1030-the-cavalier-songs-and-ballads-of-e:
Between 1642 and 1684 England tore itself in civil war, and Royalist singers answered with songs for the king, for lost battles, and for tavern cheer. This gathering preserves their ballads, catches, and laments, from marching tunes to bitter jokes at Cromwell's men.

The pieces range from high praise of Charles I to rude satire and drinking songs, and they show how ordinary folk sang their politics. Notes set each song in its fight or plot. The book is a lively source for the war's losing side, and it still sings well aloud.
10357-life-of-johnson-volume-4-1780-1784:
James Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, reaches its close in this fourth volume, covering 1780 to Johnson's death on December 13, 1784. Boswell, disappointed at missing Johnson one year, fills the gap with sayings gathered by his friend Langton, compared to treasure dug from Herculaneum. Appendices add clubs, quarrels, and last days.

Johnson's wit, talk, and final illness fill the main text, with Miss Burney's account of his last days among the appendices. Parr's epitaph and notes on his will close the record. Readers get the moving end of the greatest English biography, full of talk, friendship, and mortality.
11385-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 446, dated July 19, 1884, ranges from tin in canned foods, found in small amounts with no cause for alarm, to the windmill, the pneumatic dynamite gun. rope pulley brakes, wire rope towage on the Rhine, portable railways at Panama and Tunis, pneumatic filtering presses, Gerard's alternating current machine, automatic fast telegraphy, and the carbon microphone. A villa at Dorking, ore deposition, burrowing crayfishes, and trade schools complete the issue.

The issue's mix reflects an age when one journal could serve chemists, engineers, and naturalists. Its articles are practical, illustrated, and brief. Readers keen on Victorian machines will find here a cross-section of what inventors and makers were actually discussing in 1884.
11647-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 458 is dated 11 October 1884 and opens with chemistry and metallurgy. Starch grains, silver ore amalgamation by the Francke vat process, and facts about platinum lead the contents. Draw stones for wire drawing get a short note, with figures throughout.

Engineering follows with modern locomotive practice, a new screw steam collier called Frostburg, and the Tardes viaduct destroyed by wind. Joy's reversing and expansion valve gear and a steam bell for locomotives appear as well. Diamond mining in Brazil, with a dam on the Ribeirao Inferno, and electricity on the Frankfort and Offenbach railway complete the technical survey.
11734-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 460, dated 25 October 1884, opens with chemistry: Wolpert's method for carbonic acid in air, and Japanese camphor, its preparation and analysis by H. Oishi. Engineering follows with links in the history of the locomotive, showing the Rocket.

Water flow through turbines and screw propellers, by Arthur Rigg, covers impact on plates and in confined channels. Textile machinery from Islington, endless rope haulage, and a reliable water filter complete the technical set. A later passage on gas molecules argues that repeated collisions turn motion into ever finer vibrations. The number is a Victorian engineer's miscellany.
13062-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Issued in Edinburgh in February 1843, this number of Blackwood's Magazine packs essays, verse, fiction, and current comment into one monthly bundle. William Blackwood and Sons printed it for readers who wanted the month's serious writing and light reading side by side. Its table runs from lectures on history to poems after Schiller and a study of Reynolds's discourses on art.

Readers also find a serial tale, an imaginary talk by Walter Savage Landor, pieces on Oliver Cromwell, and a report from Kabul on the evacuation of Afghanistan. A death notice for Thomas Hamilton closes the news of the day. The mix gives a clear view of what educated Britons argued about in 1843, from art and poetry to empire and war.
13632-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for May 1884, a Massachusetts magazine, opens with Chester Alan Arthur by Ben Perley Poore. Arthur, born at Fairfield, Vermont, in 1830, was son of the Reverend William Arthur, a Baptist clergyman from County Antrim who emigrated at eighteen, graduated from Belfast University, and married Malvina Stone.

Dorchester history follows, with the first meeting house in the Bay built in 1631 and used for general purposes by an order of October 1633. Young Men's Christian Association work closes the number, with a committee urging a general secretary in every town where rooms can be kept open. The magazine mixes biography, town history, and association news for Massachusetts readers.
13680-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-:
The April 1884 number of The Bay State Monthly, a Massachusetts magazine, leads with a life of Captain George Hamilton Perkins of the United States Navy, written by Captain George E. Belknap. Perkins, a New Hampshire man, served with distinction in Civil War operations on the Mississippi, and the sketch follows his career and character.

Other pieces in the issue range over New England subjects, including a tale of a long. Fruitless search for treasure, where father and son moved rock by hand and left a small mountain of stone. The magazine mixes biography, local history, and fiction in the manner of a regional monthly. It gives a clear picture of what educated New England readers enjoyed in the 1880s.
13741-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for November 1884 leads with a profile of Grover Cleveland by Henry H. Metcalf. Cleveland, then rising fast in national politics, had come from obscurity in a short time. Metcalf compares his rise with Grant's, but stresses civil service and honest government rather than war. The profile follows Cleveland's legal training and public service.

Other pieces in the issue cover Massachusetts history and literature. The magazine aimed to honour state figures and preserve local records. Its tone is earnest and civic-minded, with portraits and careful prose. Readers get a view of Cleveland just before his first presidency. The issue also shows how regional magazines shaped political reputations.
13761-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for June 1884 presents Massachusetts history, biography, and literature. Its lead article profiles Benjamin Franklin Butler, born in Deerfield, New Hampshire, in 1818. Butler rose as a lawyer, general, and politician, and the sketch follows his Civil War service and later career. Other pieces treat New England towns, writers, and public men.

Illustrations and local detail give the issue a strong regional flavour. Readers learn how a state magazine honoured its own figures in the 1880s. The Butler profile mixes praise with plain facts about his campaigns and controversies. Shorter items round out the number with notes on books and places. It is a good sample of Victorian regional publishing.
13864-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for December 1884 leads with Daniel Lothrop, Boston publisher, by John N. McClintock. Lothrop's fame shows how merchants built cities, as burghers once built Venice, Genoa, and London. New England's sturdy, liberty-loving settlers frame the sketch. Young Lothrop scratched D. Lothrop and Co. on tin at age five and nailed it to his playhouse door.

Other pieces cover Massachusetts history and letters. The magazine honoured state enterprise and character in careful prose. Lothrop's rise from boyish ambition to publishing success gives the issue its arc. Readers learn how a regional magazine celebrated business virtue. The number offers a neat sample of 1880s New England publishing.
13962-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Number 455, dated in 1884, gathers short pieces on tools, trade, and new craft. A bridge over a deep gorge in Cape Colony opens the issue, with cuts to show the work. Ships that fire torpedoes, gas motors by Dugald Clerk, and fast work on a new rail line in the north follow. A huge digger and rope haulage for boats add more detail.

Clerk traces gas motors from Watt's tests to the first gas motor made to work. A note on fire pumps tells how fire gives them drive, not just how they put out fires. The issue served men who built, mined, and made things for a living. Its charts and cuts show old craft in use, plain and clear. The issue suits those who like the past of tools and trade.
15833-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number four hundred and forty-one, dated New York, June 14, 1884. The Supplement, five dollars a year, carried technical papers for engineers, makers, and curious readers. Scientific American itself dated from 1845. This number opens with chemistry and metallurgy.

H. Schucht writes on electrolysis and the precipitation of lead, thallium, silver, bismuth, and manganese. The electro-chemical equivalent of silver, Stolba on soluble zircon, and a new process for wrought iron direct from ore follow. Later pages treat engines, building, and natural history. The issue shows Victorian science at work: practical, detailed, and eager to turn knowledge into iron and light.
15924-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for February 1884, volume one, number two, a Massachusetts magazine. A portrait of Alexander Hamilton Rice fronts the number. Daniel B. Hagar, principal of the State Normal School at Salem, writes Rice's life. Hagar opens with Massachusetts merchants, prominent in the nation through all periods.

From John Hancock, the first governor, down to the present, merchants have often held the highest public offices. Rice, merchant and statesman, joins that list. Hagar traces his career with care and local pride. Other pieces treat Massachusetts towns and history. The number gives a fine sample of state biography: a merchant governor, told for his neighbours.
15925-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for March 1884, volume one, number three, a Massachusetts magazine. A portrait of J. W. Boott fronts the number. Colonel John Hatch George leads with a life of the Honourable Josiah Gardner Abbott. Abbott traced his line to Puritan George Abbott, who came from Yorkshire in 1630 and settled in Andover.

George follows Abbott's mother line to William Fletcher, who came from Devonshire in 1640 and settled in Concord. Law, politics, and public service fill the sketch. Other pieces treat Massachusetts towns, history, and letters. The issue gives a fine sample of state pride in print: local lives, told with care, for local readers.
15926-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
The Bay State Monthly, volume two, number one, for October 1884, bound by John N. McClintock and Company of Milk Street, Boston, in 1885. The magazine calls itself a journal of literature, history, biography, and state progress. Contents of the whole second volume fill the front pages. Massachusetts pride runs through every item.

Oliver Ames, lieutenant governor, Bartholdi's Colossus, and General Carrington's Battle of Shiloh lead the list. Early Bermuda Islands and other historical pieces follow. The October number opens a volume of wide interests, from statues to battlefields. The magazine gives a rich sample of 1880s state letters: history, biography, and progress, side by side.
16293-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Number three hundred forty of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, dated February 1844, mixes fiction, travel, and politics in the old Tory monthly's manner. Contents include The Heretic, translated from the Russian of Lajetchnikoff, thrush-hunting by Alexander Dumas, high life in the last century, news from an exiled contributor, and the prophecy of the twelve tribes. Marston, or the memoirs of a statesman, reaches part eight.

Secession from the Church of Scotland, sitting for a portrait, the land of slaves, the priest's burial, and free trade and protection complete a characteristically varied number. Blackwood's, printed by Ballantyne and Hughes, spoke for Edinburgh learning and wit. The issue offers a rich slice of early Victorian magazine life.
16353-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Number four hundred twenty-one of the Scientific American Supplement, dated New York, January 26, 1884, surveys engineering, technology, and electricity for working readers. Engineering opens with Furcot's six-horsepower steam engine, foot lathes, an endless trough conveyer, railroad grades of trunk lines, and English express trains with their average speeds. An apparatus for separating paper-mill waste waters follows.

Technology adds an English adaptation of the American oil mill and large blue prints by W. B. Parsons Jr., while electricity covers apparatus shown at the Munich exhibition. The Supplement, five dollars a year, kept mechanics and inventors current. This number offers a crisp snapshot of Victorian applied science.
16607-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
This November 1843 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine packs a dozen pieces into one monthly issue. It leads with a Texas prairie tale. Then it turns to travel in Persia, a banking-house story, and wrongs done to women. A statesman's memoirs, Ceylon, trade policy, and the senses follow. A plan for trade between the Atlantic and Pacific also appears.

Two dreams and a piece on Irish repeal close the set. The mix shows what a mid-1800s British monthly gave its readers: far travel, home politics, trade talk, and fiction side by side. Each piece speaks in the voice of its day, with strong views and long detail. The issue is a good window on 1843 tastes, fears, and hopes, read piece by piece rather than straight through.
16773-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This June 28, 1884 number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume seventeen, number 443, gathers short technical pieces from many fields. Chemistry leads with beeswax, pine phenol, and a Paris school of physics, then engineering gives air cooling machines, gas heaters, concrete pipes, screw threads, and a railway ferry boat. The problem of flight also gets a turn.

Each piece is short, plain, and full of figures, tables, and shop detail, aimed at workers, makers, and keen amateurs. The issue shows what 1884 counted as new: better heat, better metals, better flight hopes. Readers today can dip in for period science and craft, or read straight through for a snapshot of a technical age in full swing.
18278-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Number 376 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume sixty-one, for February 1847, mixes memoir, history, fiction, and politics in the magazine's familiar blend. Its contents list a memoir of the late John William Smith of the Inner Temple, modern Italian history, French players and playhouses, and the reign of George II. A tale called Mildred and pieces on direct taxation complete the number.

The memoir, by Samuel Warren, also of the Inner Temple, opens with Milton's Lycidas. It presents Smith as a remarkable man cut off in his prime before most readers had heard his name. Mildred, meanwhile, spends a last day in Rome visiting old friends before leaving. Readers get a Victorian monthly at work: law, Europe, theatre, and story side by side.
20189-recollections-of-manilla-and-the-p:
Recollections of Manila and the Philippines covers the years 1848, 1849, and 1850. The writer looks back to Spain's first push toward those islands. As Cortez, Pizarro, and Almagro won fame in America, a new idea grew. Magellan, a Portuguese in Spanish service, sought a sea road east.

By sailing south and past the new western world, spices lay within reach. That old story frames a firsthand account of mid-century Manila life. Trade, custom, and Spanish rule fill the writer's daily notes. Readers get a rare English view of the Philippines before American rule.
23180-the-denver-express-from-belgravia-: A. A. Hayes wrote The Denver Express, a story that ran in Belgravia in January 1884. In the town it describes, the train's coming and going ranks among the great events of each day. A local poet even marked it in verse in the town paper. His lines, though, were borrowed without credit from an old eastern magazine. He passed them off as his own work.
25193-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
The December 1843 number of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 54, number 338, mixes art, music, fiction, and travel in the magazine's usual rich fashion. It opens with lectures on the Royal Academy and the painter Henry Fuseli, followed by notes on music and a tale called The Purple Cloak.

Other pieces include a banking-house history, college theatricals with a frog prank in the quadrangle, the conclusion of Kerim Khan's travels, notes from disturbed districts in Wales, and Texas adventures. A sixth part of Marston, memoirs of a statesman, closes the number with an index to the volume.
25727-vagabondia-1884:
Frances Hodgson Burnett writes Vagabondia, published by James R. Osgood in 1884, opening with an author's note calling it her first work of its kind. Chapters hold counsel, camps of the Philistines, a train laid, a lily of the field, and Philistines upon the travellers.

Wanted, a young person, a spark applied, the beginning of the ending, and unorthodox ways follow, with slippery places, a wind blowing nobody good, and an explosion. A dead letter, seven long years, Switzerland, and questions of dying and grief carry a tale of young vagabonds, love, and Bohemian freedom.
2653-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's papers open in this first volume of the Constitutional Edition, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. Theodore Roosevelt supplies an introduction, Carl Schurz an essay on Lincoln, and Joseph Choate an address, framing the young lawyer's early writings.

The volume follows Lincoln from his Illinois beginnings, through law, politics, and the speeches that made his name, up to the years before his national rise. Readers meet the plain, logical voice that would later carry the republic through war. The book serves as the foundation of any serious Lincoln shelf.
29165-the-american-missionary-volume-38-:
The American Missionary Association published this issue of its monthly journal in January 1884, volume 38, number one. The issue opens the year with an editorial, Another Year, and a report that the association sought one thousand dollars a day for its work. Its schools and missions served freedpeople, Native peoples, Chinese immigrants, and poor white mountain communities.

A special section, the Bureau of Woman's Work, carries pieces on the Indian woman, the Chinese, mountain white work in Kentucky, and colored people of the South. The children's page reports Christmas giving at Mystic, Connecticut, and the issue closes with receipts and the association's constitution. Readers get a year-opening record of missionary education in the post-Civil War United States.
29556-the-american-missionary-volume-38-:
Volume thirty-eight, number six of The American Missionary, dated June 1884, reports the work of the American Missionary Association. Its contents open with editorials on seven months of work, Indian missions, spring associations, and the poor. Christian educators in council and southern manufactures follow, with early dawn notes and gifts, including those of John F. Slater.

Later pages cover the Dakota Indians in an illustrated article, forty-five years in Washington Territory, and a letter on the Chinese from Oakland, California. A bureau of woman's work adds letters from the field. Readers of mission and Reconstruction-era history will find a full month of earnest, practical reporting from the field.
29938-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 364, volume 59, is dated February 1846. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The contents open with Servia and the Servian Question. A few years before, the writer says, Servia was scarcely known to the English public, an obscure Ottoman province few travellers had entered. Lately its people, left by their suzerain the Sultan, menaced by Russia, and abandoned by Europe, won their independence.

The Student of Salamanca continues in part four, with Something More about Music and Martha Brown. Marlborough, number three, and Recollections of a Lover of Society follow. It's All for the Best, A Peep into the Whig Penny Post-Bag, East and West, and An Apology for a Review close the number. The issue mixes foreign politics, fiction, music, and satire in Blackwood's full style.
29988-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 352, volume fifty-seven, is dated February 1845, printed in Edinburgh by William Blackwood and Sons and sold in London at Pall Mall. Nine pieces fill the number: North's Specimens of the British Critics, The Tower of London by Thomas Roscoe, Poems and Ballads of Goethe number three, and Spain as It Is. The Superfluities of Life, The Overland Passage, Mesmerism, Aesthetics of Dress about a bonnet, and German-American Romances complete it.

North's specimens open with Dryden. Poetry, Lord Bacon says, is a third part of learning, a social interest of momentous power. It is extolled above history and above philosophy as more divine in origin and more immediately and intimately salutary in use. Criticism, North argues, opens to us the poetry we possess, sheltering and fostering all its springing growths like a magnanimous kingly protector. Criticism as a science is feeling known.
33938-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for December 1845, number 362, gathers the month's prose and verse for a British readership. Its contents run from a second paper on Marlborough to the second part of The Student of Salamanca. White's Three Years in Constantinople, a reign of George the Third, and poems on omens and dreams fill out the issue.

The opening paper on Marlborough takes up his march into Bavaria and the battle of Blenheim. Other pieces mix history, travel, and fancy in the magazine's familiar blend. The issue gives modern readers a snapshot of what educated Britons read and debated in the last month of 1845.
4834-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
The thirty-second volume of Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1582 to 1584. Its file header numbers it as the thirty-fourth Gutenberg volume. Chapter six opens with Parma recalling foreign troops, the siege of Oudenarde, and coolness of Alexander. Capture of the city and of Nineve follows, with inauguration of Anjou at Ghent and an attempt upon his life and that of Orange.

Lamoral Egmont's implication in the plot, Parma's unsuccessful attack upon Ghent, and secret plans of Anjou follow, with Dunkirk, Ostend, and other towns surprised by his adherents. Failure at Bruges, suspicions at Antwerp, and duplicity on all sides close the sampled scope, as Anjou's French adventure collapses into suspicion and failure. Parma advances town by town while his enemies plot against each other. Readers get Motley's account of the war's late years, with Anjou, Parma, and Orange contending.
4835-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-comp:
John Lothrop Motley's complete history from 1574 to 1584 carries the Dutch revolt from its early sieges to the death of its founder. The narrative opens with the fading Blood Council, secret peace talks at Breda, and Orange's rise to almost unlimited power as towns grow richer and more jealous of his authority.

Mediation by the emperor, shifting town governments, and Orange's repeated offers to resign all test the young republic. Motley follows the diplomacy closely, weighing the skill of envoys on both sides and the prince's steady refusal to trade away religious freedom. The complete span lets readers watch a rebellion harden into a state over a single decade.
4836-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-comp:
John Lothrop Motley, D.C.L., LL.D., corresponding member of the Institute of France, wrote The Rise of the Dutch Republic, 1555 to 1584, Complete, A History, dated 1855. An editor's note introduces the author: born in Dorchester, Massachusetts, in 1814, died in 1877, author of the novels Morton's Hope and Merry Mount. Motley served as United States minister to Austria from 1861 to 1867, and to England from 1869 to 1870.

This complete volume gathers the history's full span in this set, from Charles's abdication in 1555 and Philip's early reign. Through Alva's terror, Orange's resistance, Don John's governorship, and Parma's campaigns, it reaches the war's late years. Where single volumes cover one slice each, this file holds the whole arc together, from abdication to the final campaigns sampled in the last volumes. Readers get Motley's Dutch revolt entire, from 1555 to 1584, in one volume.
8484-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
March 29, 1884, brought readers the iron industry in Brazil, by Professor Fehrand, with methods of obtaining iron, working the ore, setting up a forge, and selling prices. The steamer Churchill, built for service at Natal, got a full page of illustrations, while three-way tunnels, a continuously primed siphon, and a system for evaporating liquids added engineering variety.

Technology pages treated coal gas as a labor-saving agent in trades, with burners for disinfection and drying, and instantaneous photography got several illustrations. Electricity pages covered electric launches. The issue shows the Supplement in its mature phase, global in range, from Brazilian forges to electric boats, and still fond of engravings.
9076-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
Dated New York, April 19, 1884, this issue of the Scientific American Supplement gathers short reports on the newest science and craft of its day. The magazine, founded in 1845, served readers who wanted plain news of inventions, not high theory. This number ranges from chemistry to guns to sea soundings.

Inside are pieces on treating ores by electrolysis, an electric railway at Vienna, a course of study for engineers, the Gardner machine gun, and the deep-sea voyage of the Talisman. Engravings and maps aid the text. The issue now reads as a lively snapshot of a fast-changing age of steam, wire, and steel.
9174-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-1:
This first issue of The Bay State Monthly, a Massachusetts magazine of literature, history, biography, and state progress, appeared in January 1884. Its contents list spans the whole first volume, from Boston's tea party and the siege of Boston to Bunker Hill and the first schoolmaster of Boston. State pride runs through it.

Writers include Henry Carrington on the Revolution and Samuel Abbott Green on old Groton. Local history, biography, and civic notes share space. The issue is a rich source for New England history, and a model of the state magazine at its earnest best.
9266-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
Dated New York, July 26, 1884, this issue of the Scientific American Supplement opens with chemistry: the bitter substance of hops, by Dr. Bungener. It asks what gives hops their bitter taste, and gives processes for hop-bitter acid with analysis. Engineering follows, with harbor works at Antwerp and a caisson for deepening the river.

Bicycles and tricycles, by C. V. Boys, treat hill steepness, maps, and ball bearings, with the Otto bicycle noted. The Canal Iron Works and Marinoni's rotary press also appear. The issue is a brisk record of Victorian craft, science, and making.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume five of Robert Kerr's voyages continues the early history of Peru after the death of Francisco Pizarro. Its chapters follow the defeat of Gonzalo Pizarro and the reestablishment of tranquillity in the country. Spanish conquest and colonial order form the volume's theme. Kerr arranges the Peruvian story within his systematic history of discovery.
abbott-flatland-1884:
Edwin A Abbott, an English schoolmaster and theologian, published Flatland in 1884 under the name 'A Square.' The short novel is set in a world of only two dimensions. It is the founding work of fiction about higher dimensions and a sharp satire of Victorian society.

The Square tells how Flatland's classes are ranked by shape, from lowly lines to priestly circles. A visit from a Sphere of three dimensions blows his mind open to worlds beyond his own. Abbott uses the tale to teach geometry and to mock rank, dogma, and fear of new ideas.
arxiv-2509-00684:
Amartya Banerjee, with three co-authors, presents VECTOR+ for drug design with scarce data. The tool steers generative models toward useful parts of chemical space. That steering is a major obstacle when training data are few. VECTOR+ aims to make the search both guided and data-efficient.

The method couples contrastive learning with controlled molecule generation. Contrastive learning pulls similar molecules together in its internal space. It works for both regression tasks and classification tasks. Tests use a PD-L1 inhibitor set and a kinase inhibitor set. Many generated candidates score better on docking than known reference drugs. Docking scores predict how strongly a molecule binds its target. Checks with molecular dynamics confirm that binding is stable.
arxiv-2509-00784:
Anjali Anjali, with three co-authors, explores idempotent and nilpotent operators in bicomplex spaces. Bicomplex numbers extend complex numbers with two imaginary units. An idempotent operator equals its own square when applied twice. A nilpotent one becomes zero after repeated use. The paper defines both kinds of matrices here.

The team derives related results for these objects. Several theorems set conditions for when such operators exist. They also describe how they behave in practice. The work extends familiar ideas from linear algebra into this newer setting. Those ideas underpin projections and decaying processes in ordinary spaces. The results clarify what carries over and under what conditions.
arxiv-2509-01284:
Galois theory links field extensions to their symmetry groups, and its standard proofs rest on ideas such as separable and normal extensions. V. V. Bavula offers a fresh route that avoids those classic concepts entirely. The new approach is built on central simple algebras, a class of rings with strong symmetry.

Bavula defines G-extensions, finite extensions where the algebra of linear maps on the extension is generated by the field itself plus its automorphism group. These turn out to be exactly the most symmetric extensions, and they coincide with Galois extensions. Applying the Double Centralizer Theorem to that algebra yields the Galois correspondences for subfields directly. In this way all the main results of Galois theory are recovered, in a shorter and more unified conceptual form.
arxiv-2509-01584:
Simultaneous localization and mapping, or SLAM, lets a camera build a three-dimensional map while tracking its own motion, but many systems need the camera's internal settings first. Ganlin Zhang, Shenhan Qian, Xi Wang, and Daniel Cremers present ViSTA-SLAM, a real-time monocular system that works without those intrinsics. That freedom makes it usable across many camera setups.

Its front end is a light symmetric two-view association model that estimates relative poses and local point maps from just two color images at once. At about a third the size of comparable front ends, it still yields stronger two-view constraints. The back end builds a pose graph with loop closures to correct drift. Tests show better camera tracking and denser, cleaner reconstructions than current methods, according to the authors' experiments.
arxiv-2509-01684:
Sherry Yang, Joy He-Yueya, and Percy Liang show that small AI agents can learn to do machine learning work better by practice. Most such agents just prompt a large fixed model, so they never improve with use. The team trains a much smaller model with reinforcement learning, where rewards guide updates after each try. Two snags arise: tasks take uneven time, and test scores give blunt feedback.

The authors fix the time snag by weighting slow but good tries more in updates. For blunt feedback, a helper model adds log lines to code so partial progress can earn partial credit. On a bench of Kaggle tasks, the small trained agent beat a large prompted model by a clear margin. The result favors learning from practice over sheer model size.
arxiv-2509-01784:
Andrea Andrisani leads five co-authors in testing neurons built from light for low power computing. Quantum optical neurons use photon interference, where light waves overlap, to do neural steps with little energy. The team builds designs around two interferometer types, devices that split and rejoin light paths. Each design tweaks the light by phase, strength, or brightness.

The designs become software modules that can train inside layered networks. Tests cover two image sorting sets, run five times each under clean and noisy conditions. One interferometer family stays stable even with noise, while another rivals classic neurons in deep nets for some tweaks. Weaker variants wobble under noise. The code is public for further work.
arxiv-2509-01984:
Quan Dao leads eight co-authors with VARIN, the first noise inversion editor for visual autoregressive image models. Autoregressive models build images scale by scale, rivaling diffusion models on text to image tasks. Editing a given image by prompt, without retraining, is just as vital for real use. Inversion means running generation backward to recover the noise that rebuilds the source image.

Their key piece inverts the argmax sampling step with location awareness to yield inverse random noises. Those noises rebuild the source faithfully, then guide targeted edits from new prompts. Tests show strong prompt fidelity while backgrounds and structure stay intact. The method gives autoregressive models a practical editing path they lacked.
arxiv-2509-02584:
Sanjay More and Anil Khairnar wrote a 2025 algebra paper introducing weakly generalised p.q.-Baer star-rings, a class of rings with an involution operation that generalises earlier Baer-type conditions. Ring theory studies such structures to understand how annihilators, sets that kill given elements, behave.

The authors prove that, under stated assumptions, every weakly generalised ring of this kind embeds inside a generalised one. They also show the stronger class has partial comparability of projections, the ring's idempotent elements. When a parallelogram law holds, each pair of projections splits into orthogonal parts. A separation theorem follows, and spectral theory yields a representation of the ring as a sheaf whose sections are injective, a geometric picture of the algebra. The results extend a long line of Baer ring research.
arxiv-2509-02684:
Bingchu Fan and Zhong-Zhi Xianyu wrote a 2025 cosmology paper. It dissects family trees. These are special functions that solve the layered time integrals behind cosmological correlators. Correlators encode how quantum fluctuations during inflation seeded today's structure.

Family trees are hypergeometric functions with many variables. Energies act as the variables. Twists act as parameters. The authors use Mellin forms, which rewrite such functions as contour integrals. With them, they catalogue all singularities in variables and parameters alike. Exact series expansions sit at each singularity, each with a finite domain where it converges. Stitching the series together continues any family tree across many regions of energy space. A corollary shows family trees factorise whenever a partial energy hits zero, at every order.
arxiv-2509-03284:
S. A. Volkov and 3 co-authors computed long-missing quantum corrections around a charged nucleus in 2025. Vacuum polarization is the process where empty space briefly spawns particle pairs that screen a charge. Its leading two-loop part near a nucleus has been known since a classic 1955 derivation.

Higher-order pieces involving three, five, and seven interactions with the nuclear field had never been calculated. The authors evaluate those potentials and use them to find energy shifts for a single electron bound to a nucleus. Their results sharply cut the theoretical uncertainty of this contribution to transition energies. That precision feeds next-generation tests of bound-state quantum electrodynamics in heavy ions. It also helps pin down nuclear charge radii from spectra.
arxiv-2509-03384:
Eva A. Gallardo-Gutiérrez, Fernando Lledó, and Laura Sáenz developed approximation theory for operators on Hilbert spaces in 2025, with quantum mechanics in view. Operators there are often infinite-dimensional, so finite approximations that respect their action are essential. Two classic schemes use growing finite projections that nearly commute with the operator, either strongly or on average.

The authors unify those quasidiagonal and Følner-type schemes and extend them to unbounded operators, which are only defined on part of the space. A generalized Halmos result says every closable quasidiagonal operator is a small perturbation of a block-diagonal one on the same domain. They also introduce sparse versions of the second scheme and tie the two together. Weighted shift examples illustrate the theory, and a detailed treatment covers the Weyl algebra of quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2509-03584:
Marija Tomašević and one co-author's 2025 research paper takes up quantum effects near the threshold of gravitational collapse, studied with an anomaly-based method. Critical collapse can, classically, end in a naked singularity visible to the outside universe. That would break weak cosmic censorship, the idea that singularities stay hidden behind horizons.

Their one-loop semiclassical analysis couples Einstein gravity to a scalar field that is free and massless. Solvable near-critical solutions are treated in both two and three space dimensions, within the dominant spherical wave sector. Regularity again selects one special quantum state, here described as Boulware-like, carrying real vacuum polarisation from the collapsing matter. Quantum corrections grow as a new mode. Tracing horizons with both classical and quantum modes reveals a finite mass gap. Collapse then switches from classical Type II behaviour to quantum-modified Type I behaviour, enforcing censorship.
arxiv-2509-03684:
In a 2025 research paper, Nodoka Yamanaka examines how magnetic fields affect light atomic nuclei and a cosmological puzzle called the lithium problem. The problem is a mismatch between predicted and observed lithium amounts from the early universe. Yamanaka studies the proton and neutron distributions of deuterium, tritium, and helium-3, computed from first principles, plus lithium-6 in a cluster model.

A magnetic field changes how the density of a nucleus fades at large distances. The tail's exponent gains a part that grows linearly with field strength, while other effects stay smaller. Because of that linear part, fluctuating fields always raise tunnelling rates, boosting low-energy reactions that must cross the Coulomb barrier. The mechanism cannot suppress beryllium-7 production in the early universe directly. It might still resolve the problem by raising one key reaction rate, if early fields were strong, or by correcting a measured cross section polluted by laboratory fields.
arxiv-2509-03784:
William J. Wesley gives new bounds for several small multicolour Ramsey numbers in a 2025 mathematics paper. A Ramsey number is the smallest board size that forces a guaranteed pattern, whatever colouring is chosen. Here edges of a complete graph are painted in several colours, and the hunt is for a one-colour copy of a target graph in its assigned colour.

Wesley uses Boolean satisfiability solvers, programs that search for assignments meeting many logical constraints, to find structured colourings. Those colourings prove lower bounds for two Ramsey numbers involving complete graphs on four vertices, one missing an edge. Some recent upper bounds for cycle cases are also tightened. Two numbers, for triangles and five-cycles against six-cycles, are pinned down exactly. Critical graphs for further families, mixing four-cycles or six-cycles with star graphs, are enumerated completely.
arxiv-2509-03884:
A neural network model that predicts coronary heart disease from urinary peptides occupies a 2025 research paper by Jesus Celis-Porras. Coronary heart disease remains a major cause of death and healthcare spending worldwide. A non-invasive test, avoiding blood draws or imaging, could widen screening considerably.

Fifty key urinary peptide biomarkers were selected by genetic algorithms, which evolve candidate feature sets toward the most informative ones. Treatment and control groups of 345 people each were balanced with a synthetic oversampling technique. The multilayer perceptron network uses three hidden layers of sixty neurons. Trained under a stratified validation strategy, it reached precision, sensitivity, and specificity all near ninety-six percent. Its area under the curve score approached 0.975 for both classes. The author presents the model as an accurate, robust non-invasive diagnostic tool.
arxiv-2509-04584:
Lura K Pitchford and six co-authors witness a giant galaxy assembling violently less than two billion years after the Big Bang in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Their target, J1607, is an extremely luminous quasar whose host galaxy shines brightly in submillimeter light. Subtracting the quasar's glare in Hubble telescope images reveals a host as massive as today's giant elliptical galaxies. Its star formation rate is enormous, and it holds a vast reservoir of molecular gas, the raw material for stars.

Two companions sit nearby: one massive but gas-free, the other gas-rich but starless. The merger may be stripping gas from the infalling galaxies, quenching them. Whatever the details, the system is headed toward an extremely massive galaxy by the present day.
arxiv-2509-04684:
Merging two digital maps so each fills the other's gaps is harder than it sounds. Farnoosh Hashemi and one co-author present KRAFT, a learning-based framework for automated map conflation, in a 2025 paper. Existing methods mostly handle linear features such as roads, and rely on fixed hand-written rules.

KRAFT first turns each geospatial database into a knowledge graph. It then matches entities across the graphs using graph alignment plus a geospatial feature encoder. Finally it merges the matched entities. Because matching is learned from data, the method extends beyond roads to the wider set of map entities.
arxiv-2509-04784:
Reinforcement learning can make a language model's answers better but also more alike. Yilei Chen, lead author with four co-authors, propose a post-training method that protects diversity in a 2025 paper. Existing fixes work only at inference time or change surface wording rather than meaning.

Their method, Diversity Quality Optimization, samples a group of responses for each prompt and embeds them. A determinant-based measure from determinantal point processes scores how much semantic volume the group spans. Training then optimises quality and that diversity measure together. Experiments across instruction following, summarisation, story generation, and reasoning show diversity gains without sacrificing quality.
arxiv-2509-04884:
Fine-tuning a large model with low-rank adapters still wastes capacity when every adapter gets the same rank. Raul Singh, lead author with three co-authors, introduce L1RA in a 2025 paper on LoRA fine-tuning. Their method dynamically distributes a fixed total rank budget across adapters during training.

L1 regularisation prunes redundant ranks, and the freed rank is redistributed where it helps more. Experiments show performance matching or beating other LoRA variants at comparable or lower overhead. Analysis of the final rank distribution also reveals which components need most adaptation, notably feed-forward layers and the attention output projection.
arxiv-2509-04984:
Deep learning controllers for robots are powerful but hard to trust because their decisions are opaque. Koji Matsuno and one co-author develop a stability-backed alternative in a 2025 robotics paper. Their framework targets robots whose Jacobian, the matrix linking joint motion to tool motion, is unknown.

A modular learning approach updates all network layer weights in real time. Lyapunov-like analysis, a standard stability method, is used to ensure the closed-loop system stays stable. Experiments on industrial robots illustrate the controller's performance. The authors present the method as a route to deploying real-time deep learning for robot kinematic control safely.
arxiv-2509-05084:
Neural solvers that build a route one stop at a time recompute almost the same state at every step. Tim Dernedde, lead author with two co-authors, propose a recurrent state encoder to reuse that computation in a 2025 paper on neural combinatorial optimisation. Their encoder builds each state embedding from the previous one as well as the current state.

The recurrent model matches or beats a non-recurrent encoder with far fewer layers, cutting latency in their tests. Results cover travelling salesman, capacitated vehicle routing, and orienteering problems. The authors also plug the models into a large neighbourhood search algorithm to show practical value.
arxiv-2509-05184:
Adding triple excitations to a quantum chemistry method improves accuracy, but the best order of correction is not obvious. Zachary W. Windom and one co-author analyse fourth, fifth, and infinite-order triple treatments in unitary coupled cluster theory in a 2025 paper. They introduce a new correction that is correct through fifth order in perturbation theory.

Benchmarks compare the corrections against the infinite-order triples method and full configuration interaction. Surprisingly, the fourth-order correction agrees most closely with the exact reference for ground-state energies. The fifth-order version largely recovers the infinite-order limit. The results matter for quantum computing, where full triples are expensive.
arxiv-2509-05584:
Shrinking large neural networks with guidance from their own performance profiles is automated by Sadegh Jafari and three co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Foundation models are costly to run, and pruning or quantisation usually follow uniform rules that ignore how layers differ at runtime.

Their multi-agent system, ProfilingAgent, lets language models reason over static counts and live signals like latency and memory, then set layer-wise compression plans. Across image benchmarks and four network designs, pruning held accuracy close to baseline and sometimes improved it. Quantisation cut memory by up to about three quarters with tiny accuracy loss and consistent speed gains. Reasoning quality of the guiding model mattered.
arxiv-2509-05684:
Pulsating stars can date their clusters only up to about a billion years, David Pamos Ortega concludes in a solo 2025 asteroseismology paper. Delta Scuti stars vibrate, and their vibration patterns encode age, but the method's reach near the cool edge of the instability strip was untested.

Pamos Ortega estimates a key spacing between vibration frequencies for thirty-five stars observed by two space missions. A grid of stellar models varying mass, composition, and rotation supplies comparison ages through a weighted probability fit. On synthetic stars the method dated older stars reliably in principle. Applied to real stars, almost none passed a billion years. Convection and rotation treatment in one-dimensional models limit the dating.
arxiv-2509-05984:
Which Tribonacci-Lucas numbers read the same forwards and backwards while splitting into two distinct repeated-digit blocks? Mahadi Ddamulira settles that number theory question in a 2025 paper. The Tribonacci-Lucas sequence grows by adding the previous three terms, starting from small seeds. A repdigit is a number like 777, built from one repeated digit, and a concatenation glues two of them together.

Ddamulira combines Baker's theory, which bounds linear forms in logarithms of algebraic numbers from below, with continued fraction reduction methods to corner all possibilities. The search ends with a complete determination of the palindromic concatenations of two distinct repdigits inside the sequence. The paper is a model of how transcendence tools finish exponential Diophantine hunts.
arxiv-2509-06084:
A lump of the KP-I equation seeds a fully localized wave on deep water in a 2025 paper led by Changfeng Gui with four co-authors. The physical problem is three-dimensional gravity-capillary water waves: a perfect fluid under gravity and surface tension, with steady waves traveling uniformly in one direction. Constant speed and depth are assumed while the velocity potential and boundary conditions are analyzed.

Using the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili I equation as the simplified model, the authors show a key point. Within a specific parameter range, the full problem admits a solitary wave like the KP-I lump, localized in every direction. The result transplants a famous two-dimensional model solution into a genuine three-dimensional water wave.
arxiv-2509-06484:
A machine learning model that cannot break the laws of thermodynamics is presented by Marco Hoffmann and six co-authors in a 2025 chemical engineering paper. Their subject is excess Gibbs energy, a quantity that helps predict how liquid mixtures behave. Guessing it for many-component mixtures from molecular structure alone has long been difficult.

The model, HANNA, builds physical laws in as hard limits, so its answers always stay consistent. It learns from experiments on vapor-liquid and liquid-liquid balance, activity coefficients at extreme dilution, and excess heat in two-part mixtures. A stand-in solver makes training on liquid-liquid data possible, and a geometric step extends results to mixtures with many parts. HANNA proves accurate and covers far more cases than leading rivals, and the trained model is freely available online.
arxiv-2509-06684:
Stars made partly of dark matter are modeled for the first time in a specific form by Jeet Amrit Pattnaik and four co-authors in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Quarkyonic stars are dense objects where matter behaves partly like quarks. The authors mix in dark matter and ask whether such hybrids match real gravitational-wave and X-ray observations.

A two-fluid treatment keeps ordinary matter and dark matter as separate, interacting components. The dark component can gather in the center as a core or spread out as a halo, and each shape leaves distinct signs. With dark matter included, the models reach the heavy mass range suggested by the GW190814 event, whose lighter object remains unexplained. Results for squeezing under tides, spin inertia, and radius agree broadly with GW170817, GW190814, and NICER limits, making a dark-matter hybrid a plausible reading.
arxiv-2509-06884:
Diamond sensors with very little nitrogen are described for delicate magnetic measurements by Jiashen Tang and six co-authors in a 2025 quantum sensing paper. Nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond are flexible sensors, and the amount of plain nitrogen nearby sets their coherence and sensitivity. Low-nitrogen stock should suit pulsed magnetometry, which gains from longer coherence.

The team grew diamond by chemical vapor deposition with low strain, purified its carbon isotopes, and used controlled irradiation and annealing to make the sensing centers. The new stock, under one part per million of the relevant nitrogen, showed even strain and dephasing limited by the spin bath. Across a wide range of light levels, its shot-noise-limited sensitivity beat a previously studied higher-nitrogen diamond at moderate and low excitation. Hands-on guidance for choosing sensor stock follows.
arxiv-2509-06984:
Institutions fine-tuning large vision-language models together, despite missing data types and unequal computers, get a framework from Lishan Yang and six co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Federated learning with low-rank adapters is efficient and privacy-aware. In practice, hospitals and transport operators hold data with missing modalities, and their hardware differs, producing adapters of imbalanced ranks.

No earlier work had tackled both problems together for federated vision-language models. Their framework, FediLoRA, is a lightweight aggregation scheme built on the observation that simple averaging plus structured editing can help both the shared global model and each site's personalized model. Results were strong across general and medical benchmark datasets, with extra healthcare experiments supporting real deployment. Code is released. The work targets settings where data cannot move and sensors cannot be trusted to be complete.
arxiv-2509-07184:
Erencem Ozbey and 1 co-author present DROWCULA in 2025, a method that finds new categories in image data without any human labels. Most learning systems need labeled examples, which cost great human effort. In open-world settings, entirely new classes can appear later, and past work has mostly used some labels to catch them. The new method uses none at all.

First, Vision Transformers, a neural network type that uses attention to weigh image parts, turn images into numeric summaries. Manifold learning then refines those summaries by using the hidden shape of the data cloud. Tests on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and Tiny ImageNet set new best results for finding and grouping new classes. The method works whether the number of groups is known ahead of time or not, and the code is public.
arxiv-2509-07484:
Wenshuo Gao's second entry in this block, written with 3 co-authors in 2025, animates vector graphics automatically. Vector graphics are drawings built from shapes and curves that scale cleanly to any size. Animating them by hand takes substantial manual effort, even though motion makes them clearer and easier to control. The method is called LINR Bridge, linking neural implicit representations with video diffusion models.

Layered implicit neural representations first rebuild the artwork while keeping its infinite resolution and exact colors and shapes. Those representations are then optimized by video score distillation sampling, which borrows motion knowledge from a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model. Finally the original graphics are warped to follow the learned motion, giving smooth animation. Experiments show vivid, natural motion and clear gains over existing techniques that struggled with artifacts.
arxiv-2509-07684:
Neutron star mergers forge heavy elements, and reading their fading light requires precise atomic data. Jérôme Deprince and Lucas Maison benchmark two fast calculation methods in a 2025 research paper. Their test case is singly ionized strontium, an element whose lines appear in kilonova spectra. A week after a merger, the ejecta leaves thermal equilibrium, so modelers need collision strengths for electron impacts.

The authors compute those strengths with a plane-wave Born method inside a Hartree-Fock code, and with a distorted waves method in another package. They compare both against trusted R-matrix reference data. They also compute radiative parameters for forbidden transitions. The benchmark shows where each cheap approximation can be trusted. That guidance supports large-scale atomic data production for all heavy elements, which kilonova modeling urgently needs.
arxiv-2509-07984:
Zhiyu Li and 4 co-authors solve wave propagation across interfaces that change in both space and time, in a 2025 electromagnetics paper. Space-time modulated materials can process signals dynamically, but most earlier work assumed abrupt parameter jumps. Graded-index interfaces, where properties vary smoothly, are more practical to build and open new ways to shape waves.

An exact solution generalises the impulse response method from ordinary time-invariant systems to these graded space-time interfaces. The analysis reveals versatile chirping effects, where a wave's frequency sweeps as it crosses the interface. Controlled chirping is valuable in radar, communications, and signal processing, so a solvable, realistic interface model widens the design space for future electromagnetic devices.
arxiv-2509-08384:
Quantum networks gain flexible logical wiring from graph states in a 2025 paper by Mateo M. Blanco and 3 co-authors. Entanglement shared between just two parties is not enough for protocols like secret sharing or distributed computing. Graph states represent multipartite entanglement that local operations and classical messages can reshape into the connectivity a protocol needs.

Earlier work used bi-star layouts; the authors extend the analysis to multi-star topologies. Maximum achievable connectivity is computed for networks of switches each serving several clients, including asymmetric cases where client counts differ. Logical connectivity on demand would let a quantum network reconfigure itself per task, the way classical networks route packets, instead of rebuilding physical links.
arxiv-2509-08584:
Karim Chahine and 1 co-author examine measurement driven changes in free fermions in a 2025 paper. They study the entanglement Hamiltonian, a tool that describes how one part of a system is linked to the rest. Repeated measurement can push the system between phases.

Numerical work finds three special points, from chaotic motion under weak monitoring to a metal-like phase and then a localized phase. Spectral tests, which study spacing patterns in energy levels, sharply locate the change and its key exponents. Longer range tests support that picture. The results give a new way to diagnose monitored quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2509-08684:
Alessandro De Luca and 1 co-author extend Dorst-Smeulders coding to arbitrary binary words in a 2025 paper. A Sturmian word is a balanced binary sequence tied to discrete lines in geometry. Its Dorst-Smeulders code is four integers that rebuild it efficiently.

A linear time algorithm finds the code for the longest Sturmian prefix of any binary word. Repeating that step splits a word into the fewest possible Sturmian factors, each with its own code. The method could help compression when inputs contain long Sturmian segments. Though the code is short, the proof rests on deep structure of Sturmian words.
arxiv-2509-08784:
L. Piscarreta and 8 co-authors probe accretion and star properties in the Orion Nebula in a 2025 paper. Some young stars there look far older than the bulk group in color diagrams, yet show signs of still gathering gas. The team tests whether that age gap is real.

Spectra from the VLT X-Shooter instrument cover forty stars with a wide range of apparent ages. Modeling ultraviolet excess gives extinction, temperature, and accretion values for each star. Most seemingly old stars then fit a young age, and strong lithium supports their youth. Three stars stay old despite ongoing accretion. Accretion light shifts stars in diagrams and can distort age estimates.
arxiv-2509-08884:
G. Degni and 5 co-authors pull a cosmic signal from voids with a new rebuild step in a 2025 paper. Voids are the low density zones in the galaxy map. The void galaxy cross link can reveal what the cosmos holds, once false warps in the map are fixed.

The Alcock-Paczynski signal is the key warp test. A rebuild step first moves galaxies back toward their true spots, which cuts warps from their odd speeds. Voids are then found in the rebuilt space, a first for this work. Small voids once thrown out can now be used. Limits on the key values get about a fourth tighter.
arxiv-2509-08984:
Souvik Biswas and 14 co-authors report quantum sensing with a spin ensemble in a two-dimensional material in a 2025 paper. Spin defects can sense tiny signals with very fine spatial resolution. Diamond sensors lose performance near surfaces, motivating atomically thin alternatives.

The team fully probes a spin system in hexagonal boron nitride, mapping its interactions with nearby nuclear spins. Magnetic and electric noise sensing can be switched, and the noise spectrum is rebuilt while accounting for control errors. A record coherence time under decoupling enables sub-microtesla sensitivity at ten nanometer distance. Defect engineering in thin hosts may yield versatile next generation sensors.
arxiv-2509-09184:
Leonard M. Verhoff and 2 co-authors study surfaces and interfaces of infinite-layer nickelate superconductors in a 2025 paper. These materials are made as thin films, so surface and interface layers differ from the bulk interior. Substrate and vacuum contacts shape those layers.

Density functional theory plus dynamical mean field theory examine how electronic correlations act in each region. Correlations can drive surface layers into a Mott insulating state, where electrons localize strongly. Termination effects create a polar field that shifts key pockets above the Fermi level, even without doping. At one interface type, titanium orbitals become electron doped. The results matter for interpreting film experiments.
arxiv-2509-09384:
How much warming is already locked in, and how much can policy still change? Anthoulla Phella, Vasco J. Gabriel, and Luis F. Martins forecast temperatures under rival futures in a 2025 research paper. They use a Bayesian vector autoregression framework with constraints on climate drivers like carbon dioxide and methane. Forecasts run to 2050 under the standard shared socioeconomic pathways.

Under the business-as-usual, high-emissions path, the conditional forecast tracks the unconditional one closely. Under strong mitigation with low emissions, the paths diverge only after about 2040. Conditional temperatures then stay meaningfully below the baseline trajectory. The lesson is about lags: emission cuts take decades to bend the temperature curve visibly. Policymakers who expect quick climatic gratitude for early action will misread the evidence. The authors stress that delay built into the climate system belongs inside policy design, not as an afterthought.
arxiv-2509-09584:
Event cameras report brightness changes within microseconds and never blur, yet language models have barely learned to talk about what they see. Lingdong Kong and 8 co-authors build the missing benchmark in a 2025 research paper. Talk2Event is the first large-scale dataset for grounding spoken-style referring expressions in event data. Its scenes come from real-world driving.

The benchmark holds thousands of scenes and well over ten thousand annotated objects. Each referring expression was carefully validated and enriched with four attributes. The attributes cover appearance, status, how it relates to the viewer, and how it relates to nearby objects. That structure supports reasoning about context, not just recognition. The authors offer Talk2Event as a foundation for multimodal perception that keeps up with fast, badly lit, real motion. Robotics and human-AI interaction are the obvious first beneficiaries.
arxiv-2509-09684:
Bruno Yui Yamate and 3 co-authors release a bilingual benchmark in 2025 for turning plain questions into database queries inside process mining. Text-to-SQL tools let people without database training ask questions in ordinary words. Process mining brings its own vocabulary and a special shape, since event logs collapse into single-table structures that generic benchmarks never practise on.

Their data set pairs Portuguese and English versions of 1,655 spoken-style questions with 205 target queries and ten qualifiers. Experts curated the material, professional translators handled the language pair, and detailed labels mark how hard each item is. A baseline run with GPT-3.5 Turbo shows the resource works, and the authors pitch it for wider semantic parsing research as well.
arxiv-2509-09784:
Amir Bahador Javadi and 2 co-authors extend a data-driven modelling tool in 2025 so it can learn equations for systems that somebody is actively steering. Sparse regression methods such as ARGOS recover compact governing laws from time series, a prize across physics, engineering, robotics, and medicine. Real systems, though, are pushed by control inputs and outside forces that the original tool had no way to represent.

ARGOSc folds those outside inputs into the discovery process, letting the true forcing dynamics surface alongside the system's own laws. On benchmark cases, a Van der Pol oscillator, Lotka-Volterra populations, and a forced Lorenz system with feedback, it found the governing equations more accurately than rivals. The method stayed robust through low and moderate noise levels.
arxiv-2509-09984:
Praphull Kumar and Dean M. Townsley study the shaking of accreting white dwarf stars in this 2025 paper. In dwarf nova systems, a white dwarf pulls in gas in bursts, then goes quiet, and in quiet times its surface can be seen to pulse. Those pulses carry clues about the star's mass, size, temperature, and spin, but which wave type causes them has been unsettled.

Earlier work blamed gravity modes, while other studies pointed to Rossby modes. Kumar and Townsley compute both together, with a full account of how each wave pattern shows on the star's surface. Neither type wins clearly on visibility. The gravity modes, though, sit at higher frequencies that fit the usual driving picture. The authors therefore favor them for the periods seen so far.
arxiv-2509-10184:
Leen Almajed and 1 co-author study a failure mode of kindness in supportive conversation in a 2025 paper on what they call incongruent positivity. Cheerful replies can misfire when they brush past real pain, sounding dismissive, minimising, or rosy past belief. The authors gather genuine user-assistant exchanges from Reddit and generate fresh model replies to the same situations, sorting every case by emotional stakes.

Mild cases cover relationship friction and everyday advice, while severe ones involve grief and anxiety. Model replies leaned toward unrealistic brightness more often than human ones, especially when stakes ran high. Fine-tuning experiments and a weakly supervised classifier pair follow, built to detect the mismatch types automatically. Generic positivity, the authors conclude, is not the same as support.
arxiv-2509-10284:
David Zahrádka and 5 co-authors present a control architecture for fleets of warehouse robots in this 2025 paper. Multi-agent path finding plans routes for many robots sharing one space, with no collisions. In real buildings, robots get delayed, and delays can make even a perfect plan slow. Replanning is costly, so the hard question is when replanning is worth it.

Their design executes plans with a robust method that tolerates delays, while tracking an estimate of the expected finishing time. That estimate predicts whether a fresh plan would actually finish sooner. The team tested the full loop in a real-time simulator built to mimic their real warehouse fleet demonstrator.
arxiv-2509-10384:
Jianxin Zhang and Clayton Scott extend rectified flow in this 2025 paper. Rectified flow is a generative modeling method. It learns straight paths between noise and data. The authors lift it from finite-dimensional data to functions themselves. Many generative techniques had already made that lift. Rectified flow had not.

The team works in a Hilbert space of functions. Their theory rests on a superposition principle. That principle concerns continuity equations in infinite dimensions. The same frame absorbs two relatives of rectified flow. Functional flow matching is one. Probability flow equations are the other. It also drops restrictive assumptions that earlier flow matching theory needed. In tests, the method beat existing functional generative models. The door opens to generating whole curves and fields, not just vectors.
arxiv-2509-10584:
Xiaofan Zhou and 4 co-authors ask whether language models can recruit clinical trial patients from social media in this 2025 paper. Trials often fail to find enough eligible volunteers, and classic recruiting is slow and local. People also share a great deal of health information in public posts, which might point to candidates who match a trial's rules.

The team built TRIALQA, a data set from colon and prostate cancer forums, labeled by experienced annotators against real trial criteria. Seven language models were benchmarked under several training and prompting strategies. The models showed real promise, the authors report, but still stumbled on the multi-step reasoning that eligibility rules demand, such as combining timing, history, and treatment details.
arxiv-2509-10684:
Vitor F. Grizzi and four co-authors improve a neutrino detector's vision in this 2025 instrumentation paper, returning to the NuGraph2 graph network for liquid argon time projection chambers. The network segments particle events well overall but misses rare classes such as Michel electrons, the decay products of stopped muons. The team tries three physics-inspired upgrades.

First, they enrich each node's inputs with context from detector geometry and track continuity. Second, they add auxiliary decoders to capture correlations between classes. Third, they add energy-based penalty terms shaped by Michel electron physics. On public MicroBooNE data, the input enrichment won by a wide margin, sharpening precision and recall for Michel electrons by untangling overlapping regions of the network's internal space. The other two ideas helped little, which the authors attribute to the network's hit-level design and address in a planned successor.
arxiv-2509-10784:
Jin Yang, Daniel S. Marcus, and Aristeidis Sotiras adapt medical vision foundation models to three-dimensional scans in this 2025 paper. Foundation models promise general skill. Volumetric segmentation remains a weak spot, though. That task outlines organs and lesions through a whole scan. Labeling enough target data by hand is expensive. Randomly chosen fine-tuning samples waste that budget.

Their framework, ASSFT, picks samples actively at test time. Two signals guide the picking. One gauges how much new knowledge a sample carries, and how varied it is. The other gauges how hard the sample's anatomy is to segment. Uncertainty inside the regions of interest supplies that second signal. A selective semi-supervised stage follows. It adds only reliable unlabeled samples. Confidence and closeness to labeled samples do the filtering. Noisy self-training is avoided. Each human annotation is spent where it teaches the most.
arxiv-2509-11184:
Partha Shah and 8 co-authors study how the labels used for skin tone affect fairness in medical AI in this 2025 paper. Models that classify skin lesions can perform unevenly across skin tones. The usual label set, the Fitzpatrick scale, sorts lighter skin into finer categories than darker skin, which may itself distort training and measurement.

The team trained lesion classifiers on data grouped by tone at different levels of detail. Group-specific models beat one general model trained on balanced data. But merging the lighter categories into a single wide group hurt performance. The authors argue the results support moving medical AI away from the Fitzpatrick scale toward one that represents the full range of human skin more evenly.
arxiv-2509-11484:
M. S. Anastopoulos Tzanis and 5 co-authors refine a standard model of tokamak edge stability in this 2025 paper. The edge of a fusion plasma, the pedestal, is limited by ballooning instabilities. The widely used EPED model pairs two such limits, but it usually approximates the kinetic ballooning threshold with a simpler ideal one, an approximation that can drift badly in squat, low-aspect-ratio machines.

The team applies a reduced model built on a gyro-fluid code, which captured the kinetic modes in both a conventional and a spherical tokamak. They also show that global high-turn modes can block access to a prized second stable region. Feeding both improvements into EPED brought its pedestal predictions closer to measured data.
arxiv-2509-11584:
Zishun Liu, Liqian Ma, and Yongxin Chen give safety-critical control a probabilistic promise. This 2025 control theory paper treats model predictive control. The system is nonlinear and buffeted by random noise. Keeping it safe with high chance is much harder than in a noise-free model.

Their trick is set erosion. The safe region shrinks by a margin sized to absorb the noise. The chance-based demand becomes a plain demand on the smaller set. Any standard predictive controller can then be used as is. A tight bound on random wander from the nominal path is the key. Analysis backs safety levels like ninety-nine point nine nine percent. Numerical tests confirm the method on complex dynamics.
arxiv-2509-12084:
Tariffs fell for decades, yet world trade stopped globalizing after 2007, and Tianyu Fan with two co-authors blame geopolitics in 2025. Their claim: worsening political alignment between countries has steadily eaten the gains from tariff liberalization since the mid-1990s.

To measure alignment, the team used language models to compile over eight hundred thousand geopolitical events across 193 countries from 1950 to 2024, distilling them into a bilateral score. Local projection estimates say a lasting one-step improvement in alignment eventually lifts trade between the pair by about a fifth. In a standard trade framework, tariff cuts raised 2021 world trade by roughly seven and a half percent, while geopolitical deterioration cut about five percent back off, with welfare effects spread unevenly.
arxiv-2509-12384:
Seth Ockerman and 7 co-authors study vector databases on a supercomputer in a 2025 paper. Vector databases store numerical embeddings of text, images, and video for fast similarity search. They now support retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model grounds its answers in external sources, yet their behavior on high-performance computing systems is little known.

The team ran a distributed Qdrant system on the Polaris supercomputer at Argonne. Their workload used biological text from BV-BRC and embeddings built from a scientific corpus with a Qwen embedding model. They measured insertion, index construction, and query latency with up to thirty-two workers. Drawing on practical lessons, the paper offers a first characterization to guide future optimization on HPC platforms.
arxiv-2509-12684:
T. Nguyen, D. Parra and S. Richard map in 2025 the full set of edge effects that alter Levinson theorem in a thin, layered scatter system. The classic theorem links scatter to bound counts, but at thresholds new paths can open or close and shift the count.

They show how each shift comes from a path change and can be read as a part turn count on new operators. Cases cover buried thresholds, shifts in path counts, and doubled thresholds. Most work is by hand, with an algebra frame for the final matches. The map helps readers predict when the plain theorem needs a fix.
arxiv-2509-12884:
Pratik Nag, Andrew Zammit-Mangion and Ying Sun model in 2025 spatial fields that change character from place to place by bending space itself. A steady field on a bent map can look uneven on the true map, but picking the right bend by hand is hard and often stops at two dimensions.

They learn the bend with neural flows, which are reversible maps that can form rich, high-size warps. In fake tests the flow model held more patterns than common rivals. On three-way float data from the Argo ocean set the frame showed clear use. The method opens uneven field work to higher sizes.
arxiv-2509-12984: Jun Chen, Xiabing Ruan and Jia Yang compute in 2025 the full calculus named for Tamarkin and Tsygan for one Koszul algebra. The algebra has global dimension larger than its count of generators, a gap that makes the case a sharp test. Hochschild homology and cohomology, the core parts of that calculus, turn out to act in intricate ways here, even though the algebra has a lean presentation and sound homological traits.
arxiv-2509-13184:
Andrea Cataldo, Rohan Yadgirkar and six co-authors steer light in circles on a programmable chip in 2025 with fake magnetic fields. Photons ignore true magnetism, yet staged drives can mimic its push and force one-way flow.

Stepwise Floquet drives mix static and shifting phases. Flow circles one way and flips when drive order flips. Flux-tuned fringes stay sharp, and tuned periods steady the flow. A phase order mark counts drift per period and flips sign with drive order. The chip route offers a flexible lab for driven light phases.
arxiv-2509-13284:
Perseas Christodoulidis studies in 2025 how open effective theories gain new structures when systems leak to an environment. Loss, noise, and bent conservation follow naturally in the Schwinger and Keldysh frame. Superfluid, Maxwell, and gravity cases are the test beds.

In gauge and gravity cases, open terms that break advanced symmetry need care. They stand only if motion identities deform in a consistent way. One such term in open gravity is built in full. Its deformed diffeomorphism identities are shown. The check sorts allowed leaks from broken ones in open gravity.
arxiv-2509-13884:
Sena Atli and Syksy Rasanen examine how the lumpiness of matter affects gravitational waves in a 2025 cosmology paper. The wave equation couples gravitational waves directly to spacetime curvature, a term usually dropped as small. But curvature spikes exactly where matter particles sit, and those spikes could shift the inferred angular diameter distance to a source.

Applying a recently introduced post-geometrical optics approximation that keeps the curvature terms, the authors model particles as localized within their Compton wavelength. The curvature from electrons alone would produce a large distance effect, yet caustics form and break the approximation before that regime is trustworthy. They conclude the method's valid window is narrow, and other tools are needed where curvature effects grow large.
arxiv-2509-14484:
Ari Athair and three co-authors optimise cross flow turbine blades in 2025, turbines whose blades spin around a vertical axis in water or wind. Three shape choices interact: chord to radius ratio, blade camber and preset pitch. Past work often varied them one at a time.

Curved blade paths create virtual camber and virtual incidence, effects the authors quantify with a conformal transformation. Two experimental data sets, one sweeping pitch and size, one sweeping true camber, are analysed together. Links between pitch and camber influence emerge clearly. The authors propose a path to cut a harmful dynamic effect while keeping efficiency. Joint optimisation matters because a pitch change can mimic or cancel a camber change.
arxiv-2509-14884:
Mateusz Bawaj and Andrea Svizzeretto discuss using reinforcement learning to lock optical cavities in a 2025 proceedings paper from the EuCAIFCon 2025 conference. Locking a Fabry-Perot cavity means holding its mirrors at an exact spacing where light resonates. The task is nonlinear and matters for gravitational-wave detectors, which need extreme stability.

A custom simulation environment with a time-domain model let the authors train learning agents on the problem. A deep deterministic policy gradient agent learned to acquire the lock reliably for both low- and high-finesse cavities, including settings like the Virgo detector.
