The paper weighs actor-critic architecture choices such as twin delayed and soft actor-critic variants. It also addresses real-time hardware limits, low-latency execution, and offline policy updates for future laboratory deployment.
arxiv-2509-15084:
Doreen Jirak, Pieter Maes, Armeen Saroukanoff, and Dirk van Rooy argue that AI tools for ships must explain themselves in ways crews can use, in a 2025 paper. Smart tools now help with steering and ship operations. At sea, where things change fast and stakes are high, crews need to know why a tool backs a choice, not just what it backs.

The authors treat good explanations as the base of strong human-machine teamwork at sea. They propose a survey built for the field to learn what sea professionals think about trust, ease of use, and clarity of AI tools. The aim is to steer future tools toward explanations that fit work on the bridge, rather than generic add-ons.
arxiv-2509-15284:
Adeline Guéret, Carlos Gaete-Morales, and Wolf-Peter Schill compare charging strategies for fifteen million electric cars in Germany in a 2025 energy economics paper. Electric vehicles decarbonize transport, but their charging load lands on the power system. The study systematically varies the mix of inflexible charging, smart charging, and bidirectional vehicle-to-grid charging, where cars also feed power back.

A capacity expansion model finds a surprise: a moderate share of bidirectional charging, below thirty percent of the fleet, already beats a fully smart-charging fleet on total system cost. At half the fleet bidirectional, costs fall below even a system with no electric cars at all. Vehicle-to-grid earns its keep by serving demand during high residual load hours. Savings also spread to other consumers, which matters for fair energy policy.
arxiv-2509-15384:
J. L. Ortiz leads a very large team that measured a small icy world beyond Neptune. The object, called 1995 SM55, belongs to the Haumea family, a rare group of icy bodies. In February 2024 it passed in front of a star. Five sites watched the star blink out, which lets the team trace the object's shape and size.

Their fit gives an oval shape about 187 kilometers across, smaller than an older upper bound. Light measures give its brightness, its slight color, and a slow change as it spins. Joined, the data show a bright surface that reflects most sunlight, a bit more even than Haumea itself. Such a bright coat fits the idea that the family came from one past crash.
arxiv-2509-15584:
Divya Bajaj leads a large team that compares ways to boost the power of chemical reaction models. These models track how species counts change through reactions. Testing whether a species count is zero can lift such models to full computing power. That test can hide in many forms: blocking, priority, or timing rules.

The team add a direct form: a new model that bumps a special species whenever any other count hits zero. They show this model can compute anything. They then show many studied variants match it through fast simulations. So blocking, varied rates, parallel runs, and growing volume add no power beyond the zero test itself. The result unifies a family of models.
arxiv-2509-16084:
Computer-designed molecules often cannot be made in a real lab, which limits their use in drug work. Seul Lee and seven co-authors present ReaSyn, a method that reshapes a target molecule into one with a workable building plan. Plans are written as trees that can be grown from the bottom up or the top down with one model.

A second stage edits whole plans by adding, removing, or swapping steps. In tests, ReaSyn led on rebuilding known makeable molecules and on goal-driven search. It also beat prior tools at growing new hits. The cycle of builds and edits explores a huge space with care.
arxiv-2509-16184:
Pinning down the fine energy levels of atoms from their spectra takes experts years for each species. M. Ding and four co-authors turn that slow craft into a game-like task that a learning agent can play. They cast the analysis as a chain of choices on a graph, with rewards learned from past human decisions.

On line lists for cobalt and neodymium species, the agent found hundreds of level energies within hours. Its values matched published ones in most cases, though match rates varied by species. Faster atomic data would serve both astronomy and fusion work, where demand keeps growing.
arxiv-2509-16784:
Mohammed Al Owayyed, Adarsh Denga, and Willem-Paul Brinkman build a training agent for child helpline staff in a 2025 paper. New counselors often train through roleplay with people, which costs time and staff. Rule-based agents give structure but can sound stiff. The team blend rules with a language model for more natural chat.

The blend keeps talks on track while letting replies flow. In tests, trainees rated the agent as more controlled yet natural. Some support for higher engagement also appeared, though it was weaker. Such agents could let helplines train more staff at lower cost. Control matters here, since the talks mimic sensitive calls.
arxiv-2509-17284:
Kanan Anwar, writing alone, builds a quantum theory of light that allows magnetic monopoles. His 2025 arXiv paper starts from a two-potential scheme due to Cabibbo and Ferrari, in which electric and magnetic sources stand on an equal footing. That frame reveals a doubled gauge symmetry at the classical level, and Anwar carries it into the quantum domain.

He applies the Gupta-Bleuler method in a stated gauge to build the physical state space and remove states with negative norm. The finished theory holds the usual photons of everyday light. It also predicts a second kind of excitation, dual photons tied to magnetic charge. Anwar closes by weighing what these dual particles could mean for electromagnetic duality and for gauge theory more broadly. No experiment is claimed; the paper is a careful piece of theory craft.
arxiv-2509-17484:
Remo Ruffini and Yu Wang point to two calm pockets of the cosmos where chemistry might grow complex. Their 2025 arXiv paper compares the Galactic Center with little red dots, compact early galaxies. Both settings host black holes of millions of solar masses. Around them sit dense, cold stores of molecules bound up with dust grains.

The authors stress that both places are electromagnetically tranquil, a rare calm in such extreme settings. That calm, they argue, lets complex molecular chemistry proceed without being blasted apart. It may also allow the synthesis of organic molecules that life needs. They offer the two settings as natural laboratories for studying prebiotic chemistry and early steps toward genetic evolution. The paper is a short, speculative essay rather than a data study, and its claims are framed as possibilities.
arxiv-2509-17584:
Shota Tateishi and five co-authors compare small quantum and classical processors that work in sequence. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies machines built from three or four modules, each handling local data. The modules may pass only a sliver of information: one qubit or qutrit on the quantum side, one bit or trit on the classical side.

For the classical machine, the team proves bounds on how well its output can track a target function. The quantum machine breaks those bounds in theory. A silicon photonics experiment then shows the break in practice. The authors also show how to find the classical bound for any target by recasting the search as an Ising-type spin-glass problem. The theory covers broader tasks too, such as low-rank binary matrix approximation, and it marks a clean line between the two kinds of hardware.
arxiv-2509-17684:
ThankGod Egbe, Peng Wang, Zhihao Guo, and Zidong Chen test a self-supervised vision backbone for robot control. Their 2025 arXiv paper evaluates DINOv3, a large vision model trained without labels, as the eyes of a diffusion policy for manipulation. The question is whether label-free features can match or beat the supervised backbones robots usually borrow from image classification.

Four benchmark tasks, including pushing, lifting, and can and square placement, run under one FiLM-conditioned diffusion policy. Three regimes are compared: training the backbone from scratch, freezing it, and fine-tuning it. Fine-tuned DINOv3 matched or beat the standard ResNet-18 on several tasks, and even frozen it stayed competitive, a sign of strong transferable priors. Self-supervised features also improved sample efficiency and robustness. On hard tasks the swap gained a clear margin in success rate, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-17784:
Jin Li and 7 co-authors use large language models to find cause links in mixed data. Their 2025 frame, MLLM-CD, works on text, image, and other modes at once. Pure data checks can miss how modes touch each other, and cause links can stay vague.

Three parts do the work in turns. A contrast step finds true factors from paired samples. A stats step maps cause links between those factors. A what-if step then uses model world facts to refine the map, round by round. Tests on fake and real data sets show the frame finds real factors and links.
arxiv-2509-18384:
Language models can turn plain instructions into action plans for robots, but they often break safety rules. Yunhao Yang and six co-authors present LAD-VF, a method that fixes plans without retraining the model. Their 2025 paper uses formal verification, a math check that a plan obeys stated rules. Failed checks feed back into the prompt, not the model's weights.

The method adds a text loss shaped by the rule checks and refines prompts step by step. That design scales, works with mixed model setups, and leaves an audit trail of prompts. In robot navigation and manipulation tests, rule compliance rose a lot. Success rates climbed from sixty percent to over ninety percent. The authors offer the method as a clear, checkable path to safer model-driven control. No costly human labeling or fine-tuning is needed.
arxiv-2509-18484:
A treatment can affect not just the person treated, but their neighbors too. Yuanchen Wu and Yubai Yuan present a method to estimate such direct and spillover effects on networks in this 2025 paper. Effects differ across people and links, which makes the job harder. Likeness between connected people also confounds the picture.

Their two-stage method first uses graph neural networks to model the nuisance parts: how traits and network shape drive outcomes. The second stage strips those parts out and fits a clear attention-based model of interference. A math trick called orthogonalization keeps first-stage errors from skewing the result. A bootstrap procedure adds uncertainty bounds for the spillover map. Tests show better estimates of varied effects. The output can flag influential neighbors and recover the sign of spillovers.
arxiv-2509-18784:
A monophonic set in a graph is a set of vertices such that every vertex lies on some chord-free path between two of them. Boštjan Brešar, María Gracia Cornet, and Tanja Dravec pin down that number for Kneser graphs in this 2025 paper. Kneser graphs link sets that share no elements. The monophonic number is the size of the smallest such set.

The team establishes that number for all Kneser graphs in the valid range. For larger parameters, they prove a stronger fact: any two non-adjacent vertices already form a monophonic set. Graphs with that trait are called strongly 2-monophonic. They give conditions for the trait and show it survives taking products of graphs. Every Johnson graph has it, as do non-complete Hamming graphs. Chordal graphs, with one family of exceptions, do not. The paper maps a tidy corner of graph theory.
arxiv-2509-19084:
Asela Hevapathige, writing alone, designs a graph neural network meant to avoid three known weaknesses of the breed. Graph networks pass messages between linked points to classify them, but deep versions blur all points into look-alikes, a flaw called oversmoothing. They also handle mixed link types poorly and lump all features together in one block. The new design, AxelGNN, borrows from a model of how culture spreads between similar people.

Its links open or close based on how similar two points are, letting groups converge or drift apart. Features are copied in segments, small meaningful groups at a time, rather than all at once. A global polarization step keeps several distinct clusters alive, fighting oversmoothing. Tests show the design matches or beats prior methods on node classification and influence estimation, on both friendly and mixed-link graphs.
arxiv-2509-19184:
Silvia Almada Monter and two co-authors simulate how a special kind of ultraviolet light escapes from galaxies. The light, Lyman-alpha, bounces through neutral hydrogen gas before escaping, and its shape carries clues about the gas. Astronomers also use it as a stand-in for the escape of ionizing light, which is harder to observe. Theory for escape through uneven, directional gas layouts has lagged behind observations.

Their Monte Carlo simulations push the light through porous, clumpy gas while varying channel shapes, outflows, and dust. Surprisingly, the light does not slip out mainly through the thinnest paths; it crosses channels of substantial depth, which dims the central peak. Splitting channels matters little next to their geometry and coverage. Outflows and dust reshape the spectra in ways the authors capture with simple analytic models. The results warn that spectra suggesting thick gas may still hide leaking channels.
arxiv-2509-19284:
Long chains of thought are the fashion in reasoning models, but Yunzhen Feng and four co-authors find that longer and more self-reviewing is often worse. Across ten large reasoning models on math and science problems, simply stretching the reasoning or adding more backtracking lowered accuracy. Judging quality by token counts confuses verbosity with good process. The authors instead view each chain as a graph and extract its structure.

One statistic stands out: the failed-step fraction, the share of steps that sit in abandoned branches. It predicts correctness better than length or review share across models. Selecting answers by that statistic at test time gives the largest accuracy gains, and deleting failed branches from chains improves them directly. Failed branches appear to bias what comes after. The lesson is to scale test-time effort by structure, favoring chains that fail less.
arxiv-2509-19584:
A spherical cap is a dome cut from a sphere, and averaging a function over such a dome raises sharp math questions. Boris Rubin introduces one-sided fractional integrals on the cap and studies where they stay bounded. Weighted function spaces set the rules for that boundedness. He then derives exact formulas that undo the averaging, recovering the original function.

The results feed into Riesz potentials, a classic smoothing operation, on the same dome. In two dimensions the inversion problem shows up in electrostatics and elasticity. Rubin's tools include flat projections of the sphere, sharp integral forms, and wave-like decompositions of functions on spheres. Exact inversion formulas matter when engineers must rebuild a source from averaged measurements. The paper gives that rebuild a firm footing.
arxiv-2509-20084:
Planning safe flight paths through cluttered spaces is the problem taken up by Guillermo Gil, Jose Antonio Cobano, and two co-authors in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their system, called C-3TO, plans smooth three-dimensional paths for aerial robots. It works with a neural map that estimates the distance to the nearest obstacle at any point.

Older methods read distances from a fixed grid, which can blur exact values. C-3TO instead asks the neural map directly while it shapes the path with smooth polynomial curves. A two-stage process then balances speed, safety, and smoothness. Tests show the paths avoid collisions and stay within what the robot can actually fly. Users can also adjust window sizes and settings to fit different tasks. The result is a flexible base for safe local replanning in flight.
arxiv-2509-20484:
Cameras at the edge of a network cannot stream everything to the cloud for labeling. Dani Manjah and four co-authors study how to pick the few images worth sending in a 2025 arXiv paper. In their setup, a large teacher model on a server labels selected images. Small models on the cameras then train on those labels and must be refreshed as scenes change.

The selection strategy mixes two instincts. Confident stream items are favored as they arrive, one by one. A diversity rule stops the chosen set from repeating the same scene over and over. For the same training effort, the paired strategy produced a high-quality edge model. It did so while asking the server for very few labels. The result matters for large camera fleets where bandwidth and labeling budgets are tight.
arxiv-2509-20584:
Data centers for artificial intelligence are outgrowing their optical links. Alireza Geravand and eleven co-authors present a comb-driven transmitter meant to scale with them in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their architecture sits on a silicon and silicon nitride platform. A quantum-dot frequency comb supplies many wavelength channels from one source, feeding dense multiplexing for co-packaged optics.

Compact microring-assisted modulators do the encoding. Single-tone tests reached four hundred gigabits per second per polarization in the O-band, at a record shoreline density and very low modulation energy. Six comb channels carried just over a terabit per second across five kilometers of fiber. System analysis suggests combined rates above ten terabits per second per fiber are realistic. The design sketches a path toward petabit-scale interconnects inside future computing clusters.
arxiv-2509-20884:
Question-answering systems that look at images often learn shortcuts from biased training data. Zhifei Li and six co-authors build IOG-VQA to fight that habit in a 2025 paper accepted by IEEE Transactions on Multimedia. The model answers visual questions by reasoning about objects and their interactions.

One part applies self-attention across detected objects, capturing how objects relate within a scene. Another part uses a generative adversarial setup to debias the training signal, producing a fairer data distribution. Together they push the model toward real visual evidence rather than superficial patterns. The authors report improved accuracy and better generalization to varied questions and images. The work targets a known weakness of visual question answering in the wild.
arxiv-2509-21484:
Online convex optimization must perform well against data that arrives over time, in geometries beyond the Euclidean one. David Janz and 2 co-authors study that setting in a 2025 paper. Losses are Lipschitz in one norm, while regularization follows another. Gradient estimates come from randomized two point finite differences. Sampling uses cone measures on spheres of a third norm.

Unified high probability regret bounds are proved for all norm choices. All moment bounds on the gradient estimator drive the analysis, in the dual regularization norm. Time uniform control of quadratic variation follows. The algorithm is anytime and data driven. Special cases recover known in expectation rates, strengthened to high probability. Lower bounds show optimality for part of the range and a gap elsewhere.
arxiv-2509-21584:
Cells measured by several omics tools share some signals and keep others private to each mode. Yu Gui and 2 co-authors learn disentangled codes of such data in a 2025 paper. Shared and mode specific features both matter for describing cell states. Ideally, mode specific features stay independent of shared ones while capturing all extra information. Information theory criteria express that trade off naturally.

Mutual information goals are hard to estimate reliably, and variational substitutes underperform. Their method, IndiSeek, combines an independence enforcing objective with an efficient reconstruction loss. That loss bounds conditional mutual information. The setup balances the two aims side by side. Single cell multi omics is the motivating use, with downstream analyses as the intended beneficiaries. The method is built to keep the two kinds of signal apart without losing either one.
arxiv-2509-21684:
Newton methods converge fast but cost much per step, while gradient descent is cheap but slow. Danny Duan and Hanbaek Lyu propose a Newton type method between those poles in a 2025 paper. Regularized Overestimated Newton uses an overestimate of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives. Behaviour is governed by the largest Hessian overestimation error. Per iteration cost stays low by design.

Globally, convergence is accelerated when the optimality gap is large and settles to a slower rate when small. Locally, convergence is superlinear when the overestimation is exact and linear when inexact. Non isolated minima are allowed under a local quadratic growth condition. A randomized low rank Hessian approximation gives a practical variant. Smooth convex optimization is the setting throughout.
arxiv-2509-21784:
Zhengyang Zhang, Conor M. Byrne, Chengyuan Wu, and Bo Wang study a rare class of pulsing stars in this 2025 astrophysics paper, accepted by The Astrophysical Journal. Blue large-amplitude pulsators swell and shrink on cycles of only minutes. They burn very hot, and astronomers still debate how they form. The team tests whether helium-burning stars can explain them.

The authors ran the BPASS population code for the Milky Way. Their model predicts well over ten thousand such stars in our galaxy. Most would have normal companion stars, while the rest would orbit worn-out or compact partners. The two groups form in different ways and end up with very different orbit lengths. Most of these stars are too dim to see today, but coming sky surveys should find several hundred of them.
arxiv-2509-21984:
Move the key object in a picture, and a large vision-language model may answer differently about the same scene. Yingjie Zhu and eight co-authors study that spatial bias in this 2025 paper. Through controlled tests, they show current models often give inconsistent outputs when identical information sits at different image locations. Their analysis traces the bias not to the vision encoder, but to a mismatch in how the vision and language parts pay attention.

To fix it, the authors propose Adaptive Global Context Injection, a light mechanism that feeds a shared global view of the image into every image token. By making each token carry the whole scene's meaning, the mechanism reduces the bias while keeping the model's skills intact. Wide-ranging tests show stronger spatial robustness, plus good results on downstream tasks and on hallucination benchmarks, where made-up content is checked.
arxiv-2509-22184:
Pavan Karjol, Vivek V Kashyap, Rohan Kashyap, and Prathosh A P present a way to teach neural networks functions that respect a symmetry group. A function is equivariant when rotating the input rotates the output in step. Many groups preserve a quadratic form, a bowl-shaped measure of size, and the authors use that fact as the key. Their 2025 method learns the quadratic form tied to the group directly from data, assuming the group is of the orthogonal kind.

The learned form has a unique symmetric matrix behind it, and building its diagonal shape into the network gives simpler, cheaper models. The framework extends to functions of several input vectors at once, using their Gram matrix to capture how the inputs relate. Tests on polynomial fitting, quark jet tagging, and inertia prediction beat baseline methods at both finding the symmetry and learning the function.
arxiv-2509-22284:
State-space models process sequences with a transition matrix that carries memory forward, but cheap designs for that matrix limit what the model can express. Aleksandar Terzić and four co-authors propose a structured sparse design in this 2025 paper, a NeurIPS spotlight. Their target is state tracking: the ability to mimic a finite-state automaton, the simplest machines with memory. Fully general transition matrices can do it, but they cost too much memory and computing even at moderate sizes.

Their model, PD-SSM, builds the transition matrix as a product of two simple parts: a selection matrix that routes each state to one destination, and a diagonal matrix of complex scale factors. That keeps the cost of the recurrence on par with the cheapest diagonal designs. In theory, one layer of the model can emulate any automaton with matching state count, a stronger guarantee than rival structured designs offer.
arxiv-2509-22584:
John C. Baez surveys double categories as a language for open systems: systems that interact with their surroundings. The focus is the variable sharing approach, where systems compose by identifying shared variables. That approach is usually built with structured or decorated cospans. Baez explains it through three running examples: open Petri nets, open dynamical systems, and Petri nets with rates.

He compares the strengths of the structured and decorated versions and draws out their shared features. Any such double category receives maps from two simpler ones, its exoskeleton and its outer shell. He also studies hypergraph double categories, a proposed common frame that should subsume both cospan styles.
arxiv-2509-22684:
Tarunesh Verma and 3 co-authors profile zero-knowledge proofs on graphics chips to find where time goes. These proofs show a secret input was used correctly without revealing it. They power private coins and blockchain scaling, and GPUs have sped up their core kernels. But a systematic study of bottlenecks on modern GPUs was missing.

Once multi-scalar multiplication got fast, the number-theoretic transform took up to nine tenths of proof time. Current transform code underuses the GPU and skips features like asynchronous operations. The arithmetic runs on the 32-bit integer pipeline with limited parallelism. The authors map tuning options, like precomputed inputs and new data formats, as a roadmap for faster provers.
arxiv-2509-22784:
Jonathan Carney leads a large team that chased the fading afterglow of the longest gamma-ray burst ever seen. GRB 250702B lasted so long that standard collapsar models strain to explain it. The team gathered optical and infrared follow-up from a suite of major telescopes, including Keck, Gemini, and Magellan. The afterglow fits forward shock emission from a relativistic jet buried in heavy obscuration.

Deep images show the host is a massive, dusty, lopsided system, likely two galaxies in a major merger. The burst's offset, host traits, and jet rule against a jetted tidal disruption around a supermassive black hole. Other progenitors remain open, from an atypical collapsar to a star disrupted by a stellar-mass compact object.
arxiv-2509-22884:
Cancer data often mixes traits shared by all patients with traits tied to one cancer type. Arhit Chakrabarti and 3 co-authors build a clustering method that uses both kinds. Older grouped clustering tools use only the shared traits and waste the rest. Their method, the global-local Dirichlet process, models the shared and group-level parts at once.

The authors describe the model in two ways and give a fast way to fit it. Tests used fake data and a real set of gut-related cancers. Extra clinical traits, like a blood marker, body mass index, and smoking rate, split broad groups into finer ones. Those finer groups may aid study of how tumors grow and differ.
arxiv-2509-23284:
Huge antenna arrays serve near users directly, but far users often sit behind blockages. Xiaomin Cao and 4 co-authors route far-user signals through a reconfigurable intelligent surface. Three precoding schemes at the array get compared: two zero-forcing types and maximum ratio transmission. Closed-form efficiency expressions are derived for one scheme. Statistical forms cover the other two.

A visibility region heuristic trims compute cost. A two-stage design then tunes surface phases and power to lift the weakest users. Gains over equal power and random phases were large for all schemes. Central zero-forcing led overall, while the local variant ran cheaper.
arxiv-2509-23484:
Guessing whether a student will answer an exam question right is a core skill for any AI tutor. Tom Quilter and 3 co-authors work on formal mathematics exams, where good training data have been scarce. They release the largest open set yet of marked formal math exam responses. Their model builds on item response theory, a classic way to link student skill and question difficulty.

Their best tool is a new discrete variational inference method, built for settings with little data. It beat classic item response and matrix methods, and pushed accuracy past eighty percent. One surprise: a single skill value per student was enough to reach top accuracy, even when topic-level skill profiles were added.
arxiv-2509-23684:
Inside a fine-tuned transformer, single neurons rarely tell the whole story; groups do the work together. Tanya Chowdhury and 3 co-authors map those groups with tools from coalitional game theory. Neurons play as agents in a hedonic game, where preferences encode how much each group adds to a layer's computation. An algorithm then extracts stable coalitions, groups whose joint removal has effects beyond the sum of parts.

The team tracks coalitions across layers as they persist, split, merge, or vanish. Applied to reranker models from three families, the coalitions showed higher synergy than clustering baselines. The authors argue these units are functional, interpretable, and predictive.
arxiv-2509-23784:
Neural networks that solve physics equations from sparse, boundary-only data can sound surer than they should. Filip Landgren and Marika Taylor explore Bayesian and extended physics-informed networks on a nonlinear equation from holography, tied to an entanglement surface. Analytic asymptotics supply training data from the boundary alone. The authors argue that standard overconfidence measures mislead here, since a model that obeys hard physics constraints may be confident for good reason.

They propose diagnostics instead: an information density and a local measure of how strongly the physics constraints collapse the posterior. The same tools are tried on Liouville-type and Van der Pol equations to probe apparent overconfidence further.
arxiv-2509-24284:
David Baraglia extends a classic duality transform to a real form of K-theory. In complex K-theory, the Fourier-Mukai transform links the K-groups of a torus and its dual through pullback, tensoring with a special line bundle, and pushforward. For families of tori, twisted K-theory makes the same link work.

Baraglia defines Real T-duality for torus bundles that carry real structures and proves such duals exist. He then builds a Real Fourier-Mukai transform for those dual pairs and proves it is an isomorphism. An application follows to the families index of Real Dirac operators, which bears on Real Seiberg-Witten theory.
arxiv-2509-24384:
Judging whether a language model's output is harmful sounds like a job for a language model, yet the judges disagree with each other. Langqi Yang and 8 co-authors built HarmMetric Eval, a benchmark that grades the graders. It holds harmful prompts paired with harmful and harmless outputs across fine categories, and scores each metric on whether it ranks the harmful output higher.

A surprise emerged: classic reference-based scores like ROUGE beat model judges at fine-grained harm checks. Analysis shows model judges stumble on irrelevant or useless outputs. The team then built a better judge, prompting with fine criteria and lightly fine-tuning with reference scores. It reached the top on their benchmark.
arxiv-2509-24484:
Prabhanjan Ananth and 2 co-authors draw a hard line around what pseudorandom unitaries can build. These unitaries look perfectly random to any efficient test, and there is evidence they are weaker than one-way functions. The open question is how they relate to other plausibly weak quantum primitives. The team focuses on primitives that use classical communication.

Their main result: bit commitments and key agreement of that classical-communication kind cannot be built from pseudorandom unitaries in a black-box way. The core step shows how hard it is for separable channels to tell identical Haar unitaries from independent ones. The separation sharpens results from both learning theory and cryptography.
arxiv-2510-00184:
Xiaoyan Bai and seven colleagues published this 2025 paper asking why transformer models fail at multi-digit multiplication. The models master many hard tasks yet stumble on grade-school arithmetic. The team reverse-engineered a model that does learn multiplication through implicit chain-of-thought. Probes and attribution tools let them watch how that successful model organizes the work.

The model caches pairwise partial products and retrieves them through attention links. Digits are stored in a Fourier-style code, and partial sums form by geometric addition. Standard fine-tuning, by contrast, settles into a shortcut that lacks these long-range links. When the authors added a helper loss predicting the running sum, ordinary training succeeded too. The lesson is that the right inductive bias, not more data alone, unlocks such skills.
arxiv-2510-00484:
Saurabh Shivpuje and a team of co-authors published this 2025 paper on quantum computing for photochemistry. Diazirines and diazo compounds release carbenes under light, a trick used across chemical biology. Modeling their excited-state paths needs large active spaces that strain classical methods. The team applies sample-based quantum diagonalization, a hybrid quantum-classical technique, on superconducting quantum processors.

Ground-state results beat the chemical accuracy threshold at nearly every stationary point for the parent molecule. For a phenyl-substituted version in a much larger active space, errors stayed near one kilocalorie per mole against strong classical references. An extended variant of the method handled excited states with heavy configuration mixing. Classical tools still ran geometry steps and diagnostics around the quantum core. The authors conclude that quantum frameworks can already trace complex photochemical landscapes with useful fidelity.
arxiv-2510-00684:
Biswas and Mandal build a unified framework for Bohr-type inequalities in this 2025 arXiv paper on complex analysis. The classical Bohr inequality says the summed absolute coefficients of a bounded analytic function stay controlled within a disk of radius one third, and that radius cannot be improved. Many variants exist for special function classes, each proved with separate tricks. The authors instead work with harmonic mappings that are K-quasiconformal in the unit disk.

Their method inserts several Schwarz functions at once into the majorant series that drives the estimates. That single framework recovers the known theorems A, B, and C as special parameter choices. It also yields new refined inequalities that fold in the function's value, its derivative, or area terms. Tables and figures in the paper track how the improved radii behave across parameter settings.
arxiv-2510-01184:
Xu and co-authors give diffusion and flow models a dial for how wildly or safely they sample. Generators normally reproduce the training distribution's spread, whether users want sharp certainties or broad exploration. Rescaling the learned score over time changes the effective local temperature of sampling.

No retraining is needed, and both deterministic and stochastic samplers accept the tweak. Toy data confirmed the mechanism before five real tasks were tried. Depth prediction gained from sharper sampling, while image generation preferred slightly flatter draws. Protein design and robot manipulation also responded well to tuned temperatures. Temperature here acts locally through time rather than as one global knob. Sharper draws raise precision where one best answer matters most. Flatter draws help exploration where diversity is the prize. Off-the-shelf models accept the method without surgery. One mechanism serves five very different tasks well.
arxiv-2510-01284:
Low, Wang, and Katyal generate sound and video together in one model instead of gluing two pipelines in sequence. Separate synthesis usually drifts out of sync, and post-hoc alignment patches never quite hide the seam. Their system, Ovi, twins two identical transformer towers, one per modality.

Blockwise fusion lets the towers trade timing and meaning at every stage of generation. The audio tower, trained on vast raw audio, speaks with identity and emotion while adding matched effects. Joint training on video corpora teaches synchronization directly rather than by rule. The clips aim at cinematic storytelling with speech that fits the scene. Scaled positional embeddings carry the timing handshake between towers. Architectural symmetry is the bet, since identical towers fuse cleanly. Hundreds of thousands of audio hours taught the sound tower its craft. Movie-grade clips are the stated ambition.
arxiv-2510-01384:
Kim and co-authors give masked diffusion generators a principled way to spot and repair their own bad tokens. These models unmask text in parallel, which invites inconsistencies between positions that sequential models avoid. Their plug-in, PRISM, learns a per-token quality score inside the same forward pass.

A self-correction loss provably ties the score to true token quality, with no reinforcement learning or external verifier. Low scorers get remasked and regenerated during sampling. Gains appeared across puzzles, plain text, and code, and grew as step budgets shrank. The method attaches to any pretrained masked diffusion model. Sudoku supplies the crisp test where a wrong digit is unambiguous. An eight-billion-parameter code model carried the largest demonstration. Dependency errors across positions are the mechanism being exploited. Few-step sampling is where self-correction earns its keep. Quality scores ride free inside existing passes.
arxiv-2510-01584:
Ximenes, Pires, and Villas-Bôas solve a quantum walk exactly for a new family of starting states spread over many sites. Quantum walks model how quantum particles wander, and the starting spread is a knob experimenters can turn. Complex hopping phases in the rules add a second knob with its own effects.

Closed-form results reveal transport with a preferred direction from completely unbiased starts. A backfire effect appears too, where wider starting spread helps early motion but hurts later spread. Staying-put probability decays with an enhanced power law only under fine tuning. The formulas give designers precise control over quantum transport. Exact solutions are rare in quantum transport, which makes these formulas a benchmark for numerics. The crossing time separates the helpful regime from the harmful one. Hamiltonian phase steers the effect, giving experimenters a tuning dial. Delocalization cuts both ways.
arxiv-2510-01684:
Jia and Liang study dark solitons in exciton-polariton condensates in this 2025 physics paper. A condensate of this kind forms when light and matter excitations merge in a semiconductor cavity. A dark soliton is a moving dip in the condensate's density. The authors ask how such solitons behave after sudden changes, called quenches, to the system settings.

The team varied the interaction strength and the pump laser intensity in their analysis. A Hamiltonian variational method gave simple equations for how soliton velocity evolves over time. Direct simulations of the full condensate equation matched those equations well. They found three regimes for the soliton's fate. At moderate pump power it travels stably, while stronger pumping breaks it apart. Quenching both settings at once can excite whole trains of solitons.
arxiv-2510-01784:
Wu and five co-authors improve long-form video generation in this 2025 computer vision paper. Making videos that run for a minute or more is hard for current models. They must remember distant context while avoiding the error build-up of step-by-step decoding. The team attacks both problems with two separate mechanisms.

The first, MemoryPack, is a learnable system that retrieves context using text and image guidance together. It models short-term and long-term links jointly while keeping linear computing cost. The second, Direct Forcing, is a single-step approximation that aligns training with inference more closely. That alignment curbs the drift that creeps in during long generations. Together the two parts raise temporal consistency across long clips. The work pushes autoregressive video models closer to practical, reliable use.
arxiv-2510-01984:
Wang builds a small artificial spine that bends and stretches for quadruped robots in this 2025 robotics paper. Mammals flex their spines to lengthen strides, absorb landings, and generate thrust. Most robot quadrupeds keep rigid trunks, which limits that agility. The SPARC module adds a three-degree-of-freedom sagittal spine between the body segments.

Three torque-controlled actuators give the spine pitch and axial motion under programmable stiffness and damping. A custom control board running at one kilohertz shapes that compliance along each axis. The whole package weighs just over a kilogram, including its protected power unit. Bench push-pull tests rendered commanded stiffness between three hundred and seven hundred newtons per meter with under two percent error. Release trials confirmed clean spring-damper responses across damping settings. A simpler controller worked too, but with more variability. The open-source platform awaits on-robot trials.
arxiv-2510-02284:
Romero and co-authors teach video generators to respect basic physics when objects collide. Their 2025 computer vision paper introduces a method called KineMask. Modern video models make pretty clips for film and ads. Their objects, though, often slide through each other or move without cause. KineMask starts from one still image plus a chosen object speed. It then renders the motion and the collisions that should follow. Training uses object masks that slowly lose future motion hints. The model must learn to predict interactions on its own.

Training began on synthetic scenes with simple motions. A version trained without interactions hallucinated fake collisions. A version trained on interaction scenes rendered pushes and crashes correctly. The skill carried over to real scenes. Robot planners need simulators that obey cause and effect. KineMask moves video models closer to that role.
arxiv-2510-02484:
Rodriguez-Sanchez, Allen, and Konidaris teach agents to split raw pixels into controllable factors. Their 2025 machine learning paper addresses a representation problem. Factored decision models learn far faster than flat ones. They need the state already split into separate variables. Deep learning agents see only rich pixel streams instead. The authors exploit a simple habit of actions. Each action usually moves only a few variables. The rest evolve by the world own rules. Their contrastive method, ACF, uses that contrast as a teacher. It recovers variables each action can move on its own.

Three benchmarks with known ground truth test the method. Taxi, FourRooms, and a MiniGrid door task supplied the worlds. ACF recovered the true controllable factors from pixels. Baseline disentanglement methods trailed it consistently. Not every useful variable is controllable, they caution. Uncontrollable factors still matter for planning ahead. Factored learning from raw sight gets closer.
arxiv-2510-02584:
Abtahi, Mojahed, and Nazari plan robot paths around moving obstacles three hundred times faster. Their 2025 robotics paper uses Koopman operator theory. Nonlinear robot motion makes optimal planning slow. Koopman methods lift the dynamics into a space where they look linear. Earlier work lifted only the motion itself. This team lifts the collision constraints as well. Data driven decomposition finds the lifted model from samples. Only the bilinear version captured the needed couplings. Linear versions failed on the quadratic avoidance terms. Planning then becomes a fast quadratic program inside model predictive control.

Tests used a unicycle style mobile robot model. The lifted planner found safe optimal actions reliably. Average compute time fell by a factor of three hundred twenty. The baseline was a nonlinear controller in the original space. Real time control on small embedded hardware becomes feasible. Moving crowds of obstacles stress exactly this speed.
arxiv-2510-03184:
Grigorescu and Moayyedi prove that finding the smallest one-sided code sparsifier is NP-hard. Sparsifiers shrink a structure while keeping its key measures. A one-sided sparsifier keeps a subset of coordinates. Every codeword must keep a set fraction of its weight there. Recent work showed small such sets always exist. Half-sized sets suffice for the half-weight demand. Existence, though, says nothing about search cost.

This paper settles the search question negatively. Minimizing the subset size is NP-hard in general. The proof reduces from the nearest codeword problem. That problem is a classic hard nut in coding theory. Approximation fares no better in their analysis. Matching hardness bounds rule out easy near-optimal search. Random or greedy picks thus remain the practical route. The gap between existence and computability is now explicit. Code designers cannot expect optimal sparsifiers from any efficient method.
arxiv-2510-03384:
Arunasalam, Pickering, Celik, and Ur present a 2025 arXiv paper on the values inside everyday choices made by AI assistants. When an assistant picks a recipe or a travel plan, its picks favor some values over others. Values like care for nature, charity, and diversity may steer those picks. The team audited six language models on thirty everyday tasks. They compared the models with each other and with one hundred United States crowd workers.

The audit found that models often stray from human value patterns. Models disagreed with each other on the values their choices implied. So swapping one assistant for another can change the moral flavor of help. Users rarely see these leanings, since the tasks look neutral on the surface. The study gives designers and regulators a method to surface leanings before assistants shape millions of decisions. It also warns users to check whose values their helper carries.
arxiv-2510-03684:
Mehrer and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper using computational models to choose where to stimulate the visual cortex of macaque monkeys, then testing those choices in the animals. Early visual prosthetics stimulate low level cortex and evoke only flashes or letters. Higher visual areas encode objects, promising richer percepts, but picking stimulation targets there is guesswork. Their framework has three parts: a module translating stimulation settings into activity changes, topographic brain models, and a mapping back to the cortex.

Model chosen stimulation sites produced shifts in the monkeys' perceptual choices during a recognition task. Per site predictions correlated strongly with the animals' behavior. Image generation from stimulated face selective sites produced face like patterns, echoing a patient's reports of face phosphenes. A model in the loop turns prosthetic design from trial and error into prediction. Richer visual experiences for blind patients are the goal.
arxiv-2510-03784:
Yu and colleagues wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on how to divide a fixed parameter budget inside Transformer models. Transformers power most modern language and vision systems, yet designers lack clear rules for sizing each layer. The authors study two choices: how many attention heads each layer gets, and how large each head should be. They combine math analysis with experiments to find better allocations.

The analysis shows a trade-off in early layers between more heads and larger heads. It also proves a saturation effect: beyond a point, larger head dimensions add little, and the waste grows for long input sequences. Because of this, later layers can often run well with fewer parameters than early layers. The authors turn these findings into practical design rules for building smaller Transformers. Such rules could cut memory and computing costs with little accuracy loss.
arxiv-2510-03984:
Kaur and colleagues wrote this 2025 conference paper arguing that personalized AI agents are graded with the wrong test. Standard benchmarks freeze a user's needs at one moment and score the agent once. Real users change their minds, refine their tastes, and return across many sessions. A static snapshot cannot show whether an agent truly adapts to a person over time.

The authors propose a three-part lens for evaluation. First, simulated users should carry preference models that evolve as interactions proceed. Second, structured interviews, modeled on library reference interviews, should draw out preferences in context. Third, scoring should track how agent behavior improves across sessions, not just final accuracy. They illustrate the lens with a case study in online shopping search using the PersonalWAB dataset. Its aim is to reframe personalization as a long process that evaluation must learn to measure.
arxiv-2510-04084:
Mayama and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper testing two theories of consciousness against each other in living neurons. Integrated information theory ties consciousness to a system's integrated causal structure, measured by a quantity called Phi. The free-energy principle instead describes brains as inference machines minimizing surprise. Whether Phi tracks inference dynamics was unknown, so the team used cultured neuronal networks already shown to perform inference.

Repeated stimulation from hidden sources taught the cultures to distinguish the sources. Across sessions, variational free energy fell while accuracy and Bayesian surprise rose. A proxy for integrated information followed a hill-shaped path, rising then falling as learning settled. Phi correlated strongly with Bayesian surprise, only modestly with accuracy, and not at all with free energy itself. The authors read Phi as marking belief updating: cores of integrated activity expand when evidence forces revision.
arxiv-2510-04284:
Lai and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on Doctor-R1, an AI medical agent trained not just to answer clinical questions but to conduct the consultation that produces a sound decision. Large language models perform well on static medical examinations, yet real outpatient care requires strategic and empathetic questioning over multiple turns. Doctor-R1 is trained as an interacting agent rather than a one-shot answerer.

A two-tiered reward separately improves diagnostic decisions and communicative inquiry, while an experience repository grounds learning in high-quality prior trajectories. On HealthBench and MAQuE, Doctor-R1 outperformed specialized open-source medical models by a substantial margin and surpassed powerful proprietary systems, despite greater parameter efficiency. The study suggests consultation behavior should be optimized and assessed as a clinical skill in its own right, not inferred from examination accuracy.
arxiv-2510-04484:
Amin Banayeeanzade and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on steering the mood and personality of AI chat models. A tutor bot might show joy to praise a student, or firmness to stress a review. The team built PsySET, a benchmark that tests both how well steering works and whether it stays trustworthy. Four models from different families faced several steering methods.

Prompting steered the models reliably, but it gave coarse control over intensity. Vector injections gave finer control, at a small cost to output quality. The trust checks covered safety, truthfulness, fairness, and ethics after steering. Some effects defied common sense in the results. Even joy, a positive mood, weakened defense against false claims and lowered privacy care. Joy also raised preferential bias toward some groups. Anger raised toxicity as expected, yet it made the model resist leaking private data.
arxiv-2510-04584:
Fernando López, Santosh Kesiraju, and Jordi Luque wrote this 2025 paper on shaky test scores for audio language models. Such models answer questions about sound, and most benchmarks grade them with multiple choice tests. A single accuracy number per test is the norm. The team suspected that small changes to a test would swing that number. They ran a systematic study across three benchmarks and four leading models.

Shuffling the order of the answer choices changed scores by large amounts. Rewording the question or the choices moved scores as well. Rephrased wrong options caused the largest drops in their runs. So a model rank on one printing of a test may not survive a reprint. The authors propose a simpler protocol with a metric that averages over such variations. Their report format shows the spread, not just the headline number. Benchmark builders gain a fairer way to compare audio models.
arxiv-2510-04684:
Shao Ping Li and Jens Chluba wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on a new way to spot hidden particles from the early universe. Extra radiation after neutrinos decoupled would raise the effective count of neutrino species. That count alone cannot say what produced the extra energy. The authors point to spectral distortions in the cosmic microwave background as a second clue. Extra energy that starts as neutrinos can still trade energy with photons through weak interactions.

That exchange leaves a faint fingerprint in the spectrum of the background light. Pairing the species count with the distortion signal breaks the tie between rival sources. Hidden sectors that couple mainly to neutrinos become visible this way. The paper maps the parameter space that joint measurements could reach. Future instruments will measure both anisotropies and distortions with far better precision. The combined probe could reveal particles that no collider or telescope sees directly.
arxiv-2510-04784:
Christopher Orrico, Hari Prasad Varadarajan, Matthijs van Berkel, and Lennard Ceelen wrote this 2025 paper on steering plasma density inside a fusion reactor. The ITER tokamak will feed its plasma with pellets fired at set moments. Controllers must shape the density profile while respecting safety limits. The system mixes dynamics, delayed inputs, and on off actuators with uncertain effects. The authors use model predictive control, which plans over a horizon.

Their multi stage variant plans over a tree of futures to face uncertainty head on. That tree makes a heavy mixed integer problem heavier still. To run in time, they shrink the prediction model with a data driven reduction method. A reduction compresses the profile description itself. The combined design keeps the safety and uncertainty handling of the method. It drops the computing load to a level a controller can carry. Density control decides fuel use and stability in plasma.
arxiv-2510-04884:
Schroeder, Funk, Guan, Okonek, and Ziegelmeier wrote this 2025 paper on choosing which links to keep when simplifying a network. Analysts prune nodes and edges to reveal structure, but the cut off is picked by feel. Small changes in the threshold can reshape the network, which makes results fragile. Most pruning sees only pairs, ignoring groups that interact together. The authors build a method on topological data analysis.

Their algorithm uses persistent homology, which tracks shapes in data across scales. It scores parameter choices by how stable the shapes stay under changes. Users can demand amounts of structure, which blocks degenerate answers. A demonstration builds networks of concepts from paper abstracts, linked when they share an abstract. The method picked thresholds that kept structure without tuning. The framework extends past networks to parameter choice problems. Science mapping is one user; biology and social data face the pruning question.
arxiv-2510-05084:
Ethan Kahn studies a side effect of tiny electric thrusters on small satellites in this 2025 arXiv paper. Electrospray thrusters sip power and push CubeSats efficiently. Their ion plumes spread out in a wide cone, though. A plume that hits body-mounted solar panels can foul them and waste thrust.

Kahn built a particle-tracking simulation, validated against experiments to within a few percent. He tested nine thruster placements across 1U, 3U, and 6U CubeSats. Rear mounting on a 3U craft fouled nearly half the array area. Deployable panels cut contamination by 77 percent compared with body-mounted ones. Side-mounted thrusters avoided impingement entirely at a small efficiency cost. The numbers give mission planners concrete design trades.
arxiv-2510-05384:
Felipe Almeida and P. F. Barker redesign the laser trap that holds nanoparticles in mid-air in this 2025 arXiv paper. Levitated optomechanics cools floating particles toward quantum states of motion. Recoil from scattered photons heats them back up and limits every experiment. Standard Gaussian beam tweezers suffer this heating badly.

The authors study traps built from cylindrically polarized vortex beams with radial or azimuthal polarization. These beams cut recoil heating by up to an order of magnitude versus Gaussian tweezers. Silicon particles in radial vortex beams showed reductions above ninefold in the best range. The beams also trap larger particles beyond the Rayleigh regime, in bright or dark configurations. Tuning the wavelength can even shape nonlinear or repulsive potentials for creating non-classical states.
arxiv-2510-05484:
Murali and colleagues at the University of Texas at Austin tackle child safety in chatbots. Language models now sit inside tutoring and entertainment tools that children use daily. Safety tests are built for adults and miss how risk changes with age. Their 2025 benchmark, ChildSafe, grades model safety through simulated child users instead.

The simulated children embody four age bands, from early elementary to late high school. Their traits rest on established developmental psychology, avoiding tests on real children. Scoring covers nine safety dimensions, including privacy, misinformation, and emotional support. Multi-turn trials found consistent weaknesses that shift with the simulated age. The youngest group proved hardest for every model tested, and no model excelled across all ages. The team released its agent templates, protocols, and conversation corpus for reuse by other researchers.
arxiv-2510-05784:
Wiesmayr and colleagues adapt wireless links using only success and failure feedback. Choosing each transmission's modulation and coding scheme trades speed against reliability. The industry standard, outer-loop adaptation, leans on channel estimates and fixed steps. Their 2025 SALAD algorithm infers channel quality from acknowledgments alone.

SALAD fits the signal quality by minimizing cross-entropy between feedback and predicted error rates. Its learning rate self-adapts online through knowledge distillation from a hindsight teacher. Hypothesis testing detects underestimated channels and probes faster schemes safely. A feedback loop holds the long-term error rate near its target. One parameter set handled every traffic regime in the testbed trials. Over-the-air 5G tests beat the standard method clearly. Reliability stayed on target while the throughput gains accumulated. Throughput and spectral efficiency rose by up to fifteen percent across traffic regimes.
arxiv-2510-05884:
Kaiser and Tilgner sharpen necessary conditions for spherical dynamo action. Dynamo theory asks how vigorous a flow must be to sustain magnetic fields. Classical bounds use the flow's maximum speed or maximum strain. Their 2025 paper adds a radially varying weight to both criteria.

Two weight families are studied: power laws and an optimal profile. The optimal profile adapts to the velocity field under examination. Weighted lower-bound Reynolds numbers follow for Childress-type and Backus-type criteria. Testing uses two known efficient spherical flows. For the most efficient field, the Backus ratio drops from about sixteen to about six. Both weight types improve both criteria for the radially varying field. A flow without radial variation gains less from the weighting. That is an improvement by a factor of roughly two point six. Tighter bounds orient expectations for planetary and stellar dynamos.
arxiv-2510-06084:
Sorensen and co-authors show that post-training narrows what language models can do in a 2025 machine learning paper. Instruction tuning boosts task scores, but many jobs have many valid answers rather than one. Creative writing and synthetic data generation need output spreads matching a target distribution.

The team names three goals: in-context steerability, coverage of valid outputs, and distributional alignment. Across three model families, post-training weakened all three. Prompts could still unlock stored knowledge, yet models grew worse at overriding priors to follow a new in-context distribution. The authors built Spectrum Suite from over 40 sources and more than 90 tasks to measure the problem. Their Spectrum Tuning method trains on that suite to restore flexibility. Tuned models often beat pretrained and instruction-tuned versions on held-out tasks, with wider coverage and better alignment.
arxiv-2510-06184:
Donovan, Hara, Kapustka, and Rampazzo produce four derived equivalences for a simple nine-fold flop. The flop transforms between total spaces of vector bundles on two Grassmannians, Gr(2,5) and Gr(3,5). Derived equivalences across flops matter for mirror symmetry and the minimal model program.

They identify four window categories inside the derived category of coherent sheaves on an Artin stack. Each window realizes one equivalence, and all commute with the pushforwards of the flopping contractions. That compatibility makes the equivalences well behaved for tracking sheaves through the flop. As an application, the approach reproves derived equivalence for a pair of non-birational Calabi–Yau threefolds. Those threefolds arise as zero loci of sections of homogeneous bundles inside Grassmannians. Four distinct windows on one flop give geometers several lenses on the same transformation. Window techniques convert hard birational geometry into manageable category theory.
arxiv-2510-06384:
Ahmadi and four co-authors show a shared thermal environment can charge a quantum battery on its own in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Most quantum battery proposals need coherent drives or engineered non-equilibrium resources. Those requirements clash with noisy real hardware.

Their design couples an ensemble of identical two-level units collectively to one thermal bath. The bath mediates interference between emission and absorption pathways. That interference steers the state away from passivity into a steady state holding extractable work. Closed-form expressions describe the steady state, and stored work scales favorably toward the many-body optimum. The mechanism survives local noise, too. With mixed dissipation, nonzero steady-state ergotropy persists and even peaks at finite temperature. As local work buffers, such batteries could speed ancilla reset and cut syndrome-extraction overhead.
arxiv-2510-06584:
Justin Cheung, Samuel Savine, Calvin Nguyen, Lin Lu, and Alhassan Yasin work on medical image analysis. Their 2025 paper studies CT scans and the deep learning models that classify them. A model trained on clean scans can fail when a scanner adds a new visual artifact. Labeling many artifact images by hand is expensive, so the team seeks another route.

They simulate ring artifacts, a common CT flaw caused by detector gain errors. Baseline models trained only on clean images failed on the ringed images. Adding other distortions during training gave no improvement on the unseen artifact type. A domain adversarial network did much better. It kept high accuracy on ringed scans while using only unlabeled artifact images in training. The result supports domain adaptation as a practical fix when labels are scarce. Hospitals could adapt models to new scanners without costly relabeling campaigns.
arxiv-2510-06684:
Kang An, Chenhao Si, Ming Yan, and Shiqian Ma study how to train physics-informed neural networks more reliably. Their 2025 paper concerns networks that solve equations by adding physics rules to their training loss. Several loss terms compete, covering equation residuals and boundary conditions. Those terms pull in different directions and have very different curvatures.

Older fixes blend the conflicting gradients before a single optimizer sees them. The authors argue that blending breaks the optimizer's own internal balancing. Their framework, AutoBalance, gives each loss term its own adaptive optimizer instead. The separate updates are combined only afterward. Tests on hard benchmarks show clear reductions in error. Both average and worst-case error measures improved over existing frameworks. The split design also steadied training by smoothing the curvature landscape. The paper supports the theory with analysis of a simple quadratic problem.
arxiv-2510-06784:
Engineers at Rarimo and Distributed Lab present Bionetta, a system for proving that a machine learning model ran correctly without revealing it. Their 2025 technical report works in zero-knowledge machine learning. Such proofs let a phone or browser convince others that a neural network produced a result. The proof must stay small and quick to check.

Bionetta builds on a modified proof protocol they call UltraGroth. The team compared it with rival tools such as ezkl and deep-prove. For custom neural networks, proving times improved by a large margin. Proofs could be generated on mobile devices. The trade-off is heavier one-time setup, including circuit compilation and a trusted setup step. The authors claim theirs is the only scheme deployable on Ethereum contracts without huge proofs. Verification stays cheap enough for smart contract use. That opens client-side proving for apps that need privacy with checks.
arxiv-2510-06984:
Masanari Kondo and four co-authors investigate why open-source design proposals get turned down. Their 2025 paper studies the proposal process of the Go language. Proposals there shape major design decisions after long debate. Declines without clear feedback frustrate authors, yet rejection reasons were poorly understood.

The team analyzed 1,091 proposals submitted to the Go project. More proposals were declined than accepted, and decisions typically took over a month. Forty percent of proposals ended in decline in their count. Only about fifteen percent of declined proposals were ever sent back. The researchers sorted the declines into nine distinct reasons. They also tested whether a language model could predict declines in advance. That forecasting worked only modestly with the model they tried. The taxonomy gives authors a clearer map of what sinks a proposal. Project leads gain evidence for giving sharper feedback earlier.
arxiv-2510-07284:
Rezaei and co-authors introduce OnlineRubrics, a way to keep grading criteria fresh while a language model trains. Their 2025 paper uses rubrics, written checklists that score open-ended answers where no simple verifier exists. Static rubrics age badly: models learn to game them, and new flaws appear mid-training. The team's method grows the rubric during training itself. It compares answers from the current model against a reference model, pair by pair. Differences surface new criteria worth scoring.

The online process catches errors as they emerge rather than after training ends. Across general and expert test sets, models trained this way gained up to eight points over static-rubric training. The harvested criteria clustered around themes like transparency, practicality, organization, and reasoning. Living rubrics could make training safer wherever quality is judged by checklists.
arxiv-2510-07484:
Han and co-authors unify retrieval and generation for question answering over knowledge graphs. Their 2025 paper critiques the standard two-stage pipeline. There, a retriever first fetches a subgraph and the generator answers from it, so any retrieval miss caps accuracy. Retrievers also tend to overfit their training graphs. Reasoning by Exploration instead lets the model walk the graph itself. At each step it picks nodes and edges to explore, building reasoning paths while generating the answer along the way. Retrieval becomes part of reasoning rather than a preliminary chore performed blind.

Training runs in two stages: supervised learning on gold reasoning paths, then reinforcement learning to sharpen exploration and generalization. On multiple knowledge graph question benchmarks, the method beat strong two-stage baselines. It also transferred to unseen graphs better than specialized retrievers.
arxiv-2510-07584:
Debris-Alazard, Gaborit, Neveu, and Ruatta build public-key encryption whose security rests only on the MinRank problem. Their 2025 paper adapts the celebrated Alekhnovich and Regev constructions. Those were the first schemes proven secure from the average-case hardness of decoding random codes and of the learning-with-errors problem alone, with no extra assumptions. Such minimal guarantees seeded today's post-quantum standards. The new variant transplants the recipe to rank-metric matrix codes.

Parameter analysis shows the scheme is practical. It runs slightly slower than FrodoKEM, the conservative lattice standard-bearer, but far faster than the original Alekhnovich and Regev schemes ever were. Adding structure later could close the remaining gap, the same path earlier code-based standards took.
arxiv-2510-07684:
Xia and four coauthors wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on a foundation model for galaxy data. Cosmologists simulate galaxies in computer universes and also observe real ones through telescopes. Linking those two views is a central challenge. The team built an encoder-only transformer that accepts many kinds of inputs. It takes single values such as mass and redshift, plus histories and spectra.

Flexible masking lets the model answer varied questions from partial inputs. It can predict a spectrum from mass and redshift, or estimate redshift from survey brightness. Training used a large set of simulated galaxies from a gigaparsec-scale run. Combining two surveys' photometry improved redshift estimates by half over one survey alone. Late-time history data improved mass estimates even more strongly. The authors see the model, called MOSAIC in the text, as groundwork for future versions that also ingest images and merger trees.
arxiv-2510-07784:
He and twenty-one coauthors present PLUM in this 2025 paper on generative recommendation at industrial scale. Large language models bring sequence skill and world knowledge to recommendation. Turning a text model into a recommender takes more than a prompt. PLUM adapts pretrained models in three stages for this job. It now runs in production at YouTube, serving billions of users.

First, items receive Semantic IDs, compact token codes that carry meaning. Continued pretraining on domain data then grounds those codes in user behavior and text. Task-specific fine-tuning teaches the model to generate the IDs of items a user should see next. Against a heavily optimized production system built on large embedding tables, PLUM improved retrieval substantially. Ablations confirmed the value of each stage and of starting from a pretrained model. The paper also reports scaling behavior and lessons for ranking and search tasks ahead.
arxiv-2510-07884:
Jiang and eight coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on weak-to-strong generalization for language models. A weak, aligned model generates training samples, and a stronger model learns from them. That route skips human feedback and explicit reward models. Its weakness is noise and bias in the weak teacher's output. The authors find a structural link that suggests a cleaner way to make the samples.

Implicit rewards, they show, are mathematically the same shape as contrastive decoding. Contrastive decoding compares a model before and after alignment to cut noise during generation. Their framework, ConG, uses exactly that contrast to produce training samples for the strong model. The samples carry higher implicit reward and less noise. Across model families, ConG improved capability transfer and robustness over standard weak-to-strong training. The work reframes a decoding trick as a supervision tool for training the next generation of models.
arxiv-2510-08484:
Simon Schmidt, Sigurd Storgaard, Michael Walter, and Yuming Zhao prove a quantum advantage in a guessing game from 1991, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Feige's game gives two players two questions and three possible answers each. Players cannot communicate, yet must guess each other's inputs in a coordinated way. Classical and quantum strategies cap success at different levels for such nonlocal games.

The authors show quantum players beat the classical ceiling in Feige's game. The game also robustly self-tests the three-dimensional maximally entangled state: near-optimal play certifies that state. Oddly, the game is the 'or' of two games, and neither of those shows quantum advantage alone. They further study parallel repetition, where many copies are played at once. For non-signalling strategies, perfect parallel repetition holds when the game is repeated an even number of times.
arxiv-2510-08684:
Ling Zhu and co-authors find the Milky Way's dark matter halo stands vertically against its disk in a 2025 arXiv paper. The halo's three-dimensional shape records the galaxy's formation history, but it is hard to measure directly. Their dynamical model makes minimal assumptions about internal structure while allowing a flexible triaxial halo. They fit six-dimensional position and velocity data for K-giant stars from LAMOST and Gaia.

The halo emerges as triaxial and nearly oblate out to about fifty kiloparsecs. Its long-intermediate axis plane stands vertical to the stellar disk, unexpectedly, yet aligns with the plane of satellite galaxies. This suggests the Galactic disk and inner halo flipped from an original alignment, likely torqued by minor mergers. Milky Way analogues in the Auriga and TNG50 simulations support that flip scenario. Tentative evidence also shows the halo twisting with radius, aligning inward and turning vertical beyond twenty kiloparsecs.
arxiv-2510-08784:
Zamoro, Grinstein, and Quílez fix a mathematical blow-up that plagues a classic tool of particle physics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Physicists split scattering events, where particles bounce off each other, into partial waves to read off the traits of new particles. When a particle with no mass is exchanged along one path, the math for straight-ahead scattering shoots to infinity. That makes the partial waves undefined, much as in the classic Rutherford scattering problem.

The authors argue the infinity is an artifact of computing in steps rather than a real effect. They give a correction factor that accounts for all orders of the calculation at once and keeps the waves finite. Applied to collisions of W bosons, the fix sharpens the limits that consistency places on the mass of the Higgs particle. The same method should help when the exchanged particle is merely very light.
arxiv-2510-08884:
Lopes, Barata, and Moreno test a hybrid learning method on one of robotics' hardest skills, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In-hand manipulation means repositioning an object using the fingers alone, without setting it down. The dynamics are intricate, and a hand must sense and adjust constantly. Their framework, developed earlier, steers a trained controller with a lookahead model that simulates candidate motions and scores them, much like model predictive control.

The team compared the guided controller against the same controller left alone. Tests used simulated hands with full and reduced sets of motors, handling assorted objects. They also changed the objects' weight and size, and even swapped in objects the controller had never trained on. Given a strong starting controller and an accurate model, the lookahead improved results in most cases, including the changed conditions. The gain came at a clear price: far more computation per move.
arxiv-2510-09084:
Ali, Banerjee, and Prasad study how an advertising provider should divide billboard slots to disappoint every client as little as possible, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Advertisers buy a promised amount of influence, meaning views likely to sway buyers. Deliver less and the provider is underpaid; deliver more and the excess is wasted. Either way the provider suffers a loss the authors formalize as regret, and the goal is to allocate slots so total regret is minimized.

They propose two algorithms with a shared greedy heart. The first adds slots one by one, each time choosing the slot that cuts regret most per unit of budget. The second sprinkles in randomness, sampling a subset of slots instead of scoring all of them at every step. Both are analyzed for time and space costs. On real-life datasets, the randomized version reached good regret levels in reasonable time.
arxiv-2510-09184:
Charpentier and Lison build stronger attacks for unmasking people in supposedly anonymized documents, in this 2025 arXiv paper. De-identification software blanks out names and other personal details before documents are shared. Judging whether the masking protects anyone is hard, so researchers play the adversary: an automated attacker uses background knowledge to guess what each blank hides. The authors ask how to make that attacker as strong as possible.

Two upgrades help. First, the order in which blanks are attacked matters, because each recovered detail informs the next guess. Trying several orders and pooling the predictions beats any single pass. Second, reasoning models, which think step by step before answering, noticeably improve the unmasking. The boost is largest when the adversary has extensive background knowledge. Together, the upgrades give a sterner yardstick for certifying masking tools.
arxiv-2510-09284:
Sergeenko studies what flies out of high-energy particle collisions using a string-based model of the strong force, with attention on the Large Hadron Collider, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most debris comes from soft interactions, where the strong force defies first-principles calculation. The Quark-Gluon String Model instead pictures quarks linked by gluon strings that snap into new particles. Sergeenko works with a modified version.

The paper treats inclusive processes, counting chosen outgoing particles without tracking everything else. It discusses diffraction dissociation, collisions where a particle excites or breaks up while keeping nearly its direction. Cross-section calculations use values for complex, curved trajectories of the Pomeron and Reggeons, the exchanged objects of Regge theory. Elastic and inelastic events at LHC energies get special attention.
arxiv-2510-09984:
Aneja, Nagender Aneja, and Murat Kantarcioglu learn joint embeddings of software graphs for malware detection in this 2025 arXiv paper in computer security. Software can be drawn as graphs in several ways. A function call graph links functions by who calls whom, while a process call graph links running processes.
