Each graph type highlights different structure, so a detector trained on one view misses signals in the other. The authors learn embeddings, numeric summaries, that fuse both graph views into one representation. That joint view aims to expose malware behavior that hides across the function and process layers. The approach treats the choice of graph as a source of strength, not a fixed decision made before analysis.
arxiv-2510-10584:
Shizhen Zhao and four co-authors test whether big pretrained vision models can spot inputs unlike anything they were trained on, in this 2025 arXiv paper. This task is called out-of-distribution detection. They study several vision foundation models and find that a pretrained DINOv2, used with no fine tuning at all, already separates unfamiliar inputs well. Its scores rival purpose built state of the art methods.

Fine tuning on in domain data can help further, but performance sags when the label space grows large, because decision boundaries get complex. To fix this, the team proposes a Mixture of Feature Experts module. It splits features into subspaces handled by different experts, refining the boundaries. A dynamic mixup strategy also adapts how training examples are blended, giving harder categories more support. Across extensive experiments, the approach significantly outperformed baseline methods.
arxiv-2510-10984:
Jingyi Wang and six co-authors make Bayesian optimization work under constraints and mixed fidelity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization steers costly searches by modeling the goal and choosing informative trials. Multi fidelity versions mix cheap rough runs with costly accurate ones. Constraints complicate everything, since the feasible region must be found while optimizing, and popular rules like expected constrained improvement need feasible starting samples that may not exist.

Their constrained multi fidelity method uses new acquisition functions with three practical virtues: closed form expressions, straightforward implementation, and no need for feasible initial samples. They test combinations of the functions on synthetic problems. Then come two real applications: a data driven design problem for inertial confinement fusion, and a high current joint design studied with finite element simulations involving contact mechanics. The method performed effectively on both.
arxiv-2510-11184:
Language model agents that can call tools, such as a code interpreter, are usually trained and tested inside a single subject area. Zhengyu Chen and co-authors ask whether tool skills learned in one domain carry over to others in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their agent was trained with reinforcement learning exclusively on mathematical problem solving, then evaluated on reasoning tasks from several distinct domains.

The experiments show that tool use learned from mathematics transfers effectively, giving strong task performance with high token efficiency elsewhere. To support that transfer, the authors propose the TGRL framework with three parts. A standardized tool interface hides domain details, a dual-component reward encourages generalizable behavior such as tool efficiency, and an XML prompt template separates thinking, tool calls, and responses. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks reached state-of-the-art performance and highlighted the cross-domain potential of tool reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2510-11284:
The Milky Way still carries chemical fingerprints of the dwarf galaxy it swallowed billions of years ago. Sven Buder and co-authors test that memory in a simulated galaxy in this 2025 arXiv paper. They use the NIHAO-UHD simulation, an ultra-high-definition rerun of a Milky Way analogue, and trace stars accreted in its last major merger from their birthplaces to their present-day orbits.

Stars born in the core of the swallowed galaxy end up more tightly bound to the host and more chemically enriched, while stars from its outskirts are less bound and metal-poor. The pattern appears in elemental abundance planes, reflecting gradients in star formation efficiency. The trends agree with idealized simulations, though they are weaker and less linear. The authors warn that selecting stars by their motion misses the enriched core, biasing reconstructions of the merger, and they outline fairer selection strategies.
arxiv-2510-11684:
C. Y. Tan leads a large collaboration reporting three new ultra-faint companions of the Milky Way. Their 2025 arXiv paper draws on the third data release of the DELVE survey, which images the southern sky with the DECam camera. Two independent search algorithms flagged the same three systems: Carina IV, Phoenix III, and DELVE 7. All three hold old, metal-poor stars.

Carina IV and Phoenix III have sizes that match known dwarf galaxies. DELVE 7 is far more compact, spanning about two parsecs, so it is more likely a star cluster. Its exact nature stays unclear without follow-up spectroscopy. Motions measured by the Gaia spacecraft suggest Carina IV is not tied to the Large Magellanic Cloud. Phoenix III is the faintest known satellite in the far outer halo of the Milky Way.
arxiv-2510-11784:
Michael Nee and Lisa Randall rebuild a popular supersymmetry scenario in five dimensions. Many models place our world in a five-dimensional space with singular points, spurred by string theory. Supersymmetry breaking in such setups is often sent by anomaly mediation, a route prized for how much it predicts. Yet most work shortcuts through a four-dimensional effective theory. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the full five-dimensional version instead.

Working with stabilized supersymmetric theories in five dimensions, the authors derive the true low-energy theory of their SCAM scenario. Several features differ from what four-dimensional reasoning expects, above all the roles of boundary superpotentials and the radion field. The famous universality of anomaly mediation also needs revision. The paper maps when five-dimensional results collapse to the naive four-dimensional answer and when they do not. Often supersymmetry breaks at the five-dimensional level, adding corrections simple treatments miss.
arxiv-2510-11884:
Klaudia Dilcher and five colleagues sharpen the math behind a sensitive kind of magnetometer. Spin-precession magnetometers read a magnetic field from the wobble of atomic spins. They serve navigation and searches for new physics. The team's 2025 arXiv paper studies the free-induction decay mode, where spins are set ringing and observed as the signal fades. The goal is tracking field changes faster than the usual response limit.

The authors derive the Bayesian Cramér-Rao bound, the ultimate precision limit for estimating the wobble frequency. A heavyweight technique called the prediction error method reaches that bound but costs much computation. Two cheaper filters, the extended and cubature Kalman filters, come near the bound while running efficiently. The cubature version wins only for large spin numbers. Focusing on the extended filter, the team shows it tracks fluctuating and sudden transient signals accurately. The methods transfer to other nonlinear sensors.
arxiv-2510-12184:
Jiwan Kim, Kibum Kim, Sangwoo Seo, and Chanyoung Park teach small multimodal models to look where their teachers look. Knowledge distillation shrinks a big model into a usable one, but distilled students keep failing to inherit the teacher's visual perception. Their 2025 arXiv paper pinpoints the cause: visual attention misalignment, students gazing at wrong regions while teachers focus on the right spots.

Their method, CompoDistill, aligns the student's visual attention head-on with the teacher's during distillation, beside the usual knowledge transfer. Broad tests show large gains on compositional reasoning tasks, the ones that demand real visual perception, like judging whether the woman is on the table or under it. Scores on standard visual question answering stay strong, matching prior distillation studies. The method also works with a newer backbone, evidence it travels well. Perception transfers only when students learn where to attend.
arxiv-2510-12284:
Li, Tamaru, and Yao classify special hypersurfaces inside the complex hyperbolic quadric, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. A hypersurface is a surface of one dimension less than its ambient space, and Hopf hypersurfaces are those whose structure vector field follows their principal curvature directions. Principal curvatures measure how the surface bends along its main axes.

The authors restrict attention to Hopf hypersurfaces whose principal curvatures are constant. For the complex hyperbolic quadric in dimension at least three, they give a full classification when there are no more than two distinct constant principal curvatures. For the cases of three or four distinct constant principal curvatures, they determine exactly which values occur and with what multiplicities, meaning how many directions share each value. The results complete a detailed picture of this family, extending earlier classification work in related spaces such as complex hyperbolic space and the complex quadric.
arxiv-2510-12384:
Li and a large team combine several kinds of molecular data to build an aging clock and uncover distinct patterns of human aging, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Biological age tracks physiological decline better than the calendar, but earlier clocks used one data type and missed much of aging's complexity. The team drew on the Human Phenotype Project, a cohort of ten thousand adults with deep long term profiling.

Their data span clinical, behavioral, and environmental measures plus transcriptomics, lipidomics, metabolomics, and the microbiome, four molecular layers measured in the same people. Machine learning models that capture nonlinear dynamics produced a multi omics clock that predicted health outcomes and future disease risk well. Clustering of the integrated profiles then revealed distinct subtypes of aging, each with its own pathway level changes. The authors argue that such integration can decode how aging differs between people and support personal healthspan monitoring and prevention.
arxiv-2510-12784:
Jin and co-authors present SRUM in this 2025 arXiv paper, a training method for unified multimodal models, which are single systems that both understand and generate images. Such a model's understanding is often strong while its generation lags. So the authors ask whether the understanding side can grade and improve the generation side. They pursue this without any new human-labeled data.

SRUM closes that loop with a global-local dual reward, meaning one score checks the whole image's meaning and layout while another checks fine object-level details. The internal evaluator sends corrective signals to the generator during post-training, and the method fits existing models of varied designs. On two text-to-image benchmarks the scores rose clearly after SRUM training, and the gains generalized across tasks.
arxiv-2510-12884:
Bril, Hu, and Bultinck map magnetic order in twisted tungsten diselenide in this 2025 arXiv paper. The material stacks two atom-thin layers at a small twist, creating a moiré pattern, a large-scale interference grid where electrons interact strongly. At one hole per moiré cell, earlier work expected a triangular antiferromagnet, but the full phase diagram held surprises.

Numerically scanning interaction strength and an applied displacement field, the authors found multi-Q order, a magnetic pattern mixing four different spatial wave patterns at once, in part of the diagram. These states, flat or non-flat in spin arrangement, deform continuously from the expected antiferromagnet while quadrupling the unit cell. They appear at experimentally realistic settings and come with softening spin fluctuations, which the authors link to the material's nearby superconductivity.
arxiv-2510-13184:
Pan, Dong, Xing, and Wu auto-tune nested compiler pipelines in this 2025 arXiv paper. LLVM's New Pass Manager organizes optimization passes in nested layers, with pipelines nested inside pipelines, but existing auto-tuners assume a flat linear sequence. That mismatch means they cannot even guarantee that a candidate pipeline is valid in form.

The authors build a framework for the nested design. A formal grammar defines the space of valid nested pipelines. A forest data structure represents them directly. A structure-aware genetic algorithm manipulates those forests so every candidate is valid by construction. Synergistic pass relationships mined beforehand guide the search, with an optional refinement stage exploring how valid arrangements differ in performance. On seven benchmark datasets with a recent LLVM, discovered pipelines reduced instruction counts by well over thirteen percent beyond the standard size optimization level on average.
arxiv-2510-13384:
Sannikov and co-authors track how lasing changes as light-matter coupling weakens in polymer-film microcavities. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses MeLPPP, a stiff ladder-type polymer with a narrow emission line. Such organic films bind light strongly, which makes them attractive for polariton devices, hybrid light-matter states. Systematic studies of this crossover in one material platform have been scarce.

By tuning the cavity length, the team moves the system from strong to weak coupling. They find the lasing threshold rises many-fold when polariton lasing gives way to plain photon lasing. In both regimes, the emission energy shifts toward the polymer's gain peak. Molecular vibrations also matter: thresholds drop near resonances tied to one exciton transition. The results help separate true polariton effects from ordinary lasing in organic devices. The authors present the films as a platform for future low-threshold lasers.
arxiv-2510-13584:
Wang and a large collaboration design Hamiltonians that move quantum states perfectly while shrugging off noise. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets perfect state transfer and remote entanglement, two primitives for quantum networks. Engineered Hamiltonians from standard methods often falter when noise enters. The team starts instead from a noise-resilient energy spectrum and builds upward.

Their dome model adds one tunable parameter that reshapes the spacing between energy levels. At one extreme it reduces to the conventional transfer model. At the other, it simplifies to a swap acting on just the two end qubits. Simulations confirm the design improves robustness against noise markedly. For long distances, a cascaded strategy chains several short transfers in sequence. The scheme suits superconducting qubits with tunable couplers, where Hamiltonians can be engineered quickly.
arxiv-2510-14184:
Mahmood Hegazy, Aaron Rodrigues, and Azzam Naeem present MAFA, a multi-agent system that annotates enterprise data at scale, deployed in production at JPMorgan Chase, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Financial firms sit on backlogs of millions of customer utterances needing accurate labels, and hand-labeling them is slow and expensive.

MAFA combines specialized agents and structured reasoning with a judge-based consensus mechanism, and it adapts to new tasks, such as FAQs, intents, entities, or custom categories, through configuration rather than code changes. The system cleared a backlog of one million utterances while averaging eighty-six percent agreement with human annotators and saving over five thousand hours of manual work per year. Most annotations come back with high confidence, so humans focus on ambiguous cases. Across multiple data sets and languages, MAFA improved top-one accuracy over single-agent baselines by nearly fourteen points in relative terms.
arxiv-2510-14284:
Yishun Luo and Martin Zubeldia develop a theory of load balancing across servers that differ in speed, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Jobs arrive at a dispatcher and must be assigned immediately to one of many queues. Policies include sending a job to the shortest queue or choosing among a few random queues. Dispatchers often work from stale, periodically updated queue information.

Their framework covers a family of policies in which the dispatcher updates at long intervals and dispatches using queue lengths and service rates. From it they derive a sufficient condition for stability. They show stability need not be monotone: raising the arrival rate can restabilize a system, and they characterize this under a bottleneck condition. When stability holds, they prove the system collapses to a state description. It achieves delay in heavy traffic. Queue lengths converge to a deterministic profile scaled by a random factor.
arxiv-2510-14484:
Ioannis Apergis and co-authors laboratory-test whether a CMOS camera, the Marana 4.2BV-11, can do the light measurements astronomy demands, in this 2025 arXiv paper. CMOS sensors are displacing CCDs in observatories, but their quirks raise doubts about photometric precision for tasks like exoplanet transit detection.

Testing the camera in its fastest-frame-rate and high-dynamic-range modes, they measured read noise, dark current, response and dark-signal non-uniformities, quantum efficiency, and transmittance. Read noise came in around one and a half electrons. The high-dynamic-range mode reached a capacity of sixty-nine thousand electrons with a dynamic range of ninety-three decibels. Linearity errors stayed at a tenth of a percent in both modes, and photo-response non-uniformity was a few tenths of a percent, worse in the fast mode. The characterization gives astronomers the numbers needed to judge the camera for photometry.
arxiv-2510-14684:
Devriendt, in a 2025 arXiv paper, gives a geometric picture of magnitude, a single number that summarizes the size of a metric space. Magnitude is defined algebraically, through a matrix built from distances between points. That definition is useful but hard to picture. Devriendt asks what magnitude looks like when the space is drawn in ordinary Euclidean geometry.

He constructs an embedding of a suitable finite metric space into Euclidean space with a special property. The magnitude of the space can then be read off from the circumradius of the embedded points, meaning the radius of the unique sphere passing through them all. Three applications follow. The embedding describes how magnitude grows when the space is scaled up. A new matrix theory links the magnitude of a space to those of its subspaces. And a newly identified limiting regime yields results resembling submodularity, where adding points to larger sets helps less.
arxiv-2510-14784:
Kudasov proves, in a 2025 arXiv paper, that the energy bands of electrons in certain metals carry a topological fingerprint that cannot change under smooth deformation. In crystals with a superstructure, the electron dispersion can wrap the Brillouin zone, the space of allowed momenta, as a multi-sheeted covering. Kudasov shows that the number of sheets and the monodromy, the way sheets permute around loops, are invariants under ambient isotopy, meaning under continuous reshaping of the covering.

As a concrete case, the paper analyzes three-sublattice models for helimagnets with a 120-degree magnetic order, in one, two, and three dimensions. The two-dimensional system shows unconventional f-wave magnetism. It also hosts a specific topological metal state whose Fermi surface has a single sheet with a textured spin pattern. Kudasov briefly discusses the transport signatures such a state should show and how it might be realized in an experiment.
arxiv-2510-14984:
Lauber and Peirlinck build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a model of an artificial heart sewn from fabric. Fabric-based soft robots carry heavy loads at low weight and bend, twist, contract, or extend easily, suiting them to medicine. The device modeled, called Less In More Out, is a fluid-driven soft artificial heart made of heat-sealed fabric layers. Experiments showed promise, but design work needs simulations.

Their model reproduces the measurements: the heart's nonlinear deformation, its strain fields, and its pressure-volume relationships under quasi-static loading. Comparing designs, devices with fewer pouches deliver higher stroke volumes, but at up to fifty percent higher peak von Mises stresses. A strain-life fatigue analysis fingers the heat-sealed seams and the regions that buckle as the features limiting durability. The framework exposes stress concentrations and fatigue life that experiments can barely measure, guiding optimization of fabric hearts.
arxiv-2510-15084:
Led by F. Murgas, a large international team reports a newly confirmed planet around the star TOI-283 in this 2025 arXiv paper. The planet, TOI-283 b, is a mini-Neptune, a type common across the galaxy yet absent from our own solar system. NASA's TESS satellite first spotted it crossing its star in 2019, and the team followed up with the ESPRESSO instrument in Chile.

Combining the transit data with precise velocity measurements of the star, the researchers pinned down the planet's size at about 2.34 times Earth's radius, with the mass near six and a half Earth masses, give or take two. It circles its bright K-type host star every 17.6 days or so, at a comfortable distance that keeps it fairly cool. Its measured density points to a world with a substantial share of lighter material beyond plain rock.
arxiv-2510-15484:
K. Sośnica, A. Fienga, D. Pavlov, N. Rambaux, and R. Zajdel define the coordinate system that future Moon missions will share. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that positioning, navigation, maps, and timing on the Moon all need one agreed reference frame. They set the system's origin at the Moon's center of mass, with axes fixed to the surface and rotating with it.

The first realization of the frame blends three independent lunar orbit and rotation solutions using a statistical weighting method. It spans laser ranging data from 1970 and extrapolations to 2052. For the years 2010 to 2030 its average error is about seventeen centimeters. Most of that error sits in the origin, blamed on the poor geometry of the retroreflector network left by Apollo-era missions. Laser ranging residuals inside the new frame run at only two to three centimeters for the best stations.
arxiv-2510-15784:
Qihao Peng, Qu Luo, Zheng Chu, and Neng Ye propose a base station in a 2025 paper. It could free small internet-of-things devices from batteries. The station transmits with conventional radio equipment. It receives uplinks through a Rydberg atomic quantum receiver. That receiver uses highly excited atoms as antennas. Devices harvest part of the incoming signal's energy. They power themselves this way.

The authors design the transmission scheme jointly with the energy split. The goal is to maximise total data rate. The problem is non-convex. They first derive guaranteed lower bounds on uplink rates. Two combining methods are covered. The design aims at self-sustained networks. Sensing devices would run on the very signals they exchange.
arxiv-2510-15884:
Faizan A. Khattak and Mantas Mikaitis extend a method for probing the hidden numerics of hardware matrix multipliers to consumer graphics cards. Data centre cards from NVIDIA and AMD had been studied before, covering traits such as rounding, normalisation, and accumulator precision. Their scheme generates test vectors without exhaustive search and without device-specific hard-coded constants.

The method works across mixed-precision input and output formats in an architecture-independent way. Applied to two consumer cards, an Ampere RTX card and an Ada Lovelace workstation card, it reveals their multipliers' features for several low-precision formats. The consumer Ampere card turns out to match the data centre A100 exactly on these traits. Khattak and Mikaitis expect the code to run unchanged on newer Hopper and Blackwell cards and on eight-bit formats.
arxiv-2510-15984: K. E. Feldman, writing alone, prices Bermudan swaptions with a new semi-analytical model. The model needs no calibration that is specific to one product. A Bermudan swaption gives its holder the right to enter an interest-rate swap on preset dates. Pricing such options in the usual way means fitting a model to market data for each product in turn. Feldman's model works from swap rate distributions and the correlations between them instead. That lack of a calibration step is the model's chief claimed gain for daily pricing work.
arxiv-2510-16184:
Zefanya Bramantasaputra, Dea Daniella Wangsawijaya, and Bharathram Ganapathisubramani study how a turbulent boundary layer heals after a shove from changing air pressure. A boundary layer is the thin sheet of air that drags along a wall, and its flow turns chaotic. They pushed the layer with short bursts of helpful then harmful pressure, then let it relax.

Fine hot-wire probes tracked the flow at set points downstream, across three flow speeds. The pressure bursts fattened the slow wake zone of the profile and stirred up extra churn far from the wall. Even long after the pressure eased off, the mean flow had not fully healed. Only when the total push fell low did the near-wall flow recover, while the outer flow kept a lasting imprint. The findings matter for wings and blades, where pressure shifts shape how air clings and drags.
arxiv-2510-17084:
Fatemeh Mahmoudi and three co-authors pick risk factors when one event blocks others in this 2025 paper. In health trials, a first event can bar later ones from view. Exact event times may also hide inside check gaps. The team needs a pick rule that fits each event type.

Their rule uses a penalty that prunes weak factors yet keeps strong ones. It picks factors and gauges their effects for each event at once. Proofs show the rule finds the true factor set in large samples. Fake-data tests back the claims, and a real HIV group set fits well. The tool aids health teams that weigh rival risks with gapped times.
arxiv-2510-17284:
Jiri Gavenda and three co-authors gauge privacy loss in Bitcoin coinjoin trades in this 2025 paper. Coinjoin pools many users' coins in one joint trade to hide trails. How much trail hides stays hard to gauge at scale. The team adapts a chain-scan tool to joint trades and builds a sharper gauge.

Their scan finds post-mix hide sets shrink by ten to fifty percent on mean. The shrink hits hardest on day one and fades by one year. Their new gauge weighs fees, code limits, and user acts after the mix. Tests on fake and real Wasabi trades back the gauge. Even so, true owners stay hard to pin down with care.
arxiv-2510-17384:
People learn where to grip a new object by watching someone else use it, and Jiajin Tang with three co-authors gives computers a similar skill. Their task, called affordance grounding, asks a model to find the part of an object that allows an action, learning from photos of people interacting with objects. Earlier methods passed knowledge one way only, from those interaction photos to plain object views.

Tang and his co-authors close the loop, letting the plain views also sharpen what is drawn from the interaction photos. Their LoopTrans system adds shared location tools and a cleaning step for the transferred knowledge. It improved scores on every measure across photo and video tests, even when a person body hid the contact region completely.
arxiv-2510-17784:
Esmaeel Zanganeh and Antonio Lombardo show how one tiny silicon block can steer the spin of light. Controlling both direction and spin at the nanoscale serves quantum and sensing tools. Their device is a single silicon nanocuboid, a block far smaller than a wavelength. The block itself has no handed twist in its shape.

Inside it, electric and magnetic dipoles combine into a Circular Huygens Dipole. Dipoles here are paired oscillations of charge and magnetism. Changing the incoming wave's polarization flips the forward-scattered spin. Output switches cleanly between right- and left-circular states. The passive design needs no power to hold its setting.
arxiv-2510-17884:
Mohammad Abdul Rehman and four co-authors test whether large language models can guess passwords from simple user profiles. They prompt three open models with facts like names, birth dates, and hobbies. Success is checked at the first, fifth, and tenth guesses, in plain text and in hashed form.

Every model scored under one and a half percent even at ten guesses. Older rule-based and mixing methods did far better on the same task. The study then traces where the models' reasoning breaks down. Security readers get measured evidence that fluent text skill does not transfer to password guessing.
arxiv-2510-17984:
Aritra Bal and five co-authors bring ideas from quantum information into plain classical neural networks for particle physics. Each particle in a collision is treated like a qubit, and a quantum Fisher information matrix sums up how the particles relate. That compact summary then feeds a graph network that sorts jets of particles.

The quantum-based features show distinct patterns for plain jets and for top quark jets, matching physical hopes. Sorting improved as a result. The authors frame the method as a broad, readable, and scalable route to quantum-informed study of collisions, without needing an actual quantum computer to run it.
arxiv-2510-18084:
Zaineh Abughazzah and four co-authors allocate radio resources for drone relays in rescue work, where security, speed, and battery life pull against each other. When ground networks fail, drones linked to open radio systems keep rescue teams connected. Delays or breaches in that setting can cost lives, so the trade-offs must be handled jointly.

Their reinforcement learning system adjusts allocations as conditions change, weighing safety checks, latency, and energy use together. Older schemes, the authors note, treated these goals apart. Emergency network planners get a design that faces all three demands at once instead of optimizing one and hoping the rest follow.
arxiv-2510-18184:
Lukas Helff, with eight co-authors, moves logical reasoning inside a language model, into its hidden activation space. Sparse autoencoders expose inner features that often match human concepts, but those features sit passive and fragile. Their ActivationReasoning frame first gathers such features into a concept dictionary, then turns active ones into logical propositions at run time.

Rules over those propositions infer higher-order structure, compose new concepts, and steer the model's behavior. Reasoning becomes an explicit layer rather than a hope pinned on fluent text. Interpretability researchers get a bridge between neural activity and formal logic that can also control output.
arxiv-2510-18284:
Nathan Grieve works on computing local Weil functions in a sole-authored 2025 mathematics paper. Local Weil functions are height tools that measure how close points on a variety sit to a chosen divisor. A divisor is a formal combination of smaller pieces inside the variety, used to track positions.

Grieve builds on the approach of Bombieri and Gubler and on his own earlier work. His route starts from presentations of Cartier divisors, meaning concrete descriptions of those divisors by local equations. From those descriptions he derives effective algorithms, meaning step-by-step methods that actually finish the computation. The setting is projective varieties, a standard class of geometric spaces.
arxiv-2510-18584:
Jona Dirks, with Nicole Schirrmacher, Sebastian Siebertz, and Alexandre Vigny, settles the difficulty of a graph problem called weighted treedepth. A treedepth decomposition arranges a graph's vertices into a rooted forest so every edge joins an ancestor with a descendant. When vertices carry weights, the cost of a decomposition is the heaviest root-to-leaf path, and the question is whether a cheap enough decomposition exists.

It was already known that the problem is NP-complete on trees, meaning no fast general solution is expected. The authors prove it stays NP-complete even on graphs of bounded degree, where each vertex has only a limited number of neighbors, ruling out an easy escape through sparsity. On the brighter side, they show the problem can be solved efficiently on simple paths and on one-subdivided stars, two narrow graph families where structure keeps the search manageable.
arxiv-2510-18684:
Mohamed Nabih Ali works with Daniele Falavigna and Alessio Brutti. They build a speech recognition system for many languages. The system rests on a newer sequence model type. Speech across languages is a hard task. Some languages have little training data at all. Their system is called MLMA. It swaps the transformer backbone for Mamba. Mamba is a state-space design built for long sequences.

Mamba absorbs language-aware conditioning on its own. It also builds shared representations across languages. No separate machinery per language is needed. Standard multilingual benchmarks tested the system. MLMA performed on par with transformer-based systems. Transformers have long dominated this field. The authors present the result as clear evidence. State-space models can back speech recognition well. They are scalable, efficient, and accurate at once. That holds even for languages with scarce resources.
arxiv-2510-18784:
Soroush Tabesh and his four co-authors close an accuracy gap in low-precision training. Neural networks are trained to run with rounded weights. The rounding still distorts learning. The standard trick passes gradients through as if rounding were invisible. That biases the updates. Their method is called CAGE.

CAGE corrects the gradient with local curvature data. It estimates how the rounding-induced loss increase bends the landscape. The method grows from a two-goal view of training. Accuracy is balanced against quantization limits. The authors prove convergence guarantees for smooth problems. They supply an efficient implementation using common optimizer statistics. In fine-tuning, accuracy loss halved versus the past best method. In pretraining, three-bit precision matched what rivals needed four bits to reach.
arxiv-2510-18984:
Kasturi Ranjan Swain, Rajesh K Malla, and Adolfo del Campo present a feedback method that uses noise itself to help open quantum systems reveal ground state properties. Noise in current quantum devices usually spoils the clean motion that algorithms need, well before fault-tolerant machines arrive.

Their approach simulates open system dynamics on a quantum computer, even allowing negative decay rates beyond the standard Markovian picture. Lyapunov-based feedback then steers the system toward a target virtual state under engineered noise. Turning a nuisance into a tool could make near-term devices more useful for basic physics.
arxiv-2510-19284:
Yoshiki Jikumaru writes down the governing equations for membrane O surfaces, a class of shell shapes that appear when a membrane in balance carries a constant load pushing straight through its surface. For such surfaces, the lines of principal curvature match the lines of principal stress. This makes the system integrable and mathematically tractable.

Equations are given for surfaces of the first and second kind, echoing a classic classification of Guichard surfaces. Jikumaru also shows these membrane surfaces form a subclass of a broader family, and that the Bäcklund transformation maps each kind back into itself, a symmetry useful for generating new solutions.
arxiv-2510-19484:
Zaifei Yang and four co-authors present KnowMol, a large language model built to understand and generate molecules. Models of this kind have been held back by weak written descriptions of molecules and by clumsy ways of encoding molecular structure during training. The team attacks both problems at once.

They built KnowMol-100K, a dataset of one hundred thousand molecules with detailed annotations written at several levels of chemical description. They also designed a chemically informed way of representing molecules for the model. Trained on these, KnowMol posted strong results across molecular understanding and generation tasks, and the dataset is released publicly.
arxiv-2510-19684:
Yutian Wen and seven co-authors report a superconducting resonator whose frequency and bandwidth can both be tuned on demand, built to address spin ensembles in diamond-like solid-state systems. Such ensembles are promising quantum memories, holding coherence for seconds at special clock transitions, but practical schemes need a resonator that can adjust dynamically. Their device tunes frequency with a direct current through a high-kinetic-inductance film.

Bandwidth is tuned separately through parametric coupling to a low-quality buffer resonator. With it, the team addressed an ensemble of bismuth donors at their clock transition and measured an echo coherence time of four hundred fifty milliseconds. They also demonstrated radio-frequency driving of the donor transitions and live control of the resonator bandwidth.
arxiv-2510-19784:
Shixuan Liu and six co-authors tackle a hidden obstacle in learning models of dynamical systems: data gathered in different environments behave differently, but environment labels are often missing. Without labels, methods that generalize across environments cannot get started, a common problem in large public and privacy-sensitive datasets. Their method, DynaInfer, infers the labels from the data itself.

Within each training round, fixed neural networks score the data, and their prediction errors reveal which examples belong together environmentally. The authors prove the procedure solves the underlying alternating optimization problem and test it on diverse systems. DynaInfer assigned environments more accurately than existing techniques, converged quickly to the true labels, and sometimes beat methods that were given the true labels.
arxiv-2510-19984:
Konstantinos Kitsios, Marcel Böhme, and Alberto Bacchelli study greybox fuzzing, a testing method that mutates seed inputs and keeps any that reach new code. They ask whether the order in which mutators are applied changes how well a fuzzer works. A fitted model on all mutator pairs shows a clear interaction effect.

Guided by that finding, the authors present MuoFuzz, which learns which mutator is likely to help next and builds sequences by sampling from those learned chances. On the FuzzBench and MAGMA benchmarks, MuoFuzz reaches the highest code coverage. It also finds bugs that two strong rivals, AFL++ and MOPT, each missed.
arxiv-2510-21084:
Juntao Li leads five co-authors on MediRec, an clear language model framework for Chinese drug advice from digital health records. Clinical support tools are strong in English data, while Chinese drug advice with readable reasoning has been largely unexplored.

MediRec grounds its suggestions clinically rather than predicting coarse drug codes alone, so doctors can follow why a drug is proposed. Interpretable output matters because prescribing errors carry direct patient risk and clinicians must defend each choice. The framework targets a gap between benchmark performance and bedside trust in a major language community.
arxiv-2510-21384:
Michał Zegrodnik and three co-authors model superconductivity in a twisted double layer of the material WSe2, two sheets rotated slightly against each other. Recent experiments found an unusual paired state there, and the team asks which conditions of electric field and electron filling let that state form.

Their model keeps one effective band and treats electron interactions with an approximation that respects strong local repulsion. A superconducting phase appears only in a narrow range of applied field, exactly where a sharp peak in the density of states, called a Van Hove singularity, crosses half-filling of the band. That match with recent data comes from a balance: the peak supplies many states for pairing. While interaction-driven shrinking of those states keeps the system in a weakly to moderately correlated regime.
arxiv-2510-21784:
Maria Nareklishvili, Nick Polson, and Vadim Sokolov build a prediction method that learns quantiles rather than full odds curves. A quantile marks a level that future values should fall below with a chosen chance. Predicting quantiles therefore gives a direct read on risk. That helps with large forecasting problems.

Their method is called Generative Quantile Bayesian Prediction. It uses generative modeling to build maps from data to quantiles. The authors set it beside rival methods such as conformal prediction and fiducial prediction. They argue it has gains in both theory and practice. Worked examples cover the classic normal-mean learning setup. A causal inference problem is covered too. The paper ends by pointing to open directions for more research.
arxiv-2510-21884:
Avinash Patil asks whether model explanations rest on the words that drive predictions. Language models give reasons for their text classifications. Patil checks those reasons against a clear yardstick. The yardstick is a set of simple, transparent classifiers. Their word-level importance scores are fully visible.

Patil sorts the predictive words into two piles. Some support the predicted label, and others argue against it. Across three benchmark collections, a steady pattern appears. He calls it support-contra asymmetry. Explanations for correct predictions lean on supporting words. They rarely mention opposing ones. Explanations for wrong predictions cite far more of the opposing evidence. Auditors gain a concrete check from this. When a model's story drifts toward the case against its own answer, the answer itself is suspect.
arxiv-2510-21984:
Faria Huq, Elijah L. Claggett, and Hirokazu Shirado ran a preregistered online experiment on how AI writing help changes group politics. Five hundred fifty-seven participants in sixty sessions debated controversial topics over several rounds and could switch groups freely, while some received live message suggestions from a large language model.

Two flavors of help diverged sharply. Suggestions tuned to a person's own stance led to more messages and stronger sorting into like-minded camps. Suggestions woven from groupmates' views produced more receptive language and more mixed, cross-cutting ties. Small differences in how the assistant framed help thus cascaded into opposite social structures, one more divided and one more cohesive. The study warns that design choices inside AI messaging tools quietly shape collective organization.
arxiv-2510-22084:
Atij Mahesh compares six ways to stop language models from producing gender-stereotyped text. The test is strict by design. Each sentence must name both an agentic and a communal trait. The occupations come from the Winogender set. Success means real compositional control, not dodging a few bad words.

The six methods span prompting alone and generate-then-filter. A formal decoding controller is included. So are supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization. The last method erases a bias direction inside the model. The headline result sits in the title. Preference learning fails at the compositional demand. Direct supervision succeeds. Mahesh also scores how natural the surviving text sounds. Each technique's gains are weighed against its costs.
arxiv-2510-22484:
Till Hauser, writing alone, studies how the spread of points under a group action can reveal order in a dynamical system. A group action means a set of symmetries moves points around in a steady, rule based way. His 2025 paper uses mean diameter, an average measure of that spread.

Hauser uses mean diameter to describe regular factor maps, which are clean links between two systems. He proves a system is diam-mean equicontinuous, meaning nearby points stay close on average, exactly when it extends such a regular system. He also shows a largest such factor exists and discusses when these links stay stable.
arxiv-2510-22584:
How many sides can a polygon have when it is exactly the union of a fixed number of triangles arranged in a ring? Giedrius Alkauskas, writing alone in 2025, studies those regular triangle unions and the counting sequence they produce.

Alkauskas shows the sequence starts with values including three, twelve, twenty two, and thirty three, and gives matching style bounds. The upper bound can actually be built, at least on paper as a combinatorial pattern. He asks whether the pattern can be drawn with pseudolines and then stretched into straight lines. A new tool, triangulation shifts, represents each union through changes to a regular polygon triangulation.
arxiv-2510-22884:
Two sided markets may reward pairs beyond each side's own quality. Federico Crippa, writing alone in 2025, studies such complementarities. Only a sparse subset of matches is realized. He adds one complementarity parameter to a Tukey model. The base model has two way fixed effects.

Variation inside a four cycle identifies the parameter. Four cycles are loops in the matching network. Connectedness identifies agent productivities separately. His cycle based estimator avoids estimating latent productivities. It is consistent and asymptotically normal under sparse asymptotics. That yields a formal test for no complementarities. An application uses World Bank manager country assignments. It finds negative complementarities in that data.
arxiv-2510-22984:
Chankyo Kim, Sicheng Zhao, Minghan Zhu, Tzu-Yuan Lin, and Maani Ghaffari design neural networks that respect broad linear symmetries. Many science problems involve matrix data such as covariances or shape tensors, yet most symmetry-aware networks handle only compact groups or plain vectors. That limits their reuse on richer data.

Their Reductive Lie Neurons work exactly with general linear symmetry and handle matrix and Lie algebra features natively. A new invariant bilinear form fixes a stability problem for reductive algebras. The design lets nonlinear layers interact in a principled way, opening symmetry-aware learning to a wider class of geometric problems.
arxiv-2510-23084:
Sunyou Hwang, Christophe De Wagter, Bart Remes, and Guido de Croon tackle wasted circling when small drones soar on rising air along slopes. Orographic soaring can stretch flight time greatly, but fights between control of the long axis and the vertical axis push the craft into energy-burning circles that risk loss of control.

Their SAOS method switches control between axes, driving only one at a time during soaring. That turns an underactuated craft into a fully driven one for those phases. Angle of attack also feeds the flight controller data. The strategy promises longer, steadier soaring for micro air vehicles in hill and ridge winds.
arxiv-2510-23184:
Junho Kim and Young Min Kim use multimodal foundation models to find analogies between three-dimensional scenes. An analogy is a smooth map that aligns regions of two scenes with shared spatial relations. Such maps let a robot transfer paths or task plans from a known room to a new one.

Older methods needed extra training and fixed object lists. The authors instead prompt foundation models that already join vision and language, avoiding task-specific training. Training-free analogies could help robots adapt demonstrations to unseen spaces, a core need for imitation learning in real homes and workplaces.
arxiv-2510-23484:
Julie Mordacq, David Loiseaux, Vicky Kalogeiton, and Steve Oudot introduce T-REGS, a minimum spanning tree regularizer for self-supervised learning. Self-supervised methods learn from unlabeled data by enforcing invariance to changes like rotation or blur. Good representations must avoid dimensional collapse, where features shrink to a thin subspace, and should spread uniformly.

T-REGS regularizes training with the total length of the minimum spanning tree over learned representations in a batch. Encouraging a longer tree pushes features to spread without collapsing. The simple regularizer gives practitioners a new lever for training label-free vision and signal models.
arxiv-2510-23584:
Feng-Li Lin and Sayid Mondal ask a basic question at the border of gravity and quantum physics: can plain Newtonian gravity create quantum entanglement? Claims that classical gravity might entangle two objects have stirred debate, because real entanglement would hint that gravity itself must be quantum. The authors test the idea on quantum bodies modeled as superposed mass quadrupoles, lumps of mass held in two arrangements at once.

They attack the question three ways: a mini-superspace model, semiclassical gravity, and stochastic gravity. Only the first entangles the separate bodies, and it does so by quantizing part of the tidal field. In the other two, the tidal field stays classical and the final state never entangles. The findings support the hypothesis that gravitationally induced entanglement needs quantum gravity, and they show how rough perturbative treatments can mislead.
arxiv-2510-23684:
Samuel G. Fadel and seven co-authors present VIKING, a method for Bayesian inference in deep neural networks. Bayesian treatment promises good predictions plus honest uncertainty, yet the standard mean-field approximations often deliver the opposite: shaky training, weak predictions, and poor calibration. The mismatch grows in today's heavily over-parameterized networks, where many weight settings fit the data equally well.

VIKING builds its approximate posterior from two independent linear subspaces of the parameter space. One captures changes that matter inside the training data's support, the other changes outside it. The result is a fully correlated posterior that respects the network's reparameterization geometry, tuned by easy-to-read hyperparameters. The team supplies scalable routines to fit the model and draw samples. Across tasks, models, and datasets, VIKING reached top performance against a wide set of rivals, arguing Bayesian deep learning is far from a lost cause.
arxiv-2510-23784:
D. J. P. de Sousa and five co-authors identify a new way for bulk metals to control light, rooted in the geometry of electron waves. Theory shows that built-in traits of Bloch states can switch on odd optical effects in metals. The new effect comes from two of those traits acting together: Berry curvature and the orbital magnetic moment of Bloch electrons.

The test material is twisted double-bilayer graphene, whose moiré bands carry strong values of these traits. There the effect gives a sizable response of a magnetoelectric kind that grows in direct step with the applied field. In the material's most symmetric form this route dominates, since the rival dipole route is banned by symmetry. The team's calculations predict gate-tunable effects on polarized light in the terahertz range. They present the material as a tunable platform for light control in two-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2510-23984:
Isabella Danhoni and three co-authors extend the symmetry energy expansion from nuclear matter to dense quark matter, the stuff inside neutron stars. The expansion connects the isospin-symmetric matter probed in laboratories to the asymmetric matter in stars. Using a formula to define isospin asymmetry for quarks, they derive how the expansion changes when quarks replace nucleons.

To test the framework, they run perturbative QCD calculations at next-to-leading order, with quark masses included. A surprise emerges: quark matter at weak equilibrium is not isospin symmetric at all, and the expansion gains a small skewness term with no hadronic counterpart. The authors draw a consequence for model builders. If equations of state must match the perturbative QCD results at high density, the symmetry energy should show a non-monotonic dip along the way. That dip becomes a checkable prediction tying star interiors to first-principles calculations.
arxiv-2510-24184:
Amandip Sangha introduces a new way to deform the algebra of smooth functions on a compact curved space, working alone. The construction uses only the spectrum of the Laplace operator, splitting functions into spectral parts. It twists the usual multiplication channels between those parts by phases of unit size, giving a well defined product on the finite spectral core.

Sangha gives a simple condition for the product to respect complex conjugation and states a boundedness hypothesis under which it extends to a full Sobolev algebra. In that setting, associativity equals an explicit identity for the twisted channels. The paper also studies gauge aspects and rigidity in simple cases, and compares the method with classic deformation approaches.
arxiv-2510-24284:
Wenhao Wang and ten co-authors introduce MCP-Flow, a pipeline that helps language model agents master the growing ecosystem of Model Context Protocol tools. Agents increasingly rely on outside tools for complex real tasks, yet research covered few servers, depended on costly manual curation, and offered little training support. That gap limits real world deployment of tool using agents.

MCP-Flow automates server discovery, data synthesis, and model training through a web agent. It gathered and filtered data from 1,166 servers and 11,536 tools, producing 68,733 high quality instruction and call pairs plus 6,439 trajectories, far beyond prior work in scale and diversity. Experiments show the training improves how models call diverse tools.
arxiv-2510-24784:
Lauri Laatu leads a team with nine co-authors who put a transformer model on a fast chip for use at a giant particle collider. Such models tag jets, sprays of parts from a hit, very well, but they are too slow for the snap choice stage of an event. Their chip run breaks the one microsecond mark, a first for this model type.

Fine cuts to number size and a math trick let the whole model fit on one chip. The team also added support for key model parts to a known open tool, so peers can reuse it. Scores matched top past tools, at a span of about a hundred billionths of a second.
arxiv-2510-25384:
Doan Nam Long Vu led twelve co-authors on synthetic therapy data. Rui Tan, Lena Moench, and Svenja Jule Francke helped. Daniel Woiwod, Florian Thomas-Odenthal, and Sanna Stroth followed. Tilo Kircher, Christiane Hermann, and Udo Dannlowski joined. Hamidreza Jamalabadi, Simone Balloccu, and Shaoxiong Ji followed. Their 2025 paper generates therapist-client conversations with language models.

Privacy rules limited earlier mental health data work. Prior studies relied mainly on generic information instead. Their SQPsych pipeline uses structured questionnaire based profiles. Real client profiles inform generation without leaking sensitive data. The resulting corpus is called SQPsychConv in the paper. They fine-tune open-weight language models on it. Automatic benchmarks and human evaluation tested the models. Trained psychotherapists judged quality in human evaluation. Standard benchmarks missed strengths of their data set. Expert judgment showed clear gains in therapist roleplaying. Experts preferred their sessions over rival mental health models.
arxiv-2510-25484:
Ben Bakary Junior Siriki and Adama Coulibaly study beam stabilization. Their 2025 math paper studies a degenerate Euler-Bernoulli beam. The beam faces a non-uniform axial force. Delayed edge feedback control acts on the system. Global exponential stabilization is their main goal. First they address well-posedness of the system carefully.

They construct an appropriate energy space for study. Weighted Sobolev settings give that functional space. Using the Lumer-Phillips theorem, they prove generation results. The linear operator generates a contraction semigroup there. Next they establish uniform exponential stability overall. A novel Lyapunov functional is constructed for proof. It incorporates weighted integral terms into energy values. System energy decays exponentially to zero, they show. A precise decay rate value is derived too. The work extends stability theory for distributed systems. Complex setting systems may benefit from these methods. Delayed controls are common in engineering uses.
arxiv-2510-25684:
Yujun He led six co-authors presenting SplitJoin. Hangdong Zhao, Simon Frisk, and Yifei Yang helped. Kevin Kristensen, Paraschos Koutris, and Xiangyao Yu joined. Their 2025 paper reduces intermediate results in database joins. Minimizing intermediates is critical for multi-join query processing. The Yannakakis method guarantees acyclic query efficiency. Cyclic queries remain an open challenge for processing.

SplitJoin presents split as first-class query operator. Input tables partition into heavy and light parts. Varied partitions can use distinct query plans. Current binary join engines execute those plans. Intermediate sizes shrink using that partition flexibility. Design space includes thresholds, strategies, and join ordering. Implementation fronts DuckDB and Umbra database systems. On DuckDB, more social network queries completed. Runtime better over twofold on average there. Intermediates shrank nearly eightfold on average too. Umbra showed smaller but consistent improvements overall. Per-split plans beat one universal join order.
arxiv-2510-25784:
Dhananjaya Gowda, Seoha Song, Harshith Goka, and Junhyun Lee propose zFLoRA. Their 2025 paper fuses low-rank adapters with zero latency. Large language models deploy with task-certain adapters widely. Adapters serve multiple downstream uses simultaneously. Adapter settings are under one percent of base model. Yet their inference compute is disproportionately great. Overhead can reach two and a half times base.

Their zero-latency fused low-rank adapter removes that overhead. Zero or negligible latency is added over base model. Tests used three model sizes and standard rivals. Eighteen tasks across three categories were tested. Commonsense thinking, math thinking, and summary-dialogue categories appeared. Latency readings ran on phone and GPU platforms. A Samsung Galaxy device and NVIDIA H100 were used. Proposed adapters present zero to negligible latency overhead. Favorable quality comparisons against rivals were found. Quick multi-adapter deployment becomes more useful on devices.
arxiv-2510-25884:
Eitan Sprejer and five co-authors tackle the problem of making language model judges match human taste. Model judges are hard to calibrate and can shift with wording of the scoring rubric, show bias, or give unstable answers. Better judges matter for training models from human feedback and for routing each query to the best model.

Sprejer and the team model varied, persona based tastes by learning how to combine scores from several judges, each tied to a rubric. They build preference labels at scale from personas, then test two combiners, an additive model and a small neural network. Case studies probe bias in both human and model judges and check how robust the combined system stays.
arxiv-2510-26084:
Di-Chang Chen leads six co-authors in a study of hot Jupiters, giant planets that orbit very close to their stars, and what their ages reveal about their origins. Hot Jupiters challenge classic planet formation theory, and several rival channels could make them. The team use a sample around single Sun like stars with measured kinematic properties, which give a handle on age.

Chen and the team find that the decline in hot Jupiter frequency with age is broken by a ridge at about two billion years, direct evidence for multiple origins on different timescales. Fitting theory to the pattern constrains the tidal quality factor for Sun like stars and the channel shares. Most form early, but about forty percent form late in their account.
arxiv-2510-26284:
Xia Jiang and Rong J. B. Zhu develop a Bayesian framework for learning across many related contextual bandit tasks at once. A contextual bandit is a repeated decision problem where context guides each choice and only the chosen option reward is seen. Multi task versions can share structure across tasks, but tasks also differ, and prior methods often ignore the covariance structure that links them.

Jiang and Zhu use a hierarchical Bayesian model that captures both shared patterns and task specific variation. An empirical Bayesian step estimates the prior covariance matrix from data, which adds practicality and flexibility. Two algorithms follow, one based on Thompson sampling and one on upper confidence bounds, each folding the estimated prior into decisions, with frequentist analysis provided.
arxiv-2510-26484:
Rasoul Amirzadeh, Dhananjay Thiruvady, and Fatemeh Shiri blend several language models to judge the mood of financial text. Sentiment analysis sorts writing into positive or negative views, which traders and analysts track closely. Single models can be unclear about their reasons, costly to tune, and uneven across topics.

Amirzadeh and his two co-authors fuse three models, FinBERT, RoBERTa, and BERTweet, inside a Bayesian network. That network treats each model's call as a node with odds attached, then weighs them together. Across three hand-labelled financial collections with different styles, the blend beat each single model by about six percent in accuracy. The authors present the gain as steady across data sets, with a clearer, more open route to each final call.
arxiv-2510-26684:
Vaibhav Kurrey, Sivakalyan Pujari, and Gagan Raj Gupta report a long-term factory deployment of camera-based failure prediction. Their setting is a steel rolling mill, where unplanned breakdowns are costly. Industrial cameras watch equipment, alignment, and the motion of hot bars along the line in real time.

Kurrey and his two co-authors process the live video on a central server with deep learning models, which keeps the heavy computing off the plant's control systems. Sensor data and visual inputs are analysed together. The system locates failures and suggests their likely root causes early enough for proactive maintenance. The authors argue the integrated approach lifts reliability, productivity, and profit, and that server-based inference scales across production lines with modest extra resources.
arxiv-2510-26784:
Arnab Sen Sharma, Giordano Rogers, Natalie Shapira, and David Bau look inside language models for a built-in filtering operation. In functional programming, filter keeps the items of a list that pass a test. The team uses causal mediation analysis across many list-processing tasks to see how models do the same job.

Sen Sharma and his three co-authors find a small set of attention heads, which they call filter heads, that hold a compact encoding of the test in their query states. That encoding is portable: lifted out, it runs the same filtering on new collections, in other formats and languages, even on other tasks. In some cases, though, models use a second strategy, marking each item with a pass or fail flag as they go. The results show transformer models can build human-readable versions of abstract operations.
arxiv-2510-27484:
Uzay Macar, Paul C. Bogdan, and two other co-authors argue that one look at an AI's reasoning is not enough, in a 2025 paper. A reasoning model can write many chains of thought, not just one. Studying a single chain can mislead anyone probing how the model decides. Their fix is resampling: freeze a partial chain, then let the model finish it again and again.

Three case studies show the power of the trick. First, stated reasons may not cause the act: pleas about self-preservation barely moved choices in blackmail tests. Second, edits pasted into a chain steer it weakly and unevenly, while resampled picks stay on-policy, drawn from the model's own text. Third, deleting a step fails when the model just repeats it later. Their resilience metric resamples again and again to keep such content out.
arxiv-2510-27584:
Ilyass Moummad, Kawtar Zaher, Hervé Goëau, and Alexis Joly propose a fast way to search large image sets in 2025. Large models give rich codes for each image, but comparing those long codes is slow. Hashing, which turns each image into a short string of bits, allows fast matching. Past hash methods need complex training and long runs.

Their rule, called CroVCA, trains bit codes to agree across matched views of the same scene. A single loss drives the match, while a second term keeps codes varied and balanced. A small network called HashCoder learns the codes and can sit on frozen model output. Quick bit search could speed huge photo archives.
arxiv-2511-00184:
Sami Davies, Venkatesan Guruswami, and Xuandi Ren study scheduling problems where a planner may drop a small share of jobs on purpose. One problem packs jobs onto unlike machines to finish fast. A twin problem, nicknamed Santa Claus, shares value among agents as fairly as possible. Both versions trade completion time against how much work gets done.

For machine scheduling, allowing a longer deadline lets their method schedule more jobs than earlier work could. For the fair-sharing problem, they prove the first hardness result: near-perfect fairness for almost all agents is hard to reach. A new set-packing variant supports the proof and may interest other researchers.
arxiv-2511-00284:
Pierluigi Contucci, Godwin Osabutey, and Filippo Zimmaro propose a single yardstick for judging whether the AI boom can last. The yardstick is economic productivity of energy, the output a country produces per unit of energy used. History warns them. The first industrial revolution raised profits before efficiency, and the ratio fell until science and social change caught up. Later waves built on firm theory and skipped that dip.

Data from three decades show rich economies raising the ratio in a steady line. Those same economies drive world output and energy use, so AI's thirst for power will hit them hardest. The authors urge open reporting of AI energy use and rewards tied to productivity, so growth does not blindly waste energy.
arxiv-2511-00384:
Isa Mammadli and eight co-authors built a brainbot: a small programmable bristlebot that senses its state, predicts where it is heading, and computes its own steering on board. Ordinary active particles just move with fixed behavior, so a self-steering particle is a step toward adaptive active matter. Their first step is a physics-informed digital twin of the device.

The twin rests on a kinematic model that reproduces the statistics of measured paths and can generate long, faithful synthetic ones. On that base they run model predictive control directly on the bot, and it follows a non-trivial target path accurately. By fusing physical modeling, data-driven calibration, and control, the platform points toward machine-learning studies of many interacting smart particles.
arxiv-2511-00784:
Zhong-Wu Xia and colleagues study small disturbances around a rotating black hole of a newer kind, one shaped by a Kalb-Ramond field. The black hole is a BTZ type solution, a simpler three dimensional model often used to test ideas about gravity.

Separating the wave equation for a scalar field leads to a Heun equation, whose solutions let the team compute quasinormal modes, the ringing tones a black hole settles with after a disturbance. They find the Kalb-Ramond parameter changes the spectrum strongly, and only one mode shows instability. Checking energy and angular momentum flows, they show the field also shifts where superradiance, a wave amplification effect, can occur.
arxiv-2511-01084:
Anton Gjokaj, David Kalaj, and Djordjije Vujadinovic find the best possible constant in an inequality for functions on the unit circle. The inequality bounds a combination of a function's analytic and co-analytic projections, weighted by a positive parameter, in terms of the function's own size in an Lp space.

Their result generalizes a sharp form of the classical M. Riesz conjugate function theorem due to Pichorides and Verbitsky, along with well known estimates for holomorphic functions. Sharpness is proved by testing the inequality on a family of quasiconformal harmonic mappings and pushing a parameter to its limiting value, where the bound is attained in the limit. The paper sits in harmonic analysis, where exact constants, not just existence, are the goal.
arxiv-2511-01284:
Karma Phuntsho and co-authors review how foundation models, large models pretrained on broad data, can be adapted to medical image analysis. Such models promise broadly useful, task agnostic help across clinical tasks and scan types, which could relieve the shortage of labeled medical data. Real clinical use, though, is blocked by domain shift, scarce labels, heavy computing demands, and strict privacy rules.

The review assesses the main adaptation routes: supervised fine tuning, domain focused pretraining, parameter efficient fine tuning, self supervised learning, hybrid methods, and multimodal schemes. For each it weighs reported gains, usefulness in clinics, and limits, naming trade offs earlier reviews often skipped. Emerging directions include continual learning for live use, federated privacy preserving training, and hybrid self supervision.
arxiv-2511-01484:
Shunyuan Shang, Emna Zedini, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini evaluate a relay chain meant to bring fast links to users beyond the reach of ground networks. A ground station fires a laser beam up to a high-altitude platform. The platform amplifies the signal and forwards it by radio to people on the ground. Intelligent reflecting surfaces help the radio leg.

The authors model fading on each leg with standard statistical distributions, including turbulence effects on the optical link, and they test both direct and heterodyne detection. From that model they derive the system's data capacity, average bit-error rate, and outage probability, using the bivariate Fox-H function, plus simpler formulas for the high-power limit. Computer simulations match the theory exactly.
arxiv-2511-01584:
Debasish Mondal, Anirudh Nemmani, and Arunima Banerjee classify a fingerprint of cold hydrogen gas in deep space: the 21-centimeter absorption line. The line can arise in a galaxy lying between us and a distant radio source. Or it can arise in gas tied to the source itself. Telling the two apart normally needs optical follow-up. Huge blind surveys cannot afford that follow-up.

Using 118 known absorption lines from the literature, the team fit each spectrum and trained six machine learning models on the fitted parameters. A random forest did best, reaching about 89 percent accuracy, and the line width at 20 percent depth proved the most informative single parameter. Retraining with just that width and the integrated optical depth kept accuracy near 88 percent, a lean recipe for survey pipelines.
arxiv-2511-01684:
R. Morales-Cabrera and Y. Bonder build a semiclassical theory of gravity in which spacetime can twist as well as curve. Torsion, the twisting part of the connection, appears in Einstein-Cartan theory, a classical modification of general relativity. Semiclassical gravity treats matter quantum mechanically while gravity stays classical, and the question is whether that hybrid can be made consistent once torsion is present.

Working with a free Klein-Gordon field coupled non-minimally in four dimensions, the authors show the theory can be axiomatized. Hadamard renormalization gives well-defined expectation values for the energy-momentum and spin-density operators, the two sources torsion couples to. They identify the renormalization ambiguities by building a renormalization Lagrangian from differential forms, and they confirm that the conformal anomaly persists even with torsion switched on.
arxiv-2511-02084:
Pallav Kumar Bera and Samita Rani Pani design a smarter protection relay for power lines that connect solar plants to the grid. Conventional relays struggle here because power electronics change how fault currents behave. Their single-ended method watches three-phase currents, builds a recurrence matrix from changes in their quantiles. It feeds the result to an InceptionTime deep learning system that spots faults, locates them, and names the faulty phase.

Simulations on two standard test grids, including the New England 39-bus system, covered switching events, high-impedance faults, sensor saturation, noise, and double-circuit lines. Semi-supervised methods such as label spreading were added so the system performs near supervised levels with little labelled data. The authors report robust performance across configurations and changing solar capacity.
arxiv-2511-02784:
Lior Alon, Dan Mikulincer, and John Urschel count sign changes along eigenvectors of random matrices. Read as operators on signed complete graphs, these vectors have a nodal count, the number of sign flips between neighbors. Their 2025 paper focuses on orthogonally invariant ensembles, with the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble as the central case.

As matrix size grows, the spread of nodal counts settles onto the same limiting law as the eigenvalues themselves. For the Gaussian case, that limit is the semicircle law. The outcome overturns a conjecture from quantum chaos and quantum graphs, which had predicted a Gaussian shape for the nodal count. The finding links two counts that were not expected to share one law.
arxiv-2511-02884:
Dariush Salami, Nima Bahmani, Huseyin Yigitler, and Stephan Sigg tackle a quiet fault in radar sensors: their readings drift as the hardware warms up. Their 2025 paper covers millimeter-wave FMCW radars, the kind used in dense wireless networks. Heat inside the device shifts its parts, and that drift can spoil measurements if left uncorrected.

Their calibration framework works from inside the device. It reads internal temperature sensors and applies a compensation model with signal processing to keep readings accurate. In experiments, the link between the signal amplitude and the temperature drift fell by up to 84 percent. The method adds little computing cost, which aids scaling in crowded networks, and it avoids sensitive external data on ethical grounds.
arxiv-2511-02984:
Alan Vazquez, Peter Goos, and Eric Schoen design better experiments by joining two screening designs into one larger plan. Their target, OMARS designs, let researchers test factors at three levels in few runs, with linear effects kept clean of quadratic and interaction effects. Full catalogs exist only up to five factors, since listing all options grows too costly. Their 2025 construction sidesteps that wall.

The method glues two definitive screening designs together, then folds and permutes columns of one parent to cut aliasing among second-order effects. The children beat their parents on statistical features. The authors study the new designs' properties and compare them with published alternatives. The result opens economical three-level testing to problems with many factors.
arxiv-2511-03084:
Gowtham Premananth and Carol Espy-Wilson turn the coordination of the vocal tract into a measurable sign of schizophrenia. The disorder can scramble speech, but most AI diagnostic tools act as black boxes that clinicians distrust. Their 2025 framework reads articulatory features, how the speech organs move together, and plots their eigenspectra, which separate tangled from simple coordination patterns at a glance.

A weighted score built from those plots separated the groups reliably, with doubt confined to a narrow band near zero. The score tracked overall illness severity on a standard rating scale. It also tracked the balance of positive against negative symptoms: stronger positive symptoms went with more complex coordination, and stronger negative symptoms with the reverse. The authors offer it as a transparent severity marker.
arxiv-2511-03184:
I. Araya and six colleagues present ISOSCELES, a model grid for measuring the properties of massive stars from their spectra. Massive stars drive galactic change through winds and chemical enrichment, but reading their atmospheres needs good wind models. The common shortcut for wind speed, the beta law, misses real complexity. Their 2025 grid replaces it with hydrodynamic wind solutions from the m-CAK theory, including fast and slow solution families.

Synthetic line profiles from the Fastwind code fill a grid spanning O, B, and A type stars at solar composition. A semi-automatic fitting routine then derives stellar and wind parameters from key lines. Tests on six stars reproduced the observed profiles closely, and the slow solution fit two early B supergiants well. Ultraviolet lines and varied composition come next.
arxiv-2511-03484:
Mahdi Ebrahimi pursues two routes toward a conjecture by Jan Saxl about representations of the symmetric group. Saxl proposed that the tensor square of one special representation, tied to a staircase shape, contains every irreducible representation of the group at a matching size. Kronecker coefficients decide whether each piece appears, and their positivity is the crux.

Ebrahimi's tools are a semigroup property of those coefficients and generalized blocks of the group. Each route certifies that certain representations do occur in the square. The conjecture remains a claimed target rather than a settled result, and partial families still count as progress. Representation theory gains whenever structured families inside the square can be named with certainty.
arxiv-2511-03884:
Kaihua Ji, Luning Sun, Shusen Liu, Fei Zhou, and Tae Wook Heo train autoregressive deep surrogate models to mimic dendrite growth during alloy solidification. Phase-field simulation captures such microstructure patterns well but costs too much for routine materials design, so a faster stand-in is valuable.

Surrogates learn from short phase-field trajectories in small domains, then predict growth at larger length and time scales more than a hundred times faster. Tests cover steady growth and directional solidification of a dilute aluminium-copper alloy. Comparisons with phase-field benchmarks show close agreement in tip-selection constant, pattern symmetry, and primary spacing evolution, supporting use in practical design workflows.
arxiv-2511-04584:
Daniel Gomm and two colleagues argue that ambiguity in data questions is not always a flaw. People querying tables often leave details open on purpose, trusting the system to fill gaps. Interfaces that treat every gap as an error miss that cooperative intent.

Their framework shares the work of specifying a query between user and system. It separates clear queries, ambiguous but resolvable ones, and uncooperative ones that cannot be resolved. Reviewing fifteen datasets, they find query types mixed without control. That mixing, they argue, makes current scores poor measures of both accuracy and interpretability.
arxiv-2511-04984:
Xinheng He and co-authors present Peptide2Mol, a diffusion model that designs small molecules that act like a peptide when bound to a protein. Drug design with AI often skips the fact that the body itself uses peptides to bind proteins.

The model reads both the source peptide and the pocket around it on the target protein, then grows a small molecule to fit. It leads on standard non-sequential design tests and yields molecules close to the source peptide. A partial diffusion mode also lets users tune a molecule or shape a peptide mimic step by step.
arxiv-2511-05084:
José Gómez-Torrecillas and co-authors study transpose and dual codes inside quotients of skew polynomial rings. Those rings yield matrix algebras at the heart of rank-metric codes, which guard data when rank, not count, is the right error gauge.

Recent work found the largest known families of maximum rank distance codes in such subsets. Here the authors give clear skew forms for transpose and dual builds. That lets them name the adjoint and dual codes for the new families, a step needed to use and check those codes in practice today.
arxiv-2511-05184:
