The authors propose an observability architecture that collects telemetry apart from the workload itself.

Because monitoring is decoupled, execution data persist across system and algorithm layers, kept for reproducible, retrospective analysis instead of being lost or forcing redundant runs. Applied to a typical workflow based on sample-based quantum diagonalization, the system exposes how the solver behaves across iterations. The payoff is transparency for infrastructure-aware algorithm design. Developers can see what the hybrid machine actually did, tune systematically, and trust that scarce quantum time was not wasted on runs nobody can reconstruct.
arxiv-2512-05584:
Haoran Yu and a large team of astronomers ask why small galaxies hold so little ordinary matter. One suspect is stellar feedback, the push of winds from young and exploding stars. Such winds can drive gas clean out of a galaxy. Direct proof has been scarce. So the team stacks spectra from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. They combine light from roughly four hundred thousand galaxies to bring faint signals into view.

In the stacked spectra they find cool gas flowing outward, traced by magnesium lines. Their sums show winds from low mass galaxies can escape the halo entirely. Sight lines to background quasars confirm extra gas around galaxies, mostly above and below the disk. Together, the results support the idea that star driven winds drain small galaxies of gas. What happens inside a galaxy is thus tied to thin matter spread far outside it.
arxiv-2512-05684:
Peter Cameron and Siavash Lashkarighouchani revisit a classic result at the crossroads of combinatorics and dynamics. A famous theorem by Kechris, Pestov, and Todorčević links Ramsey theory with how groups act on ordered spaces. One consequence says the limit object of a Ramsey family of finite structures carries a hidden total order. That in turn forced Nešetřil's older result: such structures must be rigid, with no symmetry at all.

Their 2025 paper gives a new, more direct proof of this fact. Take a Fraïssé family of rigid structures over a finite relational language. The authors show a clean either-or. Either the family's limit has a reduct that is a total order, or the Ramsey property fails outright for an explicit small pair of structures, one of them with just two elements. A short proof like this shows exactly where the Ramsey property can break.
arxiv-2512-05884:
Fabio Costa and Jing Yang build a language for watching a quantum system over time, even when it has memory. Measurements in quantum control and sensing rarely happen at instants; they stretch over time. Existing frameworks let experimenters step in at chosen moments. The missing piece is a description that never commits to one specific measuring device, so any continuous monitoring can be plugged in.

Their extension lifts process theory into continuous time, using functionals that take whole past records as input. It builds on the Feynman-Vernon influence functional and yields a continuous Born rule, separating process from watcher. Causality and Markovianity, memorylessness, gain natural definitions in this setting. A generalized Caldeira-Leggett model shows the machinery on a realistic case with memory. The framework opens the way to causal structures in the continuum.
arxiv-2512-05984:
Omar El Deeb models Saturn's F ring as a small nonlinear system pushed by two moons at once. The F ring is a thin, braided strand of ice and dust, shepherded by Prometheus and Pandora. El Deeb's model adds a clumping term to predator prey mathematics, and drives it with both moons' frequencies.

Integrating the model and reading it with the tools of dynamical systems, spectral analysis, stroboscopic maps, and rotation numbers, two regimes appear. At moderate clumping strength, the motion is bounded and quasiperiodic, with smooth amplitude waves and thin loop signatures. Push the nonlinearity slightly higher and the oscillations turn strongly modulated, with broadened bands and sideband rich spectra. Rotation number maps show organized domains, including Arnold tongue like locking bands. Model timescales match the forcing periods. The model shows how little machinery makes the ring dance.
arxiv-2512-06484:
Steven Hofmeyr and four co authors present PureMagic, a scheduler for fault tolerant quantum computers built from surface codes. Such machines need magic states, special resources that make full quantum computing possible. Growing them by a newer route, cultivation, takes only one logical qubit, but the timing is random: some states finish fast, others drag. A fixed schedule cannot cope with that spread, and older factories ate huge areas of the machine.

PureMagic schedules on the fly. Every spare patch of the machine doubles as both a road for moving data and a plot for growing magic states. When a road is needed, growing pauses and restarts later, which trims the long tail of slow grows and leaves no patch idle. Across many benchmark circuits it beat bus based routing by wide margins, used far fewer logical qubits, and cut average preparation time several fold.
arxiv-2512-06584:
Zekai Zhang and Adam Lidz propose a new way to probe magnetism spread across the cosmos. Radio waves from distant sources twist as they pass through magnetized gas, an effect called Faraday rotation. The size of the twist, the rotation measure, is catalogued for many background sources, and galaxy surveys map where matter gathers in the foreground. The authors cross match the squared rotation measures with the galaxy density field, split by separation on the sky.

That statistic dodges contamination and the noise bias that plagues simpler versions using absolute values. Sliced by galaxy distance, it can rebuild how cosmic magnetism evolved over time. The team models it with a large cosmological simulation that includes magnetic fields, and ties it to a three point statistic of gas and magnetism. The measure, they argue, can be read from near term data.
arxiv-2512-07184:
Da Zhang and co-authors forecast time series with help from the words and timestamps that surround the numbers. A sales curve, a sensor stream, or a climate record rarely travels alone: reports describe it, and the calendar structures it. Diffusion models, strong generators in other fields, had mostly been applied to the bare numbers. UniDiff brings the extra signals inside one diffusion framework built for forecasting.

The numbers are first cut into patches, each mapped to an embedding by a small network, preserving local rhythm. A single parallel fusion module then uses cross-attention to weigh structural information from timestamps and semantic context from text in one step. A guidance scheme designed for two sources lets users dial the influence of text and of time separately while generating. Across real-world benchmarks spanning eight domains, the unified model set the best scores.
arxiv-2512-07584:
The Meituan LongCat Team published this 2025 technical report on their image generation model, LongCat-Image. It is an open-source foundation model that works in both Chinese and English. The team targets weak spots in current leaders: text rendering, realism, speed, and access for developers.

Careful data curation runs through every stage of the model's training. Curated reward models then guide a final reinforcement learning phase. The payoff is sharp text inside images and strong photorealism. Chinese characters are a special strength, including complex and rare ones that rivals often garble. The core model is far smaller than the giant designs common in the field. That compact size cuts memory use and speeds up image creation. The model also edits images well, holding top results on standard tests. Meituan releases model versions and the full training toolchain in public. Developers get checkpoints from several stages, not just the finished model.
arxiv-2512-08184:
Chikun Ding, Yuebing Zhou, Yu Shi, and Xiangyun Fu, theoretical physicists in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is Einstein aether theory, a variant of gravity where a preferred vector field, the aether, breaks Lorentz symmetry. They work in a subclass of the theory and allow any number of spacetime dimensions.

The team finds an exact black hole solution carrying an aether charge, which unlike electric charge has a nonzero minimum value. Parts of the aether potential stay smooth at the horizon, while others diverge there. Even with broken symmetry, they show the Smarr formula and the first law of black hole thermodynamics still hold exactly. They also work out how gravitational waves polarize in this theory. Some wave modes travel at light speed as usual, while one expected polarization cannot propagate at all in four dimensions.
arxiv-2512-08384:
Soeren Wilkening, a quantum computing researcher in Germany, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. He presents a quantum search routine for constrained combinatorial optimization, the class of problems where one hunts the best option under rules. Earlier Grover based methods handled mainly linear constraints, which excludes many real problems with arbitrary, efficiently checkable objectives and rules.

His routine extends that approach to general constraints on discrete domains. Assuming future fault tolerant quantum hardware, he shows the method could beat the best classical solvers and heuristics in both running time scaling and solution quality. More realistic versions still promise runtime savings of a hundred to a thousand times, by his analysis. The result is not a claim about today machines, but a map of where quantum search may pay off once logical qubits mature. For optimization practitioners, it widens the set of constrained problems worth targeting with quantum methods.
arxiv-2512-08984:
Nirhoshan Sivaroopan and coauthors introduce RAG HAR, a training free method that uses retrieval augmented generation and large language models to recognize human activities. Activity recognition supports healthcare, rehab, fitness tracking, and smart environments. Existing deep learning methods need data set specific training, large labeled corpora, and heavy compute, which limits their reuse.

Their method computes lightweight statistical descriptors from sensor data and retrieves similar samples from a vector database. That fetched context guides a language model in identifying the activity. Prompt tuning improves the queries, and a language model based descriptor enriches the database with context aware entries. Across six diverse benchmarks, the system reaches leading results. It does so without any model training or fine tuning, which underlines its strength and practical value. The method can also recognize and label in a meaningful way multiple activities that were never seen while the system was built.
arxiv-2512-09184:
Siyang Hao and Kenneth Breuer study what happens to a wing that flies in the swirling wake left by another flapping wing. The setup copies a trick seen in nature, where animals ride the disturbed air behind others. The authors ran wind tunnel tests with a fixed wing placed in the wake of a pitching airfoil.

They measured the forces on the wing while also filming the airflow with a technique that tracks moving particles. The lift on the surfing wing rose and fell in step with the flow structures hitting it. Those swings followed a simple scaling based on how fast and how far the front wing flapped. Using only the local flow conditions near the wing, classic unsteady aerodynamics formulas predicted the measured lift well. The results help explain how wake surfing changes the forces on a following wing.
arxiv-2512-09284:
Reese E. Jones and three co-authors model how materials deform permanently under heat and speed, a regime called thermo-visco-plastic behavior. Many safety-critical assessments involve processes that generate much heat as they go. Materials can also slide between two regimes during one event: cool and rate-independent at first, then hot and flowing like a thick liquid.

The authors build a physics-augmented neural network framework that respects the second law of thermodynamics and proper behavior under rotations by design. Its structure combines a convex potential with a neural ordinary differential equation, trained in a way that keeps those physical guarantees. The resulting models cover the full spectrum from ordinary elastic-plastic response to fully viscous flow. They also capture complex behavior from material microstructure, and they predict how much mechanical work turns into heat when fitted to stress and temperature measurements.
arxiv-2512-09384:
J.-W. Zhao leads a team presenting a study of supernova 2022ngb, a Type IIb explosion, the death of a star stripped of most of its hydrogen envelope. The team ran a campaign of photometric and spectroscopic follow-up. Their goal was to pin down the explosion's parameters and learn what kind of star produced it.

Modeling the total light output gives a modest explosion: a few solar masses of ejected material, a typical energy, and a small mass of newly made radioactive nickel. The supernova was faint for its class and rose slowly to peak brightness. Spectra from the late, nebular phase show lopsided line profiles, meaning the explosion was not spherical and its radioactive material is unevenly spread. The progenitor appears to have been a compact stripped star of moderate mass, shaped by a binary companion, with a birth mass in the mid-teens of solar masses.
arxiv-2512-09484:
Shaull Almagor, Guy Arbel, and Sarai Sheinvald settle two questions about tropical, or min-plus, models, mathematical machines where costs combine by minimum and addition instead of the usual operations. Weighted finite automata in this setting, and the equivalent cost register automata that track costs in registers, can behave nondeterministically. The questions ask whether that nondeterminism can be reduced.

For weighted automata, they show the unambiguisability problem, whether an automaton can be made unambiguous, is decidable, resolving a long-standing open problem. Their proof reduces it to determinisability, recently shown decidable as well. The register side goes the other way: minimizing the number of counters in a cost register automaton is undecidable. That holds even when the number of registers is fixed in advance, already with seven registers. The pair of results draws a sharp line between two models that express exactly the same functions.
arxiv-2512-10184:
Koji Ishiwata and Eiichiro Komatsu find where a standard approximation of the infant universe stops being trustworthy. Their system couples an axion field to an SU(2) gauge field during inflation. The gauge field produces spin two particles, tensor fluctuations, which push back on the background dynamics. Perturbation theory handles that backreaction only while the particles' energy density stays below the background's. The authors map where the ratio crosses one. It nearly matches the strong backreaction regime.

Worse, in places the ratio exceeds one even before the system reaches that strong regime. Any perturbative study of the strong regime is therefore limited from the start. The authors' prescription is blunt: reliable answers need non perturbative methods, such as three dimensional lattice simulations of the full dynamics. The result matters because axion gauge models are a popular source of observable gravitational waves and primordial black holes.
arxiv-2512-10384:
A team led by Cong Pang benchmarks a skill image models are rarely tested on: telling nearly identical things apart. Large vision language models converse fluently about pictures, but existing benchmarks emphasize reasoning and neglect fine grained recognition, naming the exact species, model, or subcategory in view, which practical applications need. The authors present FROW, a fine grained recognition open world benchmark, evaluated with GPT-4o's help. They then propose improvements from two directions: how training data is constructed, and how training is staged.

Their data recipes include mosaic examples combining multiple short answer responses, and open world examples generated from real questions and answers. Tests show mosaic data lifting category recognition accuracy modestly, while open world data raised benchmark accuracy by a large margin, with content accuracy up several points as well. Adding fine grained data during pretraining improved category recognition by up to a tenth.
arxiv-2512-10584:
Tetsuya Takaishi models financial volatility with a single-qubit quantum circuit, about the smallest quantum learner possible. Volatility, the size of price swings, clusters and reacts unevenly to gains and losses, and a good model must keep those fingerprints. He generates test data with the Rational GARCH model, which is built to produce asymmetric volatility on purpose.

Trained on that synthetic series, the quantum circuit's predictions preserved the negative link between returns and later volatility, the hallmark of the asymmetry. Checks of the Hurst exponent and multifractal structure showed the predicted series kept the original's anti-persistent behaviour, meaning swings tend to reverse rather than run on. And its layered fractal character survived as well. The ten-page study suggests even a one-qubit learner can carry the statistical signature of realistic volatility.
arxiv-2512-10684:
Shaopeng Hu and co-authors make systems able to predict their own failures before they happen. For discrete-event systems modelled as finite automata, diagnosability means a fault can be spotted after it occurs, while prognosability means it can be foreseen. The paper first pins both properties down in formal terms, showing each equals a normality condition on a suitable part of the system's language.

From that equivalence, supremal sublanguages with each property provably exist, and the authors give an algorithm that computes the largest controllable, normal, prognosable or diagnosable sublanguage. Real systems are modular, built from parts that run side by side, yet these are global properties that purely local supervisors usually cannot enforce. A refined pre-normality lets them compute local supervisors piece by piece, and the resulting closed loop is controllable as a whole, normal, and prognosable or diagnosable, as worked examples show.
arxiv-2512-10884:
Piotr Masajada, Aby Philip, and Alexander Streltsov present entcalc, a software toolkit for measuring geometric entanglement in systems of several quantum particles. Geometric entanglement gauges how far a state sits from the nearest unentangled one, but computing it exactly is out of reach. Their package, in Python and MATLAB, takes a multipartite state and returns a trustworthy estimate.

For pure states it reports the value with an error; for mixed states it gives lower and upper bounds that bracket the truth. Several methods for the lower bound let users trade accuracy against computing cost. The team tests entcalc on three-by-three entangled states, mixtures of GHZ and W states, thermal states of three-qubit spin chains, and noisy versions of the classics. Bound gaps stayed tiny, spin-chain entanglement marked quantum phase transitions, and a tuned magnetic field switched on entanglement between distant sites.
arxiv-2512-11884:
Ranjan Sapkota and co-authors compare a giant generalist vision model against tuned specialists at finding apples in orchard photos. The generalist is SAM3, used with no task training at all. The specialists are three sizes of YOLO11, each fine tuned for the job. The test set holds 670 dense orchard images with more than 28,000 labeled apples.

At a fair overlap level, the tuned models beat the generalist on raw counts. But when the overlap bar rises, the tuned scores fall steeply while the SAM3 score barely moves. SAM3 thus draws far steadier borders, while tuning wins on counts. The team shares code and advice on when each style is the better pick.
arxiv-2512-11984:
Alireza Joonbakhsh and co-authors build ModelSelect, a decision support system for picking AI models in research software. Engineers face a flood of models and libraries, and choices are often made ad hoc from scattered notes and personal habit. That hurts repeatability and openness.

ModelSelect treats the choice as a multi criteria decision problem. Auto pipelines gather evidence into a knowledge graph, and ranking rules weigh technical fit against project context. In 50 real case studies the system matched expert reasoning closely, with high coverage and sound rationales. Against generative AI assistants it tied on quality while winning on traceability and consistency. The frame gives research teams a shared, auditable way to choose models.
arxiv-2512-12084:
Hanzhou Liu and co-authors release FloodSQL-Bench, a test set for turning plain questions into database queries about floods. Text to SQL tools are usually graded on simple tables. Flood work is messier: it joins social, infrastructure, and hazard data by keys, by place, and by both.

The benchmark bakes in those hard joins and sorts questions by difficulty. Top language models are graded under one shared retrieval aided setup, so scores compare fairly. The authors aim for a public proving ground in a high stakes field, where a wrong query can misdirect real aid. Better scores here should mean more trustworthy data tools for disaster managers.
arxiv-2512-12384:
Jesse Ponnock studies how much financial text a language model needs to specialize in a 2025 paper. Continued pretraining on domain text can adapt a general model without full retraining. He trains Llama-3.2 models of 1 and 3 billion parameters on 400 million tokens of United States SEC filings, with checks at four token budgets.

Both models improved steadily on financial validation loss, with the biggest gains in the first 200 million tokens and weaker returns after. General domain loss stayed flat, showing little drift or forgetting. Power law fits had shallow exponents, meaning financial language is regular and quick to learn. Modest budgets may suffice.
arxiv-2512-12884:
Xiangzhong Liu, Jiajie Zhang, and Hao Shen work on 3D object detection for self-driving cars. Cars often get data as object lists from smart sensors or from other vehicles, not as raw signals. Past systems fused those lists late, after separate processing.

The team instead fuses object lists with raw camera images inside one Transformer model, end to end. The lists guide the model as special queries, and a mask built from their positions steers attention to the right areas. Since no public data set has object lists alone, they fake them from known boxes with added noise. Results on nuScenes beat the vision-only base model.
arxiv-2512-12984:
Jiayin Lu and co-authors present VoroLight, a learning method that builds surface meshes from Voronoi cells. Voronoi diagrams divide space into convex cells that join cleanly, a good fit for 3D shape reconstruction. Standard methods only move the cell centers, which can leave bumpy surfaces.

VoroLight attaches a trainable sphere to each surface vertex and adds a loss that pushes the geometry toward smooth, even forms. The method keeps the clean joins and closed surfaces that make Voronoi meshes attractive. It can learn from implicit fields, point clouds, meshes, or multiple images. Extra inner centers extend the same idea to solid volume meshes.
arxiv-2512-13084:
Michael Stumpf presents FlowClass.jl, a Julia software package that sorts dynamical systems into structural classes. The classes run from gradient systems, which always flow downhill, through Morse-Smale systems, to general systems. Where a system sits shapes what it can do: gradient systems cannot oscillate, for instance.

The package runs a battery of tests on a given vector field, checking symmetry, curl, fixed points, orbits, and manifolds. It was built with developmental biology in mind, where landscape metaphors for cell fate are common. FlowClass can test whether such a landscape picture fits a given gene network model, and measure how far from gradient-like it is.
arxiv-2512-13184:
Fabio Sattin and Lorenzo Martinelli study how a charged particle gains energy from a single electrostatic wave in a magnetized plasma. The wave travels across the magnetic field at a frequency above the particle's cyclotron frequency. This setup matters for ion heating in plasmas.

Textbook results say heating needs the wave strength to pass a threshold; below it, motion should stay orderly and reversible. The authors show, by analysis and by simulation, that the motion is non-adiabatic even below threshold. When the wave is slowly switched off, the particle does not return to its start. So energization occurs even under sub-threshold conditions, though it is not strict heating.
arxiv-2512-13384:
Lukas Beringer, Mathias Steinhuber, Klaus Richter, and Steven Tomsovic argue that quantum chaos is a resource for controlling quantum systems completely. In classical physics, chaos aids control through ergodicity and sensitivity to initial conditions. Those notions do not carry over directly to unitary quantum evolution.

They identify quantum substitutes: sensitivity to weak perturbations, measured by fidelity decay, and the random matrix statistics of chaotic systems. With those, any starting state can in principle be steered to any target state past a time that grows only logarithmically with system size. Integrable systems lack both traits, so control there must break integrability. The quantum kicked rotor illustrates the ideas.
arxiv-2512-13584:
Yu. A. Shibanov and co-authors search soft X-ray survey data for known radio and gamma-ray pulsars. They use the eROSITA telescope aboard the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma observatory, which scanned the whole sky. Their paper covers the eastern half of the sky.

They found new candidate X-ray counterparts for twelve pulsars of varied ages and types, at a confidence level of at least 3 sigma. They also detected 55 pulsars already known in X-rays from other telescopes. For the new finds, they give flux estimates, first spectral traits, and short notes on each pulsar. With the western half, about 12% of known pulsars are now seen in X-rays.
arxiv-2512-13884:
Jonas Golde, Patrick Haller, and Alan Akbik release FiNERweb, a resource for multilingual named entity recognition. Named entity recognition finds names of people, places, and organizations in text. Large language models can label training data for smaller models, but past data sets were mostly side products of other studies.

FiNERweb scales that teacher-student approach to 91 languages and 25 scripts, starting from FineWeb-Edu passages. Regression models pick entity-rich passages, and multilingual LLMs annotate them, giving about 225k passages with 235k distinct entity labels. Models trained on it matched or beat baselines in zero-shot transfer on English, Thai, and Swahili, with 19 times less data. Judge scores for faithfulness and completeness were about 4 out of 5.
arxiv-2512-14084:
Li Cai unifies constructions of Kan's loop group for a reduced simplicial set, a tool in algebraic topology. Kan's loop group GX is a group model for the loop space of a simplicial set X. Different constructions of it existed, and Cai's work joins them in a topological frame.

He identifies the geometric realization of GX as different submonoids of the monoid of based Moore loops on the realization of X. He then builds a cubical subcomplex inside it, also as a submonoid. After inverting all degree zero elements there, the inclusion becomes a weak homotopy equivalence. The construction is functorial and explicit, with no inductions, in a 24-page paper. The catalog title adds twisted product language that the arXiv title, On twisting functions, does not carry.
arxiv-2512-14284:
Zhibing Li and five coauthors present SS4D in a 2025 paper on generating dynamic 3D objects from a single camera video. Older methods built such 4D content by optimizing over 3D or video models, which can break consistency over time.

SS4D trains a generator directly on 4D data, using a compact set of structured spacetime latents. It builds on a pretrained image to 3D model to keep spatial consistency despite scarce 4D training data. Added temporal layers reason across frames, and factorized 4D convolutions compress the latent sequence for long videos. A training strategy also improves robustness to occlusion. The result is high fidelity output with temporal coherence and structural consistency.
arxiv-2512-14384: Mert Baştuğ studies a sieve problem: a wall pierced by many small holes, through which a flow must pass. The holes are placed at random, and their sizes vary at random too. He finds the weakest rule on those sizes under which the fine, hole-filled flow still settles into a clean averaged limit. The result holds even when the holes cluster close together.
arxiv-2512-14584:
David Henriquez Bernal and Peter Nejjar analyze how a classic traffic-like model settles down. The asymmetric simple exclusion process moves particles along a line of sites, each site holding at most one particle, like cars that cannot pass through each other. They watch a finite segment and measure how far the system stays from equilibrium over time, in total variation distance.

Many such systems show cutoff, an abrupt drop from far-from-equilibrium to settled within a narrow time window. Their general theorem delivers that window and the exact shape of the drop whenever a KPZ-type limit result exists for the infinite line. They apply it to flat, half-flat, and step starting patterns, using purely probabilistic arguments.
arxiv-2512-14784:
Mireia Montes and many coauthors write in support of a giant northern telescope, focusing on the faintest galaxies in the sky. These low surface brightness systems shine so dimly that most surveys miss them. Yet they may hold clues to how galaxies grow, how they merge, and what dark matter is.

Models today are built mostly from bright and easy targets, which skews the picture of galaxy life. A 30 to 40 meter telescope, with sharp vision from adaptive optics, could study these faint and spread out systems in depth. Placed in the north, it could reach key nearby structures and rich fields. The authors say such data would complete the story that bright objects alone cannot tell.
arxiv-2512-15084:
Tushar Singh and a coauthor analyze S-reduced rings, a relative of the reduced rings of commutative algebra. A reduced ring has no nilpotent elements, elements that vanish when raised to a power. The S version relaxes each condition by a factor from a chosen multiplicative set S, a common way to generalize ring theory.

They prove that in an S-reduced ring, the intersection of all S-prime ideals is S-zero. An S-Artinian reduced ring, they show, is exactly a finite direct product of fields. They give an example of an S-reduced ring that is also uniformly S-Armendariz, and prove every uniformly S-reduced ring is uniformly S-Armendariz. Other results link S-reduced rings with S-strongly Hopfian rings. A structure theorem for S-reduced rings rounds out the study.
arxiv-2512-15184:
Hakima Bessaih and three coauthors extend a data assimilation method from calm fluids to noisy ones. Data assimilation nudges a simulation toward observed reality, and the AOT algorithm of Azouani, Olson, and Titi is known to sync approximate solutions with the true flow in noise free settings. The authors carry it to the two dimensional stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, with additive or multiplicative noise.

They give conditions on the nudging strength and the spatial scale of observations that guarantee the nudged solution converges to the true stochastic flow. With multiplicative noise, convergence holds in expectation, at fast or slower rates set by the noise growth. With additive noise, they get fast convergence both in mean and pathwise. The results show how random forcing, viscous damping, and feedback control jointly govern sync in noisy fluids.
arxiv-2512-15384:
Gregor Donabauer and eight coauthors present MedNuggetizer, a tool that pulls small, trustworthy facts out of long medical documents. Clinicians facing thick guidelines and studies need evidence that answers a specific question, not a pile of PDFs. The tool extracts information nuggets tied to the user's query, driven by a large language model.

It repeats the extraction several times and clusters the nuggets, so only stable, agreed facts survive as reliable evidence, within and across documents. The team demonstrates it on antibiotic prophylaxis before prostate biopsy, drawing on major urology guidelines and recent PubMed studies. Domain experts judged the results, finding the tool an efficient way to explore long texts and surface query focused evidence. MedNuggetizer is offered as support for evidence based clinical work.
arxiv-2512-15584:
Daniel Herrmann and co authors build a decision theoretic framework for delegating choices to AI systems in a 2025 paper. Alignment work mostly asks how to shape AI values. A prior question gets less attention: under uncertainty, when is imperfect alignment good enough to justify handing over a decision?

The framework balances an agent's value misalignment against its accuracy and its reach, the acts open to it. Universal delegation, trusting an agent with any problem, demands near perfect alignment and total trust. Context specific delegation can still be wise with real misalignment, when better accuracy or reach gives access to better outcomes. A new scoring method quantifies that choice in advance.
arxiv-2512-15684:
Victor Leger and Florent Chatelain analyze partial least squares in high dimensions in a 2025 paper. Partial least squares extracts latent components shared by paired data sets, and it has decades of practical success in data integration. Its behavior when both data sets are high dimensional, though, lacked precise theory.

The authors study two data matrices that share a low rank common structure plus individual parts. Using random matrix theory, they characterize how well the estimated latent directions align with the true ones. The analysis explains reconstruction performance of the SVD based variant and finds regimes with counter intuitive limits. That variant still beats separate principal component analysis at detecting the shared subspace.
arxiv-2512-15884:
Yanxuan Shao and co authors show that adding entanglement can lower fidelity in noncooperative quantum networks in a 2025 paper. Standard quantum network protocols start from an allocated entanglement budget and refine it with local operations and classical communication. More budget is usually assumed to mean better final entanglement.

For noncooperative protocols, the authors prove the opposite can happen: fidelity can fall as more entanglement is added when network states are not pure. The effect is a quantum analogue of selfish routing, where each party's local choices degrade the shared outcome. The result warns that large quantum networks may waste resources without coordination, and it appeared in Physical Review Letters.
arxiv-2512-16384:
Lorenzo Frigato, Andrea Bardin, and Luca Salasnich study atoms on a bubble in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Ultracold gases trapped on spherical shells, realized in microgravity bubble traps, let physicists explore many-body physics on curved surfaces. Most work so far covers bosons, leaving Fermi gases understudied.

The team analyzes a two-component Fermi gas with repulsive interactions, spread over a sphere's surface at finite temperature. Without interactions, the sphere's geometry already creates a shell structure and changes the cold-temperature thermodynamics versus a flat gas. Adding repulsion through a Hartree-Fock mean-field treatment, they derive the grand potential and a finite-temperature Stoner criterion, the condition for the balanced gas to turn magnetic. Shell effects and repulsion interplay throughout, a signature of curved-space quantum matter.
arxiv-2512-16484:
Yuan Li and five co-authors teach AI to judge photos like people do in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Blind image quality assessment rates pictures without a clean reference copy. Humans do it through a perception-reasoning cascade, sensing flaws and then explaining the verdict to themselves.

The team first collected human data capturing that pipeline, then used reinforcement learning with human annotations as rewards. A second reward pushes the model to infer quality purely from its own written descriptions, enforcing self-consistent reasoning. Score accuracy matched leading assessment systems on standard correlation measures. On more than 1,000 human-annotated samples, the model's reasoning chains scored a ROUGE-1 of 0.512 against human explanations, versus 0.443 for the baseline. The step toward interpretable, human-like quality judgment is the paper's main claim.
arxiv-2512-16584:
Jintao Tong and seven co-authors give AI models visual thoughts in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Multimodal language models reason in text, but tasks needing visual imagination expose a gap: humans picture things while thinking, without external tools. Since these models already store images and text in one shared feature space, pictures could in principle join the reasoning stream.

Their paradigm, Sketch-in-Latents, lets the model emit continuous visual embeddings, called latent sketch tokens, as visual thoughts mid-reasoning. The model alternates between text thinking and visual sketching across steps. A reconstruction mechanism keeps the sketch tokens tied to real visual meaning rather than drifting into noise. Experiments showed superior performance on vision-centric tasks and strong generalization across general multimodal benchmarks. Code is promised for release.
arxiv-2512-16784:
Simone Teglia and coauthors introduce R3ST, a synthetic 3D data set for traffic analysis with realistic vehicle motion. Real road data capture true behavior but lack exact labels, while synthetic data give labels cheaply yet often move cars in fake, rule-based ways.

R3ST closes that gap by placing real paths into a built 3D scene. The paths come from SinD, a bird's-eye drone data set of real driving. The result pairs exact multi-type ground-truth labels with true human driving paths. That pairing serves work on forecasting where road vehicles will go, a core input for road safety tools and self-driving stacks.
arxiv-2512-17084:
Hamed Ajorlou, Gonzalo Mateos, and Luana Ruiz give a sampling method to estimate homophily in large networks, the trait of linked nodes to resemble each other. Full smoothness scores need the whole network and all node features, which privacy, scale, or churn may block.

Their frame estimates the Dirichlet energy, a Laplacian-based variation score, from sampled subgraphs with a Horvitz-Thompson estimator, which reweights by known edge inclusion odds for unbiased results. They prove the energy can be estimated consistently from samples and test other heterophily measures as well. On benchmark heterophilic data sets, the sampled estimates tracked the true structure reliably, opening network analysis to partial views.
arxiv-2512-17184:
Y. Chen, for the VERITAS collaboration, reports a very-high-energy gamma-ray study of HESS J1857+026, a source found in 2008 that still lacks a confirmed counterpart at other wavelengths. A nearby pulsar is known, but no supernova shell or like structure has been tied to it.

VERITAS data confirm the source is extended, and the team characterizes its spectrum and shape in the very-high-energy band above 100 GeV. Guided by that shape, they test a leptonic pulsar wind nebula scenario, tracing how an electron pool would travel and radiate. The work feeds a multi-wavelength hunt for what powers this stubborn gamma-ray emitter.
arxiv-2512-17584:
Christian Cella and four co-authors plan where a wheeled robot arm should park and in what order it should work beside people. A mobile manipulator rolls to a spot, then reaches with its arm. Picking spots and task order together shapes speed, safety, and how gracefully the robot yields when a person walks close.

Their framework builds a digital copy of the shared space and treats the whole planning problem as a black box. A swarm search, where many candidate plans drift toward the best found so far, balances clashing goals. In a box-packing test with humans nearby, the tuned plans cut cycle time and sequenced tasks better. The robot also adapted its plan when people entered the space.
arxiv-2512-17684:
M Tsedrik and B Bose test two ways dark energy might misbehave: by changing over time, and by trading momentum with dark matter. The momentum-trading idea, called Dark Scattering, would slow the growth of cosmic structure late in time. The team confronts both ideas with a stack of surveys: galaxy shapes from the Dark Energy Survey, distance markers from DESI, supernovae, and the Planck microwave sky.

Both models survive, but the data show no need for the dark interaction: its strength sits consistent with zero in every combination. Plain evolving dark energy fits better, with present-day values of about minus 0.76 for its pressure ratio. Adding the shape data sharpened those numbers by up to 25 percent. The tightest pre-Euclid limits on this dark trade are the paper's deliverable.
arxiv-2512-17884:
Xinyue Yu and Hayden Schaeffer speed up a data driven way to learn solution maps for physics equations. Kernel methods can learn such maps with little training, but they slow down on large data sets and wobble when data are noisy. Their method swaps the kernel for random wave features and adds a smoothing penalty.

A second step rebuilds smooth outputs with the same mesh tools engineers use for simulations. Tests covered six standard problems, from fluid flow to heat waves and loaded beams. The new method stayed accurate under noise, trained faster than the plain random feature model, and matched far costlier kernel and neural tools.
arxiv-2512-18184:
Junho Lee, Kwanseok Kim, and Joonseok Lee at Seoul National University ask whether Gaussian noise is really the best starting point for flow matching, a popular way to generate images. Their 2025 study builds a two dimensional simulation that mirrors the geometry of high dimensional data. With it they trace how the model learns during training. The analysis yields four insights about how sources shape the learned flow.

Matching the data density too closely can hurt through mode discrepancy. Directional alignment fails when it is overly concentrated, since paths become entangled. The Gaussian's coverage in all directions keeps learning robust. Norm misalignment, meanwhile, carries a heavy learning cost. Their remedy pairs norm aligned training with pruned sampling at generation time. Pruning skips starting points in data sparse regions, and it works on any pretrained Gaussian source model with no retraining. Experiments show steady gains in image quality and sampling speed.
arxiv-2512-18584:
Marios Papamichalis, Regina Ruane, and Theofanis Papamichalis study counts that live on networks, such as crime in city neighborhoods, disease in counties, and sales at firms linked by trade. A high count at one node can lift its neighbors' counts the next period. That strength drifts over time, yet standard models hold it fixed. Their 2025 paper lets the spillover be a moving coefficient tracked by a filter.

What data reveal about it depends on the network's shape. Learning contrasts nodes whose neighbors have high counts with nodes whose neighbors have low ones. In a fully connected network those contrasts vanish, and the spillover cannot be identified. They give a measure of what a dataset reveals, the accuracy the filter can reach, and an exact test of whether the network matters. Chicago burglaries, Texas COVID-19, and Weser-Ems measles illustrate the ideas. On both disease datasets, the model outforecast every competitor.
arxiv-2512-18884:
Moreno Bevilacqua, Xavier Emery, and Francisco Cuevas-Pacheco make it fast to simulate random landscapes with realistic correlation patterns. Gaussian random fields model everything from ore grades to rainfall, and generating them at scale with flexible covariance is a core computational chore. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, revisits the spectral turning-bands method and stretches it beyond the standard Matern family.

They add two newer correlation classes: Kummer-Tricomi, with polynomially decaying, long-range dependence, and Gauss-Hypergeometric, which allows correlations that cut off completely, including the Wendland family. Exact mixture representations make simulation stable and linear in cost. Tests confirm accuracy across parameter ranges, and a climate-data application uses the simulators for bootstrap error estimates and model choice. Large spatial studies get both speed and honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2512-18984:
Amlan Sinha and Ryne Beeson design spacecraft paths that stay safe when a thruster fails to fire on time. Their method works at two levels. The upper level plans a nominal low-thrust route with full control. Each lower level plans the best recovery move after a missed burn at some point along that route.

Under mild conditions, the two levels merge into a single problem that can be solved at once. The authors also prove a certificate that bounds how long a missed burn can last before the assumptions break. Tests show the bound is fast to check across many cases, though it does not capture every failure mode.
arxiv-2512-19384:
Valentin Irkhin and three co-authors report odd heat behavior in quadruple perovskites, a family of oxides with a crowded crystal cage. Their specific heat curves bend the wrong way, and a bell-shaped bump appears in a standard derived plot. The bump is strongest when copper or manganese sits at the cage's A site.

The authors read the anomaly as rattling: a loosely held ion shaking inside an oversized cage, a trick known from skutterudites and pyrochlores. First-principles calculations for the manganese member confirm such a mode directly. A pseudo-Jahn-Teller picture is offered as the qualitative mechanism behind the rattle.
arxiv-2512-19884:
Alex Cohen and Dmitrii Zakharov prove a result in additive combinatorics. The stage is the binary vector space. For a set A, its sumset A+A holds all sums of two members of A. Sets whose sumsets stay small are called moderate-doubling. Lore says such sets must hide a subspace-like shape.

The theorem makes that shape concrete. Take any set whose sumset is at most the set's size raised to a power just below two. It must meet some subspace in a large number of points. The subspace's dimension is only logarithmic in the set's size. The count of shared points is near the set's size raised to the matching power. Such results turn a bare size fact into clear structure.
arxiv-2512-20084:
Yanjie Li leads a seven-author team fusing a language model with a geometry-native network. The task is to predict how molecules stick to catalysts. Adsorption energy is the key yardstick for screening catalysts. It is the gap between a relaxed molecule-surface system and its reference state. Errors there poison all that follows. Graph networks handle 3D coordinates superbly. Language models give readable text, but blur unlike setups of the same system.

Their model, QE-Catalytic, couples a Qwen language model with an equivariant graph transformer. Graph and text channels are aligned, so 3D facts flow into the text side. The model predicts relaxed adsorption energies with much lower error than past text-based tools. It can also write crystal structure files. That serves target-driven inverse design of new catalysts.
arxiv-2512-20284:
Da-Yong Liu, Zhe Sun, Feng Lu, Wei-Hua Wang, and Liang-Jian Zou explain a puzzling pattern in iron-based superconductors. Experiments on iron pnictides and chalcogenides repeatedly find two domes of magnetic order and two domes of superconductivity in their phase diagrams. The origin of that doubled structure has stayed unclear.

Studying three representative systems, the authors propose a unified mechanism based on nearly degenerate orbitals. Anisotropic in-plane orbitals drive the first magnetic and superconducting domes. Isotropic orbitals, nearly degenerate thanks to an approximate symmetry, drive the second pair of domes. They also propose a matching rule linking spin and orbital modes in the pairing state. The picture supports an orbital-driven, orbital-selective view of these multi-orbital superconductors.
arxiv-2512-20384:
Darsana N and Sudhansu Sekhar Rout study when two polynomial sequences can take equal values. The equation sets one power-sum sequence at x equal to another at y, over a number field. Solutions amount to unlikely coincidences between the two families.

Applying the finiteness criterion of Bilu and Tichy, the authors show that under a suitable setup the equation has solutions without end whose denominators stay controlled in a precise counting sense. They also examine decomposable polynomials inside linear recurrence families. For third-order and certain binary recurrences, writing a term as a composition forces the outer factor's degree to be bounded. Such bounds limit how structured these sequences can be.
arxiv-2512-20484:
Anamika Pandey and T Raja Sekhar construct a delicate flow pattern in a realistic gas. The setting is the two-dimensional compressible Euler equations with a van der Waals equation of state, which captures non-ideal gas behaviour. Near sonic states, where flow speed meets sound speed, the non-ideal law strengthens nonlinear effects and complicates the analysis.

Working in the self-similar approach of the four-state Riemann problem, the authors build a supersonic sonic patch. This solution joins a strictly supersonic region to a sonic boundary along a pseudo-streamline. Characteristic decomposition plus a partial hodograph transform recasts the problem as a degenerate hyperbolic system. They prove a globally defined solution with uniform regularity up to the sonic curve, extending patch theory beyond ideal gases.
arxiv-2512-20684: Huan Xiao writes a short corrective note on a determinant that seemed to be about prime numbers. Pausinger had recently investigated a special determinant whose entries involve primes, suggesting number theory drives its value. Xiao points out that this family of determinants was already understood in linear algebra. Its evaluation has nothing to do with the primes at all. The same computation goes through regardless of the numbers involved.
arxiv-2512-20884:
Zan-Kai Chong, Hiroyuki Ohsaki, and Bryan Ng call language-model agents silent scholars: they read constantly but share nothing back. That one-way habit, termed epistemic asymmetry, forces every agent to redo reasoning and stalls collective learning. Private reflection habits lack any principled measure of when speaking up is worth it.

Their framework gives agents a selfish reason to share. Beliefs are tracked with a Beta-Bernoulli model that slowly forgets, so certainty decays unless refreshed by feedback. Agents gain most by publishing exactly where their uncertainty peaks. A caching scheme keeps fresh, fast-changing knowledge prioritized. In simulations with uneven knowledge distributions, the uncertainty-driven strategy clearly beat random sharing and adapted well when topics shifted.
arxiv-2512-21184:
A. Galoyan, A. Ribon, and V. Uzhinsky compute how often charmed particles emerge from nuclear collisions inside the Geant4 FTF model, a string-based simulation used across particle and nuclear physics. Their headline calculation gives the total yield of neutral D mesons in central xenon-lanthanum collisions at 150 GeV per nucleon, a regime where experiments have begun reporting charm production.

The model's yield lands close to other Monte Carlo predictions that omit quark-gluon plasma formation, and, like them, it falls substantially below the preliminary experimental data. The shortfall itself is the physics message: real nucleus-nucleus collisions appear to enhance charm production beyond what plasma-free models deliver. The authors also supply charm yields for proton-proton, deuteron-deuteron, and helium-helium collisions at the lower energies planned for the NICA/SPD experiment, giving that program concrete expectations to test.
arxiv-2512-21384:
Pavan Hosur, a condensed matter physicist, examines why superconducting diodes that work in equilibrium are rarely very efficient. A superconducting diode lets current flow more easily in one direction than the other, which could allow rectification, meaning turning alternating current into direct current, without wasting energy as heat.

Hosur shows that a perfect equilibrium diode is ruled out by the continuity of the free energy. Near-perfect behavior is possible only when the free energy develops singularities that soften the harder direction of current flow. He demonstrates the point with an exactly solvable Ising superconductor model. For smooth superconductors, standard Landau theory sets finite lower bounds on efficiency loss, and Josephson devices obey similar bounds. The high efficiencies reported in Josephson systems, he argues, come from phase constraints, metastable switching, or external drive, which step outside the equilibrium limits.
arxiv-2512-21484:
Yuanfang Yue and Yuetao Wang revisit a dark matter candidate, the higgsino-like neutralino of supersymmetry, and ask how light it could be. A pure higgsino needs a mass near one point one tera-electronvolts to match the dark matter abundance. Lighter options would be easier for experiments to reach.

In the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the authors add nearly mass-degenerate sleptons, partner particles sharing the thermal bath with the higgsino. Through coannihilation, where particle types convert into each other, the sleptons let a higgsino as light as about four hundred giga-electronvolts match the relic density. Recent LZ direct detection results push the floor up to roughly five hundred giga-electronvolts. The outcome depends sharply on the relative signs of two gaugino mass parameters. Same-sign choices are fully excluded by the newest LZ data, while opposite-sign choices survive because interference suppresses the detection rate.
arxiv-2512-21684:
Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, Md Zabirul Islam, and Ge Wang introduce SlideChain, a framework for making AI interpretations of lecture slides verifiable over time. Vision-language models now extract concepts from material, but different models, settings, and machines give inconsistent results. For high-stakes content, especially quantitative STEM and medical material, that drift undermines trust.

SlideChain builds its test on eleven hundred seventeen curated medical imaging lecture slides from a university course. Four leading vision-language models extracted concepts and relational triples from every slide. The framework stores provenance records for each extraction and anchors cryptographic hashes of them on a local Ethereum-compatible blockchain, making the records tamper-evident. The analysis itself is a finding: models disagreed sharply, with low concept overlap and near-zero agreement on relational triples for many slides. The system showed tamper detection and reproducible results across runs, at workable cost and throughput.
arxiv-2512-22084:
Data-driven models of dynamic systems break conservation laws the true system obeys. John M. Mango and Ronald Katende solve the repair problem for linear models. Given a learned operator and a constraint matrix encoding the invariants, the closest exactly-conserving matrix in Frobenius norm is an explicit orthogonal projection.

The correction is unique, low rank, and determined by the model's conservation violation; with a single invariant it reduces to a rank-one update. The authors prove the projection enforces exact conservation while perturbing the dynamics, and verify the properties on a Markov-type example. The mechanism is elementary and general, applicable to any learned linear model.
arxiv-2512-22284:
Ernest Fokoué proposes Fibonacci Ensembles, a way of combining machine learning models that takes its weights from the Fibonacci sequence. Ensemble methods like bagging, boosting, and random forests average many learners to steady their predictions. Fokoué adds two intertwined ideas: normalized Fibonacci weights, tempered by orthogonal tweaks and Rao-Blackwell tuning, to cut variance systematically, and a second-order recursive dynamic echoing the Fibonacci recurrence itself.

Controlled 1D regression tests used random Fourier feature groups and polynomial groups as base learners. In the regimes tested, Fibonacci weighting matched or improved on plain uniform averaging, and it interacted cleanly with orthogonal Rao-Blackwellization. The author presents the method as both sound and readable, a natural design point in ensemble theory.
arxiv-2512-22584:
Philipp J. di Dio and Lars-Luca Langer extend a classification from scalar polynomials to matrix-valued ones. A positivity preserver is a linear map that never sends a polynomial nonnegative on a set K to one that dips negative there. Di Dio and Schmüdgen had characterized all such maps for usual polynomials. Matrix coefficients complicate everything, because non-negativity becomes a matrix inequality at every point of K.

Working with Hermitian matrix polynomials, the authors characterize the matrix K-positivity preservers in two cases: when K is all of real space, and when K is compact. They discuss exactly how the matrix case differs from the real-coefficient case. They also pinpoint where their proof breaks down for general sets that are neither the whole space nor compact.
arxiv-2512-23584:
Subhash Chandra and Syed Abbas extend fractional calculus to functions whose values are sets rather than single numbers. They define the Riemann-Liouville fractional integral of a set-valued mapping through its integrable selections, meaning the ordinary functions that pick one point from each set. Fractional integrals of this kind arise when memory effects and uncertainty appear together.

The authors prove the basic traits of the new integral. It keeps sets convex, it stays bounded, and it shifts in step with the sets it acts on. Good behavior carries over too. If the first map varies in a bounded way or is Lipschitz, its integral acts the same way, and smooth selections of the integral exist under matching assumptions. In the scalar case, the pointwise minimum and maximum selections are identified as extremal. Possible applications to differential inclusions close the paper, which is slated for Fractional Calculus and Applied Analysis.
arxiv-2512-23884:
Hunor Csala and five co-authors build transformer surrogates that forecast the edge of a fusion plasma far faster than the physics codes. The scrape-off layer and divertor region decide how heat strikes the vessel walls, so designers need their dynamics. The standard simulator, SOLPS-ITER, is too slow for broad parameter scans or long transients.

Trained on SOLPS-ITER's own spatiotemporal output, the autoregressive transformers predict two-dimensional fields of electron temperature, density, and radiated power. Variants trained to roll out anywhere from one to one hundred steps at a time showed a clear pattern. Longer training horizons gave far more stable long forecasts, holding together over thousands of steps and tracking features such as moving high-radiation zones. The surrogates ran orders of magnitude faster than the original code, though accuracy degraded in physical regimes missing from the training data.
arxiv-2512-24884:
Abdellaoui, Abouelkhir, and Slaoui study quantum correlations in a hybrid qubit-qutrit system under noise. The system pairs a two-level and a three-level unit with axial symmetry, and its Hamiltonian structure is analyzed first. Two local noise types, dephasing and phase-flip channels, act on the parts in balanced and uneven setups.

Entanglement is measured by negativity, and broader quantum correlations by discord based on linear entropy, so the two can be compared as noise grows. Quantum information readers see which correlations survive which noise placement. Hybrid dimensions are attractive for coding, but only if their quantumness endures real-world places.
arxiv-2512-24984:
Jacob Bourjaily shows that scattering amplitudes in pure gauge theory and gravity, which lack supersymmetry, can still be grouped by general superfunctions far beyond tree level. At tree level, gluon and graviton amplitudes are efficiently pulled from fully supersymmetric theories, but loop fixes were expected to break that ease badly. Instead, all leading singularities of non-supersymmetric theories fit the general superfunction form.

Those functions differ from the fully supersymmetric ones only by an extent fixed by loop order and related data. Particle theory readers get lean codings of all helicity parts. The result keeps strong supersymmetric tracking useful for real-world theories like quantum chromodynamics and gravity.
arxiv-2601-00184:
Xue-Jia Yu, Limei Xu, and Hai-Qing Lin review topology in systems that sit at a quantum critical point. Topology gives a modern way to sort phases of matter. It goes beyond the older Landau picture. A common belief says topology dies when the bulk gap closes. Critical systems are gapless by nature. That belief would bar them from the story.

Recent work extends topology to exactly such gapless cases. The review covers critical points and stable critical phases. Both free and interacting systems are treated. Edge states can survive without a bulk gap. Topology can even split transitions that share one universality class. The authors write in a teaching style. They close with growth paths like higher dimensions and nonequilibrium cases. Modern experiments that might host these states get attention too. The textbook picture of phase change grows richer.
arxiv-2601-00284:
Neda Mohammadi, Soham Sarkar, and Piotr Kokoszka estimate the spectral density of a time series whose values are whole functions. Climate model output and brain scans produce such data. Each function sits on a huge grid of points. Older estimators build giant autocovariance matrices from that grid. At a hundred thousand grid points, the cost can become impossible.

Their estimator is a multilayer neural network instead. Spectral functional components guide its design. The authors prove it can approximate the true density under broad limits. Training skips the autocovariance kernels entirely. The work also splits across machines in parallel. Estimates then arrive much faster than before. Simulations check the method against known truth. A brain imaging application shows real data use. Large domain functional data gain a workable spectral tool.
arxiv-2601-00384:
Md Mahbub Hasan, Marcus Sternhagen, and Krishna Chandra Roy investigate cyberattacks on 3D printers used in aerospace, car making, and health care. The danger sits where design files meet machine control. Their 2026 paper studies a man-in-the-middle attack on two widely used fused deposition printers, in which an intruder alters the machine's movement file during upload.

Such tampering can produce parts that look right outside yet are weak inside, and normal software does not flag it. As a defense, the team builds an unsupervised detection system that reads machine logs during printing. A transformer-based encoder turns behavior into features, and later stages learn to spot anomalies. Tests show the system separates normal printing runs from compromised ones.
arxiv-2601-00484:
Ali Al-Bayaty and Marek Perkowski offer a new way to design quantum gates, the basic operations of a quantum computer. Gates for several qubits are normally built by multiplying large unitary matrices, which takes heavy computation and can yield gates with a high quantum cost. The Bloch sphere, a picture of a qubit's state, is usually only used afterward to check the result.

Their Bloch sphere approach instead uses the sphere as the design tool itself. Designers pick rotations visually on the sphere, guided by the layout the gate must respect, without multiplying matrices at all. The authors aim for gates that do the same job at lower cost, making the approach attractive for building larger multi-qubit operations by geometry rather than brute algebra.
arxiv-2601-00584:
Mingyu Jeon, Sunjae Yoon, Jonghee Kim, and Junyeoung Kim work on zero-shot video moment retrieval: given a sentence, find the matching segment inside a long, untrimmed video, without any task-specific training data. The core difficulty is a mismatch of granularity, since a short query describes a moment at a different level of detail than the video representations provide.

Earlier approaches leaned on strong pre-trained video and language models, but each side's knowledge arrived at a different semantic scale, so alignment suffered. Their framework, GranAlign, is training-free and explicitly bridges coarse and fine representations from the two modalities. By rebalancing granularity before matching, the method aims for more accurate localization of the requested moment in everyday videos.
arxiv-2601-00684:
Yuxi Wang, Charu Goel, and Wonkeun Chang report the first experimental fiber that guides light in a hollow core while filtering out one polarization. Hollow-core fibers carry light through air rather than glass, which suits precision photonics, but ordinary designs support both polarizations equally, so the polarization drifts under bending and other disturbances.

Their dual-ring antiresonant design couples the unwanted polarization into lossy cladding modes while letting the other pass. Over a ten-meter length the fiber reached a polarization extinction ratio above twenty-one decibels with propagation loss as low as the reported low value per meter. The design scales across wavelength bands and keeps its filtering under mechanical bending, a practical step toward stable polarized light delivery.
arxiv-2601-00984:
Mohadeseh Shafiei Kafraj, Dmitry Krotov, and Peter Latham expand the capacity of brain-like memory networks. An earlier biologically plausible two-layer associative memory could store a number of memories exponential in its visible neurons, but only linear in its hidden neurons. The bottleneck was a winner-take-all rule in the hidden layer: each hidden unit could encode just one whole memory.

Their network swaps that rule for a threshold nonlinearity, which permits distributed representations. Hidden neurons then encode basic components shared across many memories, and complex patterns arise as combinations of those parts. That change lifts the hidden-layer bottleneck while keeping the architecture biologically plausible, a step toward memory models whose storage scales the way the earlier theory promised.
arxiv-2601-01084:
Adari Rama Sukanya and three colleagues release a large drone image data set for tracking paddy rice crops in the Vijayawada region of Andhra Pradesh, India. Flights ran from the nursery stage through harvest. A twenty-megapixel color camera and a four-band sensor, covering red, green, red-edge, and near-infrared light, gathered the views.

The set holds more than forty-two thousand raw images, about four hundred fifteen gigabytes, over five acres at a ground detail of one centimeter per pixel. Each image carries location, flight height, and weather notes, and the team checked the data by building mosaic maps and plant health maps. Few existing sets cover every growth stage of Indian paddy at this detail. The release, posted on IEEE DataPort, can support work on targeted spraying, disease study, and yield forecasts.
arxiv-2601-01184:
Suryansh Singh Sijwali and Suman Saha train language models to write code that is both correct and safe. Models often produce code that runs but fails the required tests, or that slips in risky patterns. Their pipeline, SecureCodeRL, uses reinforcement learning with a reward that mixes function and security, and it gives partial credit along the way.

Partial credit rewards code for being valid, for running, and for printing output, even before it passes a full test. That steady signal keeps learning from stalling on hard tasks. In a small pilot study on held-out problems, the tuned model raised valid syntax from forty-five to sixty percent and was the only variant to pass any test. Its output also stayed clean under a standard security scanner. The authors stress the pilot scale, but the reward design is a useful template for safer code generation.
arxiv-2601-01284:
Sudhir Pandurang Rode studies how to pick out electrons in data from a planned particle physics experiment. The MPD detector at the NICA collider will study matter under extreme conditions, and clean electron signals are vital for work on pairs of electrons and their opposites. Older selection rules can lose good events.

Rode compares those rule-based cuts with two learning methods, a small neural network and a boosted decision tree. Both were trained in two ways, using all momenta together or in separate ranges. The study, reported at a 2025 seminar, aims for more real electrons kept while background stays low for later analysis.
arxiv-2601-01484:
Itai Morad, Nir Shlezinger, and Yonina Eldar study knowledge distillation, where a big teacher network trains a smaller student, through a Bayesian lens. Students usually learn from the teacher's soft probability outputs. The theory of why that helps, and how noise in those outputs hurts, has stayed murky. The authors analyze students trained by stochastic gradient descent in two regimes.

In the first, the teacher hands over the exact true class probabilities. Learning from them cuts variance and removes penalty terms that one-hot labels impose. In the second, the teacher's probabilities are noisy, and the analysis maps how that noise degrades accuracy and generalization. The moral is to use Bayesian teachers, which estimate those probabilities better. Experiments back it: students of Bayesian teachers gained up to about four percent accuracy and trained with up to thirty percent less noise in their convergence.
arxiv-2601-01684:
Search engines usually rank documents with dense vector models, but those demand large memory and graphics processors at query time. Zhichao Xu and seven co-authors present LACONIC. It is a family of learned sparse retrievers built on the Llama3 language model. The models come in one, three, and eight billion parameter sizes. They are meant to run well on ordinary hardware.

Training follows two phases: a weakly supervised stage that adapts the language model to read text in both directions, then a focused stage with carefully chosen hard negative examples. The largest version reached a leading score on the MTEB retrieval benchmark while using about seventy-four percent less index memory than a comparable dense model. Code and trained models are released openly.
arxiv-2601-01984:
Vision-language models can describe a scene yet stumble on where things are relative to each other. Weijian Ma and five co-authors give the model a blueprint. Before answering, the model writes a structured JSON record. It lists the relevant objects. Their positions, sizes, and attributes are included. The model then reasons over that record.

Three techniques make the blueprint useful. Reasoning traces embed blueprints during fine-tuning. Reinforcement learning rewards favor blueprints with the right number of objects. They also favor answers that match the blueprint. Augmentation perturbs images and questions to block shortcut answers. Across experiments, the method beat general vision-language models. It also beat specialized spatial reasoning systems.
arxiv-2601-02284:
Phusuda Thanankullaphong and three co authors test a dark energy model with two fields acting together, one normal field called quintessence and one phantom field with opposite behavior. Together they form what is known as quintom dark energy. The setting is a flat expanding universe, with an exponential potential for one field and an inverse power law for the other.

Rewriting the equations as a five dimensional dynamical system lets them find the fixed points and check which ones attract the universe at late times. The stable endings give phantom dominated expansion that speeds up. They then fit the model with the Cobaya tool to supernova, microwave background, and new DESI distance data. The data mildly favor this changing dark energy over a fixed constant.
arxiv-2601-02584:
Zhenwei Xu, Ulrich Kuhl, and Nicolas Noiray test how self sustained oscillators synchronize when the force driving them changes over time. Locking under a steady drive is well understood. But theory predicts something stranger under slow modulation, an intermittent locking regime beyond the usual locking boundaries, with the phase holding for stretches and then slipping briefly.

Their test bed is a controllable aeroacoustic oscillator, a whistle with a robust limit cycle, driven by programmable acoustic forcing whose frequency or amplitude is slowly modulated. Three regimes appear in the experiments, strict synchronization, intermittent locking with alternating locked stretches and brief slips, and no locking, with regular slips. The observations match the theoretical predictions for modulated forcing, extending the science of locking beyond the steady drive case.
arxiv-2601-02984:
Martin Perešíni and three co-authors simulate selfish mining, an attack where a blockchain miner hides found blocks to gain unfair advantage, when several attackers run at once. Most earlier work studied a single selfish miner on one protocol. The authors build a stochastic simulation framework that can run multi-attacker scenarios across different proof-of-work consensus designs.

They model the standard Nakamoto consensus as a baseline, plus Fruitchain and Strongchain, two protocols designed to blunt selfish mining. The simulations confirm thresholds reported in the literature and uncover new ones for two or more attackers. The team released the framework's source code, so researchers can add new protocols and compare them against the modeled ones on equal terms.
arxiv-2601-03084:
Mohsen Kazemian and Jürgen Jasperneite predict wireless channels for fast-moving users in future 6G networks that use OTFS modulation. At high speed, Doppler spread and shifting paths make the channel change so fast that pilot-based estimates go stale and waste overhead. Their method, CVAE4CP, is built on a conditional variational autoencoder. That is a generative model that learns how data is spread out.

The model learns how the channel values in the delay-Doppler domain are spread, given the physical setup and the speed of motion. So it can forecast future values before they occur. A compact latent code keeps the channel's built-in uncertainty clear. In wide tests under high-speed conditions, the method beat a rival learning-based baseline again and again. The authors offer it as a step toward reliable decoding in OTFS systems.
arxiv-2601-03884:
Sanidhya Ghosal and three co-authors built FLNet, a deep learning system that assesses flood damage to crops from satellite images, to speed government relief in India. Manual damage surveys are slow and biased, while satellite methods battle cloud cover and coarse resolution. FLNet first uses super-resolution to sharpen Sentinel-2 images from ten meter to three meter detail, then classifies the damage in the enhanced images.

Tested on the Bihar Flood Impacted Croplands dataset, the sharpening step clearly improved detection of the critical full damage category. Its score nearly matched what commercial high-resolution imagery achieved, without the commercial price. The authors present the approach as cost-effective and scalable, a candidate for a nationwide shift from manual surveys to automated, high-fidelity assessment after floods, when relief decisions cannot wait for field teams.
arxiv-2601-04384: Aaron Berger, Ross Berkowitz, Pat Devlin, and Van Vu prove new anti-concentration results for sums shuffled by chance, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Classical results of this kind study a weighted sum whose random signs or coefficients are independent, and bound how unlikely the total is to land near any single value. Their version replaces the independent randomness with a random permutation: fixed weights are reassigned to fixed values in uniformly random order. And the paper establishes concentration bounds for the resulting sum.
arxiv-2601-04584:
Behzad Aalipur works out how the eigenvalues of large random graph matrices fluctuate, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is the dense graphon model, where a limit function generates random graphs and its integral operator's eigenvalues are the population values that finite graphs approximate. He studies modes tied to simple, isolated nonzero eigenvalues, and assumes no smoothness of the graphon at all.

The limit law turns on one quantity: the variance of the squared population eigenfunction. When it is positive, the scaled eigenvalue fluctuation is Gaussian. When it vanishes, the first-order term disappears and the limit becomes a weighted series of centred chi-square variables. The theory even covers degenerate modes whose eigenfunctions are constant in size but flip sign, a case continuous graphons forbid but a simple two-block model already exhibits. Adjacency matrices inherit the same limits, with Bernoulli edge noise washing out at the relevant scale.
arxiv-2601-04884:
Issa Hanou and 3 co-authors precompute help for multi-agent path replanning in a 2026 paper. When one agent in a coordinated plan is delayed, conflicts with other agents follow, and a new safe plan is needed fast. Replanning only the delayed agent can be inefficient or even infeasible, while replanning everyone risks cascading changes and heavy computation.

The authors track the temporal flexibility of other agents: how long each can be delayed without causing new conflicts. Using that slack, they replan a single delayed agent efficiently while avoiding cascades. The approach suits warehouses and traffic systems, where one stalled robot or vehicle should not force a costly rethink of every other agent's route.
arxiv-2601-05684:
Hongyaoxing Gul and 3 co-authors present FLRQ, a 2026 method for quantizing large language models faster with flexible low-rank approximation. Quantization shrinks models and speeds inference. Low-rank post-training methods can help, but choosing one compromise rank for every layer wastes potential and usually needs costly fine-tuning.

The authors first analyze how low-rank effectiveness varies across layers. Their system then selects an accuracy-optimal rank per layer using a fast sketch-based approximation that notices outliers. A second component minimizes quantization error under scaling and clipping through iteration. Combined, the pieces reportedly deliver leading quantization quality and algorithm efficiency across comprehensive experiments, giving practitioners a quicker route to smaller, still-accurate models.
arxiv-2601-05984:
Sahibzada Saadoon Hammad and 4 co-authors organize in 2026 the anomaly detection for Internet of Things temperature sensors around communities of similar stations. Large sensor networks monitor cities and settings in real time, but training one model per station is wasteful. Grouping devices by day-to-day and setting similarity offers a sharing plan.
