On public benchmarks GRAFT beats baselines on both discrimination and calibration while staying sparse under noise, a combination clinicians and biostatisticians should welcome.
arxiv-2602-08484:
Tracking a sound source usually needs array-processing math or costly labeled positions. Luan Vinícius Fiorio and five co-authors build a model that learns tracking with no labels at all, guided by physics. Their arXiv paper pairs a variational encoder with a decoder that injects geometry through time-delay likelihoods between microphone pairs.

Directions are estimated straight from array signals, with no ground-truth positions in training. Tests on real data show the method beating classical baselines and matching supervised models on accuracy and cost. It also handles mismatched array shapes and corrupted microphone-position data robustly. Readers get an unsupervised tracker that carries its physics with it, plus a sketched path to multiple sources.
arxiv-2602-08784:
Self-driving cars need accurate bird's-eye-view maps of vehicles, roads, and lane markings, and radar can help cameras where vision alone falters. Santiago Montiel-Marín and five co-authors propose GaussianCaR, which repurposes Gaussian splatting as a universal view transformer for camera-radar fusion. Their arXiv paper maps camera pixels and radar returns into one shared top-down view.

Multi-scale fusion plus a transformer decoder extracts top-down features end to end for segmentation. On the nuScenes dataset, the method matches or beats leading fusion methods on vehicles, roads, and lane dividers, while running over three times faster. Code and a project page are available online. Readers get an efficient fusion design for safe navigation in complex traffic.
arxiv-2602-09084:
Professional image editing demands restraint: change only what the user asked, across many turns, at full resolution. Ruijie Ye and twelve co-authors identify three pain points, over-editing, single-turn models, and low-resolution evaluation, and answer with Agent Banana, a hierarchical planner-executor agent. Context Folding compresses long histories into structured memory, while Image Layer Decomposition edits locally to protect untouched regions at native resolution.

A new benchmark, HDD-Bench, offers dialogue-based tasks with verifiable stepwise targets on native 4K images. Agent Banana leads on multi-turn consistency and background fidelity while staying competitive on instruction following, and holds up on standard single-turn tests. The work pushes agentic editing toward professional reliability.
arxiv-2602-09284:
Medical scan sets are prized and open to abuse: unapproved use raises copy and ethics worries, yet owner checks built for everyday photos fail on sharp scans with fine body detail. Pranav Kulkarni and two co-authors propose X-Mark, a case-specific clean-label marking way for chest X-ray copy shielding. A gated U-Net makes one-off jolts inside key zones of each scan.

A multi-part training goal weighs mark power, toughness to live resizing, checkup quality, and visual fineness, with Laplacian smoothing punishing high-rate flaws for size freedom. Black-box checking spots telling conduct in suspect models. On CheXpert, X-Mark hits a 100 percent mark hit rate and cuts false alarms in one case by 12 percent, fending off adaptive raids.
arxiv-2602-09484:
Short-video apps preload upcoming clips to prevent stalls, but aggressive preloading wastes data while cautious preloading stalls more. Liming Liu and two co-authors break that tradeoff with PromptPream, a 2026 paradigm that swaps computation for bandwidth. Instead of sending pixel-level video chunks, it sends compact semantic prompts that local generative models decode into high-quality frames.

Three techniques enable the design: gradient-based prompt inversion compressing frames into small token sets, a compute-aware scheduler balancing network and processor use, and a scalable search method for the enlarged scheduling space. Evaluations show stalls and bandwidth waste each falling by nearly a third, with viewing quality rising by nearly half against traditional strategies. The paper thus turns local generation into a bandwidth saver.
arxiv-2602-09684:
Jun-Hao Zhang and two co-authors study the S-wave spectral structure of heavy-light systems holding a single top quark. The work is motivated by a recent near-threshold enhancement in top-quark pair production from CMS and ATLAS. Their 2026 paper treats top-light, top-charm, and top-bottom systems via instant Bethe-Salpeter math. Because the top quark decays far faster than typical hadronization time, discrete eigenvalues are read as model-dependent reference positions of possible quasi-bound configurations, not predictions for fully formed conventional hadrons.

Number results place the masses of these configurations close to the top-quark mass. For the top-bottom system, the first four S-wave states sit roughly five to six giga-electronvolts above the top-quark mass; for top-charm, roughly two to three. Production and decay patterns are discussed briefly in qualitative terms, as reference for future studies or tests.
arxiv-2602-09784:
Circuit finding and firing steering in transforms have grown as apart research threads, yet both work on the same picture space. Andres Saurez and two co-authors ask whether they are two views of one deep structure in their 2026 paper. They show both follow a single shape principle: answer tokens, run alone, encode the ways that would produce them. This Circuit Print guess enables circuit finding without gradients or causal meddling, finding matching structure to gradient-based methods through shape match alone.

Tests on standard benchmarks across four model kinds show circuit finding scores matching gradient-based methods. The same ways that spot circuit parts also enable guided steering, reaching nearly seventy percent emotion sorting scores against about fifty-three percent for prompt prompting, while keeping factual scores. Reading and steering thus appear as two facets of one shape object.
arxiv-2602-09884:
Configuration spaces collect every possible arrangement of robots moving through a graph under constraints. Alessia Revelli and Steven Scheirer introduce Grouped Stirling complexes, a new kind of configuration space, in their 2026 paper. Robots are placed in groups with two rules. Each vertex must host one robot at minimum, while two robots sharing a group must have at least one full open edge lying between them.

The space has a closed cell structure, meaning it can be built from cells of various dimensions. The main results show the space is path-connected whenever there are at least three groups, and they determine the number of cells in certain cases. The paper thus gives a tractable model of grouped motion on graphs, with connectivity and cell counts pinned down for the cases treated.
arxiv-2602-09984:
Quantum theory is usually taken as a starting point, but it can also be rebuilt from rules about inference. A 2026 paper by Fabricio Souza Luiz and Marcos César de Oliveira develops such a reconstruction from inference over action space. Its core object is a density of action states counting the dynamical alternatives between configurations.

Maximum-entropy inference imposes a finite resolution scale in action, below which contributions blur together. From that blur, plus normalization and additivity, complex amplitudes and unitary evolution emerge as the minimal consistent description. The Lagrangian, the structure of Hilbert space, and the Schrödinger equation then follow as derived results, with the action scale fixed by experiment.
arxiv-2602-10084:
Type Ia supernovae are thermonuclear runaways of white dwarfs in binaries, prized as cosmic distance markers yet still mysterious. A 2026 paper led by Santiago González-Gaitán, with six co-authors, compares narrow sodium absorption lines in a large supernova sample against light-curve, spectrum, and setting data. Sodium absorption runs stronger in younger, more star-forming, central events, as expected.

Crucially, an inborn link survives apart from setting. Clustering recovers an old population with low extinction and normal ejecta velocity. The young group splits into highly extincted, high-velocity events with strong blue-shifted sodium and low-extinction, normal-velocity events with little sodium. The authors read this as lopsided light from young events hitting nearby material, viewed from different angles.
arxiv-2602-10284:
A recent paper on the SOL2012-06-03 flare reported two distinct phases of high-energy gamma radiation as a first, but two-phase emission had been seen before, first in SOL1982-06-03. A 2026 paper by Gerald H. Share and Ronald J. Murphy provides evidence that the second SOL2012-06-03 pion-decay peak marks the onset of Late Phase Gamma-Ray Emission lasting over eight minutes. That delay from the impulsive X-ray peak matches the time flare-produced suprathermal protons need to overtake the expanding coronal mass ejection and gain acceleration at its shock.

The high accelerated ion-electron ratio in SOL2012-06-03 and other late-phase events matches ratios in gradual solar energetic particle events produced by shocks, not ratios typical of impulsive flares or reconnection-driven events. The paper thus ties late-phase gamma rays to shock acceleration of protons above three hundred megaelectronvolts from coronal mass ejections.
arxiv-2602-10384:
Vision-language models handle many document tasks well, but their reliability in specialized, non-English finance documents is far less tested. A 2026 paper led by Virginie Mouilleron, with three co-authors, introduces Scribe Finance, the first multimodal benchmark for French finance documents. The dataset holds over twelve hundred expert-validated questions on text extraction, table reading, chart interpretation, and multi-turn reasoning. Six open-weight models, from eight to one hundred twenty-four billion parameters, face a language-model judge.

Models score strongly on text and table tasks, at about eighty-five to ninety percent. They struggle with charts, landing between about a third and three-fifths. Multi-turn dialogue exposes a sharper failure: early mistakes spread across turns, driving accuracy down to roughly half regardless of model size. Current models thus serve well-defined extraction tasks but stay brittle in interactive, multi-step financial analysis, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2602-10484:
Zhaowen Wang and two co-authors develop a way to estimate systemic risk when two factors rarely crash jointly in a 2026 paper. CoVaR measures a high quantile of one factor given that a related factor is extreme. It is a standard tool in quantitative risk management, but data in the joint tail are thin by definition.

The authors work within bivariate extreme value theory for asymptotically independent pairs. They model the extremal structure parametrically to squeeze information from sparse tail data, and they prove the resulting estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Simulations support the method, and an application to United States stock returns produces dynamic CoVaR forecasts that risk managers can use.
arxiv-2602-10784:
Rouven Michels and two co-authors forecast defensive schemes in American football in a 2026 paper. Anticipating man versus zone coverage is crucial for offenses, yet defenders disguise assignments before the snap, making real-time recognition hard. Player tracking data offer a window into those disguised intentions.

The team integrates supervised and unsupervised learning in a number system. Elastic net logistic fitting and slope-boosted trees forecast coverage in stages. They start from pre-motion traits, add motion paths, and finally use traits derived from a hidden Markov model. That model infers latent defensive assignments between offensive and defensive players during motion. The system shows how tracking data can decode disguise before the ball moves.
arxiv-2602-10984:
Designing new molecules is slow because good candidates are rare and costly to test. Serra Korkmaz and seven co-authors propose Joint Self-Improvement, a method that pairs a molecule generator with a property predictor in one joint model. The pairing keeps the predictor honest as search drifts to new regions.

A self-improving sampling step then steers the generator with the predictor at run time, so fresh candidates lean toward strong predicted scores. Tests on offline and online molecule tasks show the method beats leading rivals when test budgets are tight. The gain matters most where each lab test costs time and money, and where a few strong candidates beat many weak ones.
arxiv-2602-11084:
Medical forecast needs trait sets that are small, stable, and readable. Yuheng Luo and two co-authors offer GRASP, which pairs Shapley attribution with group sparsity to pick such sets. Importance scores are distilled from a pretrained tree model, then a group-regularized logistic model enforces structured sparsity.

Compared with LASSO, SHAP, and deep methods, GRASP matches or beats predictive scores while using fewer, less redundant, and more stable traits. The gain matters in clinics, where a model must justify its inputs and keep working as data shifts. The frame targets patient forecast tasks where trust and parsimony count as much as raw score.
arxiv-2602-11184:
Mixture-of-experts models are powerful but huge, and naive compression breaks them. Zukang Xu and four co-authors present KBVQ-MoE, a vector rounding frame for ultra-low-bit compression of expert models. It tackles two faults: repeated rounding of similar experts, and bias growth when expert outputs aggregate.

A transform-guided decomposition extracts shared dominant components across experts, while rounding touches only expert-specific parts. Channel-wise affine correction then steadies the quantized outputs. In tests, three-bit rounding of a Qwen expert model nearly matched its full-precision scores. The method aims to make large expert models runnable on edge devices and other tight platforms.
arxiv-2602-11284:
One-way traffic for quantum signals usually needs chiral waveguides. Zhenghao Zhang and two co-authors show that a Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya contact can engineer nonreciprocity in an otherwise achiral waveguide system. Two qubits coupled to a 1D waveguide, driven coherently, gain tunable one-way conduct controlled by drive, detuning, and contact phase.

Beyond transmission, the contact yields nonreciprocal linkage and photon bunching. At special pure-state points, decohering channels drop out and transparency becomes perfect and power-independent. Away from those points, phase control drives strong linkage nonreciprocity, and superbunching shifts from transmission to reflection. The work offers a versatile resource for isolators, routers, and novel light sources.
arxiv-2602-11584:
Shrinking gradients to cut communication is standard practice in federated learning, where models train across many devices, and it is usually assumed to cost almost nothing. Yujie Gu and three co-authors show the price is real: compression sharpens the loss landscape, especially when device data differ widely, which can hurt how well the trained model generalizes. A known fix, sharpness-aware minimization, seeks flat minima but misjudges the needed correction when data are heterogeneous.

Their remedy, FedSynSAM, builds synthetic data from the global model trajectory to estimate that correction more accurately, even under compression. The paper establishes convergence for the new algorithm and backs it with extensive experiments. The message is pointed: in federated learning, cheaper messages can quietly make models worse, unless the training method accounts for the damage.
arxiv-2602-11684:
Simulated patients help train counselors and scale therapy assessment, but the field is fragmented. Different teams use incompatible profiles, prompts, and scoring rules, which blocks fair comparison and reuse. Sahand Sabour and two co-authors build PatientHub, a unified modular framework that standardizes how language-model patients are created, simulated, and judged.

The framework offers sixteen patient simulators, a graph-based orchestrator for multi-turn and multi-session chats, and a configurable judge that scores against varied rubrics. A command-line tool lets users generate profiles, run sessions, and apply turn- and session-level evaluation. Tests under one shared protocol compare supported simulators, and a new variant prototyped with little extra code shows the design extends easily.
arxiv-2602-11784:
Pinching-antenna systems reshape wireless channels by placing antennas along dielectric waveguides, but guides fail and get repaired, and that churn affects service. Chongjun Ouyang and four co-authors build a unified framework for upkeep in which guide lifetime and repair time follow exponential distributions. Guide state follows a two-state Markov chain over time. Chances of moving between states, and long-run chances, are worked out.

Folding state churn into data rate, the method measures upkeep by the chance of nonzero rate and outage chance. It is applied to a standard single long guide system and to a segmented system with many short segments under two protocols, segment switching and segment aggregation. Closed-form expressions and scaling laws show both segmented protocols beat the standard design, with aggregation stronger than switching, and the gain grows with segment count.
arxiv-2602-11884:
Large decaying kink oscillations of coronal loops are shaped by nonlinear Kelvin-Helmholtz instability and turbulence, yet theory and proof remain limited. Sihui Zhong and two co-authors test a recent theory of damping by turbulence using 3D magnetohydrodynamic simulations and modeled UV images. Simulated cases show time-varying shifts and damping rates consistent with the theory.

They also show higher-order modes, slightly longer periods than the linear kink period, and reduced displacement amplitudes. Those features are largely preserved in synthetic views, though resolving higher modes needs finer resolution than available today. Hotter channels prove more sensitive to boundary dynamics, decaying faster with smaller shifts and larger phase shifts than cooler channels. Early agreement between simulated and synthetic cases is close, while later gaps reflect turbulence skew. Bayesian fitting pins down initial amplitude and kink period firmly, but damping-profile parameters stay tangled, so more observables would aid inference.
arxiv-2602-11984:
Primitive axial algebras have several competing notions of radical, and their links were unclear. Andrey Mamontov and two co-authors compare three of them for an axial algebra with a Frobenius form. The three are the largest ideal containing none of the axes, the radical of the form itself, and the Jacobson radical, defined here simply as the intersection of all maximal ideals.

The paper contributes to the structure theory of these systems by setting the three radicals side by side and working out how they relate. For readers of axial algebra theory, that comparison clarifies which radical carries which facts, and where the three notions agree or part ways.
arxiv-2602-12084:
Comparing two systems that behave in shades of gray, rather than simply pass or fail, calls for a distance rather than a yes-or-no verdict. Jonas Forster and four co-authors build a single framework for such distances and the logics that describe them. It centers on modalities that lift plain yes-or-no properties into graded ones.

The classic example is the probability operator, which turns a property of outcomes into a probability over distributions. Their main results give fast, polynomial-time ways to extract distinguishing formulas in two logics. One is two-valued, with satisfaction allowed up to a small slack; the other is fully graded. The results cover Markov-chain distances, metric transition systems, and fuzzy systems, including a new extraction result for epsilon-bisimulation distance.
arxiv-2602-12184:
When heavy nuclei collide at high energy, photon pairs can reveal the size and shape of the fireball, much as starlight reveals stellar size. Dariusz Miśkowiec led this work with one co-author, Klaus Reygers, on photon femtoscopy in one, two, and three dimensions. The idea has been discussed for years, but few tests were possible because photon counts were too low.

Better detectors and electronics now bring the method within reach, so the paper turns to a practical choice: which motion variables should feed the two-photon correlation function. The authors argue against using invariant momentum alone, and in favour of pairing it with energy difference. That choice shapes how future photon femtoscopy results should be read.
arxiv-2602-12384:
Deep networks trained by gradients show a strong implicit bias, yet tractable maths for that bias usually needs balanced deep linear models. Nathanaël Haas led this work with three co-authors, proposing two testable signatures of deep Jacobians instead. One is depth-induced exponential scaling of ordered singular values. The other is strong spectral separation.

Viewing piecewise-linear networks through fixed gates, Jacobians become products of masked linear maps within one activation region. The team proves Lyapunov exponents govern top singular values at initialisation, gives closed forms in a tractable masked model, and quantifies finite-depth corrections. Strong separation then forces singular-vector alignment in matrix products, yielding a roughly shared singular basis for intermediate Jacobians. Experiments in fixed-gate settings confirm scaling, alignment, and decoupled dynamics, supporting low-rank Jacobian structure as a driver of implicit bias.
arxiv-2602-12784:
Nonlinear Schrödinger-Poisson-Slater equations model quantum systems with long-range interactions, but finding their solutions in the right function space is delicate. Artur Jorge Marinho, Carlo Mercuri, and Kanishka Perera prove existence and multiplicity results for a zero-mass version of the problem in Coulomb-Sobolev spaces. Their method is a new scaling approach in critical point theory, which sorts the nonlinearity's behaviour at zero and at infinity by scaling traits.

At the heart of the argument sits a scaling-invariant equation, read as a nonlinear eigenvalue problem, whose eigenvalues come from a cohomological index. That index yields fresh critical group estimates and linking sets beyond the reach of classical genus methods. The number of solutions turns out to hinge on resonance with those eigenvalues, echoing the classical Fredholm alternative in a nonlinear setting, across a broad range of parameters.
arxiv-2602-13184:
Raw odds fits extract maximum information from data, but scanning regular doubts across many factors is too much for machines. Davide Valsecchi, with two co-authors, offers a mock run-based fitting system lifting the fit target beyond scalar settings, toward a many-factor spread of focus, a learnable two-way change of feature space. Factor-style scaling flows model regular shifts as setting-based warps without combo blow-up.

A spread-out training plan learns how the spread depends on nuisance settings in a single tuning. It skips repeat training during odds scans. A Poisson-bootstrap ensemble captures finite-sample variance of the neural spread, folded in through a mean odds, giving a complete number-based-plus-regular budget in one raw odds. Checked on mock high-energy-physics-like data, the method extends strict, fully scanned raw reading to complete fine-grained spreads, joining tuning to opening tasks.
arxiv-2602-13284:
Moltbook is a social platform used only by AI agents, and this is the first large study of what its agents actually did. Over nine days, 27,269 agents posted 137,485 times and left 345,580 comments. Within three to five days they formed governance, economies, tribal identities, and organized religion, with pro-human sentiment outweighing anti-human sentiment 21 to 1.

Safety findings cut the other way: 28.7 percent of content touched safety themes, social engineering beat prompt injection as an attack style, and hostile posts drew six times the engagement of normal ones. Yet the social life looked hollow up close, with only 4.1 percent reciprocity and 88.8 percent shallow comments. Yunbei Zhang leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13484:
Filters that test set membership in tiny space, from Bloom filters onward, now come in three new flavors. Learned filters train a model to separate members from non-members, stacked filters cascade layers using negative workload samples, and adaptive filters update themselves on false positive feedback. Each was tested alone, leaving trade-offs unclear. This paper gives the first head-to-head evaluation across real data sets and query workloads.

Learned filters cut false positives up to a hundredfold but vary widely, falter on skewed or shifting workloads, and run up to ten thousand times slower per query. Stacked filters cut false positives up to a thousandfold on skewed workloads but need workload knowledge, while adaptive filters match that cut under hostile queries with no workload assumptions. Diandre Miguel Sabale leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13784:
Explaining with examples is intuitive, but it is hard to grasp how a decision value should change relative to examples differing across many features by large amounts. Real estate valuation offers a model: known-value examples, are adjusted in theory attribute by attribute, with values changed as needed based on factors. Comparables XAI adapts that practice for AI explanations, with Trace adjustments tracing what-if changes from each match to the subject, one attribute at a time, steadily along the AI feature space.

In modeling and user studies, Trace-adjusted matches achieved the highest explanation truth and precision, user accuracy, and narrowest error ranges, compared with linear regression, adjusted matches, or plain matches. The work thus supplies a new analytic basis for example-based explanations that improve user grasp of AI decisions. Yifan Zhang leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13884:
S. G. Porsev and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv paper that predicts energy levels of the highly charged ion Cf17+ for a future optical clock. Such ions resist outside disturbance and react strongly to shifts in the fine-structure constant, but experiments need exact wavelengths to find their clock transitions.

Treating Cf17+ as a single-valence ion, the authors ran relativistic coupled-cluster calculations, adding nonlinear single-double terms and valence and core triple excitations. They also weighed quantum-electrodynamic corrections and basis truncation effects. The results pin down the low-lying spectrum and the 5f to 6p clock transition, with core-valence links and iterative triples proving decisive for precision.
arxiv-2602-14084:
Alexander Zhou and four co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv problem in signed social networks. In such networks, triangles of friends and foes test structural balance theory. Yet true edge signs are rarely known at scale, so signs must be guessed with varying confidence.

The paper adapts balanced and unbalanced triangles to uncertain signs, modeled as probabilities. It gives a baseline and a faster exact counting method that uses edge probabilities to shrink the search. It also tests sampling methods for rough counts, with the improved exact method speeding each sample so queries run up to a hundred times faster. Tests on real networks check both speed and sampling quality.
arxiv-2602-14184:
Guangyu Yu and one co-author offer a 2026 arXiv theory of fractional Chern insulators in real space. Band shape and quantum shape have guided the field, but the paper recasts these blocks through mixed bosons: electrons bound to their energetically barred nearby slots. The key step builds a radially ordered, most-local base for Chern bands with no need for round symmetry.

In that base, the many-body problem drops to a simple rule: a calm block occurs when barred slots around central electrons maximize two-body push energy. Direct number tests on the Haldane model back mixed boson birth and confirm the rule. The setup also bridges the fractional quantum Hall effect in smooth and lattice settings, giving one plain real-space picture.
arxiv-2602-14284:
Evelyn Hughes and one co-author benchmark a 2026 arXiv question: can AI models complete end-to-end data science projects? Data science blends technical, analytical, communication, and ethical skills, yet current benchmarks mostly test isolated parts. The team built 40 end-to-end projects with rubric evaluations and an automated grading pipeline.

Results varied considerably by model. Newer models handled structured tasks well, but they split sharply on tasks needing judgment. The findings suggest models can approximate entry-level data scientists on routine work, but they still require verification. The benchmark exposes where end-to-end competence breaks down, beyond narrow skill tests.
arxiv-2602-14384:
Vsevolod Biryukov and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv sorting system for matter data. AI in materials science needs data rules that grasp real forms, including faces, joins, flaws, and size drops. M-CODE, or Matter Sorting via Ontology, Size and Change, links field words to reusable ideas and provenance-aware shifts.

Forms are sorted by size, shape tangle from pristine to flawed and worked forms, and variants that grasp common making and change routes. An open-source build gives JSON schemas, cases, and Python and TypeScript types, backing repeatable data set making, checks, and group gifts. The tight system aims to make matter data sets alike and reusable across groups.
arxiv-2602-14884:
A. S. Sukhanov and colleagues probe electron-phonon coupling in EuAl4 under hydrostatic pressure, using inelastic X-ray scattering in diamond anvils. The rare-earth intermetallic hosts a complex magnetic phase diagram with a centrosymmetric skyrmion lattice, and its charge-density wave transition at 142 kelvin was earlier shown to be driven by momentum-dependent coupling.

Under pressure that coupling is renormalised and suppressed across the temperature-pressure phase diagram, the team reports, confirming its crucial role in forming the charge-density wave. Squeezing a skyrmion host tunes the very interaction that orders its charge. Pressure becomes a dial on electron-lattice interplay.
arxiv-2602-15084:
Boschi and colleagues present TokaMind, billed as the first open-source foundation model for tokamak plasma dynamics. It rests on a multi-modal transformer pretrained on mixed diagnostics from the public MAST data set. The model handles time series, 2D profiles, and videos at different sampling rates, copes with missing signals, and adapts to new tasks by loading and freezing four model parts in selective fashion.

Signals are encoded with a light fixed-basis discrete cosine transform embedding, with a clean interface for alternatives such as variational autoencoders. On the TokaMark benchmark of 14 reconstruction and forecasting tasks, fine-tuned TokaMind beats the strongest baseline on all but one task. Warm-start adaptation helps most on hard downstream settings such as long-horizon forecasting and high-dimensional equilibrium goals, and code plus weights are public.
arxiv-2602-15184:
Ma and colleagues improve neural operators with fundamental physics knowledge. They serve as powerful stand-ins for tracking dynamic change in systems governed by partial differential equations. Older methods focus on learning runs from the target equation, often missing deeper principles behind it. Taking a cue from solvers, which handle varied settings of such systems, the team offers multiphysics training that learns jointly from full forms and their simple basic forms.

The framework boosts data economy, cuts forecast errors, and improves out-of-distribution transfer, notably under shifts of parameters and synthetic-to-real transfer. It works across designs and shows steady gains in scaled root mean square error across many one-, two-, and three-dimensional problems. Tests show that direct use of basic physics knowledge greatly strengthens neural operator transfer.
arxiv-2602-15584:
Armangeon and colleagues build a public data set for a tedious industrial task: lining up functional schematics with photos and 3D scans of old plants that lack native digital models. Manual alignment from images and LiDAR does not scale, schematics often clash with reality, and public industrial data are scarce. Their IRIS-v2 set aims to fill that gap for digital twin research.

It bundles images, point clouds, annotated 2D boxes and segmentation masks, a CAD model, 3D pipe routing data, and the piping and instrumentation diagram. A case study tests alignment by pairing segmentation with graph matching, with the goal of cutting the time the task takes. Researchers building digital twins for ageing facilities gain a realistic, fully stocked test bed.
arxiv-2602-15784:
Deligkas and colleagues introduce graphical distance preservation games, a new class of network allocation games. A graph, called a topology, hosts agents that must be placed at vertices, and each agent has an ideal distance, possibly different, at which to sit from some other agents. Given an allocation, each agent suffers a cost equal to the sum of differences from ideal distances for agents in their subset. The question is whether a stable allocation exists, where no agent wants to move.

Three stability notions are studied: envy-freeness, swap stability, and jump stability. The paper performs a full study of complexity by parameter along three dimensions: graph topology, agent count, and tastes. Game theorists gain a new placement game that ties stable placements to geometry, with complexity mapped across shape, numbers, and tastes.
arxiv-2602-15984:
De Santi and colleagues push generative flow models past the data they were trained on. Flow and diffusion models learn from limited samples, such as known molecules, and so generate only a narrow slice of the valid design space. For scientific discovery, the prize lies outside that slice, in designs that are valid yet unseen.

Their fix is a verifier, a checker like an atomic bond test, that steers a pretrained flow toward new territory without breaking validity. They define strong and weak verifiers, frame global and local expansion as probability space optimization, and build Flow Expander, a mirror descent scheme with convergence guarantees. Tests on visual examples and a molecular task show wider conformer diversity with validity intact.
arxiv-2602-16284:
Adam Zweiger and coauthors tackle the key-value cache bottleneck in scaling language models to long contexts. In deployed settings, long contexts are usually compacted in token space via summarization, but summarization can prove highly lossy and harm downstream performance. Recent Cartridges work showed that compact key-value caches trained in latent space can nearly match full-context performance, at the cost of slow, expensive end-to-end optimization.

Their approach, Attention Matching, compacts context fast in latent space by constructing compact keys and values that reproduce attention outputs and preserve attention mass at a per-head level. That formulation decomposes naturally into simple subproblems, some with efficient closed-form solutions. Within the framework, the team develops methods that push the compaction time versus quality frontier, achieving up to fiftyfold compaction in seconds on some data sets with little quality loss.
arxiv-2602-16684:
Bo Pan and co-authors tackle matched molecular pair transformations, the local chemical edits medicinal chemists use daily to design analogs. Past machine learning routes work at whole-molecule level with weak edit control, or learn pair edits from narrow settings and small models. The authors cast analog generation as variable-to-variable and train a foundation model on large-scale pair transformations.

Prompting lets users state preferred transformation patterns during generation. A retrieval-augmented frame, MMPT-RAG, uses outside reference analogs as context to steer generation and generalize from project-specific series. Tests on general chemical corpora and patent-specific sets show better diversity, novelty, and control, recovering realistic analogs in practical discovery settings. Drug designers get a tool that better mirrors chemist intuition.
arxiv-2602-16884:
M. Cufari and co-authors report enhanced hot electron preheat in magnetized laser direct-drive implosions. Hard X-ray emission tied to hot electron preheat was observed to rise by about half under a ten-tesla magnetic field. The field reaches a quasi-steady state aligned with the ablation flow before laser-plasma instabilities arise in the corona.

Hot electrons that would otherwise escape the corona and charge the capsule in unmagnetized implosions are instead confined in a mirror mode of the magnetic field. Those electrons then pitch-angle scatter from the mirror onto the capsule, generating the observed hard X-ray emission. Capsule charging signatures, seen in charged-fusion product energies, fall when the implosion is magnetized. The results sharpen the need to mitigate laser-plasma instabilities, above all for magnetized implosions, to maximize fusion gain and efficiency.
arxiv-2602-16984:
Vishal Srivastava establishes basic limits of black-box safety testing, via information-theoretic and computational barriers from latent context effects. Black-box safety evaluation assumes test behavior reliably predicts field performance. The paper formalizes and challenges that assumption through latent context-conditioned policies. Those models' outputs depend on hidden internal variables rare under testing but prevalent in field use.

Passive testing: minimax lower bounds via Le Cam's method show any estimator incurs large expected absolute error. That error is tied to trigger probability in field use and loss gap. Adaptive testing: using a hash-based trigger and Yao's minimax principle, worst-case error remains large even for adaptive querying. That holds when field spread is supported over a large domain, with detection requiring many queries. Computational separation: under trapdoor assumptions, field environments with privileged information can activate unsafe behaviors. No polynomial-time evaluator without the trapdoor can detect them.
arxiv-2602-17084:
Kan Watanabe led an eight-author team studying how AI coding agents write pull request descriptions, and how human reviewers react. AI agents now open pull requests on GitHub on their own, but little was known about how their description styles differ or what those styles do to review. The paper analyzes pull requests from five AI coding agents in the AIDev dataset.

The agents showed distinct description styles, and those styles lined up with differences in reviewer engagement, response time, and merge rates. Some agents drew faster, warmer, or more thorough review than others, and merge outcomes varied too. The findings show that presentation matters in human-AI coding teamwork: how an agent frames its work shapes how humans judge and accept it.
arxiv-2602-17684:
Xiao Zhu and team present CodeScaler, a reward model built to scale code language model training and test-time inference. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards leans on unit tests, yet good test cases are scarce and unreliable. CodeScaler replaces execution feedback with learned rewards, trained on curated preference data from verified code problems.

Syntax-aware code extraction and validity-preserving reward shaping keep optimization stable and robust. Across four coding benchmarks, CodeScaler beats execution-based reinforcement learning on both tested model sizes. Scaling to tens of thousands of problems with added synthetic data lifts scores well above the base model, with no test cases required. At inference, it matches unit-test approaches while cutting latency tenfold, and it tops rival reward models beyond code as well.
arxiv-2602-18084:
Benjamin Honoré and team study the trade-off between symmetry and speed in graph flow matching. Equivariance is central to graph making models because it respects the swap balance of graphs. Strict versions, however, raise run cost through added design constraints and slow learning, since the model must stay steady across a large space of possible node swaps.

Starting from an equivariant discrete flow-matching model, the authors relax it during training through a tunable symmetry tuning scheme based on sine place codes and node swaps. Tests show breaking symmetry speeds early training with an easier learning signal, but spawns shortcut answers that overfit, with the model often making copies of the training set. Tuning the symmetry signal well delays overfit while speeding learning, reaching stronger results with about a fifth of the standard training epochs.
arxiv-2602-18184:
Aristides V. Doumas and one co-author sharpen the odds bounds for sums of overdispersed count data. Their 2026 paper builds Kolmogorov-type maximal inequalities for negative binomial variables, first under independence and then under dependence. Overdispersed counts, where spread outruns the mean, show up widely in public health, insurance, and ecology.

For independent but unlike variables, the team derives sharp deviation bounds tied to Tweedie dispersion parameters, with direct use in monitoring count models. For dependent counts sharing a Gamma mixing factor, they prove a new sub-exponential refinement that yields fast-fading tail odds. Simulations show a fifty-five percent drop in mean peak deviation under suitable dependence, and a COVID-19 surveillance example shows the bounds at work. The results extend classic inequalities to messy, dependent counts.
arxiv-2602-18284:
Lena T. T. Nguyen and four co-authors benchmark faster ways to compute light absorption for platinum-based cancer probes. Their 2026 paper starts from a clinical need: many chemotherapy drugs harm healthy tissue, so early detection and targeted killing of cancer cells matter. Luminescent metal complexes can flag DNA abnormalities because their glow shifts with surroundings.

The team tests methods on a platinum pincer complex alone and tucked into a small DNA model. Two approximations speed up time-dependent density functional theory with only modest accuracy loss, and a cheap geometry method matches that trade well. Tight-binding methods run faster still but drift further. The largest uncertainty comes from the exchange-correlation functional, where one tested choice performs well. The study gives screeners a balanced recipe for candidate probes.
arxiv-2602-18484:
David Puelz examines race in admissions at a Texas medical school before a landmark ruling. His 2026 paper notes whether and how race shapes selective admissions remains central to higher education. In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard, decided in 2023, the Supreme Court held race-based affirmative action in college admissions breaches the Equal Protection Clause, ending the practice in theory.

The report studies a public medical school before the decision. It uses applicant-level data on over eleven thousand applications to the Texas Tech medical school in 2021 and 2022. Linking decisions to merit, race, gender, and situational judgment scores, the analysis provides strong evidence of racial preferences, with African American and Hispanic applicants preferred over academically similar White and Asian applicants. Counterfactual analyses measure these disparities. The findings document the race-based preferences the decision meant to address, establishing a baseline for judging whether practice changed afterward.
arxiv-2602-18684:
A flying arm that bends like a tentacle is hard to model. The drone and the arm push on each other. Niloufar Amiri, with three co-authors, compares two ways to model such aerial continuum manipulators in 2026. One is a full coupled model. The other is a simpler decoupled model that drops the interaction terms.

Both models use Euler-Lagrange dynamics under a piecewise constant curvature assumption. They are tested in open-loop runs and in closed-loop tracking. The closed-loop test uses a new visual servo controller for a moving target. Open-loop results differ sharply. Yet closed-loop tracking matches to within a fraction of a pixel. So the cheaper model may be good enough once feedback is in the loop.
arxiv-2602-18884:
Small multimodal models often fail at time and procedure. They cannot follow what happens step by step in video or in a GUI. Zhenkun Gao, with three co-authors, traces that failure in 2026 to training data. Current paradigms lack large-scale, procedurally coherent data. TPRU is their remedy.

TPRU is a large dataset from embodied scenes such as robot manipulation and GUI navigation. It trains temporal reasoning through three tasks. Models reorder frames, predict the next frame, and review the previous frame. Hard negative samples push models from passive watching to active cross-modal checks. With reinforcement learning fine-tuning, a seven-billion-parameter model jumps from about half correct to about three-quarters correct on a curated test. Gains also carry over to established benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-19084:
Profiling UCX communication lacks fine detail. Emir Gencer, with four co-authors, introduces ucTrace in 2026, a multi-layer profiler for UCX-driven communication. UCX moves data fast across multi-node CPU-GPU clusters. It serves as the transport layer for MPI, especially GPU-aware versions. Yet existing tools miss transport-layer behaviour or tie to one MPI build.

ucTrace exposes and visualises UCX-level communication in high-performance computing. It profiles message passing at the UCX level. Operations between hosts and devices, like GPUs and network cards, link directly to their originating MPI functions. Interactive views of process and device interactions help admins and developers tune performance and debug patterns at scale. Demos cover point-to-point behaviour, Allreduce comparisons, a linear solver, NUMA binding, and large GROMACS simulations with GPU acceleration. The tool is publicly available.
arxiv-2602-19184:
Robots can learn by watching, as humans do. Thanh Nguyen Canh, with five co-authors, builds that ability in 2026 with a Human-to-Robot imitation pipeline. Video captioning models favour global scenes over task objects, yielding descriptions too vague for execution. End-to-end architectures demand huge paired datasets and generalise poorly.

The pipeline splits learning into two stages. Video understanding combines temporal shift modules with vision-language models to extract actions and identify interacted objects. Robot imitation then uses TD3-based reinforcement learning to execute demonstrated manipulations. Tests span PyBullet simulation with one manipulator and real-world trials with another, across reach, pick, move, and put actions. Action classification accuracy runs high, with strong scores on standard and novel objects. Manipulation success averages high, reaching perfection on reaching tasks.
arxiv-2602-19284:
Choosing a prediction model and then trusting its intervals is risky, because selection itself can break coverage guarantees. Yuhao Wang and Tengyao Wang propose a localized method that keeps selection honest. It selects in a balanced way across calibration points. Upper and lower stand-in intervals build a safe set of candidate models that contains the best one. The symmetry that conformal methods rely on is preserved by design.

The resulting ensemble keeps exact finite-sample marginal coverage while adapting to local patterns and to models of differing complexity. In simulations it produces markedly shorter intervals than the best fixed model, with the gains largest where data are heterogeneous. The work suits settings where the right model varies across the input space, and where valid uncertainty matters as much as a point prediction.
arxiv-2602-19684:
Opinions can sweep populations fast, yet most opinion models let only pairs interact on fixed networks. Cosimo Agostinelli and two co-authors build a bounded-confidence model where groups talk, and disagreement can split them. In their model, group discussion can drive all members to agreement, while strong internal disagreement splits groups, whose subgroups then merge with others.

Across tolerance levels, adaptivity damps key group effects, bringing back near-pairwise behavior. It lets large groups form, blocks fragmentation at low tolerance, and restores the polarization-to-consensus phase transition that a rigid group model loses. Readers get a clear lesson: group talk plus adaptive regrouping shapes both social ties and global opinion flow.
arxiv-2602-20084:
Charts mislead when they break design principles. Whether language models can check those principles directly, instead of relying on hand-coded rules, is unclear. A 2026 arXiv paper by Martin Sinnona and three co-authors presents the first evaluation of large language models and vision-language models as reasoners about visualization principles.

Constraint-based checkers encode principles as logical rules, enabling precise automated checks. The authors instead test whether models can reason about visual design, using verification ground truth from answer set programming. They compiled principles as natural-language statements and built a dataset of about two thousand Vega-Lite specifications annotated with violations, plus over three hundred Vega-Lite charts. Both detection and repair of specifications were tested. Large vision-language models show promise as flexible validators and editors, yet still trail symbolic solvers on nuanced perception. Frontier models prove better at correcting violations than at spotting them reliably.
arxiv-2602-20284:
Han Fu and five co-authors study why continuous-integration builds fail for embedded open-source software and build a tool to fix them. Their 2026 paper examines four major embedded projects and more than four thousand recorded build failures. Hardware dependencies cause most failures, followed by syntax errors and build-script problems. Most fixes turn out to be small, which suggests automated repair could help if varied setups and scarce test data can be handled.

The authors present PhantomRun, a framework that uses large language models to draft and validate fixes from build logs, source code, past fixes, and compiler messages. An adaptation layer covers two CI platforms and four build systems, bridging the varied toolchains of embedded projects. In tests, PhantomRun repaired nearly half of compilation failures across the target projects. The result supports language-model repair as a practical aid for embedded teams.
arxiv-2602-20484:
The dusty torus of active galactic nuclei is central to unification schemes, yet its origin remains mysterious. Xinwu Cao and three co-authors propose a new model in which many small dusty gas clumps collectively appear as a geometrically thick, dynamic torus. Hot gas spirals toward the central black hole, forming a rotating disk on sub-parsec scales. A fraction condenses into small cold clumps through thermal instabilities when the accretion rate is high enough.

Irradiated by the central disk, the clumps re-radiate mostly in the infrared, and radiation force holds them aloft against gravity in quasi-static equilibrium for suitable column densities. The model is robust across reasonable parameter ranges. Condensation needs accretion above about one percent of the Eddington rate. Radiation cannot lift clumps if disk luminosity falls below zero point one percent of Eddington luminosity, possibly explaining missing tori in low-luminosity nuclei.
arxiv-2602-20684:
AI-aided workflows lack a way to maintain task-level checks and regulatory tracking at machine speed. Christopher Koch and Joshua Andreas Wellbrock address that gap with Agile V, a framework embedding checks and audit output each cycle. It merges Agile iteration with V-Model checks in an Infinity Loop, deploying AI agents for needs, design, build, test, and compliance, with gates.

The paper tests claims: audit-ready artifacts emerge by default, requirement-level checks come from separate tests, and verified increments need few touches per cycle. A case study on a Hardware-in-the-Loop system supports all three: about five hundred code lines, eight needs, and fifty-four tests. Audit documentation came out by itself. A requirement-level pass rate came with only six prompts per cycle, for a ten-to-fifty-fold cost cut versus COCOMO II. The authors invite outside replication for wider use.
arxiv-2602-21084:
Recent JWST images show ionized regions in the galactic center shaped into striking filaments, unlike similar regions elsewhere. Samuel Crowe, Yisheng Tu, Zhi-Yun Li, Jeong-Gyu Kim, and John Bally simulate strongly magnetized ionized regions in this 2026 arXiv paper to explain them. Their magnetohydrodynamic models test ambient gas with pre-placed dense blobs and with turbulence-driven blobs.

When blobs predate the ionizing source, photoionized plasma stripped from them funnels into long filaments along magnetic field lines. The filaments match the observed lengths and emission measures in the Central Molecular Zone. Their density and curvature depend on blob density and configuration geometry, supporting a picture of magnetically confined flows of ionized gas.
arxiv-2602-21284:
Ferro switching usually takes charges to follow ions slowly, but that split can fail. Gili Scharf, Lara Donval, Leah Ben Gur, and Alon Ron probe the breakdown in this 2026 arXiv paper. They use time-sharp second-wave making and pump-probe shine-back to reshape the free-energy landscape of tin telluride, tracking charge order and lattice motion apart.

When a light kick briefly damps the double-well barrier, charge-order motion turns strongly bent while in-step phonon motion stays wave-like. No single slow dial can tell both. The authors offer a joining picture based on split scales for rescaling ferro stiffness, catching the mixed shift and mess nature of the stuff.
arxiv-2602-21384:
Patrick E. Farrell and three co-authors build a bridge between two ways of deriving the laws of continuum mechanics. Rajagopal and Srinivasa derive constitutive relations from energy storage and entropy production by constrained optimization, while kinetic theory reaches such laws by moment closure, above all the Chapman-Enskog expansion.

For a Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook-type approximation, the authors show the maximal-entropy-production rule equals a minimal-relaxation-time rule: among allowed responses, pick the one that relaxes fastest toward equilibrium. A hybrid Chapman-Enskog-Rajagopal-Srinivasa method then recovers the standard Euler and Navier-Stokes-Fourier laws for monatomic gases, and the paper shows how other selection rules can beat classical closure for a liquid-crystal model.
arxiv-2602-21684:
Xiaohan Lei and four co-authors propose Primary-Fine Decoupling for action generation in robotic imitation. Multi-modal distribution in robotic manipulation sequences poses challenges for imitation learning. Existing methods often model action space as discrete token sets or continuous, latent-variable distributions, with trade-offs.

Token discretization loses fine-grained action variations, while single-stage continuous generation tends to produce unstable transitions. The two-stage design decouples coarse action consistency from fine-grained variations. First, action chunks compress into a small set of discrete modes, letting a lightweight policy select consistent modes and avoid mode bouncing. Second, a mode-conditioned MeanFlow policy learns to generate faithful continuous actions. Theory proves the two-stage design achieves a strictly lower MSE bound than single-stage generative policies. Tests show Primary-Fine Decoupling beating leading baselines across 56 tasks from Adroit, DexArt, and MetaWorld, generalizing to real-world tactile dexterous manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2602-21984:
In mathematics, an origami is a surface tiled by squares and glued edge to edge, and its symmetries form orbit graphs. Luke Jeffreys and Carlos Matheus study the graphs traced by primitive origamis with a given number of squares. A guess by McMullen says these graphs, in one key family, spread out like expanders, networks that stay strongly linked even as they grow.

The authors give indirect backing for that guess by proving the graphs' Euler characteristics grow without bound as the square count rises. They extend the same finding to origamis in two Prym families, and, assuming other researchers' guesses, to further families as well. The result builds on their earlier proof that these graphs eventually stop being planar, and stands as the strongest indirect evidence yet for McMullen's claim.
arxiv-2602-22084:
Small changes to a matrix shift its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and predicting those shifts is a core task across physics and numerical analysis. Francesco Hrobat and Yuji Nakatsukasa study a structured case where the perturbation takes commutator form, built from the matrix itself and a second matrix. They show this setting generalizes an earlier block-diagonal case studied by Li and Li.

The authors extend that earlier result, showing each eigenvalue's shift scales with the squared size of the perturbation divided by its gap from neighboring eigenvalues. The tangent-space viewpoint for isospectral matrices gives the analysis its shape. The work sharpens perturbation bounds for a class of structured changes that arise in practice.
arxiv-2602-22184:
A two-dimensional Coulomb gas spreads particles across a droplet, but stray components outside the droplet, called outposts, can trap a few particles. Kohei Noda studies gases with any fixed number of outposts, extending earlier work that handled a single outpost. In the one-outpost case, the particle count near the outpost stays of order one and follows a Heine distribution as the total grows.

Noda proves the joint counts near many outposts converge to a multidimensional Heine distribution. That reveals a striking pattern: counts near geometrically separate outposts are strongly correlated with each other, not just with neighbors. The result adds a subtle long-range effect to the picture of Coulomb gases, with a stated proviso for outposts separated by an intervening component.
arxiv-2602-22384:
Dust hides much of the universe's star formation, and far-infrared data are needed to see it. Seamus McNulty and eleven co-authors release 3D-Herschel, a public photometric catalog spanning ultraviolet to far-infrared wavelengths, combining deblended Herschel imaging with legacy survey fields. They model over forty-one thousand galaxies across a wide redshift range with a seventeen-parameter Bayesian fitting code.

Comparing fits with and without far-infrared constraints, the team finds ultraviolet-to-mid-infrared models already recover stellar ages, star-formation rates, and masses robustly for most galaxies. That holds even for the small share with strong far-infrared detections. The star-forming sequence barely moves when far-infrared data join, confirming an earlier offset as robust. Dust modelers gain a catalog that tests what far-infrared light truly adds.
arxiv-2602-22884:
Aayush Mishra and two co-authors keep spread-cost Bayesian guessing honest as data streams in. Spread-cost guessing finds hidden values fast with make-believe networks trained on mocks, but weakens when models misjudge reality. Self-match training on untagged real data hardens networks, yet prior methods handle only static, single-task settings.

The new ongoing setup splits mock-based pre-training from tag-free stepwise self-match fine-tuning on real data. Total loss is fought two ways: flashback replay from a memory buffer of past sightings, and elastic weight lock-in that tames updates to protect key knobs. Across three diverse case studies, both tactics cut loss sharply and beat standard mock-only training, landing closer to Markov-chain Monte Carlo gold standards.
arxiv-2602-23184:
Sara Rosenthal and five co-authors release MTRAG-UN, a benchmark for multi-turn retrieval-augmented generation. In this popular setup, a language model answers across a conversation while pulling facts from a corpus. The benchmark holds 666 tasks with over 2,800 conversation turns across six domains, each paired with its source texts.

Tests show that retrieval and generation models still struggle on four open problems. These are questions that cannot be answered, questions left underspecified, questions that do not stand alone without prior turns, and replies that stay unclear. By naming and measuring these failure modes in one shared test, the benchmark gives builders a concrete target. It aims at making conversational assistants more robust when the user, the question, or the answer itself is incomplete.
arxiv-2602-23884:
Sandor E. Tuñón-Andrés and two co-authors study the equidistant dimension of corona product graphs. The 2026 paper defines that dimension as the smallest size of a vertex set that can separate every pair of outside vertices by equal distance to some member. It is a distance-based parameter previously unexplored for corona products.

The authors introduce an auxiliary empty bisector graph, which records pairs in the base graph that no third vertex can sit equidistant from. With that tool they prove tight bounds on the equidistant dimension of corona products and exact values for several classical graph families. They also show that for a fixed base graph, the dimension depends on the second graph only through its order, and eventually grows linearly with it. The work fills a gap in the study of distance parameters under graph products.
arxiv-2602-24284:
Pezhman Ebrahimzadeh and two co-authors report chaotic switching in the minimal three-pendulum network with global coupling. The 2026 paper analyzes stability conditions for chimera states, patterns where some oscillators synchronize while others remain incoherent, and their dependence on parameters, identifying three distinct switching scenarios.

First comes a riddling bifurcation: inside the chimera manifold, an unstable periodic orbit turns transversally unstable. Second, a blowout bifurcation scenario, where switching follows transverse destabilization of the chaotic chimera itself. Third, switchings between laminar saddle chimeras inside a global turbulent attractor. The analysis examines their multistability and the switching regime across chimera states, limit cycles, and fixed points. Where stable non-chaotic solutions coexist with chaotic chimeras, a switching trajectory may eventually escape to a stable solution, adding unpredictability since the escape moment is hard to predict. In short, swings flip the tale. Flips surprise all.
arxiv-2603-00184: Munagala presents a dual-pipeline system for bird image segmentation built on frozen SAM 2.1 as a shared backbone. The zero-shot pipeline uses Grounding DINO 1.5 to find birds from the text prompt 'bird', then prompts SAM 2.1 with boxes and no labelled bird data. The supervised pipeline fine-tunes YOLOv11 on CUB-200-2011 for detection, again prompting SAM 2.1 for masks. On 11,788 images across 200 species, the supervised pipeline scores IoU 0.912, beating all prior baselines, while the zero-shot pipeline trails it using only a text prompt.
arxiv-2603-00284: Ðurašinović and Lasserre study polynomial optimization over a compact set defined by SOS-concave polynomials. The function to be minimized need not be convex overall. They show that when the objective's Hessian admits a specific quadratic-module form, a hidden local convexity, the Moment-SOS hierarchy reaches the exact answer in finitely many steps. It needs no advance knowledge of that convexity. Strong convexity on the feasible set suffices for that form. The authors give an explicit order where exactness occurs, yielding certified global minimizers.
arxiv-2603-00384: Cuadra and three colleagues probe what five older adults grasp about voice first home helpers used for health reporting at home. Early talks and device logs feed a set of Privacy Cards that steer later interviews toward mental models and worries. The cards reveal thin models for true consent, with users unsure who can reach their data and mixing built in features with third party apps. Early calm about ethics gives way to richer concerns once the cards prompt deeper reflection.
arxiv-2603-00584: Cocchi and seven colleagues report the first Sardinia Radio Telescope detection of the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, a brightness dip toward cluster MACS J1752+4440 at 18.6 gigahertz. A symmetric beta model plus Bayesian retrieval yields a core radius, central density, and beta value matching expectations for a cluster of this mass. The Compton y value within a few arcminutes runs higher than the Planck value, as differing resolution and modelling would predict. The result shows the telescope can catch the onset of the SZ dip at low frequencies.
arxiv-2603-00884: Guo and Wei track how OCR fixes change later work in digital humanities, where fixes often overwrite earlier choices. Their framework logs each fix's span, type, source, confidence, and review state for old texts. Raw, fully fixed, and history-filtered text give different named entities and readings, and history signals flag shaky results for a human to check.
arxiv-2603-00984: Broom and four colleagues quantify Bell non-locality when signaling is present, dropping the usual rule that local stats ignore distant measurement choices. Their method asks how often locality can be kept across repeated trials, reducing the task to splitting observed links into local and truly non-local parts. Solved with linear programming in closed form for any links, it also yields a signaling measure, extending non-locality study beyond physics tests.
arxiv-2603-01084: Hamzi and Vaidya solve Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations for nonlinear optimal control with a kernel-based linear matrix inequality method. Writing the value-function gradient in a kernel space and turning the quadratic bound gives a convex semidefinite program, while a Riccati-Hessian equality at equilibrium removes the trivial solution. On a 1D test the method nearly matches the exact value, and on the Van der Pol oscillator it beats LQR on all starts while staying within 0.42 percent of the best per-case cost.
arxiv-2603-01284: Huang and three colleagues present FoSS, a dual framework for driving trajectory prediction, joining frequency-domain reasoning and linear-time sequence modeling. One branch applies a discrete Fourier transform, splitting trajectories into amplitude parts for intent and phase parts for variation. It reorders spectra step by step and refines them with two picked state-space submodules. A time-domain picked module rebuilds self-attention behavior in linear time and fuses both views with a cross-attention layer. Learnable queries plus a weighted fusion head produce rival trajectories with motion doubt.
arxiv-2603-01484:
Signals that change over time on a network, such as sensor readings, need math tools that respect both space and time. Mingzhi Wang, Manjun Cui, Feiyue Zhao, and colleagues extend those tools in this 2026 work. Older fractional transforms force one shared setting across both dimensions, which limits how well they fit mixed patterns.

Their new transform gives each dimension its own fractional order while keeping key traits like reversibility. A second version links graph and time bases along a smooth path on a curved space of transforms. On top sits a filter whose orders are learned from data end to end. Tests on real time-varying graph data and on image repair show steady gains over top fractional methods.
arxiv-2603-01984:
Xiaoyu Yi, Gus Xia, and Ziyu Wang give composers a visual way to control instrumental texture in generated music. Their 2026 work identifies instrumentation, which instruments play and in what roles, as a natural control axis. Text prompts and metadata cannot shape a multi-track piece with that directness.

Their representation, ViTex, draws texture as an image-like score for the model to read. Color encodes instrument choice, position encodes pitch and time, and stroke traits encode local texture. A discrete diffusion model, conditioned on ViTex plus chord progressions, writes short multi-track symbolic pieces. Texture-level control stays explicit while unconditional generation quality remains strong in their tests. The demo and code are public, which invites hands-on trials of visual music control.
arxiv-2603-02184:
Jinqi Wu, Sishuo Chen, Zhangming Chan, and colleagues build a public test set for ad prediction in this 2026 paper. Online ads earn credit for a sale through rules called attribution, and rules differ. Learning from several rules at once can help predict conversion rates. Public data sets, though, carry labels from just one rule.

Their benchmark, MAC, is the first public set with labels from many rules. A companion library gathers standard methods so results can be compared fairly. Learning from many rules helped most users with long paths to a sale. Adding extra targets sometimes hurt, so targets must be chosen with care. Their new model, which mixes expert parts unevenly, beat the prior best method by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-02584:
Mayank Mishra, Gwangho Choi, Wenhua He, and colleagues build a quantum photonic platform at visible wavelengths in this 2026 paper. Quantum photonic circuits need extremely low loss and fast, low-power reconfiguration. Silicon nitride waveguides with loose light confinement offer record-low losses. Their usual thermo-optic tuning, though, is slow, power-hungry, and crosstalk-prone.

Piezo-optomechanical actuation replaces heat with mechanical motion for tuning. Prior piezo platforms used tight confinement with far higher losses, capping circuit depth. This work merges piezo actuation with the ultra-low-loss loose platform. Measured propagation loss at a visible wavelength is exceptionally low. Modulation runs at megahertz rates with strong phase efficiency. The platform keeps active performance while enabling the deep circuits scalable quantum algorithms require.
arxiv-2603-02684:
HateMirage, a 2026 dataset from the FLaMe.nlp Lab at IIIT Delhi, targets hate speech that hides inside false stories. Most hate datasets catch open insults and slurs. Harmful intent wrapped in distorted news claims is subtler, and it can spread or excuse abuse.

The builders started from widely debunked false claims, then traced matching YouTube debates to gather over four thousand comments. Each comment is labeled for its target, its intent, and its likely social impact. That three-part labeling goes beyond the word-level notes of older datasets. Tests with open language models suggest clear explanations depend more on varied, reasoning-rich training than on model size alone.
arxiv-2603-02784:
Wafaa Fadlelmula, Sanaa Hamid Mohamed, and Taisir El-Gorashi design a low-energy network for rooms lit by data-carrying light. Their 2026 paper proposes a point-to-point optical network as the backhaul for visible light communication access points. Dedicated fiber links join the lights to small fog servers spread through the building.

An optimization model jointly assigns computing work, routes traffic, and tracks power use and queueing delay across the fog layers. Against a rival router-based optical design, the point-to-point layout cut power use by up to about two-thirds under power-focused settings. Delay fell by up to about three-quarters as well. Better in-building links and fuller use of spread-out servers explain the gains.
arxiv-2603-02884:
O. A. Veliev examines when a twisted version of the Dirac operator still behaves like a well-ordered spectrum problem. His 2026 paper studies the operator with a periodic two-by-two matrix potential whose values can be complex numbers. Because the operator is not self-adjoint, its spectrum can misbehave, and expansions in its modes may fail.

Veliev gives a condition on the off-diagonal entries of the potential under which the operator is at least asymptotically spectral, meaning its modes settle into spectral order at large scales. A second condition guarantees full spectrality outright. He then develops the spectral expansions valid in each case. The results extend classic one-dimensional spectral theory into the complex, non-self-adjoint setting used in advanced wave problems.
arxiv-2603-03284:
Thomas Schwetz revisits a basic question in cosmology: how heavy can neutrinos be if some dark matter decays away? His 2026 paper allows part of the dark matter to decay into massless dark radiation. That decay can offset the extra matter density that appears as neutrinos slow down, hiding the neutrino mass from some kinds of data.

Using galaxy distance measures, supernova data, and a microwave background distance estimate, Schwetz finds surprisingly heavy neutrinos still fit well, and the data even mildly prefer some decay. Adding the full microwave background data, especially its lensing signal, breaks the trick and restores a tight mass limit. The lesson is that structure growth data are essential for firm neutrino bounds.
arxiv-2603-04084: Garcia and others present end-to-end event reconstruction for sharpness physics at future colliders. Future tests demand unprecedented sharpness on Higgs, electroweak, and flavor observables. Current particle flow methods depend on detector-given clustering. The new method maps charged tracks plus calorimeter and muon hits straight to particle-level objects via shape models, condensation clustering, and dedicated identification and energy networks. Benchmarked on simulated FCC-ee collisions with the CLD concept, it beats the rule-based state of the art by 10 to 20%. It cuts charged-hadron fake rates sharply.
arxiv-2603-04184: Vidal and others propose publication and maintenance of relational data in enterprise knowledge graphs. To make legacy relational sources accessible through the knowledge graph, an RDF view of the relational data must be created, and building that view aids query results and data availability. A materialized view must be kept current to reflect relational database updates.
arxiv-2603-04284: Zacharia and colleagues offer one planner for aerial, ground, and underwater robots. OmniPlanner joins volumetric exploration with viewpoint based inspection and target reaching in a single modular design. A platform layer captures each machine's sensing, travel, and motion limits, so one strategy transfers with little retuning. Field and simulation trials in mines, forests, submarine bunkers, factories, and outdoors show steady cross domain results. It beats typical baselines on exploration and inspection efficiency. The same plan thus works in air, on land, and at sea.
arxiv-2603-04384: Chen and colleagues exploit agent reasoning traces to improve retrieval for deep research agents. Unlike human users, such agents write explicit reasoning before each search, a signal retrievers ignore. Reasoning-Aware Retrieval embeds that trace jointly with the query, and DR-Synth builds training data from standard question answering sets. Each part helps alone, and together they train AgentIR-4B. On BrowseComp-Plus, AgentIR-4B reaches 68 percent accuracy with Tongyi-DeepResearch, against 50 percent for conventional models twice its size and 37 percent for BM25.
arxiv-2603-04484: Wang and colleagues benchmark robust C and C++ code search with CLARC. Retrieval aids developers, yet benchmarks focus on Python and rarely stress robustness beyond lexical cues. CLARC draws on real GitHub repos, holding 1,245 evaluation pairs and 5,472 training pairs. Model generated queries pass human scoring and hypothesis testing. The pipeline ensures compilability, sorts by dependency complexity, and stress tests with anonymization plus Assembly and WebAssembly compilation. Six leading models drop sharply, leaning on lexical features over semantic understanding. Code meaning thus matters more than mere words.
arxiv-2603-04584: Perlin and colleagues run fault tolerant corrected quantum algorithms end to end. Scaling quantum work needs error fixes and fault tolerance, yet logical runs with safe parts stayed out of reach. On Quantinuum H2 and Helios chips with the Steane code, they run QAOA and Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd on the Poisson equation. QAOA on 5 and 6 logical qubits gains with more layers and T gates for turns, despite bare cost. Circuits with 8 logical qubits plus 9 logical T gates match bare results, while the largest, with 12 logical and 97 bare qubits, beat chance.
arxiv-2603-04784: Mould argues massive primordial black holes could accelerate early galaxy formation. If such black holes exist and form part of dark matter, they catalyze galaxy formation as high-density seeds. They shorten assembly time to as little as 100 million years for seeds up to 100 million solar masses. Rapid formation of host halos follows, explaining surprisingly massive early galaxies. Low surface brightness or diffuse galaxies may arise as residues of halos seeded by smaller black holes. Such smaller seeds fail to accrete a major baryonic component, leaving diffuse remnants.
arxiv-2603-04984: Ningning Li and team study the time-splitting scheme for answers of the nonlinear Dirac formula in one space and one time dimension. Assuming convergent initial data in L2, they prove the rough answers converge strongly in L2 to the global strong answer for any positive time. Pointwise figures support a modified Glimm-type functional, uniformly bounded in time, yielding L2 balance figures. They further prove relative compactness of the answer set in continuous L2-valued functions, so any convergent subsequence limit is the strong answer of the Cauchy problem.
arxiv-2603-05084: Xulong Yuan and Xiangdong Zhang investigate magnetic waveform imprints for Bertotti-Robinson and Bonnor-Melvin black holes, aiming to separate magnetic from environmental effects. A small black hole inspiraling into a Kerr black hole shows a leading magnetic correction at minus 2 PN. A spinning Bonnor-Melvin black hole shows a leading magnetic correction at minus 3 PN, with spin corrections at minus 1.5 PN in both cases. The corrections are not degenerate with modified gravity, but resemble gravitational pulls from matter with power-law indices 1 and 0.
arxiv-2603-05184: Muhammad Zarar and team present Logi-PAR, the first patient-action method built on learnable logic rules over symbolic mappings. Current clinical models mostly classify which action occurs, learning only implicit patterns from visual cues through attention mechanisms. Logi-PAR fuses contextual facts from many views and injects neural-guided differentiable rules learned end to end, so implicit patterns surface as explicit labels during training. Its rule traces explain why cues imply a risk and support counterfactual checks, while benchmarks show leading scores over vision-language and transformer older models.
arxiv-2603-05384: Zihan Zhou and team offer omnidirectional referring tracking with complete scene context. Omnidirectional cameras provide 360-degree reach. Current tracking relies on usual cameras, losing contextual cues when targets leave the frame, limiting reading of step by step actions, spatial relations, and group behaviors.
