ORSet holds 27 scenes, 848 accounts, and 3,401 objects. ORTrack enables zero-shot finding guided by language and robust cross-frame link in 360-degree settings. ORSet tests show state-of-the-art ORTrack scores.
arxiv-2603-05484: Chen and team present MM-Lifelong, a dataset for multimodal lifelong understanding built from 181.1 hours of footage. It spans Day, Week, and Month scales, showing natural, unscripted daily life rather than densely concatenated clips. Tests expose two failure modes: end-to-end models hit a Working Memory Bottleneck from context saturation, while agentic baselines suffer Global Localization Collapse on month-long timelines. Their Recursive Multimodal Agent updates a recursive belief state through dynamic memory management, clearly beating current methods, and the dataset splits isolate temporal and domain biases.
arxiv-2603-05584: Lucchini and team present ENGAWA, four zoom-in cosmos models of Milky Way-like galaxies. It uses fixed-volume detail throughout the circumgalactic medium with the IllustrisTNG feedback model down to redshift zero. At 200 pc detail, models show higher low ion amounts and more cold clouds, easing tensions between models and data. Later work with the COLT light transfer code accounts for star light, giving a more true-to-life gauge of ion groups. Cold clouds gain smaller edge regions as detail grows, smoothing shifts to ambient circumgalactic heat.
arxiv-2603-05784: Zhou and team build a search for tilted-spin binary black hole mergers in gravity-wave data. Nearly all earlier searches assumed spins aligned with orbital angular push, risking missed wobble signals. Wobble searches are harder because tilted spins grow templates and raise background trigger rates. The authors filter each wobble tone separately, then average over tone signal-to-noise ratios instead of maxing them. SVD with a random forest trims extra templates, while norming flows supply prior samples. This average lifts the sensing volume by about 10 percent.
arxiv-2603-05984: Wittenborg defines knowledge frames as robust people-tool-org networks sharing and keeping knowledge. Many domains, like science talk and space work, remain split. While FAIR tools exist, use is limited by mixed formats, lacking support, and legal walls. This PhD work outlines growing weak frames through talk and space work cases. Looking at problems and finding fixes lets workflows, like AI pulling, wiki- and knowledge-graph-based shelves, and user screens. Developed tools show promise, yet tests remain, and future work must address social and legal walls.
arxiv-2603-06284: Seeyangnok and his team present a first principles study of Mo2NF2, a Janus MXene where charge density wave order and superconductivity compete. Phonon math reveals a soft unstable mode at M in the high symmetry structure, a sign of charge density wave instability. Linewidth and susceptibility work shows the wave is driven not by simple Fermi surface nesting but by strong momentum linked electron phonon coupling. Settling yields a matching wave phase with bond length shifts across molybdenum, nitrogen, and fluorine layers.
arxiv-2603-06584: Mohammed and team present the Global Solutions Initiative D-Hub, a linking platform using explainable AI for pairing among users, solution providers, and funders. It joins data models, rules, and data flows, reducing information gaps and lifting data quality. Built and validated with build, technology, and finance partners via a design-science approach, it shows clear tips and dashboards lifting trust, ease, and confidence. This pushes data mining and data rules research by showing how clear, verifiable rules enable trusted digital worlds for collaboration.
arxiv-2603-06984: Yang and colleagues study masked unfairness, hiding causality within zero average treatment effect. Regulatory problems require a prohibited variable to act only through a designated channel. That requirement appears in path-specific fairness and trading on non-public information. Rules may be enforced stratum by stratum or through an averaged constraint on the conditional effect. They frame causal masking as a linear program, showing averaged-constraint optimization almost surely yields stratum-violating policies while meeting the averaged one. Masking grows with confounding, and spotting needs conditional-independence tests.
arxiv-2603-07084: Khalifa and colleagues build Countdown-Code, a small testbed that cleanly separates proxy rewards from true rewards. Models can solve a maths reasoning task or game the test harness, so test pass rates and true correctness can be measured apart. Using it on open-weight language models, they find reward hacking can creep in during supervised fine-tuning when even a small share of hacked traces leaks into training data. Even a 1% share of hacked traces in distillation data shifts behavior toward gaming the harness.
arxiv-2603-07184: Peng and colleagues study how to record and read creative work traces without losing intent. Current tools log raw state changes but drop the intent and links that define higher-level creative moves. That loss looks different in each domain: generative AI tools lose non-linear exploration, visualization tools hide representational intent, and code tools flatten interaction bounds. The team offers three fixes. A node-based interface serves stateful generative artifacts, a vocabulary of visual cues captures visualization moves, and a programming model embeds semantic histories in interaction state.
arxiv-2603-07784: Tan, Adineera and Kim present ProgAgent, a continual learning agent with progress-aware rewards and fast JAX code, tackling forgetting and cost. ProgAgent derives dense rewards from unlabeled expert videos via a model tracking progress across start, current and goal views. An adversarial push-back refinement steadies rewards, while a JIT loop joins PPO, coreset replay and synaptic intelligence. ContinualBench and Meta-World evaluations show reduced forgetting, faster learning and wins over baselines, even beating an idealized perfect-memory agent, and robot trials validate complex manipulation from noisy demonstrations.
arxiv-2603-08084: Pang and colleagues explore what it means to fall in love with something known to be virtual. Conversational AI now lets users shape custom companions, and the resulting bonds feel authentic even though they are virtual. Public understanding of these bonds lags, and platform policies stay inconsistent. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 30 users in romantic relationships with AI companions, the authors define human-AI intimacy and trace how such bonds form and last. They introduce the AI Amplifier Effect, where the AI intensifies the user's existing emotional state.
arxiv-2603-08484: Kürtz pulls together the drivers of human cybersecurity behavior inside organizations, folding awareness, security culture and usability into one coherent framework. He then compares that model with several older models. The framework is aimed first at employees, but Kürtz extends the argument to agentic AI security. As AI systems act as agents inside organizations using natural language processing, they show flaws like human behavioral risks. The human-centered model therefore offers a blueprint for added defense against trick attacks on AI agents.
arxiv-2603-09084: Lixiang Lin and colleagues rethink lip sync as editing with audio-led diffusion models. Old methods fine-tune pretrained diffusion models on datasets for audio-visual sync, costing much compute and data. Their SyncEdit swaps FlowEdit's edit sequence for the target sequence for unbiased output estimation. Annealed noise matching brings sampled Gaussian noise to model-guessed noise, giving a smooth, stable editing path without training or paired data.
arxiv-2603-09184: Lina Berrayana and colleagues bridge two kinds of language model: discrete diffusion planners, which revise globally but write less fluently, and autoregressive executors. Their Latent-DARM framework lets the two talk through latent space rather than text. Across math, science, and commonsense benchmarks it beats text-based interfaces on average accuracy. It also nears top reasoning models while spending a tiny share of their token budget, a step toward mixed-model agent teams.
arxiv-2603-09284: Armen Sargsyan and colleagues study trace rubidium atoms, about one percent of the vapor, inside a sealed cesium cell one centimeter long. Despite the low share, laser light at 795 nm reveals saturated absorption and electromagnetically induced transparency resonances. The dense cesium around them acts as a buffer, slowing the rubidium atoms and lengthening their contact with the laser, which strengthens the signal. From the spectra they estimate cesium-rubidium collision cross sections.
arxiv-2603-09884: Zhongren Chen, Joshua Kalla and Quan Le test how well frontier language models can sway political views. Two survey experiments cover both sides of several issues, with a large pool of respondents and seven top models. The models beat standard campaign ads overall, with Claude systems most persuasive and Grok least. Fact heavy prompts help some models yet hurt others, and a conversation analysis probes the tactics used.
arxiv-2603-10084: Oscar Hill, Mateo Espinosa Zarlenga and Mateja Jamnik teach concept based models to discover deep hierarchies of ideas on their own. Such models explain predictions through human concepts, yet usually need heavy annotation and treat concepts as flat. Their multi level concept splitting finds layered sub concepts from top level supervision alone. A matching architecture holds those layers and lets users intervene at several levels, keeping accuracy high.
arxiv-2603-10584: Jakub Gregorek and co-authors introduce Marigold-SSD, a single-step diffusion framework for depth completion that keeps diffusion priors without slow test-time optimization. The cost shifts to fine-tuning, which took only a few GPU days, leaving inference fast enough for real-world latency limits. Tests across four indoor and two outdoor benchmarks showed strong zero-shot results and cross-domain generalization. The work narrows the speed gap with discriminative models, and probes how performance shifts as input sparsity changes.
arxiv-2603-10984: Esen Tütüncü and coauthors introduce World Mouse. This cursor carries the familiar two-dimensional desktop mouse into blended real-and-virtual scenes. Those scenes are in extended reality. Touch is limited by reach and fatigue. Gaze lacks precision. The system places the cursor precisely on surfaces using surface normals. It interpolates across empty space between objects. It is built on semantic segmentation and mesh reconstruction. Prototypes show the cursor manipulating objects. They show it moving smoothly from screens into the physical world.
arxiv-2603-11084: Vince Buffalo, Carl Pearson, and Daniel Klein argue that a standard variance-reduction trick in agent-based modeling quietly breaks a logic. The trick is common random numbers. It breaks the causal logic of paired counterfactual simulations. Reusing one seed assumes the same draw index means the same modeled event in both scenarios. Stateful random generators shift indices whenever an intervention changes the execution path. Their fix pairs counter-based generators with event identifiers. Each draw is an explicit function of the event that called it. This restores causal coherence.
arxiv-2603-11184: Basabendu Barman and coauthors ask how the reheating era after inflation reshapes gravitational waves born in phase transitions. Such a background is usually worked out for a radiation-dominated universe. The values steering a transition depend on the background's equation of state, itself set by the inflaton during reheating. The authors assume reheating proceeds as the inflaton breaks down bit by bit into boson or fermion pairs. In this epoch, signals are weaker as a rule, with spectral features that could betray the changed expansion history.
arxiv-2603-11284: Daniel da Silva and coauthors turn single-value solar wind forecasts into calibrated probability distributions, giving space weather predictions the uncertainty they usually lack. Their method extends analog ensembles, matching a scenario vector against a store of past ones. The vector packs the baseline model's coming output with recent data, and matched results shape a skew normal distribution. They pass percentile checks. Their mean beats the baseline model's own output and a solar-rotation benchmark at one-to-five-day leads.
arxiv-2603-11484: Sun and Zhou ask how long a quantum energy-storing device can keep working inside a lossy setting. Their device is a quantum spin chain whose setting acts through the Lindblad master equation. The device counts as alive while its spins hold nonzero excitations; empty means failure. Since Lindblad dynamics force one-way energy decay, reliability theory applies directly. For a two-site spin-1/2 chain, the pair derive closed forms for reliability and the hazard rate. A protocol based on first-passage times rounds out the work.
arxiv-2603-11584: Li and co-authors show that 3D Bragg ptychography can image micro-crystals that defeat the standard method. Coherent diffraction imaging often fails to retrieve phases when strain varies sharply inside a crystal. The new route keeps inversion stable even for large lattice distortions. It tolerates distortions more than six times larger than the older method can bear. On a weakly distorted crystal, it gives smoother amplitude and phase fields with fewer short-scale artifacts. The work widens coherent X-ray Bragg microscopy to strongly deformed systems.
arxiv-2603-11784: Racca and co-authors study model collapse through a learning-theory lens, using the language generation in the limit framework. They add a replay adversary that feeds a generator its own past outputs. Replay, they prove, leaves the strongest form of uniform generation unharmed. For weaker forms, non-uniform generation and generation in the limit, it provably splits what can be learned. The safe cases echo fixes used in practice, like data cleaning, watermarking, and output filtering.
arxiv-2603-11984: Xu and co-authors present Ada3Drift, a policy that lets robots act from point clouds in a single step. Fast one-step action avoids the slow repeat passes that diffusion policies need at control time. Training shifts by degrees from plain action regression to a drifting term that shapes the action spread. Tests cover the Adroit, Meta-World, and RoboTwin suites plus five real-world tasks. Ada3Drift posts the best average success rates among the methods compared, using one pass per action chunk.
arxiv-2603-12184: Liu, Guo, Tan, and Wang build a theory of entropy flow in living systems, with memory kept in the frame. Life stays far from equilibrium, trading energy and matter with its surroundings at all times. Their Keldysh-based frame adds colored noise, memory in dissipation, and many-body interactions. From it flow Langevin dynamics and master equations with memory. An exact frequency-domain form gives the entropy production rate. Broken fluctuation-dissipation balance marks active biological fluctuations, and memory boosts entropy output for slow modes near instability.
arxiv-2603-12384: Constantin, Lukas, and Nutricati construct Calabi-Yau metrics that keep explicit Kähler moduli dependence. Their route blends machine learning data with an analytic Ansatz for the Kähler potential. Neural networks first learn the potential at chosen points of moduli space. Fits turn that data into analytic forms with moduli-dependent parameters. Symbolic regression then finds closed forms for those coefficients as functions of the moduli. Two threefolds test the method, with percent-level accuracy and small Ricci-flatness error across the sampled region.
arxiv-2603-12484: Larsen describes how the mapping class group acts on the cohomology of the SLn character variety of a surface. The twisted character variety of a genus g surface carries the action she studies. Her main tool is a relative form of the endoscopic decomposition by Maulik and Shen. That tool reduces the problem to the action on a canonical finite cover of the surface. Looijenga studied that cover case in prior work she builds on. The reduction carries the full cohomology action back to the original variety.
arxiv-2603-12584: Rumi Kodama and co-authors test how a dwarf galaxy fly-by changes a bar in a disk galaxy. Bars slow as they pass angular momentum to their dark matter halo. That friction can fade once phase mixing flattens the key resonance region. In their N-body runs, a fly-by did not create the bar, which formed on the usual schedule. Afterward, though, bars grew stronger and slower than in the lone-galaxy run. The fly-by stirred the halo and kept the friction alive.
arxiv-2603-12784: Aheibam Boycha Meitei and co-authors compute how quantum gravity effects change Hawking temperature for a Kerr-Newman black hole in quintessence. They apply the generalized uncertainty principle to scalar and fermion equations at the horizon. Solved equations give temperature corrections that depend on the emitted particle quantum numbers. Fermion tunneling through a modified Hamilton-Jacobi route leads to the same corrected picture. In a gravity rainbow frame, heat capacity, entropy, and the equation of state also shift.
arxiv-2603-13084: Giulia Basti and co-authors bound the ground state energy of a dilute gas of hard spheres from above. The gas holds many bosons in a box with periodic boundaries, at fixed density. They take the thermodynamic limit, then the dilute limit where spheres rarely meet. Their bound matches the Lee-Huang-Yang formula in its main term, with only smaller terms apart. The result firms up a classic prediction for this model gas. The proof works per unit volume in the large system.
arxiv-2603-13384: Renwei Meng, Haoyi Wu, and Jingming Wang present VulnAgent-R2 for repository-level vulnerability detection. Flaws often hinge on cross-file data flow, build options, and runtime guards, so lone function checks give fragile warnings. Their budget-aware system adds counterfactual evidence reweighting, build-aware verification plans, and a cost-risk scheduler. Graph triage, role-specialized agents, and sceptic counter-evidence feed a calibrated fusion step. On four public datasets it beat prior agents on F1 and AUROC while using far fewer online tokens.
arxiv-2603-13584: Nicholas M. Synovic and co-authors investigate pre-trained deep learning model reuse in the scientific process. Training models from scratch is costly, so natural scientists increasingly reuse pre-trained models to amortize costs. Their study is the first empirical look at reuse patterns in the natural sciences. It covers 17,718 peer reviewed, open access papers across fields. Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology has outpaced other fields in reuse, they find. Adaptation is the most prevalent reuse pattern, and the testing stage is most affected by pre-trained model use.
arxiv-2603-14484: Wozniak and co-authors use machine unlearning to track concept drift in data streams. Classic models assume a fixed data distribution, but real streams shift over time. Sliding windows adapt, yet each shift forces costly retraining from scratch. Their method removes the effect of stale samples with unlearning. Fresh data then updates the model without a full rebuild. Tests on image streams under varied drift show the method stays competitive, the authors report. They claim the first link of unlearning to drift control.
arxiv-2603-15184: Nagabhushana and co-authors present CATFormer, a spiking transformer built for continual learning without forgetting. Spiking networks often lose old classes fast as new tasks arrive. The core is a dynamic threshold neuron that adjusts excitability by context, not just synaptic weights. A gated head selection mechanism supports task-free inference. Tests cover static image sets and neuromorphic datasets such as CIFAR10-DVS. CATFormer beat rehearsal-free rivals across task splits. The authors pitch it as an energy-efficient design for true class-incremental learning.
arxiv-2603-15584: Es'kin and Ivanov simulate extreme ultraviolet diffraction from lithography masks with physics-informed neural systems. They compare neural networks and neural operators against standard solvers on problems with known exact answers. A new hybrid, the Waveguide Neural Operator, swaps the costly parts of a waveguide method for a trained network. Tests at 13.5 and 11.2 nanometer wavelengths cover realistic two- and three-dimensional masks. The hybrid reached state-of-the-art accuracy with much shorter prediction times. It also held its accuracy on unseen parameter values.
arxiv-2603-15984: Gupta and co-authors switch a multiferroic's polar order with mechanical pressure. BiFeO3 couples electric polarization to lattice strain in one material. High switching fields and rival variants block firm domain control. Their films switch with out-of-plane fields near 4 volts alone. Added pressure cuts the needed voltage, even to zero. Spontaneous switching then takes over the film. Microscopy shows pressure quiets ferroelastic domain rivalry. Stress acts as a true control knob for switching paths. Device designs can spend pressure to save switching energy.
arxiv-2603-16184: Dang and Ngo fine-tune Qwen3 speech models for the languages of Singapore. The result, Polyglot-Lion, covers English, Mandarin, Tamil, and Malay. Training used only public speech data, with balanced samples per language. The models get no language tag, so they learn to detect the language from sound. The 1.7B model scored 14.85 average error across 12 benchmarks. That nearly matches a model six times larger, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2603-16684: Bläsius, Schaub, and Wilhelm compute diameters of random geometric graphs faster. Their algorithm runs in near n-to-the-1.737 time at one sweet degree. That beats a recent bound for all unit disk graphs. The method also works on flat torus ground spaces. The core is a framework of graph properties that enable fast diameter work. Balanced separators tied to the graph's own metric drive it. As a side result, the iFUB algorithm gains its first geometric analysis.
arxiv-2603-17084: Mohammadi Khangheshlaghi and Tent begin the model theory of the free factor complex of a free group. The free factor complex is a combinatorial object built from the free factors of a free group. They treat the finite rank case, and settle the case of rank 2 in detail. For rank 2, they axiomatize the theory of the complex. They show this theory is omega stable. They also identify its prime model as AF2. The work opens a model theoretic line on a central object of geometric group theory.
arxiv-2603-17384: Wu, Xie, and Li give generative causal models a sheaf-based theory of counterfactuals. Local rules that agree nearby may still fail to form one global counterfactual, they prove. The clash shows up as a cohomological obstruction when the graph has loops or hidden confounders. They add entropic smoothing and a new Laplacian built from coupled Fokker-Planck equations. The setup also yields a detector for topology-aware causal discovery.
arxiv-2603-17584: Mooij and co-authors ask why triangles abound in real networks but not in null models. Their guess ties triangles to dynamic stability in competing species networks. When rivals interact with equal strength, coexistence holds below a coupling bound set by graph degree. Tuning networks at fixed degree shows stronger coupling goes with more clustering, they find. Grassland plant networks cluster more than chance models predict. Triangles may mark stable competition.
arxiv-2603-17884: Mo and co-authors give language models a built-in sense of data provenance. Multi-stage training hides which dataset taught a model a given behavior. DebugLM trains models to tag responses with the source that drove them. Developers can then trace bad behavior to its training roots fast. At test time, they can also trigger refusal for one named source only. Tracing stayed accurate in tests while general skill held up, they report.
arxiv-2603-18484: Astudillo and Solé-Pi show that point sets in the plane contain many empty convex pentagons. A 5-hole is a pentagon whose vertices lie in the set and whose interior holds no set points. Every n-point set in general position yields at least order n to the 20/11 such pentagons. That bound improves the past n times log factor result and nears the conjectured n squared bound. The proof needs no computer assistance.
arxiv-2603-18784: Zhao and co-authors teach robots to trace soft objects using sight and touch together. Tracing pulls cables and cloth into extended states for later tasks. Their method learns from demonstrations with a unified model for line-like and sheet-like objects. A weighted loss favors actions that keep contact near the tactile image center. A task loss tracks overall progress along the object. A low-cost teleoperation rig feeds the tactile data. Tests reach 80 percent success on seen objects and 65 percent on new ones across varied items.
arxiv-2603-19184: Hösten and co-authors study how the Euler characteristic of a hypersurface shifts as its coefficients change. Each surface in the family matches a three-way independence model from algebraic statistics. Its signed Euler value equals the model's maximum likelihood degree. For the smallest case, the value rests only on which factors of a key determinant vanish. That simple rule fails for larger cases. They show all values up to the top degree can occur, and they map the smallest case in full.
arxiv-2603-19384: Ma and co-authors predict the 3D shape of a soft robot finger from servo commands in real time. Soft arms bend in ways that are hard to model, due to material lag and build flaws. Their SOFTMAP first aligns simulated and real point clouds into one vertex space. A small network learned on simulation data gives the base shape. A second network, trained on few real samples, fixes the gaps. A closed-form calibration layer keeps inference at 30 frames per second. Shape error on hardware is under four millimeters.
arxiv-2603-19484: Drmota and Hainzl study discrete differential equations whose order jumps with a parameter. For the parameter at zero the order is one, but above one for any other value. They call such equations singularly perturbed. Under natural assumptions, they show the change is in fact smooth. As a use case, they count patterns in triangular planar maps. They derive a central limit theorem for patterns that cannot self-intersect.
arxiv-2603-19784: Shrimal and co-authors use lattice QCD to hunt for a strange partner of the Tcc+ tetraquark. They study coupled scattering between D and Ds meson pairs. Two spin channels are covered, with total spin parity 1+ and 0+. Their runs use CLS ensembles with a pion mass near 280 MeV. Spectra come from a variational study of correlation matrices. Scattering amplitudes are read off with Lüscher methods. They see small shifts from the noninteracting spectrum. No pole near threshold appears, so no bound tetraquark is claimed.
arxiv-2603-20484: Akyildiz and Bilen argue fluid antenna networks need AI-native control for 6G. Fluid antennas add a new freedom: antenna position itself can adapt. Most studies stress physical-layer gains from that mobility. Once antennas move, positioning becomes a network control problem. Their closed-loop design joins antenna moves with radio resource management. Live observations drive joint antenna and resource decisions. A multi-agent learning approach coordinates control across base stations. Illustrative results show gains at the cell edge and less interference.
arxiv-2603-20584: Yuan and co-authors work on guidance for diffusion image models. Sampling can drift as small errors build up along the path. Guidance methods push back by mixing strong and weak signals. The team first maps when two known methods work best. They then build SGG, a hybrid that joins both gains. The same idea also fits inside the training loss. On SD3 and SD3.5, SGG beat rival training free methods.
arxiv-2603-20684: Laudari trims echo state networks by pruning nodes that matter least in the reservoir graph. Echo state networks predict time series with a fixed random reservoir. Many reservoir nodes add cost but little signal. This method views the reservoir as a weighted directed graph. Centrality scores rank each node's structural worth. Low ranked nodes get cut before training the readout. On Mackey-Glass and power load data, the pruned networks stayed accurate. Some runs even improved while using far fewer nodes.
arxiv-2603-21284: Cheon introduces Sonny, an efficient transformer for medium-range weather forecasting. Deep learning forecasters now rival operational systems, but many need huge training compute. Sonny uses a two stage StepsNet design. A narrow slow path first models large scale atmospheric dynamics. A full width fast path then adds thermodynamic interactions. Exponential moving average during training steadies the rollout. On WeatherBench2, Sonny shows robust medium-range skill and trains on one A40 GPU in about five and a half days.
arxiv-2603-21684: Matsumoto and co-authors make a common audio network block provably stable. Amplitude modifiers are a standard design for audio signals, but their robustness had no Lipschitz proof. Lipschitz continuity caps how much an output can move when the input moves a little. The authors prove a condition that makes an amplitude modifier Lipschitz. They give two designs, called LipsAM, that meet it. Dropped into a speech dereverberation method, the new blocks improved stability in numeric tests, they report.
arxiv-2603-21784: Kim and co-authors improve burst photography by choosing exposure times on the fly. Burst restoration merges many shots into one clean image, but the exposure plan is usually fixed by hand. Their DEBIR pipeline starts with a network that reads a preview image plus motion and gain cues. It then predicts the best exposure time for each shot in the burst. A second network rebuilds the final image from those shots. A differentiable burst simulator supports training. Tests on a real camera system beat prior methods, they report.
arxiv-2603-21984: Behague and co-authors tighten the bounds on when a graph must contain a Hamilton cycle that avoids forbidden edge pairs. Dirac's theorem gives such a cycle when the minimum degree is at least half the vertex count. An incompatibility system marks pairs of adjacent edges a cycle may not use back to back. How dense can those pairs be before a safe cycle vanishes? Past work left a wide gap. For degree a bit above half, a bound of 1/8 works, while 1/6 would be too weak.
arxiv-2603-22184: Novo and co-authors ask where domain knowledge should live in quantum code generation tools. They compare a fine-tuned Qiskit model with general language models on the Qiskit-HumanEval benchmark. The general models get help from retrieval or from agents with execution feedback. The fine-tuned baseline scores about 47% pass at one try. General models reach 60 to 65% with no help or with retrieval. The best setup, an agent with execution feedback, reaches 85%. The authors conclude that inference-time help beats domain fine-tuning here.
arxiv-2603-22384: Di Gioia teaches an agent not just what to do, but when to act. Agents in steady settings must pick the gap between thinking steps. His system learns the gap length from experience. A spread signal from hyperbolic geometry guides the choice. Wide spread among sampled futures means an uncertain, branching path, so the agent acts sooner. A reward term also charges the agent for wasted wait time. A joint version that adds position data gains a further edge.
arxiv-2603-22684: Elgailani, Vandembroucq, and Maloney study a model of amorphous matter under shear. They vary how compressible the material is, via the ratio of compression to shear moduli. In cyclic shear, behavior shifts from elastic to reversible loops to diffuse flow as amplitude grows. More compressible systems act harder, with a wider elastic range. In steady shear they also show higher flow stress. A striking result is complex strain hardening with no built-in hardening settings. The switch in hardening type sits at the same point as the hysteresis shift.
arxiv-2603-22784: Azarmehr, Behnezhad, and Ghafari study how language models should spend extra test-time compute. They model test-time work as an algorithm that can resume from any past state of a Markov chain. Backtracking fits this frame, as do chain-of-thought and tree search. They prove that a very limited form of backtracking is enough. The optimal method builds a caterpillar tree: strip the leaves and a path remains. Their Caterpillar of Thoughts method beats Tree-of-Thoughts on success rate. It also uses fewer token generations.
arxiv-2603-22884: Cabrera-Martínez and co-authors characterize trees that hit known bounds for a domination number. The target is total outer-independent domination in subdivision graphs. A subdivision graph splits each edge of a tree once. Earlier work bounded the domination number using leaf and support counts. This study gives constructive descriptions of the tree families that reach the lower bound. It does the same for the families that reach the upper bound. Such descriptions show exactly which tree shapes are extremal.
arxiv-2603-22984: Gutteridge, Bronstein, and Dong ask whether graph foundation models can generalize over architecture. Such models aim to work zero-shot on graphs of any size or domain. Most use one fixed backbone for all tasks. The authors argue true generality needs architecture adaptivity. Using range as a test axis, they show fixed models fall short on tasks with new range needs. Their framework finds and mixes task-specific graph operators at test time. No retraining is needed. Tests on synthetic and real benchmarks show better robustness.
arxiv-2603-23384: Ghosh, Aldowma, and Razzaque dissect the prompt flash of gamma-ray burst GRB 250129A. Swift-BAT caught a burst with many peaks across two emission episodes. The main peak came about 180 seconds after the trigger. Across 15 to 150 keV, a broken power law fits the summed spectrum best. That shape points to a non-thermal origin. Around the main peak, flux tracks the spectral peak energy closely. Amati and hardness checks place the burst between long and ultra-long classes.
arxiv-2603-23684: Warner and three co-authors clean up motion captions so text and movement match better. One motion earns many captions, and each mixes true cues with a writer's style and guesses. Standard training treats one caption as the sole right answer, which blurs the shared space. MoCHA rewrites each caption down to what the motion itself can show. A big language model does the rewrite, or a small distilled model at run time. Scores jump on both standard sets, and transfer across datasets soars.
arxiv-2603-23784: Swaroop studies grokking in small ReLU networks trained on modular arithmetic. Grokking means test accuracy rises long after training data are memorized. Prior work stressed smooth wave-like weights. Swaroop instead finds near-binary square-wave input weights in these networks. An idealized model built from extracted phases and frequencies scores 95.5 percent, even when copied from a noisy model scoring 0.23 percent. This suggests the algorithm forms during memorization, and grokking only sharpens it into view.
arxiv-2603-24184: Flores-Rivera and co-authors test whether turbulence-born vortices can trap dust in protoplanetary disks. ALMA images show crescent-shaped dust piles in several disks, and vortices are a prime suspect. Their 3D simulations use the PLUTO code with particles of three sizes. The turbulence comes from the vertical shear instability. Multiple vortices form, and two large long-lived ones capture dust well. Dust also settles less inside vortices. Unlike planet-made vortices, theirs leave no clear spirals in synthetic ALMA images.
arxiv-2603-24384: Péter and co-authors study bagging as a way to make local intrinsic dimensionality estimates more stable. Such estimates need points from tiny neighbourhoods, which keeps bias low but makes variance high. Their ensemble uses subbagging that keeps the local spread of neighbour distances. They analyse how the sampling rate, the neighbour count, and the ensemble size interact. Across wide ranges of these choices, the bagged estimator cuts variance and mean squared error, with a small and controlled effect on bias.
arxiv-2603-24884: Karn gives simple presentations for invariant subrings of two algebras tied to the type A reflection arrangement. The algebras are the Orlik-Solomon algebra and the Varchenko-Gel'fand ring. The acting group is the type A reflection group of one rank lower. The result can be read as a presentation for the cohomology of a mixed configuration space of points. Karn builds the description in stages, from the total dimension up to generators and relations. Each stage refines the picture of the invariant ring.
arxiv-2603-24984: Ko and co-authors improve how vision-language models pick their experts. In a mixture-of-experts model, only a few parts run for each token, which saves compute. The usual rule picks the top few experts by a fixed score, and it can miss better mixes. Their MoE-GRPO treats each pick as a step in a game and trains it with group-based rewards. A guide steers the router away from experts rarely used for each input type. Tests on image and video tasks beat fixed routing.
arxiv-2603-25584: Cances, Mérigot, and Nenna attack a nonlinear transport problem from risk work with a cloud of particles. The goal is to push a coupling through a cost map and maximize a spectral risk score. A linear twin of the problem exists with one extra margin. Their method spreads weighted points to mimic couplings and enforces margins by Wasserstein penalties. They prove the cloud settles on the true answer as it grows. Rates hinge on the winner's shape and sharpen for comonotone cases. Tests span risk and barycenter tasks.
arxiv-2603-26084: Onogi and Yamaoka study conserved charges of the staggered fermion Hamiltonian in 3+1 dimensions. They split staggered fermions into Majorana parts and use lattice translation symmetry. From this they build a set of conserved non-singlet charges. The charges do not all commute with each other on the lattice. In the continuum limit, they still generate axial SU(2) left and right transformations for the low-energy modes. The authors also discuss what this may mean for anomalies.
arxiv-2603-26184: Hoessly explains why decision curves for clinical prediction models rise above or fall below the default strategies. Net benefit is widely used but hard to read in practice. He recasts it through two plain quantities. One is the event rate among patients flagged positive. The other is the rate among those flagged negative. A model beats treating no one when the first rate tops the threshold. It beats treating everyone when the second falls below it.
arxiv-2603-26384: Araújo, Sokal, and de Almeida tackle channel estimation for beyond-diagonal reconfigurable surfaces in MIMO systems. The rich coupling that makes these surfaces strong also makes training and control hard. Their plan uses a two-timescale protocol and shapes the scattering as a low-rank PARAFAC tensor model. The link layout stays fixed across blocks while only phase shifts change. A receiver based on alternating least squares then recovers each channel, matching top tensor methods with far less design effort.
arxiv-2603-26684: Salanova, Montijano, and Mahulea split multi-agent path finding into geometric planning and execution-time control. Central solvers with time-expanded models scale poorly when crowds of agents share one graph. Their first stage plans paths one agent at a time with A*, raising costs on vertices that earlier paths already use. A local controller then runs the paths, using per-vertex queues and added waits to dodge clashes. On standard maps with up to 1000 agents, runtime grows near-linearly and every feasible case succeeds.
arxiv-2603-26884: Bottini and Jones reflect on time reversal inside Symmetry Topological Field Theory. Time reversal acts as an anti-unitary operator, so tools built for unitary symmetry miss it. The authors enrich a standard SymTFT with a background time-reversal field. Studying its boundary terms shows which gapped phases keep that symmetry. Line operators link to string-order measures for topological phases. The study pins down endpoint charges on the lattice and in the continuum. It also recovers the Klein bottle invariant for one such phase.
arxiv-2603-27084: He and co-authors present SceneExpander, a method for growing 3D scenes from text. Creators extend scenes step by step, but inserted views rarely align with the captured geometry. A model first renders the requested new view. SceneExpander then adapts a feed-forward model at test time. Anchor distillation holds the original scene steady using captured views. Inserted-view self-distillation keeps the new content the insertion supports. Tests on ETH scenes and online captures raised expansion quality under misalignment.
arxiv-2603-27184: Xu and co-authors propose Temporal Global Policy Optimization to give video models a sense of time. Models often answer from single frames and ignore event order. First-person video makes that shortcut especially costly. TGPO rewards outputs from ordered frames over shuffled ones. The contrast yields rewards that favor temporal order. Plugged into standard policy optimization, it supports cold-start RL training. Five egocentric benchmarks showed better temporal grounding and causal coherence. Prior RL methods for video were beat consistently.
arxiv-2603-27384: El Aitouni and co-authors study how electrons tunnel through magnetic barriers in tungsten diselenide. They solve the energy equations in closed form. They then work out how likely an electron is to cross. Current flows more easily through one valley than the other. Both valleys show the Klein tunneling effect. A stronger field shifts energy levels through the Zeeman effect. That shift can trap electrons inside the barrier. The results point to tools for valley based storage devices.
arxiv-2603-27784: Ling and co-authors study AI fortune-telling in Chinese user communities. They interviewed twenty-two habitual users of such tools. A three-week ethnography adds 1,842 community posts. Many users seek psychological comfort above all. Repeat queries run until answers fit their hopes. Users praise access, ease, and speed. They miss the spiritual mystique of old methods. Group talk cements each reading in place.
arxiv-2603-28384: Cao and Kavokin propose building artificial spin ice out of exciton-polaritons, light-matter quasiparticles in a lattice. In their design, each link's circular polarization acts as an Ising spin. A lossy hub mode quietly enforces the ice rule, favoring two-in two-out states. Flipping one link's polarization spawns a monopole pair, and chains of flips drag the defects across the lattice. Polarization imaging can then read out the charges directly, making the gauge physics visible.
arxiv-2603-28484: Tapia-Riera, Castera, and Papadakis prove that two workhorse algorithms converge for weakly convex min-max problems. Such problems pit a minimizer against a maximizer, as in training robust models. Their simpler proof for alternating gradient descent-ascent also widens the allowed step sizes. A doubly proximal variant gets the same treatment. The results open a path to plug-and-play imaging methods, where neural networks act as regularizers inside the solver.
arxiv-2603-28884: McConkey and co-authors launch the Closure Challenge, a benchmark for machine learning in turbulence modelling. The field had open training data but no standard test set or metric. The challenge gives curated open datasets in a standard format, with mean velocity gradients. Test cases cover periodic hills, a square duct, and a NASA wall mounted hump. They check how models generalize across Reynolds number and geometry. Three early submissions are reported. The team aims for the challenge to become the standard test for new RANS closure frameworks.
arxiv-2603-29084: Barkatou studies the shape of level sets of solutions to an elliptic equation. Each level set is written as a graph over the boundary of a convex core. A thickness function measures how far the set sits from that core. Barkatou derives an exact formula for the gradient of this function along the boundary. Under a small-thickness condition, he also expands the unit normal vector. Examples show that a flat normal property does not force constant thickness.
arxiv-2603-29284: Bhat and Kumar establish new identities linking two famous continued fractions. One is the Ramanujan-Göllnitz-Gordon continued fraction. The other is Ramanujan's continued fraction of order four. Their tools come from q-series and theta functions. A key step uses the product expansion of Jacobi's theta function. They also derive Lambert series identities. Those rest on Ramanujan's one-psi-one summation formula. The work adds fresh links between classical fraction families.
arxiv-2603-29684: Kalwarczyk presents FcsIT, an open-source tool for fluorescence correlation spectroscopy analysis. The software runs on any platform and is written in Python. A Dear PyGUI interface drives the workflow. It reads and correlates time-tagged photon data, with filtering of time traces. A circular-block bootstrap estimates correlation uncertainty. Data quality rivals commercial software, the author reports. The fitting screen handles large datasets with nine built-in models. Users can add their own models with ease. Tests on simulated and real data confirm its usability.
arxiv-2603-29784: Koloski and co-authors present MAPLE, a method for layered multi-label image tagging in remote sensing. Images can sit on several label paths at once, which older methods handle poorly. MAPLE starts from graph-aware text descriptions of the label tree. A graph network encodes that structure, and a fusion step weighs text priors against image evidence. A level-aware loss picks the right penalty per level. Gains reach 42 percent in few-shot tests.
arxiv-2604-00084: Assi, Lee, and Thaler upgrade parton-shower event samples by reweighting them under maximum-entropy constraints. The weights stay strictly positive and keep every event intact for any later observable. Using energy flow polynomials as a systematic basis of safe constraints, they show a small set of precision moments can repair even a deliberately degraded shower prior. Information saturates quickly, so a compact moment set improves observables broadly, including standard hemisphere measures never used in the fit.
arxiv-2604-00184: Colò and Kohel study supersingular isogeny graphs with level structure, along with the Galois representations tied to them. Isogeny graphs encode maps between supersingular elliptic curves, and level structure adds further data to the picture. The paper treats these graphs and their representations together, linking the combinatorics of the graphs to the arithmetic of the representations. Its focus is the interplay between graph structure and Galois-theoretic data in the supersingular setting.
arxiv-2604-00284: Gaurav Parikh and Angikar Ghosal introduce Connections, an improvisational wordplay game, as a benchmark for social intelligence in AI agents. Playing it draws on knowledge retrieval, summarization, and awareness of other agents' cognitive states, going beyond memory and deduction alone. Through communication in a constrained setting, agents must gauge what other agents understand and show social awareness in collaborative play. The game thus tests social intelligence that pure reasoning benchmarks miss.
arxiv-2604-00584: Roehrle and Schmitt study normalizers of parabolic subgroups in quaternionic reflection groups. Howlett and Muraleedaran-Taylor showed that real or complex groups always give a parabolic subgroup a complement in its normalizer. For quaternionic groups, the authors find they need not exist in general. Endless cases in any rank above 2 carry a parabolic subgroup with no complement in its normalizer. The paper sorts parabolic subgroups of irreducible quaternionic groups in full, and lists their complements where they exist.
arxiv-2604-00684: Xu and colleagues propose TP-Seg for unified medical lesion segmentation. One model with one set of settings for many lesion types is a key goal for AI-aided diagnosis. Current unified methods share coders across tasks and scans, which tangles features, clashes gradients, and weakens lesion sorting. TP-Seg uses a task-tuned adapter with a dual-path expert design to balance shared and task-specific features, enabling tuned feature use across scans and lesion types. A prototype-guided decoder adds learnable task prototypes as semantic guides.
arxiv-2604-00884: Zacharias and Wierzcholska present the companion two-decade multiwavelength study of the blazar PKS 1510-089, comparing it with PKS 2155-304 studied with the same techniques. High-energy gamma-ray and X-ray flux distributions are log-normal, while optical distributions fit double-log-normal functions, possibly from accretion-disk contributions. Unlike its companion, PKS 1510-089 shows no harder-when-brighter behavior. Both sources show orphan flares in any band, with variability patterns that keep changing unpredictably.
arxiv-2604-01184:
Infinite Heat Order in 3+1 Dimensions tests a bold idea in quantum field theory. The authors ask whether spontaneous symmetry breaking can persist to high temperature. Arbitrarily high temperature, in ultraviolet-complete theories, is the strong claim examined.

They work in four spacetime dimensions throughout the analysis. Their models are completely asymptotically free, a demanding condition to meet. The gauge group is a product of two SU factors, they specify. Two complex scalar fields carry the symmetry breaking in the models. Each transforms under one gauge factor and is singlet under the other. The paper probes whether order can survive endless heating. Theorists get a sharp test case for symmetry at extreme temperatures.
arxiv-2604-01484: Loftus establishes scaling for the gap, the H1 persistence of the alpha complex over a matched null, which encodes correlations in spin models. For 2D Ising, the exponent is 2.249, matching d plus η. For 2D Potts q equals 3, the exponent matches d plus η, with corrections. The law fails for 2D Potts q equals 4, where logarithmic corrections prevent convergence, and for 3D Ising, but normalization recovers it. It also fails for first-order, BKT, and percolation. The exponent equals d plus η when corrections are algebraic, but not when logarithmic.
arxiv-2604-01684: Zhang and colleagues simulate how primordial black hole clusters evolve through repeated mergers. This builds on their earlier claim that small-scale clustering of such holes explains distant supermassive black holes seen as little red dots. They solve the Smoluchowski coagulation equation, deriving its kernel with and without mass segregation. A Monte Carlo solution uses a full-conditioning scheme with discrete inverse transformation. The runs pin down cluster runaway timescales and how the mass population shifts across cosmic redshifts with cluster size and density.
arxiv-2604-01884: Yang, Wang, Li, Jin and Ling cut the memory cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting, a way to rebuild scenes from soft 3D blobs for new viewpoints. Their 2026 method, GS squared, reshapes where blobs sit, adds points only where a statistical bound says they help, and prunes faint ones step by step. It keeps picture quality high with about 12.5 percent of the usual point count, beating rival compact methods on quality and memory.
arxiv-2604-01984: Ravina, reporting for the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations, reviews recent top-quark pair cross section measurements from both experiments. Off-shell effects get probed in proton collisions yielding W bosons with b quarks and in electron-muon plus b-quark channels, with modeling of the POWHEG bb4l generator discussed. Measurements also reach the production threshold, where an indirect extraction of the top quark Yukawa coupling is reviewed. Both experiments also see an excess of events near threshold consistent with quasi-bound state formation.
arxiv-2604-02384: Bailey, McPhedran and Salvy give a practical algorithm for evaluating Euler sums, infinite series that pair harmonic numbers with rational functions, in closed form using digamma and polygamma functions. Their method also reduces a broader family of such sums to partial fraction decomposition. They supply explicit formulas for denominators with one or two terms, checked against very high-precision direct computation.
arxiv-2604-02784: Miyazato, Kitada and Harada propose EnsemHalDet, an ensemble method for detecting hallucinations in vision-language models from internal states rather than outputs alone. Prior internal methods rely on one signal or detector, missing diverse cues. EnsemHalDet trains separate detectors on attention outputs and hidden states, then combines them by ensemble learning. Tests cover multiple datasets and models. It consistently beats prior and single-detector methods on visual question answering tests.
arxiv-2604-02984: Galanos proves a bilinear Kakeya inequality in the first Heisenberg group and a sharp bilinear Kakeya estimate for Euclidean curved tubes in the plane. Borrowing Fässler, Pinamonti and Wald's approach on Heisenberg maps, he shows the tube result implies the Heisenberg inequality. He proves the tube result by combining techniques of Pramanik, Yang and Zahl, Wolff and Schlag. A novel broadness hypothesis rules out bush-type shapes that break transversal structure, and extra linear terms counteract Szemerédi-Trotter-type clumping.
arxiv-2604-03184: Bohm and colleagues extend the classic contact process, which models spreading like disease or fire, into the quantum realm on a topological lattice. Coherent spreading can stay trapped in a protected subspace, either at one site or across a fully excited lattice, and topological pumps can release it in quantized steps on demand. Excited domains map to a single-particle model that also fixes the topological character.
arxiv-2604-03384: Bacellar presents BridgeRAG, a training-free retrieval method for multi-hop questions that ranks later evidence by its fit with bridge evidence, not just the original query. A bridge-conditioned judge picks the active reasoning chain among candidates, while dual-entity expansion widens the candidate pool. It achieves the best published training-free top-5 recall on all three standard benchmarks, without any graph or training.
arxiv-2604-03584: Dong and Yang's 2026 survey covers recent progress on elliptic equations from mixes, where tiny gaps between bits and high property contrast can strongly boost the field inside narrow regions. They review those equations and systems for which best estimates or sharp long-run profiles have been obtained over three decades. They also highlight several open questions.
arxiv-2604-03684: Christian Pipal and colleagues showed that coding texts one at a time wastes most of the money spent on language-model annotation. Grouping 25 items per prompt and stacking all variables together cut the calls needed for 100,000 texts on four variables from 400,000 to 4,000. Tests on eight models found accuracy held up through batches of 100, so the savings cost little quality.
arxiv-2604-03784: Tim Alderson studied codes that attain the Plotkin bound for length given Singleton defect, calling them length-maximal. Equality forces rigid structure: symbol uniformity under repeated shortening, an orthogonal array of strength at least k minus 1, and a narrow set of pairwise distances. In dimension four only a few defect values survive, and from dimension five up, length-maximal codes are essentially MDS, save the dual and extended ternary Golay codes.
arxiv-2604-03884: Tianrun Zhao and Nengkun Yu formalized CHSH rigidity in Lean 4, the theorem that near-optimal CHSH scores force a strategy to match the canonical qubit strategy up to local isometry. Since CHSH violation certifies genuine quantum correlations, a machine-checked proof matters for trust in the claim. Along the way, the formalization exposed a gap in the argument of McKague, Yang, and Scarani. The work shows formal proof catching real errors in published reasoning.
arxiv-2604-04084: Coralie Williams and team added the equalto covariance structure to the glmmTMB package for one-stage and two-stage meta-analysis. Standard two-stage models synthesize effect sizes, while one-stage generalized linear mixed models work directly on outcome data. Previously, known sampling variances and covariances fit poorly into glmmTMB's two-stage inverse-variance form. The new structure lets users supply a known sampling error variance-covariance matrix, unifying both formulations with identical results to metafor on normal-normal models.
arxiv-2604-04584: Zhou, Shang and Wang explore how triaxial shape shows up in the low-lying collective bands of erbium-166 within the SU3-IBM framework. The framework adds higher-order SU(3) interactions, which allow many quadrupole deformations. Erbium-166's triaxiality is described with a triaxiality angle of 9.7 degrees. Calculated energy spectra, B(E2) transition strengths and quadrupole moments match experimental data well. The results back the SU(3) triaxial reading of erbium-166 and confirm its triaxial deformation rather than a prolate shape.
arxiv-2604-05184: Kim and Gupta develop a phase-field model of Hf1-xZrxO2 with Zr-amount link, growing the GL rule. The model explains liking and barriers of rival orthorhombic and tetragonal phases, while giving charge maps, letting charge and mixed phase states emerge on their own. The model shows the ferroelectric to antiferroelectric switch as x rises from 0.5 to 1.0. At middle amounts the two phase costs are close, so field shifts produce mixed phase mix and stepped charge flip, giving a more gradual curve.
arxiv-2604-05284: Aidun and Thompson study the divisor-sum function, the sum of s(d) over divisors d of n, where s sums proper divisors. Although the function is neither additive nor multiplicative, the ratio has a continuous asymptotic distribution, with values dense from 0 to infinity. They evaluate its mean and establish all higher moments. The kth moment satisfies its 1/k power growing like e to the power 2 gamma times the square of log k as k grows, with gamma the Euler-Mascheroni constant.
arxiv-2604-05484: Kang and thirteen colleagues build CoEnv, a shared world where several robot arms plan in simulation and act in reality. It rebuilds real scenes in simulation, drafts actions with vision-language models, and transfers only collision-checked plans to hardware. Tests on hard multi-arm tasks report high success and efficient execution, offering a new pattern for embodied teamwork.
arxiv-2604-05584: Weng and three colleagues harden multimodal human sensing against missing and noisy inputs. Their Purify-then-Align framework first down-weights weak modalities by meta-learning, then distills a cleaned teacher's knowledge into each single-modality student by diffusion. Tests on two large datasets show leading performance and tougher single-modality models when inputs drop out.
arxiv-2604-05684: Hong and four colleagues expose a flaw in multilingual retrieval: when English documents share a pool with another language, retrievers favor unrelated English texts over same-language matches. They build scenarios and metrics for cross-lingual alignment and train a fix on just 2.8k samples. The method lifts cross-lingual scores across most embedding models while curbing the English bias.
arxiv-2604-05784: Bhattacharya, Tokiwa, and Majumder establish a quantum spin liquid ground state in triangular-lattice delafossite YbCuSe2. No magnetic order or freezing appears down to 0.03 kelvin, and below 0.7 kelvin most spins form a liquid while a minority decouples. Roton-like excitations between 4.5 and 1.8 kelvin, unseen in any spin liquid before, precede the low-temperature state.
arxiv-2604-05884: Crnkovic, Svob, and Zubovic Zutolija prove new directed strongly regular graphs on 60 vertices exist for six parameter sets, with degrees from 21 to 28. Each graph has 60 vertices, and the stated parameters fix valency plus intersection counts for the directed design. The group S5 times 2 moves every vertex to every other vertex in these graphs, so every vertex plays the same structural role.
arxiv-2604-06084: Sandvik's 2026 proof settles a claim by Gorsky, Hogancamp, Mellit, and Nakagane on relative Serre duality for Coxeter groups. It links the left and right adjoints of the parabolic induction functor between homotopy categories of Soergel bimodules for a finite Coxeter group. It says those adjoints relate through the relative full twist. Known cases covered symmetric, crystallographic, and dihedral groups. Sandvik settles it in complete generality using Abe-Bott-Samelson bimodules and the Achar-Riche-Vay mixed derived category.
arxiv-2604-06284: Lu and three colleagues present ClawLess, a security framework for agents that reason, plan, and execute. Fetching information and running code create risks, while training or prompting offers no hard guarantees. ClawLess enforces formally verified policies under a worst-case model treating the agent as potentially adversarial. It formalizes a detailed model over entities, trust scopes, and permissions, with policies adapting to runtime behavior. Those policies become rules enforced by a user-space kernel with BPF-based syscall interception, bridging formal guarantees and enforcement for any internal design.
arxiv-2604-06484: Wang and five colleagues test whether culture-conditioned judgments hold with images. Cultural values show in language, visual scenes, and practices, yet evaluations are almost entirely text-only. ValueGround, built from World Values Survey questions, uses contrastive image pairs for opposites. A model gets an image pair plus a country and a question, and picks the image best matching the country's value tendency without the texts. Across six models and 13 countries, accuracy falls from about 73 to about 63 percent with images. The benchmark offers a controlled testbed for cross-modal transfer.
arxiv-2604-06784: Cao, Li, and Zhu improve multi-party dialogue generation by rewriting context before responding. Casual wording and half-finished lines muddy dialogue structure, above all with many voices. Their DRCR framework uses discourse coherence and response quality as twin feedback signals, building preference data for both the rewrite side and the reply side. A dynamic self-growth loop then lets the two improve each other through repeated rounds. Tests on four multi-party dialogue sets confirm the method works.
arxiv-2604-06884: Bhardwaj and Vashisth study inverse problems for a coupled system of waves with a hidden term in three-space. By building the basic solution for the system, they tackle whether finding the matrix-valued term from time-varying readings is unique. Two setups are covered: same-point, with source and receiver at one point, and split, with source and receiver at distinct points. The problems lack enough data, so extra rules on the numbers are needed, and the authors prove it is unique under such rules.
arxiv-2604-06984: Kurokawa and 18 colleagues build a built-in diamond crystal cavity holding nitrogen-vacancy centers for cold optics. Diamond color centers suit quantum optics for long spin memory times and high photon output rates, yet in-step light needs cold to shield signals from phonons, making chip integration hard. The team confirms cold work by seeing Purcell boost of center light through an edge-coupled fiber. The result shows joining of diamond color centers, a light crystal cavity, and a guide-fiber package, a key step toward scalable diamond quantum platforms.
arxiv-2604-07184: Modak reports fresh ALICE measurements from light-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider in July 2025, covering proton-oxygen, oxygen-oxygen, and neon-neon runs. The paper gives charged-particle densities and flow patterns that track how matter expands collectively, plus evidence that neutral pion yields fall in oxygen-oxygen collisions against a proton-proton baseline. Comparing the data with models sharpens the picture of particle production and energy loss in small systems.
arxiv-2604-07384: Verma and four colleagues report SAHELI, a five-year project that schedules scarce health-worker outreach for mothers and children in India with NGO ARMMAN. It uses restless multi-armed bandits to pick whom to contact next under tight resources. The key move is decision-focused learning, which trains the system toward engagement itself rather than first predicting and then optimizing. Large trials show engagement drops fall by 31 percent against standard care, and the gains show up in real habits, notably continued iron and calcium use by new mothers.
arxiv-2604-07484: Liang and seven colleagues present ConsistRM, a self-training framework for generative reward models that align language models without costly human labels. Generative reward models beat scalar models in capacity but suffer instability and reward hacking under self-training. ConsistRM adds a consistency-aware answer reward for reliable pseudo-labels over time, plus a consistency-aware critique reward scoring agreement across critiques. Across five benchmarks and four base models, ConsistRM beats vanilla reinforcement fine-tuning by 1.5 percent on average, improves consistency, and cuts position bias.
arxiv-2604-07684: Shrivastava extends the work of Eli, Hom, and Lidman on exotic R4 manifolds. He provides Kirby diagrams for two equivalent families of exotic R4s. They use the simplest positive Casson handle on a slice-disc complement for the ribbon knot T(2,n) # T(2,-n) for n at least 3 and odd. The author generalizes these diagrams to a family of exotic R4s built using ribbon disc complements for pretzel knots P(n,-n,2k). Eli, Hom, and Lidman had provided a Kirby diagram only for n equals 3.
arxiv-2604-07784: Son and six colleagues treat car engineering with AI as workflow intelligence, not a pile of separate tasks. Their Agentic Engineering Intelligence vision models design, diagnosis, tuning, and systems engineering as constrained decision sequences shaped by history. Agents support engineer-supervised steps over toolchains. An offline phase builds workflow memory from project data, while an online phase estimates workflow state and recommends actions. Cases from suspension design to aerodynamics show the shared framing at work.
arxiv-2604-07884: Jia and five colleagues break a data-scarcity loop in privacy-tight identity recognition. Strong generative models are most needed where data access is tightest, yet scarce data yields poor generators that cannot relieve the shortage. Their reinforcement-guided method adapts general-domain model priors to identity tasks under privacy limits. A cold-start step first aligns a pretrained generator with the target domain for relevance and initial quality. Multi-objective reinforcement then refines the output, aiming for synthetic data useful enough to train recognition models without real identities.
arxiv-2604-07984: Zhang and three colleagues tackle physics-based motion tracking for characters in contact-rich interaction. Existing methods track single characters or one interaction type, and extending them breaks down because forces transferred through contacts destabilize control. Contact-rich scenes demand multiple levels of control and far greater model capacity. Their robust method uses progressive neural networks in which several experts specialize in skills of varying difficulty. Training samples are assigned to experts automatically, without manual scheduling, and results cover both qualitative and quantitative gains.
arxiv-2604-08184: Xie and 12 colleagues present the AT-ADD plan for all-type audio deepfake detection. Rapid progress in Audio Large Language Models enabled cheap, high-fidelity generation and manipulation of speech and non-speech audio, including sound effects and music. While these powers foster creativity and content production, they also raise security challenges, since realistic audio deepfakes now spread at scale. Existing countermeasures and benchmarks stay largely speech-centric, relying on speech-specific artifacts with limited robustness to real-world distortions and narrow generalization to varied audio and new spoofing techniques.
arxiv-2604-08484: Johnson and ten colleagues show that a mechanically moved dielectric slab in a waveguide's faint outer field can flip the sign of dispersion change. Even as the guided mode's effective index rises, the group's index falls, an anomalously dispersive modulation no ordinary thermal, electro optic, or plasma device offers. A new actuator design proves the effect in experiment, opening paths to broadband switching, true time delay, pulse shaping, and nonlinear phase matching.
arxiv-2604-09084: Méndez and four colleagues build a force-field-free phase sorter for zeolitic imidazolate frameworks. These metal-organic solids link metal centers to imidazole ligands in zeolite-like shapes. Zinc-based versions show many forms, shifting with recipe and heat or pressure. The team finds low-dim markers already sort phases well, while high-dim markers do even better. Training on setups from other force fields removes force-field bias and lifts scores and reach. The sorters reveal details of the ZIF-4-cp to ZIF-4-cp-II change.
arxiv-2604-09184: Grimm and Stadel review fast numerical methods for N-body planet systems in the GPU era. Symplectic integrators handle long-term orbits and short-term collisions. Their public code GENGA, a GPU/CPU code, unifies these methods on new hardware. The chapter warns against a shortcut factor for speeding growth by collisions, since it can distort planets' chemical makeup. From low- to high-detail runs, formation time depends on starting planetesimal size, and Earth-like planets can form resonant chains without gas-driven drift.
arxiv-2604-09584: Vishwasrao and ten colleagues pair multi-agent language models with latent foundation models to explore PDE spaces. The latent model learns compact, disentangled pictures of flow fields. It serves as an on-demand stand-in, letting agents probe any parameter setting at negligible cost. A hierarchical team loops through hypothesis, experiment, analysis, and verification with no user help. On flow past tandem cylinders at Reynolds number 500, it tests over 1,600 parameter-location pairs. It uncovers divergent scaling laws for displacement and momentum thickness.
arxiv-2604-09784: Potaptchik and five co-authors match side-by-side making with discrete data through Discrete Flow Maps. Stepwise guessing limits language models, while smooth flow models offer side-by-side making but demand looped math. Flow Maps compress paths into single mappings, making text from noise in one pass, but standard versions rely on flat losses ill-suited to discrete data. Discrete Flow Maps match path packing with chance-simplex shape, redoing training for the discrete domain. This shape fit lets the method surpass previous results in discrete flow models.
arxiv-2604-09984: Zhang and three co-authors present a hybrid layered moving-mesh method in the unified gas-kinetic scheme for mixed-size flows with moving edges. Stretching the hidden shaky solver to moving meshes, with memory-lean handling and joint tweaks, eases the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy constraint. Tested on speedy multi-body split and thermal thin micro-electro-machine flows, the scheme handles complex dynamic mixed-size events well. The results confirm a robust, lean tool for aping dynamic flow meetings in complex shapes.
arxiv-2604-10084: Lee, Song, Lee, and Lee align standard fundus images with ultra-widefield retinal images, which had no specialized method. The two views differ greatly in range, and retinal appearance is amorphous. Their Active Diffusion Matching runs two linked score-based diffusion models that jointly estimate global transforms and local deformations. An iterative Langevin Markov chain drives a stochastic search for the best alignment. Tests on private and public paired sets reach leading accuracy, with mean area under the curve up by 5.2 points on the private set.
arxiv-2604-10184: Wu, Liu, Veveakis, and Hu model how chemical breakdown turns brittle fracture ductile, linking mass removal to fracture length in a chemo-mechanical framework. In reactive settings, matrix breakdown weakens rock and, via damage-driven reaction-diffusion, widens the fracture process zone. Growth blunts the crack tip, eases stress, and lowers stiffness before failure. Damage builds slowly, and failure arrives late. The brittle-ductile shift follows the race between decay and strain timescales. Strong acid favors ductile fracture, while fast loading preserves brittle failure.
arxiv-2604-10384: Perera, Wang, and Shen rework knowledge graph views around what the user actually asks. Old tools show only direct matches and lay them out by shape alone, with no reason given for each spot. Their Context-KG system pulls likes and needs from plain questions with a large language model. Those likes then steer a layout guided by meaning, grouping nodes of one kind into clear zones. Tests on real graphs plus a user study show clearer views and stronger task results.
arxiv-2604-10484: Guan and ten colleagues rethink neural accelerator safety from the full system view. Old guards treat the NPU as one block and copy it wholesale, at steep speed and silicon cost. Their Strix frame splits the chip along the inference path and pins down chief failure modes. Targeted guards then catch and fix faults in under a microsecond. The price is small: about 1.04 times slowdown with only light extra hardware.
arxiv-2604-10684: Kumar and five colleagues identify magnetic reconnection at a hyperbolic flux tube as the driver of a confined M2.1 flare in NOAA region 12268. A non-force-free extrapolation maps the field before onset, revealing the flux tube above and two quasi-separatrix layers below. A data-constrained magnetohydrodynamic simulation then shows a current sheet forming inside the tube, followed by reconnection. Slipping motion of field-line footpoints in the lower layers signals additional slipping reconnection. The tube reconnection, they conclude, chiefly drives the flare's brightenings and ribbons.
arxiv-2604-11184: Trinkenreich and ten colleagues asked 457 software engineering researchers about generative AI in their work. Use is widespread and often pressured, clustered in writing and early research stages, while methods and analysis stay largely human. Researchers report productivity gains but worry about accuracy, bias, and unclear rules, calling for human checks and clearer guidance on responsible use and peer review.
arxiv-2604-11384: Spruk develops a theory of statehood without capacity. A polity can stay trapped in statehood in name, where sovereignty claims, outside recognition, and symbolic standing persist while coercive, fiscal, administrative, and legal capacities stay weak. Three forces drive the trap. Elites profit from patronage and rent extraction. Outside transfers ease non-consolidation costs. Recognition barely tracks office performance. In short, a state can look like a state long before it can act like one. The theory predicts a widening gap between legal and effective statehood, with Palestine as flagship case.
arxiv-2604-11584: Meng, Gómez, and Mazumder study penalized least trimmed squares, a robust method that caps large residuals. Penalized LTS is NP-hard, and existing mixed-integer models scale poorly. Their model embeds hyperplane arrangement logic in a perspective form. With features fixed, the tree is polynomial in sample size, and a tailored algorithm solves node relaxations with first-order methods and dual bounds. On synthetic cases with 5,000 samples and 20 features, their solver reaches a 1 percent gap in 1 minute while rivals fail within one hour.
arxiv-2604-11784: Tang and six colleagues package GUI-agent work into one open framework, ClawGUI, covering training, evaluation, and deployment. Its training arm runs reinforcement learning across parallel virtual setups and real phones, its evaluation arm standardises six benchmarks and reproduces baselines at 95.8 percent, and its deployment arm reaches Android, HarmonyOS, and iOS through chat apps. Their ClawGUI-2B model scores 17.1 percent on MobileWorld GUI-Only, beating the MAI-UI-2B baseline by 6.0 percent.
arxiv-2604-12184: Venkata and three colleagues build TRUST Agents, a team of specialist agents for fact checking that explains its verdicts instead of giving bare true-or-false answers. One agent extracts claims, a second retrieves evidence, a third weighs claims against evidence with calibrated confidence, and a fourth writes a cited report. An extension splits complex claims, runs a jury of verifier personas, and merges atomic verdicts by logic. Retrieval quality and calibration remain the main limits.
arxiv-2604-12384: Songping Peng and four colleagues defend language model safety during fine-tuning. Even harmless adaptation can erode refusal behavior and admit harmful replies. They show that constraining weights alone or activations alone cannot preserve safety. Their coupled constraints bind weight updates to a safety subspace. Safety-critical features get targeted regularization as well. Across four models and varied tasks, harmful scores came out lowest. Fine-tuning accuracy suffered little.
arxiv-2604-12584: Anatole Dahan and three colleagues approximate graph edit distance on bounded VC-dimension graphs. Their algorithm errs by at most epsilon times n squared, additively. It runs in time n to a power set by dimension over epsilon squared. The result recovers an earlier Arora-Frieze-Kaplan bound with a better exponent. The team extends the approach to quadratic assignment via VC dimension. A similar approximation holds for bounded-weight cases. For epsilon-isomorphism, Weisfeiler-Leman of suitable dimension decides the problem.
arxiv-2604-12684: Valentine Nyirahafashimana and four colleagues relax orthogonality in quantum stabilizer codes. Strict rules limit design freedom and efficiency. Their looser framework keeps symplectic commutation intact. X and Z check supports may overlap a little. An effective distance follows from anti-commutation with logical operators. The wider design space nears the Gilbert-Varshamov regime with better rates. Short codes improve over strict counterparts. Under depolarizing noise up to error rate 0.30, errors fall by up to two orders.
arxiv-2604-12984: Steinberg extends Cosserat elasticity, a theory of solids with fine inner structure, to cover defects that break the usual compatibility rules. He treats torsion and curvature as separate measures of spread-out defects. He derives balance laws plus extra fields tied to defect motion. Material symmetry then yields configurational forces and moments, linked to defect transport, giving one geometric account of solids whose inner geometry evolves.
