Standard master-worker checking bottlenecks on the master, but the supervised approach outsources checking to workers. Robust efficient solutions are shown for any constant beta below one, with honest worker effort close to one execution per task.
arxiv-2605-14984: Ming Qian and eight colleagues introduce Sat3DGen, which builds street-level 3D scenes from a single satellite image. Geometry-colorization methods stay building-focused, while feed-forward models yield rich but coarse geometry. The team puts geometry first, adding geometric constraints and perspective-view training to fight the viewpoint gap. On a new benchmark pairing VIGOR-OOD with elevation data, geometric error fell from 6.76 meters to 5.20 meters, and image realism improved sharply too.
arxiv-2605-15084: Justin Applegate and Andreas Kellas probe Python's pickle format, widely used to save machine learning models despite known insecurity. Defenses that limit imports or scan code rest on exact readings of pickle virtual machine opcodes, yet Python's three native implementations disagree. Their PickleFuzzer builds pickle objects from a grammar made for the missing spec and compares run behavior across implementations. It uncovered 14 new mismatches that can weaken detection of hostile payloads.
arxiv-2605-15184: Sahil Sen and four others ask whether plain grep can rival vector retrieval inside agent harnesses for agentic search. Two experiments compare grep and vector retrieval on LongMemEval questions across a custom rig and vendor-native CLIs, varying how tool results reach the model. A second test buries queries in growing amounts of unrelated conversation history. The study maps how retrieval choice, harness design, and result presentation mix, filling a gap in systematic comparisons of retrieval inside agent loops.
arxiv-2605-15384: Songwei Dong and five others argue that one score is not enough for evaluating sequentially evolving language-model memory. Overall final accuracy or total results hide forgetting and harmful transfer. Their SeqMem-Eval framework targets test-time settings where memory is outside, channeled, and updated without changing weights. It gauges online utility, hold-out generalization, backward transfer, and forgetting alone. Experiments show strong final gains often coexist with large loss or harmful transfer, so memory quality needs the finer-grained view.
arxiv-2605-15484: Libo Sun, Po-wei Harn, Peixiong He, and Xiao Qin ask when sparse expert routing aids vision nets. They find a compute-leverage pattern. Gains need a large share of all compute to pass through experts. At ImageNet scale, routing to at least two experts is also a must. Set tests rule out backbone kind as the cause. A per-sample Soft MoE variant rescues one data set. It shows batch-axis dispatch is the main fault in per-sample CNN setups.
arxiv-2605-16184: Lu and three colleagues present Asteria, a runtime system that makes second-order LLM training practical by moving optimizer state off the critical GPU path. Instead of holding all preconditioner state on the accelerator, it spreads state across GPU memory, CPU memory, and optional NVMe storage. Shadow states prepared in advance let inverse-root computations run asynchronously on the host. On GH200 systems it lowered optimizer overhead and latency spikes for a 7B model, while a single GB10 GPU handled a 1B model.
arxiv-2605-16384: Huang and four colleagues give patch tokens help from above: global tokens that track shared information across patch tokens. A Dynamic Token Filtering step drops redundancy by cumulative conditional entropy. That design answers a rigid habit: tokenization squeezes every picture at one fixed rate, ignoring how unevenly information is spread. The authors name two faults: patch tokens alone cannot rebuild a picture fully, and patch tokens repeat each other. Handing out tokens in line with information richness, TaTok reports a 1.3-fold gFID improvement and an 8.7-fold inference speedup.
arxiv-2605-16584: Zhang, Cansever and Li study how to place few sensors so an unknown high-dimensional linear system can still be fully observed. Their two-stage method first identifies the system by combining trajectories that each watch different state coordinates. It then adapts a classic allocation method to the learned parameters. Theory shows the allocation is near-optimal in sensor count when any coordinate may host a sensor. The method also extends to coordinates that cannot be sensed.
arxiv-2605-16684: Waterhouse and colleagues implement an entropy-stable discontinuous Galerkin solver for compressible Euler equations with buoyancy on graphics processors. On NVIDIA A100 hardware, the most expensive kernel reaches nearly 70% of 64-bit floating-point peak speed. The graphics kernels run ten times faster and over thirteen times more energy-efficiently than a tuned CPU code. The solver also doubles speed at 32-bit precision and scales strongly and weakly across problems.
arxiv-2605-16784: Ma, Bian and Ozbay propose placing mobile charging trucks on the fly to support fixed stations during mass evacuations, when heavy EV demand can swamp fixed sites. Their ARMD framework splits placement into risk sharing of trucks among stations and dynamic routing to chosen stations, solved offline-to-online. Sharing uses a spread-out, partly seen Markov decision process with multi-agent policy tuning, pre-trained offline and refined online. In a mock storm exodus from Hillsborough County data, ARMD cuts average risk by up to 71.1% under demand shifts.
arxiv-2605-16984: Bourgois, Seminck and Poibeau report their winning submission to the language-model track of the 2026 CRAC shared task on coreference resolution. Their system, built on Gemma-3-27b and fine-tuned in two stages, scored 74.32 CoNLL F1 on the official test set, ranking first in its track and third overall. A multilingual base adapter comes first, then dataset-specific adapters, with mention spans marked by headword in an XML-style format with local reindexing and documents annotated iteratively. The design held up across languages, document lengths, and annotation guidelines.
arxiv-2605-17084: In his 2026 paper, Xu studies how the inner layout of a language model lines up with its word-predicting output layer. He tests a new score, Subspace PGA, across ten models of varied size and family. Mid-layer layouts track prediction closely, but small models lose that link late in training while large ones keep it. A few strong directions drift off course and hide the pattern, and removing them restores it.
arxiv-2605-17284: Zhu and colleagues address rare, safety-critical driving scenes that defeat end-to-end vision-language-action models, like construction zones and tricky yields. Their CLAP framework adds per-roadblock soft prompts to a frozen driving model, fetched on demand over vehicle-to-everything links. A two-stage method first finds a hard-scene direction, then tunes prompts along it, cutting planning error on hard scenes 24 percent with no loss on normal ones.
arxiv-2605-17484: Tsou studies stability for the inverse conductivity problem of recovering a convex polyhedral body in a uniform isotropic medium from a single boundary reading. His tools are singularity split for elliptic equations in non-smooth domains, smallness propagation and microlocal analysis. Together, they yield a logarithmic estimate. The estimate bounds the Hausdorff distance between bodies in terms of reading error. That shows how reading quality controls shape recovery.
arxiv-2605-18084: Christoph Langenbruch summarizes results on flavour changing neutral current decays from LHCb. These decays are forbidden at lowest order in the SM, allowed only via loops, so New Physics can contribute through corrections. Semileptonic and radiative b to s(d) decays allow New Physics searches. They probe its operator structure through branching fractions, angular observables, and CP-asymmetries. Tensions with SM predictions appear in b to s muon decays. Their significance depends on assumptions. The proceedings include the B0 to K*0 muon-antimuon measurement, using 8.4 inverse femtobarns from Runs 1 and 2.
arxiv-2605-18184: Giorgia Modi's 2026 paper treats views from fixed outside RGB cameras as common prior maps for robot scene mapping. Those wide views seed a semantic and geometric prior before the robot moves at all. An RGB-only pipeline then fuses on-board and outside views alike into an incremental 3D scene graph, with no hardware changes. A graph-guided search steers the robot toward zones of high semantic doubt, and even one outside camera lifts initial object recall by up to 79 percent.
arxiv-2605-18384: Andre Marinho, Gisele Freitas, and Camila da Silva report a university outreach activity that took physics experiments built from low-cost materials into a public space. Undergraduate students in physics teacher training designed and presented the demonstrations to visitors, aiming to share basic physics ideas and spark public interest in science. Questionnaire responses from fifty-two visitors in the 2026 study point to gains in student learning and communication skills.
arxiv-2605-18684: Sanderson Oliveira de Macedo and Ronaldo Martins da Costa present Reversa, a 2026 setup turning legacy software into working specs for AI agents. A multi-agent chain maps the surface, probes modules, extracts rules, drafts architecture, writes unit specs, and reviews claims. Traceability links code to spec, confidence is marked, and gaps stay open for checks. An ATM porting study from COBOL to Go gave 517 claims, 10 gaps, 53 Gherkin scenarios, and 9 of 11 tasks done at inventory time. Final parity checks and cutover were not done.
arxiv-2605-18984: Yuqi Tang and twenty-three colleagues benchmark how well multimodal models spot flaws in AI-made video. Artifact-Bench builds a three-level taxonomy of realism artifacts across photorealistic, animated and CG styles, and sets three tasks: telling real from fake video, comparing pairs for realism, and identifying specific artifacts. Tests on 19 leading models reveal substantial limits, with many scoring near or below chance on hard settings. Model judgments also diverge sharply from human perceptual preferences, casting doubt on their reliability as general evaluators of video realism.
arxiv-2605-19284: Thomas Howe and David Wingate show that language models often wall off the same idea when it appears in different forms. A fact in English and Swahili, or a function in Python and Haskell, may be learned twice over instead of once. That duplication wastes capacity and weakens learning as more versions pile up, and added parallel data may not fix it. In small models, early multilingual learning stays almost fully split, and every fix they test flips in effectiveness once the count of versions passes a threshold.
arxiv-2605-19384: Hu and Han propose CDiT, a conditional diffusion transformer that generates terahertz wireless channels for ultra-massive antenna systems. Older models lean on sparsity or fixed parametric shapes that miss complex spatial change across far and near fields. Their method treats channel creation as geometry-aware learning in a sparse beamspace, feeding position in as a condition. Tests on realistic channel data show stable training and clear gains over standard benchmarks, offering a data-driven route for next-generation wireless design.
arxiv-2605-19584: Maran and Restelli study online market making where a learner posts bid and ask prices to traders with valuations. Unlike bandit models with censored feedback, their model reveals supply and demand whenever no trade occurs, while valuations stay hidden when trades happen. That extra information changes learnability. An elimination method achieves square-root-of-T regret with high probability, no smoothness needed, extended to mean-reverting prices under local or global drift. With oblivious prices an explore-then-perturb method guarantees T-to-the-two-thirds regret in expectation.
arxiv-2605-19684: Sanner, Michel and Kammer study missing bonds and fracture resistance in spring networks. Fracture energy measures resistance to a dominant crack; disorder raises it through crack arrest, but its dependence on disorder level stays unclear. In a triangular spring network they vary missing-bond concentration and find fracture energy rises with crack advance. Mapping missing bonds onto an energy landscape, fluctuation spread grows with the square root of the missing fraction, so average fracture energy follows the same scaling. The landscape's exponential tail yields a logarithmic rise with crack advance.
arxiv-2605-19984: Andreas Triantafyllopoulos and five colleagues outline how machines might learn to listen using reward alone, without detailed labels. Their framework centres on curiosity-driven search for new sound sources, an idea still little explored for audio compared with vision. The paper reviews earlier attempts, sets out open technical challenges and offers a first proof-of-concept implementation showing the approach can work.
arxiv-2605-20184: Lawrence Hollom tightens the bound on colour changes along a geodesic between antipodal vertices in a two-coloured hypercube. Norine's conjecture, in Feder and Subi's form, puts it at one. The previous best was about five sixteenths of n, from Kirchweger, Peitl, Subercaseaux and Szeider. Hollom finds a geodesic with at most about pi over two times root n colour changes, answering a question of Leader and Long. That count is also the expected number for a random start, and it is optimal up to the constant for random starts.
arxiv-2605-20384: Wang and two co-workers build training data for machine-learned interatomic potentials with entropy-guided sampling. Local entropy steers molecular dynamics toward varied snapshots, while a global entropy score keeps only setups adding genuinely new information. With a pretrained Allegro-OAM-L model, the method reaches near- or sub-meV per atom accuracy from only hundreds of labeled structures. On carbon, silicon and NaCl, it cuts energy error by roughly 3 to 10 times versus random sampling at matched sizes.
arxiv-2605-20484: Perruchot-Triboulet and two co-workers anchor graph SLAM for legged robots without GNSS signals. LiDAR sensors drift in height in sparse or repetitive scenes, so they add a leg-odometry lane to the LIO-SAM framework. A selective-noise identity constraint couples that lane to the main LiDAR-inertial lane. On a Linxai D50 quadruped over two outdoor loops beyond one kilometer, elevation drift falls from over 30 meters to under 30 centimeters, and a scene that defeated the baseline now converges.
arxiv-2605-20684: Linus Ng Junjia and four colleagues tackle retrieval for corporate credit underwriting, where analysts mine long, multilingual financial files. Standard retrieval ranks by meaning similarity, which often surfaces passages that are on-topic but useless for a decision. Their two-phase design first gathers a broad pool with word-based and dense multilingual retrieval. A controller then filters by query intent and file structure, and a judge model ranks passages by use for analysis.
arxiv-2605-20784: Yosuke Miyanishi and Tetsuro Morimura propose interaction locality, a framework for measuring whether information flow in reasoning models stays local. Spatial reasoning needs both place-bound computation and place-invariant plans, yet it was unclear how local model updates really are. They instantiate the idea with sparse-autoencoder ablations and finite-noise activation patching, with extra checks in the appendix. Applied to HRM and TRM on maze, Sudoku, and ARC tasks, patching gives the clearest pattern.
arxiv-2605-20984: Koen van Hove, Jeroen van der Ham-de Vos, and Roland van Rijswijk-Deij study the security of domain registrars and the risk of domain name takeover. Domain names anchor an organization's online presence and reputation, serving as a linking pin for web services and email. A malicious takeover can therefore cause significant damage. Organizations register names through registrars, businesses that play a key role in safeguarding against malicious takeovers. The paper empirically studies how the top ten registrars for the Dutch country-code domain implement security controls against takeovers.
arxiv-2605-21184: Stefan Hoffelner proves that a dual assertion about graphs of total projective functions is consistent at the third projective level. It is known that the graph of a total Sigma-one-n function is Pi-one-n. He builds a model of ZFC in which every total Pi-one-three function has a Sigma-one-three graph. That principle clashes with Pi-one-three uniformization and hence with the usual projective-determinacy picture, and the construction repairs the last step of an earlier failure-of-uniformization argument.
arxiv-2605-21684: Deskins and colleagues present a uniform Bayesian analysis of NICER soft X-ray spectra from eight comets. They identify lines from charge exchange, measure ion fluxes, and infer solar-wind freeze-in temperatures. The spectra fall into carbon-dominated, intermediate, and nitrogen- and oxygen-dominated families. Carbon diagnostics cluster near one and a half million kelvin, while nitrogen-oxygen diagnostics run systematically higher. Short-timescale flickers in the inferred conditions point to solar-wind fluctuations rather than changing coma composition as the main driver of spectral differences.
arxiv-2605-21884: Daniel Gervini and Simon Kopischke introduce estimators for trend and seasonality in point-process time series, where events arrive at scattered times. They model the processes as doubly stochastic Poisson models with log-Gaussian intensity functions, and propose simple M-estimators for the job. The paper derives the estimators' asymptotic distribution and tests their finite-sample behavior by simulation. As a real test, the authors track bike demand patterns in Chicago's Divvy bike-sharing system.
arxiv-2605-22184: Michela Artebani and co-authors study Cox rings of smooth Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces in toric Fano varieties. Using primitive pairs of the ambient Fano polytope, they identify cases where the hypersurface is a Mori dream space with explicit Cox ring forms. Other cases force an infinite automorphism group. In dimensions three and four this yields a split between finite Cox ring generation and infinite automorphism group. For a class of non-Mori dream examples, they prove the Morrison-Kawamata cone conjecture for the movable cone.
arxiv-2605-22284: Ganey and Nienkemper-Swanepoel present moveEZ, an R package for animated PCA biplots. It shows how multivariate structure shifts across ordered levels of a category. Built on the biplotEZ package, it offers three animation frames of rising complexity. In the fixed frame, variable vectors stay put while sample points move. In the two dynamic frames, both are recomputed at each level, with Procrustes alignment keeping the view steady. The package suits publication graphics and works wherever repeated measures span an ordered category.
arxiv-2605-22384: Collmann, Nimr and Fettweis compare local and over-the-air phase calibration for MIMO arrays. Phase impairments, such as phase noise, limit coherent transmission and channel estimation. Over-the-air methods assume steady phase and known channels. The team tests a live local method against over-the-air calibration on USRP X310 radios. Both remove phase drift and whiten phase noise at low and high sync bandwidths. Local calibration proves more stable and channel-free, while over-the-air calibration needs no extra hardware but suffers multipath effects.
arxiv-2605-22484: Méndez and team study whether vision model class heads can serve as semantic prototypes. Vision-language models map images and text to a shared space, but need costly training on paired datasets. Post-hoc methods link pretrained encoders through light mappings, yet still need much paired data. The team repurposes class heads, discarded after pretraining, as semantic anchors. This unlocks zero-shot alignment and data augmentation mixing prototypes with real pairs. With leading post-hoc methods, the approach boosts accuracy in retrieval and zero- and few-shot classification.
arxiv-2605-22584: Beck and Stamm study how smoothly coupled cluster amplitudes vary when nuclear positions shift, with an eye to interpolation from few reference shapes. Under non degeneracy assumptions at Hartree Fock and coupled cluster level, they show the amplitudes behave as real analytic functions, a very strong form of smoothness. They then dissect the artefacts that canonical orbitals inject in practical runs and suggest ways to soften them. Numerical interpolation tests against exact amplitudes back the theory.
arxiv-2605-22684: Rodríguez and others adapt time series foundation models to specialized classification, where quadratic attention costs and tangled variability block progress. Their ChronoVAE-HOPE model swaps attention for a memory HOPE block: Titans modules hold short term dynamics while a continuum memory system abstracts long term context. A disentangled latent space splits trend and seasonal parts through separate encoder heads and decoder paths. Pre trained on the Monash archive and tested on UCR benchmarks, the encoder yields results across temporal domains, above all where causal structure is strict.
arxiv-2605-22784: Gurram builds one algebraic system around the formal Bell transform, linking Dirichlet convolution of arithmetic functions to endless Euler type products. Through log slopes of exponential generating functions, he maps Bell powers to Möbius inversions in plain terms. The system yields exact vanishing rules and mod patterns for old series including Ramanujan's tau function and prime coloured partitions. Inverse Bell transforms recover old partition recurrences and generate special polynomial families such as Appell and Sheffer types.
arxiv-2605-22884: Swain and four colleagues propose Tensor Cache, a two-level memory for Transformers that rescues tokens evicted from a sliding window instead of discarding them. Recent tokens stay in exact local attention, while evicted key-value pairs compress into a fixed-size outer-product memory read by later queries. A learned gate fuses both levels. The design improves the memory-quality frontier against bounded-state rivals, and fixes a training shortcut that silently added spurious cross-token products.
arxiv-2605-22984: Antonelli, Akhondzadeh, and Bojchevski show that test-time training, which adapts model parameters during inference, opens new jailbreak paths. Across three threat models, attackers exploit adaptation to bypass safety filters, reaching average attack success over ten trials of 95 percent under LoRA few-shot attacks and 93 percent under generation-phase attacks. The flaws transfer to production fine-tuning APIs. The authors propose a validity-aware evaluation to correct inflated scores from degenerate outputs, plus a lightweight provider-side detector as a first defense.
arxiv-2605-23084: Batte, Bravo, and Luca determine every Woodall number in the Padovan sequence plus all Cullen numbers in the Perrin sequence. Both sequences satisfy the recurrence U_{n+3} equals U_{n+1} plus U_n, with different starting values. A Cullen number has the form m times 2 to the m plus 1, while a Woodall number has the form m times 2 to the m minus 1. They prove 1 and 7 are the sole Woodall numbers in the Padovan sequence, and 3 is the sole Cullen number in the Perrin sequence.
arxiv-2605-23184: Adachi and three coauthors study Iwasawa lambda-invariants of constant Zp-towers over supersingular l-isogeny graphs, fixing primes r and p and letting l vary over infinitely many primes. This graph analogue of Iwasawa theory, begun by Gonet and Vallieres, connects graph theory, elliptic curves, and Galois representations of newforms. The graph adjacency matrix has eigenvalues from the l-th Fourier coefficients of a weight 2 Eisenstein series and newforms at level r. The paper ends with a conjecture on the Galois orbits of newforms.
arxiv-2605-23584: Hite and Siwach map how quantum resources organize in collective neutrino oscillations, using entropy, non-local magic, and matrix product state bond dimension. In tensor network simulations of two-flavor neutrinos, sharp energy-dependent flavor swaps, called spectral splits, appear exactly where entropy peaks and non-local magic dips locally. That anticorrelation shows splits come from structured redistribution among flavor modes, not generic resource growth. Resource paths trace constrained arcs in entropy-magic space, linking compute complexity to astrophysical observables for future simulations.
arxiv-2605-23684: Allaham and Diakopoulos audit search citations for AI-generated sources. Generative search engines answer questions by synthesizing web information, but AI content now floods the web, and engines may still cite synthetic sources. Treating synthetic sources as equal to trusted ones puts users at risk. The audit covers ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity over 712 queries on politics, health, and environment. About 16 percent of cited sources prove AI-generated across all four engines, with few domains cited repeatedly alongside many rarely cited ones.
arxiv-2605-23784: Schotland and Yu investigate the phaseless inverse scattering problem for the Schrödinger equation and develop methods based on the inverse Born series. They consider three types of phaseless data: far-field total field, total field, and far-field scattered field. In the far-field setting, they propose a Fourier-based method that exploits scattering reciprocity between incident and observation directions to recover Fourier coefficients of the scattering potential. For phaseless scattered-field data, they employ a polarization-based approach to recover phase information and enable inverse Born series reconstruction.
arxiv-2605-23984: Wang and six co-authors move factory anomaly spotting from central, offline analysis to distributed, online operation across edge devices. Their system, MODIAD, plans multi-class model updates by weighing data supply against update frequency, solved with a greedy algorithm that picks the largest marginal gain at each step. A low-rank adapter strategy, REC-LoRA, cuts compute and message cost while keeping spotting scores. On two multimodal factory data sets, MVTec 3D-AD and Eyecandies, the approach beat rivals on performance and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-24284: Zhao, Lavrentiadis, and Asimaki build a big ground-motion model for Los Angeles from CyberShake runs. Built as Gaussian-process fitting, it takes the ASK14 model as prior median and learns site and path effects through Matern kernels. Scaling to a million-plus points needs sparse Cholesky solve, side-by-side compute, and GPU speed. The full hundreds-of-millions dataset stays too big, so random spread is handled apart. The model fills partly observed fields and predicts unseen cases, and a Puente Hills size 6.7 case study closely matches runs.
arxiv-2605-24384: Kondapally and seven co-authors measure covert dialect bias in language models. They test how models tie stereotype traits to meaning-matched tweets in two English dialects. Earlier work found more negative stereotypes tied to AAVE tweets judged alone. The team finds the bias grows sharply when SAE and AAVE pairs are judged side by side. Naming the dialects outright worsens it further. Fairness tuning cuts gaps for single tweets for some traits, but gains do not hold steadily in side-by-side judgments, and overt bias stays strong.
arxiv-2605-24584: Łukasz Struski and others introduce LAPLEX, a trainable Laplace-kernel operator that acts like a dense matrix without storing one. Defined implicitly by learnable coordinate anchors, it runs with Fourier-like scaling. It supports trainable matrix-vector products at dimensions up to a billion on modern graphics hardware. As a neural layer it gives compact projections and classification heads that read as soft, trainable routing. The same primitive serves as a Gram operator for covariance models on three-million-dimension flattened images, keeping visible spatial structure without imposing convolutional bias.
arxiv-2605-24684: Hao Yan and others diagnose why graph learning can lose to plain MLPs once encoders grow large. Under pretrained priors, forced aggregation mixes topology noise into node features, drowning the signal. It also throttles gradient flow while a shared loss lets dominant modalities crush weaker ones. Their SUPRA design decouples the paths. Topology-free MLPs handle modality features while a light shared graph network captures structural synergy, with extra supervision fighting starvation. Tests reach top results with 3.5 times lower peak GPU memory and much faster training than graph transformers.
arxiv-2605-24784: Zhuocheng Shang and Ahmed Eldawy demonstrate GRAIL, an agentic system translating Python geospatial workflows into Spark programs for satellite data. Domain scientists write Python scripts for satellite imagery but lack large-scale scalability. Rather than fine-tuning a specialized model, GRAIL adapts RDPro, a Scala satellite-analysis library, for model use with structured docs and API aliases. Translation runs as a LangGraph pipeline splitting generation into sections with guided inputs and outputs, allowing targeted fixes without full regeneration. Real-world geospatial workflows showcase correctness and scalability.
arxiv-2605-24884: Rodrigo Sandoval-Orozco leads a fresh look at extreme accretor quasars as tools for measuring the cosmos. The team uses a cleaned sample drawn from many prior sources. They test three rival models of cosmic expansion and land on a Hubble constant near 70 from quasars alone. That value sits close to the one found when supernovae, cosmic clocks, and microwave background data join in. Both dynamical dark energy models earn a weak edge over the standard model, yet the spread inside quasar samples stays large.
arxiv-2605-25084: Shumon Koga and Miroslav Krstic address safe tracking for the Stefan problem with a moving edge. The model pairs a parabolic partial differential equation on a moving domain with an edge governed by second-order rules under a Neumann rule. A series-expansion feedforward control solves the inverse Stefan problem for a reference trajectory, and the series is proven to converge. An energy-shaping controller keeps the constraint safe in closed loop. The system is globally stable with fast decay in tracking error, and a sine-wave simulation shows tracking.
arxiv-2605-25184: P. K. Minnumol and P. G. Romeo look at the ideals of a commutative principal ideal ring through two lenses at once. As an ordered semigroup, the collection I(R) turns out to be regular. As a category, the collection I_R has subobjects. The paper then establishes a correspondence between these two structures, linking the semigroup view with the categorical view of the same ideals.
arxiv-2605-25284: Jinyan Su and Claire Cardie probe a gap between spotting ambiguity and acting on it in language-model assistants. Models often recognize that a question admits several readings when asked directly. Yet in ordinary question answering they mostly answer straight away instead of seeking clarification. Added retrieved context widens the split: it makes questions easier to answer while making clarifying questions even rarer. The study tests ambiguous, clear, and disambiguated questions across three settings, with a judge model sorting replies into answers, refusals, and clarifications.
arxiv-2605-25384: Yingji Zhang, Yong Dai, and André Freitas study how geometry problem solving mixes reasoning with code. Their GeoMathCode setup lets program-like representations serve as intermediate visual steps, including added lines or points that clarify a figure. Experiments show reasoning steps and code steps separate cleanly in the model's hidden space. Supervised fine-tuning makes the reasoning landscape more structured and informative, while layered code syntax forms its own subspaces. Those code subspaces carry more mathematical symbol information than visual representations alone, revealing how the two reasoning modes divide labor.
arxiv-2605-25684: Santacreu and Sevilla-Peris define boundedness and ergodicity for maps on locally convex spaces, tied to one endless matrix. Given two matrices, they study when maps bounded for one matrix are ergodic for the other. From this matrix-action view they recover matching forms of the classical trio: power boundedness, then Cesàro boundedness, then mean ergodicity. The work thus unifies three classical operator notions under one transference frame.
arxiv-2605-25984: Orme, Yu and Tan make chatbots safer at run time without retraining them. Their SafeCtrl-RL method treats a chat as a run of choices. A learning agent picks prompt tweaks from live feedback. Unsafe replies are curbed by repeat tweaks, a kind of unlearning at run time. Tests on several models and unsafe chats show safer replies and better answers than older prompt methods. Cost and quality also trade off well.
arxiv-2605-26184: Yuelin Hu and four colleagues derive a noise-aware rule for blending supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning in large language models. Fixed mixing schedules fail as the noise in each signal shifts, so their Guided Adaptive Controller estimates the best balance from training statistics, with smoothing and capped updates. The controller alone beats the best rule-based rival by three points on AMC. The full system gains nearly four points across math, code, science, and logic tests, while cutting drift and large weight swings.
arxiv-2605-26284: Koyo Fujii and six colleagues' 2026 system, PhyPush, estimates an object's mass and friction from a single push, using only end-effector velocity, via a physics-guided Transformer. Newton's second law plus Coulomb friction enter through a physics-guided loss, improving consistency and generalization to unseen objects and surfaces. In simulation, it cuts error by more than ten percent against a baseline with privileged force data. It transfers zero-shot from simulation to the real world, beating a purely data-driven baseline.
arxiv-2605-26384: Denisa-Andreea Constantinescu and David Atienza's 2026 controller, GridPilot, is a three-tier system turning AI supercomputers into grid-responsive loads. It works across millisecond, second, and hour scales, with a safety-island bypass guaranteeing fast response. On a three-GPU V100 testbed, response hits ninety-seven point two milliseconds, nearly seven times faster than the Nordic Fast Frequency Reserve requirement of seven hundred milliseconds. A power-usage-effectiveness correction keeps commitments robust at the meter, closing two point five to five point eight points of cooling drag across six grids.
arxiv-2605-26484: Wenjie Zhou and five colleagues uncover a rank-1 subspace effect in late language-model pretraining. Raw optimization steps swing, yet merged checkpoints collapse onto a near one-dimensional manifold. A river-valley account explains it: averaging works like a geometric low-pass filter, damping high-curvature noise to reveal the descent path. Their Extra-Merge strategy, needing no extra training, extrapolates along this subspace to cut loss without gradient updates. Tests on GPT-2 and LLaMA models from 124M to 2B beat merging baselines, with Pythia-12B zero-shot gains.
arxiv-2605-26584: Peiran Wu and four colleagues cut video cost with O-MARC. Long token runs make inference costly, and benchmarks poorly isolate audio-visual links in noisy videos. UGC-AVQA holds 1,000 videos and 4,816 pairs, with an audio-removal test requiring acoustic and visual evidence. OMAC, a training-free plug-in, compresses while keeping visual memory and audio anchors. O-MARC distills compression so compact models stay robust. On Qwen2.5-Omni-3B, it scores 45.8, beating full inference at 44.1 and OmniZip at 41.0, with latency and memory down 35 percent.
arxiv-2605-26784: Luo and seven colleagues replace the hard clipping used in on-policy reinforcement learning with a softer constraint on policy ratio variance. Hard clipping truncates high-return, high-divergence updates wholesale. Their ratio-variance limit instead acts as a soft brake, keeping useful gradient signals and reusing stale off-policy data. Their R2VPO method, built on primal-dual optimization, beats PPO baselines on math reasoning and robotic control, with the largest gains on smaller models.
arxiv-2605-26984: Xu and five co-authors build TED, a graph neural network model for tax evasion detection guided by related party transactions. Existing tools lean on company statistics but miss the rich interaction patterns in tax scenarios. TED models the scenario as a heterogeneous graph, filters low-level noise with transaction groups, and uses hierarchical attention to capture deeper structure. Tested on two real labeled datasets and a live tax bureau system, it clearly beats state-of-the-art rivals.
arxiv-2605-27084: Boccaletti and twenty-five co-authors present near-infrared polarized images of the AB Aur disk at three epochs over 3.85 years, plus hydrogen-alpha images at one epoch. The disk follows Keplerian rotation, but departs inside about 60 astronomical units, with a deviation up to about 12 degrees at the smallest radius. Two bright spirals inside the millimeter cavity trend differently, linked to planet candidates. Compact sources f1, f2, and f3 orbit in planes tilted tens of degrees to the disk, and shadow changes point to optically thick regions there.
arxiv-2605-27284: Xintong Hu and colleagues build FineVLA, a framework for teaching robots from fine-grained instructions about how a task should be done. It unifies nearly a million trajectories from ten robot datasets into a checked set of fine-grained examples, plus a benchmark for testing. Mixing fine-grained and goal-only instructions beats goal-only training, with the largest gains on pose, color, and approach direction.
arxiv-2605-27984: Kim and colleagues build Korean benchmarks for speech-language models without corrupting the language through naive translation. Two human-agent pipelines transfer spoken-question tests and convert Korean speech corpora into understanding tasks, yielding three public sets totaling over twelve thousand samples. Tests of eight models show English-Korean gaps that vary sharply by model and task.
arxiv-2605-28084: Lee and colleagues teach language models to read laughter as a social cue, not just a sign of joy. Their SMILE-Next set spans three jobs: spotting laughs, sorting laugh types, and working out what a laugh means in real scenes. A laugh-tuned instruction recipe plus a team of laugh experts beat strong multimodal baselines by a wide margin.
arxiv-2605-28184: Wang and colleagues make multi-token prediction work inside reinforcement learning instead of detaching its gradients. Decomposing each step's effect into a correlation term and a perturbation penalty explains why detaching, cross-entropy, and policy-loss regimes each succeed or fail. Their adaptive coefficient calibration tracks the best blend online, matching or beating the detach baseline on six math reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-28384: Alan Ferrari proposes Meta-Attention, a scheme routing each token in a transformer to its best-suited attention method: full, linear, or local sliding-window attention. A Bayesian controller balancing accuracy against computing cost makes the choice and reports its confidence, curbing collapse toward always using full attention. A small language-model test cut projected cost to about a quarter under hard routing, against nearly three fifths for a prior-free baseline.
arxiv-2605-28484: Yongseok Jang gives Finnish morphophonology a compositional algebraic framework built on comonads. Each context-dependent rule becomes a map from a focused local context to one output segment, and length-changing rules compose as coKleisli arrows. A new Writer comonad lets deletions pile up as a monoid action instead of needing intermediate materialization. Thirteen arrows reproduce behavior that Omorfi encodes with 874 continuation classes, and the same arrows serve both analysis and generation, with strong accuracy on a Finnish treebank.
arxiv-2605-28684: Amirpasha Hedayat and four colleagues build history-aware adaptive reduced-order models to speed up high-dimensional flow. Their method uses incremental singular value decomposition, with occasional full checks supplying correction snapshots for basis updates. Each update flows through the basis to the reduced operators and hyper-reduction gear, and the evolving singular structure keeps a record of past flow. On Burgers flow, the Sod shock tube, and a ten-species spinning detonation engine, history-aware updates beat others, and the method tops a Direct adaptive baseline on the engine.
arxiv-2605-28884: Faruk Alpay and Baris Basaran study how cone-shaped ordering rules shape languages that assign vector values to strings. Extreme rays of a dual cone split every possible continuation into negative, tight, or positive sign patterns. These patterns form a stable carrier for the whole observation family, and a bounded-horizon version can be computed by listing accumulated futures. Tests show the cone layer spots qualitative blocks before numerical work begins.
arxiv-2605-29084: Yubo Li, Rema Padman, and Ramayya Krishnan argue source-dependence is a missing axis of NLP evaluation. The same question can draw different answers depending on the source retrieved, a failure single-answer evaluation cannot diagnose. In transplant education, where sources disagree, they release TransplantQA, a benchmark of patient questions from multiple handbooks. They add HERO-QA, grounding and auditing each answer, and a judge scoring source relationships on a five-label taxonomy. At scale, better retrieval reveals far more disagreement than prior estimates suggested.
arxiv-2605-29184: Evgeny Saveliev and colleagues introduce Influence-Guided Symbolic Regression, which frames equation discovery as iterative generation plus selection. A language model proposes terms for a linear model, scored by each term's marginal contribution to accuracy. This influence score drives pruning that refines the model, inside a Monte Carlo tree search balancing new forms against high-influence terms. Tests span drug, disease, and genomic benchmarks, and a case study found a link between DNA methylation and RNA Polymerase II pausing, later backed by lab work.
arxiv-2605-29284: Ziyu Li and colleagues present a fast approximation for the Kriging prediction step for Gaussian processes on a regular grid. Exact Kriging and conditional simulation are too slow for modern spatial work with many observations and dense grids. Their method approximates each off-grid covariance vector by a sparse mix of on-grid values within a local neighborhood of grid points. This cuts compute sharply while keeping accuracy. A factorial study shows error falls with more smoothness, higher neighbor order, and finer grids, matching kernel theory.
arxiv-2605-29384: Benjamin Clavié presents Latent Terms, showing that retrievers learn forms that split into sparse parts. Trained on frozen retrievers, sparse autoencoders with no tweaks for retrieval extract a vocab with Zipfian stats. That vocab is ready for sparse retrieval scoring via BM25. This enables sparse retrieval with no learned expansion goal or sparse supervision, and applies to any retriever. Latent Terms matches or beats its base model scoring and SPLADE variants. It beats its base model by a lot on LIMIT, a task to highlight failures.
arxiv-2605-29684: Paolo Baglioni and six colleagues model Bayesian deep nets where training size and width grow together, the proportional-width regime. Shallow nets here are well mapped, but deep non-linear nets have resisted the same treatment. Their equivalent Wishart Ansatz captures the main random swings of layered kernels, letting strong representation learning collapse to at most as many scalar terms as layers. Stretched to convolutional nets, the idea tracks how finite width reshapes the kernel. Tests on benchmarks match the theory well, with two kinds of systematic drift.
arxiv-2605-29784: Zdenek Hradil and Jaroslav Rehacek tie quantum inference resolution to a sampling Gram operator. That operator marks which degrees of freedom data can reach and how wide a reconstruction band they support, acting like a transfer function in imaging. With deviance scaling, it gives a working test to tell resolved features from flaws of thin sampling, noise, or model guesses. Rebuilding in the Gram eigenbasis shrinks the problem to modes the measurements support. The frame links tomography, inverse rebuilding, and sharpness into one check on fine phase-space claims.
arxiv-2605-29984: Lukas Liehr settles which grids and which compactly supported window functions can generate a Gabor orthonormal basis, a complete set of time-and-frequency shifted copies that spans square-integrable signals. He states the answer in geometric language, through translation tilings and discreteness of grid projections. The result closes a conjecture of Han and Wang against such bases on certain irrational grids. He also builds Gabor bases that no product set can realize, answering a question posed by Iosevich and Mayeli.
arxiv-2605-30084: E. S. Benilov applies an Enskog-Vlasov kinetic model for dense fluids to supercooling liquids. He computes the spinodal temperature where a liquid turns unstable and freezes. Cooling at fixed volume reaches lower temperatures than cooling at fixed pressure, he finds. He then shows the surface tension of a supercooled liquid-vapour interface diverges at that temperature. An oscillating region spreads without limit when its waves stop fading. Argon and other fluids illustrate the results, which he argues should hold beyond the model's approximations.
arxiv-2605-30184: Fanny Lehmann and six colleagues benchmark AI weather models on year-long rollouts, sorting long-horizon failures into blow-up, drift and loss of seasonality. Short-range forecasts excel, but rolled-out models develop instabilities. Stability turns on small scales: unstable models boost high-frequency energy, while stable ones denoise added noise. Stable models generate unique trajectories from the initial state, not mere stochastic parrots. Ablations on Vision Transformer designs confirm the findings across nine leading models.
arxiv-2605-30384: David C. Flynn presents the EPS Astro-RAG Platform, a set of five star data sets and 149 Jupyter notebooks. A fix notes a past omega sign flip came from a code error; with the fixed formula, all eight Z1 spinners give positive omega values. KROSS omega values are withdrawn, since their edge points came from templates. The platform spans redshift zero to six, linking spin curves, star cluster motion, mid-range sky motion, and ALMA motion data. The five sets hold 2,064 records in all.
arxiv-2605-30684: Ragone and Lucarini build a frame for dynamic emergent constraints in climate science, relations linking responses to forcing across signals to narrow forecast uncertainty. Using linear response theory, they show traditional dynamic constraints are a special case of broader integral ones. These links compute a predictand's response from a predictor's response and the pair's proxy Green's function. Existence hinges on the proxy Green's function's causality and observation time scales. Applied to MPI-ESM warming simulations, the frame puts constraints on firm ground and suggests a protocol for identifying conditions.
arxiv-2605-30884: Li and colleagues sharpen how agents point at screens, tackling two weak spots in training. First, old methods treat all training cases alike, though their value varies with hardness, which can waste training or cause collapse. Their GUI-D pipeline scores each case by hardness to weight training. Second, their GUI-C2 method narrows the view in steps, guided by the model's doubt, keeping wide context for large targets and fine precision for small ones. Tests show state-of-the-art grounding with less added inference time.
arxiv-2605-30984: Maye-Lasserre and colleagues diagnose and fix template collapse in 3D CT reports. Modern vision-language models write fluent text yet detect few problems, falling to forms that under-report rare findings. This failure stems from limited data, label skew, and weak signals from volume inputs. Their CLarGen splits what to say from how to say it. It joins a query model for problem spotting, recall of matched cases, and a medical language model to write the report. CLarGen lifts medical scores while keeping reports fluent.
arxiv-2605-31084: Brandner and colleagues present Beeline, a fast path for service meshes enforcing application-layer policies in kernel space. Service meshes provide a uniform abstraction for communication, implementing encryption, routing, and balancing, but proxies on data paths cost performance. Beeline synthesizes an eBPF-based data plane from policies, enforcing most application-layer policies directly in the kernel. It accelerates microservices without modification, falling back to proxies for unsupported policies. With TLS and HTTP/2 support, Beeline cuts latency by up to six times versus meshes while sustaining three times more throughput.
arxiv-2605-31484: Castin and colleagues present Balanced LoRA, a fix for low-rank adaptation. This is the most widely used way to fine-tune large language models. LoRA is overparameterised: many pairs of low-rank factors give the same adapted weight matrix. Yet those pairs can have very different condition numbers, which changes how fast training converges. Balanced LoRA projects each step onto a balanced manifold. That improves conditioning while keeping the adapted matrix intact, and it converges faster than standard LoRA with better results across fine-tuning tasks.
arxiv-2606-00084:
Jayakody, Thenahandi, and Jayarathna turn thousands of hotel reviews into management intelligence with SentimentLens, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Travel platforms collect both free-text reviews and star ratings, but the two often disagree, hiding operational problems. Their system applies aspect-based sentiment analysis, which scores feelings about specific service aspects rather than the review overall. It extracts aspect terms, classifies their sentiment, assigns them to service categories, and analyzes patterns at region, hotel, and category levels.

Applied to more than 10,000 real hotel reviews, the framework mapped how traveler sentiment varies across regions, service categories, and hotel types. A cross-modal check compared textual sentiment against numerical ratings to expose latent conflicts in service quality. Importance-performance and entropy-based analyses then flagged high-impact fixes. The authors argue the approach travels beyond their national case study to other destinations and review-driven service industries.
arxiv-2606-00184:
Schweitzer, Danilchenko, and Stulman test if a hidden shield in a mobile net can be sniffed from outside. Such nets form on the fly with no fixed base. A route plan named OLSR steers their traffic. Shields hide in plain control chatter and add no new packet types.

The team runs sims in four states: plain, attack, shield, and both. They test still and moving nets. Traits come just from route shifts a quiet watcher can see. Group models spot the shield with high marks in home tests. A slim set of four traits moves well both ways across still and moving nets. The shield thus leaves a faint but real trace.
arxiv-2606-00284:
Ahuja and Blevins ask how to teach a model new tongues with no loss of old skill. More pre-training on fresh tongues is a plain way to grow a model. Plain fine steps tend to wear down what the model knew. That wear is called vast forgetting in the field.

The pair blend model states from pre- and post-growth stages slice by slice. Mid slices, when rolled back, heal read skill most. Tongue-pair shifts vary by kin group and path. Four fix plans are then put to the test. These span slice freezes, pull-back fines, late slice swaps, and soup blends. Freeze of key slices cuts read loss most, and can top the base model. Shift tests stay mixed, so picks should fit tongue and task.
arxiv-2606-00384:
Rudman and co-authors give sight-word models a tool kit that grows as they probe data. Fit of a math form to data is a core step in lab work. It is also one of the least auto-bound steps. Past agent tools draft and hone forms by talk loops, yet stall on hard tasks.

Their frame, VESTA, adds stats tools to the loop in a live way. Tools reshape data, draw tests of a claim, and run firm checks. Tools made on the fly pile up for use in rounds to come. A new bench, DAWN, spans form fits and time-line tasks in tiers. It ends with real sky tasks, like star mass forms and wave chirps. Live-made tools beat past pipes most on hard tasks.
arxiv-2606-00684:
Cao and co-authors tackle a safety task for AI in this 2026 paper: spotting inputs that fall outside the data a model was trained on. They use continuous normalizing flows, which assign each input a density score. A known flaw is that such models can give odd inputs a high score.

Their frame, called Lagrangian sub-flow, splits the input space in two. One part holds the traits that matter, and the rest gives context. Density is then judged on the key part alone. In speech tests, the same flaw shows up: odd sounds can score as likely. The team adds signals drawn from the shape of the flow path itself. These signals beat score-based checks on a real test of spotting mispronounced sounds, they report.
arxiv-2606-00984:
Yu and Oh study bandit learning when updates must stay rare in this 2026 paper. In a linear contextual bandit, a learner sees a context, picks an action, and earns a reward. Real systems may fold feedback into their model only a few times. Past batched methods often freeze the action rule inside each interval as well. That extra freeze is a separate, stronger curb.

The pair give two practical algorithms that update parameters only on the order of log log T times. The first, BLCE-G, hits minimax optimal regret in both small and large action regimes at once. The second, BLCE, drops a costly design step that slowed prior methods. It keeps optimal regret and posts the lowest known run time among such methods. The ideas extend to generalized linear bandits with near optimal results.
arxiv-2606-01384:
Terada sums Apostol's Möbius functions of order k over integers. Apostol defined this function in 1970 for each positive k. It generalizes the classic Möbius function, the k equals 1 case. Apostol proved an asymptotic form for the full sum. His error term involves x to the 1 over k times log x. In 2001, Bege conjectured sharper estimates for a restricted sum. That sum runs over n coprime to a given q.

Terada settles the conditional version of that conjecture fully. The unconditional version gets a partial solution. He also gives a mean square estimate for the error term. The work sits in analytic number theory. It extends a line of results over fifty years old.
arxiv-2606-01584:
Arronte Alvarez and Xie Fincham hunt high-confidence bias in tutoring chatbots. Tutoring agents can improve engagement and student outcomes. LLMs now supply scalable, personalized feedback in such systems. They may also perpetuate or amplify social stereotypes. That risk weighs heavily in educational settings. High-confidence biases are the target of this study. These are cases where a model misses biased judgments yet stays confident. Such misses can shape its reasoning and feedback to learners.

A new dataset method regenerates student-tutor interactions. Controlled bias turns get inserted from a benchmark dataset. Multiple LLMs face detection tests on the data. Bias detection proves much harder in tutoring chats than benchmarks. Top models are overconfident in their wrong assessments.
arxiv-2606-02184:
Brzozowski and Chung show that language models default to the same invented people again and again. Across hundreds of separately produced AI generated documents, the invented pair Elena Vasquez and Marcus Chen keep turning up. They appear as volcano experts, astronauts, thriller protagonists, podcast hosts, and academic co-authors, though neither person has ever lived. Models do not merely default to likely single names when inventing fictional experts. They produce correlated ensembles of names, pairs and trios whose joint rates far exceed chance.

Those priors are specific to each model family and each version, and they are actively suppressed at model release boundaries. That leaves dateable behavioral fingerprints in model output, the authors argue. Claude, Gemini, and GPT each show distinct favored ensembles. The findings matter for anyone auditing AI generated text on the web or in publishing. Correlated name priors can haunt both long after generation.
arxiv-2606-02384:
Tschalzev and co-authors argue that tabular data benchmarks miss a key step. Real modeling work leans on feature engineering. It builds new input columns from raw ones. Modern benchmarks skip that step in full. The gap this leaves has never been measured. Their pipeline, TabPrep, fills it with light preprocessing.

TabPrep uses feature generators aimed at three structural patterns in data. Many model classes show clear blind spots for those patterns. Adding TabPrep lifts scores across the TabArena benchmark. Tree, neural, linear, and foundation models all gain. The gains often beat those from new model designs alone. TabPrep also tops past automated feature tools. It wins on accuracy, speed, and range of use. The team releases it for direct use in benchmark setups.
arxiv-2606-02484:
Chen and co-authors present Iteris, an AI research system for open problems in computational mathematics. Such problems need more than proofs. They also need numerical tests, adversarial constructions, and algorithm design. Language model agents have won ground in pure math. Computational math has seen less of that progress.

Iteris runs agentic research loops on open questions. The team tests it on two problems from a Simons Workshop collection. The system produced numerical evidence, constructions, and proof drafts. Expert review and correction turned those drafts into verified results. One result is a phase diagram. It compares conjugate gradient with randomized coordinate descent on power-law spectra. The other is a counterexample for QR factorization with column pivoting. It fails to pick well-conditioned submatrices under low coherence. Human validation stays essential in the loop.
arxiv-2606-02984:
Noonan and Kareta report Hubble and ground-based imaging of a rare comet, P/2023 V6 (PANSTARRS). V6 is one of only two known Jupiter co-orbital comets. Such objects link outer solar system bodies to comets seen near the Sun. The other known case, P/2019 LD2, will make that transition in 2063.

The team tracked V6 through late 2024 and early 2025. Ground-based images stopped detecting it after early October. Deep Hubble imaging in early December found a point source at its expected spot, at magnitude 28.06. The authors read this as a sign that V6 stopped being active in late 2024. Its thermal state thus differs from LD2, despite both having large active fractions. The brightness implies a diameter near 340 meters. That would make V6 the smallest object directly observed by Hubble beyond the main belt, and the smallest known Centaur.
arxiv-2606-03184:
Sun and co-authors build a synthetic benchmark for finance forecasting. Real markets are hard to learn from: the signal is faint, tails are heavy, and regimes shift. Real data also hide causes. When a model fails, no one can tell which hidden force hurt it, and only one path of history is ever seen.

FinStressTS fixes causes by design. It holds 30 test settings built from six force families, such as volatility clustering, regime switching, and self-exciting jumps. Fifteen models are tested on point and probability forecasts, from classic time series tools to transformers. Three lessons stand out. Which model wins depends on the force at play, and simple models often beat transformers. Models whose assumed spread matches the true one score well on calm data. Neural models need more data to match simple baselines, and gain most on latent regimes.
arxiv-2606-03284:
Chomphooyod and co-authors build a benchmark for cultural understanding in Southeast Asia. Frontier models do well in Western settings but are barely tested on the cultures of this region. Past inference benchmarks lean on Western content, translations, or one language. Their set, SEA-NLI, is native and culture-grounded.

The benchmark covers eight Southeast Asian countries. Items appear in English and in native regional languages, checked by native speakers. Seventeen encoder and decoder models are tested. All score low, above all on knowledge-heavy classes such as Languages and Science and Technology. A failure study finds the main cause: models lack Southeast Asian cultural knowledge. Models adapted to the region do better. Culture-aware prompts help too. Chain-of-thought prompts add little. The authors offer the set as a lens on how far model knowledge still is from this part of the world.
arxiv-2606-03484:
Lyon and Taher speed up proof search for Gödel-Löb logic, known as GL. They work in CSGL, a tree-hypersequent system for that logic. Poggiolesi had asked for a syntactic decidability proof in that system. Maggesi and Perini Brogi had sought a PSPACE proof-search method there. Both open asks are answered here.

The method is called linearization. It builds just one branch of a proof and one branch of a tree sequent at a time. That avoids the exponential blowup of naive search. The resulting algorithm decides validity in PSPACE, matching the known hardness of GL. When search fails, fragments of tree sequents combine into finite counter-models. That device proves the algorithm correct. Every valid formula also gets a proof made only of line sequents. This links depth-first search to linear nested sequent systems.
arxiv-2606-03784:
Sun and co-authors revisit embodied chain-of-thought for robot control at record scale. Reasoning traces should bridge language and physical action. Their best form and integration stayed unclear. The team curates the largest embodied CoT corpus yet. It holds nearly a million trajectories and over 2,500 hours of data.

Effective traces ground high-level meaning in concrete action guidance. End-effector moves and image-space paths work; abstract reasoning alone adds little. Explicit traces also fail as an autoregressive prefix, since errors compound at inference. Their model, ERVLA, trains with a CoT-dropout plan. Rich traces teach the model, yet it predicts actions directly at run time. Success reaches about 87 percent on LIBERO-Plus and 53 percent on VLABench. Real-robot tests beat strong rivals, above all on ambiguous and long tasks. Code, data, and checkpoints are public.
arxiv-2606-04184:
Weidong Tang and a large team introduce GroupToM-Bench in 2026. It is the first test suite for group theory of mind in a multimodal setting. The task: predict how a group's beliefs and tensions harden into shared outcomes.

The suite pairs video and text scenes with questions about what a group believes, wants, and will do. Models must track each member's view and the group's shared view at once. Top models did well on single-person questions but stumbled on group ones. The gap was worst where members held clashing views. Nonlinear group dynamics, where one voice sways the rest, proved hardest to model. The authors offer the suite as a yardstick for social reasoning in AI.
arxiv-2606-04284:
Yifan Wang and a team of co-authors propose in 2026 a reward model design that respects the diversity of human preferences instead of averaging them into one universal score. Reward models steer language model training, yet people genuinely disagree about what good looks like.

Their sparse mixture-of-experts reward model routes each comparison to a few specialist experts, with training pressure toward sparse routing and diverse experts. On controlled and real-world preference data, the experts learned interpretable specializations, and routing patterns were readable rather than arbitrary. At test time, adjusting expert weights personalized the model to individual users, and watching those weights shift gave a qualitative view of how the model adapted. The approach needs no extra annotation beyond ordinary preference pairs.
arxiv-2606-04384:
Xiaobo Huang and Fang Xie revisit in 2026 the privacy accounting of a selective-release variant of private gradient descent, and find the books did not balance. The parent algorithm had posted remarkable accuracy, but its privacy proof ignored how selective release changes each example's sampling probability.

The pair re-derive the analysis from scratch, accounting for that variation, and propose a corrected algorithm built on clipped gradients with the tighter analysis baked in. Across four datasets spanning images and text, the corrected method kept strict, honestly computed privacy guarantees while still achieving exceptional model performance. The work is a cautionary tale for the field: utility claims in privacy research are only as good as the accounting behind them.
arxiv-2606-04484:
Fu and colleagues present AgentJet, a flexible framework for training AI agents with reinforcement learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Centralized frameworks tightly couple agent activity with model optimization, which limits what can be trained. AgentJet decouples the two: swarm server nodes hold the trainable models and run optimization on GPU clusters, while swarm client nodes execute arbitrary agents on arbitrary devices. That split enables training teams of different models together, mixing several tasks with isolated runtimes, and surviving failures in outside environments without halting training.

Developers can even edit an agent's code live during training by swapping a client node. A context tracking module with timeline merging consolidates redundant context and speeds training by 1.5 to 10 times. AgentJet also includes an automated research system that takes a topic as input and runs multi-day reinforcement learning studies on large clusters by itself, reproducing workflows researchers normally drive by hand.
arxiv-2606-04684:
Mobeen presents a five-stage pipeline for reading license plates from real traffic video in real time, in a 2026 arXiv computer vision paper. Field conditions are harsh. The pipeline chains deep learning detection, kinematic multi-object tracking, and temporal data interpolation into one end-to-end system. It is designed to recover from those failures rather than discard the affected vehicles.

A YOLOv8 nano model first localizes vehicles. The SORT algorithm links them across frames. A second plate-specific detector crops plates for an EasyOCR reader guarded by positional syntax checks. An offline interpolation mechanism then rebuilds fragmented tracks by imputing missing bounding boxes over time. On 3,599 continuous surveillance frames tracking 45 vehicles, interpolation raised the dataset from 2,247 raw detections to 4,536 coordinates. That is an increase of about 102 percent. Top OCR confidence reached 0.982. The average stayed 0.414, reflecting unstable frame quality in real footage.
arxiv-2606-04784:
Frydrych proves that a classical data structure from hysteresis theory captures everything any rate-independent system can remember, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Rate-independent functionals respond to inputs in a way that does not depend on the speed of time's passage, only on the sequence of extremes. The Preisach extremum stack records exactly those extremes.

He proves a characterization theorem: every computable, causal, rate-independent functional factors through the stack. The main result goes further: the stack is a Shannon-minimal sufficient statistic. As a corollary, maintaining the stack online suffices for rate-independent estimation. The stack is thus the complete memory of hysteresis, provably without waste.
arxiv-2606-04984:
Meysam Bagheri Tagani and Carmine Autieri study topological electronic responses in a kagome altermagnet in this 2026 arXiv paper. Altermagnets split electron spins by momentum yet carry no net magnetization. The material here hosts a compensated coplanar 120-degree magnetic texture, and the authors model it with a tight-binding model, a simplified picture of electrons hopping between nearby atoms.

They show the noncollinear exchange field alone creates strong spin splitting and spin-polarized Fermi surfaces. Yet a hidden symmetry forces the Berry curvature, a quantity that bends electron paths, to stay exactly zero even with spin-orbit coupling present. Adding an orbital chiral flux term breaks that symmetry and switches the curvature on, creating local hot spots even with no spin-orbit coupling at all. Mapping the anomalous Hall response then reveals a hierarchy of energy scales behind the change.
arxiv-2606-05084:
Tingjun Lyu and Yunmei Shi analyze radar sensing with AFDM waveforms in this 2026 arXiv paper. AFDM, affine frequency division multiplexing, is a chirp-based waveform proposed for high-mobility systems that combine sensing and communication. Numerical bounds existed, but no closed-form analysis showed how the chirp shapes delay and Doppler estimation, the two quantities radar must pin down.

The authors identify a cancellation in the AFDM likelihood: chirp-induced frequency drift is exactly offset by a phase correction in the chirp-periodic prefix, leaving a small residue. From that cancellation they derive a closed-form Fisher information matrix set by the chirp through a single scalar, plus Cramér-Rao bounds. AFDM proves less delay-Doppler-coupled than OFDM at any nonzero chirp rate. Its delay bound improves quadratically with chirp rate, the Doppler bound stays unaffected, and the theory reduces to the OFDM result as the chirp vanishes.
arxiv-2606-05184:
Yingjin Bi studies monoidal categories associated with Kac-Moody open Richardson varieties in symmetric type in this 2026 arXiv paper. Open Richardson varieties are crossings of Schubert cells in a flag variety. Their coordinate rings carry cluster algebra structures built from generalized minors, special functions introduced by Fomin and Zelevinsky. The paper connects that structure to a categorical framework of Kashiwara, Kim, Oh, and Park.

Bi studies how the minors factorize inside the ring, checking their simple factors in the monoidal category. The main result shows that cluster monomials in the coordinate ring match exactly the isomorphism classes of simple modules in that category. The Grothendieck ring of the category contains the cluster algebra structure built by Bao and Ye. In finite type, Leclerc's seeds coincide with Ménard's seeds for them, and the enlarged setting provides a monoidal categorification of the cluster structure.
arxiv-2606-05284:
Visal Sok and a large team link clump formation in galaxies to accretion of metal-poor gas in this 2026 arXiv paper. Star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon are often clumpy, and those clumps constrain how the galaxies assembled. The team analyzed abundances in about 300 star-forming galaxies between redshifts 0.6 and 2.6 using the LEGA-C, MOSDEF, and CANUCS surveys.

They found clumpy galaxies sit below the mass-metallicity relation, with lower metallicities than expected for their mass, while non-clumpy galaxies sit above it. In a subset with resolved data, clumps in metal-poor hosts are younger and form stars faster than clumps in metal-rich hosts, with no mass difference. Merger statistics classify most clumpy galaxies as non-mergers. The results suggest the clumpy appearance of cosmic-noon galaxies is driven by inflows of metal-poor gas that dilute metallicities and trigger star formation, rather than by mergers.
arxiv-2606-05384:
Srimonti Dutta and Akshata Kishore Moharir test whether language model judges stick to their decisions when challenged, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The authors study post-decision manipulability: how far a verdict can be moved by talking with the judge after it has decided. In tests on MT-Bench and AlpacaEval, judges proved highly stable under neutral re-evaluation, yet reversible under targeted post-decision challenge.

An anti-baseline challenge overturned stable judgments through motivated pressure, while a counterbalanced check kept that reversibility apart from net steering toward a chosen answer. The reversals matter: they lowered agreement with human choices, shifted benchmark rankings, and changed outcomes despite judges reporting high confidence. Authority framing unsettled judges most, and revised judgments arrived with reasons barely matching the first ones, suggesting post hoc rationalization. The authors propose an Evaluation Robustness Score combining reversal risk with direction effects.
arxiv-2606-05484:
Paul Janson, Edouard Oyallon, and Eugene Belilovsky present MAPL in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method for compressing the communication that pipeline parallelism requires. This trains models too large for one device by splitting them across stages, but passing activations between stages becomes the dominant bottleneck on low-bandwidth networks. Fixed projections can compress those activations, yet they degrade results and force awkward constraints on training.

MAPL, Manifold Aware Projection Learning, instead learns a separate low-rank projection for each pipeline stage. It treats compression as a projection optimized under Stiefel manifold constraints, the requirement that the projection stay orthogonal throughout training. Each stage discovers and continuously adapts its own task-optimal subspace by constrained steepest descent. Across LLaMA models from 150 million to one billion parameters, MAPL achieved high compression with minimal loss and a far better tradeoff than the fixed-subspace approach.
arxiv-2606-05684:
Yunxiang Zhang and colleagues let language agents refresh their guidance mid-task in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most agent memory systems fetch past lessons once, at the start of a job. Long jobs drift, though, and early guidance goes stale. AdaMEM keeps two memory layers instead. A long-term store holds raw past trajectories gathered offline. A short-term layer writes fresh strategy notes as the task unfolds.

No model weights change during a run; adaptation lives in the memory. Users can trade token cost against flexibility at run time. On the ALFWorld household benchmark, relative gains reached about thirteen percent over static memory. WebShop gains reached about eleven percent, and search tasks on HotpotQA also led the field. A fine-tuning step that teaches better strategy writing added further gains. The authors frame test-time memory as a new axis for scaling agent skill.
arxiv-2606-05984:
Ruma Maity and colleagues let a three-bead microswimmer invent its own strokes in a 2026 arXiv paper. At microscopic scales viscosity rules, and swimming needs clever non-reciprocal motion. Artificial swimmers need autonomy: no external puppeteer in deployments. The team trains a two-dimensional bead trio with reinforcement learning. Neuroevolution searches for the smallest controller that still swims well.

Five characteristic gaits emerged from training. Three produced directed travel at varying efficiency. Two spun in place instead. Every gait ran on neural networks with fewer than ten nodes and weights. Minimal computation thus achieves robust low-Reynolds swimming. The result echoes biology, where simple organisms swim capably with tiny nervous systems. Algal swimmers like Chlamydomonas are the named comparison. For engineers of medical microswimmers, the message is liberating: autonomy does not require a supercomputer on board. Design the body right, and a handful of neurons can steer it.
arxiv-2606-06384:
Jason Liu, Min Xu, and Jinchuan Xing study a basic estimation problem in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Sub Gaussian variables are those whose tails decay at least as fast as a Gaussian's, and one number, the variance proxy, captures how wide that decay is. The proxy is used everywhere in probability and machine learning, yet how to estimate it from data was barely understood. The natural estimator maximizes an empirical version of the function that defines the proxy.

The authors prove that estimator is consistent and pin down its speed. Under mild assumptions it converges at nearly the square root rate, and at the full rate when the maximizing point is also bounded. They also show the assumptions cannot be dropped: without them, the worst case risk stays constant however much data arrives. Stronger tail assumptions trace a continuum between slow logarithmic rates and impossibility.
arxiv-2606-06484:
Evangelos I Sfakianakis, Barmak Shams Es Haghi, and Katherine Freese rescue the axion from an inflation problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The axion is a hypothetical particle favored as dark matter. But high scale inflation should imprint isocurvature fluctuations on it, density ripples that observations rule out. Their fix couples the inflaton, the field driving inflation, directly to gluons. The coupling raises the QCD confinement scale during inflation. That makes the axion temporarily heavy, so its fluctuations stay suppressed.

As inflation ends, the confinement scale falls. The axion lightens, and fresh fluctuations can seed the observed dark matter. Working inside alpha attractor inflation models, the authors map the viable parameter space. In the minimal setup, deconfinement must come shortly after the microwave background window closes. Reheating through heavy neutrinos creates a loop correction tension that supersymmetry can resolve. The paper bounds the supersymmetry breaking scale to keep the mechanism alive.
arxiv-2606-06584:
Nisarg Chadha, Michael G Scheer, and Eslam Khalaf sharpen a rigorous estimation method for quantum magnets in this 2026 arXiv paper. The bootstrap approach bounds ground state properties by imposing every necessary consistency constraint on operator expectation values, then optimizing. Its bounds go loose in symmetry broken phases, because local operators cannot rule out domain walls, the seams between differently ordered regions. The fix here is to add string operators, nonlocal objects stretched across many sites, aimed squarely at those walls.

With strings included, the program works directly at infinite system size. On the transverse field Ising chain, bounds in the broken phase tightened a lot. On the axial next nearest neighbor Ising model, the tightening located phase boundaries quantitatively. The method also tracked the three state chiral clock model's phase diagram. Loose bounds themselves became a signal, flagging where one phase gives way to the next.
arxiv-2606-06784:
A single post rarely betrays anyone, but a feed full of them can map a life. Peng and co-authors measure that cumulative privacy leak in this 2026 arXiv paper. They build SopriBench, a synthetic benchmark modeled on real leakage patterns from Rednote and Instagram, covering fifty user profiles and over fifteen hundred images with labeled private attributes.

Their Privacy Exposure Score grades each leak by how fine grained the exposed detail is and how sensitive its context makes it, going beyond a simple right or wrong mark.
