They also present Argus, an agent system that forms guesses from scattered clues, checks the evidence, and merges hints across posts into a privacy profile. Argus scored a quarter better than the strongest rival system, with its biggest edge exactly on the cross post leaks that single post tools miss.
arxiv-2606-06984:
Optimizing several goals at once means no single best answer, only trade offs. Rahat, Chugh, Fieldsend, and Allmendinger speed up that search in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is multi objective Bayesian optimization. A Gaussian process model stands in for the costly true objectives. An acquisition function then picks the next point to test.

Their catalyst adds gradient information from the surrogate model itself. Those predictive gradients hint at local stationarity, where improvement stalls. The catalyst augments standard acquisition functions without replacing them. Two versions are tested. One adapts its gradient weights on the fly. The other fixes weights in advance for tight budgets. On the DTLZ benchmark suite, catalysis accelerated convergence toward the Pareto set. Gains were strongest when the surrogate models were accurate. Stationary problems benefited most from the extra signal.
arxiv-2606-07284:
Khennoufa and colleagues design drone networks that power themselves from radio signals in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fleets of uncrewed aerial vehicles can restore connectivity after disasters, but limited batteries shorten missions. Their hierarchical network lets drones harvest energy wirelessly from neighboring drones, using a realistic non-linear model of how harvesting circuits behave. Communication uses rate-splitting multiple access, a scheme that splits messages into shared and private parts to manage interference.

The authors derived formulas for outage probability, the chance a link fails to meet its quality target, including hardware impairments and imperfect channel knowledge. They then optimized drone pairing, cluster selection, and hovering positions to minimize outages. Against several benchmarks, the rate-splitting design beat the main alternative access scheme by 3 to 4 decibels of signal margin. Harvesting from other drones rather than ground sources gained far more, 8 to 12 decibels depending on the scheme.
arxiv-2606-07384:
Chao Correas, Feng, Style, and Kammer show that drying hydrogels obey simpler mechanics than swollen ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hydrogels are polymer networks saturated with water, used in medicine and robotics. Their mechanics couple fluid flow with elastic deformation in tangled ways, and most modeling targets the swollen state. Real use often involves dehydration, so the authors combined experiments and theory to study gels below swelling equilibrium, where water content stays under its natural maximum.

In that regime the coupling simplifies sharply. The attraction between polymer and water controls hydration, while the much weaker network elasticity merely sets the shape. That separation enables a simplified model predicting stresses and deformations in their tests. The finding answers a question: drying does not shrink and stiffen a gel, it changes which physics dominates. Engineers designing drying-tolerant gel devices can exploit the simpler regime rather than fighting the coupled theory.
arxiv-2606-07484:
Wulff, Cao, and Aurnou derive how part of a planet's magnetic field scales with its driving power, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rapidly rotating stars and planets generate fields through dynamo action, convection of conducting fluid sustaining magnetism. Their fields range from dipoles to multipolar tangles, and work suggested multipolar forms arise when rotation matters less. The authors ran 40 three-dimensional dynamo simulations in a spherical shell, bistable pairs where the same settings can settle into either a dipolar or a non-dipolar state.

The 2 branches had similar convective velocities, but the dipole strength differed by a factor of 10 between regimes when scaled by driving power. The non-dipolar field strength was the same on both branches, yielding a scaling law. The warning is that predicting a rotating planet's field cannot assume dipole geometry. In the non-dipolar regime the dipole component should be 10 times weaker than naive estimates suggest.
arxiv-2606-07684:
Ma and colleagues attack a serving bottleneck for large language models in this 2026 arXiv paper: moving key-value caches between machines. A cache holds attention data that avoids recomputing context. Split serving eases memory limits, but cache transfer can dominate the wait for the first token. Caches built by one model variant also misalign with another. Their answer, Semantic Cache Distillation, sends compact semantic codes instead of raw caches.

Two mechanisms do the work. Most layers are rebuilt from low-rank approximations, which capture the main patterns cheaply. A patch step corrects sparse transition layers to stop errors compounding. In tests the method sped time to first token by up to about two point seven times over a prefill baseline. It also beat quantisation and selective recomputation on the quality-versus-latency trade-off. Answer quality stayed within five percent of the uncompressed reference in tight-bandwidth settings.
arxiv-2606-07884:
Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarıoğlu, at Bahçeşehir University in Istanbul, refine a modal logic of safe choices with values and certificates, in this 2026 arXiv article. The starting object is a greatest fixed point: a set of states from which some choice always has all its successors inside. This is a kernel of admissible, safe behaviour. On top of it they build a completion where choices must be certified by finite tests before value is assigned.

Only certified choices feed a discounted value transformer in the style of Bellman equations. Value-refined modal bisimulation is the coarsest equivalence preserving everything at once: formulas, kernels, certified choices, values, greedy sets, and certificates. A canonical distance refines it, arising as the unique fixed point of a choice-matching construction. Distances behave well: the value changes by no more than the distance between states, and distance zero means equivalent.
arxiv-2606-07984:
Takeshi Fukasawa studies a number solvers compute but few watch: the Lagrange multiplier on a constraint, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In constrained maximum likelihood and least squares problems, multipliers measure how hard each constraint binds. Fukasawa shows a clean fact: when the model is correctly specified, the multipliers converge to zero as the sample size grows.

The intuition is that a correct model eventually satisfies its constraints on its own, so the enforcement pressure vanishes. The observation is old in statistics but little used in solver or algorithm design. Nor is it confined to small problems. Even in high-dimensional settings like deep learning, where parameters can outnumber data points, the same reasoning applies. A vanishing multiplier could serve as a signal: persistent nonzero values would flag a misspecified model.
arxiv-2606-08084:
Selim Gatti turns a popular machine learning method into a calibration auditor for regression models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A regression model is calibrated if its predicted means match the true average outcomes for every group of similar cases. That ideal is unreachable with finite noisy data, so actuaries rely on auto-calibration: among cases given the same prediction, the average outcome should equal it. In insurance pricing this is what stops one risk cohort silently subsidising another.

Gatti shows that gradient boosting trees can test necessary conditions for both properties. Fitted in a particular way, the trees expose systematic gaps between predictions and realised outcomes: evidence against calibration. On a large insurance dataset the tests prove powerful, detecting miscalibration that aggregate metrics smooth over. For pricing teams the contribution is practical: an off-the-shelf learner, repurposed as a diagnostic, flags when a tariff model's averages cannot be trusted.
arxiv-2606-08184:
Sobhani and colleagues describe a method for shrinking text files while keeping their meaning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, TextEconomizer, pairs a transformer, the neural network design behind modern language tools, with denoising, which teaches the network to rebuild clean text from corrupted input. An entropy coding step, a classic technique that assigns short codes to common patterns, then squeezes the result further. The goal is lossy compression, where some exact wording may change but the core sense survives.

On their tests, the framework cut input size by half to four fifths while keeping quality scores close to perfect on overlap measures. One version reached a compression ratio above five to one while using far fewer parameters than rival models. A variant built on an older recurrent design compressed even more aggressively. The authors present this as a practical route to storing large text archives in much less space.
arxiv-2606-08284:
Yufei Wei and colleagues address how to find the relative position between two groups of camera images in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task, recovering a six-degree-of-freedom pose, means three position coordinates plus three rotation angles. Each group already carries internal geometry from odometry or calibration. Modern multi-view models bake that geometry into their features, yet current systems treat all views as one unstructured set.

Their method, G2G, keeps the large foundation model entirely frozen and trains only three lightweight modules: a perceiver resampler, a cross-group bridge, and a multi-frame pose head. The trainable parts total roughly thirty-two million parameters, under six percent of the full model. They are supervised only by relative poses. Across four datasets, exploiting within-group geometry improves pose estimation between groups.
arxiv-2606-08484:
Shufeng Kong and colleagues model where species live together, including the rare ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Joint species distribution modeling enables biodiversity monitoring and conservation planning. It predicts many species' distributions together, so community structure informs each prediction. Two challenges stand in the way. Environmental drivers change across space and time. Species co-occurrence also shows complex nonlinear structure and severe long-tail imbalance driven by rare species.

Their framework, STELLAR, learns a shared latent space where dynamic habitat context and community structure are optimized jointly. Its components integrate a graph-temporal model of community relationships with latent alignment and refinement steps that keep rare species from being drowned out by common ones. By tracking how community structure evolves rather than a single snapshot, the model can use a species' companions as evidence for where it persists.
arxiv-2606-08584:
Kasenbacher, Ruepp, and Ecke run a brain-inspired vision algorithm on a neuromorphic chip, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse coding represents a signal as a combination of only a few basis functions. The idea has roots in models of the visual cortex. The Locally Competitive Algorithm computes such codes through dynamics that map naturally onto neuromorphic hardware, processors built from spiking neurons. Prior work studied the non-convolutional algorithm on Intel's Loihi 2 chip. The convolutional setting is more typical of real workloads.

Convolution adds spatial structure, weight sharing, and overlapping receptive fields. The authors present a Loihi 2 implementation of convolutional sparse coding. It follows a one-layer recurrent formulation, with local inhibitory kernels from the convolutional structure. They evaluate it against a graphics processor baseline on the same problems.
arxiv-2606-08784:
Kotowski and Kotowski study how cheaply a quantum operation can be faked with a small helper system, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A quantum channel is the most general change a quantum system can undergo. Implementing one exactly usually requires an ancilla, extra quantum memory, as large as the system squared. Their simulation uses randomization and postselection: it sometimes reports failure, but success is exact.

For unital channels, those that preserve the fully mixed state, they prove a sharp trade-off between ancilla size and success probability. Every unital channel on n qubits can be simulated with constant success probability using only on the order of log n ancillary qubits. A matching construction shows the trade-off is best possible. Highly noncommutative channels, a class including random ones, need just a single ancillary qubit for constant success. The model provably fails, however, for strongly non-unital channels.
arxiv-2606-09384:
Diego Campos, Narasimha Reddy Gosala, and Arundhati Dasgupta suggest turning a quantum computer's weakness into a tool in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum measurement is random by nature, which usually spoils precise answers from quantum algorithms for nonlinear equations. The authors propose reading that randomness as genuine chance behaviour, the kind classical simulations fake with random number generators.

They test the idea on the Lorenz system, a classic chaotic model of convection with three coupled variables. Two quantum algorithms, FABLE and unitary time evolution, were run in noise-free simulated circuits using Qiskit. Their measured outputs reproduced the spread of behaviour of a classically randomised Lorenz model, rather than one exact trajectory. They argue that quantum hardware, already at one hundred twenty-seven qubits, suits such modelling tasks, where spread matters more than precision.
arxiv-2606-09484:
Kumar Thushalika, Sukumar Kishanthan, and Asela Hevapathige test whether large language models truly understand graph structure in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their probe is graph isomorphism, deciding whether two graphs are identical in structure under some renaming of their nodes. Genuine structural reasoning must be permutation invariant: renaming the nodes cannot change the answer, because the underlying graph has not changed.

On straightforward questions of this kind, the tested models scored near perfectly, with accuracy reaching the high nineties. Yet when the same graphs were presented with permuted node labels, the models often failed to recognise them as identical. The authors argue that the apparent success comes from surface pattern matching on the written representation, not from reasoning about topology. Without such tests, benchmark success can badly overstate what a model understands about structure.
arxiv-2606-09884:
Shree Murthy and Rohan Pandey pin down two ways learning agents misbehave in nonstop pricing duels in this 2026 arXiv paper. The agents use deep reinforcement learning in a continuous-time market. Prices tick by a Poisson clock, and each firm sees the other with a lag. Two failure modes show up on cue in their shared test bed.

Mode one is a tacit cartel: paired agents settle on prices far above the fair fight level, with a collusion score of zero point six nine. No word passes between them. Shifting to staggered clocks cut the score by forty-eight percent. Adding view lag drove it to a floor of zero point two eight, still above the honest mark. Mode two is a blow-up of the critic, the agent's value judge, at five events per unit time. The fix helps one mode and not the other.
arxiv-2606-10184:
Jung makes a reinforcement learning method work for models that reason in continuous hidden states instead of written steps, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Group Relative Policy Optimization compares several rollouts of a model and learns from their relative rewards, so it needs diversity between rollouts. Latent-reasoning models like Coconut feed continuous hidden states back recurrently, and that phase is deterministic: repeated rollouts produce identical trajectories, the advantage collapses to zero, and learning stalls. His fix sources the needed randomness from structured dropout.

A single Bernoulli mask, held constant across all latent recurrence steps within one rollout, creates trajectory variance. He backs the method with theory covering unbiasedness, variance reduction, and gradient well-definedness. On the GSM8K math benchmark, the method improved a Coconut baseline's pass-at-one accuracy from about twenty-seven percent to about twenty-nine percent in the reported runs.
arxiv-2606-10384:
Ren and Feng find signs of criticality, the tipping-point regime between order and chaos, inside trained recurrent neural networks, in a 2026 arXiv paper on neural dynamics. Criticality is proposed as an organizing idea in living neural systems, but its origin and relevance in artificial networks are unclear.

To explain how subcritical branching can coexist with robust long-range timing links, they introduce a mixture branching process framework linking mixed branching dynamics to such links. The results identify critical-like behavior in these networks as an emergent, size-dependent regime rather than a designed property. Training time matters too: the near-critical window appears near optimal epochs, so overtrained or oversized models drift away from it. The framework connects artificial network behavior to the physics used to describe real brain activity.
arxiv-2606-10484:
Li and a large team from Ant Group present AgentCanary in this 2026 arXiv paper, a security evaluation framework for autonomous AI agents. As agents move from chatting to executing, failures shift from bad text to compromised systems. AgentCanary organises threats in a matrix crossing five entry routes, such as prompt injection, memory contamination, and skill poisoning, with seven impact categories. Agents are tested in a real executable environment with working inboxes, pages, and calendars, keeping state across steps.

Scoring uses the action trajectory rather than the final reply, and splits into outcome safety, security awareness, and task utility. Frontier models faced single-round injections, iterative red-teaming, and long attack chains across three frameworks. The results show current agents often fail to recognise the attacks they face, especially under poisoned skills, persistent state, and long-horizon execution. The framework is offered as a baseline for more secure agent systems.
arxiv-2606-10784:
Andriulli speeds up electromagnetic scattering solvers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Solving the electric field integral equation for conducting objects yields large dense systems, and solvers pay in memory and time for every product with them. Filtering tames this by compressing the operator beforehand; known filters come from spectral formulas that sit awkwardly inside fast solver schemes. This work builds the filter from the matrices themselves, inside the Adaptive Integral Method.

Working directly on the discrete matrices makes the filtered kernels fit fast solvers, which the formula-based forms often do not. Numerical tests show results matching those filters, including on the Calderón-preconditioned equation for transverse-electric cases from a 2D object, where conditioning matters most. The point is practical: filtering becomes something a solver computes from its own matrices, not a bespoke derivation per kernel, taking the technique to problems with no tidy spectral formula.
arxiv-2606-10984:
Yang, Ren, and Li design a rotation sensor from virtual excitations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their platform couples a spinning ring cavity to a two-level system and an extra bosonic mode. Through the Sagnac effect, rotation becomes a direction-dependent detuning, reshaping the hybrid light-matter dressing.

Ultrastrong coupling also generates virtual excitations, and because the Sagnac-Fizeau shift enters their energy denominators, the polariton response to rotation grows and turns nonreciprocal: clockwise and counter-clockwise driving give different readings. The quantum Fisher information for angular velocity rises without ever extracting them directly. Bundle-emission coincidence counting offers a matching direction-sensitive readout.
arxiv-2606-11384:
Kudasov, a solo author, shows an unusual half-metallic state can exist in helimagnets in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Half-metallic ferromagnets have a gap in the density of states for one spin projection, gapless for the opposite spin. In the state Kudasov describes, which spin projection gets the gap is determined by the direction of the wave vector. The state originates from the nontrivial topology of the band structure, a multi-sheeted covering over the Brillouin zone.

He presents two-dimensional tight-binding models for p-wave and f-wave half metals, realizable in crystalline and van der Waals systems. He also discusses the complex band structure of the unusual p-wave half metal in nanostructures. In a quantum well, a standing wave with a helical spin structure forms, and a persistent spin current exists. The work links half-metallicity to unconventional magnets like altermagnets.
arxiv-2606-11584:
León, Torreblanca, Autieri, and González show one symmetry governs both spin and lattice waves in an altermagnet in a 2026 arXiv paper. Altermagnetism gives spin splitting that depends on momentum, through non-symmorphic crystal symmetries, but whether the same rules also govern spin and lattice excitations was open. From ab initio work and linear spin-wave theory, they study monolayer copper fluoride.

They find chiral-split magnons and cycloidal phonons, both controlled by the same rules. The magnon chirality is strongly anisotropic, driven by symmetric anisotropic exchange, with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling a weak modulation. The two responses are complementary: cycloidal phonon angular momentum appears exactly where magnon chirality is suppressed, and vice versa. The magnon bands carry quantized Chern numbers of plus or minus two, a sign of nontrivial topology. It thus unites spin-wave, lattice-wave, and topological responses under one framework.
arxiv-2606-11684:
Mingfei Xu and Xiaojin Zhang work on a long-standing conjecture in algebra in this 2026 arXiv paper. The finitistic dimension of an algebra measures how complicated its modules can get. A famous open conjecture says it is always finite. The authors approach it through tau-tilting modules, a modern class used to organise an algebra's representations.

They define two new quantities relative to such a module, depth and delooping level, both counting steps in a certain resolution process. Their main theorem bounds the finitistic dimension of the opposite algebra of the module's own symmetry algebra by these two quantities. Applications follow directly. When the starting algebra has finite representation type, or is minimal representation infinite, the relevant finitistic dimension is finite. Worked examples compute the bound for small algebras given by quivers, diagrams of arrows with relations.
arxiv-2606-11784:
Yuke Zhang, Wenbo Zhou and Pengfei Zhang find a way to make quantum chaos stronger in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a closed quantum system, local information scrambles across the whole system, becoming effectively unreadable. Coupling the system to an environment usually drains information away, slowing that scrambling. The authors identify the opposite process.

Their setup connects an equilibrated system to a second environment acting as an entropy reservoir. When entropy flows into the system, through heat or particles, the space of states the system explores grows larger, and many-body chaos intensifies. They demonstrate this with a solvable model, a complex Brownian SYK system, a standard toy model of strongly interacting quantum matter. Both the relaxation toward the steady state and the steady-state quantum Lyapunov exponent, the rate measuring chaos, can be computed exactly in the model. Entropy flow becomes a controllable tuning knob for scrambling.
arxiv-2606-11884:
Gregor Grote, Juan E Tapia and Christian Rathgeb test whether face image quality tools work on identity cards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Remote identity checks, for banking or government services, depend on customers photographing their ID cards. Presentation attack detection systems, which spot fake or printed documents, perform worse on poor images.

The authors adapt capture-related measures from the Open Face Image Quality standard, built for face photos, to whole ID cards. A preprocessing pipeline detects card corners, corrects perspective and masks the foreground so scores are unbiased. They then check how quality scores correlate with the performance of three attack detection systems across four datasets, two with genuine cards and two with printed mock cards. Of thirteen candidate measures, ten prove applicable. Sharpness and underexposure assessment clearly improve attack detection across all systems and datasets, while overexposure has no effect.
arxiv-2606-12184:
Ditzen and co-authors supply new tools for a popular way to model economic turning points, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Threshold regression splits data into regimes at a cutoff value, so a factor can act one way below the line and differently above it. Panel data follow many units over time, but here the time span is fixed and short. Interactive fixed effects, shared factors hitting each unit with its own strength, further tangle estimation.

They build a least-squares style estimator that stays simple, accurate, and fast, plus tests for the threshold and other parameters. They then revisit how inflation affects economic growth using the newest data. The relationship proves nonlinear, with a threshold between 1.1 and 3.5 percent depending on the sample used. The toolbox is the first built for fixed-length panels with interactive effects in threshold models.
arxiv-2606-13484:
William Chèvremont and colleagues introduce a technique for watching gels yield at tiny scales in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a soft solid is sheared back and forth with growing amplitude, it eventually flows: it yields. How microscopic structure rearranges for good during that process remains hard to observe. The team combines rheology, the study of flow, with echo X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, synchronising nonlinear data acquisition to the oscillatory shear. Their sample is a carbon black colloidal gel with a fractal structure.

They resolve time-periodic echoes in the measured intensity correlations, whose decay encodes non-affine rearrangements, motions that do not simply follow the applied strain. The decorrelation behaves ballistically at all strains, with a typical velocity that scales linearly with the loss tangent, a standard ratio describing how liquid-like the material is. Further findings link the microscopic irreversibility to the large-scale mechanical response.
arxiv-2606-13584:
Chu and colleagues probe the limits of simple material models for gels under violent impact in this 2026 arXiv paper. Characterising soft materials at high strain rates is hard because they are nonlinear and history-dependent. Inertial microcavitation rheometry uses a laser to blast a bubble inside the material and simulates the bubble's motion to infer material properties. Users noticed the inferred values depend on which window of the event is fitted, suggesting a constant-parameter model cannot describe the whole cavitation. The authors turn that window dependence into a diagnostic tool.

They estimate the model's constants over moving, overlapping windows using an ensemble Kalman smoother built for repeated data fitting. Within a standard gel model, they pinpoint where and how the constant-value assumption breaks down, rather than reporting one averaged set. The findings matter for uses from medical ultrasound to protective materials, wherever gels are characterised by cavitation tests.
arxiv-2606-13784:
Kapahtia and colleagues use large simulations of the early universe to ask which dark matter haloes host the brightest black holes. A halo is the huge clump of dark matter holding a galaxy. An active galactic nucleus is a galaxy center shining as gas falls onto its black hole. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares several simulation suites, including TNG300, TNG-Cluster, and FLAMINGO, at redshifts three to seven.

Brighter active nuclei sit in heavier haloes on average, but only up to a point. Past roughly a trillion solar masses, the link flattens in FLAMINGO and even turns down in the TNG runs. Quasars in the TNG runs usually live in haloes between ten to the twelfth and ten to the twelve point five solar masses. The spread reaches three orders of magnitude in brightness at one halo mass. Halo growth and black hole feeding therefore stay weakly linked.
arxiv-2606-14084:
Nguyen and colleagues improve robot policies at test time by choosing better noise, not retraining. Diffusion-based vision-language-action policies generalize well but latch onto spurious visual cues and produce jittery actions. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces Selected Diffusion Noise, a training-free method using the diffusion noise space as a control knob. Candidate noise vectors are sampled far from a reference set, reducing reliance on spurious cues, and scored for trajectory coherence.

Tests covered two simulation benchmarks, Google Robot and Widow-X, two real-world datasets, and policies including pi-zero and GR00T variants. Success rates rose by eight percent in simulation and ten percent in real-world settings. Actions became smoother and more stable, even with objects masked out. Since no model weights change, the technique sidesteps fine-tuning costs and forgetting risks. Theory backs it: failure probability decays exponentially in the number of candidates.
arxiv-2606-14484:
Gershteyn and Alber assess quantum computing as a threat to Bitcoin and Ethereum in a 2026 arXiv paper. Public debate often mixes up two quantum algorithms. Shor's algorithm can break the elliptic-curve signatures that authorize spending, while Grover's algorithm gives only a modest speedup against proof-of-work mining, further blunted by fault-tolerance costs and difficulty adjustment.

Folding hardware scaling, falling resource needs, readiness lags, and expert surveys into one Monte Carlo forecast gives a wide, two-peaked arrival distribution for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. The authors estimate roughly a one-in-six chance by twenty thirty-five, near thirty percent by twenty forty, and about sixty percent by twenty fifty. Of roughly six million exposed Bitcoin coins, only about two point three million are irreducibly at risk, and timely migration to post-quantum signatures would beat even an early machine.
arxiv-2606-14884:
Huang and coauthors build a consensus-based optimizer that works directly on curved spaces in a 2026 study. Consensus-based optimization steers a cloud of particles toward a shared point biased toward low-cost states. Noise keeps the cloud exploring, so the method can find global minima without gradients. Most theory assumes flat Euclidean space, while many problems live on spheres or other manifolds.

The authors formulate the particle system with the manifold's own distance, using its logarithmic and exponential maps. They prove the system and its mean-field limit, a McKean-Vlasov dynamic, are globally well-posed. Under stated conditions, the mean-field equation converges to a global minimizer of the objective. Numerical tests run on the sphere, on hyperbolic space, and on the special orthogonal group of rotations. The intrinsic dynamics handle nonconvex problems on all three spaces, matching the theory where its curvature bounds apply.
arxiv-2606-14984:
Unger and coauthors study long-term beam stability for the Electron-Ion Collider's ring electron cooler in a 2026 study. The cooler circulates electrons at modest energy to cool protons at top energy, fighting emittance growth from scattering inside the beam. Strong damping wigglers keep the electron beam tight, but their focusing fields add nonlinear effects. Those effects can shrink the safe aperture and shorten beam lifetime.

The team optimizes the lattice, including chromatic fixes, placement errors, orbit fixes, and space-charge effects. A novel sextupole-like wiggler field cuts chromatic spread sharply compared with quadrupole-like focusing. With realistic alignment and monitor errors, apertures in both planes exceed the five-sigma target. Space-charge runs with a Gaussian beam show a modest tune spread and limited emittance growth. Together the results support the cooler design at its required parameters. Further work targets a wider momentum acceptance margin.
arxiv-2606-15084:
Marron outlines the Bosque API toolkit, a spec-centered way to build software for humans and AI agents, in a 2026 tool paper. A specification states what a system should do, what it needs, and what limits apply. Vague specs let agents guess wrongly and act unsafely, as a loose bank transfer API shows. The paper argues specs should become the main artifact of the work.

The BAPI language covers data, behavior, time-based rules across API calls, and resource access, in many programming languages. Its rich type system adds guards that block common errors early. Tools check both the code that implements an API and the code that uses it. Test generation, sandboxing, and cross-language runtimes round out the toolkit. For agent-built software, clear resource limits bound what an agent may touch. Marron presents BAPI as shared ground for stakeholders, developers, agents, and automated tooling.
arxiv-2606-15184:
Kapoor and coauthors present TODDLERS 2.0, a 2026 upgrade of a framework that models young star-forming regions. The tool follows an expanding shell pushed by stellar feedback, then computes the light it emits. The first version assumed instant star birth, uniform clouds, one fixed stellar mix, and fixed dust. The upgrade removes each of those limits. It now handles varied stellar populations, cloud structures, and modes of star formation.

New population codes allow arbitrary initial mass functions and binary star evolution. Clouds can have non-uniform density profiles that themselves evolve as radiation escapes. Concentrated clouds fragment earlier, starting the shell's momentum-driven expansion sooner. A top-heavy stellar mix drives stronger feedback and earlier fragmentation than the standard mix. At low metallicity, escaping radiation can thin the unswept cloud a thousandfold. For small clusters, random sampling of stars makes feedback vary by tenfold between runs.
arxiv-2606-15284:
He and coauthors pretrain a general encoder for pulse signals from wearables in a 2026 health informatics paper. Photoplethysmography, or PPG, tracks blood flow optically and underpins many wearable health features. Existing encoders learn from waveform shape alone, ignoring who the patient is. Similar waveforms can hide different health states, though. The authors built a paired dataset linking PPG recordings with patient-level health records. Their method, CAP, aligns signal codes with those clinical records during pretraining.

Paired training anchors each patient's signals to their health state. A patching scheme bridges duration and frequency mismatches between training and use. On four downstream tasks, CAP beat strong baselines across the board. Respiratory rate prediction improved most, nearly doubling the accuracy gain. Average relative improvement across tasks reached about twenty-seven percent. Ablations and plots confirmed each design piece contributes. The work argues signal foundation models should be patient-centric, not signal-centric.
arxiv-2606-15484:
Saleem bounds how fast entanglement can grow as an interaction strengthens, in a 2026 quantum physics paper. The setting is two qubits coupled by an interaction with a tunable strength. Entanglement is measured by concurrence, and its speed is the rate concurrence changes as the strength varies. The bound involves quantum Fisher information, which sets the ultimate precision of estimating a parameter from measurements.

The paper proves the speed of concurrence can never exceed the square root of the quantum Fisher information, for any pure two-qubit state under any nonlocal interaction. Equality holds exactly when all the state's distinguishability converts into entanglement change, and the author derives those saturation conditions. Both quantities are measurable in today's ion, atom, and superconducting platforms, so the bound is testable in the lab. The same information geometry that empowers quantum sensors caps how quickly entanglement can respond.
arxiv-2606-15684:
Yi and colleagues present TickingCollabBench in 2026, a Minecraft benchmark for multi-agent tasks where collaboration is both compulsory and rushed. Real teamwork mixes agents with different abilities, partial views, changing conditions, and hard deadlines, a combination earlier benchmarks rarely capture. The tasks are built to require complementary skills: no single agent can finish alone.

A companion framework generates dynamic events during play and lets designers specify tasks declaratively in YAML files. An automated pipeline drafts structurally diverse task configurations with a language model, then filters out infeasible ones with a verifier. Baseline evaluations show current language models frequently fail in these dynamic settings. Long response latency and the difficulty of coordinating under partial observability and mixed abilities leave them far short of an oracle with global knowledge. The benchmark makes a pointed case: multi-agent systems need to be faster and better coordinated before real-time teamwork is realistic.
arxiv-2606-15784:
Le introduces BN-LTE in 2026, a Bayesian network for modelling Alzheimer's progression as a staged causal process, not a black-box forecast. The amyloid-tau-neurodegeneration cascade is usually imposed as a fixed biomarker sequence or ignored entirely. BN-LTE instead infers a latent disease time, pseudotime, from each patient's baseline biomarker profile.

Directed links are constrained by the plausible cascade ordering, and spline-varying equations link baseline measures to future yearly change in tau PET signal. On ADNI data, across repeated subject-disjoint tests, the model reconstructs tau spread's spatial pattern better than forecast baselines. Its analysis recovers stage-varying effects that prediction scores cannot show. It finds a mid-course window of amyloid effect, backed by g-formula contrasts, adjusted causal contrasts, ablations, and robustness checks. The framework ties forecasts to mechanism, which is what treatment timing decisions need.
arxiv-2606-15884:
Onami and colleagues analyse legal reasoning inside large language models at the neuron level in 2026, across seven open-weight models and seven tasks. They rank neurons by attribution score, then suppress the top ones. Suppressing the identified neurons collapses target-task accuracy, while suppressing random neurons does not, so the ranking finds genuinely load-bearing units.

A small subset of neurons proves influential across all seven tasks. Once those are removed, suppressing the rest degrades only its own task, exposing truly task-specific neurons in every model. Within law, the three benchmarks share high neuron overlap and are affected jointly, suggesting legal components that span jurisdictions. The work also qualifies a popular belief: influential neurons are not reliably in middle MLP layers; location depends on input format and content. Targeting domain neurons could become a cheaper route to domain adaptation than full retraining.
arxiv-2606-16084:
Sinha and Chavan test in 2026 whether sperm whale communication shares a famous design feature of human language. Duality of patterning means meaningless units combine into meaningful ones, which then combine further. Whales talk in codas, short rhythmic bursts of clicks that they share and recombine. Acoustic similarity alone can fake layered structure, so the authors test the layers separately.

Studying 1,483 codas from the Dominica Sperm Whale Project, they find a two-tier system whose tiers follow different rules. At the lower tier, clicks form a coda by which clicks are present with their rhythm, not by click order. Order statistics sit near zero, and ordered embeddings fail to beat a simple bag baseline. At the upper tier, codas sequence into bouts with measurable second-order dependence. The result supports a narrow duality in whale codas, with different evidence at each tier.
arxiv-2606-16284:
Desai and Robens study in 2026 how well a future electron-positron collider could spot a light scalar particle that decays invisibly. The setting is the FCC-ee at a collision energy of 240 GeV, producing a Z boson alongside the new scalar. Such states appear in several extensions of the Standard Model, and current data do not rule them out. The team uses a simplified model with an added scalar singlet and a scalar dark matter candidate.

They scan scalar masses from 15 to 120 GeV, using a parametric simulation of the IDEA detector concept. A cut-based selection is combined with a boosted decision tree from XGBoost to separate signal from background. Expected sensitivities reach cross sections near 0.01 to 0.1 femtobarns for masses below the Z boson mass. Heavier masses, up to about 1 femtobarn, are harder, and sensitivity dips near the Z and Higgs masses.
arxiv-2606-16584:
Pawlaschyk solves in 2026 a boundary-value problem for a class of complex functions on domains that stretch to infinity, where classical envelope methods usually break. The domain is unbounded in complex space, and a bounded continuous function is prescribed on its boundary. The question is whether the values extend to a maximal function of a given plurisubharmonic type, built as a Perron-Bremermann envelope. The q-plurisubharmonic functions generalize the plurisubharmonic functions central to several complex variables.

Under two geometric conditions on the domain, r-peak points on the boundary and bounded type, Pawlaschyk shows the extension exists. The boundary function extends to a maximal bounded continuous function on the closed domain. Inside, it is q-plurisubharmonic and simultaneously (n minus q minus 1)-plurisuperharmonic, and its top-degree form vanishes. That limit function coincides exactly with the Perron-Bremermann envelope formed from bounded q-plurisubharmonic functions.
arxiv-2606-16784:
Tucker leads a large team testing quantum nonlocal games in a 2026 physics paper. In these games, two players who cannot communicate must coordinate actions using shared entanglement, a link with no classical counterpart. One task is rendezvous: meeting on a network without talking, where quantum players have shown an edge under ideal conditions.

Real settings add uncertainty about the network itself. The authors build a theory of graph ensembles, families of possible networks, to capture that uncertainty. They then demonstrate the quantum advantage between physically separated ion-trap systems sharing remote entanglement, not just inside one processor. Broader problems are simulated on superconducting hardware. Surprisingly, giving players more local information increases the quantum advantage, something classical play cannot reproduce. The results point toward portable quantum devices helping groups make joint decisions in uncertain settings, from search coordination to distributed sensing tasks ahead.
arxiv-2606-16884:
Dicker and colleagues separate two ways of driving a tiny resonator in a 2026 nanomechanics paper. A carbon nanotube can be pushed directly at its resonance, or driven in a second way, by changing a system property near twice the resonance. The second route powers sensitive amplifiers, but normal electrical readout cannot reveal the frequency of motion, so the two are easy to confuse.

The team turns the nanotube into a mixer and listens to microwave sidebands through a low-noise amplifier. That gives a frequency-resolved view of the motion, separate from the drive. Direct motion of the first overtone splits cleanly from parametric motion of the basic mode, even when drive frequencies nearly match, and their power trends differ too. Beyond the usual resonance, responses appear at three and four times the base frequency. Those match high-order effects from nonlinear stiffness, opening control knobs for nanotube devices.
arxiv-2606-16984:
Hou and colleagues study AI in emergency medical services in a 2026 paper on human-computer interaction. Ambulance crews work in stages, from the emergency call through transport to hospital handover, under extreme time pressure. AI tools built for calm, desk-based settings may clash with that rhythm.

The researchers interviewed twenty-five EMS clinicians across the United States about current tools and hopes for AI support. Crews coordinate through shared awareness spread across roles, linking pattern recognition straight to protocol-driven action. Clinicians worry AI could threaten that link through legal and privacy exposure, unreliable outputs, missed context, threats to their autonomy and plain workflow friction. The authors distill five design principles for AI that supports shared awareness instead. They stress openness about how outputs arise, the ability to trace them, resilience when offline, and genuine human authority over decisions.
arxiv-2606-17084:
Tzanavaris revisits the action principle for relativistic perfect fluids in a 2026 paper on gravitation theory. An action principle derives the equations of motion from one functional, but boundary data must be fixed carefully for it to be well posed.

The formulation is manifestly covariant, built from differential forms. For flows slower than light it amounts to a geometric rewriting of the classic Schutz action. The interesting case is null flow, where the fluid moves at light speed. Extending the same principle there does not give a generic perfect fluid at all. The equations of motion force the enthalpy density to vanish, energy density plus pressure pinned to zero. The stress-energy then splits into a vacuum-like term with variable pressure plus null dust. The obstruction, Tzanavaris shows, is dynamical rather than kinematical. Because the matter action stands alone, it can travel to modified gravity theories.
arxiv-2606-17284:
Boshkayev and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on the shadows and light-bending of dilatonic black holes, exotic objects from gravity theories with a scalar field tied to electromagnetism. The holes studied are static, round, and carry both charge and a dilatonic coupling parameter. Black hole shadows are now observable, thanks to telescope images of the holes in M87 and our own galaxy, so model predictions can face real data directly.

The team computes the photon sphere, the critical impact parameter, and the shadow radius as the charge and coupling vary. Raising either parameter shrinks all three, giving a smaller apparent shadow on the sky. Predicted angular sizes are compared with the M87 and Sagittarius A observations to constrain the model. The paper also estimates the high-frequency energy emission rate and derives the leading coefficient governing strong-field light bending.
arxiv-2606-17384:
Darkhalil, Damen, and Fouhey present a 2026 arXiv paper on detecting hand-object interactions in images, a core skill for action understanding, reconstruction, and robotics. Their system, HOI-DETR, extends a detection transformer to model not only hands and the objects they touch directly. It also handles second objects, the things a held tool acts upon. The links joining hands to first objects and first objects to second ones are predicted in a single pass too.

Alongside the model, the paper assembles an evaluation suite of four varied data sets for the task. One is a new video benchmark drawn from a kitchen activity corpus, and fresh annotations also repair a widely used still-image benchmark. The released trained model lifts the state of the art on all four data sets tested. Gains passed twenty points of mean average precision on two of them, and ablations credit each component.
arxiv-2606-17784:
Colléaux and colleagues classify a family of modified gravity theories in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Quasi-topological gravity tweaks Einstein's theory with higher-curvature terms while keeping black hole equations unusually simple. The authors ask which theories keep that good behavior for a wider set of symmetric spacetimes, including Taub-NUT, the near-horizon extreme Kerr geometry, the swirling universe, and the Eguchi-Hanson instanton.

For theories built only from the Riemann tensor, they show that only third-order equations can stay analytic for these metrics. They also prove there is a unique theory with first-order field equations at each curvature order, matching the tidy structure of general relativity itself. From infinite towers of these corrections they build regular static black holes and give closed-form solutions for every symmetry on their list, checking each one makes physical sense.
arxiv-2606-17884:
Böhning and colleagues test a cheap shortcut for a deep construction in algebraic geometry, in a 2026 paper. The modern theory of atoms breaks a variety's quantum cohomology into pieces using multiplication by the Euler field, but computing in big quantum cohomology is notoriously hard. The authors define a naive version that needs only the small quantum cohomology, where the operator is multiplication by the anticanonical bundle.

They then check whether the naive pieces obey Iritani's blowup formula, a key rule for how decompositions change when a variety is blown up. Their examples are chosen to be rich enough to show the theory's features yet computable by elementary means. The naive formula holds in several cases, but a four-dimensional quadric example shows the naive and small decompositions can genuinely differ, marking where the shortcut stops being safe.
arxiv-2606-17984:
Plazas Malagón and colleagues weigh a set of galaxy clusters with gravity itself, in a 2026 cosmology paper. The Planck satellite picked these clusters by the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, a shadow hot gas casts on the cosmic microwave background, but turning that signal into a mass needs calibration. Weak gravitational lensing, the slight bending of background galaxy shapes, supplies an independent scale.

Using the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey's third-year shape catalogue, the team stacks the lensing signal of nineteen clusters and forward-models the whole selection process. Their fit accounts for miscentered clusters, scatter in the mass proxy, and selection bias. The result says Planck-style masses run high: the bias factor lands near three quarters, with roughly a tenth of uncertainty either way. Such calibrations anchor cluster counts as a probe of cosmic structure and dark energy.
arxiv-2606-18184:
Campos asks whether gravitational-wave hunters are wrong to treat every burst as a plane wave, in a 2026 paper. Detectors like LIGO and Virgo fit signals with flat wavefronts arriving from far away. A collimated burst, though, is a wavepacket with finite width, and its curved front could imprint geometric phase differences across a detector network that plane-wave templates would miss or misread.

Campos builds a paraxial wavepacket model and derives the coherent response of a network to such structured signals. For today's LIGO and Virgo baselines the difference proves negligible, vindicating the plane-wave habit for now. Third-generation networks change the picture. A toy event study shows a wavepacket-constrained search gaining a three to four fold detection efficiency at fixed false-alarm rate. It stays sharp on ordinary signals too.
arxiv-2606-18684:
Mínguez and Minondo build a theory of why firms export in different ways, in a 2026 trade paper. Export markets contain four kinds of participants. Some producers sell their own goods directly abroad. Some rely on intermediaries. Pure intermediaries export other firms' goods, and hybrid firms do both. Models do not produce this heterogeneity from firm traits.

In their model, firms differ in manufacturing capability, which lowers production cost. They also differ in commercial capability, which lowers the variable cost of reaching foreign customers. Fixed export costs are paid once per portfolio, and costs of scope are convex. Together, these two dimensions sort firms into the four types from within. The model predicts positive assortative matching: commercially stronger intermediaries pair with more manufacturing-capable producers. It also predicts broader variety portfolios for more capable firms. Using Spanish firm-level export data, the authors find suggestive evidence for both predictions.
arxiv-2606-18784:
Bautista Gonzalez and the team achieve nanometer-precise 3D localization across large biological volumes, in a 2026 optical microscopy paper. Localization microscopy sees molecular organization far beyond the diffraction limit. But taking it from flat planes to deep volumes forces a trade-off among precision, speed, and field of view. Point spread functions that encode depth over ranges blur and crowd.

The team combines a twin Airy engineered point spread function with two-photon light sheet fluorescence microscopy. They model the broadband light of real fluorophores. They reached precision better than twenty nanometers sideways, and about forty-two nanometers axially. That held across volumes hundreds of micrometers wide and one hundred deep. An expected path leads to sub-ten-nm precision in millimeter-scale specimens. Tests in bead phantoms and live mammalian oocytes showed robust performance. This sets a scalable route to super-resolution imaging over large volumes.
arxiv-2606-19984:
Juntian Huang, Jürgen Kurths, and Ying Tang merge reservoir computing with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks in 2026. Reservoir computing forecasts dynamical systems cheaply by training only a readout, but fixed reservoirs can miss long-range structure, while recurrence-free variants suffer exploding feature counts. Their method, KARC, swaps the reservoir for explicit basis-function expansions drawn from the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem.

The authors show KARC is a lightweight form of a Kolmogorov-Arnold network, keeping the expressive power while restoring closed-form training. At comparable cost it beats existing reservoir methods on hard benchmarks, including partial differential equation systems. It can even plug into diffusion models to aid text-to-image generation. Two fashionable frameworks turn out to be one, with the forecasting side gaining rigour and the network side gaining speed.
arxiv-2606-20084:
Zhuo Cao and five colleagues introduce a way to edit data with flow-based generative models when the goal cannot be written as a smooth, differentiable formula. Their 2026 paper starts from conditional flow matching, which splits each sample into a condition-set part and a leftover residual carrying the sample's individual character. Gradient search fails on black-box goals, such as a crystal property computed by an external tool. The authors therefore search the residual space with evolutionary methods.

Two search modes divide the work. Self-pollination refines one sample's residual for local gains, while cross-pollination mixes residuals across unlike samples to explore broadly. Tests on MorphoMNIST, a counterfactual image benchmark, and on crystal data show the split balances hitting the target, keeping the original intact, and staying diverse. Since the method wraps any flow model without retraining, the recipe extends from images to scientific design tasks.
arxiv-2606-20284:
Ariel Guzmán, Mohsen Fathi, and J. R. Villanueva study how light bends around a rotating black hole when electromagnetism is nonlinear. Their 2026 paper uses the rotating García-Díaz solution. Here light is not governed by the metric's null cone alone: the field acts as an optical medium, and its constitutive response sets the physical light cones. The team projects the field onto a principal tetrad to rebuild the local response law tied to Maxwell theory.

Inserted into the Fresnel problem, the response splits the quartic into two quadratic branches, each with its own optical metric, a birefringence with no Maxwell analogue. Both branches separate in Carter style, giving separate critical constants and unstable orbit families. On a distant observer's sky, these become two critical contours that coincide in the Maxwell limit and split as the nonlinear response activates. The shadow, in such theories, should be double-edged.
arxiv-2606-20884:
Stephen Kleene proves a decay estimate in a solo 2026 mathematics paper for the stability operator of the helicoid, a classic spiral minimal surface. The setting is a Poisson problem on a vertical strip. The source term is supported on a strip of fixed height. The question is how fast solutions fade away from that support. Natural orthogonality conditions on the source are assumed.

Kleene shows solutions decay at a definite rate away from the support. The stability operator governs whether small deformations grow or shrink. Its behavior shapes how the helicoid responds to perturbations. Decay estimates are technical but powerful. They let later arguments localize effects, treating far regions as negligible. Minimal surface theory relies on such control to pass from local equations to global geometric conclusions about shape and stability under change.
arxiv-2606-21284:
Yoonho Kim, Seongsu Kim, Sungsoo Ahn, and Honghui Kim present MADField in 2026, a model that predicts how gas settles inside nanoporous materials used for storage and separation. Screening such materials needs adsorption equilibrium data, but particle simulations are slow and density-based theory is less accurate. MADField reframes the task as predicting the full density field of the adsorbed gas, learning from both cheaper theory data and scarcer high-fidelity simulation labels.

Uptake accuracy improves sixfold over the best theory baseline and over fifteenfold against simulation labels, and predicted fields also warm-start theory solvers, halving their iterations. Screening 270,000 metal-organic frameworks for methane working capacity, the model ranks candidates so well that checking the top 1.7 percent recovers 95 percent of the rare top performers. Inference runs about five orders of magnitude faster than simulation.
arxiv-2606-21884:
Patel tests, in 2026, a tempting assumption: that any task a short program can solve can also be taught to a language model as a written chain of thought. He built nine reasoning tasks from deterministic generators, reverse-engineered the generators into Python solvers, and distilled their step-by-step procedures into a large open model. Forward-computable tasks installed readily and transferred well.

Cryptarithm, a letter-arithmetic puzzle solved by backtracking search, resisted every attempt. Across eleven chain-of-thought designs, reinforcement learning, and self-training, accuracy stayed between one and seven percent, even though a search solver answers 71 percent of instances. The model did the arithmetic correctly on nearly every line. What it could not do is carry a search forward as a left-to-right derivation. Revealing the cipher key, which removes the search, lifted the same instances from three percent to 57 percent accuracy.
arxiv-2606-22084:
Parikh, Liu, and Wang present Patched Flow Matching in 2026, a method for reconstructing a turbulent flow's full wall-pressure field from very few sensors. Wall pressure spans fine viscous scales and broad outer scales at once, which neither short simulations nor sparse measurements capture alone. Their framework learns a patch-local prior from short-domain simulations and fuses it with sparse sensor readings.

Built patch by patch, the field reconstructs domains far larger than the training setup. Expressing the prior in inner-scaled coordinates lets the method climb to higher Reynolds numbers with as few as five hundred extra snapshots. On compressible channel-flow simulations, it rebuilt full-resolution pressure fields on a domain four times longer than the training one from sensor coverage as low as 0.25 percent of the surface. Zero-shot tests at unseen Reynolds numbers confirmed the approach.
arxiv-2606-22584:
Jouko Väänänen argues a provocative thesis about logic and set theory in this 2026 paper. Second order logic lets quantifiers range over sets and relations, not just individuals, and it is formalized in a second order language. Set theory, by contrast, is written in a first order language, which looks weaker at first glance.

Väänänen argues the appearance is misleading: second order logic is, in a meaningful sense, a weaker form of set theory rather than a rival foundation above it. The argument proceeds historically as much as technically. The paper reviews the long history of interactions between second order logic and set theory, tracing how the two fields borrowed from and reacted against each other. It also surveys modern trends in that relationship. The paper is a perspective piece, aiming to reframe how logicians describe the relative strength of the two frameworks.
arxiv-2606-22984:
Lu Zhong and colleagues build a transformer for spin glasses in a 2026 physics and machine learning paper. A spin glass is a disordered magnet where tiny spins interact through random couplings that frustrate each other. Drawing fair samples from its energy distribution is central to statistical mechanics and hard optimization. Earlier neural samplers gained little from growing larger, unlike language models. They also cost too much on big systems, erasing their edge over classical methods.

Zhong and colleagues design attention that mirrors the physics, with sparse links and position codes tailored to spins. A fast attention method lets them sample whole configurations in parallel. The result runs up to a hundred times faster than earlier autoregressive samplers. It handled record system sizes on one graphics processor. It also recovered full probability distributions, plus free energies and overlap statistics, for standard spin glass models across temperatures.
arxiv-2606-23484:
D. S. Cabral and colleagues develop thermo field dynamics for de Sitter spacetime in a 2026 paper. De Sitter space is the geometry of an expanding universe. The authors study a massive scalar field coupled non-minimally to gravity there. A comoving observer sees the Bunch-Davies state as empty vacuum. A static observer sees that same state as a thermal bath held at the Gibbons-Hawking temperature. That observer dependence motivates a thermal formulation. Thermo Field Dynamics doubles the system, and the paper combines two doublings: the geometric one tied to the horizon and the statistical one of a heat bath.

Cabral and colleagues track the Bogoliubov angle over time and compute particle densities in both frames. In the radiation limit, the comoving density stays conserved, as the cosmic microwave background suggests. In the static frame, thermal effects drive particle creation. The two temperatures together create a characteristic thermal scale.
arxiv-2606-23584:
Jayarajan, Kannan, and Mondal prove new bounds linking the spectrum and coloring of signed graphs, in a 2026 paper on spectral graph theory. A signed graph is an ordinary graph whose edges carry plus or minus signs. Its adjacency matrix records those signs. The spectral radius is the largest eigenvalue magnitude of that matrix. For unsigned graphs, deleting one vertex changes the largest eigenvalue in a controlled way, with a known bound tied to degree. The same claim fails once signs enter.

The authors prove that the bound does hold for the spectral radius of signed graphs. They also revisit coloring bounds. The chromatic number is the fewest colors needed so that adjacent vertices differ. Earlier work extended some classic bounds but stalled on a version using all eigenvalues. This paper supplies a lower bound built from all eigenvalues of the signed graph and its negative edge subgraph.
arxiv-2606-23684:
Ueda, Numasawa, De Vos, and Watanabe show how a purely structural lattice defect can mimic a famous reflection effect, in a 2026 paper on quantum physics. In Andreev reflection, an electron hits a superconductor. It bounces back as a hole, its antimatter like counterpart. Meanwhile a pair enters the superconductor. The same math appears in impurity and monopole problems with no superconductor in sight. What mechanism unites them?

From a Majorana description of a magnetic chain, the authors build a folded lattice where a boundary impurity shifts a staggered chain by one site. In the continuum limit that shift flips the sign of one moving Majorana mode. Recombined into an ordinary fermion, the flip is exactly the Andreev boundary condition itself. The picture gives a small scale account of classic impurity physics. It identifies the boundary as an interface between a topological phase and a gapless chain.
arxiv-2606-23784:
Ransome and a large team introduce a survey designed to shadow the coming Legacy Survey of Space and Time. Their 2026 paper also reports its first study, of a restless variable star. The Shadow Survey uses the Dark Energy Camera to watch galaxy cluster fields nightly, in step with the main survey. It aims to catch extremely young supernovae and precursor eruptions at unmatched cadence and depth. The paper describes the survey's workflow, pipeline, and candidate vetting.

Its first result follows AT 2017des, a luminous blue variable in a Virgo cluster galaxy. The star erupts on roughly ten day timescales, peaking brighter than normal variables of its class. Spectra resemble supernova impostors, stars whose eruptions mimic true explosions. Long baseline records show the peaks growing brighter, reaching five times their earlier flux.
arxiv-2606-24184:
Morgunov and Batista reframe planning a chemical synthesis as writing text under instructions. Retrosynthesis works backward from a target molecule to buyable starting materials. Classical planners search step by step with single-reaction models. Constrained searches, such as demanding a set route depth or a required starting material, usually need specialised algorithms. Their 2026 generator, Ariadne, instead places target, constraints, and route inside one prompt-and-completion sequence for a decoder-only model.

One trained checkpoint follows the prompt fields. Adding a depth constraint or a required starting material sharply raises the share of routes that satisfy it. Against DESP, a bidirectional search planner, Ariadne wins on required-starting-material measures. It also runs in minutes rather than hours of GPU time. On ordinary reconstruction it matches a leading competitor at about half the inference time. Gains are clearest on route-holdout tests, where whole routes were withheld.
arxiv-2606-24384:
Ortega and colleagues model whether radiation dose meters stay truthful at the extreme dose rates of FLASH radiotherapy. FLASH delivery, tens of grays per second, spares normal tissue while controlling tumours. The ionisation chambers that verify dose were designed for gentler beams, though. In air-vented plane-parallel chambers, ions recombine before collection, and the charge cloud itself distorts the field. Both grow vicious at ultra-high dose rates.

A self-consistent Monte Carlo model, built with the Garfield++ toolkit, simulates charge collection efficiency. Space-charge effects and ion recombination are included together, rather than corrected for each in isolation. Self-consistency matters. The drifting charges reshape the very field that moves them. The 2026 model, developed at the Université libre de Bruxelles, gives FLASH researchers a physics-based way to predict chamber response. There, the classical recombination corrections, derived for conventional dose rates, can no longer be trusted.
arxiv-2606-24484:
Ye and colleagues tackle reading text that was designed to be looked at, not read by machines. WordArt, artistic text with custom fonts, textures, and layouts, breaks ordinary scene text recognition. Its datasets and fixed template models assume regular lettering. Their 2026 effort advances the task from both the data and model sides at once.

A two million image synthetic dataset dwarfs earlier artistic text resources, by hundreds of times. One subset comes from an upgraded rendering pipeline, giving accurate, controllable WordArt. The other mines prompts with a vision language model, and makes images for real range. The companion recogniser pairs a visual encoder accepting arbitrary shaped inputs with an autoregressive decoder. The decoder models complex layouts directly, breaking the fixed template bottleneck. Tests show the design beating prior scene text methods on artistic material. Ye's team frames data scale and shape freedom as the twin keys to reading WordArt.
arxiv-2606-24884:
Maggie Wang and five Stanford colleagues present InSight, a framework that lets robot policies teach themselves new skills. Vision language action models learn manipulation from demonstrations, but only the skills those demonstrations contain. InSight makes such a model steerable at the level of primitive actions: move the gripper to the bowl, lift upward, then pour the bottle. Two stages make this work.

First, a pipeline segments demonstrations into labelled primitives, using a vision language model to decompose plans and end effector poses to cut boundaries. That data fine tunes the policy for steerability. Second, a data flywheel spots primitives a task needs but the policy lacks. The system attempts them under model proposed control, then labels and integrates the successes into training. Skills like block flipping, sweeping, and pouring are acquired with no human demonstrations of them. Learned primitives then compose into long horizon tasks, Wang and colleagues report.
arxiv-2606-25384:
Classical commutative algebra leans on the Noetherian assumption that chains of ideals stop growing, but modern applications include rings where they do not. Ryoya Ando studies Cohen-Macaulay style properties for such rings in 2026, using the Hamilton and Marley definition built on polynomial grade. Two basic operations are put to the test: adjoining a variable, and localising, which means focusing on one prime ideal at a time. Both behave politely in the standard theory.

Ando shows the good behaviour can fail for polynomial extensions in general, then rescues it where rings are stably coherent with finite weak global dimension. A claimed strengthening in an earlier reference falls to an explicit counterexample. The final part characterises exactly when localisation keeps modules torsion free, using regular saturation, total fraction rings, and a special class of prime ideals.
arxiv-2606-25684:
Model predictive control steers a system by repeatedly solving for the best future moves, then applying only the first. Sebastian Steffen and Mark Cannon, at Oxford, tackle a guarantee gap in 2026 for robust nonlinear control that uses separate learned predictors for each future step. Such multi step models simplify the maths, but predictions made at different times can clash, and the optimisation can suddenly have no feasible answer at all. Single step schemes carry classical guarantees against that failure; naive multi step ones do not.

Their fix checks ahead for possible infeasibility of the robust problem. When trouble looms, the controller falls back on previously verified reachable sets, sets of states already proven safe to occupy. A predictor substitution strategy swaps the offending model for the certified fallback. A small numerical example shows the machinery working, restoring the recursive feasibility and stability assurances that safety critical control demands.
arxiv-2606-25784:
Mixing two photos together trains image models to generalise, but the blend scrambles both pictures' meanings. Khawar Islam, Arif Mahmood, Xin Jin, and Naveed Akhtar keep augmentation inside a single image in 2026. Their self saliency mixup cuts out the most informative patches of a picture, at several scales, and pastes them into its own dull regions. The label stays truthful, nothing foreign enters, and the model learns features that survive changes of scale. A second scheme, FracMix, stirs fractal self similarity patterns into the salient regions at adaptive ratios, adding structured complexity.

The unified framework lets one image teach both its ordinary and fractal structure at once. The authors analyse the advantage theoretically, then test widely: seven benchmarks spanning coarse and fine grained classification, robustness, calibration, detection, and transfer learning. The method reached state of the art results across that sweep, without the computational overhead of cross sample mixing.
arxiv-2606-25984:
Mingguang Chen builds a benchmark that tests whether language models can think like expert investors. Models increasingly help with investment research. Yet no test checks whether they can rebuild a named investor's decision framework and apply it faithfully. InvestPhilBench fills that gap. Its tasks span eight tiers of difficulty. The lowest tier asks for principle identification. The highest asks for extending a framework to new ground.

Materials come from primary sources only. The release holds 118 verified principle cards and 25 framework cards. It also holds 243 questions, split between a development set and a held-out test set. Scoring runs through an automated pipeline with five metrics. A failure-mode protocol flags six computable error patterns. A small four-model study shows a sharp split between provider tiers. The composite score saturates at the frontier, while a per-gate accuracy metric still separates strong models.
arxiv-2606-26084:
Sudip Chakrabarty, Bivas Mallick, Ananda Maity, and A. S. Majumdar build practical tests for Wigner negativity. A negative Wigner function marks a quantum state as truly nonclassical. Such states power quantum advantage in light-based systems. Full tomography can find the negativity, but it costs too much. Their tests need only a few copies of the state.

Constraints on positive phase-space distributions generate the criteria. Three families of tests emerge: Hankel-matrix checks, norm inequalities, and log-convexity relations. Together they form a ladder of stronger and stronger witnesses. An exact formula rewrites each Wigner moment as a parity-based observable, so labs can measure the moments directly. Simulations of randomized measurements and classical shadows show the scheme working. The same tools also spot entanglement between two or more parties.
arxiv-2606-26284:
C. Zhang reports the making of a light-boosting lining for a neutrino detector. The Short-Baseline Near Detector at Fermilab is a liquid argon chamber that reads particle tracks from ionization and scintillation light. More light, evenly spread, means better triggers and sharper reconstruction. Sixty-four double-sided plates now line its cathode. Each plate stacks fibreboard, mirror film, and a coating of tetraphenyl butadiene, a shifter that converts invisible ultraviolet scintillation into visible light.

Production needed care at every step. Physical vapor deposition laid the shifter down evenly, and mass plus surface-profile checks verified the coat. Blue and ultraviolet room light can degrade the shifter, so filtered handling and controlled storage guarded the plates. Meshes around the assembly keep it compatible with the cathode's high voltage. The coated area is the largest of its kind in a neutrino detector. Early measurements show uniform, strong light response.
arxiv-2606-26484:
Ji Qiang presents a fast solver for space-charge effects in particle accelerators. Space charge is the mutual repulsion of particles inside a dense beam. In high-intensity machines it grows the beam, forms halos, and loses particles. Tracking many particles is the standard study method. Full three-dimensional solvers are accurate but slow, especially for long beam bunches.

Qiang's solver is two-and-a-half dimensional and symplectic. Symplectic means it preserves the geometry that keeps long simulations physically faithful. He first derives a semi-analytical formula for a smooth beam shape in open space. The solver then adapts to arbitrary beam shapes. It also handles beams inside rectangular and round conducting pipes. Finally, he extends it to circular accelerator layouts. Tests show the fast solver closely matches the full three-dimensional one for long bunches. That makes it practical for large circular machines.
arxiv-2606-26684:
Jana Schulz introduces the non-forgetting model of parallel communicating finite automata. Such systems team several small automata together. Each can ask another for its current state. In the classical model, asking makes the asker forget its own state. The new model lets automata keep their state while querying, a more realistic behaviour.

Schulz compares the computing power of many variants. Most non-forgetting variants match multi-head finite automata exactly, in both deterministic and nondeterministic cases, when the counts of automata and heads agree. One special case breaks the pattern: deterministic centralised systems in non-returning mode sit strictly below their counterpart. Proving that exception also completed a proof left open in earlier work. The results answer questions for the new model that remain open for the classical forgetting one.
arxiv-2606-27284:
Meng and colleagues study how gay dating app users in China spot and handle deception. Such apps offer vital meeting spaces where social acceptance stays limited, yet they also host rich deceit. Interviews with twenty-two users across platforms including Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul ground the study. The practices form a typology reaching beyond fake profiles. Relational, emotional, financial, and commercial forms all appear in this interview study of 2026 of grassroots safety knowledge.

Trust judgements turn out layered and probabilistic, not binary. Users weigh multiple signals over time, treating each verdict as provisional. Risk recognition is also collaborative: experiences circulate, tactics get abstracted, and shared rules get codified by the community. Long platform use builds that collective craft. Semi-closeted status heightens vulnerability to exploitation throughout. Designers of dating platforms inherit clear lessons about supporting community-grown verification habits rather than ignoring them.
arxiv-2606-27384:
Black describes a pipeline that digests published papers into a shared, queryable knowledge base. Published papers hold validated measurements in clashing formats and vocabularies. The Materials Explorer Pipeline extracts structured records from those papers, each carrying its measurements, source details, and a confidence score. Records stay portable and citable, so other scientists can build on them directly. Interactive browsing surfaces correlations and candidate hypotheses for expert review in this systems paper of 2026.

A test on recent superconducting qubit papers yields a corpus of two hundred thirty-three samples spanning ten material classes. The sources come from a national quantum research centre's community. Papers stop being a pile of PDFs and become a database. Cross-group comparison and hypothesis testing gain the shared resource they lacked. Extraction quality, not access, becomes the bottleneck.
