arxiv-2606-27584:
Filling in missing parts of a three-dimensional scene is hard when damage or narrow viewpoints hide whole regions. Hana Kim, Minje Kim, and Tae-Kyun Kim present CoIn in 2026. CoIn repairs scenes by passing information back and forth. One side is flat image editing. The other side is a 3D representation built with Gaussian splatting, a fast format of soft coloured blobs.

CoIn first paints content into the damaged images. A diffusion model does the painting, and diffusion models build pictures from noise. This allows masks of any shape. It also allows tasks beyond removal, including inserting new objects. A reference-aware reconstruction then builds a 3D scene. The scene is weighted toward one trusted view. It guides the image editor so all viewpoints agree. A final step sharpens texture and realism. In experiments, CoIn reached the best performance on both removal and insertion, while keeping views consistent.
arxiv-2606-27684:
Recommender systems increasingly reason with large language models. One style reasons in latent space, using hidden vectors instead of words. Such reasoning often starts from an unconstrained point. The start may sit far from the target item, and the path then wanders. Chang Liu and six colleagues propose IntuRec in 2026 to anchor the start. Their idea borrows from cognitive neuroscience, where intuition guides human reasoning.

IntuRec works in two stages. First, the recommender generates a top candidate set from the user's history. That set serves as the source of intuition. Second, attention turns the set into a preference-aligned embedding. The embedding initialises the latent reasoning start point. Later reasoning steps are guided from that grounded start. Experiments on several real-world datasets followed. IntuRec consistently beat state-of-the-art baselines, the authors report. The work was presented at the KDD 2026 conference.
arxiv-2606-27784:
Adversarial attacks fool neural networks through non-robust features. Earlier defences prune, mask, or recalibrate those features. Taïga Gonçalves and three colleagues take a different route in 2026. Their plug-in module, A3, learns to scale activation signals up or down. The scaling needs few added parameters. It can be inserted into networks with minimal changes.

A learnable mask and a factor read from the signals themselves set each scale. Flipping one sign switches between the two modes. In the up mode, signals are amplified. In the down mode, they are attenuated. The amplified outputs serve as negative references for new contrastive and ranking losses. Experiments expose a useful coupling. Training the model to fail on amplified signals makes it more robust on attenuated ones. Across backbones, datasets, and training methods, robustness improved consistently. Added compute and memory costs stayed negligible next to rival plug-in defences.
arxiv-2606-28084:
Renormalisation group equations govern how coupling constants run with energy. A. S. Fedoruk and D. I. Kazakov construct simple analytical solutions in 2026 for two Standard Model couplings. They are the strong coupling and the top quark Yukawa coupling. The solutions hold in the asymptotic regime. They have explicit form, containing only logarithms and no special functions. Leading and subleading logarithms are summed to all orders of perturbation theory.

The two couplings influence each other asymmetrically. The top Yukawa coupling's effect on the running of the strong coupling is negligible. The strong coupling's effect on the top Yukawa coupling is essential. Higher orders give a noticeable contribution there. Getting elementary formulas required neglecting terms that are inessential in the asymptotic regime. The strategy can be pushed further, the authors note. Summing further series with changed arguments improves the approximation. Such closed forms make the running transparent without numerical integration.
arxiv-2606-28584:
Fábio Amaral, Geovani N. Grapiglia, and Cassio M. Oishi teach a data-driven modeling method to ignore bad data. Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics builds a compact governing equation from measurements by sparse regression. But noise and outliers poison the fit, and standard pipelines treat every observation as equally trustworthy.

Their pipeline separates cleaning from modeling. A least-trimmed-squares stage first sums only the smallest squared residuals, again and again, to pick out the most trustworthy observations without being told which points are corrupt. A thresholded regression then recovers a lean model from the survivors. Across tests with varying amounts of bad data, the method clearly beat current robust variants. It held up even when a fifth of the observations were corrupted, a regime where dynamics learning usually falls apart.
arxiv-2606-28884:
Tu and many colleagues introduce GigaSpeechBench, a benchmark for speech recognition drawn from real-world recordings, not clean studio audio. Modern systems post low error rates on high-resource test sets, yet those numbers flatter them in daily conditions. The benchmark holds 680 hours of human-annotated speech. It stresses the weak spots: dialects, accents, age variation, specialist words and languages with little training data.

Five modules organise the material. One covers low-resource languages of the Middle East and South-East Asia, plus Japanese and Korean. Others cover six Chinese dialects and six English accents. A fourth holds dense terms across twelve domains in Chinese and English. The last holds speech from older adults and children. Human translations support speech translation tests for eleven languages. Evaluating leading foundation models and commercial services, the team found performance dropped sharply in these settings. Those gaps expose blind spots that standard benchmarks hide.
arxiv-2606-28984:
Spivak builds one compositional framework in which machine learning and classical mechanics appear as two readings of the same diagrams. Compositional means big systems are wired from smaller ones, with the whole's behaviour assembled from the parts. His syntax is an operad, a formal system for plugging interfaces together, whose pieces pair input-output interfaces with a reactive parameter space, smooth input and output maps, and a real-valued potential.

The key result is lens internalisation, a functor that turns lens-like descriptions into systems inside any suitable category. Two translations follow. One stores position and momentum; the other stores position only. Applied to a parameterised function, the position-only reading recovers gradient descent training, with backpropagation as the backward pass. Applied to harmonic particles wired on a graph, the two readings give the wave and heat equations from one diagram. Both compile to state machines that can run.
arxiv-2606-29084:
Kimiaei proposes a derivative-free method for minimising rough, nonsmooth functions when gradients are unavailable or unreliable. The method builds discrete gradients from function values alone, sampling enough points to form a model of the Goldstein subdifferential, a generalised gradient for such functions. The smallest element of that sampled set serves both as a measure of near-optimality and as the reference for building descent directions.

To go beyond plain steepest descent, the method adds a matrix memory correction, curving the search using past steps. Coefficient damping, diagonal scaling, a bounded-angle correction and stability safeguards help too. A two-point line search accepts a serious step or enriches the local model. Under stated assumptions, the method computes approximate stationary points. In tests up to a thousand dimensions, the matrix variant stayed most reliable at the strictest tolerance.
arxiv-2606-29584:
Polat and three colleagues improve machine-learned interatomic potentials, models that predict the forces between atoms for molecular simulation. Potentials built on geometric algebra predict force magnitudes well but force directions poorly. The cause lies in the structure: the geometric product of two vectors supplies only part of the mathematical content, leaving a rank-two piece missing from every message-passing layer.

Their model, CliffordSTF, couples the Clifford multivector with symmetric-traceless tensor tracks in closed form, at ranks two and three. A learned bilinear form connects the tracks, with no Clebsch-Gordan tables or Wigner matrices needed. On the rMD17 benchmark, force direction accuracy jumps by an order of magnitude over the base Clifford model, while force and energy errors fall. On catalysis datasets, it attains the best out-of-distribution energy error in their study. An ablation over eleven variants confirms the two tracks complement each other.
arxiv-2606-29984:
Peng and eleven colleagues tackle a failure mode of reinforcement learning for vision-language models: reasoning that reads fluently but ignores the image, leaning on language habits instead. Their fix is to steer the model into a faithful regime before reinforcement learning begins.

The Faithful Warm-Start strategy first builds FaithfulQA, a dataset drawn from six visual question answering benchmarks where each item spells out its visual observations, question requirements, background knowledge, and answer. A model judge then purifies the dataset. Training on this data teaches causally grounded vision-language patterns. Experiments show the warm start improves answer accuracy, stabilises the later reinforcement learning under sparse rewards, and cuts reasoning that the image does not support.
arxiv-2606-30484:
Giorgio Maria Cavallazzi, Miguel Pérez Cuadrado, and Alfredo Pinelli show that a neural flow estimator can be superb on recorded data yet wreck the control loop it feeds. Opposition control cuts skin-friction drag in turbulence. It needs velocity readings above the wall. Wall sensors cannot measure it directly. A recurrent estimator infers it from wall shear stress.

Offline, the estimator is excellent on fixed flow data. Correlation reaches zero point nine nine with near-unity coherence. Inside the loop, it fails within moments. The controller shifts the flow off its training distribution. Small errors push the flow away from the learned attractor. Filtering and averaging only postpone the breakdown. They even accelerate the decorrelation from the true field. Retraining on the estimator's own closed-loop data fixes it. Spectral consistency on actuation completes the fix. Much of the ideal drag reduction survives with wall data alone.
arxiv-2606-30884:
Yongbo Chen, Yan Zhu and Rebecca Faust ask how programmers debug data-intensive workflows. In such work, code runs over large datasets through many stages. Visual debugging tools exist, but most research targets traditional software. Data work stays uncharacterised. The trio interviewed nine practitioners from varied data-intensive fields. They read the transcripts for shared themes, hunting for problems that visuals could ease.

Three challenges cut across the interviews. Evidence lies scattered across artefacts, and assembling it is hard. Spotting where behaviour departs from what was expected is hard too. So is tracing how state evolves across workflow stages. Each challenge maps to a need that current debuggers meet only partly. Tools should align evidence across artefacts. They should compare behaviour against expectations. And they should make state evolution traceable.
arxiv-2606-31084:
Feng and five colleagues speed up a costly tool inside VVenC, the reference encoder for the Versatile Video Coding standard. The tool, Merge with Motion Vector Difference, refines a block's motion by trying many direction and distance offsets, which improves prediction but makes the encoder search exhaustively and slowly. Their goal is to skip candidates that cannot pay off.

The team approximates the encoder's 8-tap interpolation filter with a 2-tap version and derives a criterion from spatial gradients and prediction residuals that estimates each candidate's likely gain. Implementation tricks, including symmetric offset inference and a cross-shaped downsampled dot product, keep the added cost tiny. Against existing fast methods, their algorithm cuts the average search ratio from 21.07 percent to 11.05 percent.
arxiv-2606-31184:
Li and Simchi-Levi ask whether a transformer can run adaptive experiments for average treatment effects on its own. Good designs assign treatments by a Neyman rule that depends on unknown outcome variances for each arm. Their Bayesian in-context experimenter is a transformer trained to copy a Bayesian teacher that updates beliefs from trial history.

The teacher's rule converges to the oracle design, and the transformer rebuilds that updating with attention-based summary statistics and projected gradient steps. Unknown smoothness is handled by a mixture-of-experts version whose gate acts like a posterior over smoothness classes. Bounds on the transformer class show the policy can be learned by supervised pretraining, and experiments confirm close teacher imitation plus sharper treatment effect estimates than baselines.
arxiv-2606-31384:
Fu and two colleagues study decentralized online estimation when the messages between nodes carry noise. Each node in a fixed directed network measures an unknown parameter and runs its own estimator in continuous time. No central point exists, so the nodes must reach agreement through noisy links alone.

The team turn the convergence question into a stability question for a stochastic differential equation with random, time-varying coefficients. Gains can be set so the estimates converge in mean square, as long as the measurements and the graph are jointly rich enough over time and space. A special case where the measurement matrices follow a Markov chain is worked out, and a numerical example confirms the theory.
arxiv-2606-31484:
Al-Khalili and three colleagues propose Fork-Think, a cheaper way for language models to reason in parallel. Parallel thinking samples many reasoning paths and then picks among them, which wastes tokens on paths that were never promising. Fork-Think flips the order: decide first where branching is worthwhile, then think.

A single seeding path is scanned for forking points, spots where model confidence marks a meaningful choice. Sampling then branches only at those points, and the continuations are aggregated into the final answer. Across three models and three reasoning benchmarks, token use falls by up to 30 percent and runtime by up to 57 percent, with quality matching or beating parallel thinking. Later forking points often yield better generations than early ones.
arxiv-2606-31684:
Kheirabadi and Shokri calculate how stretching bilayer graphene changes its nonlinear optical response when the two valleys of its electronic structure are unequally populated. In balanced bilayer graphene the second-order response cancels between valleys, so no second-harmonic generation, the doubling of light frequency, appears. Valley polarization breaks that cancellation.

Using a low-energy Hamiltonian with trigonal warping and strain-induced anisotropy inside a quantum kinetic calculation, the pair find a strongly directional second-harmonic spectrum. It has resonant enhancements at photon energies near the Fermi energy and twice it. These are tied to two-photon and one-photon interband transitions. Flipping the sign of the strain reverses the induced second-harmonic current, giving a mechanical switch for nonlinear optical transport and a route toward tunable mid-infrared valley devices.
arxiv-2606-31784:
Farrell and three others derive continuum equations for nematic liquid crystals from kinetic theory, now including viscosity and heat flow. Nematic fluids consist of rod-like molecules with shared orientation. Earlier kinetic derivations produced only inviscid Leslie-Ericksen type models, and they imposed alignment rather than letting it emerge.

Starting from a kinetic theory of ordered fluids with a BGK collision operator and mean-field alignment, the team separates fast orientational relaxation from slower momentum relaxation. Chapman-Enskog expansions at two orders yield the free energy form and the entropy production structure. A constrained maximisation step then fixes the stress, couple-stress and flux laws. Both compressible and incompressible versions of the thermal viscous theory are given.
arxiv-2606-31884:
Marin, Padhiar and Shillito give intuitionistic justification logic a semantics, where before it had only syntax. Justification logic refines modal boxes into explicit proof or evidence terms. The intuitionistic version adds satisfier terms for native diamonds, which cannot be defined from boxes intuitionistically. A proof-theoretic realisation theorem already linked it to intuitionistic modal logic.

Two classes of models are added. Basic modular models extend possible-world semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic. Richer modular models add Kripke-style machinery that keeps the semantics backwards compatible with modal logic. Soundness and completeness are proved for both classes. Using the modular models, the authors then establish a semantic realisation theorem, completing the bridge to the underlying modal system.
arxiv-2608-00184:
Schlitt studies sums of a random multiplicative function with periodic weights. A Steinhaus random multiplicative function f supplies the randomness. A one-periodic function g of bounded variation supplies the weights. An irrational number alpha scales the argument of g. He studies the distribution of the weighted sums up to N.

He finds a necessary and sufficient condition for Gaussian limits. Normalized by standard deviation, the sums converge to the standard complex Gaussian under it. A second result restricts summands by prime factor size. When all prime factors exceed z, and z grows slowly, a central limit theorem always holds. Readers get sharp limit laws for a delicate random sum.
arxiv-2608-00284:
Moraes and co-authors present a hybrid attention pipeline for human-robot interaction. Their case study uses an expressive robotic head from the InMoov ecosystem. One layer is fast and geometric in form. It gives high-frequency face and head-pose data for timing control. A second layer is semantic, built on a vision-language model.

The semantic layer sees only raw camera frames from the robot. It labels attention toward the robot, phone use, or attention elsewhere. A finite state machine merges both signal streams. It governs activation, waiting, resumption, and return to rest. Ten participants ran 40 trials across baseline and adaptive conditions. Interaction starts were reliable in every trial. Pause behaviour in the distraction condition was consistent. The two layers carried non-redundant information, they report.
arxiv-2608-00484:
Visentin and co-authors tune soft robotic reservoirs to match digital ones. Soft bodies suit reservoir computing: their springy motion gives memory and rich state changes. Such bodies are used as-is, though, with no pretraining or tuning. That may cap their scores next to digital reservoirs. This study asks if a soft reservoir can be pretrained to mimic strong digital dynamics.

The scheme tunes body settings, a state map, and control laws at once. A model you can differentiate and an equation-error score avoid step-by-step simulation. Test robots are soft bots trained against a network of random oscillators. Many restarts of gradient descent do the tuning. On sort and forecast tasks, tuned reservoirs beat untuned ones by 33.7 percent on average. They also stayed near the digital target.
bailly-rapport-commissaires-magnetisme-a:
In 1784 the French king set a royal commission to test Mesmer's animal magnetism. Jean-Sylvain Bailly drafted its report, and Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier, and Joseph Guillotin were among its signers. The commission ran careful trials, blindfolding patients and swapping magnetized objects for plain ones.

The verdict was firm. No fluid could be found, and the effects came from imagination alone. The report is a landmark of scientific testing, a debunking carried out with wit and rigor. It did not end mesmerism, but it set the standard for judging such claims. Enlightenment reason speaks here at its most decisive.
beal-buddhist-records-western-world-vol1:
Samuel Beal translated the Si-yu-ki, the record of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's journey to India, as Buddhist Records of the Western World. Volume one appeared in 1884. Xuanzang traveled from 629 to 645, crossing Central Asia to study at the great Indian monasteries.

The record describes kingdoms, roads, relics, and monasteries of seventh-century Asia in a pilgrim's faithful detail. Xuanzang names the doctrines he heard, the stupas he worshipped at, and the rulers who fed his party. Historians of India and China alike mine Beal's volumes for facts found nowhere else. Beal's notes name modern places for the pilgrim's ancient stops.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-53:
The February 1843 Blackwood's leads with Arnold's Lectures on History, mourning Dr. Arnold of Rugby lately dead. His premature loss to the literature of his country, the reviewer says, the volume proves almost irreparable. Schiller's poems and ballads reach their fifth number, Reynolds's Discourses their second part, and Landor stages Oliver Cromwell against Sir Oliver Cromwell in an imaginary conversation.

Caleb Stukely walks through part eleven with his comic miseries. One Mr. Thompson, we learn, holds that Satan took advantage of his Sabbath absence and drew his wife to chapel, making her a dissenter. Thompson calls it severer punishment than ever was inflicted for Sabbath-breaking. Eyre's Cabul and the evacuation of Afghanistan bring the Afghan disaster home, and the World of London continues its second series among the upholsterers and ale-houses.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-54:
November 1843 in Blackwood's rides first to Texas. Adventures in Texas asks if the reader was ever in a Texian prairie. The answer comes with a land-scrip: a paper from the Galveston Bay and Texas Land Company, come to a young man one fine morning. The scamper in the prairie of Jacinto follows. Travels of Kerim Khan, the Wrongs of Women, Ceylon, and Marston's tale fill the body of the number.

Storm takes the sampled pages. A whole crowd rushes forward, clashing pikes and muskets. Cannon worked by deserters from the royal troops join in. The Marseillais — galley-slaves and port ruffians — lead the attack. The palace windows cease firing at once, promising sure success. A piece on the senses, a banking-house tale, and a scheme for joining the Atlantic and Pacific by trade round out the number.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-55:
February 1844 in Blackwood's opens with the Heretic. Next it sends Alexandre Dumas thrush-hunting, in a piece turned from the French. High Life in the Last Century recalls the grand world gone by. The Prophecy of the Twelve Tribes looks forward, and Marston's tale reaches part eight. The split from the Church of Scotland — the Disruption's late shock — gets its hearing. The Land of Slaves and a free-trade debate close the state papers.

A soldier's memoir gives the sampled scene. Varnhorst, who did everything and was everywhere, shakes the returned officer's hand. French light horse has slipped between the foot columns in the night, picking up stragglers. The duke, with whom the writer stands in favour, must be warned. A sitting for a portrait, a lament from Bath for poor old maids, and Prudence fill out the number.
blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-volume-61:
February 1847 gives Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine number CCCLXXVI, volume LXI, printed in Edinburgh for the Blackwood house. By then the monthly was a fixed part of British reading life, blending memoir, history, fiction, and fiscal debate. Its pieces appear unsigned in the house manner.

Samuel Warren opens with a memoir of John William Smith, a barrister of the Inner Temple cut off before age thirty-seven. Essays follow on modern Italian history, French players and playhouses, and the reign of George the Second. Fiction comes with Mildred, a tale, and lighter verse includes The Early Taken. A ride to Magnesia supplies the travel writing. A closing argument on direct taxation weighs how the state should raise its revenue, giving the number a practical end.
bovet-pandaemonium-english-1684:
Richard Bovet published Pandaemonium, or the Devil's Cloyster, in 1684. The title page promises a further blow to modern Sadducism, the age's word for doubting spirits. Bovet wrote as Joseph Glanvill's popular successor in the English war for belief in the invisible world.

Apparition stories and witchcraft cases pile up as his evidence. Each tale is told with gusto and offered as proof that spirits walk among us. Bovet presses ghost stories into the service of theology. Doubters, he argues, will end by doubting God himself. The book shows popular print defending the spirit world with narrative firepower rather than dry argument.
britten-nineteenth-century-miracles-1884:
Emma Hardinge Britten swept the globe for marvels in Nineteenth Century Miracles, her vast book of 1884. Her faith held that the dead speak and heal in her age. She set out to prove it with tales from land past land, faith past faith, town past town.

Each part gives names, dates, and sworn tales of cures and ghosts. The sheer bulk is her case. She meant the book as a store of proof no foe could shrug off. It is the faith's world tour in one tome. She knew the chief names of the faith at first hand in her tours. That close reach gives her vast claims a weight mere hearsay lacks.
bruno-de-infinito-1584:
Giordano Bruno wrote these talks in Italian in 1584, while he lived in London. The full title speaks of the vast whole, the world, and the worlds. Bruno held that the stars are suns with worlds of their own. The Church later burned him at the stake in Rome.

Five talks pit Bruno's voice against men who cling to the old closed cosmos. He says space has no edge and no core point. Earth is one world among a vast host of worlds. The book is a root text for the claim that life fills the sky.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol1-1:
Thomas Burnet's Sacred Theory of the Earth reached English readers in 1684. Volume one holds the two first books of his four part theory. The first book treats the Deluge, the second treats Paradise, the Earth as it first was. Burnet pictures the young Earth as smooth, fair, and without seas or mountains.

The Flood, in his telling, cracked that smooth shell and drowned the world. Ruined fragments of the crust became our mountains and ocean beds. The work founded modern catastrophist cosmology, Earth history by great sudden blows. Its grand style won readers across Europe for a century. The English translation spread the theory widely. Few books shaped early geology so much.
cavendish-experiments-on-air-1784:
Henry Cavendish, a rich and shy English scholar, read these papers on air in 1784 and 1785. He was famed for the care and truth of his trials. His work bore on the great fight over phlogiston that then split chemistry. Few trials of that age can match his for care, and few men hid from fame as he did.

Cavendish joined two gases with a spark and got pure water, weight for weight. The result showed water is a compound, not a base stuff as men had long held. He also wrote back to Kirwan in the same work. The proof shook the old scheme hard.
cia-0000009784:
Loc Ninh district, in Binh Long province, is named in a July 1973 report on an American pilot's death. Loc Ninh, near the Cambodian border in South Vietnam, saw heavy fighting in 1972. Pilots lost over the south were fewer than in the north, but their cases ran just as long.

A death in the south could be checked against nearby bases, witnesses, and graves more easily than in the north. Even so, this report came months after American combat ended. It shows southern losses still being documented in the postwar accounting. The pilot's case joined the record with district and province attached.
cia-0000011484:
France was fighting to hold its North African empire in 1958, and a CIA paper that June tracked events in Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco. Algeria's war for freedom had already run for years and was tearing French politics apart. Tunisia and Morocco had won independence in 1956, yet France still held great sway over both.

The paper follows the fighting in Algeria and the pressure on Paris from all sides. General de Gaulle had just returned to power in France as the crisis deepened. The study captures an empire in its last years and a region being remade by nationalist revolt.
cia-0000012284:
Developments concerning a blacked-out subject are tracked in a CIA note from July 1961. The note belongs to the Penkovsky file's moving stream of progress reports. As the operation matured that summer, officers logged each turn: meetings held, material received, and risks weighed and answered in turn.

Only the outline survives the censor's pen; names and places do not. Even so, the note shows the rhythm of a case reporting on itself at regular beats. For readers, it is a pulse reading from the operation's busiest season, when the paper trail grew with every turn of events.
cia-0000012384:
Chalk lines on a pavement and a dead drop in a hollow place anchor an undated diagram, its year estimated as 1960. The plan lays out where marking signals should be placed and how drops should be served. Diagrams like this were the working drawings of covert action. In their way they are as precise as any engineer's plans for a bridge.

The sheet belongs to the Penkovsky era's tradecraft, when signals and drops carried a colonel's secrets across Moscow. Its lines and labels map an operation's geometry on paper. For readers, it is the blueprint layer of espionage, rarely preserved.
cia-0000013784:
American prisoners were believed held in a jail in the center of Hanoi. A CIA paper from September 1966 records that view and weighs it. The belief came from the early accounting's fragments: sightings, reports, and inference. The analysts labeled their picture honestly as a view, not a certainty. The capital's prisons were closed to any outside eye. Their inmate lists were guarded as state secrets by Hanoi's government.

The paper weighs the prisoners' likely places in the city's heart. The 1966 picture was fragmentary, but the fragments pointed to the system taking shape. For readers, it is the first map of the missing, drawn while the war was young.
cia-0000014784: Labor's reactions to May Day 1954 and the September 1953 elections in Portugal fill a CIA file dated June 3, 1954. The file also reaches further, the title notes, beyond its first topics. Portugal then lived under a strict right wing regime. Reading its workers' mood mattered to a Washington that prized stable allies.
cia-0000015384: Match magazine carried an article on a UFO sighting, in a CIA file dated February 1, 1956. The title adds that Mars will enter the story, clipped mid thought. A French magazine's saucer piece joined the clipping file that winter. Foreign press on saucers was read in Washington as a gauge of the fever abroad.
cia-0000015484: Leon Davidson's letter gets another staff workup in an untitled CIA record dated in 1958, with a memo attached. The memo is dated July 25, 1958, in the clipped code of the title. Davidson wrote so often that his mail drew set handling inside the agency. The attached memo shows readers passing his words along with their own remarks added.
cia-0000026784: Prospects in South Vietnam are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1962. American advisers were then arriving in growing numbers to help President Diem's government fight the Viet Cong. A prospects paper had to judge troops, politics, and morale together. From 1962 the road ran to full American war within three years, which darkens every line of such a forecast.
cia-0000028284: Probable developments in Iran through 1955 are forecast in a CIA paper dated in 1954. Iran had just come through the 1953 coup that restored the Shah's full power. A forecast past that shock had to judge oil, the army, and a shaken public mood. The paper's horizon, 1955, shows planners working one careful year at a time. The new order rested on the army, the court, and oil income paid under fresh terms.
cia-0000046484: Ross Perot, the Texas businessman who campaigned for American prisoners, clashed with officials over a report of prisoners in Laos. A CIA item dated July 2, 1980, kept the story. Perot had spent his own money on the cause since the war years. The item preserves a public fight over who spoke for the missing.
cia-0000048984: Gunfire and explosions broke up Archbishop Romero's funeral in 1980 and sent mourners fleeing in a stampede. This CIA item holds the file on that day, kept with the Truth Commission records. The attack on a funeral crowd became one of the civil war's most shaming scenes, mourned and studied ever since.
cia-0000049084: A New York Times article dated March 3, 1984, is preserved in a CIA item, filed with the Truth Commission records. The Times covered El Salvador's war closely, and its reporting often forced official Washington to answer in public. Clippings like this one were kept because press accounts shaped the politics around the files.
cia-0000049184: The record of a meeting held on May 16, 1990, with its subject blacked out, survives in a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. Meetings at that level, in that season, circled the Jesuit case and the war's endgame. What was said sits behind the redactions, which is itself a fact about the file.
cia-0000049284:
Military developments in El Salvador are tracked in a CIA paper from 1983, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. That year the Salvadoran army was being rebuilt with American money, advisers, and new battalions, while the guerrillas held much of the countryside. The paper takes the war's machinery as its subject.

Inside, the subject is change itself: units formed, tactics shifted, and ground gained or lost between reports. Papers like this one let Washington judge whether its investment was buying a stronger army or a longer war. The paper survives as a snapshot of the buildup at mid-course.
cia-0000049384: Assassination of Ignacio Ellacuria and five other Jesuit priests is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049384, dated October 1, 1989. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item names Ellacuria and counts the other victims. It is a short declassified record of the killings, its heading giving the central facts that the file was created to note.
cia-0000096484: Statements on the Cultural Revolution, reduced military training, and poor morale are gathered in declassified CIA document 0000096484, dated July 4, 1967. The heading lists three unlike topics in one breath. Readers find a short declassified statements item from China reporting, its mixed contents announced plainly in a title that reads like a contents line.
cia-0000096584: Views of a redacted source on the refugee problem are recorded in declassified CIA document 0000096584, dated June 5, 1967. The heading marks the speaker as deleted. The brief file preserves reported views on refugees with the source withheld. It is a short record. Its redaction is part of what a reader learns from the catalog entry itself.
cia-0000098284: Possible Additional Agency Support Furnished Howard Hunt is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098284, dated May 6, 1973. Hunt is named, and the support is called possible and additional. The brief file is a Watergate-era record hedged in its own title, preserved among the agency's other 1973 items touching the scandal's figures.
cia-0000098684: Letter to Mancon regarding a February 18, 1992 quotation submitted for fiscal year 1992 costs, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000098684, dated February 4, 1992. The recipient is named as Mancon. Readers get a short procurement letter record, its subject a submitted price quote, filed beside the business justification item. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000118684: New Mobilizaitn Group Meets Press in Hanoi is the heading, with mobilization misspelled and its date an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000118684, dated January 2, 1971. The title reports a new group meeting the press in Hanoi. The misspelling sits inside the group's name in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the misspelling as released.
cia-0000119584:
A November 1963 CIA report describes a political crisis in Czechoslovakia. The communist party still held firm control, but strains were showing years before the Prague Spring. The report treats the trouble as more than routine friction inside the regime.

Crisis reports from inside the Soviet bloc were prized in Washington, where hard facts about allied communist states were scarce. This one records the early tremors of a problem that would grow through the decade. For readers, it offers a baseline: the mood in Prague as the agency saw it five years before reformers briefly took the country in a new direction.
cia-0000126884: An October 1968 CIA report states that the Czechoslovak leadership faces an uncertain future. Two months after the invasion, no one could say whether Dubcek would keep his post. The paper weighs the chances of the men Moscow had humbled that summer. Uncertain-future papers are wagers in print; Dubcek in fact held on until the following spring, when the last of the reform leadership was finally cleared away.
cia-0000132284: Situation Report 593 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 4, 1991, is labeled a special spot commentary on Saddam Hussein. Its headline breaks off after the words Saddam calls for, so the demand itself is missing from the title. Spot commentaries were quick analytical takes rather than full studies. The entry preserves the agency's rapid reading of one Saddam statement.
cia-0000132484: American refineries in Cuba being ordered to process Soviet crude oil fill part three of a CIA item dated April 6, 1960. The section is headed the West. The headline word oil is cut short in the record title. The order set up the showdown that soon led to the refineries being seized. The short item reports the order as analysts received it.
cia-0000132684: The Cuban situation fills a CIA item dated March 5, 1961. It stands beside a second item on the same subject from the same month. Two items with one subject show the pre-invasion watch running at double pace that spring. Each fresh report fed the plans then being finished in Washington. The short item gives the situation as analysts summed it up that week.
cia-0000132784: Cuban Developments, dated 4 October 1960, is a declassified CIA paper in a running series that tracked events in Cuba. By that autumn Castro's government had been in power for well over a year, and relations with the United States had badly soured. The title promises developments rather than a single theme, and the catalog gives no further detail on which events this installment covers. It stands here as one dated entry in the agency's near day-by-day record of Cuba in 1960, released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135884: One item dated 5 January 1954 in the declassified CIA files turns to a pouch manifest from Lincoln, listing what the sealed mail pouch carried that day. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000135984: Dated 4 February 1954, one CIA cable in the open files deals with contact between Calligeris and President Remon, reported before the heading breaks off. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136784: A Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade, dated only to 1961 in the catalog record. The brigade's year ran from final training to the failed April landing and its aftermath, and the record does not place this item within it. No subject is stated. The document is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, part of the declassified archive of the exile force.
cia-0000138984: Military information on Russian aid to the Chinese Communists is the whole subject of document 0000138984, a 1946 report now in the CIA's declassified files. The year matters: China's civil war had flared again after Japan's defeat, and American officers were trying to gauge how much Soviet help Mao's forces were getting in Manchuria and beyond. Reports of this kind fed Washington's early picture of the communist bloc taking shape across Asia.
cia-06768784:
Memorandum dated 10 July 1964, from the Executive Registry to the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence, concerns delegation of authority. The memo states it is for information only. It sums up an attached detailed study of what the Deputy Director could pass to the Executive Director-Comptroller.

In short, the study holds that the Director cannot delegate power to terminate employees, or to serve on the Atomic Awards Board, a power never invoked. The Deputy Director cannot delegate certifying confidential, extraordinary, or emergency spending under section 8(b) of the CIA Act. Entry of up to 100 aliens a year should not be delegated without the Attorney General's concurrence, the memo says. Most other administrative powers under sections 4, 5, and 8 of the Act were judged delegable, some of them further down the chain.
clarin-la-regenta-1884:
Leopoldo Alas, who signed himself Clarín, published La Regenta in Spain in 1884 and 1885. The text here is the Spanish original; no English translation of the novel is in the public domain. Ana Ozores, wife of a retired judge in the provincial city of Vetusta, suffocates in piety, gossip, and boredom.

Two men circle her: her confessor, Fermín de Pas, and the local dandy Álvaro Mesía. Faith, ambition, and desire pull Ana toward a fall the whole town watches for. Clarín builds Vetusta street by street, soul by soul, with patient irony. Spanish readers rank La Regenta as their greatest novel of the nineteenth century. Its scale invites comparison with Madame Bovary and Anna Karenina.
collectanea-chymica-a-collection-of-ten-:
Collectanea Chymica, printed in London for William Cooper in 1684, gathers ten treatises in chymistry, as its title page spells it. The subjects named are the liquor alkahest, the mercury of the philosophers, and other curiosities worthy of perusal. Its authors include Eirenaeus Philalethes, Van Helmont, Dr. Francis Antony, Bernard, Earl of Trevisan, and Sir George Ripley.

Roger Bacon's Speculum Alchymiae and a piece called the Tomb of Semiramis close the roll. The alkahest treatise was, the preface says, bestowed on the editor by a generous stranger. Projection figures swell as the work proceeds: after repeated multiplications, one part of the medicine is said to convert a million parts of imperfect metal into gold and silver.
collins-idyll-of-the-white-lotus-1884:
A tale of old Egypt frames Mabel Collins's The Idyll of the White Lotus, her tale of 1884. A boy with sight past the veil is drawn to a shrine of the white lotus. Priests of two paths fight for his soul. One path serves self and rite. One serves the hid light.

Collins wove her creed into tale form here. The book charmed fans who found dry creed hard. It grew to be the creed's best loved tale of the path. Its soft glow still wins new fans each year. A sage of the creed is said to have blessed the tale in draft. Fans took that nod as proof its lore rang true and deep.
des-langst-gewunschten-und-versprochenen:
A judge's guide to alchemical books fills Hermann Fictuld's Probier-Stein, or touchstone, in this 1784 issue. A preface to the third edition tells its history. The little book first came out at Leipzig in 1740, from Michael Blochberger, and a second edition followed in 1753.

Fictuld sorts the writings of the true adepts, and of others found worthy, by their inner worth and content. This first class of the work sets out the sound authors and warns off the rest. One life told here is of Gualdus, who won a count's title at Venice and a prince's rank elsewhere. He loved seekers of chemical secrets and taught them kindly, Fictuld says. The book is a buyer's guide to a crowded, tricky shelf.
dorsey-omaha-sociology-1884:
James Owen Dorsey was a missionary turned ethnologist who knew the Omaha language deeply from years among the Omaha and Ponca. His 1884 report for the Bureau of American Ethnology describes how Omaha society was organized, down to its smallest rules.

Dorsey explains the gentes, the kin groups that fixed each person's duties, marriages, and place in the tribe. He describes the sacred tents and their holy objects, and the tribal circle, the camp arrangement that mapped the whole social order on the ground. His detail is dry but unmatched. Scholars still rely on this report for the structure of Siouan tribal life.
europmc-pmc10447584:
O'Mahony chaired an expert panel in 2023 to update drug safety lists for older patients. The lists are called STOPP and START. STOPP flags drugs that may harm older people more than they help. START flags good drugs that doctors often forget to offer. A European panel of drug experts checked each item.

Version 3 holds 190 rules, a sharp rise from 114 in version 2. O'Mahony ties the growth to new drugs and fresh trial proof since the last list. The aim is safer reviews of drug sets for older people. Risk runs highest in patients with many illnesses who take many drugs at once. The lists help cut bad drug reactions and events.
europmc-pmc10917684:
Murdock and colleagues show how light and sound pulses help the brain wash out waste in this 2024 mouse study. The glymphatic system is a flow network that rinses the brain with fluid and clears waste. One waste product, amyloid, builds up in Alzheimer disease. Pulses at 40 cycles per second had eased disease signs in mice, but the reason was unclear.

In a mouse model of Alzheimer disease, the pulses boosted fluid inflow and outflow in the outer brain, the team found. Blocking the rinse system erased the amyloid clearing, they showed. Vessel widening and water channel shifts supported the flow. A nerve signal chemical helped drive the effect by tuning artery pulsing. The authors say the rinse path is a real lever for clearing brain waste.
europmc-pmc11254784:
Strain and colleagues pool 507 surveys to track adults who move too little from 2000 to 2022 in this 2024 study. Insufficient activity raises the risk of chronic disease, poor function, weight gain, and mental ill-health. The last global estimate covered 2016, with limited trend data. The team aimed to update prevalence for 197 countries and territories.

Too little activity meant under 150 minutes of moderate activity, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, per week. Surveys came from 163 countries and covered 5.7 million participants. A Bayesian statistical model produced estimates by country, year, age, and sex. Global prevalence in 2022 was 31.3 percent, they report. The team also judged whether the world is on track for the 2030 target of a 15 percent relative cut, if 2010 to 2022 trends continue.
europmc-pmc11474384:
Bai and colleagues track the global burden of congenital birth defects from 1990 to 2021 and forecast it to 2040 in this 2024 study. Congenital birth defects are conditions present at birth that strain health systems worldwide. Prior studies were geographically limited. This analysis uses the Global Burden of Disease 2021 data for four major defects.

The four are congenital heart defects, neural tube defects, digestive anomalies, and Down syndrome. Burden is measured in disability-adjusted life years, a combined count of years lost to early death and years lived with disability. Patterns are reported globally, regionally, and nationally, with emphasis on health inequalities. The authors aim to supply scientific evidence for better resource allocation. High-burden populations are singled out for focus. The forecast to 2040 extends the planning horizon.
europmc-pmc11555284:
Ajoolabady and colleagues review swelling as the engine of atherosclerosis in this 2024 paper. Atherosclerosis is plaque build-up in arteries. It underlies coronary artery disease, where heart arteries narrow, and heart failure. Strong evidence from clinics and labs ties swelling inside plaques to how the disease grows.

The review works through the cell and molecular steps that drive plaque swelling, in macrophages and other white blood cells. Macrophages are the immune cells that fill plaques and eat debris. Signal cascades that fan the swelling are spelled out. The authors then weigh drug targets, with the pros and cons of current treatments. Closing sections cover treatments that calm swelling and shield artery walls. The aim is to flag targets with real promise for patient care.
europmc-pmc1247384:
Satarug and Moore reviewed low-level cadmium harm from food and smoke in 2004. Cadmium is a kidney toxin that the body barely removes. Levels in liver and kidney rise with age. Food and cigarette smoke are the main sources for most people.

Recent studies link cadmium to kidney trouble and bone density loss. The harm appears in general populations with sound nutrition. That finding challenges the old view tying Japanese itai-itai disease to diet gaps. Harm showed at intakes within the then-current weekly safety limit. Satarug argues that limit needs revision downward.
europmc-pmc12662184:
Alonso and co-authors profiled the virus family Asfarviridae in 2018. The family holds one species, African swine fever virus. Its DNA genome runs 170 to 194 thousand base pairs. Virus particles stack a core, two lipid layers, and a geometric shell.

Infection gives pigs and wild boar an acute bleeding fever. Spread occurs by contact, ingestion, or Ornithodoros ticks. Wild pigs form a reservoir in Africa where disease is endemic. Outbreaks periodically spill into Europe from there. Alonso summarizes the official taxonomy report for the family. The profile follows the ICTV report format for virus families.
europmc-pmc1661684:
When a yeast cell's folding workshop swells, it eats the excess back down. Bernales, McDonald, and Walter found that in 2006. The unfolded protein response can expand the endoplasmic reticulum at least five-fold to handle misfolded proteins.

Under the microscope, the swollen membranes were packed into autophagosome-like sacs, the cell's recycling bags. Genes for this self-eating were switched on by the stress response and proved essential for survival under severe stress. Oddly, the digestion enzymes inside the sac were dispensable. Bernales argues that sequestering the extra membrane, not destroying it, is what saves the cell.
europmc-pmc1851984:
Will, Stadler, Backofen and colleagues built a way in 2007 to sort newly found noncoding RNAs by shape. Databases group these RNAs into families by sequence likeness, but whole classes, such as microRNAs, are united by folded structure instead. Genome surveys were turning up thousands of candidate RNAs that fit no known family.

Their tool, LocARNA, aligns RNAs by both sequence and predicted folded shape, using a faster variant of a classic algorithm. It can cluster several thousand candidates at genome scale. The method also tolerates contaminated input, including unstructured or non-conserved sequences slipped in by survey errors. Tests showed it could pull plausible new RNA classes out of genome-wide lists of structured candidates. That gives unclassified RNAs a first sorting into groups worth deeper study.
europmc-pmc1885284:
Tian, Gao and co-authors investigated in 2007 a devastating new pig disease that swept China in 2006. Farmers called it high fever disease, and it spread to more than ten provinces, hitting over two million pigs and killing about 400,000 of them. Unlike typical disease from the PRRS virus, adult sows also fell ill.

Sick pigs ran fevers of 40 to 42 degrees, shivered, and showed red skin rashes. Autopsies and immune tests found highly pathogenic PRRS viruses infecting many organs with severe damage. Whole-genome reading of isolated viruses revealed a unique hallmark change that sets these variants apart. The team dissects that molecular signature and argues the outbreak was an atypical, fatal form of PRRS, a viral disease already costly to pig farming worldwide.
europmc-pmc1913584:
Bell, Ebisu and Belanger studied in 2007 whether the air a pregnant woman breathes affects her baby's birth weight. Earlier studies disagreed, and most came from Southern California or outside the United States. This analysis covered 358,504 births in Connecticut and Massachusetts from 1999 to 2002.

Exposure was estimated from county-level pollution averages across pregnancy and by trimester, at the mother's home county. Models adjusted for pregnancy length, prenatal care, delivery type, and many maternal traits. A typical spread-wide rise in nitrogen dioxide across pregnancy lowered birth weight by about nine grams. Carbon monoxide lowered it by about 16 grams, coarse particles by about eight grams, and fine particles by about 15 grams. Timing mattered: several effects concentrated in the first or third trimester.
europmc-pmc1959184:
Matouk, Hochberg, Galun and co-authors showed in 2007 that a non-coding RNA named H19 is required for human tumors to grow. H19 is an imprinted gene, read from only the mother's copy, and it makes no protein. It shuts off in most tissues after birth but wakes again during tissue repair and in tumors.

Low oxygen, a common tumor stress, raised H19 levels. Silencing H19 in liver and bladder cancer cells stripped their tumor-forming power in animals and cut their colony growth after oxygen stress. Adding H19 back boosted the cancer cells' tumor potential. Silencing also blunted induction of the protective gene p57kip2 under low oxygen. The team catalogs further candidate targets of H19. The results nominate H19 itself as an anti-tumor drug target.
europmc-pmc1974784:
Shi, Fredrickson and co-authors reviewed in 2007 how two bacteria breathe solid rust-like minerals despite a physical barrier. Shewanella and Geobacter gain energy by reducing iron and manganese oxides, a process called dissimilatory reduction. The minerals barely dissolve in water and cannot cross the cell envelope, so electrons must travel outward instead.

Both species deploy cytochromes loaded with multiple heme groups, the iron-holding units that pass electrons along. In Shewanella, proteins named CymA and MtrA ferry electrons across the inner membrane and the middle compartment. A secretion system then places the ten-heme proteins MtrC and OmcA on the cell surface, where they reduce minerals directly. In Geobacter, surface cytochromes OmcE and OmcS likely feed electrons to hair-like pili that relay them to the mineral. The shared multi-heme strategy is the review's central thread.
europmc-pmc2125284:
J. Bronfenbrenner of the Western Pennsylvania Hospital in Pittsburgh dissected the Abderhalden reaction, then the most argued-over test in medicine. The reaction was claimed to reveal defensive ferments in blood against a chosen tissue, famously in pregnancy. Bronfenbrenner's first finding is that the reaction is specific.

The serum property behind it, he shows, develops in experimental animals at the same time as antibodies during immunization. Yet no digesting ferment can be directly observed in immune blood. That self-digestion, in turn, is traced to a removal: the sensitized test material strips antitrypsin from the serum, unguarding its proteins. His controls run the pregnant and male sera side by side in the ice box. Readers get a fashionable test pulled apart and rebuilt on the ferment-and-antiferment scheme, specificity kept and mystery removed.
europmc-pmc2125484:
Robert A. Lambert of Columbia's Presbyterian Hospital pathology lab compared germ-killers against germs and human tissue cells side by side in 1916. He used tissue cultures to mimic conditions in the body. The uncomfortable headline: human connective tissue and wandering cells, though hard to kill with many of them, are in general easier to kill than Staphylococcus aureus.

Nine agents were tested, among them mercuric chloride, potassium mercuric iodide, phenol, tricresol, hydrogen peroxide, Dakin's hypochlorite fluid, argyrol, and alcohol. One approaches the ideal germ-killer: iodine, which kills germs at strengths that do not seriously injure the tissue cells. Lambert notes that broth tests flatter these chemicals; serum demands stronger doses, and infected wounds stronger still. Readers get wound cleaning graded by what it costs the patient's own cells.
europmc-pmc2125784:
Hans Zinsser and Julia T. Parker studied bacterial anaphylaxis, the violent reaction a sensitized body makes to a germ product, for the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1917. Working with guinea pigs, they used the isolated uterus as their test organ and asked how fast tissues become sensitive, and what part of the bacterium the sensitive tissue actually answers to.

Sensitizing the uterus took three to five days, even when sensitivity was passed over from another animal, matching what was known for serum anaphylaxis. Whole bacteria and whole red cells drew no response at all. The tissue reacted only once bacterial matter had been extracted or dissolved, and blood tests during infection showed that germs do shed such matter into the circulation. Harm in a sensitized patient, they argue, works partly through this released material meeting new antibodies.
europmc-pmc2126684:
O. T. Avery and Glenn E. Cullen measured the acidity at which pneumococcus cultures grow best and the acidity at which growth stops. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1919. They grew the germ in broths with varying sugar content, starting at different reactions, and they retested used broth after filtering out the bacteria.

Growth ran best at a mildly alkaline reaction. In broth with enough fermentable sugar, growth continued until the culture turned fairly acid, and that acidity alone seemed to halt it. With less sugar, growth stopped earlier from simple exhaustion of the food. Plain broth, with only meat-extract sugar, stopped growth near neutral. Filtered used broth supported no new growth unless sugar was added back. Used dextrose broth, reset to the best reaction, grew pneumococci again. Food supply and acidity together, the work shows, set the culture's limit.
europmc-pmc2128384:
Edmund V. Cowdry and Peter K. Olitsky compared mitochondria, the thread-like bodies inside cells, with bacteria, side by side. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. A standing suggestion held that mitochondria are really symbiotic microbes living in cells, an idea that would reshape biology and medicine if true.

The pair examined both in the living state and in fixed preparations, under the same treatments and the same stains. The two answered differently in chemical and staining behavior across the board. Such differences, they argue, can only rest on a basic dissimilarity in chemical makeup. Mitochondria behave as parts of the cell's own substance, not as tenant organisms of another kind. The comparison is direct and controlled, which gives the negative answer its weight: same handling, same tests, different nature.
europmc-pmc2128484:
Alexis Carrel and Albert H. Ebeling grew lymphocytes in blood serum and found the white cells feeding their neighbors. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923, from the Rockefeller Institute. Fibroblasts, the connective tissue cells, cannot multiply on serum alone, which raised the question of what they live on in the body.

Lymphocytes and large mononuclear cells, by contrast, live and increase greatly in plain serum. While living there, they make and secrete substances that fibroblasts can use as food. The authors judge it probable that these white cells build, from the nitrogen compounds in serum, the very substances fibroblasts and surface cells need in order to multiply. The blood's wandering cells thus act as cooks for the fixed tissues, preparing food the tissues cannot prepare themselves.
europmc-pmc2130984:
P. Lecomte du Noüy tracked physical changes in blood serum after immunization, in the thirteenth paper of his surface tension series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. Injecting an antigen into an animal, he found, slowly alters the blood fluid itself in ways a physicist can follow.

Two signs mark the change: the surface tension of serum solutions falls, and diluted serum drying under set conditions forms a special crystallization pattern. The change peaks around the thirteenth day after the first injection and fades until it usually vanishes near the thirtieth. One large dose or many small ones give the same course, and reinjection does not alter it. The signs seem independent of antigen still circulating. The protein molecules of immune serum, he adds, are about the same mean length as those of normal serum, so the change lies elsewhere than in size.
europmc-pmc2131184:
Louise Pearce and Chester Van Allen, at The Rockefeller Institute, began a 1926 series on the effects of light on normal rabbits. Part one records clinical and postmortem observations. Fifty male rabbits lived in constant light lacking the shorter ultraviolet rays. Fifty more lived in constant darkness. Both groups were kept so for two to twelve weeks, with other groups under normal room conditions as controls.

The general health of the rabbits was not hurt by steady light or by darkness. Weight gain took place in all groups and was strongest in the constant light group. Sickness seen during the test was rare and mild. At postmortem, though, about six in ten rabbits from every housing group showed some visible lesion, most of them slight.
europmc-pmc2140684:
Crozier and Pilz, at Rutgers College, opened a study of slug locomotion in 1924 with the giant slug Limax maximus. The slug creeps by waves that run along the sole of its foot. They measured wave speed, wave frequency, the advance from one wave, and the speed of upward creeping, then asked how temperature governs the rhythm.

Wave speed, wave frequency, and single-wave advance each rose in direct proportion to the speed of progression. With the work rate held constant, wave frequency followed Arrhenius' equation as temperature changed, with a fixed temperature characteristic. The speed of a single wave carries nearly the same characteristic. The same value appears in nerve net transmission in the sea pansy Renilla, a hint of shared machinery.
europmc-pmc2265484:
Eriksson and co-workers traced the yellow skin trait of domestic chickens in 2008 to its gene and wild source. Yellow skin comes from a recessive allele letting yellow carotenoid pigments deposit in skin. The team showed the trait stems from regulatory mutations that silence the BCDO2 gene in skin. That gene normally breaks carotenoids down. In white-skinned birds the pigments are taken up from blood but degraded in the skin.

Comparing gene sequences across junglefowl species overturned a long-held view. Darwin held that domestic chickens descend solely from the red junglefowl. The yellow skin allele instead most likely comes from the grey junglefowl, a close relative. That was the first conclusive proof of a hybrid origin for the domestic chicken, and it reshapes views of how domestication proceeded.
europmc-pmc2265684:
Storla, Yimer and Bjune systematically reviewed 58 studies in 2008 on delay in tuberculosis diagnosis and treatment. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are essential for control, since most transmission happens between cough onset and treatment start. Definitions of delay varied widely between studies, so instead of a strict meta-analysis the authors extracted solid findings from all of them to build a global picture.

Delay clustered with many factors: HIV infection, chronic cough or other lung disease, negative sputum smear, disease outside the lungs, and rural residence. Poverty, old age, female sex, alcohol misuse, immigration and low education also featured. The core problem was a vicious cycle of repeated visits to the same care level. Patients received non-specific antibiotics and never reached specialised tuberculosis services. Once diagnosis was in reach, treatment began promptly.
europmc-pmc2376384:
Tolcher and a large team measured how long dosing of a cancer drug drains a DNA repair enzyme in 2003. The drug, temozolomide, damages DNA in tumor cells. The enzyme, shortened to AGAT, undoes exactly that damage, so draining it should make the drug bite harder.

They tracked AGAT in blood cells of 52 patients on two stretched schedules: daily for 7 days every 2 weeks, or 21 days every 4 weeks. After seven days the enzyme's activity had fallen by 72% on average, and it stayed markedly low a week after treatment stopped. Longer courses cut it by 63% to 73% across all doses tested. On the 21-day schedule, patients with the deepest enzyme loss, near 90%, suffered the worst drops in platelet counts. The authors said stretched dosing gives deep, lasting enzyme depletion.
europmc-pmc2410284:
Rittling and Chambers reviewed osteopontin as a cancer marker in 2004. Osteopontin is a protein first spotted in transformed cells 25 years earlier, and it helps cells stick, move, and signal. The question was whether its levels in tumors or blood can forecast how a patient's cancer will behave.

In animal work, injecting cells or breeding mice with altered osteopontin changed tumor growth and spread, though in complex ways. Across many human cancers, high osteopontin in tumor tissue or blood tracked more advanced disease. The authors weighed those studies and found the pattern consistent enough to call it a candidate prognostic marker. They also cautioned that the protein's many jobs in the body complicate reading its levels. Its exact cancer-driving mechanism, they noted, was still unclear.
europmc-pmc2667184:
Paolacci and colleagues searched in 2009 for steady yardstick genes in wheat, needed to measure gene activity fairly. Lab tests of how strongly a gene is switched on must be scaled against reference genes that stay constant. The usual picks, borrowed from housekeeping roles, in fact wobble a good deal, which skews results.

Starting from public wheat databases, the team picked 32 candidate genes, mixing old standards with twenty fresh ones. They measured all of them across 24 samples: varied tissues, growth stages, and heat and cold stress. Two scoring programs agreed on which genes held steadiest. Three new genes beat the classic picks, including actin, which proved shaky. A test on a real target gene showed the point: with a poor yardstick, its pattern looked wrong; with a good one, the reading came clean.
europmc-pmc2669884:
McVicker and colleagues measured in 2009 how strongly natural selection has shaped the genomes of humans and their primate kin. Selection leaves a shadow: when it removes harmful variants near a useful gene, neutral variation nearby drops too. The team compared human variation and differences among five primate species against maps of conserved DNA stretches.

Near those conserved stretches, neutral diversity fell sharply. Across the whole genome, selection had cut average diversity by roughly a fifth to a quarter on the regular chromosomes. The effect ran stronger still on the X chromosome, and strongest of all near gene parts that code for proteins. The pattern fits background selection, the steady weeding of harmful changes in ancestral populations. Long-term selection, they conclude, explains the patchy divergence between humans and chimpanzees better than tangled histories of splitting populations.
europmc-pmc2675784:
Bates reviewed in 2007 how Leishmania parasites, single-celled organisms that cause skin and organ disease across the tropics, get from sand fly to mammal. Knowing the handoff in detail is the first step to blocking it. More than 30 species of the parasite exist, and the bite of a female sand fly is the only proven route in.

The main trick is a gel the parasites secrete in the fly's gut. The gel, packed with ripe infective forms, plugs the gut so the fly cannot feed cleanly. Trying to drink, the fly coughs the plug back out, gel and parasites together, into the skin of its victim. Bates also weighs side possibilities: damage to a valve in the fly's throat, parasites in spit glands, and parasites leaving in droppings. The three parasite subfamilies, he notes, weight these routes differently.
europmc-pmc2678084:
Oshlack and Wakefield warned in 2009 that a built-in bias in RNA sequencing skews lists of genes that differ between samples. RNA-seq, the new method of counting gene messages by sequencing them, was fast becoming the tool of choice for reading which genes are on. The authors checked three published datasets for hidden distortions.

The distortion was clear: the longer a gene's message, the easier it is to call that gene changed. Long messages simply collect more sequence reads, so their counts are steadier and pass significance tests more often. The bias is not a flaw of one lab's protocol; it follows from counting itself. It warps ranked gene lists, and it can mislead pathway tests that ask which gene groups change together. A gene set rich in long genes can look active for purely technical reasons, the authors caution.
europmc-pmc2696084:
Uronis and colleagues showed in 2009 that shifting the gut's bacterial mix changes a mouse's risk of colon cancer driven by inflammation. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease develop colorectal cancer more often, but whether the microbes themselves drive the cancer step was unproven. The team built a model using mice lacking IL-10, a calming immune signal, dosed with a cancer-triggering chemical.

Sixty-two percent of those mice developed colon tumors, against 20 percent of normal mice given the same chemical. Tumor counts rose and fell with the severity of gut inflammation. Mice raised germ-free stayed tumor-free with healthy colons. Mice colonized with a single mild bacterium strain had far less inflammation and fewer tumors. Removing a key alarm pathway, MyD88, abolished tumors entirely. Changing the microbial tenants, the authors conclude, truly changes cancer susceptibility.
europmc-pmc2701284:
Cobos and colleagues reviewed in 2008 the sigma-1 receptor, an enigmatic protein once mistaken for an opioid receptor, and the drugs that bind it. The receptor is unlike any other known protein in sequence. It lives largely in the cell's internal membranes, where it tunes calcium signals, and it also adjusts ion channels and several neurotransmitter systems, most notably glutamate.

Its binding list is a who's who of brain drugs: the antipsychotic haloperidol, antidepressants such as fluvoxamine, and stimulants such as cocaine and methamphetamine all grip it. Certain steroids made in the body may be its natural partners. Animal studies tie its activity to memory, mood, pain, and drug craving. That breadth makes its ligands candidates across psychiatry and pain medicine, and blockers of it candidates against stimulant abuse. The review gathers the behavioral evidence behind each claim.
europmc-pmc2702084:
Kao and colleagues profiled in 2009 fifty-two widely used breast cancer cell lines, the lab stand-ins on which much cancer research and drug testing rests. Real breast cancers split into molecular subtypes with different behaviors. The open question was which lines faithfully model which subtypes, and which model nothing found in patients.

Reading both gene activity and DNA copy changes, the team sorted the lines into one luminal subtype and two basal-like subtypes, A and B. Luminal lines carried the estrogen-receptor signature of their tumor counterparts. Basal-A lines matched basal tumors and carried BRCA1-pathway marks. Basal-B lines looked more like stem and mesenchymal cells, further from any common tumor. Copy changes in lines broadly echoed tumors, though lines ran more scrambled. The catalog tells researchers which model to pick, and flags candidate cancer genes where copy and activity move together.
europmc-pmc2702684:
Ganguly and Carmena reported in 2009 how the brain forms a stable map when it controls a prosthetic device, which is a machine that moves by brain signals. They worked with monkeys that moved a cursor with brain activity alone. Past work changed the set of brain cells or the decoder each day, so lasting learning stayed unclear.

With a fixed decoder and the same brain cells tracked for up to 19 days, the monkeys built a map that held steady over time. They could recall it at once and keep it even when a new task got in the way. The pattern acted much like a learned motor skill, such as riding a bike.
europmc-pmc2711084:
Nguyen Ba, Pogoutse, Provart, and Moses presented in 2009 NLStradamus, a simple hidden Markov model for predicting nuclear localization signals in proteins. These signals are short stretches of amino acids that tag a protein for import into the cell nucleus. Yeast uses many import pathways, yet the signals for most of them lack clear patterns, and existing prediction tools missed most known cases.

The team first compiled sixty experimentally verified signals in yeast and analyzed their residue patterns. Despite the many pathways, the signals showed similar patterns of amino acids. Current methods scored a low true positive rate on this set; one leading tool found only a tenth of the signals. Their hidden Markov model, a statistical pattern matcher, consistently found thirty-seven percent of the signals while keeping false alarms low. It held that rate on data beyond the yeast set used for training.
europmc-pmc2722084:
Blazkova and co-authors showed in 2009 that DNA methylation, a chemical silencing tag, helps keep HIV locked in latency inside resting immune cells. Modern drug cocktails suppress HIV but cannot clear this hidden reservoir, which is the main bar to a cure. Whether methylation truly controls that hiding, rather than just marking it, had never been proven in patients.

In a lab latency model and in patients with no virus in blood, the viral promoter region was heavily methylated and hard to reactivate. Patients with active virus carried unmethylated promoters instead. Methylation acted late as latency settled, not at first silencing, and even dense methylation could still be partly reversed by some drugs.
europmc-pmc2813284:
Knoth and colleagues mapped signs of new neuron growth in the human hippocampus across the whole lifespan in 2010. The hippocampus is a brain area central to memory, and rodents there grow new neurons throughout life. Whether the same happens in adult humans was nearly untested.

Working with tissue from fifty-four people aged from birth to one hundred years, the team tracked a marker protein called DCX that young neurons carry. DCX cells appeared at every age, but their numbers fell steeply as age rose. Early in life those cells co-carried all fourteen rodent-linked markers tested, and a few key markers persisted even in the oldest brains. The pattern closely mirrors the rodent course.
europmc-pmc2819884:
Bitar and colleagues measured how often a rare but deadly fungal infection struck France between 1997 and 2006. The infection, called zygomycosis or mucormycosis, is caused by common molds whose threads invade blood vessels and kill tissue. It mainly hits people with weak immune defenses or diabetes, and death rates in some forms reach sixty percent.

Using national hospital discharge records, the team tracked cases across the whole country rather than at single hospitals. Their population-based count confirmed a real rise over the decade, matching what scattered hospital reports had suggested. They also profiled which underlying illnesses patients carried and how often the infection proved fatal, giving France its first national baseline for this disease.
europmc-pmc2858084:
Deng and a large team mapped in 2010 where a stem cell marker called ALDH1 appears across common cancers that start in surface tissues. ALDH1 is an enzyme, a protein that speeds chemical work, and bright ALDH1 cells can behave like cancer stem cells. The team compared tumors with the healthy tissues they came from.

Staining nearly eight hundred tumors from six cancer types, Deng found each cancer kept a distinct ALDH1 pattern that matched its tissue of origin. Enzyme activity tracked the staining, and lab culture did not change it much. In ovarian cancer, high levels meant worse outcomes for patients, and the bright cells resisted chemotherapy while showing stem-like traits in tests.
europmc-pmc2916884:
Walker and co-authors mapped in 2010 which antibody targets explain the rare HIV patients whose blood neutralizes many virus strains at once. A vaccine will likely need such broadly neutralizing antibodies, yet nobody knew which viral sites the natural versions aim at. They dissected the serum of nineteen donors with the most potent cross-strain activity recorded, using a battery of binding and depletion tests.

In most donors, just one or two antibody specificities accounted for nearly all the breadth and power. Two targets dominated. One site spans the conserved parts of the viral spike's loops, defined by two famous antibodies. The other overlaps where the virus grips the CD4 entry receptor. A short shopping list for vaccine designers replaces a fog of possibilities.
europmc-pmc2918584:
Pluskal, Castillo, Villar-Briones, and Oresic released in 2010 MZmine 2, a rebuilt open-source workbench for mass spectrometry data, the molecular profile files behind metabolomics and proteomics. Raw instrument output must be cleaned, peaked, identified, and aligned across samples before biology emerges, and the original MZmine had aged. The rewrite separates a stable core from plug-in processing modules.

New tools include multi-stage fragmentation support, sharper isotope pattern handling, peak identification against online databases, and scatter plot views for comparing samples. A fresh alignment method borrows the RANSAC algorithm from computer vision to line up peak lists robustly, and it beat older methods on both synthetic and real data. Live previews of every parameter setting make the pipeline far less of a black box.
europmc-pmc2920084:
De Hartog, Boogaard, Nijland, and Hoek calculated in 2010 whether swapping short car trips for cycling helps or harms the individual Dutch traveler. A shift brings more physical activity but also more inhaled pollution and more crash exposure. They combined systematic reviews of all three factors and modeled half a million people switching to bikes for daily short trips, expressing outcomes in life years.

For the switchers, activity gains dwarfed the harms: on the order of three to fourteen months of life gained per person. Extra pollution cost at most a few weeks, and crash risk a similar small amount. Society gains further through cleaner air and fewer emissions, though not counted in the personal ledger. The arithmetic strongly favors the bicycle for short urban trips.
europmc-pmc2926784:
