Lévesque and a genome consortium sequenced in 2010 Pythium ultimum, a water mold that rots seeds and roots across a huge range of crops and ornamentals. The genome runs about forty-three million DNA letters encoding some fifteen thousand genes. Its layout closely parallels its notorious relative Phytophthora, the potato blight genus, letting the team spot what a root-rotting lifestyle adds and drops.

RNA sequencing showed most genes active, with whole suites switching under stress and during host attack. The predicted proteins include a large arsenal for invading plant tissue, from wall-digesting enzymes to effector proteins that manipulate host cells. Some famous blight effector families are missing, marking a genuinely different attack recipe. The genome hands plant pathologists the parts list of a model for the whole Pythium genus.
europmc-pmc2944084:
Alonso-Magdalena and colleagues tested the plastic chemical bisphenol A in pregnant mice in a 2010 study. The chemical, used in hard plastics, can mimic hormones, and human studies had linked exposure to diabetes and heart disease.

Doses matching everyday environmental levels worsened the insulin resistance that comes with pregnancy and raised blood insulin, fats, and leptin. Months after birth, treated mothers stayed heavier and more insulin resistant than untreated ones. Male pups exposed before birth showed disturbed sugar control and pancreas function by six months of age. The work flags pregnancy as a sensitive window.
europmc-pmc2946684:
Rawat and Nair reviewed extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, bacterial enzymes that defeat many modern antibiotics, in a 2010 article. These plasmid-carried enzymes spread fast and complicate care in hospitals and the community alike.

The enzymes break down third-generation cephalosporins and a related drug, yet are blocked by clavulanic acid, a trait labs use to detect them. Strains carrying them often resist several other drug families too, narrowing treatment choices. Infections range from simple bladder infections to life-threatening sepsis. Carbapenem antibiotics remain the choice for serious cases, though resistance to them has begun to appear.
europmc-pmc3002984:
Gahan, Pauchet, Vogel, and Heckel pinned a caterpillar's resistance to a bacterial crop toxin on a broken transport protein in a 2010 study. Sprayed and engineered Bt crops rely on the Cry1Ac toxin, and the cotton pest Heliothis virescens had evolved to withstand it.

Breeding over a thousand offspring and mapping the trait, they separated this resistance gene from a previously known one. Resistant insects carried a disabling mutation in ABCC2, a membrane transporter, and their gut membranes lost the tight toxin binding seen in susceptible insects. The transporter apparently helps the toxin punch into gut cells.
europmc-pmc3017084:
Kofler and colleagues introduced PoPoolation, a toolbox for reading population genetics from pooled DNA samples, in a 2011 article. Sequencing many individuals mixed in one pool is cheap, but standard formulas misread such data.

Their programs estimate classic diversity and selection statistics. They correct for pooling bias and sequencing errors while doing so. They can also measure divergence between species. Results display as sliding window plots across the genome. Tests of mapping choices, error rates, and coverage show where pooled estimates stay trustworthy, helping smaller labs run genome-wide population studies within modest budgets.
europmc-pmc3178584:
James Chandler and colleagues surveyed bacteria living with wild fruit flies in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. The laboratory fruit fly is a rising model for friendly host-microbe relations, but lab results mean little if wild flies carry different microbes. The team profiled bacteria from fourteen fly species and relatives gathered worldwide, spanning fruit, flower, mushroom, and cactus feeders.

Wild communities proved narrow: just four bacterial families made up the great bulk of the gut flora, and the leaders appeared across many hosts despite varied diets and homes. Diet still shaped the mix strongly in controlled tests, yet the gut kept only a filtered subset of environmental bacteria. Worryingly, the species used in lab experiments are rare or absent in wild flies, while wild dominants are rare in labs. Lab models, the authors warn, only partly mirror nature.
europmc-pmc3253084:
John Wieczorek and colleagues described Darwin Core, the community standard for sharing biodiversity data, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Records of species and specimens live in countless formats on incompatible systems, blocking any unified view of global biodiversity. A shared vocabulary of terms is the essential first step toward putting those records together.

The paper traces how the standard grew and is maintained by its community. It explains the categories of terms the standard defines, the difference between its simple and relational forms, and how people have put it to work. Case studies show extensions into new fields such as metagenomics and genetic resources. The authors close by showing how standardized records combine into knowledge products that map species distributions and track how they shift with environmental change.
europmc-pmc3257684:
Walter Hurley and Peter Theil reviewed the antibodies in colostrum and milk in this 2011 article in Nutrients. Immunoglobulins are a core part of the immune protection in these secretions and form the link by which a mother hands passive immunity to her offspring. How that transfer works differs widely among mammals, and the review sets the mechanisms side by side.

Cows give large volumes of antibody-rich colostrum and milk. That makes them attractive sources of immune products for people. Such immune milk preparations have been tested against several human diseases. The authors consider which antibody types each secretion carries and how they are secreted. They ask how a newborn, or an adult drinker, gains protection from them. How well the antibodies survive processing and digestion is a further theme. Those survival questions decide much of the practical value of milk antibodies.
europmc-pmc3261984:
Yuming Guo and colleagues modeled how temperature affects deaths in Tianjin, China, in this 2011 paper in Environmental Health Perspectives. Evidence from China was scarce, and it was unclear which temperature reading predicts mortality best. They combined a case-crossover design, which controls for season, with a flexible model that captures curved relationships and effects spread over following days.

The relationship was U-shaped: both cold and heat raised mortality. Cold effects arrived after about three days and persisted for ten. Heat effects were immediate and lasted about three days. They were partly offset by a dip afterward, as the frailest deaths were brought forward. Average temperature predicted deaths better than daily maximum or minimum. The authors note the combined method can be reused for air pollution studies.
europmc-pmc3297584:
Henn and a large team used deep sequencing to watch HIV change during the first weeks of infection, in a 2012 study. Older methods read only the most common virus versions and miss rare ones. Their new platform read the whole virus genome at great depth in one patient, paired with detailed tracking of the immune response.

Most early rare changes in the virus were escapes from killer T cells, showing intense immune pressure as virus levels first fell. Some transmitted changes quickly reverted, and even rare versions were enough to spark fresh immune responses. When the virus escaped the strongest T cell attacks, the early drop in virus levels stalled. The authors argue that vaccines must aim T cells at parts of the virus that cannot change easily.
europmc-pmc3323384:
Hsu and colleagues investigated the return of Nipah virus brain illness in Bangladesh, reporting in 2004. The virus first appeared in Malaysia and Singapore in 1998 and 1999, mainly infecting pig farmers, and fruit bats were identified as its likely natural home. Bangladesh saw a deadly cluster of fever and brain inflammation in 2001, then another in a district not far away in 2003.

The team reconstructed both outbreaks, comparing symptoms, testing stored samples, and looking for risk factors and animal sources. Antibodies and illness patterns tied both clusters to Nipah virus. Unlike the Malaysian outbreak, where sick pigs drove spread, the Bangladeshi pattern raised the possibility that the virus passed directly from person to person. The authors say this second route changes how future outbreaks there should be contained.
europmc-pmc3325284:
Dong, Liu, Yu, Wang, and Zhou hunted for the most changeable stretches of the plant chloroplast genome, reporting in 2012. Botanists rely on chloroplast DNA to trace family trees and to barcode species, but the genome changes slowly, leaving few useful markers for telling close relatives apart. The team scanned the full chloroplast genomes of twelve plant genera to find the spots that vary most.

They picked out twenty three promising regions, including four gene stretches, two introns, and seventeen spacers between genes. A handful of spacers varied the most and look best for separating species. The team designed starter DNA pieces that frame each region and confirmed they work across a spread of flowering plants, from ancient lineages to grasses and roses. The catalog gives plant scientists a ready shortlist for fine scale family trees and DNA barcoding.
europmc-pmc3334584:
Jiao led a large team that dated an ancient genome multiplication in the history of flowering plants, reporting in 2012. The event, called gamma, tripled the genome of an early ancestor of the largest plant group, the eudicots. Exactly where it fell in the family tree was disputed, and settling it matters for understanding how these plants exploded in diversity.

The team built family trees for hundreds of gene groups using gene readouts from many plant lineages, including fresh sequencing of plants outside the well studied groups. Nearly all traces of the event landed in one window, after the split from buttercup relatives but before two great branches, the rose and aster families, parted. Dating placed the burst around one hundred seventeen million years ago. The great flowering of eudicot diversity, source of most plant species alive, followed soon after.
europmc-pmc3387384:
Guitart-Masip and co-workers probed in 2012 how people learn when rewards and punishments demand opposite actions. Choices carry two pulls: whether the outcome is good or bad, and whether success needs acting or holding back. Their task crossed those two demands so each combination could be learned separately.

Volunteers learned active choices far better under reward, and passive choices better under punishment. Computer models split the effect into a hardwired Pavlovian push and flexible learning. Brain scans tied learned action values to the striatum and midbrain dopamine centers, with opposite signals for act and hold choices. Two frontal regions had to engage for learning to succeed, the scans showed.
europmc-pmc3390384:
Loper led a genomic comparison in 2012 of ten Pseudomonas strains that live with plants and can protect them. The bacteria differ widely in their gifts: some fight plant diseases, others affect insects and microbes. Seven of the ten genomes were newly sequenced for this study.

The strains fell into three sub-groups, with close kin sharing much of their DNA. The shared core made up barely half of any single genome, and the group's total gene pool was huge. Surprise finds included genes for new antibiotics, insect toxins, and several secretion systems. Most interaction genes sat in strain-specific regions that look recently acquired, showing how each strain tailors itself to its lifestyle.
europmc-pmc3396284:
Tangermann and many colleagues reviewed the BCI Competition IV in 2012, the fourth open contest for brain-computer interface methods. These contests release high-quality brain data freely so teams worldwide can test their decoding methods. Entrants ranged from deep specialists to students, across many countries.

Six challenges pushed the field: signals without cues, artificial data, many-class continuous control, carrying learning between sessions, magnet-based recordings of direction, and finger movements read from the brain's surface. Each was chosen to demand fresh ideas rather than polish old ones. The review explains the tasks and results. Organizers hoped winning entries would strengthen the analysis methods future interfaces rely on.
europmc-pmc3400084:
Araujo, Zhang, and Yin reviewed in 2012 how one protective enzyme guards arteries against atherosclerosis, the buildup that causes heart attacks. The disease grows as fats and immune cells crowd the vessel wall and oxidize. The enzyme, heme oxygenase-1, breaks down heme and is switched on by the master regulator Nrf2.

Its three breakdown products each help: easing oxidation, calming inflammation, and slowing cell growth and death in vessel walls. Levels are normally low but surge under the stresses that drive plaque. Oddly, switching on its regulator can worsen plaque instead, a wrinkle any therapy must respect. Trials are already testing treatments built on this enzyme's actions.
europmc-pmc3441384:
Stern, Adiseshaiah, and Crist highlighted in 2012 two underappreciated ways engineered nanomaterials can poison cells: jamming their recycling system and their waste sacs. The usual explanations, oxidative stress and inflammation, leave the machinery vague. Most routes by which cells swallow nanoparticles end at the lysosome, the cell's digestion sac, making it the prime meeting point.

Some materials also trigger autophagy, the cell's self-eating program, perhaps as an attempt to digest the invaders. But durable particles that refuse to break down can themselves wreck both systems, with toxic knock-on effects. The review gathers that growing evidence. Safer nanotechnology, they argue, must reckon with what particles do to the cell's housekeeping core.
europmc-pmc3461484:
Sousa da Silva and Vranken presented ACPYPE in 2012, a Python wrapper that readies small molecules for motion simulations. Such simulators need a topology file describing each molecule's atoms and forces, and the standard maker, ANTECHAMBER, is fiddly to run inside other software. Their tool produces ready topologies for several major simulation programs, including GROMACS and CHARMM.

The tool also computes the partial charges simulators require. Its output was checked three ways: against standard amino-acid topologies, across a large set of drug-like ligands from the protein data bank, and by rebuilding five protein-ligand complex structures. All checks passed cleanly. Released as free, open-source code and a web portal, it slots into Python-based toolkits for structural work.
europmc-pmc3488584:
Tumors breathe poorly in their low-oxygen cores, and Hamish W. King, Michael Z. Michael, and Jonathan M. Gleadle test whether that stress changes the tiny packets breast cancer cells shed. Their 2012 study grows three breast cancer cell lines at 1 percent and 0.1 percent oxygen and counts the exosomes, small vesicles cells use to signal neighbors.

Both moderate and severe hypoxia raise exosome release clearly in all three lines. The fractions also carry more miR-210, a small RNA tied to low-oxygen responses. The team links the boost at least partly to the HIF oxygen-sensing pathway. More packets under hypoxia could help tumors talk to surrounding tissue and spread.
europmc-pmc3561084:
Gordan Lauc and a large team of collaborators published a genome-wide association study in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on the sugars attached to antibody proteins. The sugar chains on immunoglobulin G, a main antibody type, change how it binds cell receptors and drives immune responses. The group hunted for DNA regions that control this sugar pattern, called N-glycosylation, in thousands of Europeans.

Measurements on 2,247 people, checked in a second group of 1,848, flagged nine genome regions. Four held genes for enzymes that build sugar chains. The other five had not been tied to this process before, yet most were already linked to autoimmune diseases such as lupus and Crohn disease, or to blood cancers. A mouse experiment on one gene supported its role. The overlap hints that sugar patterns sit upstream of several illnesses.
europmc-pmc3561684:
Mary Wisz and many co-authors reviewed species distribution modelling in Biological Reviews in 2013, focusing on the living interactions that shape where species occur. Models that forecast where a species can live usually lean on climate and landscape. Encounters with other species, such as predators, prey, competitors, and food plants, were long treated as local detail that washes out at large scales.

Evidence from present-day ranges, fossil records, and richness patterns shows otherwise. Interactions leave clear marks from small plots up to whole continents, within feeding levels and across them. The review then surveys modelling tools that can fold interactions into forecasts instead of leaving them out. For readers planning conservation under climate change, the message is direct: a map built on weather alone can misplace a species whose neighbors also move.
europmc-pmc3566584:
Mark Walton and colleagues studied learning in the macaque brain in Neuron in 2010, focusing on the orbitofrontal cortex, a frontal region tied to flexible choice. Monkeys played a three-armed bandit game where the best-paying option changed without warning. After selective damage to this region, the animals struggled to find the new best option after each switch, a deficit often blamed on simple stubbornness.

Closer analysis told a different story. The monkeys were not rigid; they switched too much, bouncing among all options. Their choices stopped tracking which exact choice had earned which exact reward, the credit assignment called contingent learning. A fallback based on recent history still let them roughly favor good options. The study recasts this brain region's job: it binds rewards to the specific choices that caused them, which later flexibility depends on.
europmc-pmc3593184:
Klas Stenlöf and colleagues tested a new diabetes drug, canagliflozin, in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism in 2013. The drug blocks a kidney transporter that normally recaptures sugar from urine, so more sugar leaves the body and blood sugar falls. The phase 3 trial enrolled 584 adults with type 2 diabetes whose diet and exercise alone were not controlling their blood sugar. It assigned them to one of two daily doses or a dummy pill for twenty-six weeks.

Both doses beat placebo on the headline measure: hemoglobin A1c, a three-month sugar average, fell by 0.77 and 1.03 percentage points against a slight rise on placebo. Fasting and after-meal sugar, body weight, and systolic blood pressure also fell, while protective HDL cholesterol rose. Side effects were modestly more common on the drug, notably genital yeast infections and urine-related complaints, with few dropouts. The results position the drug as a workable single therapy.
europmc-pmc3602084:
Raúl Herzog and colleagues reviewed why health workers do or do not promote vaccination in BMC Public Health in 2013. European vaccine experts had urged work on staff knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes, assuming these drive whether workers recommend shots to patients. The review tested that assumption by gathering studies from developed countries, published between 1998 and 2009 in any of seven languages, that statistically tied those inner factors to vaccination intentions.

From 2,354 first hits, fifteen studies survived the rules. Their designs and measures differed too much to merge, so each was judged alone. Every study pointed the same way: workers who knew more, whose beliefs matched the scientific evidence, and who felt positive about vaccines intended to vaccinate more. Quality scoring of each study accompanied the summary. The link the experts assumed is real, though the patchy evidence base cannot yet say which lever moves intentions most.
europmc-pmc3668284:
Sometimes the act of reading a gene, not its product, does the regulating, Kornienko, Guenzl, Barlow and Pauler review in a 2013 BMC Biology article. Their subject is long non-coding RNAs, stretches read into RNA that never builds a protein. Under two percent of the human genome codes for protein, yet most of it is read into RNA. About ten thousand such genes are logged in humans.

The review sorts cases where the RNA product itself acts from cases where the mere act of transcription switches a neighbour gene on or off. That second route works in place, along the same DNA stretch. The authors give tactics for telling the two apart in the lab. The split matters, they argue, because the tool you build differs if the act is all.
europmc-pmc3714284:
Rolando Herrero and a large team of co-authors reported a vaccine trial result in PLoS ONE in 2013 from Costa Rica. A vaccine against human papillomavirus types 16 and 18, which cause most cases of a throat cancer that is becoming more common, was tested against mouth infection. In the trial, 7,466 women aged 18 to 25 got either the HPV vaccine or a hepatitis A vaccine as a control.

Four years later, 5,840 women gave mouth samples. There were 15 cases of oral HPV16/18 infection in the control group and only one in the vaccine group, a claimed efficacy of about 93 percent. The matching figure for neck-of-womb infection was about 72 percent. The authors say the vaccine gives strong protection against oral infection.
europmc-pmc3715784:
Martin Schlapschy and seven co-authors described a method called PASylation in Protein Engineering, Design and Selection in 2013. Many protein drugs are cleared from the blood too fast by the kidneys, which weakens their effect. The team built loose chains of three simple building blocks, proline, alanine, and serine, that take up space in the blood much like a widely used synthetic coating called PEG.

Unlike PEG, these chains can be fused to a protein drug at the gene level, so the whole product can be made in bacteria with no extra chemical steps. The chains break down in the body, showed no toxicity or immune reaction in mice, and kept proteins such as interferon and growth hormone in circulation much longer, boosting their effect.
europmc-pmc3718784:
Jevin West and co-authors published a large-scale study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on gender in scholarly authorship. They studied over eight million papers across the natural sciences, social sciences, and humanities, drawn from the JSTOR collection. Their question was whether gender gaps in academic life show up in who gets named as an author, and where.

Even where total publication counts looked close to equal, closer checks found lasting gaps. In some fields men held most of the prized first and last author spots. Women were also much less likely to be the sole author of a paper. The authors warn that these quieter patterns of inequality can hide behind headline numbers that look fair.
europmc-pmc3738984:
Barbara Prietl, Gerlies Treiber, Thomas Pieber, and Karin Amrein wrote a review in Nutrients in 2013 on vitamin D and immune function. Vitamin D is best known for bone and mineral health. But the receptor for it, and the enzyme that activates it, turn up in many immune cells, including T cells, B cells, and monocytes.

Lab studies show that vitamin D calms some front-line immune cells and pushes the system toward a more tolerant state. Animal work and human supplement studies point to benefits for immune function, above all in autoimmune disease. The review gathers the evidence on inflammation control and on regulatory paths tied to autoimmune conditions, with special attention to type 1 diabetes.
europmc-pmc3739884: Tomochika Fujisawa and Timothy Barraclough revised a method for drawing species boundaries from single-gene data in Systematic Biology in 2013. Their hosted text is short and carries the study's abstract. The GMYC method fits branching models to a gene tree to separate species-level splits from within-species ones. Tests on simulated data showed accuracy depends mainly on average population size relative to the time between species splits, and that the single-threshold version beat the multiple-threshold one.
europmc-pmc3849184:
Yasumasa Kato, Shigeyuki Ozawa, Chihiro Miyamoto, Yojiro Maehata, Atsuko Suzuki, Toyonobu Maeda, and Yuh Baba review acid around tumors in Cancer Cell International in 2013. Tumor tissue often sits in an acidic bath, unlike healthy tissue. That acid state may help tumors grow and spread.

Lactic acid from sugar burning without oxygen was long blamed as the sole source. Cell pumps and carriers that push acid out of cells add to it, and carbon dioxide from a side sugar path adds more. Acid wakes enzymes that chew through tissue and turns on genes that aid spread, by a signal path apart from low oxygen. The review treats acidity as an active force in cancer, not a side waste, and a possible treatment target.
europmc-pmc3946184:
Mandy Truong, Yin Paradies, and Naomi Priest review the reviews on cultural competency training in health care in BMC Health Services Research in 2014. Such programs aim to help services work better with racial and ethnic minority patients and shrink health gaps. The team searched for review articles published from 2000 to mid-2012 and appraised each for quality, gathering nineteen reviews covering between five and thirty-eight studies each.

Outcomes fell into three groups: effects on patients, on providers, and on access to care. Most reviews found moderate evidence that provider behavior and care access improved, but weaker evidence that patients' health itself improved. Many underlying studies relied on self-report and weak designs. The authors call for rigorous trials that measure patient health and organizational change, not just provider attitudes.
europmc-pmc3961184:
Constant V. Edi and a large team dissect extreme insecticide resistance in the malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Around Tiassalé in Côte d'Ivoire, these mosquitoes had evolved very strong resistance to bendiocarb, a carbamate sprayed indoors, on top of resistance to pyrethroids and other classes. That combination threatens malaria control, which leans on treated nets and spraying. Genome-wide scans compared resistant and susceptible mosquitoes from several sites.

Overproduced detox enzymes from the CYP6 family stood out. Two of them, CYP6P3 and CYP6M2, conferred resistance to bendiocarb and pyrethroids when switched on in fruit flies, and CYP6M2 also covered DDT, spanning three insecticide classes. Strongly resistant mosquitoes also carried extra copies of the ACE-1 gene, including its resistant form, from a gene duplication. The authors call the pairing alarming for control programs.
europmc-pmc4029684:
Thomas Seel, Jorg Raisch, and Thomas Schauer present methods to measure joint angles from body-worn sensors, in Sensors in 2014. Such sensors, called inertial measurement units, track motion without cameras. Human bodies lack the flat faces and right angles of robots, so sensor placement cannot be assumed.

Their methods need no set mounting direction. They first find the joint axis and centre from the sensor data itself. They then read bending angles at the joint using only spin and acceleration sensors, with no reliance on a steady magnetic field. Trials with a leg amputee walking compared the method against a camera-based motion capture system. Knee angle errors stayed under a degree on the prosthetic side and near three degrees on the natural leg. Ankle errors sat near one degree.
europmc-pmc4047484:
Mudassar Ahmad, Melanie Hirz, Harald Pichler, and Helmut Schwab review protein making in the yeast Pichia pastoris, in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology in 2014. The yeast, now renamed Komagataella, grows to very dense cultures on methanol. Strong, tightly controlled promoters switch production on. Yields can reach grams of protein per litre.

It began over forty years ago as a feed protein project, killed by an oil price shock, then reborn as an expression host. Drug proteins and industrial enzymes are now made in it at trade scale. Hard cases remain: proteins built of many parts, ones that sit in membranes, and ones the yeast chews up. The review covers fixes on both sides, from redesigned expression vectors to engineered host strains and screens for champion producers. Membrane protein work gets special note as a recent breakthrough area.
europmc-pmc4086084:
Qi Zhao, Jian Ren, and colleagues developed GPS-SUMO, a tool that predicts where SUMO proteins attach to other proteins and where they dock without attaching. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. SUMO tags regulate many cell processes, but finding their sites across whole protein sets is slow work in the lab.

The tool covers both covalent attachment sites and SUMO-interaction motifs, the docking patches. A new prediction engine, tuned with a swarm optimisation method, was tested critically against existing tools and judged substantially better. A free web service is provided. With proteome-wide predictions in hand, researchers can now probe how attachment and docking cooperate in SUMO regulation, the authors say.
europmc-pmc4096384:
Glenda E. Gillies, Ilse S. Pienaar, Shiv Vohra, and Zahi Qamhawi reviewed sex differences in Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroendocrinology in 2014. Men develop Parkinson's more often than women, and sex is now recognised as shaping the risk and character of most major complex diseases.

The authors gather clinical and experimental evidence on the dopamine pathway that fails in Parkinson's. That pathway differs by sex in its basic organisation, which may explain male vulnerability. Female hormones, above all estradiol, protect against dopamine loss in experiments. Male hormone patterns fail to protect and may even worsen loss. The review argues that sex-specific, hormone-based therapies could improve treatment for both men and women.
europmc-pmc4147684:
Ruth McBride, Marjorie van Zyl, and Burtram C. Fielding reviewed the coronavirus nucleocapsid protein, a structural piece with many side jobs. Their review appeared in Viruses in 2014. Coronaviruses infect humans and many animals, causing illnesses from colds to fatal disease, and carry the largest genomes of any RNA virus.

The N protein wraps the viral genome into a complex and works with the membrane protein during assembly of new virus particles. It also boosts how efficiently the virus copies and assembles itself. The review covers the protein's layout inside the particle, where it sits in infected cells, and its many functions. Inside host cells it can derail the cell cycle and blunt interferon defences, underlining its multifunctional character.
europmc-pmc4176484:
Daniela E. Eigenmann, Mouhssin Oufir, and four co-authors compared four human cell lines as lab models of the blood-brain barrier in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS in 2013. Drug makers need a fast lab test for whether a new compound can cross into the brain. Human cell layers grown in dishes could serve, if they seal tightly enough.

The team grew each line, named hCMEC/D3, hBMEC, TY10, and BB19, and measured electrical resistance across the layer plus leakage of two marker dyes. All four lines made the expected junction proteins, though in differing amounts. The hBMEC line gave the tightest barrier in the best dish setup. Adding astrocyte or pericyte partner cells did not tighten any line, a result that narrows how such models should be built.
europmc-pmc4177084:
Osamu Tohyama, Yasuhiro Funahashi, and seven co-authors tested the drug lenvatinib in thyroid cancer models in the Journal of Thyroid Research in 2014. Lenvatinib blocks several receptor proteins that tumours use to grow new blood vessels and to drive their own growth. Thyroid cancers that no longer respond to standard care have few options.

Given by mouth to mice carrying human thyroid tumours, lenvatinib shrank growth in five differentiated, five anaplastic, and one medullary tumour models, and it cut vessel growth in most of them. In dishes it stopped growth directly in only two of eleven cell lines, one with high FGFR1 and one with a mutant RET protein, both targets of the drug. The main effect, the team concludes, is starving the tumour of blood flow.
europmc-pmc4271684:
Shefali Oza, Joy E Lawn, Daniel R Hogan, Colin Mathers, and Simon N Cousens estimate what newborn babies died of, country by country, from 2000 to 2013. Their study appeared in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2015. Deaths split into the first week of life and the three weeks after, since the causes differ between those spans.

For countries with strong death records the team used the records directly; for the rest they built models from study data in similar settings. Most causes fell over time, yet preterm birth problems stayed the top killer in 2013. The estimates show where newborn care efforts can save the most lives.
europmc-pmc4306884:
Natasha Khamisa, Brian Oldenburg, Karl Peltzer, Dragan Ilic, and Paul B Tchounwou surveyed nurses in South African hospitals about stress, burnout, satisfaction, and health. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in 2015. Most research on nursing strain comes from rich countries, leaving the picture in developing health systems thin.

Twelve hundred nurses at four hospitals were invited and about three quarters answered five questionnaires. Staffing problems linked most strongly to both burnout and low satisfaction, and burnout explained more of the variation in mental health than any other factor. Safety risks at work also dragged on satisfaction and health. The authors note the cost to patient care when nurses run empty.
europmc-pmc4355684:
David MacIntyre and colleagues tracked the vaginal microbiome through pregnancy in a British group of women, reporting in Scientific Reports in 2015. Most earlier work of this kind came from North American groups. The team sampled 42 women who went on to deliver at term, taking swabs at four points in pregnancy and again six weeks after birth, and read the bacteria by gene sequencing.

During pregnancy the community was mostly Lactobacillus, a group of bacteria, with low variety, but after birth it shifted sharply to less Lactobacillus and more variety in all women. Some women carried a form led by Lactobacillus jensenii, a pattern not stressed in North American reports. Which forms appeared also varied with ethnic background. The work warns that findings from one region may not fit another.
europmc-pmc4366184:
Graham Moore and co-authors set out Medical Research Council guidance on process evaluation in The BMJ in 2015. Complex health programs, such as anti-smoking or obesity efforts, combine many parts that interact, and trials of them report whether they worked but not how or why. Process evaluation fills that gap by studying delivery, quality, mechanisms, and setting. Earlier council guidance praised the idea but gave no method for doing it.

The new framework organizes process evaluation around implementation, mechanisms of impact, and context. It advises planning the work early, linking it to the trial's outcome measures, and reporting it clearly enough that others can repeat a program in a new setting. A good process study, the authors argue, tells policy makers whether a result came from the program itself, from patchy delivery, or from local conditions.
europmc-pmc4392984:
Massimo Masserini reviewed nanoparticles as ferries for drugs into the brain, in ISRN Biochemistry in 2013. The blood-brain barrier seals the brain's delicate environment, admitting ions and few small molecules while blocking most else. That seal also blocks most medicines, leaving many brain disorders hard to treat. Nanoparticles, engineered carriers about a billionth of a meter across, are a young strategy to slip drugs past the barrier or ride its own transport routes.

The review first explains the barrier's structure and physiology, then surveys the nanoparticle types most used in medicine, including lipid and polymer carriers that can be decorated with targeting molecules. It closes with hard questions: the possible toxicity of the particles themselves to nerve tissue, and the technical steps needed before laboratory promise becomes clinic routine. Heavy investment, Masserini argues, is justified by the unmet need.
europmc-pmc4601084:
Andrew P. Bailey and colleagues' 2015 fly study centres on fat droplets that protect stem cells from oxygen damage. In fruit fly larvae, glial cells form a niche that keeps neural stem cells dividing during starvation. The team tested that niche under low oxygen and oxidative stress. The work appeared in Cell and focuses on lipid droplets in the glial cells.

Droplets formed in the niche glia when stress rose. They pulled fragile fatty acids out of cell membranes and stored them in their cores, where damage spreads less easily. That lowered harmful oxygen byproducts and shielded both glia and stem cells. The study gives fat droplets a new job as antioxidants, a role that may apply in many tissues.
europmc-pmc4620584:
Working with colleagues, Benjamin S. Freedman published a 2015 study growing kidney organoids from human stem cells and editing them to model disease. Lab-grown kidney tissue could help study inherited kidney disorders. The team started from stem cells grown as hollow balls called epiblast spheroids. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

With one signal blocked, the spheroids formed segmented, nephron-like organoids holding tubule, podocyte, and vessel-type cells. The tubules moved test cargoes and reacted to a toxic chemical as real kidney tissue does. Using CRISPR editing, the team knocked out podocalyxin and saw cell junction defects. Knocking out either of two polycystic kidney disease genes produced cysts. The system offers a repeatable human model for kidney disease and repair.
europmc-pmc4663484:
A 2015 theoretical analysis by Mikhail A. Livshits and colleagues deals with isolating exosomes by differential centrifugation, the field's standard method. Exosomes are tiny vesicles, forty to one hundred nanometres wide, that carry disease markers. Labs using the same protocol with different rotors got inconsistent results. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

The authors derived formulas for what share of vesicles of each size pellets under given force and time, for both swinging bucket and fixed-angle rotors. They define a cut-off size above which vesicles fully sediment. Tests on vesicles from HT29 cell cultures matched the predictions. A free web calculator lets any lab adjust its protocol to its own rotor, which should make exosome preparations comparable across studies.
europmc-pmc4740184:
Johnson and a large melanoma team ask why only 30 to 40 percent of advanced melanoma patients respond to anti-PD-1 therapy. They also ask whether tumour cells' own antigen-presentation machinery predicts who benefits. Across 60 melanoma cell lines, the class II presentation molecules, MHC-II, appear in a distinct subset of tumours while class I is universal.

In two separate patient cohorts treated with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 drugs, MHC-II on tumour cells tracks with response, longer progression-free and overall survival, and heavier T-cell infiltration. Because a routine stain for HLA-DR can flag these tumours, the authors propose MHC-II testing as a practical way to select patients for checkpoint therapy.
europmc-pmc4749084:
Katie M. O'Brien, Kristen Upson, Nancy R. Cook, and Clarice R. Weinberg compare ways to correct chemical exposure measures for sample dilution, in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2016. Urine tests are usually adjusted for creatinine, and blood tests for fat-loving chemicals are adjusted for serum lipids. The authors argue that the standard fixes can leave bias behind.

They set up six causal scenarios in diagrams, covering influences like age and hydration on creatinine, and body mass and recent fat intake on lipids. Across 1,000 simulated studies for each case, they test seven adjustment methods for bias and coverage. Their new approach, standardization plus the dilution measure as a model covariate, stays nearly unbiased with honest coverage, and they recommend it for exposure studies.
europmc-pmc4757784:
Shohei Koyama leads a broad author team in Nature Communications in 2016 on why some lung tumors stop responding to immune therapy. Drugs that block the PD-1 checkpoint can shrink lung cancer, yet tumors often adapt and grow again. The team traced that rebound in mouse lung tumors and in samples from two patients.

Tumors that first shrank and then grew carried a second checkpoint, TIM-3, raised on the very immune cells the first drug had engaged. In mice, adding a TIM-3 blocker after PD-1 failure extended survival. The two patient cases showed the same TIM-3 rise at the point of relapse. The authors propose TIM-3 as both a warning sign of this escape route and a next target to block.
europmc-pmc4759884:
Panagiotis F. Sarris and four colleagues scan plant genomes in BMC Biology in 2016 for odd-shaped immune sensors. Plant cells guard themselves with NLR proteins, which spot germ invaders and raise the alarm. Some sensors carry extra parts fused on, and those parts may work as bait: germ weapons grab them, and the grab itself trips the alarm.

The team catalogued these fused sensors across flowering plants, among them 19 crop species, and checked a subset by hand in wheat and brassica lines. Some bait parts recur in distant plant families, and many match proteins that germs are known to attack. That match supports the bait idea. The catalogue, the authors say, points breeders toward fresh sources of disease resistance.
europmc-pmc4786684:
G. O. Sipe and five co-authors show in Nature Communications in 2016 that the brain's immune cells help rewire the seeing brain. When one eye is covered in young animals, the visual cortex shifts its allegiance to the open eye, a classic test of brain flexibility. Microglia, long cast as guards, were caught here acting as electricians.

During the sensitive period, covering an eye changed microglia shape, movement, and their touching of connections. The team focused on P2Y12, a sensor found on calm microglia that steers their reaching arms. Mice lacking the sensor kept their microglia response dull and lost the cortex shift entirely. The result gives immune cells a direct hand in experience-driven rewiring of the young brain.
europmc-pmc4802384:
Maria Carmen Collado and four co-authors challenge a textbook idea in Scientific Reports in 2016: that a baby's gut starts sterile and meets microbes first at birth. Early gut microbes program immune and metabolic health for years, so when the seeding starts matters. The team sampled fifteen mother-baby pairs, all full-term planned cesarean births, to keep collection clean.

Womb fluid and the placenta each carried a distinct microbe mix, sparse and low in variety, dominated by one broad group. Features of that mix matched the baby's first stool, hinting at transfer before birth. By three to four days old, the gut mix had shifted toward the microbes of first milk. The authors propose seeding begins before birth and continues through feeding.
europmc-pmc4866784:
Martin Ogonowski and co-authors tested in 2016 how tiny plastic bits affect the water flea Daphnia magna. Worry grows that microplastics harm small water animals that filter food from water. Most lab tests used smooth factory spheres, yet wild plastic is mostly weathered shards of mixed size. The team compared natural and human-made particles in the flea's food water.

At the tested sizes, two to five micrometers, and shares up to most of the food mix, flea life traits answered plastic much as they answered natural inert grains. Filter feeders handle grit well, which tempers alarm at these levels. Real-world risk checks should still use realistic shards and doses.
europmc-pmc4874484:
Ahmed Elbediwy and co-authors showed in 2016 that grip signals from the skin's base layer control two growth regulators, YAP and TAZ. Skin renews itself from stem cells in its basal layer and heals wounds fast. In that layer, YAP and TAZ sit in the nucleus, switched on, and they rise further after wounding. Removing both from adult mouse skin slowed basal cell growth, caused hair loss, and weakened repair.

Touch with the base membrane, through grip proteins called integrins and a Src signal, keeps YAP and TAZ in the nucleus. Daughter cells that lose that touch switch them off and mature. The same grip rule appears in other layered tissues and their cancers, a shared control for renewal.
europmc-pmc5000484:
Edin Smailhodzic, Wyanda Hooijsma, Albert Boonstra, and David J. Langley published a systematic review in BMC Health Services Research in 2016. They asked how patients use social media for health reasons, and what effects that use has on patients and on their ties with health workers. Their search first found 1,743 articles, of which 22 met the rules for full review.

The review sorts patient use into six kinds, led by seeking support, facts, and a sense of worth from others. Reported effects include better self-care and well-being, but also lost privacy, unwanted marketing, and habit-forming use. Ties with doctors could grow more equal and open, or turn strained, with some patients switching doctors. The work gives clinics a clear map of both the gains and the risks of health-related social media use.
europmc-pmc5007684:
Jeffrey L. Spees, Ryang Hwa Lee, and Carl A. Gregory review how mesenchymal stem and stromal cells aid repair, in Stem Cell Research & Therapy in 2016. These cells, first found in bone marrow, can form bone, cartilage, and fat. Early hopes held that given cells would settle in hurt tissue and rebuild it directly, but study results have shifted that view.

The review centers on three other routes. The cells release proteins and hormones that calm immune cells and help nearby cells survive. They pass mitochondria, the cell's power units, to damaged cells through tiny tubes or parcels. They also shed small vesicles loaded with RNA and other cargo. Knowing which route matters most for each injury could yield safer, more standard cell products and even cell-free drugs for tissue repair.
europmc-pmc5081484:
Fredrik Edfors and seven co-authors test whether RNA levels can stand in for protein levels in human cells, in Molecular Systems Biology in 2016. Biology often assumes a gene's transcript count mirrors its protein count, but reports conflicted. The team used targeted proteomics to count actual protein copies for a set of human proteins across tissues and cell lines, then compared those counts with matching RNA measurements.

Transcript and protein levels correlated poorly on their own. The fix is a conversion factor specific to each gene: once that RNA-to-protein ratio is applied, protein counts become predictable, and the factor holds across tissue types. The ratios vary hugely, from a few hundred protein copies per RNA molecule to several hundred thousand. So the world's growing transcriptome atlases can be used to estimate protein abundance, so long as each gene's own conversion factor travels with the data.
europmc-pmc5118584:
Jane Topolovec-Vranic and Karthik Natarajan reviewed social media recruiting for medical studies in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2016. Enrolling enough volunteers is a common bottleneck, and researchers have turned to social platforms as a new channel. The hosted text opens under a journal masthead that names the journal's editors; the review itself is the work of these two authors.

They found 30 studies that used social media alongside at least one other method. In 12, social media recruited best; in 15 it did not, and in 3 it tied. It shone for hard-to-reach groups, winning in six of eight such studies. Yet in most studies reporting demographics, its recruits differed from those reached by standard routes, and cost results were mixed, so the channel suits some studies better than others.
europmc-pmc5177284:
J. R. Adie and Mrs. Adie reported an inquiry into malaria and mosquitoes in the Kashmir Valley in The Indian Medical Gazette in 1913, in abstract of a paper given to the 1912 Malaria Conference. Their survey covered the valley floor around Srinagar and Ganderbal, some twenty miles by ten, worked from April to October 1912.

Local practitioners held that Srinagar itself has practically no malaria and no anopheline mosquitoes. Cases seen in July to September, they said, are imported from the lowlands. The Adies' observations generally confirm this. They describe a high valley of rice fields and a robust, well-fed population, and note Dr. Neve's rule that malaria grows commoner as one descends from the capital toward places like Uri and Punch.
europmc-pmc5197584:
P. V. Gharpure, of Grant Medical College in Bombay, counts primary cancers in fifty years of post-mortem records. The records run from 1877 to 1926 and cover some six thousand autopsies. From them he gathered just 36 cases of primary carcinoma. His paper, read before the Bombay branch of the British Medical Association, concentrates on four organs where telling primary from secondary growth is hardest: the liver, stomach, pancreas, and gall-bladder.

Fourteen cases named the liver as the primary site, but Gharpure accepts only two as beyond doubt. In the rest, details such as missing notes on the uterus or prostate left room for a hidden primary elsewhere. The two solid cases shared a pattern: a little-changed organ size, marked multilobular cirrhosis, and a fast-growing tumor. His scrutiny is a lesson in how loosely the label "primary" had been applied.
europmc-pmc5253684:
Zhen Liang and ten colleagues reported DNA-free genome editing of bread wheat in Nature Communications in 2017. CRISPR editing usually delivers its machinery as DNA, which can lodge in the plant's genome and adds stray mutations elsewhere. For crop breeding, avoiding foreign DNA entirely and cutting off-target changes are the top goals.

Instead of DNA, the team delivered ready-made CRISPR protein-RNA complexes, called ribonucleoproteins, into immature wheat embryos. The full protocol takes seven to nine weeks and yields four to five independent mutants per hundred embryos. Deep sequencing showed off-target changes were far rarer than with DNA delivery, and no off-target mutations were found in the mutant plants. Because no foreign DNA is used, the plants are fully transgene-free. The authors argue the method should transfer to other crops and ease public acceptance of edited varieties.
europmc-pmc5312084:
Robert P. Dickson and co-authors mapped bacteria in healthy lungs in mBio in 2017. DNA tests had shown that healthy lungs are not sterile, as once thought. Doubters warned that scopes pick up mouth bacteria on the way down. The team set out to test if scope samples show the true lung mix, and how bacteria reach the lungs.

Eight healthy adults had careful scope sampling, with shielded brushes and lung washes, plus strict controls for stray DNA. Mouth and lung samples matched far more than the controls did, so scope passage added little noise. Signs of entry peaked near the split of the airways. That pattern fits tiny, silent inhaling of mouth fluid as the main route, more than spread along the airway walls. Lung burden and variety were lower than in the mouth, as a thin settled community would suggest.
europmc-pmc5390384:
Brisa S. Fernandes and five co-authors set out a case for a new field they call precision psychiatry, in a 2017 paper in BMC Medicine. Precision medicine tailors care to each person's genes, setting, and way of life. Psychiatry has lagged other fields in lab tests and tools that guide care for one patient, so the gain from catching up could be large.

The core promise lies in biomarkers, body measures that can sort patients and predict which treatment will help. New tools for genes, brain scans, and blood tests now make such finds more likely. The authors argue that giving the field its own name will build a clear identity and push work ahead. They sketch the near future they expect this shift to bring.
europmc-pmc5398984:
Benjamin M. Ellingson, Patrick Y. Wen, and Timothy F. Cloughesy propose updated scan rules for glioblastoma trials in a 2017 paper in Neurotherapeutics. Glioblastoma is a fast, deadly brain tumor. Trials judge new drugs in part by whether scans show the tumor shrinking or growing. The standing rules, called RANO, fixed many flaws of older guides, but hard cases remain, such as swelling that mimics growth after radiation.

The authors suggest measuring tumor volume rather than flat size, and using special scan maps that make tumors stand out. They drop the need to grade non-bright tumor parts by eye. They set the scan after radiation as the start point for new cases. Their rules also sort true growth from fake growth or fake shrinkage in both new and returned disease.
europmc-pmc5439484:
Bouis and Saltzman review the HarvestPlus evidence that biofortified crops improve nutrition. Their review appeared in Global Food Security. Micronutrient deficiency afflicts over two billion people. That is one in three worldwide. Biofortification breeds vitamins and minerals into staple crops. It reaches people with limited diet diversity. HarvestPlus has led the effort since 2003. More than 20 million people now grow these crops. Farm households eat them as well.

The review weighs efficacy and delivery experience. Farmer and consumer adoption get close attention. Breeding works; the evidence is strong, they conclude. Attention should shift to scaling up. The goal is one billion people by 2030. Three challenges block that path. Biofortified traits must enter public breeding programs. Consumer demand must be built deliberately. Policies and investments must integrate the approach. Institutional leadership is the missing ingredient, they argue.
europmc-pmc5461484:
Grancini and co-authors make perovskite solar cells last a full year by joining two forms of the material. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Perovskite cells now convert over a fifth of sunlight to power. They still break down far too fast for market use. Moisture, heat, and ultraviolet light all degrade them. A device for sale must hold its output for decades. The team layered a stable flat form over the stronger three-dimensional form.

The joined cells still performed well. Carbon-based versions reached about 13 percent efficiency. Standard porous versions reached just under 15 percent. Output held steady for a year of running. The team then scaled the idea up. They printed modules ten centimeters square. The process matched industrial practice. The modules reached about 11 percent efficiency. They ran over 10,000 hours with no loss at all. Low cost completes the case for the design.
europmc-pmc5535284:
Stein and the WHO World Mental Health Survey collaborators report a global study in BMC Medicine on social anxiety disorder. Most prior data came from rich Western countries. This survey pooled 28 community studies with 142,405 respondents. It measured prevalence, onset, impairment, and treatment across income levels. The patterns proved strikingly consistent worldwide.

Lifetime prevalence averaged 4.0 percent across all countries, they report. Rates ran lowest in poorer countries and highest in the Americas. Onset came early everywhere, and impairment hit work and social life alike. Women, the young, and the unmarried faced higher risk. Treatment lagged most where incomes were lowest.
europmc-pmc5541084:
Aide and co-authors present a review on PET scan measurement in cancer care. Scans at different hospitals can give different numbers for the same tumor. Such gaps weaken trials that span many centers. The authors explain how shared standards can close those gaps.

Much of the review covers the EARL accreditation program for FDG PET/CT. It sets common rules so uptake values and tumor volumes can be compared across sites. The authors describe checks of the program across tumor types. They also report a survey of 51 accredited centers. Readers get a clear guide to making scan numbers more alike in daily work and research.
europmc-pmc5606984:
Kim and co-authors report a cancer immunotherapy study in Nature Communications. Gram-negative bacteria shed tiny spheres called outer membrane vesicles. These packets are not alive, yet they stir the immune system. No one had tried them against cancer before.

Given into the body, the vesicles gathered in tumor tissue. They triggered output of two antitumor signals, CXCL10 and interferon-gamma. Established tumors were fully wiped out in the mouse tests. The protection lasted, and later tumor challenges were rejected too. Mice lacking interferon-gamma got no benefit, proving that signal is required. No notable side effects appeared. The vesicles came from engineered E. coli with tamed toxin. Readers see a new, cell-free way to wake up antitumor immunity.
europmc-pmc5627684:
Hopkins, Gillilan, and Skou describe updates to the BioXTAS RAW software in the Journal of Applied Crystallography. Small-angle X-ray scattering reveals the size and shape of molecules in solution. Raw detector images must be reduced before analysis. Many tools cover only part of that chain.

RAW is a free, open-source Python program with a graphical interface. It turns two-dimensional detector images into scattering profiles. Standard steps like averaging and subtraction are built in. It estimates radius of gyration and molecular weight. Advanced work includes inverse Fourier transforms and shape envelopes. Data from chromatography-coupled runs get their own tools. The program runs at beamlines and on personal machines alike. It covers Windows, Mac, and Linux. Readers get a single no-cost pipeline from detector image to publishable analysis.
europmc-pmc5636984:
Hamam and co-authors review tiny RNA molecules in the blood as signs of breast cancer. Their review covers microRNAs that travel in the blood of patients. Such markers could aid early diagnosis and track how treatment works. The authors note that blood tests for these molecules are still hard to standardize.

The review explains how microRNAs form and how they silence genes. It weighs the strengths and limits of blood microRNAs as tests. The authors warn that many of these molecules come from normal body responses, not the tumor itself. Open questions cover disease specificity, sample handling, and how to normalize test results.
europmc-pmc5644184:
He and co-authors report a cancer study in a clinical cancer research journal. It examines a circular RNA in triple negative breast cancer. Microarray screening found circGFRA1 raised in these tumor cells. PCR tests confirmed the rise in cell lines and tissues. Higher levels tracked with poorer patient survival.

Knocking down circGFRA1 slowed cell growth in lab tests. It also promoted cell death and shrank mouse xenograft tumors. Reporter assays showed circGFRA1 binds miR-34a directly. The GFRA1 gene product binds that microRNA too. So the circular RNA acts as a sponge, or competing endogenous RNA. This raises GFRA1 expression. The authors propose circGFRA1 as a biomarker and therapy target.
europmc-pmc5748484:
Sigismund, Avanzato, and Lanzetti review fresh roles of the EGFR receptor in cancer. EGFR normally guides growth and upkeep of epithelial tissue. In lung and breast cancer and glioblastoma, it drives tumor growth. It also marks tumors that resist drugs.

The review first covers the standard ligand driven pathway and its control by cell uptake. It then turns to newer, non-standard roles of the receptor. These include stress driven movement inside the cell, autophagy, and energy use. The authors close by weighing what these roles could mean for future cancer drugs.
europmc-pmc5755684:
Mägi and co-authors present MR-MEGA, a method for pooling genome studies across ancestry groups. Shared causal variants can boost power when studies span many populations. Yet effect sizes can differ in ways tied to ancestry. Standard pooling handles that gap poorly.

MR-MEGA models each variant's effect as a function of genetic axes. Those axes come from allele frequency gaps between studies. Tests show more power than fixed and random effects pooling. Fine mapping also sharpens, with small credible sets at diabetes loci. Use on kidney data from 71,461 people gave stronger signals where ancestry tied effects differed.
europmc-pmc5770584:
Lu and co-authors review ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron and lipid damage. This death path differs from apoptosis and other known paths. It runs when a key defense enzyme fails or its fuel runs out. Small molecules that trigger it can slow tumor growth in tests.

The review sets out how ferroptosis works at the molecular level. It then weighs the role of this death path in cancer growth. Drug resistance is a special focus, since ferroptosis can restore drug sensitivity. Strategies to tune the process for treatment close the account.
europmc-pmc5784884:
Varma and co-authors hunt for chemical signatures of Alzheimer disease in brain and blood. The metabolic roots of the disease stay poorly understood. The team measured set panels of metabolites in brain tissue from an autopsy cohort. Machine learning picked the markers that split disease from control samples.

A panel of 26 metabolites, mostly from two lipid classes, separated the groups well. The team then tested the same panel in blood from two large aging cohorts. Blood levels tied to brain shrinkage measures and spinal fluid markers of disease. Such signatures could track early, silent stages of Alzheimer disease.
europmc-pmc5797284:
Chiurchiù and co-authors review how fatty signaling molecules shape long-term inflammation. Some of these lipids start and sustain immune attack. Others help switch it off. When control fails, brief defense turns into lasting disease.

The review sorts the lipids into four families. It covers classic eicosanoids and pro-resolving mediators. It also covers sphingolipids and endocannabinoids. The authors link each family to cell signals in diseases like arthritis, diabetes, and bowel disease. Readers get a clear map of which lipids drive harm and which aid repair. The diseases traced run from arthritis and diabetes to lupus and multiple sclerosis.
europmc-pmc5807384:
Barbui and co-authors explain the 2016 WHO rules for myeloproliferative neoplasms. These are blood cancers where marrow makes too many cells. The world guide sorts them into seven types. Clear rules help doctors tell look-alike diseases apart.

Focus falls on three types tied to JAK2, CALR, or MPL gene faults. Tables lay out the test results each diagnosis needs. Changes sharpen the line between masked polycythemia vera and thrombocythemia. They also split early from advanced primary myelofibrosis. The authors flag disputes and give practice tips. Readers get a working guide to a complex rule change.
europmc-pmc5808284:
Bonaz and co-authors review the vagus nerve in the gut-brain axis. Gut microbes, the gut, and the brain talk both ways. The vagus nerve is a main wire for that talk. It senses microbe products and carries word to the brain.

The nerve also sends calming signals back down. One pathway damps gut inflammation and seals the gut wall. Stress weakens vagus tone, and low tone shows in bowel disorders. The authors weigh nerve stimulation as a fix. Readers get a tour of the nerve that links microbes, mood, and gut health.
europmc-pmc5821084:
Goodall and co-authors map the essential genome of E. coli K-12. Some genes are so vital that losing one kills the cell. Finding them guides drug hunts and genome notes. A method called TraDIS spots them with swarms of gene disruptions.

The team built a dense disruption library in this lab workhorse strain. They checked its calls against gold-standard deletion sets. Careful statistics corrected for gene and genome size. Manual reading found fine features that math alone missed. Some genes were newly marked essential, and some old marks were wrong. Readers get a benchmarked list and a sharper method for other genomes.
europmc-pmc5836084:
Roche opens a special issue of Cancers on the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in cancer. The editorial frames why this cell program matters. Epithelial cells can loosen their bonds and turn mobile. Tumors hijack that switch to spread.

The switch is rarely complete in real tumors. Hybrid cells carry traits of both states and travel in clusters. Reversing the switch may seed growth at distant sites. Triggers range from low oxygen to signals from nearby stroma. The issue's reviews then track the program across head and neck, breast, and ovarian cancers. Drug resistance is a recurring cost.
europmc-pmc5877384:
Camomilla and co-authors review wearable inertial sensors for sport performance. Their systematic review appeared in Sensors. Tiny magneto-inertial sensors are now cheap and non-invasive. They suit measures taken during training or competition. The team searched four databases for studies in athletes. Screening 2,040 papers left 286 studies and 23 reviews. Tasks that predict injury or count activity were excluded.

Most kept studies analysed technique, with 163 papers. Others assessed motor capacity, physical demands, or activity type. Elite and sub-elite athletes formed most of the samples. Sessions ran mainly in the field during training. Team, water, and winter sports featured strongly. The authors give reliability notes and future trends.
europmc-pmc5905184:
Zhang and co-authors review methods for extracting and isolating natural products. Their comprehensive review appeared in Chinese Medicine. Natural products have long driven new drug discovery. Their active amounts in source material are usually tiny. Getting them out is slow and labour heavy. That bottleneck limits wider use in drug work.

The review covers both classic and modern techniques. Solvent extraction, distillation, and pressing are set beside newer tools. Isolation methods, including chromatography, get full treatment. Each method's strengths, weaknesses, and examples are given. Readers can match a method to their material and goal. The paper serves as a practical handbook for the field.
europmc-pmc6003984:
Lin and co-authors develop single-breath-hold photoacoustic computed tomography of the breast. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The system images blood vessels deep in breast tissue. It reaches 4 centimetres deep in living patients. In-plane detail is 255 micrometres, at ten frames per second. A full volume scan takes about 15 seconds. One held breath thus avoids motion blur in the images.

Tumours stand out through their denser vessel networks, they report. The method needs no ionising radiation or injected contrast. Patients ranged from B to DD cup sizes. All tumours were found in the test group. Dynamic imaging can also probe tissue stiffness.
europmc-pmc6005684:
Nakane, Kimanius, Lindahl, and Scheres present multi-body refinement for cryo-EM data in RELION. Their paper appeared in eLife. Flexible molecular complexes challenge standard single-particle analysis. Their tool treats a complex as several rigid bodies. Each body moves on its own within the whole. Separate focused refinements improve each body's reconstruction. Partial signal subtraction sharpens the results step by step. The process runs in a fully automated way.

Orientation data across all particles feeds a motion analysis, they report. It yields movies of the most important movements. Test cases were a malaria parasite ribosome and a yeast spliceosome. The method reveals structure and dynamics together.
europmc-pmc6023384:
Lundstrom reviews viral vectors used in gene therapy. His article appeared in Diseases. Viral vectors are altered viruses that carry genes into cells. They now treat metabolic, heart, muscle, blood, and eye diseases. They are also used against infections and many cancers.

Better vector design and delivery drove this revival. The review walks through the main vector families. Adenoviruses, retroviruses, and adeno-associated viruses all feature. Gene silencing appears as a reversible option. Animal studies and human trials supply the evidence. Several vector-based drugs have won approval worldwide. Readers get a broad map of a field back at the front of medicine.
europmc-pmc6101584:
Rambaut and co-authors present Tracer 1.7, software for reading Bayesian phylogenetics output. Their article appeared in Systematic Biology. Evolutionary trees are often built by Markov chain sampling. That sampling leaves huge trace files behind. Checking them by eye is slow and error-prone.

Tracer summarizes the sampled values automatically. It draws density plots and joint views. It flags poor mixing through sample size scores. Files from many popular programs load directly. Users can merge runs and compare them side by side. Demographic history can also be rebuilt from traces. The tool is open source. Readers get a standard checkpoint before trusting an evolutionary tree.
europmc-pmc6117384:
Wang and co-authors present a research article in Frontiers in Microbiology on a probiotic strain and gut health in piglets. Weaning often harms the gut barrier of young pigs. That raises the risk of infection. The strain studied is Lactobacillus plantarum ZLP001.

The team tested the strain against harmful E. coli in piglets. Pretreatment kept the gut from leaking a tracer dye. It also kept key sealing proteins in place. Levels of inflammatory signals fell. Gut microbe mixes shifted toward bacteria that make butyrate. Those bacteria tracked with higher fatty acid levels in feces. The authors say the strain guards the gut in two ways at once.
europmc-pmc6163284:
Avery and Hoffmann wrote a review in Nutrients on selenium, selenoproteins, and immunity. Selenium is an essential trace nutrient needed for development and many body processes. The immune system depends on getting enough of it from food. Selenium acts mainly through proteins that contain it.

Humans have 25 such selenoproteins, with varied jobs. The review sums up how they regulate immune cell functions. New high-throughput methods and computer tools have sharpened that picture. When the system goes off balance, inflammation and immune disease can follow. The authors suggest that targeting single selenoproteins may one day tune immunity more precisely than diet alone.
europmc-pmc6179084:
Hill and co-authors present a study in Medical Education Online on the stressors facing medical students, in their own words. Student stress is tied to depression, burnout, loss of empathy, and poor grades. Yet recent multi-school studies asking students directly were lacking. The team focused on the millennial generation of trainees.

Students at Florida's nine medical schools answered an anonymous online survey on wellness and distress. Their open answers name scheduling chaos and unclear academic demands as top burdens. Many said school used their time badly and changed plans without warning. The authors aim to guide programs and policies that cut student distress. The quotes give the findings a direct, human voice.
europmc-pmc6205984:
Keller and co-authors reviewed cell counts in the mouse brain. The mouse brain is the most studied brain of any species. Yet basic cell numbers are still patchy. The review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy. It gathers counts for the whole brain and its parts.

The team searched past studies for density values. They covered neurons and support cells such as astrocytes and microglia. For well-studied areas, counts exist for main cell types. For most areas, counts are sparse or absent. Values also vary a lot between sources. The authors say new methods are needed. A full, shared dataset would help both theory and lab work.
europmc-pmc6265284:
Zhao and co-authors catalogued long non-coding RNAs across the Arabidopsis plant genome. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. These RNAs do not code for proteins, yet they steer gene activity. The team found 6,510 of them under normal and stress conditions. Many run opposite to a protein coding gene. Those reverse copies are called natural antisense transcripts.

One such RNA, named MAS, drew deep study. Cold switches MAS on. MAS is needed to switch on its partner gene, MAF4. That gene holds back early flowering after cold. MAS works by guiding a helper protein to the gene. The helper adds a chemical mark that favours activity. The catalogue widens what is known about plant gene control. It also shows how reverse RNAs can raise, not just lower, gene output.
europmc-pmc6272784:
He and co-authors review how curcumin links inflammation to chronic disease. Their review appeared in Molecules. Lasting oxidative stress can drive lasting inflammation. That inflammation in turn feeds many chronic diseases. Cancer, diabetes, heart disease, and bowel disease are on the list. Curcumin blocks oxidation and calms inflammation in lab tests.

The review traces how stress signals switch inflammation on. Curcumin acts on several of those switches at once. Trials have tested it in bowel disease, arthritis, and eye inflammation. Many other chronic conditions are also covered. Safety looks strong across those tests. About one hundred firms now sell curcumin products of many forms. The authors argue that the stress to inflammation chain is the key link. Breaking it could prevent more than one disease at once.
europmc-pmc6342984:
Wang and co-authors present MuSiC, a method to read cell mixes in bulk tissue. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications. Bulk RNA data blend signals from many cell types. That blending hides which cells drive disease. Single-cell data give pure type profiles instead. MuSiC bridges the two kinds of data.

The method weights genes that stay consistent across people. It also weights genes consistent within a cell type. That makes single-cell profiles transfer well to bulk samples. The team tested it on pancreas and kidney tissue. Human, mouse, and rat data were all used. It beat older methods, above all for close cell types. The tool lets researchers mine vast bulk datasets. Those datasets cover many diseases single-cell work has not reached.
europmc-pmc6356784:
Van Belleghem and co-authors review how bacteriophages interact with human immunity. Their review appeared in Viruses. Phages are viruses that infect bacteria, not human cells. The body hosts them in enormous numbers. They were once seen as mere bystanders. Their immune effects were thought to run through bacteria alone.

New work shows phages act on immunity directly. Their effects are usually anti-inflammatory in nature. They shape early defenses through cell uptake and cytokines. They also steer antibody production and T cell balance. That can change how bacterial infections end. The authors present a computer model of these dynamics. It predicts a broad role for the phage community. Phage therapy may gain from that insight.
europmc-pmc6370184:
Voerman and co-authors present an individual participant data meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine. They pooled data on 162,129 mothers and children from 37 pregnancy cohorts in Europe, North America, and Australia. The study asked how a mother's weight before pregnancy and her weight gain during it affect child obesity risk.

Higher maternal BMI and excess gain both raised the risk of child overweight at every age band. Effects grew stronger in late childhood, with odds over fourfold for children of mothers with obesity. Excess gain added only a small extra risk within each BMI group. The authors urge prevention efforts to focus on weight before pregnancy.
europmc-pmc6533084:
Verbruggen and co-authors give a consensus guide to the stop-signal task. Their guide appeared in eLife. The task measures how fast a person can cancel an action. Such response inhibition matters in daily life. Its failure links to many brain and mental disorders.

Small design choices can spoil results from this task. Studies vary in design, delay settings and analysis. The authors agreed on 12 easy-to-follow recommendations. They flag what goes wrong when each rule is skipped. Open-source tools come with the guide. Those tools help plan sample size, run the task and analyse data. The goal is more accurate and comparable stop-signal research.
europmc-pmc6566984:
Soliman reviews the evidence linking dietary fiber to lower cardiovascular risk, writing in Nutrients. Fiber is plant carbohydrate that human enzymes cannot digest. Its soluble forms, found in oats, barley and fruit, dissolve into gels that drag cholesterol out of the body. Its insoluble forms, in bran, nuts and whole grains, add bulk and speed the gut along.

Recommended intakes run to 38 grams a day for men and 25 for women, yet most Americans fall short. The review explains fiber's chemistry and gut fermentation, then weighs animal and human evidence on cholesterol and atherosclerosis. One striking result: adding gel-forming soluble fiber to statin treatment doubled the drug's cholesterol-lowering effect in pooled trial data.
europmc-pmc6617684:
Jayaraj and co-authors review the double role of inflammation after ischemic stroke. Their article appears in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. Stroke ranks third among causes of death and disability worldwide. Most strokes are ischemic, from a blocked artery. The damage does not end when blood flow stops.

After the first injury, immune signals wake resident brain cells. Neutrophils, monocytes, and T cells then enter the damaged zone. Their attack can kill more cells and widen the injury. Yet the same response later supports repair and recovery. Timing decides which face dominates. The review covers oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and matrix enzymes as amplifiers. The authors argue that time-aware therapy could protect the brain better.
europmc-pmc6631684:
Liu compares plasmid DNA and mRNA as vaccine technologies. Her review appears in Vaccines. Both platforms date back to the 1990s. Both build vaccines straight from a protein's gene sequence. That allows fast, generic manufacturing. It also suits personalised cancer vaccines. DNA vaccines reached licence first in veterinary medicine. Recent excitement, though, has swung toward mRNA.

The review weighs theory against trial evidence. Both platforms needed potency boosts over the years. Teams tweaked the constructs, added adjuvants, and improved delivery. mRNA provokes stronger innate inflammation than DNA. That helps immunity but raises toxicity questions. Liu closes with the clinical status of mRNA candidates. She sets it against human DNA vaccine results.
europmc-pmc6646484:
Hesamian and co-authors appraise deep learning methods for medical image segmentation. Their review appears in the Journal of Digital Imaging. Segmentation outlines organs and lesions in scans like CT and MRI. It is a first, critical step in diagnosis pipelines. Hand-built feature systems dominated for years. Deep learning has now taken over the task. The authors survey the leading network designs. They compare strengths and weaknesses structure by structure.
