GAO found that excluding the allowance would substantially raise the share of troops eligible to apply. The effect was large under an income limit of 50 percent of area median income. But GAO warned that other factors may limit real use of the programs. Awareness, supply of units, and program rules all shape take-up. The report separates paper eligibility from likely outcomes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-84:
A new way to surge Navy ships is tested in GAO-06-84, a report GAO released on November 22, 2005. Since 2000, Congress has given the Navy about $50 billion a year to operate and maintain its forces, which support around 376,000 personnel. The Fleet Response Plan aimed to send more ships to sea on short notice. It changed how ships train, maintain, and deploy. GAO judged the plan's management and testing.

GAO found that the Navy had taken many positive steps to set up the plan. But it had not fully built a comprehensive management approach to guide it. Sound practice calls for a clear mission, linked goals, and ways to monitor progress. Rigorous testing of the new deployment model was also lacking. GAO urged the Navy to manage the change as carefully as the operations it enables.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-384:
Three federal agencies judge the same schools for different aid programs, and their reviews overlap. GAO revisited the duplication in GAO-07-384, a report dated March 8, 2007. The veterans agency paid about $2.1 billion in education aid in fiscal year 2006. Over 470,000 people received it. State approving agencies vet schools for the veterans program. They received about $19 million that year. GAO first flagged the overlap in 1995.

State agencies gained new duties in 2001, GAO found. They now promote apprenticeships and license testing too. Their funding rose from $13 million in fiscal year 2003 to $19 million in fiscal year 2006. It is set to fall from fiscal year 2008. Many programs they approve also pass education or labor reviews. Coordination between the reviewers is rare. GAO asked what extra value the state layer adds. It urged joint steps to cut the overlap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-584:
Trucking firms with the worst safety records do not always face review first, and GAO-07-584, a GAO report of August 28, 2007, studies the queue. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration targets carriers for compliance reviews using SafeStat scores. The scores blend crash rates and violations. GAO asked whether the queue in fact puts the riskiest carriers at the front.

The policy does catch many high-risk firms, GAO found, and that saves lives. But it skips some of the worst. A companion GAO report in June 2007 showed a math model beats the score formula at spotting crash risk. This study adds field checks at nine offices on how reviews stay thorough and even. It also tracks fines: the law calls for maximum fines in set cases, and the agency levies them less often than required. One fix offered: fast-track carriers in the worst 5 percent on crash scores.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-84:
Doctor shortage areas are mapped in GAO-07-84, a report dated October 24, 2006. The Health and Human Services Department marks areas that lack primary care doctors. Over 30 federal programs use the marks to steer funds and benefits. A 2002 law told GAO to review it. GAO counted the areas and read studies of the method.

More than 5,500 shortage areas existed as of September 2005. About half cover places or groups of people. The rest are clinics and other facilities in every state. Bonus pay for doctors and loan relief for health workers ride on the marks. The lure of those gains can skew the map, GAO noted. Some areas keep marks they no longer merit. GAO urged the department to drop stale marks in a public list. It also urged a finished plan to revise the system. The department agreed with both calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-984:
A new business model for the reserves is urged in GAO-07-984, dated June 20, 2007. Over 580,000 reservists were activated between September 2001 and March 2007. Repeated call-ups strain families, employers, and units. Homeland defense duties compete with war missions. The force was built for a different era's demands. GAO ties the case to fiscal and security facts. Pay and bonus systems get close review. Some jobs sit overfilled while others run short. Bonuses flow even where staffing exceeds targets.

Defense leaders lack a full map of those mismatches, GAO found. Services do not report every over- and underfilled specialty. Reasons for the gaps go unreported as well. GAO urged yearly reporting on specialty fill rates. It also urged a management plan for recruiting and retention. Bonus use should be justified post by post. The department agreed that tracking matters. The statement blends testimony with a same-day pay report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-284:
Workers' compensation payments are stress-tested in GAO report GAO-08-284, issued February 26, 2008. The federal program paid over $1.8 billion in fiscal year 2006 to staff hurt on the job. The Labor Department's compensation office runs the payments. GAO opened the review on its own authority. It sampled claim files at random and visited five district offices.

GAO judged how well the office guards against improper payments. It hunted for weak points in how wage-loss checks are made. It also checked how fully known overpayments are clawed back. The title points the way: better data and management would strengthen the fight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-384:
GAO covers aviation noise research at two agencies in its report GAO-08-384, dated February 15, 2008. Community anger over aircraft noise blocks airport growth that the nation needs to meet rising travel demand. The Federal Aviation Administration studies noise effects on communities, while NASA works on quieter engines and airframes.

GAO found the two agencies' plans cover a wide range of projects and line up well, through joint planning groups and shared advisory panels. Their goals aim to cut the number of people exposed to heavy noise, mostly by quieting aircraft at the source. But success is far from sure: new technology must still be proven, built into production aircraft, and taken up by fleets. Both agencies had no comment on the draft report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-684:
Land swaps between Washington, D.C. and the federal government were set by a 2006 law. Poplar Point is the best known site in the deal. GAO-08-684, dated June 13, 2008, tracks the status of each transfer and the steps still left before building can start.

As of June 6, 2008, no land had changed hands by title, though control transfers took effect on December 15, 2006. Nine swaps were set to finish by the end of summer 2008. Poplar Point may move by fall 2009 if its land-use plan wins approval. Other swaps hinge on a side deal over 12 acres. Full build-out will take many years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-84:
Reform at the United Nations has been a U.S. push for years. GAO-08-84, dated November 14, 2007, grades reform steps in five areas: ethics, oversight, buying, head office operations, and review of old mandates. An October 2006 GAO report found progress slow at that time.

The ethics office has moved furthest, with staff in place and a whistleblower shield. A new audit advisory panel should start by January 2008. The internal watchdog office grew stronger but still depends on UN funding in ways that curb its freedom. Buying and mandate review lag. GAO urges the State Department to grade reform results each year in its report to Congress.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol1-188:
Eduard von Hartmann, a young German ex-officer, published his Philosophie des Unbewussten in 1869 and startled Europe. W C Coupland's English translation of 1884 fills three volumes, and volume one here treats the phenomenology of the unconscious. That is: Hartmann gathers the signs of unconscious mind at work in body, instinct, and feeling.

His claim is large: an unconscious will and idea steer nature and human life beneath our waking thought. Decades before Freud, Hartmann made the unconscious a central concept of philosophy. The first volume builds his case from reflex, instinct, and the healing wisdom of the body. It is a strange, powerful book that its century could not ignore.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol2-188:
Volume two of Coupland's 1884 Hartmann turns from the signs of the unconscious to its metaphysics, its inner nature and law. Eduard von Hartmann's Philosophy of the Unconscious, first published in German in 1869, argues that one unconscious principle works through all nature. Volume one had surveyed its effects; this volume asks what that principle is.

Hartmann joins Schopenhauer's blind will to Hegel's unfolding idea, and finds both at once in the unconscious. From atoms to human genius, one striving, knowing power drives the whole, on his account. The system swept Germany and reached England in Coupland's careful English. Volume two is where the bold architecture stands tallest.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol3-188:
Coupland's third volume of Hartmann, from 1884, carries the Philosophy of the Unconscious into religion and history. Eduard von Hartmann's German work of 1869 had grown through many editions into a system touching everything. Having traced the unconscious in nature and in mind, he now asks what it means for faith and for the fate of mankind.

Hartmann reads history as the unconscious slowly schooling humanity out of its illusions of happiness. Religion, on his view, moves through stages toward a clear-eyed, somber wisdom. His pessimism, argued at full scale, made him one of the most debated thinkers of his age. Volume three completes Coupland's English Hartmann, system and all.
hering-condensed-materia-medica-1884:
Hering's guiding symptoms filled ten big volumes, and The Condensed Materia Medica of 1884 shrinks that wealth to pocket size. The second edition keeps Constantine Hering's marks and choices, so the strongest signs still stand out. A prescriber could carry the great man's life work in a coat pocket.

Condensing meant hard choices: only the symptoms Hering trusted most survive the cut. What remains reads like the distilled voice of the larger set, terse and ranked. Country doctors riding between patients prized such books, and this one ranks among the most portable forms of the great materia medica.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands, complete for 1600 to 1609, gathers chapters thirty-eight to fifty-three. Military events and the Nieuport campaign open the file. The siege of Ostend concentrates the war's middle years. Elizabeth's death, James's peace with Spain, and Spinola's command follow in sequence.

Peace deliberations in Spain meet a court that calls the truce beneath its dignity. Henry IV's designs and Spain's internal decay receive Motley's survey chapters. The States-General vote on the groundwork of the treaty near the close. A conclusion chapter ends the whole history with the truce of 1609. This single file holds the entire last act of Motley's epic. Readers can watch a war of religion settle, at last, into a treaty of exhaustion and recognition.
huysmans-against-grain-1884:
Joris-Karl Huysmans published Against the Grain in 1884, a French novel with almost no plot in the usual sense. Its hero, Des Esseintes, is a rich and tired nobleman. He shuts himself away in a house outside Paris. There he surrounds himself with rare books, scents, jewels, and art.

Most of the book lists what Des Esseintes loves and what he hates. His tastes stand against the plain tastes of the world outside. The novel became a guide for the Decadent movement, which prized art and artifice over nature. Its strange hero still draws readers who like beauty pushed to an extreme.
jacko-ape-man-yale-british-colonist-1884:
A Victoria newspaper told British Columbia a strange tale on July 4, 1884. The Daily British Colonist reported a creature called Jacko, caught by a train crew above Yale. The headline asked what the thing was, and the report calls it a kind of gorilla.

Jacko was small, hairy, and strong, the crew said, and was kept in town for show. No trace of him stands past the news reports of that summer. Most now take the tale for a hoax or a tall yarn of the rails. Still, the report is read as the first draft of the Bigfoot legend.
jevons-investigations-currency-finance-1:
Jevons died in 1882, and his Investigations in Currency and Finance appeared in 1884, edited by H. S. Foxwell. The volume gathers the papers Jevons had written on money, prices, and trade crises across his career. Foxwell, a fellow economist, arranged them as a memorial to the marginal revolution's most empirical mind.

The papers track the value of gold, chart price movements with early index numbers, and test the idea that trade cycles follow a rhythm. Jevons even tried to link commercial crises to sunspots and harvests, a bold guess that later scholars judged wrong but fertile. Throughout, statistics serve theory: he hunts patterns in the numbers the way a detective hunts clues. The book preserves the working side of a founder of modern economics, counting and measuring where his rivals only reasoned.
jewett-country-doctor-1884:
A Country Doctor, printed in 1884, opens with chapters named The Last Mile and The Farm-House Kitchen. Later heads follow a great change, a stay at Dr. Leslie's, and new outlooks for its heroine. The book grew from Jewett's own life beside a country physician father.

Nan Prince, a bright farm girl raised by that doctor, resolves to study medicine herself. Her choice costs her a marriage offer and the good opinion of proper society. She holds her course all the same. When women doctors were still rare, the novel gave American readers a serious and early portrait of a professional woman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-phine: Aaron ben Phinehas sat on the rabbinical college of Lemberg. In that role he was among the rabbis who had to decide a case in matrimonial law. The case concerned the widow of a man killed by the bands of Chmielnicki. Aaron died at Lemberg on June 20, 1651. The case is cited from a responsum printed at Ostrog in 1796.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abd-servant-184:
Abd is an Arabic word meaning servant, placed first in many compound names of Jews in Arabic-speaking lands. The name that follows it is always the name of a god, the entry explains. In early times it could be the proper name of a god, as in Abd-Uzza or Abd-Shams. Phoenician, Aramean, and even Hebrew cases of the same pattern are given.

As belief in one God grew, first among Jews and later among Mohammedans, the second part changed. It became an adjective for one of God's traits, used as a name for God Himself. Abd-ul-Aziz, servant of the Mighty, is the case given. This shift in form, the entry says, helps a student date the men who bore such names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abot-the-father:
Abot, or Pirke Abot, is a small Mishnah tract of ethical sayings by rabbinic sages. It stands last among the nine tracts of Nezikin. Its name, the Fathers, points to the chief teachers whose maxims fill it.

Five chapters trace the chain of teaching from Moses through the Great Synod to Mishnah teachers. Sixty teachers speak across about four hundred and fifty years. Hillel asks who will care for him if he does not care for himself. Ben Zoma defines the wise, the hero, the rich, and the honored. Jews later read Abot in summer Sabbath services.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-b-minyomi-: Adda b. Minyomi was a Babylonian amora of the third century. He was a younger peer of Rabina I. and of Huna Mar b. Iddi. At times he is quoted with no name at all. The quote runs as the Court of Nehardea. Three Talmud tracts hold such cites. The hosted text is very short. It gives his age, his land, his two peers, and that court tag. It gives no teaching in his own words and no facts of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aga-benjamin-88:
Benjamin Aga led the Karaites of the Crimea. He died in 1824. He was royal cash keeper to Selim Ghyrey Khan, the last Tatar ruler of the Crimea. Karaite books call him Ha-Neeman, the Trusted. His father Samuel, who died in 1770, bore the same call name and most likely the same post. When the khan fled his rebels, Aga went with him to St. Petersburg.

In 1795 Aga led a Karaite team to the capital. They asked the empress to free their sect from the double tax laid on Jews. They won that freedom. They won land grants and rights they had not sought as well. The win set a mark for later Karaite claims in law. A marble stone at Guzlowo marks the trip. Aga had lent the khan large sums and hoped to claim them back on that first trip north.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahikar-984:
Ahikar is the hero of a wide-spread legend and the supposed author of many proverbs. In the Book of Tobit he appears as a kinsman of Tobit. He is also lord chancellor of Assyria under Sennacherib. Greek writers know a like figure under forms of the same name.

In the legend, childless Ahikar adopts his nephew Nadan and trains him as his heir. The nephew betrays him with forged letters, and Ahikar is sentenced to death. A friendly executioner hides him instead, and he returns in time to serve the king in Egypt. There he answers hard tasks, even building a castle between heaven and earth. Nadan dies in prison, fed on the proverbs he once scorned. The entry compares the Arabic, Armenian, Syriac, and other versions, and weighs their Jewish roots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-albo-joseph-108:
Joseph Albo was a Spanish preacher and theologian of the fifteenth century. He is known chiefly for his book on the groundwork of Judaism, the "'Ikkarim," or Principles. Little of his life is certain. He took part as a Jewish delegate in the long debate at Tortosa in 1413-14. Graetz puts his birth no later than 1380, and his death in 1444.

His teacher was Hasdai Crescas, author of "Or Adonai." His use of medical pictures hints that he may have practiced medicine. The first part of the "'Ikkarim" came out alone. A storm of abuse then drove him to add three more parts. He was charged with stealing his teacher's thoughts without credit. The entry finds that charge unproven, since master and pupil will naturally agree. His book, it argues, is best read as a defense of Judaism under attack.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfaquin-also-a: Alfaquin is a surname used in Spain. It was given, in general, to the king's physician. It was also borne by the king's secretary and interpreter. In Spain, Portugal, and Provence it matches the name hakim. That is the Arabic word for a physician, or for a sage. The entry is only a few lines long. It explains the name and its use, and names no single bearer of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almeyda-jose-he: Jose Henriques de Almeyda was a writer in Amsterdam. He worked early in the eighteenth century. He wrote in Portuguese. His first book came out in Amsterdam in 1706. It is built of odes on words made from the letters of Torah. It was given to a patron in Amsterdam. The entry calls the book very rare. A second book of verse came out in 1712. It praised an envoy of the king of Portugal. That book is rare as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anaw-abraham-be: Abraham ben Jehiel ha-Rofe Anaw was a physician and rabbi in Rome. The entry places him at the start of the thirteenth century. It names him as father of two known sons. One son, Zedekiah, wrote the ritual work Shibbole ha-Leket. The other, Benjamin, was a liturgical poet. The entry is brief and cites Vogelstein and Rieger's history of the Jews in Rome for more detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antinoe-1584: Antinoe was a city in the south of Middle Egypt, on the east bank of the Nile. The emperor Hadrian founded it in the year 122. Jews seem to have come there with the Greeks, drawn by trade with the Red Sea port of Myso Hormus. In February 1896, C. Schmidt found a Hebrew inscription of the second century in the old Christian cemetery at Antinoe. Its letters had once been covered with red paint. Beside the worn text stand a seven-branched candelabrum and a cypress tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arabian-nights-:
Arabian Nights is the popular name of a set of tales written in Arabic as Alf Lailat wa Lailah, One Thousand and One Nights. Galland's French version of 1703-1717 made them known to all Europe. Burton's edition, the fullest, holds more than 230 stories, many with tales inside them.

Joseph Jacobs, as cited here, sorts the tales into four layers. A Persian-Indian core came first, framed in Persia. An Arabic reworking followed at Harun al-Rashid's court in the ninth century. Cairo added tales from the twelfth to the fifteenth century and gave the set an Egyptian tone. Galland's version alone added Ali Baba and Aladdin, traced to a Christian teller from Aleppo named Hanna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arles-latin-are:
Arles, in the department of Bouches du Rhone, was the ancient capital of Provence, and Jews may have lived there from the first centuries of the common era. A legend says Vespasian set Jews adrift on three ships, one reaching Arles. The first firm document is a decree of 425, in which Valentinian III barred Jews and heathens from arms, office, and owning Christian slaves.

Later rulers brought sharp turns. Under the Arian Visigoths, Jews held full civic rights and helped defend the city in 508. Under the Merovingian kings, pressure to convert grew so strong that Pope Gregory rebuked Bishop Virgilius of Arles for his zeal. The entry follows the community through these early centuries of favor, defense, and forced preaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascari-or-azkar:
Elazar ben Moses Ascari, also Azkari, was a sixteenth-century rabbi at Safed. Azulai styled him Ir we-Kaddish, Angel and Saint. He studied under Joseph Sagis, a colleague of Joseph Caro. At Safed he helped found the Sukkat Shalom, Tabernacle of Peace, a society given to religious meditation. For that circle he wrote his book Haredim, The Devout Ones, in 1585.

Haredim rests on three pillars: knowledge of God, strict keeping of his commandments, and penitence. Its commandment section treats required and forbidden acts one by one, including laws that can be kept only in Palestine. On penitence, Ascari opposes needless fasting as a path to repentance. Though he knew the Cabala and knew Isaac Luria in person, the entry does not count him among the cabalists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athens-modern-2:
Athens, in its modern Jewish life, had a young community when this entry was written. It was hardly thirty years old. One of its oldest families was that of Max Rothschild, a Bavarian Jew. He came to Greece in 1833 with King Otho. For years the community had no synagogue and no rabbi. A Turkish ḥakam led services in poor rooms.

Most Athenian Jews were of Levantine-Spanish stock, living close together, and worked as craftsmen or peddlers. In 1899 they set up a committee to revise their rules and find means for a modest synagogue. They hired a hall for prayer and won land for their own cemetery. The entry also recalls the duchess of Plaisance. In 1855 she left the community land for a temple to the God of Israel. The gift sat unclaimed for thirty years and was lost by law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-awia-saba-the-e: Rab Awia Saba, the Elder, was a Babylonian teacher of the Law. He belonged to the third generation of the amoraim, in the third and fourth centuries. He was born at Pumbedita but often studied under Rab Huna the First, who held him a great scholar. The Talmud keeps two cases where his deep reasoning wore his teacher out. Rab Huna, drained from lecturing, cut the debate short with a dodge: a raven has flown past. Awia was probably the father of Aḥa, son of Awya.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-babski-refues-b:
Babski is the Yiddish name for folk medicine among the Jews of Russia and Poland. The cures mix plain drugs with magic means. A practical cabalist, called a ba'al-shem or good Jew, was called on to charm away toothache or wounds. He drove out evil spirits and broke the evil eye.

Cures for pregnant women and children get special care in the entry. One rite, called Bleigiessen, poured molten lead into water. A wise woman read the shapes the metal took. From them she named the beast or thing that had caused a fright. Two popular handbooks spread such cures among the people. Their items run from a horse's tooth hung on a child for teething pain to a small engraved tablet worn against the evil eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bakhmut-2384: Bakhmut is a city in the Yekaterinoslav government of Russia. The entry is a brief count of its Jews. The city holds 4,000 Jews in a population of 19,000, and the district 9,469 Jews in a total of 332,171. Until 1882 Jews nearby rented land to farm. Since the law of May 3, 1882, only 10 or 15 hold land, in Christian names, and sublet it. Among the Jews are 583 artisans, including 185 tailors in a hard state. Schools named are a Talmud Torah, a private school, and 9 ḥeders with 155 boys.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-on-the-: Baraita on the Creation is a two-part heading. Its first part is only a cross-reference to Ma'aseh Bereshit. The second part carries the substance. Under this title, L. Goldschmidt published a work at Strasburg in 1894 and gave it out as an Aramaic apocryphon. A. Epstein showed, in the "Monatsschrift," that the work is spurious and is Goldschmidt's own. He had turned the Ethiopian Hexæmeron of Pseudo-Epiphanius into Aramaic, then edited his own rendering as though it were an old Jewish apocryphon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-b-samuel:
Baruch b. Samuel, called Baruch of Mayence, was a Talmudist and prolific payyeṭan who died at Mayence on April 25, 1221. He studied under Moses b. Solomon ha-Kohen of Mayence and Eliezer b. Samuel of Metz, and often cites their decisions. He was one of the most eminent German rabbis of his time and a leader of the Mayence synod of 1220. Several of his responsa survive, mostly on rabbinic civil law. His "Sefer ha-Ḥokmah" (Book of Wisdom) is now lost.

His poetry is better known than his law. His penitential poems, dirges, and hymns entered the German and Polish rituals. They made him one of the most popular payyeṭanim. The seliḥot in particular show genuine poetic fervor. The entry prints a translated specimen beginning "Jeshurun's God, beyond compare." It also warns against confusing him with Baruch of Greece, a Tosafist quoted in the Tosafot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-be-abidan-and-b:
Be Abidan and Be Nazrefe are supposed names of places where, by Talmud report, Jews and non-Jews met for religious dispute. Scholars in the entry dispute the words themselves. Some take them as scornful labels for houses of Jewish Christians.

The entry rejects that reading, since the Babylonian teachers lived where Christians had little sway and the foes seem pagan. It ends by treating both as real places in Babylonia. There, in the first half of the third century, Jews and Persians argued over religion. Later ages no longer name them. Books tied to the first of these places are named in the Talmud as sacred writings of Jewish Christians.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beirut-syria-an:
Beirut, in ancient times Berytus, is a city in Phenicia on the Mediterranean, between Byblus and Sidon. Old letters name it Birutu, and Greeks called it Berytus. The entry opens by weighing two roots for the name, a well and a cypress tree.

Much of the long piece sorts Beirut from other towns of like name in Bible and Talmud. It then follows Jewish presence there across the ages, through travelers who name its trade and at times say nothing of Jews at all. Sources in several tongues close the account. Cakes from Berytus earn a passing mention in a Talmud passage on foods, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-samu: Benjamin ben Samuel of Coutances was a Talmudist and French liturgical poet of the first half of the eleventh century. Old scholars gave him the proud title of payyeṭan. Thirty-one of his pieces survive in the rite books, most in the French rite, which helps place him in France, not at Constance. He wrote chiefly for the three feasts and the New Year. The entry also credits him as a great Talmudic voice and notes a lean toward mysticism in his verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-congress:
Berlin Congress names the meeting of the great European powers at Berlin from June 13 to July 13, 1878. Its task was to settle the questions left by the Russo-Turkish war. Many former Turkish provinces gained freedom at that table. For Jews, the key point is a condition the congress set.

In case after case, full civic and political rights for Jews were made a term of a new state's recognition. Clauses in like form went into the treaty for Bulgaria, Montenegro, Servia, and Rumania. The entry prints the Rumanian clause in full and traces its stormy debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-besor-3184: Besor is a wadi, or river-bed, named in First Samuel. Two hundred of David's followers stopped there. They were too worn out to go on. The rest of the force chased the Amalekites. The entry gives a modern identification for the place. Guerin linked Besor with Wadi el-Ghazza. That wadi reaches the Mediterranean southwest of Gaza. The entry offers no other details about the site.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bielgoraj-3284: Bielgoraj is a district town in Russian Poland. It lies in the government of Lublin. During Chmielnicki's uprising its Jews were all killed. That slaughter fell in 1648-49. Rabbi Hirsch died among them. In 1890 the town held 3,430 Jews. The total population was 7,812. The district held 6,811 Jews in all. The town had one synagogue and three prayer-houses. It also had a Hebrew school and a hospital. Many of its Jews worked as artisans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-gustave-3: Gustave Bloch was a French historian and archeologist. He was born at Fegersheim, Alsace, on July 21, 1848. He passed through the Ecole Normale Supérieure. He taught rhetoric at the Besançon lycée. He belonged to the French schools at Rome and Athens. At Lyons he taught Greek and Roman archeology. By 1902 he led ancient history at the Ecole Normale. His books treat the Roman Senate's origins. He also wrote on Celtic and Roman Gaul. That work opens Lavisse's History of France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boleslaw-iii-kr: Boleslaw III Krzywousty, the Wry-Mouthed, was king of Poland from 1102 to 1139. The entry is very short. It says Jews in his time spread through Poland and Lithuania as far as Kiev. There they ran a lively trade, chiefly in salt with Holics and Przemysl, and probably in slaves. From his fame as a brave and generous ruler, the entry infers that Jews likely held much freedom then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-borrower-3584:
Borrower in Jewish law is one who takes another's property for free use. He must return the very thing he took. That sets him apart from a borrower of money, who may repay in kind.

Biblical law holds the borrower to the strictest account. If the thing is lost, stolen, or dies in his hands, he must make full payment. One exception holds: if the owner went with the property, no payment is due. Talmudic rulings add more exceptions. Wear from proper use does not count against him. A set time for return also limits his duty after that time ends.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breslau-aryeh-l:
Aryeh Lob ben Hayyim Breslau was a German Talmudist and rabbi born in 1741 at Breslau. He died on April 22, 1809, at Rotterdam. He lived at Lissa and Berlin before serving as rabbi at Emden.

In 1781 Breslau was called as chief rabbi to Rotterdam. Great scholars sent him Talmudic questions, a mark of his standing. His responsa, Pene Aryeh, came out at Amsterdam in 1790. The entry praises its logic and its plain, clear style. He also knew secular sciences well and won friends among Christian scholars. When French troops entered Holland in 1793, he wrote synagogue prayers for the occasion. His three sons all became rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buchbinder-bern: Bernhard Buchbinder, who wrote as Gustav Klinger, was an Austrian journalist born July 6, 1854, in Budapest. He was meant for a mercantile career, but a one-act comedy played in Budapest set his course. Both parents died while he was young, and his father had been a poor pedler. Buchbinder had to support younger brothers and sisters. Under real hardship he took up journalism. He made his name as a novelist and dramatic writer. The entry lists novels from 1882 to 1894 and a long string of dramas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-caballeria-de-l:
De la Caballeria was a Marano family of Aragon, wide branched and strong through wealth and learning, above all in Saragossa. It descended from Solomon ibn Labi, who had nine sons. The eldest, Bonafos, accepted baptism, and most brothers followed. They took Christian names and rose to high office in church, Cortes, treasury, and university.

One Pedro of the family arranged the marriage of Isabella of Castile to Ferdinand of Aragon. He presented the bride a necklace worth 40,000 ducats and paid part of its cost. Yet office did not shield the family from the Inquisition. Alfonso joined the plot against the inquisitor Arbues. In 1488 Luis and his son Jaime did public penance at Saragossa, and one member's remains were burned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cadenet-3884:
Cadenet was a small village in the French department of Vaucluse, along the river Durance. Like its neighbors, it held a Jewish community in the Middle Ages. A charter of 1283 let Cadenet and seven other towns keep a synagogue and cemetery. The price was a yearly tax of two pounds of pepper paid to the archbishop of Aix.

Most of the entry follows a lawsuit from 1385. Maestro Duran of Cadenet falsely claimed he had married a woman of Arles who had refused him. Two witnesses backed the claim and were later convicted of perjury. Rabbinical courts in four cities heard the case in turn. Isaac ben Sheshet gave the final, severe judgment against Duran and his partners.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantheras-3984:
Cantheras is a surname tied to a high priestly house in Josephus. Josephus makes Simon, son of the high priest Boethus, bear the name, and names Elioneus, son of Cantheras, as a high priest set up by King Agrippa between 41 and 44. Two Hasidic leaders, though, cursed the house of Boethus and the house of Cantheras as two houses, not one.

That clash drives the whole short entry. Grätz blamed Josephus for mixing the names up. Schürer accepted Josephus as right. A Mishnah passage names Elioneus as a son of Joseph Caiaphas instead. The entry lays out the sources and the two scholarly verdicts without settling the matter itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cartagena-4084: Cartagena is an old city on the east coast of the Spanish province of Murcia, named in the Talmud. Jews settled there at an early date. A decree of the fourth Council of Cartagena, in 436, barred bishops from keeping any hearer, Jew included, from hearing the word of God up to a set point in the service. Many Jews expelled from Spain sailed from Cartagena. Many Maranos also settled there, and fell into the hands of the Inquisition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cerfberr-anatol: Anatole Cerfberr, a French journalist and author, was born at Paris in 1835 and died at Neuilly in 1896. He wrote for many papers under pen names, among them Arthur Clary, Antoine Cerlier, and Fulgence Ridal. An admirer of Balzac and Victor Hugo, he held socialist views and knew the stage well. He published poems, biographies, and studies. His guide to Balzac's Comédie Humaine, printed at Paris in 1887, was crowned by the Académie Française.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cheese-4284:
Cheese is the curd of milk run into molds and left to set. Ancient Hebrews knew the food. Three Hebrew expressions point to kinds of cheese in use. One names the common article, still made in Syria by straining milk through cloth, salting the curd, and drying disks in the sun. Another may name a sweet-milk cheese, much like cottage cheese.

In later days a guild of cheese makers plied the trade. Talmudic writings speak often of hard cheese making. Cheese and water counted as a very poor meal. Cheese also fell under a ban on buying certain foods from idolaters. That ban was one of eighteen rules adopted at a famous meeting, rules their makers died for. One kind, from Bet Oneiki, was barred outright. Rabbi Meïr would bar its use for any purpose, a view the Rabbis did not accept.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cicero-marcus-t:
Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator, lived from 106 to 43 B.C., and the entry gathers what he said about Jews. In 59 he spoke for Flaccus in the Aurelian Forum at Rome. Flaccus stood accused of seizing Temple money sent by Jews under his rule in Asia. Cicero attacked the Jewish crowd at the trial and called their faith a barbaric superstition.

The entry doubts he spoke from deep conviction; the plea served his client. It also notes a weak legal point in his case, since Judea then lay inside the Roman empire. A pun at the trial of Verres in 70 B.C. and a slur in another speech round out the record quoted here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-josiah-44: Josiah Cohen, an American lawyer and judge, was born at Plymouth, England, on Nov. 29, 1841. His family had long been settled in Cornwall. He made his name in western Pennsylvania. He chaired the Allegheny county Republican executive committee. In 1884 he sat on the presidential election board for Pennsylvania. In 1901 he became judge of the orphans' court of Allegheny county. Jewish posts fill the rest of the entry. He served the Union of American Hebrew Congregations and led District Lodge No. 3 of the B'nai B'rith order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-concordance-lat:
Concordance, from the Latin for agreement, names an alphabetical list of all the words in a book, with the passages where each word stands. In Jewish use the term covers concordances of the Bible and of the Talmud only. Hugo de Sancto Caro first built one for the Latin Vulgate, about 1244.

Isaac Nathan of Arles made the Hebrew counterpart from 1437 to 1445. Polemic fights with Christian scholars drove him: he needed every Bible passage at his fingertips. His Meir Natib split the Hebrew text into chapters and numbered verses on the Vulgate pattern, a first for a Jewish work. Later sections weigh Furst's concordance, praised for fresh word studies yet faulted for forcing his root theories onto the order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cosmogony-4684:
Cosmogony means a theory of how the world began. The entry defines it as the mythic, pre-scientific view kept in the traditions and folk poetry of ancient peoples. Nearly all races hold such accounts, it notes. They form a large part of each mythology. Local climate and culture shape them, so later written versions often clash. System and order come later, when a theology reworks the raw material.

Much of the article then sets the Bible's creation accounts beside those of other peoples. It gives the order of creation in Genesis, from heaven and earth to man. It also describes the Hebrew picture of a flat earth swimming on water, under a solid vault of heaven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cruelty-to-anim:
Cruelty to Animals opens with a puzzle. The Bible sets man as sole ruler over the creatures, free to use them as he wills. Yet its laws hold many rules for the rights of dumb beasts. The Rabbis took those rules to prove that kindness to animals is a Bible command. Eating a limb cut from a living animal was banned for all nations, under the Noachian laws.

Set precepts follow. An ox threshing grain must not be muzzled, but left free to eat as it works. The term ox covers all animals, and the owner's faith does not matter. Maimonides and the Shulḥan 'Aruk are cited for the details. A later section defends the Jewish mode of slaughter as more humane than rival modes, against European bans.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-gorodok-4: David-Gorodok is a town in the government of Minsk, Russia, presented here through its 1895 figures. The population was 10,086, including 4,902 Jews, most of them in business and industry. There were 672 artisans, 564 of them running their own businesses. Goods such as bricks, timber, boats, and fish went by boat to Minsk and Kiev. About 20 families farmed, and 140 people hired out as day-laborers. The entry counts schools and ḥadarim, and notes that the town had no charitable institutions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diderot-denis-5:
Denis Diderot was a French philosopher and encyclopedist born at Langres on October 5, 1713. Like the other encyclopedists he preached tolerance. Yet this entry finds little sympathy in him for Jews and Judaism. His article on Jewish philosophy in the "Encyclopédie" is bright but shallow and not free of errors, it says.

A fine passage on the Jews of Amsterdam in his "Voyage en Hollande" draws the same verdict. Two anecdotes in "Neveu de Rameau" star Jews, one a renegade who robs a rich Jew of Avignon, the other an Orthodox Jew of Utrecht in a shady bargain. The entry calls both tales unlikely and says they show only the common prejudice of the age. Diderot died at Paris on July 30, 1784.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dormitzer-meir-: Meïr ha-Levi Dormitzer was an Austrian scholar who died at Prague on Jan. 25, 1743. The whole entry is only a few lines. It names one work as his, a book called Ha'ataḳah, or Translation. That book explains the foreign words found in Bertinoro's commentary on the Mishnah. The entry gives the book's printing as Prague, 1809, long after its author's death. No birth date, post, or other writing is recorded for him here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dyer-isadore-53:
Isadore Dyer was an American merchant and communal worker born in Dessau, Germany, in 1813. He came to America young and lived first at Baltimore. In 1840 he moved to Galveston, Texas. There he traded until 1861, when he retired after a strong business career. He died at Waukesha, Wisconsin, in 1888.

From 1866 Dyer presided over Galveston's Union Marine and Fire Insurance Company, until it closed in 1880. He ranked high in the Odd Fellows and was among its earliest grand masters. Galveston's first Jewish services met at his house in 1856. His will provided for the two Hebrew cemeteries. It also left money for more seats for poor families at Congregation B'nai Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-einhorn-ignatz-:
Ignatz Einhorn, known as Eduard Horn, was a Hungarian preacher and political economist. He was born at Vágh-Ujhely on Sept. 25, 1825. He died at Budapest on Nov. 2, 1875. He studied at Talmud schools and at Budapest University. Journalism in the capital was his first work.

In 1847 Einhorn began preaching at Alt-Ofen's new temple. In April 1848 he founded the weekly Der Ungarische Israelit. It sparked Budapest's Reform congregation, whose first preacher he became. In the freedom struggle he spoke for the revolution, then served as army chaplain. Police pursuit drove him to Leipsic by March 1850. There, as Eduard Horn, he wrote on Hungary's recent past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliakim-ben-mes: Eliakim ben Meshullam was a German Talmudist and prayer poet. He was born about the year 1030. He died at Speyer at the end of the eleventh century. He studied at Mayence and at Worms. Eliakim set up a famed school of his own at Speyer. He wrote notes on nearly all the tractates of the Talmud. Scholars used those notes into the fourteenth century. Only his notes on Yoma survive today. He also wrote a poem for a circumcision held on a Saturday.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elisha-ben-abra: Elisha ben Abraham ben Judah was a Russian rabbi. He died at Grodno on July 1, 1749. He was rabbi and head of the school at Lucicz in Volhynia. His book Kab we-Naki gives short notes on the Mishnah. Amsterdam printed it in the year 1697. He also put out notes on a famed Mishnah commentary. That volume came out at Altona in 1735. One handbook dates his first book to 1664 instead. On that count he lived past a hundred years of age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ethan-5884:
Ethan is the name of three men in the entry, each drawn from Chronicles or Kings. The first Ethan was famed for wisdom, though Solomon surpassed him. Chronicles places him in the third generation after Judah. The second Ethan descended from Gershom, eldest son of Levi, and stood in the line of Asaph. The third Ethan came from Merari, Levi's third son.

That third Ethan, also called Jeduthun, forms a famous trio with Heman and Asaph. David set them over the music of worship. The entry credits Ethan-Jeduthun with the music of Psalm 39. It also calls him a prophet of the second class and the king's seer. His descendants appear in the days of Hezekiah and after the Exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-exorcism-5084:
Exorcism is the driving out of evil spirits by spells, and the entry collects its Jewish traces. In the Bible, David's harp playing drives an evil spirit from King Saul. The angel Raphael teaches Tobit how to ban a spirit. Terms for the act appear in Greek and Hebrew sources quoted here.

Josephus supplies the entry's set piece. A man named Eleazar drew a demon out through a sufferer's nostrils with a ring holding a root Solomon had named. He swore the demon never to return, then ordered it to tip over a basin of water as proof it had left. Rabbi Johanan ben Zakkai is also quoted on the practice. Later sections follow exorcism in rabbinic writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-faitusi-jacob-b:
Jacob ben Abraham Faitusi was a Talmudist who lived in Tunis and later in Jerusalem. He died at Algiers in July 1812. He traveled on behalf of the Jerusalem community. His Berit Ya'akob, printed at Leghorn in 1800, holds sermons and comments on Sotah and on Geonic notes. Mizbah Kapparah followed in 1810, with comments and sermons on charity.

His Yerek Ya'akob gathers cabalistic notes on the Pentateuch, Talmud pieces, and responsa. His son David Hayyim edited that work. A second edition of Mizbah Kapparah appeared at Lemberg in 1861, long after his death. The entry's sources are Cazes on bibliography and Zedner's catalogue of Hebrew books in the British Museum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferdinand-phili: Philip Ferdinand was a Hebrew teacher born in Poland about 1555 who died at Leyden in 1598. After a roving life in which he turned first Catholic, then Protestant, he reached Oxford and then Cambridge, entering in December 1596. He drew a pension from the Domus Conversorum, receipting it in Latin, Hebrew, and Greek. Scaliger drew him to Leyden in 1598 with a professorship, and admitted learning much from him. His one book renders the 613 commandments, printed at Cambridge in 1597.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischel-eliezer:
Eliezer ben Isaac Fischel was a Russian Talmudist and cabalist who lived at Strizhov. He lived in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The entry lists many cabalistic and homiletic works by him. Several of their titles begin with the word Olam. One book gives homilies on the unity of God.

Another explains contrasts. A third holds seventy cabalistic homilies on one verse of Genesis. Thirty treat the spheres and lights, and forty treat the Jewish holidays. It came out at Zolkiev in 1800. Two named scholars also ascribe a commentary to him, printed in 1805.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fleischl-von-ma:
Ernst Fleischl von Marxow was an Austrian physician born at Vienna on Aug. 5, 1846. He died there on Oct. 22, 1891. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1870. The next year he became a prosector at the university's anatomy institute, under Rokitansky. In 1873 he began to teach physiology there. He rose to assistant professor in 1880. In 1887 the Imperial Academy of Sciences chose him as a corresponding member.

Fleischl invented several tools for his science. Two named here measure electric current in fine tubes and the coloring matter of blood. His essays treat the laws of nerve action and the bending of light in fluids and in magnetic fields. He translated Maxwell's Matter and Motion into German in 1887. His gathered papers were edited at Vienna in 1893. A mural portrait of him was set in the university arcade in 1898.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-frankel:
Fränkel is a family of scholars and Talmudists. Its earliest known member was Koppel Fränkel, dated 1650. He was the richest Viennese Jew of his time. When the Jews were banished from Vienna in 1670, his children settled at Fürth. One daughter, Esther, married a Prague preacher of the Spiro family. Their children bore the double name Fränkel-Spiro. Simon, the first of them, headed the Prague community.

A second marriage later joined the two families again. A Fränkel of Fürth wed a daughter of Elijah Spiro, a cousin of the first bridegroom. That branch also married back into the main Fränkel line in time. From this triple joining descended the scholar Zechariah Frankel. His father took the simple name Frankel. The entry closes by pointing to a pedigree printed on the page before it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedman-lob-be:
Löb Behr Friedman, also called Aryeh Dob, was an author and teacher born in 1865 at Suwalki, Russian Poland. He was schooled at Boskowitz in Moravia and afterward moved to Warsaw. There he became one of the movers of Zionism. With Samuel Mohilever he founded a Zionist society in the city. In 1892 he went to America and became editor of a Hebrew paper.

He has written a good number of school books and other works. Among them are a Hebrew book on teaching and lives of the Talmudists. One book sets rabbinic law before the young in the Jewish-German tongue. Others gather tales and pearls from the Talmud. He has also written novels and pieces for Hebrew journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gallico-samuel-: Samuel Gallico, an Italian Talmudist and cabalist of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, studied under Moses Cordovero. He later taught Menahem Azariah di Fano. Gallico compiled Asis Rimmonim from parts of Cordovero Pardes Rimmonim, adding notes by Mordecai Dato. The book came out at Venice in 1601. Fano later revised it and added a comment of his own. Another comment by Mordecai ben Jacob also joined the work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-genoa-6584:
Genoa, a great Italian seaport and former republic, likely held Jews from Rome before the Second Temple fell. The first firm records are two letters of the emperor Theodoric in the fifth century. They touch on a synagogue and past grants. In 1134 a tax on Genoa Jews paid for oil for church altars. Soon after, Jews were driven out or left under attack.

Benjamin of Tudela found only two Jews there about 1165. A rule barred Jews from staying more than three days. Spanish exiles landed in 1492 and begged leave to mend their ships. Many died on the wharves that winter. Leave to settle came and went in short grants. A ghetto was set out in 1660.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-golyatovski-joa:
Joanniki Golyatovski was a Little-Russian cleric and anti-Jewish writer. He died in 1688. He studied at the Kiev-Mogilian College and took holy orders. He later headed the Little-Russian schools as rector. He declared himself the enemy of Catholics, Jews, and Moslems alike. His sharpest hatred fell on the Jews, which won him popular favor.

The rise of Shabbethai Ẓebi gave him his chance. He answered it with a dialogue between a Jew and a Christian. Its title was "Messia Pravdivi." The work, written in Little-Russian, later passed into Latin and Russian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gross-charles-6:
Charles Gross was an American author and history professor. He was born at Troy, N. Y., on Feb. 10, 1857. Troy High School and Williams College trained him first. Paris, Berlin, and Göttingen followed. His Göttingen doctorate rested on a study of the Gilda Mercatoria. Harvard made him professor of history in 1888. It also gave him an honorary master's degree.

His field was medieval and English history. His books include "Gild Merchant" (1890) and a bibliography of British municipal history (1897). His "Sources and Literature of English History" came in 1900. In 1887 he lectured on the Jews' Exchequer in medieval England. The entry calls that lecture a gain for English and Jewish history alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gunzburg-6684:
Günzburg was a town of Bavaria, in Swabia, on the Danube. A small but thriving Jewish community lived there in the sixteenth century. In 1566 its Jews asked Emperor Maximilian II to confirm Isaac ha-Levi as rabbi. He had served thirty years already. Family quarrels inside the community made formal standing needful. Among the members was Simeon Günzburg, rich and influential. He was the ancestor of the Günzburg family.

Solomon Luria marveled that discord could enter so pious and learned a congregation. The community has long since vanished. Yet the town's name stays familiar to Jews. It was the birthplace of the Günzburg, Günz, and Gaunz families.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haida-abraham-b:
Abraham ben Simeon Haida, also known as Abraham Lemberger, was a printer in Prague between 1612 and 1628. He was a son of Simeon Haida. In 1610 he helped print Samuel Laniado's "Keli Ḥemdah" with Moses Uṭiẓ and Gershon Popers. From 1612 he worked with Uṭiẓ on further books.

His press turned out a long list of Hebrew works. It printed Immanuel ben Solomon's "Maḥberet ha-Tofet weha-'Eden" in 1613, Joseph ben Moses' "Bi'ure Rashi" in 1614, and Solomon Luria's "Yam shel Shelomoh" on Baba Ḳamma in 1616. It also issued Solomon ben Jacob's "Shir ha-Shirim" in 1626. He worked in the houses of Samuel Meisel, Judah ben Jacob Cohen, and Jacob Bak. His sons were still printing in 1641.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halberstadt-708:
Halberstadt is a town in the Prussian province of Saxony. The first proof of Jews there is a letter of protection from Bishop Volrad dated 1261. Through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the town's Jews appear as a prize fought over by bishop and city council. The community throve in the mid-fifteenth century, then took a blow when Bishop Ernest II expelled the Jews in 1493.

Jews returned, grew again, and were expelled once more in 1594, then readmitted for the tax money and allowed a synagogue. A mob wrecked that synagogue in 1621, and another in 1669, with troops helping. Heavy taxes ground the community, yet it grew to about 120 families, kept a burial society from 1679, and drew noted rabbis to its Talmud school. The entry ends with its list of rabbis from 1661 to the present incumbent of 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-hanina:
Hananiah b. 'Aḳabia was a tanna of the second century, a fellow of Judah b. 'Ilai and likely a younger pupil of Gamaliel II. He seldom appears in haggadot, but he stood firm in the Halakah, and Rab praised his sharpness of mind. Even his name is unsettled: Hananiah and Ḥanina, 'Aḳabia and Akiba, swap places across the sources for one and the same ruling.

He was fearless in debate and opposed even the nasi and his deputy. He lived at Tiberias, where he lifted many restrictions that had cramped the people's comfort. The entry closes with a warning for readers: a bare "Hananiah" in a text may be this man or an elder namesake, R. Joshua's nephew. The company he keeps in the passage — Meïr's age, or the age before — tells which one is meant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-solomon-al:
Solomon Alexander Hart, born at Plymouth in April 1806, was an artist and the librarian of the Royal Academy in London. He entered the Academy as a student in 1823. His first shown work was a small portrait of his father. He moved on to oil painting and won full Academy membership in 1840.

Hart taught painting at the Academy from 1854 to 1863, then became its librarian in 1864. A trip to Italy in 1841 and 1842 filled sketchbooks that fed later pictures. His Jewish subjects include Hannah, mother of Samuel, and a scene of Manasseh ben Israel with Oliver Cromwell. He died on June 11, 1881.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heckscher-samue: Samuel ben Meir Heckscher was a German scholar who lived at Altona in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. One work of his is known. It is a lament, written in Hebrew and German, on a great fire. That fire raged at Altona in 1711. The entry is only a few lines long. It gives no dates for his birth or death and names no other writing. Two Hebrew book catalogs are cited as the sources for this short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herczeghy-moriz:
Moriz Herczeghy, born in Budapest on Aug. 19, 1815, was a Hungarian physician and author. He studied medicine in Budapest and Vienna. He joined the Revolution of 1848 in Vienna, then went to Paris. In 1860 he moved to Italy.

Herczeghy became chief physician in Garibaldi's army. Later he served eight years as chief military physician at Constantinople. A severe wound in the Russo-Turkish war ended his practice. His writings covered politics, cretinism, and epidemics. His chief work was a study of the woman question, printed in French in 1864 and Hungarian in 1883. He died in Vienna on Dec. 23, 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiel-7684: Hiel was a Bethelite who rebuilt Jericho in the reign of Ahab, in First Kings. The entry says Joshua's curse on that rebuilding fell on him. He laid the foundation at the cost of Abiram, his first-born. He set up the gates at the cost of Segub, his youngest son. An attempt to identify Hiel with Jehu is also noted, with a source given. No other acts, dates, or family facts are offered in this short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-kara-7784: Ḥiyya Ḳara was a Palestinian scholar of the third and fourth centuries. He was a pupil of Samuel, son of Naḥman. In that teacher's name he said that since the Temple fell, neither good wine nor white earthenware could be had. The name Ḳara was given him for his deep knowledge of the Bible, the entry explains. A note in a Lamentations commentary is cited for that point. No birth place, death date, or written works are given for him here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horschetzky-mor: Moritz Horschetzky was an Austrian physician and writer born at Bydzov in Bohemia in 1788. He died on November 7, 1859, at Nagy-Kanizsa in Hungary. He had practiced medicine there since 1811. As a writer he worked chiefly on Josephus. He translated the Antiquities and added notes, in editions of 1826, 1843, and 1851. His humor showed in a set of invented travel reports by Nathan Ghazzati. Julius Furst mistook that piece for a translation from Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-imber-naphtali-:
Naphtali Herz Imber was an Austrian Hebrew poet born at Zloczow in Galicia in 1856. After Talmudic schooling he began to wander, reaching Vienna and Constantinople. There he met Laurence Oliphant and spent time with him in Palestine, with a side trip to Egypt. After Oliphant died in 1888, Imber moved to England.

In London he knew Israel Zangwill and wrote for the Jewish Standard. In 1892 he crossed to the United States and drifted through Boston, Chicago, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. Mysticism drew him, and he wrote pamphlets on it. His fame rests on Hebrew verse. His poem Ha-Tikwah voices the Zionist hope with force and has been taken up as the movement's anthem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-judah:
Isaac ben Judah was a Talmudist of the twelfth century and the teacher of Solomon ben Isaac, known as Rashi. He was a native of Lorraine, but he settled early in Germany, where he studied under Eleazar ha-Gadol. He headed the rabbinical schools of Mayence and then of Worms. It was at Worms that he taught Rashi.

The entry calls him one of the greatest Talmudic authorities of his time. Rashi cites his commentaries on the Talmud in several places. His responsa survive scattered through works such as the "Pardes ha-Gadol," the "Or Zarua'," and the responsa of Meir of Rothenberg. A French Mahzor manuscript names him as head of the school of Paris, but the entry judges that claim highly improbable.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-noah-: Isaac ben Noah Cohen Shapira was a Polish rabbi of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, a grandson of Hirsh and the teacher of Joel Sirkes. He trained in the yeshibah of Hayyim ben Samuel of Kremenetz. After serving as rabbi at Gorodnitza and Beresnitza, he was called to Meseritz. His "Sefer Zikkaron" set all the paragraphs of the Shulhan Aruk in alphabetical order, rimed as a help to memory. It was printed at Cracow or Prague in the seventeenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-of-krems:
Israel of Krems was an Austrian rabbi of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. He was the great-grandfather of Israel Isserlein, who quotes him on the Pentateuch. His own work was the "Haggahot Asheri," notes printed with R. Asher's Talmudic compendium. Grätz identifies him with the Israel whom Emperor Rupert named chief rabbi of all German communities on May 3, 1407.

Because the post carried civil control of the Jews, above all tax gathering, the German rabbis resisted it fiercely. Some even threatened Israel with excommunication if he would not resign. A second decree that November fined any who refused him twenty gold marks. The edicts did little, and the office soon died. By 1415 Israel appears in an imperial document as a superintendent of the Jewish taxes, under the chamberlain Conrad of Weinsberg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-b-aaron-o: Jacob b. Aaron of Karlin was a Russian rabbi and author who died at Karlin, in the government of Minsk, in 1855. He was a grandson of Baruch of Shklov, the mathematician. He was also one of the earliest and best-known graduates of the Volozhin yeshibah. For about thirty years he held the rabbinate of Karlin, and his age counted him among its greatest authorities. His "Mishkenot Ya'akob" (Wilna, 1838) holds responsa on all four parts of the Shulhan Aruk. A volume of novellae followed after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobson-ludwig:
Ludwig Lewin Jacobson, a Danish surgeon, was born in Copenhagen on Jan. 10, 1783, and took his medical degrees there in 1804. He served as a military surgeon during the British bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807. In 1816 the University of Kiel made him a professor, and he died in Copenhagen on Aug. 29, 1843.

His fame rests on comparative anatomy. In 1809 he announced a previously unknown organ in the human nose, later named the Jacobsonian organ. He also devised a tool to stop arterial bleeding and a lithoclast for crushing bladder stones, and he won prizes for research on kidneys in birds and reptiles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jephthah-8584:
Jephthah was a judge of Israel for six years and the victor over the Ammonites. A Gileadite, he was driven from his father's house by his half brothers and led a band of free fighters in the land of Tob. When war with Ammon came, the elders of Gilead begged his help and made him their chief at Mizpah. Talks with Ammon's king failed, and Jephthah beat him and took twenty towns.

His fame rests on a rash vow: he promised God the first thing that came from his house if he won. His only daughter came out dancing to greet him. After two months of grace he kept the vow, and Israel's daughters mourned her four days each year. His men later slew 42,000 Ephraimites at the Jordan fords.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joab-yhwh-is-fa:
Joab, son of Zeruiah, David's sister, was commander-in-chief of David's army. He first appears at the pool of Gibeon in a fight with Abner's men. On the retreat Abner killed Joab's young brother Asahel. Joab later lured Abner back to Hebron and killed him there in revenge, and David forced him to walk in penitent dress at Abner's burial.

His great chance came at the siege of Jerusalem. David had promised the chief's post to the first man to strike the Jebusites, and Joab won it. He then strengthened the taken city and led David's wars, above all in Edom and against the Ammonites. The entry presents him as a skilled general and a model of loyalty whom David both prized and feared.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-samuel-b: Joseph Samuel ben Abraham was a French rabbi born at Aix in Provence who flourished at Avignon toward the end of the thirteenth century. Like his father, he backed Abba Mari of Lunel. A fierce dispute over religion shook southern France in the years 1303-1306. During that fight Joseph sent word of his support to Solomon ben Adret of Barcelona. In their letters Adret calls him by his full chain of names, Joseph ben Samuel ben Abraham. The entry gives no works or death date for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-eli-o: Judah ben Eli, the Tiberian, was a Karaite grammarian and liturgical poet who died at Jerusalem in 932. There he had headed a school. His grammar, Me'or Enayim, sorts the Hebrew nouns into thirty-five classes. Pinsker took him to be the Jerusalem scholar whom Abraham ibn Ezra names as author of eight grammar works. Judah also wrote two liturgical poems and a lament on the ruin of Zion with his name in acrostic. Later scholars matched him with several men of like names in other books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-julius-archelau: Julius Archelaus was a son of Chelcias and, to judge by his name, a Hellenized Jew of a rich and noble house. King Agrippa I chose him as husband for his first daughter, Mariamne. She was ten when her father died in the year 44, and the wedding took place under her brother Agrippa II. A daughter, Berenice, came of the match. Mariamne later left Archelaus and married the alabarch Demetrius. Josephus cites Archelaus as one who knew Greek culture well and could vouch for his history of the war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaminka-armand-:
Armand Kaminka was a Russian scholar born at Berdychev on May 5, 1866. He studied at Berlin in several schools at once. His fields were philosophy, Eastern languages, state economy, and theology. He took a doctorate at Berlin University. In 1887 he went on to Paris for more study at the Sorbonne.

In 1893 Kaminka became acting rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. That same year he took the Prague pulpit left by S. I. Kämpf. From 1897 to 1900 he served at Esseg, in Slavonia. In 1901 he moved to Vienna as preacher and as secretary of the Israelitische Allianz. In 1903 that body sent him to Kishinef. His task was to look into the massacres of Jews there. The entry lists his books on Galilee, the geonim, and Hebrew verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-theodore-:
Théodore Klein was a French physician. He was born at Durmenach, in the Upper Rhine, on May 30, 1845. He died in Paris on May 4, 1902. He was a son of the chief rabbi of Colmar. Klein studied medicine in Paris. As a student he helped translate Helmholtz's handbook of optics into French. His thesis of 1873, on lighting and visual sharpness, won a faculty prize.

Klein edited the scientific page of "L'Opinion Nationale" from 1872 to 1876. He wrote on diabetes, on circumcision, and on other medical subjects. In 1900 the minister of the interior gave him a gold medal. It honored his long and disinterested service to the poor. He sat on the Jewish Consistory of Paris. For eighteen years he presided over the Société de l'Etude Talmudique.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kossarski-ludwi: Ludwig Kossarski, a German poet and writer born at Bromberg in 1810, died at Berlin on Nov. 3, 1873. He was a brother of Julius Kossarski. He studied medicine at Berlin but soon gave himself fully to German literature. He wrote for several journals and papers. His books include poems dated 1834, tales dated 1840, and sketches of Frederick William III in poetry and prose, also dated 1840. A later volume, Hier und Dort, appeared in 1855. The entry stays brief and lists no posts or honors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lesser-edmund-9:
Edmund Lesser, a German physician, was born at Neisse on May 12, 1852. He studied at Berlin, Bonn, and Strasburg and took his degree in 1876. He worked at the skin clinic at Breslau, then taught at Leipsic from 1882. In 1892 he became assistant professor at Bonn.

In 1896 Lesser headed the syphilis ward at Berlin's Charité Hospital. A year later he led the university's new clinic for skin and venereal disease in that city. His textbook on those diseases reached a tenth edition in 1890. He also wrote on herpes, on mercury shots, on syphilis in the innocent, and on the leper houses of the Middle Ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-family-of-: Levy Family of America is the heading of a genealogical tree. The hosted text gives the tree itself in no words at all. It holds one line only. That line says the tree traces the family descended from Benjamin Levy of Philadelphia. No member of the family is named in the text, and no dates or places beyond Philadelphia are given. A reader gets the family's stated root and nothing more from this entry as hosted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lilienthal-max-:
Max Lilienthal, a rabbi and educator, was born at Munich on Nov. 6, 1815. He died at Cincinnati, Ohio, on April 5, 1882. He took his Ph.D. at Munich in 1837. In 1839 he became principal of the new Jewish school at Riga, and its preacher as well. The school opened on Jan. 15, 1840.

In December 1841 the Russian state sent Lilienthal on a mission. He was to learn how Jews felt about planned state schools for them, and to calm their fears. Many Jews feared the schools were a path to conversion, and trust in him thinned as he traveled. At Minsk the crowd's anger forced him to seek police protection. Discouraged, he went back to St. Petersburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loewe-louis-100:
Louis Loewe was an English Orientalist and theologian born at Zülz in 1809, and he died in London in 1888. He studied at several Jewish schools and at the University of Berlin. In London the Duke of Sussex made him his Orientalist in 1839. He traveled widely in the East and learned many languages.

Loewe joined Sir Moses Montefiore on nine missions to help Jews abroad. On the Damascus trip in 1840 he spotted a key word error in a ruling, and the wording was changed from pardon to acquittal. He later led Jews' College and the Ramsgate college. His books include work on Egyptian and Circassian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lumbrozo-jacob-:
Jacob Lumbrozo, a Lisbon-born physician, planter, and trader in colonial Maryland, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Cyrus Adler and J. H. Hollander. He reached Maryland on January 24, 1656, by way of Holland. He built a profitable medical practice, took up land, and grew wealthy.

Lumbrozo is the first Jew in Maryland whose faith is proven by documents, the article stresses. In 1658 he was arrested for blasphemy under the Toleration Act of 1649, a charge that carried death and loss of property, after denying the Trinity. A general amnesty freed him ten days later, and no new attempt followed. He later traded with the Indians by commission and exercised most rights of a citizen. The entry uses one man’s case to test how far religious toleration in Maryland really reached.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-oz-zur-10384:
Ma'oz Zur, the great Hanukkah hymn, is examined in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The hymn was first sung at home after kindling the festival lights. It later entered the synagogue service as well. Its acrostic spells the name Mordecai. Zunz placed its author in the middle of the thirteenth century.

Much of the article is given to the famous tune. The bright melody became so bound to the feast that four other Hanukkah hymns are sung to it. Gottheil's English paraphrase, Rock of Ages, carried it into the Union Hymnal. Scholars traced the air to an old German folk song known among Jews by 1450. Luther used the same melody for one of his first chorales. The entry thus follows a hymn from a medieval Jewish home into churches and hymnals far beyond it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mah-nishtannah-: Mah Nishtannah, literally wherein is distinguished, is given a stub entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The words open the child's questions to the father in the Passover Haggadah. By extension, the whole home service of Passover is sometimes familiarly called by this name. The questions are often chanted in the study chant of the Talmudical schools. The intoned text appears elsewhere in the encyclopedia's pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattersdorf-joa:
Joab ben Jeremiah Mattersdorf was a Hungarian rabbi who died about 1807. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He owed his pulpit to family connections. Aaron Chorin had been a disciple of Joab's father, and through his influence Joab became rabbi of Deutschkreuz. The town lay near Mattersdorf, from which his name is taken.

Two books define his record, among them “Hen Tob,” printed at Zolkiev in 1806, which comments on part of the marriage-law code Eben ha-Ezer. The printed volume adds a companion work by his son-in-law. His earlier “Sha'are Binah” offers fresh readings of an older legal work. The entry also catches him in a shared scholarly error. Like Joseph Caro and others, he mistook the author Isaac ben Reuben for a grandson of Isaac Alfasi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-simeon:
Meir ben Simeon of Narbonne was a Talmudist and controversialist of the later thirteenth century. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a disciple of Nathan ben Meir of Trinquetaille. He corresponded as an equal with Nahmanides and enjoyed a high reputation as a commentator. His fame in his own day, though, rested on religious disputation with Christians.

His “Milhemet Mizwah,” the War of the Commandment, survives in a Parma manuscript and falls into five parts. It opens with his account of a formal disputation held in 1245 before the bishop of Narbonne. It collects his controversies with churchmen. It explains the messianic passages Christians pressed into service, and comments on the Shema and the thirteen attributes of God. It ends boldly, with a letter declaring the revered “Sefer ha-Bahir” a forgery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menken-ada-isaa:
Ada Isaacs Menken was an Anglo-American actress. One daring role made her name. Joseph Jacobs and Edgar Mels profile her in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in Louisiana in 1835. She began as a child dancer in New Orleans, survived capture by Indians in Texas, and wrote for newspapers. In 1856 she married Alexander Isaacs Menken, publicly embracing Judaism. In 1861 the Mazeppa of Albany's Green Street Theater made her famous. She rode strapped to a horse in the part. It made her famous on two continents. The entry calls the part more acrobatic than histrionic.

The life that follows is restless. She married the prize-fighter John Heenan, the humorist Orpheus C. Kerr, and James Barclay, played the London and Paris stages, and wrote two books of poems. The last, "Infelicia," was dedicated by permission to Dickens. She died in Paris in 1868. Dickens, Swinburne, Dumas, and Hugo admired her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-max-107:
Max Michael, a German painter born in Hamburg on March 23, 1823, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman, published in 1906. He studied at Dresden's art academy, spent five years in Paris, and then twenty years working in Rome and Venice. His first known work, Country Girl Writing, dates from 1866.

Michael returned to Berlin in 1870 and, five years later, became professor of painting at the Royal Academy, a post he kept until his death in 1891. The entry names his Girls' School in the Sabine Mountains, now in Hamburg's Kunsthalle, a cardinal visiting a monastery, Job disputing with his friends, and Bertini painting an altar-piece among the Camaldolites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miter-10884:
The miter is the priestly head-dress of the Bible. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein sort it out in a Jewish Encyclopedia article published in 1906. The high priest's miter, the miẓnefet, was fine linen. It carried a gold diadem engraved Holiness to the Lord, tied on with a purple cord. Ordinary priests wore the migba'ah, likewise of linen.

The article then follows the word pe'er beyond the sanctuary. It was a festive head-covering for a bridegroom and for the daughters of Zion. Precisely because it was an ornament, mourners took it off. The Bible never describes the miter's shape. Its names suggest a turban wound round the head. Exodus, Ezekiel, and Isaiah supply the evidence throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-10984:
Mordecai, in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Cyrus Adler and A. S. W. Rosenbach, published in 1906, is not the biblical hero but an American family of German origin settled in the United States in the later eighteenth century. Its fame is military, and its brightest name is Alfred Mordecai of Warrenton, North Carolina, born January 3, 1804.

Alfred entered West Point at fifteen and graduated first in his class in 1823, into the engineer corps. He taught natural philosophy at the academy, built Forts Monroe and Calhoun in Virginia, and rose to captain of ordnance. For two decades he sat on the Board of Ordnance, inspected arsenals, and toured Europe's cannon-foundries. He died at Philadelphia in 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-hasid-110: Moses Hasid was an Austrian ethical writer who lived at Prague in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His one work is a Zawwa'ah, a book of ethical instructions, printed at Prague in 1717. Part of it, as Iggeret ha-Musar, was reprinted with Moses Alshech's commentary on the Prophets in 1720.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mother-hebrew-e:
Mother, in Hebrew em and in Aramaic imma, is treated here as a subject in Bible and rabbinic teaching. Wilhelm Bacher and David Philipson wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article. Legally the father headed the Hebrew family, and the mother stood below him. In the honor owed her by her children, though, she stood on his level.

The article gathers the texts: the Decalogue bids children honor mother and father alike, and Proverbs sets a mother's teaching beside a father's. Scripture pictures God's comfort as a mother's comfort and grief as Rachel weeping for her children. Rabbinic tales add Tarfon's devotion to his mother. The entry closes on the mother's supreme place in rearing and teaching the young.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-natronai-b-nehe:
Natronai b. Nehemiah, called Mar Yanka, headed Pumbedita's academy. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Mendelsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was gaon there from 719 to 730. He married into the exilarch Hasdai's family. Pride in that tie marked his rule.

Sherira Gaon reports that students fled his arrogance. Many left the academy and returned only after his death. Two responsa are ascribed to Natronai by name. One readmits followers of the false Messiah Serenus. The other bars children of heretics who renounced Judaism. Weiss, though, gives both rulings to Natronai b. Hilai. Many more responsa under his name remain uncertain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuwiedel-elias:
Elias Neuwiedel was a Russian teacher of Hebrew grammar. Crawford Howell Toy and Max Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Neustadt-Sugind in 1821. He died at Warsaw on Sept. 16, 1886. He studied Talmud at the yeshivah of Volozhin.

Neuwiedel taught Hebrew and modern languages after Volozhin. Rossieny, in Kovno, and Warsaw were his school towns. At Warsaw he published his Hebrew grammar in 1874. More Sefat Ibrit follows the method of Ollendorf. In 1882 came Ab le-Banim, talks for the young. Its title means a father to his children. He was grandson of Benjamin-Benish Neustädter, a noted name. The entry keeps his record in these few firm lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-noph-11584:
