David Galan-Madruga and colleagues report a 2026 study that estimates daily ozone in city air. Ozone near the ground harms lungs and public health. The team built a math formula from pollution and weather data for three European capitals: Madrid, Stockholm and Rome. Data spanned the years 2004 to 2021, with daily ozone from low to high levels.

The formula fit the data well, at near eighty five percent, with a mean error near zero. It held up on new time data not used to build it, and on a new place not in the build set. Both checks met European legal limits for short term ozone models. Exceedance days, when ozone topped safe marks, were rare in the count. A light formula that travels well can aid city health alerts.
pmc-13279584:
Shota Hoshika and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta analysis of surgery timing for thigh bone breaks near the knee in older adults. Such breaks, called distal femur fractures, are grave in old age. Whether early surgery helps was unclear. Two reviewers searched five sources to late 2024 under standard review rules.

Of more than six thousand records screened, sixteen cohort studies with more than thirty one thousand patients fit. The main outcome was death at thirty days, with later death and side effects as second checks. In the pooled result, early surgery showed no clear link to lower thirty day death rates. Bias and proof strength were graded with standard tools. The null find urges care plans past speed alone, like patient fitness and team readiness.
pmc-13279684:
Nitzan Aizenbud and colleagues report a 2026 study that translates a dry mouth form in Hebrew and tests its worth. Xerostomia, or dry mouth, harms oral health and life quality, yet no tested Hebrew form existed. The team turned the Xerostomia Inventory, a standard dry mouth form, in Hebrew by cross cultural rules. They then checked its steadiness and fit with real saliva flow.

One hundred two dry mouth patients filled the Hebrew form. Most were women, and mean age was near sixty four years. Internal steadiness scored very high on the standard alpha scale. Scores linked strongly, in the reverse way, with unstimulated saliva flow: worse dryness meant less spit. Links with other saliva measures were strong as well. Scores did not link with unrelated social facts, which backs the form as a true dry mouth gauge for Hebrew care.
pmc-13279784:

Seizure drugs curb fits but do not stop the disease process. Rust like stress, called oxidative stress, can both cause and follow seizures. Yet all time antioxidant care blurs normal cell signals. Their therapy turns on just in overactive nerve cells.

A promoter called cfos, which wakes in hyperactive neurons, drives Nrf2, a master switch for antioxidant defence. A virus carrier took the build in brain cells. In sham animals, the build stayed near silent. After drug induced status epilepticus, a long seizure state, the build lit up in neuron cells of two memory zones. It rose within four hours, peaked at twelve to twenty four hours, and fell by forty eight hours.
pmc-13279884:
Masamichi Yano and colleagues report a 2026 study that groups heart failure patients who also have atrial fibrillation. Atrial fibrillation is a fast, uneven heart rhythm that often pairs with heart failure, a weak pump state. Its effect on outlook was unclear. The team seek patient subgroups, called phenotypes, with distinct traits and risks. Records held four hundred seven patients admitted with both conditions.

Key risk facts like age, sex, blood markers, kidney scores and drug use fed a cluster analysis, a grouping method. Four phenotypes with clear profiles emerged. The first held younger, mostly male patients with low pump share but sound body state and the highest use of guideline drugs. They fared best on the joint outcome of death or heart failure return. The second group sat mid way on frailty and drug use. Group based risk can tailor watch and drug plans.
pmc-13280384:
Xiang-Rong Wu and a large team present a 2026 AI framework to tailor dual HER2 blockade in breast cancer. HER2 positive breast cancer grows via the HER2 protein, and dual blockade with two antibodies plus chemotherapy is standard before surgery. Responses vary a lot, and practical forecast tools were lacking. Their framework, HER2-LADDER, joins clinical facts with spatial features from routine tissue slides. Slides held standard dye and HER2 stain images.

The model predicted response to the dual therapy in three cohorts. Cohort sizes were two hundred seventy six, eighty two and eighty five patients. Accuracy scores ran high in all three, with the build cohort on top and two validation cohorts close behind. Scores then split patients for tailored advice. Spatial tissue reads from routine slides could guide who needs full dual therapy and who may need a shift.
pmc-13280484:
Iham F. Zidane and colleagues present a 2026 study of venturi based thrombectomy devices tested by simulation and bench work. Mechanical thrombectomy removes clots in stroke, and the Circle of Willis artery geometry poses major challenges for navigation. Five designs were assessed in a simplified cerebral artery segment for the middle cerebral artery, a frequent occlusion site. Designs held three venturi angles, a taper and a cylindrical control.

Computer fluid simulations used standard turbulence models with blood clot interaction physics and non Newtonian blood rheology. In vitro, three dimensional printed prototypes were tested with porcine thrombi in silicone arterial phantoms. Simulations forecast extraction times near two seconds for the control and near one and a half for the forty five degree venturi, with efficiency plateauing beyond that angle. Experimental results confirmed the trend: the forty five degree design was optimal and all venturi devices beat the control.
pmc-13280584:
Catherine Shteynberg offers a 2026 personal reflection, Hope without certainty, after a third brain tumour recurrence. Her care team recommended radiation and chemotherapy. Treatment might offer temporary disease control, but no reliable way existed to predict the outcome. Her husband worried about potential harms, including cognitive decline and diminished quality of life. She chose treatment anyway. The decision exposed a central tension in serious illness: hope framed around anticipated futures, while patients live in profound uncertainty.

Dominant clinical models structure hope around anticipation, goal orientation and pathways to future outcomes. Snyder Hope Theory frames hope as agency and pathways toward desired goals. The Herth Hope Index operationalizes hope through future oriented expectation and goal attainment. Its items even reverse score fear of the future, assuming fear marks low hope. The reflection questions whether such frameworks fit patients who must hope without a clear future to aim at.
pmc-13281284:
Aakriti Sharma and colleagues ran a 2026 trial on blood flow patterns during heart surgery. In bypass surgery, a machine pumps blood while the heart is stopped. Pumps can push blood in a smooth stream or in pulses, like a heartbeat. The team sorted eighty patients by chance into pulse or smooth groups. All had planned surgery to close a heart hole or fix a valve. One team did all the operations, from 2019 to 2020.

Seventy-seven patients were in the final count. Time in intensive care and in hospital was much the same in both groups. Kidney and liver tests and problem rates also matched. One kidney marker ran slightly higher in the pulse group. The authors say pulse flow showed no clear gain here. They do not advise its routine use on this proof.
pmc-13281884:
Qian He and colleagues reviewed nano-scale drug carriers for rheumatoid arthritis in a 2026 paper. The disease is a long-term immune attack on joints that swells and slowly destroys them. Standard drugs help many patients but hit the whole body and stir side effects. They also fail to reset the joint's hostile inner climate. Tiny carriers can ferry drugs straight to inflamed joints. The review sorts the newest platforms by how they aim and what else they do.

Many carriers do double duty once inside the joint. They mop up corrosive oxygen waste, ease low oxygen, and reprogram immune cells toward calm. Some pair diagnosis with care in one package, tracking disease while treating it. The authors weigh what blocks clinic use, from safe large-scale making to proof in patients. They map a path toward smart, joint-fitted nano care.
pmc-13282084:
Ciana M Bowhay published a 2026 education study of an assignment designed to turn animal science students into critical evaluators of media. Students arrive awash in online claims about farming, nutrition, and animal welfare, and they overrate their own ability to spot misinformation. Across two semesters of an undergraduate animal nutrition course, 42 students completed media pieces tied to course content and judged their credibility, then reflected. The author coded the coursework and reflections for themes.

Before the assignment, students leaned on cues: how expert the author seemed and how popular the piece was. Afterward they reported hunting for bias, planning to research claims before believing them, and checking who is speaking before accepting a message. Bowhay frames the shift as transformative learning, where facing one's own habits loosens them. The paper argues media literacy belongs inside the animal science curriculum, since graduates must communicate credibly in a noisy information environment.
pmc-13282684:
Isha Bhardwaj and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review on digital twin technology in orthodontics, the dental field that straightens teeth and aligns jaws. A digital twin is a virtual model of a patient that can simulate treatment and predict results. Its role in orthodontics was underexplored. The team searched four databases for English studies from 2005 to April 2025, following standard scoping methods.

Only nine studies qualified, showing the field is young. Uses ranged from static skull and face twins built from three-dimensional scans to richer twins merging scan types, including mouth and face scans. The authors say the theory base from other industries is elaborate and could transform diagnosis and treatment planning. They judge the potential immense for accuracy, efficiency, and patient experience. Yet they stress the evidence is limited and diverse rather than proven, so clinical adoption should grow from pilot work and validation, not hype.
pmc-13282984:
A 72-year-old man without HIV developed fungus in lung, blood, urine, and brain lining, a 2026 case from Fengzhen He and team. The fungus Cryptococcus neoformans most often strikes people with weak immune defenses. Spread to many organs is rare when HIV is absent, as in this case.

Cultures later grew it from blood, urine, and chest fluid. A spinal fluid test for fungal antigen confirmed spread to the brain lining. Strong antifungal drugs improved lab markers, but organ failure followed and discharge came after 98 days.
pmc-13283384:
Five symptom clusters and three recovery paths emerge around cervical cancer surgery in Yuting Zhang's 2026 longitudinal tracking. Symptom groups and paths over time were not well mapped for this care stage. The team also built a model to flag high-risk patients early.

Patients at one cancer hospital were tracked before surgery, after surgery, and before discharge. Five stable symptom clusters emerged, from body pain to mood and eating issues. Patients split into three paths: good recovery, lasting moderate strain, and severe distress. Age, surgery length, and blood markers shaped risk in the model. Low albumin and potassium raised risk, while the full model sorted risk well.
pmc-13283784:
Yizhuo Fu and co-authors reviewed in 2026 a small adaptor protein called TIFA that sits at a crossroads of immune signalling. TIFA helps switch on TRAF6, a step that fires the NF-κB pathway, a master control of inflammation. A second route, through the sensor ALPK1, lets cells detect bacterial products and raise defences. When TIFA is switched on by phosphorylation, it assembles into larger complexes that gather partner proteins.

The review covers the structure behind that assembly, the signalling routes it feeds, and its roles in immune cells, long-term inflammation, and cancer. TIFA can push tumour growth in some settings and restrain it in others. The authors weigh its promise as a drug target given those two faces.
pmc-13284884:
Kong Qingfei and Xiao Wen write a letter, published in 2026, on hepatitis B prevention among students in Bangladesh. They respond to a study by Khatun and colleagues that found low vaccine coverage in university and college students and wide knowledge gaps, even among the well educated. The letter praises the focus on a key public health problem.

Awareness alone will not close the gap, the writers argue. Work must name the real blocks to action, such as cost, access, ease, trust in the messenger, and felt risk. Older students may have missed childhood vaccine programs and may fear side effects. The letter calls for intervention research that tests concrete steps, not just more education.
pmc-13285684:
Le Tan Hung and colleagues test whether trimming the jaw angle during jaw setback surgery keeps the jaw steadier afterward, in a 2026 randomized study. The surgery treats people whose lower jaw juts forward. Muscles that sling under the jaw can pull it forward again during healing, causing relapse.

Twenty patients were split evenly between standard setback surgery and setback combined with angle removal. X-ray tracings tracked chin landmarks over three months of healing. The standard group drifted forward, while the combined group settled slightly backward. The authors argue that removing the angle shortens the muscle sling and eases its pull. They suggest larger studies covering other jaw patterns.
pmc-13285884:
Rajvi D. Doctor and colleagues compare tools and washing methods for redoing failed root canal treatments, in a 2026 laboratory study. Sixty lower premolar teeth were filled with a modern bioceramic sealer, then retreated with one of two file systems. The team measured how much tooth wall was lost and how well leftover sealer was cleaned out.

Scans showed the ProTaper system removed more dentin than the NeoEndo system. For cleaning, laser-activated irrigation removed the most sealer, followed by ultrasound-activated washing, with plain needle irrigation last. Microscope images supported the scan findings. The authors note the dentin difference between file systems was not statistically firm, while the cleaning ranking was clear.
pmc-13286284:
Nancy M Y Teng and colleagues probe the lung's bacterial community in people left breathless after COVID-19 in a 2026 clinical study. Some survivors keep scarred scans and symptoms long after the virus clears, and a disturbed airway flora is one suspect. Wash fluid from 38 such patients went through gene sequencing and stood against samples from healthy lungs.

Patient lungs held more kinds of bacteria, spread more unevenly, than the comparison set. A handful of genera, including familiar mouth residents, shifted in share between the groups. Yet almost no clinical measure tracked those shifts, apart from scan cloudiness easing as variety rose. The authors judge the changes real but faint, unlikely to explain the lasting damage, and note oral bacteria turning up in the wash could itself mirror the illness state.
pmc-13286484:
Takuro Tomino and co-authors report a tiny colon growth hiding an aggressive cancer in a published 2026 case report. The man, 75 and under care for liver cancer, had a screening colonoscopy that found a 4 mm slightly raised spot with a dipped center in his transverse colon. Magnified imaging showed scrambled vessels and a blurred surface, patterns that warn of deep trouble despite the small size.

Snare removal revealed poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma already burrowing into the wall's lower layer, with lymph channel invasion but clean edges. Stains ruled out both hormone-type tumors and spread from his liver cancer. No further surgery followed because his liver cancer had reached his lungs. pmc-13286784:
Amey Oak and a large team evaluate a software platform that pulls cancer registry data straight from electronic medical records at Tata Memorial Centre in India. The 2026 study checks completeness and the time abstractors need per case. The hospital runs one of India's largest cancer registries, but gathering scattered record details by hand is slow.

pmc-13286884:
Zernila Zaheer reviews how drug-proof germs harm life and wealth in Pakistan. The 2026 review pulls in twenty-nine studies found through a set search. Germs that shrug off key drugs are on the rise in gut, lung, and hospital wards. Old drugs fail more and more, and proof of spread is strong.

pmc-13287184:

Heat-formed aligners pushed much harder in the front-to-back direction and then lost force quickly after an early peak. Printed versions, with either a straight or a scalloped edge, delivered gentler forces that rose slowly and levelled off. Printed aligners also matched planned thickness more closely. The authors say the steadier force control deserves testing in patients before clinical claims are made.
pmc-13287884:
Eric K Rowinsky and colleagues outline a phase 3 trial of nanvuranlat for advanced bile duct cancer in a 2026 abstract. Nanvuranlat blocks a transporter that feeds amino acids to tumor cells. pmc-13288684:
Patrice Degoulet and fellow senior scholars sort out two overlapping labels in a 2026 perspective article drawn from a MEDINFO 2025 panel in Taipei. pmc-13288884:

pmc-13289384:

pmc-13289784:

pmc-13289884:

pmc-13290084:

pmc-13290984:
Leqin Chen and co-authors ask in a 2026 survey study whether growing up in a city or in the countryside relates to how well new college students handle emotions. pmc-13291284:

pmc-13291984:

pmc-13292384:

pmc-13292584:

pmc-13292784:

pmc-13292984:

The authors suggest training should build emotional skills alongside tech skills.
pmc-13293284:

Change varied widely, so the authors urge fixing barriers at both personal and workplace levels.
pmc-13293884:

pmc-13293984:
Teng Hu and colleagues describe SCas12aV2 in a 2026 protocol for finding RNA directly, with no copying or pre-amplification step. pmc-13294384:

pmc-13294484:

pmc-13294984:
Tao Wu and colleagues test whether bouts of thin air can help the aged brain mend after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. pmc-13295884:

Outcome data on diabetic maculopathy came from the FinnGen group in Finland. pmc-13295984:
Megan R Rajah, Anton F Doubell and Philip G Herbst use heart scans in 2026 to study severe narrowing of the aortic valve in South Africa. They compare patients whose heart pump fraction had fallen with those whose pumping stayed normal, testing whether weak wall thickening explains the drop.

Wall thickness, though, was identical between groups, and muscle mass differed little. The authors conclude chamber stretching and valve tightness, not failed thickening, track with the weaker pumping.
pmc-13296684:
Xinyue Li and co-authors review sensors built from tiny engineered materials for brain and mental-health tests in a 2026 article. The authors point to combined platforms, closed brain loops, and prediction models as next steps.
pmc-13297084:
Izabela Rams-Pociecha, Paulina C. Mizia and Rafal P. Piprek chart, in 2026, gonad development in bearded dragon embryos slice by slice. The popular pet lizard may model how genes and nest temperature set sex, including temperature-driven sex reversal.

Gonads first appeared on day eight and already diverged by sex a day later, unusually fast for reptiles. Testes quickly formed their tubules, while ovaries kept a thick outer layer, gained germ cells and grew large inner cavities, perhaps suiting clutches of up to thirty eggs. The timeline anchors future gene and temperature studies.
pmc-13297784:
Jiaqi Li and colleagues work out how phloridzin, a flavonoid from apples, binds to whey protein, in a 2026 study. Whey protein isolate can carry such plant compounds in foods, but the grip between them was unclear. Lab measures and computer simulations were combined to watch the pairing form.

The protein took up a small load of the compound, just over one percent by weight. Heat measures showed the binding runs on disorder gains, driven mainly by water-shunning and electric forces. The protein's coiled shape adjusted only modestly on binding. Knowing the grip's nature helps food designers build carriers that hold flavonoids through processing and digestion.
pmc-13297984:
Hope grew measurably among grieving people who completed a community support program, according to a 2026 pilot study by Yoojung Kim and Carmen G Loiselle. Eleven participants in Living with Loss, run by the Montreal organization Hope and Cope, answered surveys and interviews before and after the program.

Hope scores rose significantly by completion. Participants valued learning fresh coping strategies, hearing varied perspectives on loss, and sharing experiences with people who understood. At the same time, attending in person brought emotional and logistical strains for some. The authors treat the small pilot as evidence of genuine benefit, while flagging delivery changes that could ease participation burdens.
pmc-13298184:
A bile duct cancer drug set off a rare and deadly skin disease in a case told by Katarina Čular and her team in 2026. A 43-year-old woman with spread liver bile duct cancer took pemigatinib, a drug that blocks the FGFR2 growth switch. Seven months in, she broke out in calciphylaxis, a grim state where small blood vessels crust with calcium and skin dies.

A skin biopsy proved the cause. The team stopped the drug and gave germ-fighting drugs and full support care. She still worsened and died of sepsis as the cancer grew too. The team urges doctors who use this drug class to watch the skin with care. Early spotting and a fast stop may be the one chance to help.
pmc-13298384:
Early softening of a stiff fatty liver tends to continue, show Shohei Kimura and co-authors in a 2026 imaging study. They followed 100 patients with metabolic liver disease who had magnetic resonance elastography at baseline, about one year, and about three years.

Twenty-two patients counted as early responders, meaning liver stiffness had dropped at least 19% by the second scan. Those patients were far more likely to keep that improvement at year three, 59% versus 27% for the rest, and the link held after adjustment with an odds ratio of 3.41. Stiffer livers at baseline also improved more often. The authors say short-term scans can hint at the longer trajectory.
pmc-13299884:
D Kim and colleagues re-analyse a randomised trial of stopping blood thinners after successful atrial fibrillation ablation, splitting patients by left atrial size, in a 2026 post-hoc study. The original trial found net benefit from stopping treatment in patients free of rhythm recurrence for a year. This analysis asked whether atrial diameter changes that answer.

Outcome rates at two years were low and statistically similar across size groups and treatment strategies. Events in the smaller-atrium group occurred only among patients who continued treatment. The authors conclude decisions may hinge more on staying rhythm-free than on atrial enlargement, supporting individual choices backed by systematic rhythm monitoring after ablation.
pmc-13300384:
S Iqbal and colleagues report early rhythm relapse after pulsed field ablation from the SINGLE-SHOT CHAMPION trial, published in 2026. Patients with symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation were randomized to pulsed field ablation or cryoballoon ablation, and every patient received an implantable heart monitor at the procedure. A ninety-day blanking period was set, during which early recurrences are usually discounted.

Early recurrence struck about forty percent after pulsed field ablation against sixty percent after cryoballoon treatment, and the fibrillation burden during blanking was also lower with the newer energy. Timing mattered most: recurrences confined to the first thirty days often settled, while those appearing later rarely did and drove more hospital visits and repeat ablations. Success rates at one year rose as the blanking window lengthened. The authors argue the evidence supports shortening the standard blanking period.
pmc-13300984:
Fever after a foreign trip sends emergency doctors down a wide diagnostic maze, and Liesbeth Van Dessel with colleagues offer a practical map in a 2026 overview. Built for stable patients outside intensive care, their summary ranks travel-linked causes by how often they occur, how long they incubate, and how they present.

Malaria, dengue, and typhoid fever top the imported list, though ordinary infections still cause most post-travel fevers. The authors stress travel and exposure history as the sharpest tool for choosing tests, with early empiric treatment where severity demands it. Their bottom line for most cases is simple: work systematically, treat early when needed, and pull in specialists promptly.
pmc-13302084:
Xiaoyi Wang and co-authors propose, in a 2026 computer vision paper, a detection system that fuses ordinary camera images with infrared images. Visible pictures fail in darkness or glare, while heat images lack fine detail, so combining them should help machines spot objects. Their design pairs convolutional networks, which read local detail, with a deformable transformer that tracks wider context.

Tests ran on standard benchmark sets that include street scenes and low-light surveillance footage. The fused system posted the best detection scores among compared methods on both datasets, with clear margins over the runner-up approach. Gains were largest in hard cases such as occlusion and cluttered backgrounds. The authors present the architecture as practical support for driving and security systems.
pmc-13302584:
A one-line correction fixes heart-scan timing for patients with a blocked left electrical pathway, Tsubasa Morioka and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 imaging study. Ninety-four patients, split among normal rhythm, right bundle branch block, and complete left bundle branch block, had the quiet mid-diastolic window of the right coronary artery measured. Standard formulas predict that window from heart rate and conduction time.

In left-block patients the standard formula overshot by an average of 37.9 milliseconds, enough to blur images. Subtracting the excess QRS width erased the bias and halved the prediction error. Rebuilding the model from scratch proved unnecessary, the authors conclude; the physiology holds, only the offset changes.
pmc-13302984:
Syed Muhammad Anas Ibrahim and Jungyul Park design, in a 2026 engineering study, acoustic resonators that both block low traffic noise and harvest its energy. Noise below five hundred hertz has wavelengths so long that ordinary resonators grow impractically large. Their approach lets an active-learning algorithm propose cavity shapes, checking only the most promising with heavy simulations.

The search paired a statistical surrogate model with a genetic optimiser, retraining after each verified round. A scaled prototype amplified pressure about twentyfold near the target tone, and a revolved three-dimensional cavity did better still while cutting transmitted sound. Fitted with a stack of piezoelectric elements, the device produced a measurable trickle of power under loud test sound, enough for small sensors.
pmc-13303284:
Kun Zhou, James C Kosmopoulos, and Karthik Anantharaman present, in a 2026 paper, a software toolkit that classifies bacteria- and archaea-infecting viruses down to species level. Existing tools handle broad family ranks well but blur at genus and species, where ecology questions live. Their method builds on family trees of single-copy marker genes matched to the official taxonomy framework.

Benchmarks showed agreement with the official classification in the mid-eighties to low-nineties percent range at subfamily and genus levels. Adding genome-wide identity measures pushed species-level agreement above ninety-two percent against a major virus database. Assignment rates matched or beat rival tools in head-to-head tests. The toolkit is released publicly for standardised viral naming in microbiome studies.
pmc-13305184:
Marco A. Obregón-Mendoza and colleagues report two new crystal forms of diacetylcurcumin, a relative of the turmeric pigment curcumin, in a 2026 study. Crystal form can change melting, dissolving, and patent value for drug-like compounds.

Different solvent mixes grew the new forms alongside the one already known. Nuclear magnetic resonance in solid samples and X-ray work confirmed a canoe-shaped form and a balloon-shaped form that grew side by side. A cheap pairing of microscope shape checks and infrared scans quickly mapped the crystal options. Such simple screening may guide work on other natural product families.
pmc-13305684:
Maria Patsiliva led a 2026 Greek study linking Mediterranean eating habits with harmful sugar-related compounds in type 2 diabetes. Sixty-one adults took part, and diet was scored on a scale running from 0 to 55 points.

Eye and skin levels of advanced glycation end-products were read with light-based tools, and blood levels were measured by lab assay. Stronger diet adherence appeared more often in women and went with lower blood sugar control marker HbA1c in the reported results. After adjustment, higher scores still linked to lower eye and skin readings, suggesting diet quality may relate to tissue damage markers.
pmc-13306084:
Dorottya Nyáry wrote a 2026 narrative review tying long-term low-grade inflammation of ageing to muscle wasting. Both processes feed frailty, poor metabolism and loss of physical ability, and share roots in immune drift, cell power faults and oxidative stress.

Evidence from lab, population and trial studies covered plant chemicals such as polyphenols and carotenoids, omega-3 fats, exercise and wider eating patterns. Pathways in focus included NF-κB, AMPK–mTOR and Nrf2 signalling, which govern inflammation, cell energy and muscle upkeep. The authors present combined lifestyle and nutrient steps as a plausible way to slow both processes together.
pmc-13306584:
Jung-Tien Lo mixed spent coffee grounds into PLA plastic for 3D printing in a 2026 materials study. Grounds were added across a range up to 20 wt% in filaments and printed parts to test heat, strength and handling traits.

Coffee lowered the softening point slightly and raised crystallinity, while heat breakdown began sooner yet stayed above printing temperatures in reported checks. Filament strength and stiffness fell, and printed parts grew lighter, darker and thirstier for moisture. Bending and impact strength also dropped, so the authors frame grounds as a tailoring filler with clear trade-offs.
pmc-13306784:
Jonggwon Kim trained a semi-supervised adversarial system to spot attacks on car networks in a 2026 study. Vehicle CAN buses carry safety signals without built-in identity checks, so injected or spoofed messages can mislead control units.

Message runs become 64×9 grey images for learning, starting from a small labelled set to set an early boundary. Later rounds refine that boundary with distribution goals and generated fakes, then train the generator against it. The staged plan aims to keep the low false alarms of supervised tools while still catching unseen attacks.
pmc-13306884:
Ahmed Almotairy delivered two eye drugs through moulded inserts holding a self-emulsifying mix in a 2026 study. Corneal infections from amoebae and fungi resist standard drops because much of each dose washes away before entering tissue.

Voriconazole and diclofenac were loaded into tiny droplets sized under 100 nm with spread below 0.35 in reported optima. Inserts could be tuned for fast or slow release, and tissue tests outside the body pushed voriconazole into cornea above the level needed to block growth. The design aims to raise drug entry while cutting drop waste.
pmc-13307184:
Na An hunted drug targets for ulcerative colitis among lactylation genes in a 2026 genetics study. Starting from 46 such genes, overlap with blood gene-control data narrowed the field to 29 candidates for causal testing.

Outcome data covered 482,657 participants in a Finnish database in the reported design. Multiple causal models, a second validation method, corrected expression data and single-cell profiles from a public set all filtered the list. A cell model using inflamed colon lining then checked how shortlisted genes change during inflammation. The short list gives drug hunters fresh leads for calm gut drugs with clear gene roots.
pmc-13307384:
Josephine Paparo and Elizabeth Pizarro-Campagna survey in 2026 how supervision, money strain, and overall placement joy shape how competent psychology interns feel in Australia. A total of 122 interns on the 5 + 1 path to registration filled in an online survey.

Interns felt happier when providers put learning ahead of service demands, and good supervision also tracked with higher joy in the placement. For current interns, the link from supervision to felt competence ran fully through placement joy, and it was strongest under money strain. Stronger oversight of providers could protect trainees and help keep them in the workforce.
pmc-13307684:
Patrick William Chambers writes a 2026 letter that extends a recent thesis on long COVID by adding magnesium and sex hormones to the account. The thesis casts the mTOR pathway as a core driver, and the letter asks what might push that pathway into overdrive for so long.

Low magnesium could blunt the energy sensor AMPK, which in turn would free mTOR from a key brake in the system. Mild lack might thus worsen fatigue, while a deeper lack could flip the balance the other way. The letter also links low oestrogen patterns, vitamin D, and a skewed calcium to magnesium ratio, and it floats combined fixes for trial testing.
pmc-13308284:
Lan Ma and colleagues follow the udder microbe community of dairy cows in 2026 across the dry period between lactations. Milk was sampled before dry-off, just after calving, and one month into the new lactation. The dry weeks reshape the gland completely, and dry cow antibiotic therapy adds its own pressure.

Before dry-off, the gland held a diverse but unstable community fed by environmental exposure. Calving created a bottleneck: colostrum immune factors cut diversity and numbers sharply. Early lactation rebuilt the community only partly toward its old state. Resistance genes and mobile genetic elements followed the same dip and partial recovery pattern. Host changes and dry therapy together drive the reset, the authors conclude. Knowing the rhythm could help farmers time interventions and spare antibiotics.
pmc-13308484:
Cora Delling and co-authors test in 2026 how two gut parasites change sugar transport and cell seals when they infect pig gut cells at the same time. They tracked four seal proteins and two sugar carriers at 24, 48, and 72 hours, plus sugar levels inside cells at the middle point.

Seal protein genes did not shift in a firm way under either parasite in this cell model. One sugar carrier, GLUT2, fell in cells with Cryptosporidium parvum at 48 hours versus both clean cells and Giardia only cells. Sugar inside cells rose when both parasites were present at once. Giardia alone left the checked markers alone, so the first parasite drove the sugar effects seen.
pmc-13309084:
Kouichi Kajiwara, Shinsuke Sakoda, and Kimiaki Kawano recount in 2026 how thinking traps delayed treatment of a young rugby player's infected hip joint. The twenty-one-year-old arrived after a match with fast-worsening pain and raised inflammation markers. Fluid drawn from the joint looked cloudy, yet antibiotics were withheld because a sports injury seemed more likely.

Rest and anti-inflammatory medicine briefly improved him, which reinforced the first impression, and he went home. He returned the same evening unable to walk, with inflammation climbing further. Culture then grew Staphylococcus aureus, targeted antibiotics began, and keyhole washing of the joint followed. He returned to competitive rugby twenty weeks after surgery. The authors name anchoring bias and premature closure as the culprits. Cloudy joint fluid, they argue, should force an immediate diagnostic timeout in any athlete.
pmc-13309284:
Silvana R Oliveira and co-authors map in 2026, cell by cell, the element mix of algae that live on glaciers and lasting snow banks, where cold, fierce light, and scant food rule. They used single cell plasma mass checks on three cold species and two warm water kin, and cross checked the sums with bulk digests.

Per cell bulk, cold algae held less phosphorus, magnesium, and calcium, a fit for the slow burn of cold life. Starved of phosphorus, one cold species held its inner mix steady, while a second shed phosphorus and magnesium and gained copper. The maps show how ice algae guard their stores when food runs thin on the ice.
pmc-13309384:
Nicole M Spanier and co-authors describe a 2026 greenhouse study on whether soil microbes remember past drought. Soil microbes help plants cope with dry spells, but it was unclear if past dry soil changes how young trees handle new drought. Three eastern hardwood species were used to test that idea.

Saplings grew in field soil that had faced past drought or normal moisture, then faced new drought or steady water. One species, chokecherry, kept normal leaf function under new drought only when its soil had a dry past. The other two species gained no such help. The authors suggest that soil history can buffer some trees, but the effect depends on the species.
pmc-13309584:
Anna Hinterberger and colleagues test whether a chat model can turn free-text prostate scan reports into standard codes in a 2026 study. Scans that target a prostate marker help stage prostate cancer, and a shared rule set called PROMISE V2 grades spread. Most reports still arrive as plain narrative, which slows shared reading.

ChatGPT-4o read narrative reports from two scan types and assigned standard stage codes. Accuracy reached 79.8 percent for one scan type and 91.0 percent for the other, a clear gap in the trial data. Grading of the main tumor showed the widest gap, while distant spread grading matched closely. The authors see promise for low-effort structuring, with human checks still required.
pmc-13309684:
Kezar and colleagues set reference intervals in 2026 for blood and serum tests in captive-born owl monkeys, a nocturnal primate used to model malaria and viral infections. Vets need normal ranges to spot illness and judge study effects, but the values in use were over thirty years old and came mostly from wild-caught animals of unknown age. The team analyzed samples from 191 healthy monkeys, split by age class and sex.

The new intervals cover juveniles, adults, and older animals, with adult values also split by sex. Many measures differed by age or sex, and some patterns clashed with older data from this and related species, which underlines the value of fresh, colony-specific ranges. The authors offer the intervals as a practical tool for health monitoring and for reading intervention effects in owl monkey research.
pmc-13310684:
Julia Martinez-Sanchez and co-authors track vessel injury markers during a blood-filtering therapy for graft-versus-host disease in a 2026 study. After transplant, donor immune cells can attack the gut, skin, and liver, and vessel lining damage sits under much of that harm. Photopheresis, a light-based blood treatment, serves patients who fail steroids.

Blood from 35 patients was sampled before treatment and one month into it, then split by response into 18 good and 17 poor responders. A panel covered vessel activation, graft disease markers, complement activity, and neutrophil traps, plus a composite vessel stress index. Vessel markers ran high in all patients at baseline without splitting the groups. One month in, some markers rose or fell by response group.
pmc-13310784:
Babatope Akinyemi and Janice Siegford survey pig vets on smart farm tools in a 2026 study. Sensors and cameras can spot illness early and improve pig welfare and output on large farms. Vets advise farmers on buying choices, yet what drives a vet to urge these tools was poorly known.

Answers came from 61 United States pig vets met at four work meetings from 2022 to 2023. Vets scored expected gains and desire for help highest, while views on cost sat near the middle. Plans to urge wider use linked to those views in test models. Small numbers mean results are early and need care.
pmc-13310984:
Jiamin Guo and colleagues review mitochondria focused plans to boost cancer radiotherapy in a 2026 paper. Radiation kills tumors by direct DNA harm, by stirring reactive oxygen, and by waking immune attack. Mitochondria sit at the hub of oxygen stress and cell death signals, so they offer many leverage points.

Small drugs can raise or lower mitochondrial stress, while nano carriers, gene edits, and diet plans aim at the same hub. Stress signals from harmed mitochondria help immune cells mature and attack tumors. Most nano and gene plans rest on lab proof alone, while some diet and immune pairings have entered early human tests.
pmc-13311284:
Qian Zhang and co-authors give a 2026 study of a two-protein loop that feeds sugar burning and growth in kidney cancer. The deubiquitinase JOSD2 and the transcription factor CREB1 each keep the other active.

Lab and animal work showed JOSD2 is raised in renal cell carcinoma and that high levels track with worse outcomes. JOSD2 shields CREB1 from breakdown, while CREB1 switches on the JOSD2 gene, forming the loop. The pair raises sugar-use genes such as GLUT1, HK2, and PFKP, speeding growth and spread. Blocking the loop could offer a new drug target for this cancer.
pmc-13311684:
Wendy LM Leurs and co-authors compare three ways of counting hospital falls in a 2026 Dutch study. Incident reports miss many falls, so the team tested an AI text model against hand chart review.

The study covered 76 patients who fell and 1547 who did not, with over thirty thousand nursing notes. Hand review found 124 falls. The AI model caught 79.8 percent of them with high accuracy for non-falls, while incident reports caught only 37 percent in this study. The model also saved staff time. The findings support automated watching as a fairer base for fall prevention.
pmc-13311784:
Guifang Yang and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how emergency medical rescue works after debris flow disasters. Debris flows are fast surges of rock, soil, and water, usually triggered by heavy mountain rain, melting snow, or earthquakes. Most research on them covers prediction and engineering, so the authors focus on the neglected medical side: reaching victims, treating them in the field, and organizing care under difficult terrain.

The review weighs recent advances by how ready they are for real use, including drones, bedside ultrasound, and mobile medical systems. It gives particular attention to crush syndrome care before hospital arrival, where better field treatment has improved survival. Delayed access, complex ground, and long stretches of field-based care stand out as the problems that define these events. The authors close with guidance on training standards, resource placement, and planning for climate-driven disasters.
pmc-13311984:
Xingyu Wang, Haijin Wang, and Huiyu Luo report a 2026 trial on whether esketamine given during chest surgery improves sleep afterward in patients who slept poorly before the operation.

One hundred patients having planned non-heart chest surgery under general anesthesia were assigned to esketamine or placebo, dosed at induction and at skin closure. Sleep disturbance on day one hit 50 percent of the drug group against 82 percent of controls in this trial. Day three rates also favored the drug. Pain, anxiety, mood scores, blood markers, and sleep stage shares were tracked as secondary measures for a fuller picture.
pmc-13312084:
Marjory Güilgüiruca-Retamal and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, how the DASS-21 questionnaire is structured when used with Chilean healthcare workers. The 21-item scale is widely used to screen for depression, anxiety, and stress, but whether it truly measures three separate states in working groups has been debated.

The team surveyed 239 workers at a hospital in northern Chile in 2021 and compared four statistical models of the scale's structure. Every model fit acceptably, and a bifactor model fit best, yet extra checks showed one general distress factor carried nearly all the reliable signal. Scores also behaved the same across sexes. The authors conclude that the total score works as a simple screening measure of overall distress in such settings.
pmc-13312484:
Xianhua Zhao and colleagues report a 2026 analytical study profiling the color compounds of Marselan wines, a grape variety gaining ground in China. Anthocyanins and their derivatives shape a red wine's color and stability, and their fingerprint also records variety, origin, and vintage, which makes them useful for checking authenticity and quality.

The team built a targeted mass spectrometry method able to characterize 58 of these compounds in one run. Twelve compounds differed significantly by vintage, with acetylated anthocyanins and pyranoanthocyanins standing out as candidate year markers, and total levels fell with aging while the pyranoanthocyanin share grew. Wines from Ningxia, Hebei, and Xinjiang separated clearly by profile, though subregions inside Ningxia blurred together. A support vector machine model topped 96 percent accuracy at the regional level, backing fingerprints for origin tracing.
pmc-13312584:
David Maiershon and colleagues report a 2026 randomized pilot feasibility trial of mixed reality support for basic life support training in medical students. Manikin practice builds the physical skill of resuscitation but lacks a believable patient and setting, so the team layered virtual patient cues over hands-on practice with headsets shared in the same room.

Within an eight-hour course, 61 first-year students were split between mixed reality and conventional training. The technology slotted into the scheduled teaching with no failures blocking delivery and no safety incidents from the headsets. Students' reported workload matched the conventional group, and secondary measures of self-efficacy, motivation, and satisfaction also showed no significant differences. Feedback flagged headset stability and avatar responsiveness for improvement, and views on added value were mixed, leaving the door open to a larger trial.
pmc-13312684:
Arika Poudel and co-authors assess, in a 2026 study, whether measuring the macular ganglion cell complex with optical coherence tomography can pick out glaucoma in a Nepali eye hospital. The team also wanted reference values for healthy eyes and glaucoma suspects in this population, since the inner retinal layers thin as glaucoma destroys nerve cells.

The Kathmandu study covered 203 patients and 406 eyes: 76 with primary open-angle glaucoma, 62 suspects, and 65 controls. All three thickness measures ran significantly lower in glaucoma eyes than in suspects or controls, even after adjusting for age. Average and inferior complex thickness performed best, each reaching an area under the curve of 0.83 for separating glaucoma from healthy eyes. The authors endorse the measurement as a diagnostic aid while noting the single-center design as a limit.
pmc-13312784:
Vellithiruthi Thazhath Aaruni and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, the building and testing of a home literacy questionnaire for Malayalam-speaking preschool children in Kerala, India. The home literacy environment shapes early reading development, yet no validated tool existed in Malayalam to measure the practices, resources, and beliefs involved.

The team drafted items from established frameworks, had experts rate their content validity, revised the wording, and gave the questionnaire to 300 parents. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the intended structure, and internal consistency came out satisfactory. Answer patterns sketched how parents read with children, what children do with books, what parents believe about literacy, and what the home offers physically. The authors present the instrument as a valid, reliable way to assess home literacy in this population and guide early support.
pmc-13313184:
Jessica K Josephson and co-workers examine gut and brain links in chronic bowel disease in a 2026 study. They note that inflammatory bowel disease keeps rising and often comes with anxiety, low mood, and memory loss, yet the paths that join gut illness to these brain effects stay unclear.

Their test used Muc2 knockout mice, a model of lasting colitis, raised with or without gut microbes, plus normal mice for contrast. The mice were checked for anxious and low-mood behavior and for memory faults. The team also measured tryptophan and its breakdown products in colon, blood, and brain, and looked at the blood-brain barrier. The design lets them ask whether microbe-driven shifts in tryptophan use track with the behavior changes seen in colitis.
pmc-13313284:
Mohamed A. Osman and colleagues test a drug pairing against tongue cancer cells in a 2026 lab study. Head and neck cancers have low survival and often resist care, and tongue and mouth floor are the most common sites, so new options are needed.

Their plan pairs light-based therapy, which uses methylene blue plus laser light to kill cells, with metformin, a diabetes drug that may slow cancer growth. On HNO97 tongue cancer cells, they measured killing with a dye test and tracked proteins such as mTOR and AMP-activated kinase with kit assays. The aim was to see if metformin makes the light therapy hit harder and to map the paths involved. If the pairing works in later tests, it could give a gentler option for oral cancer.
pmc-13313884:
Durah Fares Hashem and Siraj Muneer Al-Kafagy chart, in a 2026 veterinary anatomy study, how two testicular cell types change across the life of Scottish fold cats. Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm while Leydig cells make testosterone, and both shift with age. The researchers collected testes from healthy cats classed as kittens, adults, or seniors. They applied tissue processing and immunohistochemical staining for cell-specific markers, comparing staining strength and cell distribution between groups.

The age gradient was clear. Kittens showed weak staining and unfinished sperm-producing tubules, a picture of immaturity. Adults showed the strongest staining and orderly tubules, matching peak sperm production and hormone function. Seniors lost staining intensity, their tubules degenerated, and Leydig cells thinned out. The authors conclude that testicular structure and function crest in adulthood and erode with age. That baseline is useful for breeding work and for interpreting reproductive disease in this breed.
pmc-13314084:
Ayesha Taranum and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a phone-based deep learning tool that flags skin and eye diseases in dogs from photographs. These conditions are frequent and worsen when veterinary care is far away, as it is for many owners in remote areas. The team assembled an image set spanning nine disease classes and applied augmentation to broaden it. They trained a MobileNetV2 network chosen for its small footprint, and embedded the model in a mobile application for instant classification.

The model reached 93.22 percent accuracy in training and 86.31 percent on held-out validation images. Head-to-head comparisons showed it beating two heavier architectures, InceptionV3 and ResNet50, on the balance of accuracy and efficiency that phone deployment demands. The authors present the app as an inexpensive first-look diagnostic aid for owners and front-line workers in remote settings, meant to speed referral rather than replace the veterinarian.
pmc-13314184:
Akmam Ali Habeeb reports a 2026 study of plant-made zinc oxide nanoparticles as a greener weapon against aphids on okra. Aphids drain the crop and spread viruses, while conventional sprays breed resistance and pollute. Habeeb synthesized the particles using seed extract of Moringa peregrina and characterized the product. He sprayed infested okra leaves at three concentrations, tracking aphid death and reproduction over three days, plus gene activity in the survivors.

Killing power climbed with dose. It reached 85 percent mortality at the top concentration of 100 micrograms per milliliter, while reproduction fell by 60 percent at the same dose. Gene measurements explained the damage: a nerve enzyme gene and a mitochondrial gene were turned down by roughly fourfold and just under fourfold respectively in the treated aphids, matching the mortality pattern. The author concludes the nanoparticles suppress the pest at molecular level and merit development as an eco-safe option for okra protection.
pmc-13314784:
Yapeng Wang and co-workers shorten a Mandarin scale for demoralization in cancer patients in a 2026 study. Loss of morale is common in Chinese cancer care and drags down treatment adherence and quality of life, yet the full 24-item scale is too long for busy clinics.

The study enrolled 1050 patients from June 2022 to June 2023, of whom 971 filled the full scale face to face, as counted in the report. Factor math and Rasch modeling trimmed and checked the items for fit, bias, and difficulty. A subgroup of 50 steady patients retook the scale to test repeat reliability, by the design given. The short form aims to let clinics screen morale fast and often, as world guidelines urge for distress in cancer care.
pmc-13316084:
Lena Klein, Matthias Brand, and Elisa Wegmann test in 2026 a two-path model of problematic social network use, separating pleasure seeking from compensation seeking. People use social networks for many reasons, time online grows, and use can turn problematic, a process the I-PACE model frames through motives, traits, stress appraisal, and coping.

In a preregistered German multicenter study, 306 participants, 81 percent female with mean age 26.41 years, completed mixed methods including a diagnostic interview adapted from gaming disorder criteria. Both reward paths were expected to raise symptom severity and usage time, and structural modeling tested those links.
pmc-13316184:
Sara Maghami, Kimmo Rumpunen, and Örjan Johansson tested in 2026 a gentler way to pasteurize apple juice using a flow-through sound device at reduced heat. Standard heat treatment keeps juice safe but damages heat-sensitive nutrients and flavor, so combined acoustic and fluid cavitation was tried instead.

The device design was checked by simulation and experiment. Dual-frequency treatment at 50 to 55 degrees worked best, cutting yeast by a log value of 3.6 and mold and general microbes by values near 2.7 and 2.8 after 450 seconds of effective treatment. Microscopy showed progressive cell breakage, and smaller particles improved juice stability.
pmc-13316284:
Sami Shoucair and colleagues published a 2026 review that pools the world experience with robot-assisted liver transplant surgery in recipients. The team gathered reports from several countries to judge whether the new approach works safely in its earliest phase.

Ten studies covering 93 operations met the entry rules, and three larger series fed the pooled math. Most grafts came from living donors and most patients were carefully chosen, lower-risk cases. Bleeding, kidney injury, and bile duct problems stayed uncommon, major illness affected about one in six patients, and pooled survival at six months reached 98.0 percent in the combined data. The authors argue the method is workable now, while wider registries should test it in harder cases.
pmc-13316684:
Larissa L da Cruz and colleagues summarise, in 2026, a long Arkansas cohort that followed infants fed soy formula, cow milk formula or breast milk into adolescence. Breast milk is regarded as the ideal infant food, yet many families use formula. Long-term safety data for soy formula have been limited.

The Beginnings studies enrolled 600 healthy term infants, with 200 in each feeding group. Breastfed infants gained weight more slowly and kept lower body mass and waist measures into adolescence. Formula groups matched breastfed infants on bone mineral, most thinking measures and reproductive development. Heart rate and vagal tone differed by group, and gut microbe profiles carried distinct early signatures. Overall, soy and cow milk formulas looked more alike than different.
pmc-13318384:
Nika Bakshi, Gayaneh Nazarian and Stephanie Wong present, in 2026, two cases of womb tearing discovered after successful vaginal birth following a previous caesarean. Rupture is rare and can be fatal, and most reports focus on events during labour rather than findings after delivery.

One woman, aged 34, bled persistently after delivery. Surgeons found a small two-centimetre defect in the front wall of the womb and repaired it successfully. The second woman, aged 31, became unstable from blood loss. She had a much larger rupture plus a second defect at the back. Massive transfusion stabilised her at first, but renewed instability led to removal of the womb. The contrast shows how widely presentation and outcome can vary.
pmc-13318784:
Maha Abdullah Momenah and Wedad Saeed Al-Qahtani present a 2026 exploratory study of bladder cancer in smokers and non-smokers. They examine a marker called BLCA-4, genetic repeat patterns, and urine cell appearance. Blood and urine samples came from patients and healthy controls. In total, 273 people were enrolled across three groups.

Cancer patients, with or without smoking history, showed higher BLCA-4 levels than healthy controls. The difference held in both blood and urine. Cell examination found low-grade tumours in non-smoking patients. Smoking patients showed high-grade tumours with large malignant cell clusters. Four genetic loci changed in urine samples, while five stayed stable. The authors suggest urine testing could help diagnosis and gauge smoking impact.
pmc-13318884:
Eduardo Leonarski and co-authors review, in 2026, kombucha production using Brazilian raw materials. Brazil is a giant fruit producer with huge variety. Researchers there brew both traditional kombucha from tea and analog drinks from other extracts. The review gathers those studies and the rules around them.

Most analog production uses fruits from the Northeast and South regions. Other bases include coffee, yerba mate, and yams. Byproducts such as cocoa, acerola, guava, and tamarind residues also appear. Mango and grape peels have been tried as well. During fermentation, phenolic content and antioxidant activity tend to rise for every extract type. Open challenges include alcohol control, unproven probiotic claims, and rules for alternative starters.
pmc-13318984:
Yang Lyu and co-authors report a 2026 national survey of cancer health literacy among urban adults in China. They compared knowledge scores for colorectal, oesophageal, lung, and kidney cancers. The sample held 1,226 adults, reached through workplace networks. A tested questionnaire scored literacy for each cancer.

Colorectal literacy scored highest, at 7.50 points on average in the results. Kidney cancer scored lowest, at 4.30 points across the group. Education and household income predicted literacy for every cancer. Other factors varied by cancer: age, sex, work status, and family history counted for some. The authors call overall literacy moderate. They urge focused teaching for adults with less schooling and lower income, run through local health services.
pmc-13319484:
Orla Mitchell and co-authors test brain age software in depression in a 2026 study of scans and life stress. Low mood and brain aging may share roots in stress, yet how they link is not settled. Three ready made tools that guess age from brain scans were tried head to head to pick the most exact one.

Scans came from 190 adults, with 110 healthy peers and 80 people with major low mood illness. The best tool was then used to score how old each brain looked next to true age. Older adults with low mood showed brains that looked older than expected, while a stronger morning stress response linked to younger looking brains. Women also showed younger looking brains than men.
pmc-13319884:
Salvatore Fundaro and co-authors test how firmly barbed face threads grip tissue in a 2026 lab study with turkey breast flesh. Threads that dissolve over time are a low surgery route to lift sagging skin, and their hold depends on how they are placed. A custom rig measured the peak force needed to pull each thread free.

Placement method changed the grip strength in clear ways. Thinner needles near the lower size tested tended to give a firmer grip than wider needles, as if a snugger track holds the barbs better. No single method won on all counts, so placement skill matters as much as thread choice. Findings come from flesh outside a living body and need care in clinic use.
pmc-13320484:
Midila Bapineni and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a fungal illness that spread through the body and was first read as a skin problem. The germ, Blastomyces dermatitidis, lives in soil in parts of North America and most often starts in the lungs. Skin sores from spread can look like cancer or bacterial infection.

The patient was a 53-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes who had raised, crusted sores on his face, trunk, and limbs for about a year. Repeated antibiotics had failed. A urine test and skin samples supported the fungal cause, and lung disease without clear chest symptoms was also found. The case shows why lasting sores that resist antibiotics need prompt fungal testing.
pmc-13321084:
Anna P. Brogan, Ernst W. Schmid, and David Z. Rudner identify a conserved cell wall factor in a 2026 study of gram-positive bacteria. Large computer screens can predict protein partners and gene roles, but turning those lists into mechanisms is hard. Pairing both screen types pointed the team to a lipoprotein they name ClcR.

ClcR boosts class B penicillin binding proteins in the Rod complex that lengthen the cell. It proved important for wall building in Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus aureus. In Bacillus anthracis, growth depended on it entirely. The finding adds a shared part to the wall making machinery of a wide bacterial group and a possible point of attack for new drugs.
pmc-13321384:
Donghai Lin and colleagues propose a shared circuit for two fuel molecules in a 2026 framework article. Lactate and beta-hydroxybutyrate were once seen as mere waste or backup fuels. The authors argue they form a redox coupled circuit across liver, kidney, heart, and muscle that balances energy use.

Linked enzyme steps and shared transporters let the pair join sugar and fat burning and support fast fuel switching during fasting, exercise, low oxygen, and stress. Breaks in the circuit are tied to fatty liver disease, diabetes, kidney disease, heart failure, and muscle loss. Exercise, ketone diets, and certain diabetes drugs are among the tools that might restore the coupling.
pmc-13321884:
Margaux de Seilhac and co-authors widen the list of gut germs that activate a calming T cell group in a 2026 study. DP8 alpha regulatory T cells respond to the gut germ Faecalibacterium and guard against bowel inflammation and graft-versus-host disease. The team asked which other helpful gut species these cells recognise.

Three more species, Blautia obeum, Roseburia intestinalis, and Akkermansia muciniphila, supplied antigens that switched on and primed these T cells. The germs seem to work by prompting tolerant antigen presenting cells. The findings deepen the picture of how gut germs and regulatory cells keep balance in the gut and beyond, with relevance for inflammatory bowel care.
pmc-13322484:
Maria Lúcia Vaz Masson, Léslie Piccolotto Ferreira, and Claúdia Giglio de Oliveira Gonçalves announce a policy milestone for voice health in Brazil in a 2026 letter. Writing for a working group of the Brazilian speech pathology society, they report that the Ministry of Health now officially recognises voice disorder as a work related condition.

Teachers and call centre staff are among the groups most in need of voice care. The path ran from early concern over teacher demand at a Recife hospital through seminars, union debate, and research to a formal care protocol. The writers note that studies often omit work setting and organisation, which weakens proof of the causal link that recognition requires.
pmc-13323584:
Yongfang Zhou and co-authors review fat-activating enzymes in sudden ischaemic events, in a 2026 article on myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke. When blood flow stops abruptly, heart and brain tissue must rewire energy use fast to stay alive under low oxygen.

The ACSL enzyme family turns long-chain fatty acids into fuel-ready forms, shaping lipid metabolism, energy output and cell signalling. Their activity shifts by cell and tissue under low oxygen, oxidative stress and inflammation, which alters injury and recovery paths. The authors weigh whether these enzymes make good drug targets for limiting damage and aiding nerve repair, and they map gaps where evidence stays thin.
pmc-13323684:
Gabrielly Santos Pereira and co-authors review magnetic brain stimulation for motor overflow, in a 2026 review. Overflow means stray muscle firing during planned motion. It appears in stroke, cerebral palsy, dystonia and Parkinson's disease. Weak braking signals within and between brain halves are thought to drive it.

Seven controlled trials qualified. Plans varied in rate, target area and add-on therapy. Only two trials checked overflow head-on, which limits firm claims. High-rate treatment over the sensory cortex cut overflow in dystonia, judged by writing tests. In Parkinson's disease, treatment shifted braking measures but left mirror movements unchanged. Proof in stroke and palsy stayed indirect, so the authors call the evidence early and tied to each disease.
pmc-13324384:
Shujuan Chang and co-authors trace a gene and chemistry chain behind learning harm after fetal growth restriction, in a 2026 mouse study. Growth-restricted pups face lasting learning harm. Hippocampal nerve cells in their model showed sharply reduced SIRT6 levels.

Deleting Sirt6 only in those neurons copied the synaptic and learning faults. The loss acted through histone deacetylase work by the protein. It raised acetyl marks at the Tdo2 gene promoter. That sped the kynurenine path and piled up kynurenic acid in the hippocampus. The acid in turn cut AKT and mTOR signals and slowed synaptic protein building. Blocking TDO2 or switching mTOR back on reversed the harm, and restoring SIRT6 in FGR mice fixed chemistry and learning.
pmc-13324684:
Kai Jiang and Kai Wang design a time-matched hydrogel for healing bone defects in diabetes in a 2026 study. Diabetes disrupts blood vessel growth and cell energy use, and gene data showed energy needs differ between early and late healing stages.

Their injectable gel pairs strontium-doped hydroxyapatite, released steadily, with berberine held in chitosan spheres for later release. Strontium helped vessel cells move and form networks under high sugar. Berberine later switched on the AMPK and PGC-1α pathway, restored cell power output, and aided bone cell growth. In diabetic mice with skull defects, the gel raised bone volume and vessel counts. Timing the release to each healing stage is the core idea.
pmc-13326084:
Erica Sutcliffe, Jonathan P. Aalto, and Ryan G. Hadt read molecular spins with light alone in tungsten complexes in a 2026 study. Paramagnetic molecules could serve as tiny quantum sensors, but most need bulky high-symmetry shapes for optical readout.

Circular light pulses started spin coherence in axial tungsten-oxo molecules at room temperature. The coherence lasted several nanoseconds, long enough for time-domain detection of resonance spectra. The method picked up g-value direction differences inside a polymer and sensed steady magnetic fields down to 5 mT in solution. Excited-state orbital motion, not ground-state motion, provided the light link. Tunable low-symmetry molecules now join the sensor toolbox.
pmc-13326284:
Yakup Gezer and team tested how fatty liver disease affects noninvasive scarring scores in chronic hepatitis B. Their 2026 multi-site look-back study studied patients with the virus who had liver biopsy, calling major scarring ISHAK stage 3 or higher and fatty buildup as at least 5% fat on biopsy. Twenty simple tests were set side by side, including newer scores FIB-8 and FIB-9 made for fatty liver disease but new in combined virus and fatty liver disease.

Test results varied by fatty liver status: FIB-8, Lok, and ATA scores performed significantly better in patients with fatty liver disease, suggesting metabolic factors shape how well scarring markers discriminate. Across all groups, however, every test showed only low-to-moderate results, limiting standalone clinical use. The authors conclude that fatty liver status must be considered when interpreting scarring scores in the virus, and that more accurate simple models are still needed here.
pmc-13327884:
Zhaoyang Yin, Ge Gong, and Jian Yin review two-way traffic between spinal cord injury and gut microbes in a 2026 article. Cord injury disrupts bowel control and unbalances gut bacteria, while bacterial products can cross into the cord and fan inflammation there. The authors sum up lab and clinical work on this gut-spinal axis.

Microbe shifts may mark how severe an injury is, and products such as short-chain fatty acids may shape the second wave of damage. Many studies try shifting gut microbes to aid recovery, yet no standard, proven clinical treatment has emerged. Naming the pathways clearly is a step toward trials that target the gut to help the cord heal.
pmc-13328384:
Lin Hu and co-authors study blood levels of the antifungal voriconazole in patients with HIV in a 2026 review of records from Changsha. Invasive fungal disease complicates HIV care, and the drug's levels swing widely between people. The study gathered 55 trough measurements from 44 patients treated between 2021 and 2025.

The median trough was 2.44 mg/L, with 70.9 percent of readings inside the 1.0 to 5.5 mg/L target band and wide personal variation, at a coefficient of 63.6 percent across patients. Liver scores, steroid co-use, and the CD4 to CD8 ratio shaped levels, and side effects struck 20.5 percent of patients, whose levels ran higher. Monitoring pays off most where liver function or steroids enter the picture.
pmc-13329384:
Jose-Carlos Sauri-Barraza and colleagues chart how surgeons learn full endoscopic lumbar surgery in Mexico in a 2026 study. The operation treats slipped discs in the lower back through small openings. The team reviewed 114 patients in a row, with 68 treated through the back route and 46 through the side route.

Skill turning points came near case 18 for the back route and case 20 for the side route, with an overall point near 44 cases. Operating time fell sharply from early to late cases for both routes. Over 76 percent of patients met the success mark across pain and disability scores at 12 months in the reported results. Error and switch rates did not differ by phase. The authors call the method safe and repeatable.
pmc-13329484:
Cullen M Lilley and co-authors test whether patient labels in exam questions sway trainee choices in a 2026 study. Medical students in their third and fourth years joined first year residents, 376 people in total, to answer case questions in two forms. One form gave no patient labels. The other added race, gender identity, or sexual orientation to the same cases.

On questions where labels could mislead, the plain form group scored higher than the labelled group in the reported results. Gaps appeared on topics such as infection testing, sarcoidosis, artery inflammation, and anaemia care. Over half of trainees said race shaped their choices. Most blamed early training for pro-White bias. The authors warn that labels in tests can reinforce bias.
pmc-13330684:
Jana Nano and a large team review repeat external beam radiotherapy for returned breast cancer in a 2026 article. When cancer returns near the first site after prior radiation, repeat treatment may allow breast-saving surgery instead of removal. Proof is mostly backward-looking, with the firmest support held by internal radiation.

Searches of seven databases to November 2025 yielded 24 studies with 1,252 patients in the reported pool. Most were single-centre, backward-looking groups of mixed quality. Repeat treatment was mainly partial-breast photon therapy on standard schedules. Evidence stays too thin to set best dose, timing, or patient picks, the authors conclude. Careful case-by-case choice keeps the option feasible.
pmc-13331184:
Masafumi Segawa and team tell of bridging vein rerouting for clipping a posterior cerebral artery aneurysm. Their 2026 note presents a 48-year-old man whose right posterior cerebral artery aneurysm was found by chance. Over eight years, the aneurysm enlarged with perifocal edema in the right cerebral peduncle, prompting surgery. Such aneurysms are very rare and hard.

Direct neck clipping used a front temple approach with bridging vein sacrifice and rerouting via side-to-side sylvian vein anastomosis, keeping drainage and opening exposure. Later imaging showed no stroke damage or venous backup, and angiography confirmed complete closure with preserved patency and a rebuilt venous route. The patient was discharged with a Rankin Scale score of 0, symptom-free at three-year follow-up. The team concludes that clipping with vein sacrifice and rerouting was safe and worked, with sinus shifting giving best exposure while cutting problems.
pmc-13331284:
James Clark and colleagues report freeing a trapped pacing lead tip with heat in a 2026 case. Left bundle branch area pacing places leads deep in the heart wall, where the screw tip can lodge in muscle or scar. In this case early readings were poor, yet screw retraction and counter-turning both failed to free the lead for a retry.

Following the sole prior case report, the team applied brief diathermy to the lead end pin for 3 seconds at the set power described in the report. Current passed to the tip and tissue joint, freeing the screw at once. Removal finished without mechanical or clinical harm. The rescue suits a rare stuck case, the authors note.
pmc-13332484:
Gokula Krishnan B and colleagues review 2026 clinical and life-science evidence for medicinal plant-based naturopathy. Plants have long served traditional care and remain a rich source of active compounds relevant to preventing and managing disease. Interest in plant-based naturopathy has grown, prompting systematic study of whether these interventions work and how they act. The review asks what therapeutic potential the combined clinical and experimental record actually supports.

Searches covered PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for studies from 2014 through 2026, screened by preset rules focused on plant interventions. Eligible clinical and lab studies were assessed for effect and mechanism. Readers gain a structured view of where plant-based naturopathy shows promise, where evidence stays thin, and which compounds deserve rigorous trials. The review separates traditional use from tested effect, a distinction clinicians and patients need.
pmc-13333284:
Natalie Schoemann and colleagues asked whether a new mother's mental state predicts how faithfully she will use a health app, in a 2026 study of the I-PREGNO program. The app supports healthy weight and mental health after birth by training stress handling and emotion skills, but it only works if women keep opening it.

Pooling 154 postpartum women from two randomized trials, the team tested depression symptoms, parenting stress, emotion regulation trouble, self-confidence, and partnership status against four kinds of app use. No predictor survived correction for multiple testing. A few weak early signals appeared, such as more depressive symptoms going with more typing inside the app, but the authors warn these may be chance given limited power. Grouping women by use pattern gave low, moderate, and high adherence groups at 24.0, 60.4, and 15.6 percent, which mental traits did not separate. They suggest looking instead at social and design factors.
pmc-13333384:
Qi Liu and colleagues asked whether the timing of brain radiation matters for lung cancer patients whose tumors carry EGFR mutations and have spread to the brain, in a 2026 retrospective study. All patients received targeted EGFR blocker drugs, but radiation was given early for some and held back for others.

Records covered 135 patients treated between January 2015 and December 2020, with 70 receiving early radiation and 65 delayed. Early radiation independently lengthened the time before brain disease progressed, at 14.6 months against 10.4 months for delayed treatment. Mutation type also mattered: patients with exon 19 deletions lived a median of 37.5 months against 25.1 months for those with the L858R change, and limited spread beyond the brain predicted longer survival too. The authors conclude that pairing the targeted drugs with prompt brain radiation improves control inside the skull for this group.
pmc-13333484:
Zi-xuan Wang and colleagues show in a 2026 study that a pre-surgery biopsy undersells the immune activity inside stomach and bowel tumors. Checkpoint immunotherapy decisions lean on T cell counts and PD-L1 staining, yet those readings come from a biopsy fragment, not the whole tumor.

The team stained biopsy and resection samples from 38 gastric and 40 colorectal adenocarcinoma patients for CD4 and CD8 T cells and PD-L1. Resections read hotter: gastric tumors showed higher CD4, CD8, and PD-L1 levels than their biopsies, and colorectal resections carried more CD8 cells. Immune ratios at the tumor centre tracked those at the invasive margin, and blood neutrophil ratios grew with tumor size. Biopsy readings predicted surgical ones weakly, with AUC values around 0.5 to 0.7, worst in colorectal cancer. The authors warn that biopsy-based immune scoring, especially in gastric cancer, can misdirect immunotherapy choices and needs tumor-specific rules.
pmc-13334084:
Jad F Zeitouni and co-authors wrote a 2026 policy commentary on Medicare's overhaul of payment for skin substitutes, the wound-care products billed in offices and homes. Spending on these products exploded more than 40-fold under the old rules.

Annual Medicare Part B spending rose from 250 million dollars in 2019 to more than 10 billion dollars in 2024. The old system paid average sales price plus 6 percent, yet makers were exempt from reporting actual sales prices, letting some clinicians profit from spread pricing on undiscounted list prices. The January 2026 reform sets a flat, site-neutral rate, with a three-tier system tied to FDA classification planned for 2027. The authors argue further steps, such as bundled payment and prior authorization, may still be needed.
pmc-13334784:
Jessica Oga and colleagues argue in a 2026 viewpoint that the frame, not just the outcome, is the problem in a Kenyan case.
