Among 868 positive women, about one in eleven carried dangerous cell changes. Extended virus typing plus cell testing gave the best balance of catching disease and sparing the healthy. Where neither cell tests nor inspection exist, treating the eight highest-risk virus types directly balanced best. Where they do exist, the winning route treated the top type at once and triaged the rest. The authors frame the menu as risk-adapted guidance clinics can match to their means.
pmc-13499484:
Kosuke Yamagata and co-authors report in 2026 a simpler surgical fix for cryptotia, a birth defect where the top rim of the ear sits buried under temple skin. Misplaced ear muscles drive the deformity, yet standard repairs focus on skin flaps or grafts to cover the freed ear. Their patient was a 35-year-old woman with a mild form of the condition, which can also block wearing glasses or masks.

Under a microscope the surgeons found two ear muscles attached in the wrong places. They moved each to its correct anatomical position, one behind the ear's bowl and one at the base of the rim fold. No skin flap or graft was needed, and the rebuilt groove behind the ear held its shape. Correction stayed stable with no return of the deformity or functional problems across three years of follow-up.
pmc-13499784:
Şahan, Cantürk, and Seyhan examine a detail with courtroom weight. How far away a shotgun was fired can be judged from the spread of its pellets, but screw-on barrel extensions change that spread. The 2026 team fired shotguns with no extension and with extensions of three lengths at targets from close range out to several metres.

Beyond one metre, longer extensions tightened the pellet cloud significantly, with the dispersion diameter shrinking as choke length grew. Entry holes also narrowed for shots fired in the two-to-four-metre band, and the farthest satellite holes crept closer to the main pattern at intermediate distances. At very close range, by contrast, extension length made no detectable difference to the central hole. The authors warn that distance estimates built only from target damage, without examining the actual weapon and cartridge, can mislead investigators.
pmc-13499984:
Eric Chun-Pu Chu reports in 2026 a case linking years of smartphone posture, dubbed text neck, to early neck arthritis in a young adult. Holding the head forward strains neck joints, and wear-related neck arthritis is appearing more often in young people as device hours climb. His patient was a 25-year-old college student with five years of recurring headaches and persistent neck and shoulder pain. Her symptoms worsened during the pandemic, with eight to ten hours of daily phone use plus laptop study.

Neck X-rays showed enlarged facet joints and narrowed disc spaces consistent with cervical osteoarthritis, unusual at her age. Care combined ultrasound therapy, massage, spinal adjustments, and neck traction over ten months. She reported less pain, better alignment and mobility, and wider disc spacing afterwards, a course the author uses to argue for posture awareness and early treatment in heavy device users.
pmc-13500384:
Sakaguchi and colleagues look at what happens years after spinal surgery in small dogs with slipped discs, a common problem in breeds like Dachshunds. Hemilaminectomy, removing part of a vertebra to relieve the squeezed spinal cord, is the standard fix for type I thoracolumbar disc herniation. Their 2026 study gathered nineteen dogs that later suffered a recurrence. It compared scans at the original surgery site between first episode and relapse to see whether the healed site itself had caused the new trouble.

The operated disc had clearly thinned over time, with its height index significantly reduced at recurrence, and the maximal cord compression at that site was actually milder the second time around. Two dogs had regrown bone where the vertebra was opened, yet in no case did regrowth or the old site explain the new symptoms, which traced to fresh herniation instead.
pmc-13500784:
Cumsille and colleagues argued in 2026 that the surroundings of microbe communities are the missing key to finding new natural products, the bioactive compounds behind many antibiotics and medicines. Genome mining has revealed far more compound-building gene clusters than the products seen in lab culture, and screens keep rediscovering known compounds. The gap, the authors say, is that most clusters stay silent without the right community and environmental cues.

Nature-inspired tricks have already woken some clusters: copying wild conditions, adding natural compounds as triggers, and growing species together so they interact. Yet the rules linking conditions to compound output remain murky. The authors urge joining context thinking with genome and chemistry data to build rational elicitation plans, ways to switch silent clusters on purpose. Their goal is a steadier flow of genuinely new compounds rather than repeats.
pmc-13501584:
Sakshi and Moonjelly Vijayan Smitha report a 2026 cross-sectional study comparing planned and unplanned pregnancies among women in Odisha, India. The team interviewed 430 ever-married women in the Khordha District who had conceived within the previous three years, recruiting from both rural and urban areas. Interviews captured social and birth details, and logistic regression identified factors tied to unplanned pregnancy, along with outcomes and care-seeking behaviour.

Nearly one woman in four, 26 percent, reported one that was unplanned; 64 percent of them continued the pregnancy while 36 percent chose to end it. Unplanned pregnancy was linked with age 30 or older at conception, more than two earlier pregnancies, birth spacing of 24 months or less, and a history of abortion. These cases also carried more complications before and after delivery, plus later testing and later first visits. The authors press for wider access to birth control and earlier contact with maternal care.
pmc-13501684:
Tianci Hu leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 genome-wide survey of WRKY transcription factors in Coffea arabica. That coffee species supplies over 70 percent of world beans and nearly all of China's crop in Yunnan. Cold snaps during fruiting are a major constraint there. Scanning four arabica genomes, the team catalogued 400 WRKY family members in three phylogenetic groups, with segmental duplication as the main engine of expansion. Cold-stress physiology tests on fruiting trees showed rising electrolyte leakage and soluble sugars alongside falling photosynthesis.

Transcriptome profiling flagged 47 cold-responsive WRKY genes in five clusters. Five of them, including CaWRKY28, switched on under cold treatment. When CaWRKY28 was expressed in yeast, the yeast tolerated cold far better, confirming the gene's protective role. The authors nominate CaWRKY28 as a prime candidate for breeding cold-tolerant coffee, and present the family catalogue as a resource for further work.
pmc-13501784:
Nanette Ryan writes a 2026 philosophy paper on what dignity can mean in end-of-life court cases involving infants. Charlie Gard, Alfie Evans, and Isaiah Haastrup were British babies with irreversible brain damage whose cases reached the High Court. Judges authorized withdrawing life support so each child could die with dignity. Yet the grounds of dignity, such as sentience, reason, or flourishing, were absent in these infants or not threatened by treatment. That mismatch leaves dignity unable to do the deciding work the rulings assigned it.

Ryan proposes a fresh account of dignity. Treating someone with dignity is a process of moral reflection and action rooted in recognition respect, the respect owed to a person as a person. On that reading, the account can decide all three cases while keeping the courts' assumptions intact, namely that the infants merited consideration and that forcing invasive treatment would have affronted their standing.
pmc-13503384:
Hervé Borrion leads a nine-author team writing a 2026 paper on crime script analysis. The criminology technique reconstructs an offence as a sequence of steps so prevention can target the weak points. Three decades after the approach was founded, scripts are used by police colleges and United Nations programmes alike. Yet scripts are built loosely, with stages too coarse to reveal where an offender could be stopped. The authors set out eight principles for building and judging scripts.

The principles, alliteration aside, cover constitution, chronology, composition, cardinality, categorisation, completeness, clarity, and consistency, and they rest on distinguishing states from activities. A good script, on this account, orders steps, subdivides them to a fine grain, counts parallel options honestly, and never contradicts itself. The team criticizes templates such as the universal script and calls for a flexible method that keeps chronological and functional cues while working at any level of abstraction.
pmc-13503684:
Zhipeng He leads a team that built a vision model to spot crabs in rice paddies, reported in 2026. Crabs blend with mud and plants, and light and weather shift a great deal in the field. Fast, sure spotting would help farms feed crabs well and watch how they act.

The model, called YOLO-RCCS, upgrades a small standard detector in four ways. New attention blocks sharpen target traits and place, a rebuild step keeps fine detail when images grow, and a loss rule gives hard cases more weight in training. Scores rose over the base model, with recall up by 4.3 points. The cost of running the model stayed about the same, which suits live farm use.
pmc-13503784:
Serkan Örücü compares four quantum-inspired search methods for heart disease prediction, in this 2026 study. The methods tune both which inputs a model uses and how the model is set, in one joint search. Past comparisons often differed in setup, which skewed the results.

All four methods ran under one shared protocol on a well-known heart data set, with the same prep steps and the same trial budget. Four kinds of classifier were tested with each method. Which method won depended on the classifier: swarm-based search led for two, and a binary form led for a third. For one classifier all four tied. Dropping inputs helped one classifier a lot but hurt two others, so input choice needs care by model type.
pmc-13504784:
Lasiah Susanti, Adi Utarini, and Siswanto Agus Wilopo study why women in Indonesia stop short-acting contraception, in a 2026 analysis of a 2017 national survey. Pills and injections are widely used, yet users quit them at high rates. Service quality at family planning clinics was the suspect.

Among women who had used such methods in the prior five years, about 44 percent of use spells ended early. Only 30 percent of spells came with full method information, the survey's quality marker. Oddly, fully informed users stopped sooner, perhaps because they knew the side effects to expect. Side effects were the top stated reason for quitting. Pill users quit sooner than injection users. Many who stopped switched methods, so the authors urge better counseling at the start.
pmc-13505084:
Junming Huang leads a team using genetics to test whether insomnia causes carpal tunnel syndrome, and whether a hormone carrier protein sits in between, in a 2026 study. The wrist condition is the most common trapped-nerve disorder and often travels with poor sleep. Which one drives the other was unknown.

Of nine sleep traits tested with genetic causal tools, only insomnia raised the odds of carpal tunnel syndrome. The reverse test found no effect of the syndrome on sleep traits. A two-step analysis suggested the carrier protein, which ferries sex hormones, explains a small slice, about two percent, of the insomnia link. The authors frame sleep care as a possible prevention route and ask for lab and clinic proof.
pmc-13506184:
Thomas Graf and colleagues examined the physics of phacoemulsification, the ultrasound method surgeons use to break up and remove a cloudy lens during cataract surgery. Six physical effects might in principle do the work or cause harm, from pressure waves and bubble collapse to heat and free radicals. Using computer simulation and bench experiments with a modern surgical system, they tested four safety-relevant processes directly.

Their analysis credits the tip's mechanical jackhammer action with fragmenting the lens. Cavitation, the formation and collapse of vapour bubbles, did not contribute to fragmentation in their tests. Heat and pressure from the ultrasound stayed too small to matter clinically. Free radicals did form during power delivery, but earlier work by the group found amounts negligible when the tip is properly engaged with the lens. The findings reassure cataract surgeons that this long-standard technique's main risks lie elsewhere.
pmc-13507184:
Xiaolong Li, Qianyi Li, Xiaoyu Zhang, and Tural Khudiyev report 2026 work on long cooling fibers that store and release heat as a core material melts and freezes. Such phase-change fibers could cool clothing without power, yet liquid cores normally break up beyond centimeter lengths. Their drawing method shrinks size while matching injection speed to pull speed.

Fibers reached thirty-five meters long and about two hundred micrometers thin, with strong heat storage and low extra cooling before freezing. Strength and stretch set records for this fiber type. Cloth with half phase-change fibers cut temperatures by three to six degrees in realistic tests, beating cotton on sun and battery heat. Scalable passive cooling looks within reach.
pmc-13507584:
Shota Sato and eight co-authors propose a tiny hollow tube made of gel that can sit inside a blood vessel and release drugs there, in 2026 work. Fiber-shaped carriers used before carried a risk of blocking flow and harming tissue. Their tube is made of barium alginate gel, a seaweed-based material that holds a stable network in flowing blood. A catheter delivers the tubes one by one into place.

The team tested the carriers in lab models that mimic vessels and in the kidney arteries of rats. Tubes stayed fixed in place while blood kept passing through the open center. They also delivered a model drug into a small kidney artery as intended. The design points toward targeted treatment inside vessels without cutting off the flow those tissues need.
pmc-13508284:
Gafarou Agounde leads an eight-author team recording traditional knowledge about mosses and their kin in Benin, in work published in 2026. These small non-flowering plants, called bryophytes, play real ecological roles yet are rarely studied for human uses in Africa. The team then checked how knowledge varied with age, job, schooling, and ethnic group.

People named sixteen species, and twelve had documented traditional uses, mostly in medicine. Local names leaned on where a plant grows rather than how it looks. One species stood out as widely known and culturally central. Elders, healers, and a few groups held the deepest knowledge, and variety thinned from the wet south toward the dry north. Forest clearing and farm expansion were named the main threats.
pmc-13508584:

Regulators now expect trial objectives to be translated into clinical questions using an international framework with five attributes. They are the treatment, the population, the outcome variable, how it is summarized, and how events after treatment starts, such as stopping the drug or dying, are handled.

The authors argue that naming the estimand aligns design, analysis, and interpretation, and that readers cannot compare effect sizes across studies without knowing which estimand each used.
pmc-13511084:
Siyu Chen, Meng Yang, Chuyan Xu, and Conghui Liu report a psychology experiment, published in 2026, on how sharing attention with another person shapes emotional reactions, and whether friendship changes the effect. Pairs of people viewed neutral, positive, and negative images while the researchers recorded their ratings and brain activity from both partners at once.

Thirty-nine pairs took part, twenty-two of friends and seventeen of strangers. Sharing attention shifted emotional judgements toward positivity, and the shift was stronger between friends. Brain recordings showed front-of-brain synchrony between partners rising for friends during shared attention but falling for strangers, which the authors link to how closeness supports sharing positive feelings.
pmc-13518784:
Lijun Meng and five colleagues follow a huge Chinese cohort in 2026 to test whether a combined blood index predicts first heart attacks. The index, called CTI, joins C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation, with a triglyceride-glucose measure tied to insulin resistance. Participants came from the Kailuan Study in Tangshan, Hebei Province.

After screening, 94,509 people were tracked for a median of about 15 years, during which 2,062 first heart attacks occurred. Risk rose step by step across the index quarters, with the top quarter showing roughly double the risk of the lowest after adjustments. Each one-unit rise in the index linked to a 29 percent higher risk, supporting its use in screening.
pmc-13518884:
Xiaoqing Jiang and colleagues test in 2026 whether the spatial arrangement of amino groups on additive molecules changes how well perovskite solar cells perform. The four-group molecule, spread in 3D, gripped the ingredients most strongly, suppressed lead defects, and improved crystal quality. Cells reached a stabilized efficiency of 26.26 percent and kept over 95 percent after 1,000 hours of operation. Modules also performed strongly.
pmc-13519484:
Aparna Aparajita and colleagues mapped the genetics of drug-resistant gut bacteria in intensive care. Family group B2 led the collection, alongside risky clones ST131, ST405, and ST648, with broad co-resistance to other drug classes. pmc-13520184:
Seep Sonali and Shweta Shenoy develop SERV-India in 2026, a questionnaire for measuring healthcare service quality tuned to Indian realities. Both questionnaire parts showed excellent internal consistency, and factor analysis fit acceptably. Patients paying cash scored significantly higher than insured patients. Distinctly local indicators entered the measure, including informal payments and personal recommendation, called Baksheesh and Sifarish in the study.
pmc-13520284:
Vemund Øvstehage leads a six-author study in 2026 asking elite para-sport coaches what makes training truly good. Eight Norwegian coaches with Paralympic and World Championship experience described daily practice with disabled athletes, and their accounts were sorted into themes.

Four themes defined quality for them: a supportive environment with adapted facilities and integrated support staff, and flexible organization with collaborative planning and careful load management. The other two were deep coach understanding of each athlete's impairment and sport, and athlete ownership that builds autonomy. Coaches framed quality as a living negotiation among coach, athlete, and support team, adjusted in real time. pmc-13521084:
David Hollo and colleagues compare in 2026 short versus standard-length stems in reverse shoulder replacement, focusing on straightness of the implant in the upper arm bone. Short stems were meant to spare bone stress, yet shorter contact might allow tilting.

Registry patients numbered 114, split evenly between stem lengths, with X-rays checked at least six months after surgery. Tilt beyond five degrees counted as malalignment. Bone density and collar fill were measured from scans and films. Short stems showed larger tilt deviation in early results. Adjusted models then test whether stem type alone explains alignment, informing implant selection.
pmc-13521484:
Faisal M Sanai leads a 2026 review of primary biliary cholangitis in the Middle East, an autoimmune liver disease that scars bile ducts toward liver failure. Most guidance comes from Western cohorts, while regional data stay thin and scattered.

Published regional studies were small and single-centre, blocking firm population estimates. Experts described underdiagnosis, uneven specialist referral and patchy access to confirmatory antibody testing. First-line treatment reliance contrasts with inconsistent access to second-line drugs, despite many incomplete responders in global data.
pmc-13522084:

The fibrin-focused reading showed a weaker raw gap, yet both thresholds stayed independent predictors after adjustment. Uncontrolled bleeding was the leading cause of death in flagged groups, supporting early targeted clotting support.
pmc-13522784:
Chloé Savignac and collaborators examine whether inheriting Alzheimer risk from a mother or a father leaves different traces in adult children in a 2026 study. Cognitive and cardiovascular markers, together with linked genetic variants, showed the strongest separation by parent of origin. The work maps how the parent who carried the risk shapes different parts of a child's risk profile.
pmc-13523184:
Nokwethemba Monica Ngcobo, Vino Dorsamy, and Chauntelle Bagwandeen set out a protocol for a systematic review on low-dose aspirin and blood levels in pregnancy in a 2026 paper. No results are reported, because the paper describes the planned review.

Two reviewers will independently screen studies, extract data, and judge quality. Results will be pooled where suitable, with subgroup analyses for differences between studies. The authors aim to balance preventive benefits against anemia and bleeding risks in future guidance.
pmc-13523384:
Andrea Hruštincová leads a team showing that different mutations in one splicing gene produce distinct disease biology in a 2026 study of myelodysplastic neoplasms, a group of bone marrow disorders. Data from one hundred twenty-one mutated patients were analyzed alongside RNA sequencing of patient marrow cells and engineered cell lines carrying single variants. Splicing, gene activity, and mitochondrial energy function were profiled in depth.

Compared with the common variant tied to favorable outlook, one alternative variant brought shorter progression-free survival, more retained introns in gene messages, and widespread mis-splicing of mitochondrial genes. Engineered cells showed impaired energy production, strongest for one specific amino acid change. The authors argue that these marrow disorders should be read variant by variant, and that mitochondrial weaknesses may offer precision treatment targets.
pmc-13523484:
Jianqiang Yang and colleagues review, in 2026, how tumors rewire their metabolism and why that rewiring differs across a single tumor. Different cell groups may rely on sugar burning, oxygen-based energy, or scavenged nutrients.

Consequences include immune evasion, as tumor cells compete for nutrients and release suppressive byproducts, plus cell states that tolerate treatment. Proposed responses include blocking context-specific fuel pathways, pairing metabolic drugs with immunotherapy, and grouping patients by metabolic profile. The authors frame such personalization as essential for better outcomes.
pmc-13527284:

The dipoles suppressed the lateral lobes and pushed the field deeper into the cord region, predicting about a thirty-five percent gain in efficiency per unit of absorbed energy. pmc-13527684:
Gereltuya Dorj and colleagues mapped penicillin markets for syphilis and rheumatic heart disease across South-East Asia. Prices varied wildly, with one drug form costing over twenty-three times more in Timor-Leste than in Bangladesh, and another varying up to fifty-five-fold across the region. Shortages hit benzathine penicillin in five countries and other drug forms in Sri Lanka and Maldives. Demand runs into hundreds of millions of doses yearly, led by India. The authors call for joint demand guesses, shared rules, and pooled buying to secure fair access.
pmc-13527984:

Treated cells showed more reactive oxygen species and weaker mitochondrial charge. Autophagy-related proteins shifted as well. Sequencing found broad changes in pathways for the cell cycle, protein transport, and cell death control. The authors present lactoferrin as a low-toxicity candidate worth more study.
pmc-13528284:
Wang and colleagues simulated, atom by atom, what happens in the first instants after radiation knocks an electron out of an inner level of pyrrole surrounded by water. Pyrrole is a ring molecule found in many biological compounds. Their 2026 computational study treats electrons and moving nuclei together, because earlier fixed-atom simulations may miss how atomic motion redirects the decay of the excited state.

Wang found that when the vacancy starts on a water molecule, energy usually transfers to pyrrole through intermolecular Coulombic decay. In that process, one molecule's energy ejects an electron from its neighbor. A second transfer pathway appeared in a minority of runs. When the vacancy starts on pyrrole, a mix of that transfer decay and Auger decay, where the molecule ejects its own electron, occurs. Freezing the nuclei changed the predicted pathway completely, proving nuclear motion decisively steers these ultrafast processes.
pmc-13529584:

Protein profiling tied each enzyme to different surface remodeling in the cancer cells. The authors propose these enzymes as targets for blocking metastatic adaptation.
pmc-13529884:
Lawrence Cheng Kiat Ng leads a 2026 report on brexucabtagene autoleucel, a CAR T-cell treatment for mantle cell lymphoma that has come back or stopped responding. Every treated patient responded, and most reached a complete response. Fever-like cytokine release occurred in most patients without severe cases, while one person had mild nerve-related side effects. Results compared well with the transplant group despite harder starting disease. The report presents early Asian real-world support for this cell therapy.
pmc-13530184:
Gaurav Kumar and colleagues test in 2026 whether hydrogen sulfide gas can protect learning ability during long-term high blood pressure. Sustained pressure harms brain vessels and inflames tissue, eroding memory over time. Rats received a pressure-raising hormone through an implanted pump, with a sulfide donor given before and during exposure.

Treated rats kept better spatial learning in a water maze and held onto more synaptic proteins in the hippocampus. Vessel activation and inflammatory immune cell states eased in both tissue and vessel-linked cells. Several inflammatory signals fell as well, tying protection to calmer vessels and brain tissue.
pmc-13530584:
Magnussen and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 79, a comparison of how three kneecap stabilization operations change patellar height. Patellar height is the kneecap's vertical position, which matters because a high-riding kneecap dislocates more easily. The retrospective cohort included 169 patients: 129 with ligament reconstruction alone, 23 with added forward-shifting bone surgery, and 17 with deliberately lowering bone surgery. On all three standard height indices measured from X-rays, the forward-shift group changed by amounts statistically indistinguishable from reconstruction alone. The lowering group, as intended, dropped the kneecap significantly more on every index. pmc-13530684:
Ernat and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 105, a study of leg fasciotomy for chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Fasciotomy cuts open tight muscle compartments, and the syndrome is a cause of lower leg pain in runners and military personnel. They asked whether returning symptoms spoil the result.

The retrospective review included 38 patients with at least two years of follow-up, most operated on both legs. Three quarters reported pain much improved, over half reported function much improved, and ninety-two percent were satisfied or very satisfied with the surgery. Symptoms recurred in about thirty-nine percent of patients, four fifths of them women. Yet even in that subgroup, over half called their pain much improved and eighty percent stayed at least slightly satisfied. Only one patient needed a repeat fasciotomy.
pmc-13531584:
Francesca H Dakin and colleagues studied how team bonds sustain staff in modern United Kingdom general practice. Published in 2026, the multi-site case study covered ten practices across England, Wales, and Scotland, using observations, interviews, and focus groups. Staff now juggle in-person and digital care amid high workload, constant change, and recurring crises, with morale often low and turnover high.

Clinics that valued and nurtured team bonds showed stronger team identity, smoother task coordination, and better staff wellbeing than those that left bonds untended. Bonds grew through everyday actions and routines, forming what the authors call a shared support frame. The study names elements of that frame that may harden clinics against change and crisis. Readers get a culture portrait with practical levers attached.
pmc-13531784:
Guibin Huang and colleagues formulate in 2026 an injectable bone glue that bonds in wet conditions, where ordinary repair materials fail. The mix combines bioactive glass, a calcium phosphate, short fibers, and a bonding amino compound in phosphate fluid. Bench tests measured strength and chemistry, while cell and rat studies checked safety.

Bond strength to titanium rose as curing completed, and fluid extracts stayed near body pH for three days. Lab cells survived well at every strength tested. Rats showed no illness, organ damage, or weight effects over 12 weeks. Dental fixing and bone gap repair are the target uses.
pmc-13531884:
Alëna A Balasanova and colleagues evaluate in 2026 a short training on opioid prescribing for older adults given to primary care clinicians. Sixty-five clinicians across 13 clinics took pre, post, and one-month surveys on knowledge, confidence, and planned safety strategies. Older patients face unique harms from long-term opioid use.

Knowledge of long-term opioid limits and confidence in offering non-opioid options rose right after training. Nearly every clinician planned at least one safety strategy. At one month, adoption ranged widely by strategy, from about one in ten to over three quarters. Brief training moved practice, unevenly yet meaningfully.
pmc-13532184:
Maisha Samio and colleagues profile in 2026 Klebsiella bacteria from urinary infections at a Bangladesh hospital for virulence, drug resistance, and slime-layer building. Of 718 urine samples, 22 confirmed Klebsiella isolates had gene testing for attack and resistance traits plus biofilm assays. Most isolates came from female patients.

Nearly every isolate resisted multiple drugs, and three resisted nearly all drugs. Key resistance genes against frontline and last-resort drugs showed up widely. Stronger biofilm builders resisted more drugs, and three virulence genes tracked with biofilm strength, painting a stubborn treatment challenge for local clinicians treating these infections.
pmc-13534384:
Hongyan Xu and colleagues explore in 2026 the role of PIEZO1, a channel that senses mechanical force, in lung adenocarcinoma. The cancer is the most common lung subtype, and drivers of its spread remain partly unknown. Database analyses compared tumour and normal lung tissue, with lab checks in cancer cell lines.

PIEZO1 levels ran lower in tumours, yet high levels linked to later stage, lymph node spread, and poorer survival. Lowering PIEZO1 in cells cut movement and lowered PD-L1, an immune shield protein. Readers see a puzzling dual pattern that needs deeper study before any clinical use.
pmc-13534484:
Ali Asgarian studies in 2026 whether the pattern of built-up land, not just its total area, shapes surface heat in an arid city landscape. Hard surfaces drive urban heating, yet layout effects beyond area were poorly known. Satellite data gave 8,130 land units linking built pattern to summer surface temperature.

Adding pattern measures to area-only models clearly improved heat prediction. Compact layouts with few large patches ran notably warmer than fragmented or balanced layouts at the same built area. Planners in dry regions gain proof that street and block layout itself affects heat exposure.
pmc-13536184:
Vo, Woo, and Maddern ask whether surgical conflicts of interest are a problem, and answer with a structured review of the literature and of policy from surgical colleges. The colleges span Australia, Canada, Ireland, Britain, and the United States. Surgeons wear many hats, clinician, manager, teacher, researcher, inventor, and industry collaborator, and each hat can tug against the duty to patients. Their 2026 synthesis checks how consistently the profession defines and manages those tugs.

The colleges agree on definitions and on disclosure as the bedrock response, but diverge widely on the practical depth of guidance for spotting, grading, and managing a conflict once declared. Their prescription is a formal pipeline: identify, disclose, assess risk, manage, monitor, and stay transparent. It is supplemented by tests like asking whether an impartial observer, or the public, would accept the arrangement.
pmc-13536684:
Abimbola Yomi Adeloye and co-authors describe mouth findings in Nigerian children with hormone disorders in a 2026 clinic study from Lagos. Fifty patients aged 6 to 18 years who attended a pediatric hormone clinic answered history questions and received standard mouth exams. Type 1 diabetes was the most common condition, followed by underactive thyroid. The team recorded soft tissue and tooth findings for each child.

Dry mouth was the most frequent soft tissue finding, seen in just over half the children, followed by darkened mouth lining, gum inflammation, and mouth sores. Tooth problems included enamel defects, bite problems, crowding, and cavities, each seen in a similar share of children. The authors argue that dental checks should become a routine part of hormone care, with dentists and hormone specialists working together.
pmc-13536784:
Li Xing and colleagues test a mitochondria-derived peptide called MOTS-c in human repair cells in a 2026 laboratory and animal study. Repair cells from fat tissue lose power in obesity, and the peptide was expected to restore energy signaling. Cells from six lean donors and six donors with obesity were treated in dishes. Pretreated cells were also tested in mice with narrowed kidney arteries.

Treated cells from donors with obesity regained peptide levels and switched on energy signaling, yet they grew more slowly and showed more aging and inflammation signals. In mice, pretreated cells failed to improve kidney blood flow, scarring, or tube injury, and treatment also weakened repair by lean cells. The authors conclude that restoring energy signals alone does not restore repair function.
pmc-13540884:
Ahmed Javed leads a 2026 analysis of United States death records asking how mortality tied to chronic lung disease among people with chronic kidney disease changed between 1999 and 2023. The two conditions worsen each other when they coexist.

Using the CDC WONDER database, the team counted 242,665 such deaths in adults aged twenty-five and over. Age-adjusted mortality roughly doubled across the period, climbing at an average of about three percent a year. Men had higher rates throughout, while women's rates rose faster. Non-Hispanic white Americans, the oldest patients, Midwestern states, and non-metropolitan areas carried the heaviest burden. The authors press for fairer coverage and stronger prevention.
pmc-13541584:
Daljeet Kaur Saggu and colleagues warned that a fast, broad, uneven heartbeat is not always an atrial rhythm problem. Published in 2026, the case series drew seven such patients from a 615-person heart-swelling registry. All seven had normal-shaped hearts and no sign of pre-excitation or typical atrial rhythm trouble on baseline tracings.

The seven ran near 40 years old on average, and four needed tube-based ablation for drug-proof rhythm storms, with extra rhythms set off in three. On their own, starts and stops plus shifting shapes marked the spells, while voltage maps found no target for tissue change. No atrial rhythms could be provoked in this group. All seven answered illness-targeted care, so the authors urge keeping a lower-chamber fast beat in mind when FBIT lacks atrial clues.
pmc-13542084:
Aníbal A Teherán and six colleagues measure, in a 2026 natural experiment, how much COVID-19 quarantine strictness cleaned the air of Bogotá, Colombia. Successive national, smart, and focalised quarantine phases during the pandemic created a rare graded test of traffic and industry shutdowns.

Pollutant levels during the smart and focalised phases were compared with matching pre-pandemic periods in 2019. Coarse and fine particle levels, plus sulphur dioxide in one phase, fell significantly, with the strictest focalised phase showing the largest standardised effect sizes. All values stayed below legal thresholds, prompting the authors to propose an added notion of environmental significance for judging whether a drop truly matters for wellbeing.
pmc-13543584:
N McCloskey's team interviewed everyone involved in precision oncology for children and young people with poor-prognosis cancers in British Columbia, for a 2026 study. Between 2021 and 2023 they spoke with nine patients aged twelve to twenty-one, ten parents, and seventeen health professionals who had taken part in genome-profiling studies. Themes were built from what people said about hopes, information, and access.

Five themes emerged. Talk between families and the many professionals involved must be clear. Results need support to be disclosed, understood, and used. New therapies are hard to reach and need active mitigation. Hopes and expectations require careful handling, and taking part itself brings personal strain. Practical fixes include coaching oncologists in explaining genomic results. Findings also need validating so families can actually obtain suggested treatments. The science, participants implied, is outrunning the system around it.
pmc-13544784:
Kem-Maria McCook and co-authors present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 62-year-old woman, a breast cancer survivor. She developed a new lump in her remaining breast. Thirty years had passed since mastectomy and chemoradiation on the other side. Imaging first read the lump as a harmless lymph node. Repeat scans showed growth. This prompted a needle biopsy.

The biopsy showed a schwannoma. This is a benign nerve sheath tumour. It accounts for only a tiny fraction of breast tumours. Fewer than seventy cases are reported. She chose surgical removal. A radioactive seed marker guided it. The authors urge a low threshold for tissue sampling. Survivors presenting new lesions deserve sampling even when imaging looks benign.
pmc-13545184:
Xuan Luo, in a 2026 study, built a survival prediction score for lung adenocarcinoma from genes linked to ADP-ribosylation, a chemical tagging process that helps control DNA repair and cell death. Luo compared tumor and normal gene data from a large cancer database, then narrowed the candidates through several layers of statistical selection. Five genes survived into the final risk model.

Patients with low scores showed more immune cells inside their tumors and a lower mutation burden than high-score patients. The two groups also differed in predicted sensitivity to several chemotherapy and targeted drugs. Lab tests singled out one gene, ARL6IP1, which helped lung cancer cells grow, move, and resist death.
pmc-13545584:
Qin and co-authors tested a 2026 prospective study of ultrasound derived fat fraction, a scan measure of liver fat, asking whether probe position and depth change the reading. Standardising such measures matters if clinics are to swap results interchangeably. Two hundred and thirty-eight volunteers were scanned at five liver windows and four depths.

Readings differed significantly across anatomical windows even at one fixed depth, Qin found, with left lobe measures biased roughly five to six percentage points high against the reference window. Shallow sampling at one centimetre biased readings about two points high, while deeper sampling biased them slightly low instead. A thicker fat layer between skin and liver independently widened deviations from the reference configuration. Under the standard reference setup, repeatability between operators was good, supporting a fixed protocol.
pmc-13546584:
Zhang and co-authors track cancer DNA in the blood, in this 2026 longitudinal study. They followed 124 patients with stage II to III colorectal cancer. All were treated at a Kunming hospital between 2017 and 2024. A single negative test for minimal residual disease, tumor DNA shed into blood after surgery, usually reassures, yet some negative patients still relapse. The team followed test trajectories over time rather than single readings.

Postoperative test positivity ran at 29.03 percent, 36 of 124 patients, and status independently predicted both progression-free and overall survival. The trajectory told the deeper story. In patients who relapsed, circulating tumor DNA signals kept climbing. In non-relapsing patients they faded or vanished. Total mutation signal was highest in the positive-and-relapsed group. Standard blood markers added further risk information. The authors conclude that watching the trend beats any single snapshot and propose a three-dimensional scoring framework for it.
pmc-13547884:
P. J. Robinson summarized in 2026 ten years of adult referrals to an Australian diagnostic service for primary ciliary dyskinesia. In this rare inherited disorder the airway's sweeping hairs fail, causing lifelong chest and sinus disease. The Melbourne service is one of only two full testing centers in the country, using high-speed video of ciliary beating, electron microscopy, and genetic tests.

Ninety-one adults were referred over the decade, and 28, about thirty-one percent, received the diagnosis. Blocked, widened airways, called bronchiectasis, were the commonest reason doctors sent patients in. Symptoms often date from birth, yet low awareness lets the condition hide behind ordinary cough labels for decades. The author urges clinicians to consider the diagnosis in adults with unexplained chronic airway disease.
pmc-13548484:
Ye Shao and a large team showed in 2026 that stem cells from human umbilical cords can donate their energy factories to injured lung cells. A protein called caveolin-1 controls how generous that donation is. Scarred, stiff lungs in pulmonary fibrosis suffer exactly this epithelial injury and energy failure. The team used cell cultures and a drug-induced lung scarring model in animals, imaging the transfer directly and measuring its efficiency.

Donated mitochondria restored the injured cells' energy output and survival while trimming harmful oxygen by-products. Raising caveolin-1 in the stem cells boosted transfer and protection, while silencing it weakened both. The delivered mitochondria latched onto fat droplets, burned more fatty acid, and cleared stored lipid, easing fibrosis. The authors offer the mechanism as a design rule for stem cell therapies.
pmc-13548584:
Hang Li and colleagues appraise questionnaires that measure nursing students' ability to practice from evidence, in a 2026 systematic review using the COSMIN framework. Reviews existed for qualified nurses, yet student tools had never been gathered and judged together. The team searched five databases for studies published up to April 2025 and rated each instrument's measurement qualities against international standards.

Content validity looked doubtful across the board, even where the internal structure of the tools tested well. Few studies checked reliability over time, measurement error, or agreement with outside standards, and none examined cross-cultural validity or sensitivity to change. Two instruments, the S-EBPQ and the EBP-COQ, stood out as most promising despite their content gaps. The authors advise educators to refine student tools under the COSMIN guidance before trusting their scores.
pmc-13551684:
Cláudia Gomes and six colleagues asked in a 2026 study whether blocking a chemical tagging process can protect the blood-brain barrier in cerebral malaria. Malaria parasites damage the barrier lining brain vessels, and no add-on treatment addresses that loss. The team exposed human brain vessel cells to lysates of infected red blood cells and also used a mouse model of cerebral malaria.

Adding the lipid tag building block worsened barrier disruption, while inhibitors of the enzyme farnesyltransferase protected the barrier in cell tests. A related enzyme's inhibitors did not help, sharpening the target. Mice given the inhibitor tipifarnib developed cerebral malaria later and survived better, suggesting a candidate add-on therapy worth pursuing alongside parasite-killing drugs.
pmc-13551784:
Yiwen Ma, joined by five colleagues, authored a 2026 study of a new compound against breast cancers that resist the antibody drug trastuzumab. About a fifth of breast cancers are HER2-positive and over a third of treated patients relapse through resistance. Working with chemists at Dalian University of Technology, the team synthesized ZQL-4c, a derivative of oleanolic acid from plants, aimed at a fat-metabolism enzyme called SCD.

By blocking that enzyme, the compound disrupts lipid handling in resistant cells and pushes them into a toxic, self-killing state the authors call lipotoxicity-mediated apoptosis. The abstract frames the work as an attractive future direction rather than a proven therapy. Such metabolism-targeted drugs, the authors suggest, could complement existing HER2 treatments when resistance emerges.
pmc-13551884:
Sun and co-authors traced a 2026 resistance pathway in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the commonest kidney cancer, against the targeted drug pazopanib. Resistance to such therapy drives the poor outlook for many patients with this disease. The team hunted genes changed both when a regulator called SMYD2 was silenced and when cells became drug resistant.

One gene, DDIT4, rose and fell with SMYD2 across cancer data and 150 patient samples, Sun found. SMYD2 places a chemical mark on a distant enhancer, a DNA switch, which recruits the factor SPI1 to switch DDIT4 on strongly. DDIT4 in turn promoted tumour growth, spread, and pazopanib resistance in cells and mouse models alike. Knocking DDIT4 down restored drug sensitivity, and the pathway signals onward through STAT3, the authors show.
pmc-13551984:
Firas Shammas, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 case report of Wilson disease, an inherited copper overload disorder, presenting first with psychiatric symptoms in a child in Syria. An eight-year-old showed rising aggressiveness, learning difficulties, slurred speech, drooling, and trouble walking with limb tremors, followed by weight loss and jaundice. Copper problems usually surface in early adulthood, so the picture risked delay in a low-resource setting.

Blood tests showed liver dysfunction, the copper-carrying protein ceruloplasmin was markedly low, and urine copper ran high in the reported workup. Brain MRI lit up deep nuclei, eye examination found the classic copper rings, and scans showed an enlarged liver and spleen with varices. Treatment with the copper chelator penicillamine, a low-copper diet, and physiotherapy brought marked recovery of movement, speech, and jaundice.
pmc-13554184:
Sylwester Michał Ciećwież leads an eight-author team testing a gene variant's link to overactive bladder and to a bladder treatment in a 2026 study. The variant sits in a gene for a brain growth factor found at higher levels in patients' urine. The group compared 160 women with the condition against 359 healthy women in Poland. Patients also received one bladder injection of botulinum toxin, with checks six months later.

Gene patterns matched between patients and healthy women almost exactly. Among patients, the variant tied to nothing measured: not symptom counts, not survey scores, not bladder function tests. Treatment response also ignored the gene split. The authors conclude this variant neither raises risk for the condition nor predicts who gains from the injection in this group.
pmc-13555084:
Sinan Julian Keleş leads a large team presenting the genome of the lesser white-fronted goose in a 2026 Darwin Tree of Life report. A single female goose supplied the sample. Two versions of her genome were assembled, the longer running to about 1,340 million letters. Most of the first version sits in forty-one chromosome-like pieces, including both sex chromosomes.

The mitochondrial genome was assembled as well, at a compact size beside the main set. The bird is the smallest of the grey geese, marked by a pink bill, a white face blaze, and a bright yellow eye ring. It migrates long distances and signals wetland health. Males and females look alike, with males slightly larger on average.
pmc-13558484:
Paola Facheris and ten colleagues reviewed in 2026 four and a half years of real-world safety data for JAK inhibitor drugs used in eczema and alopecia areata. Trials had suggested a friendly safety profile, yet routine practice data were thin. Their single-centre study pulled records for 376 adults treated with one of four such drugs between December 2020 and June 2025 and catalogued every recorded side effect.

Side effects appeared with all four agents and were mostly mild to moderate, led by small cholesterol rises, weight gain, and chest infections. Stopping treatment was driven mainly by the drug ceasing to work rather than by harm. One blood clot occurred in a patient with other risk factors, no major heart events were recorded, and four cancers were noted during follow-up. Weight gain clustered in women, a sex difference the authors flag for monitoring.
pmc-13558884:
Anamai Thetkathuek and Wanlop Jaidee compared two risk models for formaldehyde exposure among fibreboard furniture workers in Thailand, publishing the cross-sectional study in 2026. Resins used in medium-density fibreboard release formaldehyde gas, a known health hazard, during production. The team sampled full-shift personal air exposures for 439 workers across ten departments of a factory in Chachoengsao Province and surveyed symptoms.

Average formaldehyde reached 5.47 milligrams per cubic metre, peaking in the Clearing department. The Thai standard rated 80 percent of departments very high risk, against 50 percent under the US EPA model, and every department's lifetime cancer risk exceeded the acceptable threshold. The authors call for urgent exposure controls in the highest-risk departments and routine cancer-risk surveillance.
pmc-13559084:
Gao and co-authors build a prediction chart in this 2026 study for how long a scalded child will stay in hospital, a number families and burn units both need early. They reviewed 191 children with second- to third-degree scald burns. All were admitted to a national children's hospital in Zhejiang between July 2024 and August 2025. Most were toddlers aged one to three.

Seven admission features independently predicted length of stay. They were how long the burn went untreated before arrival, total body surface burned, blood albumin, and blood glucose. White cell count, hemoglobin, and skin condition completed it. Assembled into a nomogram, a point-based visual calculator, the model explained a moderate share of the variation, with a cross-validated R-squared of 0.31 in internal testing, and calibration stayed acceptable under bootstrap resampling. The authors offer the chart for early counseling and resource planning while calling for multicentre validation.
pmc-13560284:
Elena Bozzola and colleagues report Italian hospital surveillance for respiratory syncytial virus in babies hospitalized with lower respiratory tract infections. Their 2026 multicenter retrospective study spans twelve pediatric centers and three seasons, from 2018/2019 through 2020/2021. Infants under twenty-four months were sorted by nasopharyngeal test results into RSV-positive and RSV-negative groups.

Of 1,547 infants, 1,263 tested positive, making RSV the overwhelming cause. Positive babies were younger and more often previously healthy, without a family history of atopy. Their course ran harder: two thirds needed oxygen against about forty percent of negative cases in the reported rates. Intensive care admission was also more than three times as common in the positive group. Use of preventive antibody prophylaxis was rare in both groups. The authors present the network as ongoing surveillance for a burden that shifts with changing viral circulation.
pmc-13562384:
Soumya J. Niranjan and six colleagues write, in letter form, about how often veterans actually receive lung cancer screening with low-dose CT scans. Veterans smoke more, develop lung cancer more, and survive it less often than the wider public. National guidance during the study years covered people aged 55 to 80 with a smoking history and no prior lung cancer. The 2026 letter sets out a national look back at screening across 140 VA health care centres from 2014 to 2019.

Records came from the Veterans Health Administration's central data warehouse. The team planned to measure screening rates centre by centre, find what predicted whether a veteran got scanned, and check for racial gaps. Those years predate a 2021 VA programme built to widen screening, so the work offers a baseline. Knowing where uptake lagged, and for whom, can guide fairer expansion under newer rules.
pmc-13562584:
Xiaoxiao Wang and six colleagues identify a gene that holds breast cancer back by pushing tumour cells into an iron-driven form of death. The gene, TFCP2L1, runs low in breast tumours, and patients with the lowest levels fare worst. In the 2026 study, raising the gene's activity in cancer cells slowed their growth and movement, while silencing it did the opposite. Tumour grafts in animals backed the cell results.

The mechanism centres on GPX4, a guardian enzyme that normally stops ferroptosis, the iron-linked death pathway. TFCP2L1 turns GPX4 down both directly and through a growth signalling route called PI3K/AKT. A drug that blocks ferroptosis cancelled the gene's benefit, proving the death pathway carries the effect. Reactivating AKT partly restored GPX4, confirming the indirect arm. The authors nominate TFCP2L1 as a possible treatment target and a marker for tumours that might answer ferroptosis-based therapy.
pmc-13563784:
Yao He and six colleagues spray bacteria-eating viruses onto the surfaces intensive care units touch most, aiming at a drug-resistant germ that haunts wards. Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae survives antibiotics and lingers on steel and cloth. Chemical disinfectants corrode surfaces and breed tolerance over time. Their 2026 team timed the germ's survival: at least 72 hours on stainless steel, and as long as two weeks on cotton. Two phages, viruses named XDRKpn-1 and XDRKpn-2, were tested alone and as a cocktail, in liquid, against biofilms, and on four surface materials.

In liquid the cocktail cut the germ population by ten-thousand-fold within twelve hours. Biofilms fell by two-thirds to four-fifths depending on the dose. On cotton, steel, plywood, and plastic, reductions exceeded 99.7 percent, the cocktail reaching 99.998 percent on steel. The authors present phages as a green partner for chemical cleaning, while insisting ward trials must follow.
pmc-13563984:
Bjarne Nielsen and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 study at the RadiMax semi-field facility, how wheat roots grow at different soil depths across many varieties. Five years of June measurements covered 1,500 rows and 513 winter wheat varieties, with genetic data for most of them, and root intensity was recorded from shallow soil down to deep layers.

Genetic differences between varieties grew much larger in deeper soil, with the strongest signals well below one meter. That pattern matters because deep roots help wheat reach water and nutrients during dry spells. Breeders learn where in the soil profile selection for root traits is most likely to pay off, and which depth gives the clearest genetic signal.
pmc-13564084:
Jordana C. B. Bloom and co-authors chart, in a 2026 mouse study, how the hypothalamus, a brain region controlling hormones and body temperature, changes after the ovaries are removed and estrogen is lost. Gene activity was measured in two hypothalamus areas at two weeks and at four months, alongside hormone levels and temperature, then compared with human data across age.

Inflammation and support-cell activity rose over time, strongest at four months in the rear hypothalamus, and certain hormone-linked brain cells changed their signaling. Human aging showed similar pathway patterns, which supports the mouse as a model of reproductive aging. The timeline gives researchers a platform for testing treatments for menopause-related brain changes.
pmc-13566384:
Marcus Vinicius Batista da Silva, Christopher A. Bresette, and Viviana Clavería argue, in a 2026 review, that dangerous artery clots should be understood as a mechanical system, not only a chemistry problem. Blood flow forces, platelet clumps formed under high shear, and a clotting protein that unspools in fast flow can build tough clots even without the classic clotting cascade.

Lab chips that mimic vessels, computer models, artificial intelligence, and tiny robots could together measure, predict, and eventually steer clot behavior for each patient. Current platforms still miss much of that complexity and patient variation. The authors chart a move from static lab tests toward active, personalized control of thrombosis.
pmc-13569184:
María Cuenca-Medina and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, how a pest-killing fungus living inside melon plants changes the scents those plants release, and whether the changes ripple through food webs. Three melon varieties were colonized by the fungus Beauveria bassiana, their airborne chemicals were profiled, and one variety was tested with aphids and a lacewing predator.

Colonization succeeded in roughly three quarters or more of plants and produced variety-specific scent blends, some known to attract or repel insects. Lacewings preferred plants carrying both the fungus and aphids in smell tests. Growers interested in biological pest control get evidence that an internal fungus can recruit natural enemies through plant scent.
pmc-13569884:
Makbule Berfin Büker and Zuhal Kaynakcı Elinç develop, in a 2026 study, an expert-refined audit for judging how well community day centers for older adults respond to aging bodies and senses. Experts in architecture, interior design, and gerontology shaped an eighteen-item checklist over three Delphi rounds, covering access, environmental quality, and safety, then applied it to eight municipal centers in Turkey with photographs.

Total scores barely differed between center types, yet safety-critical details such as flooring, color contrast, and handrails did. Compact layouts with clear entrances seemed to ease orientation, while fragmented layouts demanded more. Designers get a tool that looks past basic compliance toward coherent, legible spaces.
pmc-13571484:
Chi and colleagues report a human antibody aimed at the coronavirus's most conserved part. Their 2026 paper screens for antibodies against the S2 subunit of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Unlike the fast-mutating S1 region that most antibodies target, S2 changes little across variants, making it attractive for broad protection as the virus keeps evolving.

The team isolated an antibody specific to S2 and characterised its neutralising activity across viral variants. They report broad-spectrum neutralisation, supporting its potential as a therapeutic agent that frequent mutations are less likely to escape. The authors also frame the target as useful for diagnostic reagent development. More broadly, they present the S2-focused strategy as a template for vaccine and antibody design against other coronaviruses, not just the current pandemic virus.
pmc-13571584:
Snow Adler and colleagues hunt, in a 2026 study, for genes behind the chalky stiffening of shin arteries that blocks limb-saving treatment in peripheral artery disease. Public gene data from fourteen data sets comparing diseased and healthy tissue yielded eighty-nine differing genes. Fourteen candidates tied to vessel cell calcification were then checked in real human tibial arteries and cultured vessel cells.

Three genes stood out in diseased arteries taken during amputations, matching their ranking from the data screen. The differing genes clustered in inflammation, bone-like, and metabolic pathways. Naming concrete drivers gives drug researchers footholds against a calcification process that currently has no targeted treatment.
pmc-13572084:
Mahamud and co-authors shrink a large vision model into a smaller one that classifies brain tumours better. Their 2026 paper proposes dual-level knowledge distillation, transferring both the soft answer patterns and the internal feature representations of a frozen vision transformer teacher into a compact Swin transformer student. The benchmark covers 44 classes of MRI scans, combining fifteen tumour types across three imaging modes, with 4,479 images in total.

Averaged over five runs, the student reached about 98 percent test accuracy, beating its own teacher, which scored about 95 percent, and a student trained without distillation. Logit-only and feature-only distillation each helped, but together they added the largest gain, showing the two signals complement each other. Four standard convolutional networks, from about 92 to 94 percent accuracy, all trailed the distilled student under identical training conditions.
pmc-13572384:
Kangjia Fan, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 model of slow rock strain, or creep, in thawing sandstone. The work speaks to deep mine shafts in cold parts of China, where frozen walls thaw after building ends. As pore ice melts, the rock weakens and can deform under steady load, which puts shaft linings at risk.

The team ran load tests at set heat levels while NMR scans tracked unfrozen water in the rock. In the key thaw band, from minus 6 to minus 2 degrees, unfrozen water rose from 1.24 to 6.23 percent. The steady creep rate rose three to four fold in that band. Their math model, built on that water measure, matched test data over 90 percent across all creep stages.
pmc-13573384:
Yanxiu Yang, with 11 colleagues, led a 2026 study of a combined index that flags fatty liver risk in people with type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver tied to metabolic strain worsens outlook for these patients, and scans for all are impractical. The index joins a sugar-fat score with body mass, and the team weighed it against rival markers.

Two groups fed the work: 449 patients in a Chinese cohort and 306 in a Japanese one for outside checks. A two-step selection method ranked the combined index top among candidate markers. Higher values went with far higher liver odds, and the risk rose in a straight line with the index. Adding it to a base model lifted sorting accuracy a clear notch. Its joint read with LDL cholesterol, the harmful form, sharpened the split further. The authors offer the pair as a cheap early flag.
pmc-13573484:
Donya Mohammadi, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 network review of how diabetes drugs compare on heart outcomes. Heart disease is the top killer of people with type 2 diabetes, and drug classes differ in far more than sugar control. A network method lets trials that never met head-on still be ranked through shared rivals.

Searches to the end of 2024 found 133 trials with 289,558 patients. One class, GLP-1 agonists, cut heart deaths and strokes with high-grade certainty. Another, SGLT2 blockers, cut heart failure and hospital stays for heart causes, also with high-grade certainty. A side signal that favoured a third class on heart deaths came with a warning about network imbalance. The authors urge picks matched to each patient's risk profile and costs.
pmc-13574884:
Domenico De Santis and colleagues tested whether virtual non-contrast images from spectral CT can replace true non-contrast scans of the abdomen, publishing the study in 2026. Dropping the unenhanced phase would cut radiation by a third, but only if virtual images measure tissues, lesions, and calcifications faithfully. Both virtual types underestimated tissue and lesion density, shrank calcification density, and looked blotchier to radiologists, with only 12 percent of venous-derived sets judged fully interchangeable. Lesion size held steady, and signal ratios were similar or better. The authors conclude virtual images cannot yet replace true non-contrast scans in routine abdominal protocols.
pmc-13576184:

This uveitis is the most important complication of the childhood joint disease outside the joints. Past reviews found the measures in use wildly varied, blocking comparison between trials.

Fifteen outcome measures fell into three groups: disease activity, structural damage, and severe course. Counting cells in the front chamber was the most used activity measure, followed by visual sharpness. Four studies used newer objective tools such as laser flare readings and detailed eye scans. The authors call for an agreed core set and a combined score to guide trials and care.
pmc-13576284:

Five profiles emerged, from low regulation to high regulation. The flexible group, high on rethinking and low on holding in, reported the lightest symptoms. Two middle groups reported the heaviest. Symptom network maps differed by profile, with uncontrollable worry and restlessness acting as core and bridge symptoms in several groups. pmc-13576384:

Online settings strip away the body cues that normally police honesty.

People cheated more when they already held a scoring advantage, especially once the match was decided, and higher-ranked players lied more readily. pmc-13576884:
Baker and colleagues wrote a 2026 guide on drawing Indigenous students into college science. Native students remain scarce in science degrees despite a growing population. Inclusive classes, close mentoring, and early research chances all appear. Dedicated campus spaces help students beat isolation and build community links. pmc-13578284:
Qi Zhang and colleagues propose a 2026 method for catching illegal radio broadcasts and tracing who stands behind them. Pirate stations are cheap to set up and can push scams or banned content over normal channels. Their content is scattered and hard to spot by hand, so the team let a topic model read broadcast text for hidden themes.

Those themes set the rules for flagging a broadcast as abnormal. A second method, borrowed from shopping basket analysis, links flagged content to groups that recur with it. In trials the system flagged bad broadcasts with accuracy above nine in ten, and traced sources with somewhat lower but still strong accuracy. The authors cast the pair as a tool for investigators who must sort large piles of recordings.
pmc-13579584:
Hodan Jibrell, Sara Malik, Claire King, and Waheeda Samady interview caregivers about starting babies on solid food, in a 2026 study from Chicago clinics. Many felt support fell short, so the authors ask for guidance that bends to family life.
pmc-13582084:
Fuk Kei Fong and colleagues tell of a 77-year-old frail man with bad leaks in both the mitral and tricuspid heart valves who had keyhole valve repair. The MitraClip tool had to be pushed deep after a high puncture through the wall between the atria, which hurt control and grip on the leaflets. A turn of the tube's L-knob cut the height above the mitral valve and gave back fine steering, so the clip landed well. pmc-13583984:

pmc-13585084:

Michigan holds huge archives of baseline environmental assessments, documents that record chemicals in soil and groundwater at contaminated sites. Much of that chemical data sits in tables with mixed formats from many laboratories.

Two versions were tried on historic brownfield files, one using a single AI model and one using two. Across ninety-nine candidate addresses the pipeline handled ninety-eight percent correctly, rebuilding usable tables or rightly excluding files with no relevant data. Human review stayed in the loop for quality control throughout.
pmc-13587284:
Getachew Gezehagn Kussia and colleagues search Addis Ababa's water supply for bacteria carrying drug-resistance genes. Some bacteria make enzymes, called ESBLs, that break down key antibiotics, and drinking water can carry those bacteria straight to households. Their 2026 study sampled raw, treated, stored, and tap water across the city over a year and ran standard culture and gene tests on what grew.

From 45 samples came 94 bacterial types, led by E. coli. Nearly two thirds of the isolates resisted drugs from three or more families at once. Gene tests on those tough isolates found ESBL genes in about a quarter, including pairs of genes riding together, and some genes sat on plasmids, the loose DNA rings bacteria swap. The authors call for routine watching of the water system and a hunt for where the contamination enters.
pmc-13591684:

One measure, the body roundness index, gauges body shape from height and waist. The other, HOMA-IR, estimates insulin resistance from fasting blood tests. Each measure predicted liver disease on its own, even after full adjustment. People high on both faced over three and a half times the risk of the group low on both measures. The two did not amplify each other, which the team reads as proof they flag distinct risks. Lee and colleagues advise watching both shape and insulin together.
pmc-13591884:
Hala S Abd-Rabbu and two colleagues feed geraniums with extracts of Azolla fern and Moringa leaves to see whether natural boosters can beat poor sandy soil. Geranium earns its keep from scented oil, yet sand holds little food or water. Plants got one of two doses of each extract through their irrigation water across the season, with two harvests taken and growth, oil, and leaf chemistry all measured.

Both extracts beat plain water on nearly every trait. The stronger Moringa dose led the field, roughly doubling or tripling height, branching, and biomass. Oil yield and its prized scent parts rose sharply, as did leaf nutrients and protective compounds. The team calls such extracts a green stand in for synthetic fertilizer on desert farms.
pmc-13592584:
Si Yang and five colleagues compare gut microbes and metabolism in aging mice, split by sex and by whether a protective gene, Nrf2, was missing. Nrf2 guards cells against oxidative damage and also steers fat and sugar handling. Female knockout mice showed notably thinner gut microbe diversity. Yang and the team conclude sex shapes how aging rewires the gut metabolism axis.
pmc-13595484:
Maria Nikolaeva leads a twenty-six-author multicenter study of whether doctors actually profile the genes of brain metastases, and whether the results change care. Records for patients operated on between 2010 and 2022 for metastases from melanoma, lung, or breast cancer were checked across centers for molecular testing of the spread tumors.

Where tissue from the original tumor was also available, the metastasis disagreed genetically in nearly half of breast cases, about a fifth of lung cases, and rarely in melanoma. Profiling prompted a change in drug therapy in a substantial minority, and profiled patients lived notably longer, especially in recent years. pmc-13597484:
Yajie Wang and colleagues found a brain circuit answer for why treadmill running calms stress-driven anxiety in mice. The answer shifts attention from excitatory signals to the brain's inhibitory brake cells. Chronic restraint stress pushed parvalbumin interneurons into overdrive. These are a fast inhibitory cell type in the prelimbic prefrontal cortex of male mice in their 2026 study.

Faking the interneuron change with chemogenetics reproduced the relief. That confirmed the cells' necessary role, not a side effect of fitness. The authors argue the inhibitory pathway has been missed in exercise neuroscience, and they name these prefrontal brake cells as targets for new anxiety treatments.
pmc-13598384:
Jing Li and co-authors engineered self-propelled nanomotors as eye drops for dry eye disease, a common condition tied to runaway oxidation and faltering mitochondria in surface cells. Inside cells, the cargo releases hydrogen in the acidic interior, and together the components quench damaging oxygen radicals, calm inflammation, and reduce cell death. pmc-13601384:

Vitamins and trace elements support the cell's energy factories, oxidative defense, and the immune system, yet shortfalls are common in older adults. Low intake, body changes with age, and common medicines drag status down, and organ decline from midlife may speed up as a result.

Low levels of the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA are also widespread and favor inflammation; these fats work with micronutrients to contain it. The authors recommend routine risk checks and selected blood tests from midlife, plus better trials, so topping up becomes standard in aging well.
pmc-13602284:

pmc-13602584:
Julia Stellmann Wrenn leads a six-author team mapping in 2026 why drug trials for myotonic dystrophy struggle to get ready. This inherited, whole-body disorder varies hugely between patients, which tangles trial design. The team gathered views from every side: focus groups, surveys, and interviews with 65 pharmaceutical partners, 35 patients and caregivers, 12 lead investigators, and 12 research coordinators. Qualitative themes were then blended with survey numbers.

Companies share data poorly and guard natural history information, which smaller firms often cannot afford. Trial designs also burden participants with cost, travel, and access problems. pmc-13610584:

Reports gathered here suggest some patients instead harbor primary hyperparathyroidism, a separate gland disorder.

The reviewers stress that nothing yet proves causation. pmc-13611084:

Second, analog combiners are tuned on that map to carve spatial nulls toward the interferers before conversion, respecting the hardware's coarse phase steps. pmc-13614184:

They found 53 percent of emissions occur inside Japan, while nearly all mining damage happens abroad. Car size, how often plug-in hybrids run on electricity, and battery size all pushed the totals up or down. pmc-13615584:

The score guides whether a painful spinal fracture in brittle bone should get surgery or gentler care. pmc-13616284:

pmc-13618384:

pmc-13621584:

pmc-13621684:

Warsaw teenagers reported suicidal thoughts and attempts more often than Ukrainian teenagers, and girls reported more than boys in both places. pmc-13623084:

Women and middle-aged adults carried the heaviest burden. Different test definitions agreed poorly, with very few people classed as ill by every method at once. pmc-13623284:

By changing flow speeds and the amount of soap-like additive, the researchers found three formation styles, including drop-in-drop and drop-in-thread patterns. Their size formula matched experiments within about ten percent when the additive was plentiful. For leaner mixtures, adding the changing surface tension over time kept the predictions just as close. The authors present the model as practical guidance for setting up controlled encapsulation in microfluidic systems.
pmc-13623384:

pmc-13624584:

pmc-13625384:

pmc-13625584:

pmc-13627484:

FAT1 testing, they argue, belongs in the workup even when the usual antibody pattern looks wrong.
pmc-13631284:

pmc-13634684:

Twelve case reports described severe episodes blamed on the drug. pmc-13635184:

pmc-13636184:

pmc-13638484:

pmc-13641184:

Mismatches tracked with uneven structural damage between knees, so the authors warn against using one knee to predict the other.
pmc-13645584:

pmc-13646784:
