The two receptors share stretches of DNA binding and many helper proteins, so each can bend the other's gene program. The review adds adrenal-made androgens, newly recognized as potent, that may amplify the signal further. Evidence from molecular, animal, and patient studies is woven into one testable framework. The authors propose the crosstalk as a source of biomarkers and of future treatments aimed at the mechanism rather than at symptoms alone.
pmc-13646884:
Eduard Flores Ventura and seven colleagues systematically review studies linking a baby's early gut microbes with later food allergy, in a 2026 paper. Food allergy is rising worldwide, and the first months of life may train the immune system toward tolerance or reaction. Five databases were searched through March 2026 for human studies that sampled microbes during pregnancy or childhood and recorded allergy outcomes. Forty studies with 6,530 participants qualified.

Children who developed allergies tended to carry less diverse gut communities, with early blooms of certain bacterial families and fewer of the groups that make calming short-chain fatty acids. Functional profiles suggested slower maturation of the gut community in cases. Study quality was middling and definitions varied, which the authors flag. Even so, the pattern supports distinct early microbial setups for allergy versus tolerance, and it points prevention research toward that early window.
pmc-13647384:
A correction notice in Case Reports in Plastic Surgery and Hand Surgery republishes the corrected abstract of a case report by De Maria and five colleagues on giant lipomas of the thigh. The original online version carried an error in its abstract, and the notice supplies the fixed text in full. The case concerns a fifty-six-year-old woman with a growing left thigh mass that caused pain, limited function, and swollen skin.

Scans showed a fatty tumor measuring eighteen by ten by eight centimeters, pressing on the femoral vein without blocking it. Surgeons removed the encapsulated mass whole, relieving the vein, and the specimen weighed just over seventeen hundred grams. Tissue tests confirmed a benign lipoma, her recovery was uneventful, and she reported full satisfaction at six months. The corrected text stresses careful imaging and planning when such tumors sit near major vessels.
pmc-13647584:
Midas M Kuilman and six colleagues hunt for blood chemicals that track Alzheimer's disease protein markers in the Rotterdam population study, in a 2026 paper. More than three thousand participants gave blood for the disease proteins, and two platforms measured hundreds of metabolites in overlapping subgroups. Models adjusted for lifestyle, demographics, and genetic risk, with splits by sex and by the APOE gene. Sensitivity checks removed people with dementia, stroke, or weak kidneys.

Fat-carrying particles rich in triglycerides tracked upward with both amyloid proteins, strongest in the smallest particle class. Protective HDL fractions moved the other way. An inflammation marker and a kidney marker rose with every disease protein, while albumin fell as damage markers rose. Certain one-carbon chemistry products also climbed across the board. The authors say the pattern sketches the metabolic backdrop against which brain disease unfolds, and may yield risk markers cheaper than brain scans.
pmc-13647884:
Cristiane da Silva Fonseca and four colleagues cure epoxidized linseed oil, a plant-based epoxy stand-in, with two hardeners and map how each network forms. One hardener was an anhydride, the other a fatty amine. The amine reaction starts more easily on paper, with lower energy barriers. Time-temperature-transformation diagrams charted each system's race between curing and vitrification, the moment the growing network freezes into glass and slows its own chemistry.

The anhydride network ended dense and stiff, with a high glass transition, near-complete gel content, and the stronger, harder solid. The amine network stayed flexible and stretchier, tore later, and even tolerated higher heat before breaking down. The authors show that freezing and diffusion, not raw reactivity, govern which system wins on speed. Their maps give makers of sustainable resins a practical guide for picking a hardener and processing window to match the job.
pmc-13649384:
Malak AlHakeem and three colleagues survey fourth-year medical students at King Saud University in Riyadh about teaching and assessment in their obstetrics and gynaecology programme. Schools must protect educational quality as cohorts grow, and student perceptions offer one check on whether new methods actually land.

Three hundred students answered a questionnaire spanning the course guide, teaching methods, and assessment tools. Fewer than half were satisfied with programme outlines and timings, and satisfaction with assessment clarity was lower still, while the skills laboratory drew the weakest ratings for meeting clinical objectives. Men and women answered differently on several items. Satisfaction did not track grades, and the authors recommend reviewing the guide and the skills laboratory.
pmc-13649684:
Michael Sharwood Smith asks whether a model of the human mind, rather than of the brain, could guide the design of machine intelligence. His focus is the Modular Cognition Framework, a theory that treats mind and brain as linked but distinct. The piece lays out how the two relate before drawing lessons for builders of generative systems.

In this model, no single centre runs the mind. Instead, a web of special modules works side by side, sharing general and task-specific rules, and builds eleven kinds of knowledge from lived experience with built-in tool kits. The author asks if such supple, creative skill can be copied in machines at all, and where else biology might offer design hints.
pmc-13649784:
Yukie Kashima and seven colleagues built a single-cell dataset of immune cells from the blood of 105 Japanese adults, published in 2026. Gene activity in immune cells varies a lot from person to person, shaped by age, genes, and life exposures. Japanese donors are scarce in such atlases, so this set fills a gap.

Age shifts hit hardest in fresh T cells, memory B cells, and one class of natural killer cells, each tied to first-response defence. In monocytes, by contrast, the chemical tags on DNA shifted with age before gene activity did, most of all at immune genes. The authors offer the data as a base for work on aging and disease risk in this population.
pmc-13649884:
Care for lupus and systemic sclerosis with lung involvement in two German states is surveyed in a German-language paper led by Haßdenteufel. These connective-tissue diseases affect many organs at once and need specialist care. Yet lung involvement carries weight for prognosis, and real care patterns remain poorly mapped. Haßdenteufel and colleagues sent a questionnaire to more than two thousand practices between late 2024 and early 2025. It collected data on structures, patient numbers, and treatments.

Sixty-seven facilities reported over fifteen hundred patients, about eighteen percent with lung involvement, with care centred in special centres. Outside centres, glucocorticoids at higher doses were used more often. Centres achieved far lower high-dose steroid use through greater use of biologics and other drugs, notably mycophenolate mofetil. Haßdenteufel and colleagues identify steroid, uneven care as a key deficit. They call for more clinics and earlier specialist referral.
pmc-13650784:
Ethan Gulledge led a 2026 field study of what semi-free-ranging lemurs eat and where they roam at the Myakka City Lemur Reserve in Florida. Lemurs face severe threats from habitat loss and climate change, so knowing how they adapt diets to new habitats matters for both wild survival and captive care. The team tracked two groups each of ring-tailed lemurs and red ruffed lemurs in forested enclosures, recording activity, foods, plant species, and home ranges.

Ring-tailed lemurs rested 64.5 percent of the time and fed 13.4 percent, favoring mature leaves and detritus across fourteen plant species, nine new to the record, within tiny ranges near the ground. Red ruffed lemurs rested less and fed more, favoring young and mature leaves, flower buds, and unripe fruit across forty-three species, all previously unreported for this setting, over larger ranges.
pmc-13650984:
Yun Zhao and two colleagues review transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation, a technique that delivers mild electrical pulses through the ear to reach the vagus nerve, the body's long autonomic control cable. The approach needs no surgery, and interest has grown across gut disorders, mood, epilepsy, and stroke recovery.

Seventy-two articles inform this narrative summary. Signals from the ear's vagus branch reach a brainstem hub, then fan upward to shape emotion and cognition and downward to tune autonomic output. A signature mechanism is an anti-inflammatory reflex that quiets body-wide inflammation through a cholinergic route. Evidence hints at value in depression, epilepsy, migraine, and post-stroke rehabilitation, plus anesthesia and gut function. The authors are frank that the review is not systematic and carries no formal bias checks. They call for tuned stimulation settings, deeper mechanism work, and personalized protocols before clinical rollout.
pmc-13651884:
Joud Hirbawi and nine colleagues study how signals from neurons control protein quality in distant parts of the body. Working in worms, the team focused on gtr-1, a gene for a neuronal receptor already linked to protection against the toxic amyloid peptide tied to Alzheimer's disease. Lowering gtr-1 activity changed gene expression, including genes for neuropeptides, the small signaling molecules neurons use to talk to other tissues.

The knockdown also sped up protein breakdown and altered aggregation in worms carrying different toxic proteins, though the effects varied with the protein involved. The findings suggest that neuropeptide signals act as body-wide coordinators of proteostasis, the system that keeps proteins folded and clears damaged ones. That coordination weakens with age, and the paper points to one route by which the brain may influence that decline.
pmc-13652084:
Jiwoo Park and three colleagues work out how a cytokine called MIF leaves cells without using the normal secretion route. MIF carries no signal sequence, so its exit path stayed undefined for years. The team focused on TRPML3, a calcium channel inside the cell that also helps control autophagy, and tested its role alongside the channel protein TMED10 and a related channel, TRPML1.

TRPML3 bound both partners and pushed TMED10 to assemble into larger complexes, which opened a channel that carried MIF into membrane-bound compartments. From there, MIF release depended on secretory autophagy, a backup disposal pathway turned to outward delivery. Only TRPML3, not its relative, drove the channel step, and it did so without needing calcium. The two-route account gives cell biologists a concrete mechanism for a long-standing puzzle in unconventional protein secretion.
pmc-13652284:
Yun Seok Jeong and six colleagues track how the gut microbes of frogs change as the animals grow from egg to adult. Frogs move from water to land during development, and that habitat switch offers a natural test of how environment shapes the microbiome. The team sampled gut communities at each life stage and compared the patterns with host and microbe relationships across other vertebrate groups.

Microbes from the surrounding environment made up the largest share of the gut community at the egg stage, and that share shrank as development went on. The community also shifted from oxygen-loving types toward oxygen-avoiding types, matching the changing gut. Habitat preference analysis suggested mammals show stronger host filtering than the frogs did. The study frames frog development as a window on a general rule: young animals start open to environmental microbes and grow more selective.
pmc-13654384:
Reza Valimoradi and eleven colleagues build a language-processing model that reads emergency physicians' notes to flag dangerous chest pain. Chest pain sends huge numbers of people to emergency departments, and sorting true heart risk quickly is hard. The model estimates suspicion of acute coronary syndrome from free-text notes, and the team tested whether adding its output improves the standard HEART scoring system for predicting major cardiac events.

Working from past cases at an Ottawa hospital, the researchers compared the combined approach against the score alone. Turning messy clinical prose into a usable risk signal could standardize judgments that now vary between doctors and shifts. The study also frames the tool carefully, as decision support inside an established score rather than a replacement for it. Which is how such systems are most likely to earn clinical trust.
pmc-13658484:
Paula Zwicky led a 2026 lab study of how printing layer thickness and silica-coating air abrasion affect bonding of resin cement to 3D-printed dental polymers. Printed resins now serve for crowns and provisional restorations, yet their smooth, low-energy surfaces can resist adhesion. The team printed four resins at polished, 20, 50, and 100 micrometer layers, 1,280 specimens, with or without silica coating. They bonded them with Panavia V5 cement, and tested dry or after 5,000 thermal cycles.

Material, layer thickness, and conditioning all shaped roughness, which generally rose with thicker layers. For bond strength, material and layer thickness mattered in both conditions, while silica coating mainly helped polished surfaces. Two materials bonded best at 20 micrometers, one stayed stable across layers, and one bonded weakest, with thermal cycling inconsistently reducing adhesion. Dental technicians get a tailoring rule: choose layer thickness and conditioning per material, rather than applying one protocol to all printed resins.
pmc-2918584:
Pluskal, Castillo, Villar-Briones, and co-authors present MZmine 2, a modular framework for mass spectrometry data. Mass testing, paired with sorting methods, profiles molecules in living samples for metabolomics and protein work. Such profiling serves systems biology, functional genomics, and the hunt for biomarkers.

MZmine 2 processes and shows those profiles in one open framework. Its modular design lets users build a workflow that fits their instrument and question. Shared open tools matter because raw instrument output is complex, and each lab handling it differently would make studies hard to compare.
pmc-3461484:
Sousa da Silva and Vranken present ACPYPE, a Python tool that makes getting small molecules ready for molecular dynamics simulations simpler. Simulations need layout files and settings describing how each molecule acts. ACPYPE wraps the ANTECHAMBER software, which generates those inputs, in a friendlier interface.

It produces files for a range of simulation programs, including GROMACS, CHARMM, and CNS. Automating a fiddly switch saves researchers days and prevents silent errors in setups. The tool is widely used in drug simulation work, where small molecules meet their protein targets in silico.  Settings files it writes can be checked and tuned by hand later.
pmc-4366184:
Moore, Audrey, Barker, and their co-authors wrote Medical Research Council guidance in 2015 on process evaluation. Complex interventions, such as programs to change diet or care, have many moving parts. Testing whether they work is not enough; researchers also need to know how they work.

Process evaluation looks inside a trial at delivery, reach, and context. The guidance gives a framework for planning and reporting such studies. It helps teams tell whether a weak result means a bad idea or just poor delivery. Funders and journals use the framework to demand clearer accounts of what actually happened in a trial.
pmc-6101584:
Andrew Rambaut, Alexei Drummond, Dong Xie, and coauthors described Tracer version 1.7 in 2018. Bayesian methods build evolutionary trees by sampling many possible histories. Checking those samples is a key step before any result is believed.

Tracer plots and summarizes the samples so users can see whether the run settled down. It reports uncertainty for dates, rates, and tree traits in clear tables and graphs. Poor mixing shows up fast, which saves wasted trust. Nearly every Bayesian phylogenetics project uses Tracer or a close cousin to vet its runs before publishing by research groups.
pmc-6679484:
Michael DeTure and Dennis Dickson reviewed the brain pathology diagnosis of Alzheimer disease in 2019. Alzheimer disease slowly erodes memory and thinking. Less common forms that start with language or vision trouble are now better recognized.

Definite diagnosis still rests on brain tissue seen after death. Plaques of amyloid and tangles of tau protein are the cardinal marks, known for over a century. The authors explain how pathologists stage and grade those changes. Their guide links what clinicians see in life to what the microscope confirms, which anchors research criteria in modern practice.
pmc-7068984:
Yan-Rong Guo, Qing-Dong Cao, Zhong-Si Hong, and coauthors reviewed the origin and treatment of COVID-19 in early 2020. The disease, caused by the new SARS-CoV-2 virus, had spread across China and drawn worldwide attention. The World Health Organization declared an emergency as the review appeared.

The authors summarize what was known about the virus's likely animal origin and human transmission routes. They review symptoms, diagnosis, and the candidate treatments then in use. Much was provisional, and later evidence revised several points. The paper preserves a clear snapshot of expert understanding in the outbreak's first weeks.
pmc-8208984:
Michael Feldgarden and co-authors described in 2021 AMRFinderPlus, a tool for finding genes of concern in bacterial genomes, together with the reference gene catalog behind it. Antimicrobial resistance is a major public health threat, and affordable genome sequencing lets laboratories scan a bacterium's DNA for known resistance mechanisms. Done well, such scanning can also flag genes tied to stress response and virulence.

The authors explain how the tool and its curated catalog work together to give accurate, consistent calls. They show how the system supports public health laboratories tracking resistant infections. Shared tools and catalogs matter because a resistance call in one lab must mean the same thing in another.
pmc-8724284:
Jiaqi Liu and co-authors reviewed in 2022 the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway, a system that guides how embryos develop and how adult tissues renew themselves. The pathway centers on beta-catenin, a protein whose levels the Wnt signals control. When this regulation breaks down, serious diseases follow, including many cancers as well as disorders outside cancer.

The review explains how the pathway works, the checks that normally keep it in balance, and the ways it fails. It then surveys attempts to turn that knowledge into treatments, from blocking the signal to restoring its controls. Because the same pathway is essential in healthy tissue, the authors stress the care needed in aiming drugs at it.
podcast-joerogan-COyRH27wc84:
Stephen C. Meyer, a leading advocate of intelligent design, joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2008. Meyer argues that life's complexity points to a mind behind nature, a claim mainstream science rejects. Rogan hosts the case at full length, as he often does with dissenters.

Meyer lays out his best-known points, from the sudden spread of animal forms in the fossil record to the code-like nature of DNA. Rogan asks how the idea differs from plain creationism and where its proof is thin. The episode is a clear statement of the design case, useful for anyone who wants it from its own side.
podcast-tuckercarlson-KI9sn4esE84:
Pastor and author Cliffe Knechtle has spent decades answering students' hardest questions about Christianity on university campuses, and he brings that practice to Tucker Carlson's program. The announced subjects are the Bible, demons, Israel, Judas, free will, and death: the core difficulties of the faith, taken in order.

Knechtle answers in the plain, patient style that made his campus videos popular, reasoning from scripture and experience. Carlson plays the sincere inquirer more than the debater here. Listeners inside the faith will find a respected apologist's current answers; listeners outside it get the clearest available statement of how those answers are built. The episode preserves evangelical apologetics in its most personable form, addressed to an audience its host has been steadily catechizing.
pseudomonarchia-daemonum-weyer-scot-1584:
Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum reached English in Reginald Scot's version of 1584. Scot printed it inside his Discoverie of Witchcraft, the first English text of Weyer's demon lore. Weyer, a Dutch physician, had listed the ranks of hell to mock credulous witch fears.

The catalogue names dukes, princes, and counts of hell, with their legions and seals. Each demon gets a rank, an office, and the hour to call him by name. Scot's larger book argues that most witch charges are fraud, pity, or cruel delusion among judges. His skepticism cost him favor, and King James later ordered his book burned in Scotland. The list still feeds grimoires and occult lore in print to this day.
puysegur-memoires-magnetisme-animal-1784:
The Marquis de Puységur, a French noble and follower of Mesmer, published his Mémoires on animal magnetism in 1784. Treating a young peasant on his estate, he stumbled on something Mesmer had missed. His patient fell not into convulsions but into a calm, sleep-like trance.

Puységur called the state artificial somnambulism. In it, patients spoke, answered, and seemed to read their own illnesses. His reports shifted attention from Mesmer's fluid to the patient's mind. That turn points toward hypnosis and later talk-based cures. The Mémoires are the hinge between mesmerism as physics and the study of the inner life.
rachilde-monsieur-venus-1884: Monsieur Vénus, by Rachilde, is shown here in a Paris edition of Félix Brossier, 1889, with a preface by Maurice Barrès; only the author's book list and the title page are present. The list names her other works with their editions. La Marquise de Sade stands in its fifteenth. Madame Adonis and À Mort stand in their fifth. La Virginité de Diane stands in its third. Single volumes follow. They include Monsieur de la Nouveauté, Histoires Bêtes, and Le Mordu.
recueil-pieces-magnetisme-animal-1784:
The Recueil of 1784 gathers the most interesting pieces on animal magnetism into one anonymous volume. Paris in that year argued about Mesmer in salons, pamphlets, and royal reports. An anthology let readers hold the whole quarrel in their hands at once.

Its pages include Mesmer's own propositions and letters from his disciple d'Eslon. The chief tracts for the fluid stand beside the chief tracts against it. Official reports and private defenses jostle in one binding. As a result, the volume is the essential one-stop source for the debate. Historians use it to hear every side of 1784 speaking at full strength.
sammlung-von-mehr-als-hundert-wahrhaften: Sammlung von mehr als hundert wahrhaften Transmutationsgeschichten, 1784. The transmutation tales. This book preserves that collection. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
sbe-21-saddharma-pundarika-1884:
H. Kern gave the Saddharma-Pundarika English dress in 1884. The work is Book Twenty-One of the Sacred Books of the East. Its short name in the West is the Lotus Sutra. The Lotus is one of the great texts of the Mahayana faith.

The Buddha tells tales of skill in means: how one path serves all kinds of men. A lost son, a burning house, and a rain that falls on all grass form famed tales. The text holds that all beings may reach full Buddhahood in time. Kern's dress was the first full one in English.
schiller-love-and-intrigue-1784:
Love and Intrigue, known in German as Kabale und Liebe, is Schiller's tragedy of 1784, Englished in the Bohn Standard Library set. Ferdinand, a president's son, loves Luise, the daughter of a humble music teacher. Their love crosses the hard class line of a small German court.

The president plans a rich marriage for his son and plots to break the match. A forged letter poisons Ferdinand's trust and leads the lovers to a grim end. Schiller aimed his fire at court corruption and class pride alike. The play made such oppression fit for the stage as it had not been before. It remains the most performed of his early works.
scientific-american-supplement-no-421-ja: Volume XVII, Number 421, dated New York, January 26, 1884, opens with Furcot's six horse power steam engine, shown with several figures. Foot lathes, an endless trough conveyer in two engravings, railroad grades of trunk lines, and English express trains with average speed and long runs follow. Apparatus for separating substances contained in waste waters of paper mills, in two figures, closes the first section. Technology gives an English adaptation of the American oil mill, with old and new processes and several engravings, and W. B. Parsons Jr.
scientific-american-supplement-no-430-ma: The iron industry in Brazil, by Professor P. Fehrand, leads Supplement No. 430, dated New York, March 29, 1884, in Volume XVII. Fehrand's heads cover methods of obtaining iron, operation of the system, elaboration of the ore, setting up a forge, and selling price of iron. The steamer Churchill, built by Hall, Russell and Company for service at Natal, with a full page of illustrations, follows.
scientific-american-supplement-no-433-ap: A new analogy between solids, liquids, and gases opens the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 433, dated New York, April 19, 1884, in Volume XVII. Hydrogen amalgam and treatment of ores by electrolysis by M. Kiliani follow. Engineering lists an electric railway at Vienna with engraving, and Professor R. H. Thurston on instruction in mechanical engineering, sketching a course of study for technical and trade education. An improved double boiler in three figures and the Gardner machine gun, shown in single barrel, two barrel, and five barrel forms, come next.
scientific-american-supplement-no-441-ju: On electrolysis, with precipitation of lead, thallium, silver, bismuth, and manganese, by H. Schucht, leads the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 441, dated New York, June 14, 1884, in Volume XVII. The electro-chemical equivalent of silver, F. Stolba on making zircon soluble, a new process for making wrought iron directly from the ore, and remarks on determination of hardness in water follow. F. J. Lloyd on changes in conversion of hay into ensilage closes the section.
scientific-american-supplement-no-443-ju:
Supplement No. 443 appeared in New York on June 28, 1884, as part of Volume XVII. Chemistry leads the issue. One piece tests beeswax, lists what is mixed into poor stock, and shows how buyers can spot the fraud. Another reports phenol in a pine, Pinus sylvestris, found in its cones, leaves, and stem, and links the find to ancient plant life and the origins of petroleum.

A Paris school for physics and chemistry is pictured with its laboratory. G. Gore contributes a study of heat and electric effects in metals under electrolysis. Engineering pages that follow cover a refrigerating machine, a gas heater, concrete pipes, standard screw threads, a railway ferry boat, and the challenge of building a flying machine. A technical section begins with concrete farm buildings.
scientific-american-supplement-no-446-ju: Tin in canned foods, by Professor Attfield, opens Supplement No. 446, dated New York, July 19, 1884, in Volume XVIII. Attfield reports a small amount of tin found, asks whence the particles come, and finds no cause for alarm. Engineering gives James W. Hill on the windmill, covering the Eclipse windmill and others with their operation and use. A pneumatic dynamite gun with an engraving of a torpedo vessel, a rope pulley friction brake in three figures, and wire rope towage as used on the River Rhine follow.
scientific-american-supplement-no-447-ju: Dr. H. Bungener on the bitter substance of hops leads the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 447, dated New York, July 26, 1884, in Volume XVIII. Bungener asks what gives hops their bitter taste, and gives processes for obtaining hop-bitter acid and analysis of the same. Engineering opens with improvements in the harbor of Antwerp, with an engraving of a caisson for deepening the river and notes on progress of Antwerp and recent harbor works. C. V.
scientific-american-supplement-no-455-se: Gallisin, a substance in starch sugar that will not ferment, heads the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 455, dated New York, September 20, 1884, in Volume XVIII. A piece on the weights and gravities of elements and compounds follows. So does a study of zinc ash and burnt pyrites made with ammonium carbonate. Engineering gives Thomas Urquhart on oil as fuel in steam engines. His piece covers a spray injector, driving, and storage.
scientific-american-supplement-no-458-oc: Chemical nature of starch grains opens Supplement No. 458, dated New York, October 11, 1884, in Volume XVIII. E. P. Rathbone on amalgamation of silver ores follows, describing the Francke tina or vat process in six figures. Interesting facts about platinum, with draw stones used for drawing wire of precious metals, complete the chemistry section. Engineering and mining then give H.
scientific-american-supplement-no-460-oc: Wolpert's method of estimating the amount of carbonic acid in the air, in seven figures, leads Supplement No. 460, dated New York, October 25, 1884, in Volume XVIII. H. Oishi on Japanese camphor follows, covering preparation, experiments, and analysis of camphor oil. Engineering gives links in the history of the locomotive, with two engravings of the Rocket, Arthur Rigg writes on the flow of water through turbines and screw propellers. His piece gives test work on impact, in four figures.
sienkiewicz-with-fire-and-sword-1884:
Henryk Sienkiewicz published With Fire and Sword in 1884, first volume of his immortal Trilogy of Poland's wars. The 1648 Cossack uprising is seen through the eyes of Polish knights in a vast historical epic. Sienkiewicz wrote to lift Polish hearts under foreign partition, and the Trilogy became Poland's national prose epic.

Jan Skrzetuski, a hussar envoy, loves Helena Kurcewiczówna and is swept into Bohdan Khmelnytsky's great Cossack rising of 1648. Zagłoba, the fat, witty old soldier, steals scene after scene with his stratagems, boasts, and unbreakable good cheer in camp. Tartars, sieges, and the sack of towns fill a canvas of steppe war in its full horror and dash. The defense of Zbaraż closes the volume in a siege Poles read as their Thermopylae of national memory in arms. Its sweep and color made Sienkiewicz, in time, a Nobel laureate.
societe-royale-medecine-rapport-magnetis:
The Royal Society of Medicine in Paris issued its own report on animal magnetism in 1784. France's medical establishment thus gave its verdict beside the better-known Franklin commission. The society's doctors examined Mesmer's claims and the cures said to follow from his fluid.

Their conclusion matched the commission's. No fluid could be shown, and no cure held up as proof of one. The power of suggestion, they held, did the real work on patients. With this report the profession closed ranks against Mesmer. Read together, the two reports of 1784 show organized science and medicine speaking with one voice against a popular craze.
spencer-man-versus-state-1884:
Herbert Spencer published The Man versus the State in 1884, a set of essays against expanding government. Spencer argues that new laws often repeat the harms of old controls. Each reform, he claims, breeds fresh coercion and fresh evils. The coming slavery is his warning phrase for a state that manages daily life.

He attacks state education, state charity, and regulation of trade and health. His ideal is a state limited to defense and the enforcement of contracts. The book became a classic statement of small-state liberal thought. American readers later took it up as a libertarian text. It shows Spencer in his most polemical mood.
spinoza-chief-works-elwes-vol-2-1884:
Volume 2 of Elwes's Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza appeared in 1884. Where Volume 1 held the political tracts, Volume 2 holds the heart of the system. It opens with On the Improvement of the Understanding, Spinoza's unfinished guide to clear thinking.

The Ethics follows, built in geometric order from definitions and axioms, treating God, nature, mind, and the passions. Spinoza argued that God and nature are one, and that freedom means understanding necessity. Select Letters close the volume, showing the system under discussion with friends and critics. In Elwes's Victorian English, this volume gave generations their Spinoza: austere, logical, and quietly radical about religion and the good life.
spr-proceedings-vol2-1884:
Scholars and scientists founded the Society for Psychical Research in London in 1882. Volume two of its Proceedings, dated 1884, holds parts five through seven. The society set out to test claims of telepathy, apparitions, and trance speaking by strict methods. Its journal of record printed the evidence for all to judge.

Early thought transference trials fill many pages, with their scores and safeguards. Reports of apparitions arrive with names, dates, and cross checks. Sittings with mediums get the same hard treatment as lab work. Skeptical voices sit inside the society itself, by design. The volume shows a young field inventing its standards. Later debate kept returning to these records.
stephens-handbook-old-northern-runic-188:
George Stephens, an English scholar who worked in Denmark, made this guide to the old rune stones in 1884. It covers carved stones and other rune works from Scandinavia and from England. Stephens spent years on trips to read the stones in place.

The guide gives drawings of the stones, reads their texts, and tells where each one stands. It sorts the signs by age and land so the reader can trace how the script changed. For its time it was the main English book on the rune stones of the north.
strindberg-married-1884:
August Strindberg published Married in 1884, a story collection of twenty tales of marriage as war. The book got him prosecuted for blasphemy in Sweden for a passage on the sacrament in one tale. It was the scandal-book of 1880s Scandinavia, and its trial made Strindberg a national figure overnight there.

The tales show husbands and wives in trades of money, pride, faith, and thwarted love at home. Some are tender, most are acid, and all distrust the romantic gloss on wedded life in Sweden. A doll's house of his own, in one tale, answers Ibsen's Nora with a colder eye. He was acquitted, but the case and the book fixed his name as marriage's great accuser in print. English readers met here the prose fighter behind the later battle-of-the-sexes plays.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-1-janu: Volume one of a Massachusetts magazine of literature, history, biography, and state progress opens with a contents list for the whole volume. Entries run in alphabetical order and include pieces on Beacon Hill, the Boston Tea Party, the siege of Boston, and Bunker Hill. Authors named in the opening pages include Mellen Chamberlain, Elizabeth Porter Gould, Samuel Abbott Green, and Henry B. Carrington. No article text itself appears in these opening pages.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-2-febr:
February 1884, volume one, number two, of a Massachusetts magazine opens with a portrait and a life of Alexander Hamilton Rice. Daniel B. Hagar, principal of the State Normal School at Salem, wrote the sketch. Rice, born in Newton Lower Falls on August 30, 1818, was a paper maker's son.

Hagar traces Rice from public schools and academies in Needham and Newton to work in a Boston dry-goods store. Illness from a fever forced him home for many months. He later joined a Boston firm known for music books, dictionaries, and paper. Hagar presents merchants, from John Hancock onward, as men often called to high public office in Massachusetts.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-3-marc:
March 1884, volume one, number three, opens with a portrait of J. W. Boott and a life of Josiah Gardner Abbott by John Hatch George. Abbott traced his line to George Abbott, a Puritan from Yorkshire who came in 1630 and settled in Andover. Another ancestor, William Fletcher, came from Devonshire in 1640.

George follows the two families down to Caleb Abbott and Mercy Fletcher, the subject's parents. He stresses plain yeoman roots, long residence in Massachusetts, and service in war. Both of Abbott's grandfathers served in the Revolution, and earlier kin served in French and Indian wars. A Burns line about rank and worth closes the opening passage.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-4-apri:
April 1884, volume one, number four, was entered for copyright that year by John N. McClintock and Company. A portrait of G. H. Perkins faces a life of Captain George Hamilton Perkins of the United States Navy, written by Captain George E. Belknap, also of the Navy.

Belknap starts at a homestead in Contoocookville, in Hopkinton, shaded by maple trees near a river bridge. Perkins, eldest of eight children, was born there on October 20, 1836. His father Hamilton Eliot Perkins, a lawyer, built the local mills and founded the settlement. His grandfather Roger came from near Salem and became a leading citizen of the town.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-5-may-:
May 1884, volume one, number five, opens with a portrait of Chester A. Arthur and a sketch by Ben Perley Poore. Arthur was born at Fairfield, Vermont, on October 5, 1830. His father William, a Baptist clergyman from County Antrim, Ireland, had studied at Belfast and edited a journal called The Antiquarian.

Poore dwells on the father, a writer on family names, a friend of Gerrit Smith, and a firm opponent of slavery. Arthur's father helped form a New York anti-slavery society that a mob broke up at Utica in 1835. Young Chester, eldest son among several children, was taught at home by this outspoken father.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-1-no-6-june:
June 1884, volume one, number six, carries a portrait of Benjamin Franklin Butler and an unsigned life. Butler was born in Deerfield, New Hampshire, on November 5, 1818. His father John, a captain in the War of 1812 who served at New Orleans, died on a foreign voyage in March 1819.

Left an infant, Butler was raised by his mother, descended from Scotch Covenanters and Irish patriots. In 1828 she moved the family to Lowell for better schooling and work. The sketch calls the boy small, sickly, and fond of books, with a strong memory. A belt of New Hampshire, it notes, also produced Webster, Greeley, and Chase.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-1-octo: Volume two of a Massachusetts magazine of literature, history, biography, and state progress was published in Boston by John N. McClintock and Company in 1885. Its opening pages list the contents of the whole volume. Titles include a life of James Gillespie Blaine, a piece on the Bartholdi Colossus, a battle of Shiloh account, and a history of the Bermuda Islands. Authors named include James W. Clarke, William Howe Downes, and Henry B. Carrington. No article text itself appears here.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-2-nove:
November 1884, volume two, number two, opens with an engraved portrait of Grover Cleveland and a sketch by Henry H. Metcalf. Metcalf says no name save Ulysses S. Grant rose from obscurity to national standing so fast. Grant's fame came through civil war, Cleveland's through public service of another kind.

Great crises, Metcalf argues, call forth leaders fitted to the hour, while self-seeking men who push forward in calm times seldom master an emergency. Grant had no part in bringing on the war that made him known. Cleveland, by the same logic, is presented as a man shaped and revealed by the demands of his moment.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-3-dece:
December 1884, volume two, number three, was entered for copyright by John N. McClintock and Company. A portrait of Daniel Lothrop faces a life by John N. McClintock. Lothrop headed the Boston publishing firm D. Lothrop and Company, called a people's publishing house.

McClintock first praises merchants, once called burghers, for building famous cities such as Venice, Genoa, Antwerp, and London. New England, he says, welcomed Pilgrims, Puritans, Huguenots, and Cromwell's soldiers rather than titled nobles. Lothrop is cast as a product of that mix, descended from John Lowthroppe, a landed gentleman in the reign of Henry VIII.
the-cavalier-songs-and-ballads-of-englan:
Charles Mackay edited this gathering of English Cavalier songs and ballads from the years 1642 to 1684. The edition used here came out in London in 1863 from Griffin Bohn and Co. Mackay, who held a doctorate of laws, frames the songs as records of public life under the early Stuarts.

His long introduction argues that ballads once did the work newspapers do now. When print reached only a small, schooled group, songs carried news of great events to everyone else. They spoke to feeling more than to reason, yet they taught the crowd the leading facts of the day. Mackay compares them with the later Jacobite ballads of England and Scotland. For readers of social history, he calls such songs rich mines of fact about manners and daily life.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, September 29, 1827, No. 275, leads with Kew Palace. The article opens among princes who built to perpetuate their memories, from Nero's golden house onward. Modern palaces win on comfort, it concedes, but cannot match antiquity's boldness of design. On Kew Green stands the new palace begun for George III under the late James Wyatt, its north front the only part open to public inspection.

A contemporary verdict, quoted at length, damns the building as an Anglo-Teutonic, castellated, gothized structure of bad taste and defective judgment. Small windows and diminutive turrets make it seem a house of windows that exclude the light. Work stopped during the royal architect's unhappy seclusion, leaving the palace unfinished. The article piles censure on an abandoned royal project. Readers of the thrifty twopenny Mirror were invited to judge a king's folly for themselves, turret by turret.

Number 264 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, July 14, 1827, opens its Architectural Illustrations series with a new church in Regent's Park. The article marvels at St. Marylebone's transformation. The parish now holds more than ten thousand houses and a hundred thousand inhabitants. In 1707 plans it was a small village a mile from London, separated by fields known for robbery and murder.

A newspaper of 1716 reports four gentlemen robbed and stripped in those fields. The Weekly Medley of 1718 wonders at a whole magnificent city rising near Tyburn Road, soon to be called Hanover Square. The writer extracts building dates from early papers to chart London's progressive improvement. Correspondents are invited to supply fuller lists of dates. Readers get urban history assembled from old journalism, with a fashionable church as the peg.
the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-linco:
Volume One of The Papers and Writings of Abraham Lincoln, covering 1832 to 1843, appeared in the Constitutional Edition edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. The title page names an introduction by Theodore Roosevelt, Carl Schurz's essay on Lincoln, and Joseph Choate's address. The same introductory pages also open the record called the complete papers, word for word.

The introduction opens with Lincoln's off-hand speech of November 10, 1864, after his re-election. Lincoln asks whether a free government can be strong enough to maintain itself in great emergencies. He counsels studying the war's events to learn wisdom, not to avenge wrongs. The editor holds the speech up as typical of the man.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-complete-: John Lothrop Motley's history of 1855 is headed in these pages as covering 1555 to 1566 in complete form, although the record title promises the longer span through 1584. An editor's note sketches Motley from his Dorchester birth in 1814 through ministries in Austria and England, quoting Holmes on sympathy with popular liberty. Here only the heading and the opening of that note are present, so the narrative itself does not appear. The heading matches the shorter complete record in the set.

Motley's third volume, covering 1574 to 1576 in its first chapter here, summarizes the latter days of the Blood Council and insincere peace talks. Secret conferences between Leoninus and Orange test the Prince's steadfastness while municipalities gain power and jealousy of Orange is rebuked.

Orange refuses to resign, accepts near-unlimited power, and leads a union of Holland and Zealand, while negotiations at Breda stall in adroit insincerity. His marriage to Charlotte de Bourbon, after the fate of Anna of Saxony, excites indignation, and tortures by Sonoy darken the close. Diplomacy and atrocity share the summary.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-32:
Headed volume thirty-four in its own pages, though the record calls it volume thirty-two, this final portion covers 1582 to 1584 in chapter six. Parma recalls foreign troops and besieges Oudenarde while Anjou is inaugurated at Ghent and survives attempts on his life and Orange's.

Anjou's secret seizures of Dunkirk and Ostend, his duplicity, and the French Fury at Antwerp bring disgrace, letters, and a provisional settlement that leaves Orange in a difficult position. Orange's marriage to Louisa de Coligny appears near the summary's end. The history closes amid treachery endured rather than resolved.
thouret-recherches-doutes-1784:
Michel Augustin Thouret, a Paris doctor, published his Researches and Doubts on Animal Magnetism in 1784. It was the year of the great royal commissions against Mesmer. Thouret's inquiry gave the medical establishment's own skeptical case, cool and clinical in tone.

He reviews the claimed cures and finds imagination, fraud, and natural recovery behind them. His doubts march in step with the commissioners' verdict of the same year. Where Mesmer's followers saw a new force of nature, Thouret saw old human weakness. The book is doubt organized into an argument. It shows French medicine defending its ground at the height of the craze.
tob-0184:
Syriac Christians kept a luminous poem, the Hymn of the Robe of Glory, inside the Acts of Thomas. G. R. S. Mead translated it in his Echoes from the Gnosis series, as volume ten. A prince is sent from his father's eastern palace into Egypt to recover a pearl guarded by a serpent.

Egypt's food makes him forget his mission and his royal robe. A letter from home wakes him; he charms the serpent, takes the pearl, and returns to wear the robe of glory again. Gnostic readers take the tale as the soul's exile and return. Mead's rendering keeps the poem's dreamlike glow.
tob-10784:
Thompson traced the strange double life of alchemy in The Mystery and Romance of Alchemy and Pharmacy. On one side stood the quest to turn lead into gold. On the other, the ovens and stills of the adepts slowly gave birth to the drug trade. Thompson treats the old adepts as pioneers, not mere cranks or fools.

Paracelsus, Basil Valentine, and hosts of elixir hunters pass through his pages, with their patrons, their labs, and their flops. He writes famed, vivid history for the plain reader. Those who ask how a hunt for a magic stone could help birth real drugs will find his tale both fun and fair.
tob-14184:
The second volume of R. H. Charles's great Oxford edition of 1913 holds the Pseudepigrapha, writings that bear false or borrowed names from Bible times. Charles gathered texts scattered across old tongues and rare editions. The volume completes his intertestamental library in English.

Here stand the books of Enoch and Jubilees, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, and the Psalms of Solomon, each with expert introduction and notes. These works show the beliefs, hopes, and fears of Jews in the centuries before Christ. Scholars still start from Charles when they study the world that produced both Judaism and Christianity as we know them.
tob-4161-70484:
Volume two of Tylor's Primitive Culture turns to religion itself. His famous theory of animism holds that belief in souls and spirits is the seed from which all religion grew. Early humans, he argues, reasoned from dreams and death to a world full of spirits.

From that seed Tylor traces growth: spirits of ancestors, gods of nature, and at last one high God. He also shows how old rites survive inside modern life, long after their meaning fades. Students of religion still start with animism, even when they argue against it. Tylor's calm, orderly case changed how the West explained faith.
tob-4184:
Diogenes Laertius compiled The Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers around 200 AD, and C. D. Yonge's translation presents ancient philosophy's great gossip column. Thales falls down a well while stargazing. Diogenes the Cynic, living in his tub, tells Alexander the Great to step out of his sunlight. Epicurus's will disposes of his garden and his slaves' freedom.

Serious treatises omit such things; Diogenes preserves sayings, scandals, wills, and death stories for dozens of Greek thinkers, from the Seven Sages to the Stoics and Epicureans. Much would be lost without him, since the originals of many works perished. Philosophy with the bark on, the Lives remain the liveliest introduction to the Greek schools.
tob-4284:
Ancient Egyptians placed guides to the afterlife in tombs so the dead could pass safely through the underworld. E. A. Wallis Budge, the British Museum keeper of Egyptian antiquities, translated and edited those texts for English readers. His version of the Book of the Dead became the one most readers have known.

Inside are spells and prayers for breathing air after death, for not dying a second death, and for living on as a spirit. Chapter by chapter, the dead face judgment, demons, and dark gates. The work shows how strongly Egyptians hoped for life beyond the grave.
twain-huckleberry-finn-1884:
Mark Twain published Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1884, complete in the first edition text. Many call it the great American novel, the book modern American writing starts from in earnest. Twain set it in the slaveholding South of his own boyhood on the Mississippi River.

Huck, fleeing his drunk father's beatings, fakes his death and takes to the river. Jim, fleeing slavery, joins him on a raft down the wide Mississippi at night. Feuding families, con men, and a lynch mob test Huck's growing conscience on shore. He decides to help Jim though he believes it damns his soul to hell. Twain's vernacular voice and moral depth keep the book central and contested still.
un-ga-res-384:
Chinese troops had poured into Korea by the time the General Assembly passed Resolution 384 on 14 December 1950. The Assembly views the state of the Far East with grave concern. Its aim is twofold: keep the Korean fight from spreading to fresh ground, and end the fighting in Korea itself. A lasting fix for the open questions must then follow, on the terms of the Charter.

The vote asks the President of the General Assembly to form a group of three people, himself among them. The group must find the base on which a sound cease-fire in Korea can be struck. It must then report its counsel to the Assembly as soon as it can. The bid failed, and the war ran on for over two more years.
un-ga-res-a-69-84:
Radiation and its effects on people and the earth are tracked in Resolution A/69/84, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The work falls to the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation, set up in 1955. The text voices worry at the harm that present levels of radiation may do to those alive now and to those yet to come.

The need to gather and weigh facts on atomic radiation grows, the text holds, as the stock of such facts grows in size and range. Fresh worry came from the wreck of the Fukushima plant in Japan in 2011, after the quake and wave that struck that year. The committee's work is backed, and its growing load is noted.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 384 (V) was adopted on 14 December 1950. It answered the entry of Chinese forces into the Korean War. The Assembly viewed the Far East situation with grave concern. It asked its president to form a group of three persons, himself included. The group was to work out the basis on which a sound cease-fire in Korea could be arranged. It was to report back with proposals as soon as possible.

Resolution 69/84, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the effects of atomic radiation. It concerns the work of the United Nations Scientific Committee, set up in 1955 to study them. It commends the Committee's 2014 report on radiation exposure from the Fukushima Daiichi accident. The accident followed Japan's March 2011 earthquake and tsunami. It endorses its next global survey of medical radiation use and exposure. It stresses secure funding and wide publication of its findings.
un-sc-res-1284: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1284, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 1995. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1384:
On 14 December 2001 the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 1384 on Cyprus. The island's peacekeeping force faced another mandate deadline. Cyprus again agreed the force should stay. Limits placed on its patrols in June 2000 were still in force.

The Council extends the force, called UNFICYP, until 15 June 2002. It repeats the call to lift the limits placed on the force in 2000. The old military position at Strovilia should also be restored. The parties are pressed to treat missing persons as an urgent human issue. A report on the work is due by 1 June 2002.
un-sc-res-1484:
Fighting and atrocities in Ituri pushed the Council to act fast in May 2003. The town of Bunia in the eastern Congo faced a grave humanitarian crisis. On 30 May 2003 the Council authorized an emergency multinational force for Bunia. It would deploy until 1 September 2003. The force worked closely with MONUC troops already in the town. Its task was to steady security and improve conditions for civilians.

The deployment was strictly temporary. It bought time for the Secretary-General to reinforce MONUC in Bunia. States were called on to give troops, equipment, and money. The force acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The French-led mission that followed became known as Operation Artemis.
un-sc-res-1584:
Côte d'Ivoire's arms embargo gained inspectors on the ground on 1 February 2005. The embargo had been set by resolution 1572 (2004) that November. Ceasefire breaches by Ivorian parties continued, and both the government and the Forces nouvelles owed full cooperation to UNOCI. African Union mediation under South Africa's president was under way.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restated the embargo decision in full. It authorized UNOCI and the French forces backing it, within their means and areas of deployment, to monitor the embargo. They could inspect, without notice, the cargo of aircraft and vehicles and any site where they suspected arms were held. Seized weapons and documents were to be collected and disposed of safely. The Secretary-General was to set up a small expert group to gather and analyze information on arms flows. All Ivorian parties were told to give the inspectors free access at once.
un-sc-res-1684: Resolution 1684 stands in the Security Council's numbered run, held here as an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. Such acts are short by design, meant to be implemented rather than admired. Reading one closely shows how much weight a single operative verb can carry for the governments and missions it governs.
un-sc-res-1784:
The question of Sudan came to a vote in Resolution 1784, adopted on 31 October 2007. Work on the Comprehensive Peace Agreement lagged behind schedule. The pullback of forces due by 9 July 2007 was late and unverified. The north-south border still lacked marks on the ground, and Abyei stayed disputed.

The text extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2008. Reports on the peace deal and the cease-fire are due every three months. Both sides must speed the pullback of forces and accept full monitoring in Abyei. The mission should help ready the census and elections, back disarmament work, and support the new Darfur mission as it takes over.
un-sc-res-1884:
UNIFIL was extended for a further year at Lebanon's request on 27 August 2009. The foreign minister's letter of 4 July asked for one more year without change. The Secretary-General advised the same on 6 August. Fresh breaches of resolution 1701 (2006) caused deep concern. The zone between the Blue Line and the Litani River had to stay free of arms outside the state's and UNIFIL's hands.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2010. The force's positive role beside the Lebanese Armed Forces was praised once more. All parties were strongly called to respect the halt to hostilities and the Blue Line in its whole length, Ghajar included. The parties were urged to mark the Blue Line visibly with UNIFIL's help. The Secretary-General had to keep reporting on resolution 1701's working. The Council welcomed the coming findings of the force's strategic review.
un-sc-res-2684: On 2 June 2023, Resolution 2684 on Libya was adopted. An arms embargo on Libya has stood since 2011. Since 2016 the Council has let states inspect suspect ships on the high seas off Libya to enforce that ban. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends those inspection powers for twelve more months. The Secretary-General must report on how the powers are used, first within six months and again within eleven.
un-sc-res-284: The text numbered Resolution 284 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 1970. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-384: The record catalogued as Resolution 384, dated 1975, preserves one formal decision of the United Nations Security Council. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-84:
One command for all forces in Korea was set up in Security Council Resolution 84, passed on 7 July 1950. North Korea's armed attack on the Republic of Korea had been held a breach of the peace. Member states had been urged to give the Republic such aid as it needed to throw back the attack and restore peace in the area.

The prompt and strong aid of states and peoples is welcomed. States that send forces are urged to place them under a single command. That command would be led by the United States, whose flag the force would fly beside the UN's own. Reports on the course of the war must come back to the Council. So began the U.S.-led UN war in Korea.
un-sc-res-884: Year 1993 in the catalog holds Resolution 884, a formal Security Council decision of the United Nations. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-984: The text numbered Resolution 984 belongs to the Security Council's official record, catalogued at 1995. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1284, adopted on 17 December 1999 under Chapter VII, rebuilds Iraq's weapons inspection system. It establishes the United Nations Monitoring, Verification and Inspection Commission, UNMOVIC, as a subsidiary body of the Council. UNMOVIC replaces the Special Commission (UNSCOM). It gives it the old commission's job of verifying Iraq's compliance with resolution 687 (1991). A reinforced system of ongoing monitoring and verification backs that work.

The Council decides that Iraq must allow UNMOVIC teams immediate, unconditional and unrestricted access to any site, record or person they wish to inspect. It keeps the IAEA in charge of the nuclear file, and has Iraq pay the full costs of both bodies. On the humanitarian side, it lets Iraq sell any volume of oil under the oil-for-food programme of resolution 986 (1995). It speeds approval of humanitarian goods. It asks for a high-level coordinator on missing Kuwaiti and third-country nationals and stolen Kuwaiti property.

On 14 December 2001 the Council returned to its oldest peacekeeping file: Cyprus. Resolution 1384 passed unanimously. The Secretary-General's report of 30 November 2001 had reviewed the UN operation there. It urged both communities to face the painful issue of missing persons. Cyprus's government agreed the UN force should remain.

Members extended UNFICYP's mandate until 15 June 2002. A report on progress was due by 1 June 2002. The text repeats a demand from the previous year. Turkish Cypriot restrictions on the peacekeepers, in place since June 2000, had to end. The military situation at Strovilia was to be restored. Routine renewals like this one kept the buffer zone stable.

Mass killing tore at Bunia, a town in Congo's Ituri region, in May 2003. Local militias fought for the town's streets. The UN force there was too thin to stop the bloodshed. The chief wrote on 15 May to plead for help. Congo's president backed the plea. Resolution 1484 passed with no dissent on 30 May 2003.

A stopgap world force could deploy to Bunia at once. Its life was fixed: to 1 September 2003. It would guard the airfield and camps for the displaced. If need be, it would shield townsfolk and aid staff too. Its troops could use all means the task required. In that gap, the UN force in Congo would grow stronger. All sides in Ituri were told to halt the fight at once.

Resolution 1584, adopted unanimously on 1 February 2005, gives peacekeepers in Côte d'Ivoire the job of hunting embargoed weapons. An arms embargo had been imposed in November 2004, and ceasefire violations by both the government and the Forces nouvelles kept breaking out despite the Linas-Marcoussis and Accra agreements. Both sides were reminded of their duty to honor the May 2003 ceasefire and shield civilians.

The Council authorized UNOCI, with the French forces supporting it, to monitor the embargo's implementation. That included inspecting, without notice, the cargo of aircraft and vessels and seizing illicit arms. The decision turned peacekeepers into customs enforcers for a war the Council was determined to starve of weapons.

Eleven permanent judges of the Rwanda war crimes tribunal have their terms extended on 13 June 2006. The judges had been elected in 2003 for four years ending in May 2007. Their trials, however, were not on course to finish within that time, and the Secretary-General had asked for the extension.

The eleven judges named in the text will stay in office until 31 December 2008, setting aside the usual term limits in the tribunal's Statute. States are also asked to keep working to ensure their nationals serving as ad litem judges can be made available to the tribunal. The aim is to keep experienced benches in place until the tribunal's remaining trials conclude.

Sudan's peace agreement is behind schedule in Resolution 1784, adopted on 31 October 2007. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement's deadline for verified redeployment of forces, 9 July 2007, had passed unmet. The North-South border was still undemarcated and the Abyei dispute unresolved. Displaced people were returning to the South, and UNMIS was also helping the new Darfur mission, UNAMID, take over there.

The Council extends the UN Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2008. It demands full, fast implementation of the peace agreements and unrestricted UNMIS monitoring in Abyei. It urges both sides to pull their forces back from the disputed 1956 border line there. It also urges them to set up an interim administration. It presses for faster redeployment, working Joint Integrated Units, disarmament planning, and support for the national census and the elections and referenda the agreement promises. Reports are due every three months.

An isle of spice won its freedom days before this vote. Zanzibar left British rule on 10 December 1963. Its sultan took the throne of a free state. A bid for a UN seat came at once. Resolution 184 passed with no dissent on 16 December 1963. The vote shared a meeting with Kenya's own seat bid.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Zanzibar. The Assembly did so with speed. The free state did not live long. A revolt toppled the sultan in January 1964. By April, the isle had merged with Tanganyika. That union grew into Tanzania. The UN seat passed to the merged state. This text marks one of the UN's briefest lives: a state that joined, fell, and merged in the span of a few months.

Southern Lebanon and the UN Interim Force there, UNIFIL, are the subject of Resolution 1884, adopted on 27 August 2009. Lebanon's government asked for one more year of the force with no change to its mandate. The Council voiced deep worry about breaches of Resolution 1701, which had ended the 2006 war. It worried about keeping the zone between the Blue Line and the Litani River free of armed groups other than Lebanon's own forces and UNIFIL.

The Council extends UNIFIL until 31 August 2010. It praises the force's work with the Lebanese Armed Forces in setting a new pattern in the south. It strongly calls on all sides to respect the halt to fighting and the Blue Line in full, guard UN staff safety, and give UNIFIL free movement. Reports on Resolution 1701 are to come every four months, along with a review of the force's size and gear.

Resolution 2684, adopted by the Security Council on 2 June 2023, renews the Libya arms-embargo enforcement regime at sea. Acting under Chapter VII, it extends for a further 12 months the authorizations set out in Resolution 2635 (2022). Those authorizations allow member states to inspect vessels on the high seas off Libya. The vessels are suspected of violating the arms embargo imposed by Resolution 1970 (2011). Member states may seize and dispose of banned items. The Secretary-General must report on implementation within six months and again within eleven months.

The Namibia question went to the International Court of Justice in 1970, sent there by Resolution 284. A sub-committee set up under Resolution 276 had suggested asking the Court for an advisory opinion. The Council agreed that the Court's answer would guide its next steps. The resolution was adopted on 29 June 1970.

The Council put a single question to the Court. What are the legal consequences for states of South Africa's continued presence in Namibia? Resolution 276 had already declared that presence illegal. The Secretary-General was told to send the resolution to the Court. All documents that could shed light on the question went with it. The Court was asked to give its answer at an early date.

East Timor slid toward war in December 1975 as Indonesian forces moved into the territory. East Timor had been a Portuguese colony, on the path to independence. Representatives of its people spoke to the Council in their own voice. Resolution 384 was adopted unanimously on 22 December 1975.

The Council recognized the right of the people of East Timor to self-determination and independence. It deplored Indonesia's military intervention. Indonesia was called on to pull all its forces out of the territory without delay. The Council also regretted that Portugal, the power in charge, had not fully met its duties. Portugal was told to work with the United Nations. The people of East Timor had to be free to choose their own future. A special envoy was to be sent at once to assess the situation on the ground.

The Korean War was two weeks old when the Council organized the forces sent to fight it. North Korea's attack on the Republic of Korea had already been judged a breach of the peace. Member states had been asked to help repel the attack. Governments had responded with prompt and strong support. Resolution 84 was adopted on 7 July 1950.

The Council welcomed that support and noted the offers of help sent in. It recommended that all members providing forces or other aid place them under a unified command. The United States would lead that command, and Washington was asked to name the commander. The unified command could fly the United Nations flag in the course of operations. It would fly alongside the national flags of the states taking part. The United States also had to report to the Council on the course of the action taken.

The war over Nagorny Karabakh flared again in the autumn of 1993. The region lies inside Azerbaijan and has a mostly Armenian population. Fighting had broken earlier cease-fires. Civilians were fleeing the Zangelan district and the city of Goradiz, which had been occupied. Resolution 884 was adopted on 12 November 1993.

The Council condemned the renewed hostilities. The occupation of the Zangelan district and Goradiz was condemned in particular, and so were attacks on civilians. Armenia's government was called on to use its influence. The Armenians of Nagorny Karabakh had to be made to obey the Council's earlier resolutions, 822, 853, and 874. The cease-fire proposals of the Minsk Group, which led the peace process, were welcomed. The Council restated Azerbaijan's sovereignty and the rule that territory may not be taken by force.

Countries that had given up nuclear weapons wanted safety in return, and the Council answered on 11 April 1995. More than 170 states had joined the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. The states without such weapons had promised not to build them. Resolution 984, adopted unanimously, gives them security assurances.

The Council welcomed statements by the five nuclear-weapon states. Each had promised not to use nuclear weapons against non-nuclear parties to the treaty, with limited exceptions. The Council recognized a key right. A victim of nuclear attack, or a state threatened with one, could bring the matter straight to the Council. The Council would then act at once. The text set out how states could help such a victim, with aid and with claims for compensation. All states were also urged to pursue talks on nuclear disarmament in good faith.
upanishads-muller-vol2-1884: Part 2 of The Upanishads closes Muller's rendering of the Hindu scriptures for The Sacred Books of the East, where it stands as volume fifteen. The Clarendon Press at Oxford issued it in 1884, five years after part one. F. Max Muller edited the series and made this rendering himself. Pages present here stop at the title page and the head of the contents list, so the texts and notes themselves are not shown. A header line in the file gives an earlier date, but the printed title page reads 1884.
zola-joy-of-life-1884:
Chatto and Windus issued The Joy of Life in 1901, edited with Vizetelly's preface. The French title, La Joie de Vivre, promises more cheer than the tale delivers. Chapter one opens as a cuckoo clock strikes six and Chanteau loses all patience.

On the stormy Brittany coast, kind Pauline gives her life to others. She nurses her cousin Lazare through endless failures and fears of death. His gloom wars with her selfless love of living across the years. Tender above all Zola's books, this 1884 novel forms the gentle counterweight to his darker visions, and Vizetelly prized it highly.
zosimus-new-history-1684:
Zosimus, a pagan official at Constantinople, wrote his New History around 510 CE to explain why Rome was falling. The English text here is the anonymous version of 1684, the only one in the public domain. His six books run from Augustus to the sack of Rome in 410.

Zosimus blames the emperors who dropped the old gods, above all Constantine and Theodosius, for the empire's wounds. He gives the fullest narrative of the late empire's fall that survives. His voice is the last great pagan answer to Christian Rome. The old spelling of the 1684 print, with its long s, takes a page to get used to.
